0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
Luke is the longest book in the New Testament. It is also, in the judgment of many, the most beautiful — a Gospel written by a physician who was also a literary artist, a historian who was also a theologian, a Gentile who understood the Jewish roots of everything he was describing better than most of his contemporaries. When Luke sets out to write an orderly account of the things that have been accomplished among us, he produces something that is at once a careful historical document, a theological masterpiece, and a pastoral letter addressed to a world hungry for good news.

The author never names himself, but the ancient tradition is unanimous: this is Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), the companion of Paul (2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24), the man who stayed with Paul when everyone else had left. He was almost certainly a Gentile — the only Gentile author in the New Testament — and this shapes everything he writes. He sees in Jesus the fulfilment not just of Israel's hopes but of the deepest longings of the whole human race. His Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, probably a Roman official of some standing, and through him to the entire Gentile world. Luke wants the world to know that what happened in Judea was not a local religious event. It was the turning point of all of history.

Luke writes in two volumes: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Together they tell the story of what Jesus began to do (the Gospel) and what he continued to do through his Spirit in the church (Acts). The Gospel ends where Acts begins — with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. This two-volume structure matters for reading Luke: his Gospel is not a self-contained biography but the first act of a larger drama, the story of how the good news of the kingdom moved from a manger in Bethlehem to the centre of the Roman world. The Gospel is movement toward Jerusalem; Acts is movement from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Luke's great themes are the themes of the kingdom come in unexpected ways. He gives more space than any other evangelist to women, to the poor, to Samaritans, to Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners — the people whom polite religious society had written off as beyond the reach of God's grace. He is the Gospel of the outsider welcomed in. He shows Jesus praying at every major turning point of his ministry. He is the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, who appears from the first chapter to the last. And above all, he is the Gospel of joy, because at the centre of everything is the announcement that the Saviour has come, and his name is Jesus.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Luke 1 sets out, before Jesus has said a word in public, what kind of Gospel this will be. It opens with a formal preface like those of the Greek historians: Luke has investigated everything carefully and written an orderly account, so that Theophilus may be certain of what he has been taught. This is history, set in a named reign and a known country.

Then the style changes and the story walks back into the world of the Old Testament. The long story of promise has reached its fulfilment. After four hundred years without a prophet God speaks again: to an old priest in the temple, and then to a girl in Nazareth, about the Son of the Most High.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In the prologue (vv. 1–4) Luke steps out before the story and says how he wrote it. He has traced everything from the source, from those who were eyewitnesses and servants of the word, and set it in an order you can follow. He writes to one man, most excellent Theophilus, already taught the faith, so that he may have certainty (asphaleia), the firm ground of knowing that what he believes is true.

A book researched like this is still God’s word: the Spirit was at work in the physician’s research.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events: the birth, the miracles, the death and the resurrection took place in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

And Luke’s goal is pastoral. He writes not to entertain, nor mainly to persuade outsiders, but to confirm the faith of someone already taught. That is what preaching rooted in history does in every generation: it settles believers in a faith that rests on what God has done.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue shows how to handle the gospel: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, set out the findings in order, and do it for the hearer’s sake. A Christian wrestling with doubt is rarely helped by being told just to trust. He is helped by being shown why trust is reasonable, which is what the rest of this Gospel does.

The certainty Luke offers is not the brittle confidence of someone who has never been challenged, but the settled confidence of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid, and who can give a reason to anyone who asks (1 Peter 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke opens with one long, balanced sentence (vv. 1–4) in polished literary Greek, like the prefaces of the Greek historians: what follows is researched, reliable history. The chapter is the morning of the gospel: God breaks four hundred years of silence, an old priest and a young virgin receive impossible promises, two mothers meet, and two songs are sung that the church has never stopped singing. Its theme is Zechariah’s own name, the LORD remembers, and at its centre is the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit.

Who was Luke? The early church consistently named Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), as the author of this Gospel and of Acts, which is its second volume (Acts 1:1). He was a companion of Paul; in Acts, he slips into “we” when he was present (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–28:16). He was probably a Gentile (Colossians 4:10–14 lists him apart from the men of the circumcision), and if so he is the only Gentile author in the New Testament. His two books make up over a quarter of the New Testament.

He opens with paperwork. Luke does not open with a vision or a genealogy. He is about to tell a story with an angel in it, and he begins by saying where he got it.

Many have undertaken. Others had already written accounts of Jesus, narratives that carry a reader through the events. Luke does not attack them. A man forging a religion would be tempted to suppress the rival accounts. A man reporting an event can welcome them, because more witnesses make a case stronger, not weaker.

Who were the many who had written before Luke? Most likely they included Mark, probably the earliest Gospel, and other written and oral accounts from the eyewitnesses. Luke shares much material with Mark and Matthew, and has much that is found only in his Gospel, such as the birth of John, the shepherds, the Good Samaritan and the prodigal son. He was not an eyewitness himself, but he says he investigated everything carefully from those who were (v. 2).

Accomplished among us. The word (peplērophorēmenōn) means fulfilled, brought to completion. Luke is not describing incidents that merely happened. He is describing promises that landed. This is a key theme of the whole book, and the risen Christ will say it in the last chapter: everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44).

Eyewitnesses. The apostles and others who had been with Jesus from the start (Acts 1:21–22). The word is autoptai, those who saw it with their own eyes. The Gospel rests on eyewitness testimony, not legend.

Ministers of the word. Servants, attendants (hypēretai), the word Luke uses of the synagogue attendant who took the scroll from Jesus (4:20). They did not invent the message; they served it, and spent their lives handing it on.

The word they served had a face. Luke names one group with two roles, eyewitnesses and servants of the word, because what they handed on was what they had seen. Luke does not call Jesus the Word, as John does, but his witnesses could have said what John says: that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life (1 John 1:1). The gospel is not an idea about God illustrated by a life. It is a life: a birth, a ministry, a death and an empty tomb.

Delivered. Handed down (paredosan), the technical word for passing on a tradition carefully, the word Paul uses when he says he delivered as of first importance what he also received (1 Corinthians 15:3). Luke places himself in the second generation. The chain between Jesus and your Bible is short and can be named: the men and women who saw him, then a careful writer who questioned them, then the book in your hands.

If Luke did research, how is this God’s word? It is both Luke’s careful work and God’s word, and the one does not crowd out the other. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah later in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there, guiding the questions he asked, the witnesses he found, the material he kept and the order he set it in (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass Luke’s mind. He used it. The research is not a crack in the doctrine of inspiration; it is how, in this case, inspiration went about its work. So you can read Luke with both a historian’s confidence and a worshipper’s reverence.

In everyday life. When someone at work says the Gospels are legends written long afterwards, you do not need to panic or to bluff. You can say, honestly, that the author tells us he checked his material against the people who were there, and invite them to read him and judge.
verseByVerse.note: Luke did not claim to be an eyewitness himself; he gathered the testimony of those who were.

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Followed all things closely. One word in Greek (parēkolouthēkoti): to follow alongside, to trace a matter back along its course. Luke did research. And for some time past is stronger than it sounds: anōthen, from the top, from the source. He had opportunity: he was in Judea for the two years of Paul’s imprisonment at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), and could have met Mary, James the brother of Jesus (Acts 21:18), and others. The birth narratives may come from Mary herself, who treasured these things and pondered them in her heart (2:19, 51). And he goes back to the very start: not, as Mark does, to a grown man at the Jordan, but to an old couple in the hill country and a girl in Nazareth.

An order that leads to a cross. Luke’s order has a shape, and the shape is Christ’s. The Gospel opens in the temple with a priest who cannot bless the waiting people (1:22), and it closes in the temple with disciples praising God after Jesus has lifted his hands and blessed them (24:50–53). Its long middle is one journey: when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51). An orderly account of this life cannot help but lead where he himself was going, to a city, a cross and an empty tomb.

An orderly account. In sequence (kathexēs), each thing in its proper place. Luke is not promising a diary timed to the day but an account with a shape that can be followed, as when he sets the rejection at Nazareth at the head of the ministry because it is the doorway into everything after it (4:16–30). Nothing has been thrown in at random.

Most excellent Theophilus. The name means friend of God or loved by God. Most excellent (kratiste) was a title for Roman officials and people of rank; Luke uses it of Governor Felix and Governor Festus in his second volume (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). Theophilus was probably a real person of high social standing, perhaps Luke’s patron who paid for the copying and circulation of the book. He was already instructed in the faith (v. 4). Luke addressed the longest book in the New Testament to one man who needed it, by name.

Does it matter that the Gospels differ in order? No, and seeing why helps you read them well. Ancient writers, like good modern biographers, often arranged material by theme as well as by date, and no one thought that dishonest. Each Gospel writer tells the same Jesus from his own angle, with his own emphases, for his own first readers. Where they differ in order or detail, they are like four honest witnesses describing one event: their differences show they did not copy each other mechanically, and their agreement on everything that matters is all the stronger for it. When you meet a difference, ask what each writer is emphasising. It is usually illuminating.

But was Luke not biased, writing as a believer? Every historian writes from somewhere, and a writer who cares about his subject is not for that reason unreliable. The question is whether he tells you his sources and lets you check him. Luke does: he names rulers, places and dates that could be tested (3:1–2), and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed the titles and details of his second volume. And see what he does not hide: the doubt of a priest (v. 20), the slowness of the disciples, the denial of Peter (22:54–62). A man inventing heroes does not write like that. Bias would have made him tidy. Luke was simply faithful. Not every question about his dates is settled (the census of 2:2 is the best known), but a writer who gives you the means to check him is not hiding from you.

In everyday life. Read a Gospel straight through in a sitting, as Theophilus would have heard it. And remember that God’s largest works often come with one person’s name at the top: the letter, the book, the conversation you give to one particular person may be the thing God uses.
verseByVerse.note: Theophilus means “friend of God.” “Most excellent” was a title used for Roman officials, which suggests a man of rank.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may have certainty. The word is asphaleia: firmness, security, the word Luke uses of a prison locked securely (Acts 5:23). It is built from a (not) and sphallō (to trip, to make to stumble): literally, un-trippability. It comes last in the Greek sentence, for emphasis. Luke did not write so that Theophilus would feel warmer about Jesus. He wrote so that when Theophilus put his weight down, the floor would hold. God is not content that his children should merely hope. He wants them to stand on ground that will not give way, and so he gave us not a mood but a record, written by a man who checked his sources, about a Saviour who really lived, really died and really rose. Our certainty rests on him, and he does not trip.

The things you have been taught. The word (katēchēthēs) gives us catechism: instructed by word of mouth. Theophilus had been instructed in the Christian faith, perhaps as a new believer or an enquirer, and Luke thinks he needs a book anyway. Evidence is not entry-level material a believer graduates from: a whole Gospel was written for a Christian’s certainty.

Know for certain who he is. Luke uses the matching adverb, asphalōs, at the climax of the first Christian sermon: let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (Acts 2:36). That is the certainty Luke’s two volumes exist to give, and it is first the risen Lord’s own gift. When the disciples met him, frightened and doubting, he did not tell them to believe harder. He said: see my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see (24:39). Christ himself handed over the evidence, and Luke is only carrying it on.

Afraid to look. Some readers fear examining what they believe in case it does not survive. Luke is not nervous. He tells you how he worked and invites you to hold him to it (John 20:31; 1 Peter 3:15). Certainty, in this book, is not a temperament. It is the settledness of a man who went and looked.

Is certainty the same as assurance of salvation? They are related but not identical. Luke’s certainty is first about the facts: that these things really happened and mean what the apostles said they mean. Assurance of salvation is a believer’s confidence that he himself is in Christ. The first feeds the second. The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both say that assurance rests on the truth of God’s promises, on the inward evidence of grace, and on the witness of the Spirit (Westminster 18.2; 1689 18.2). The promises come first, and they are only as solid as the history behind them. So when your assurance wavers, do not begin by examining your feelings. Begin where Luke begins: with what God has done in Christ.

What if I still have doubts after reading? Doubt is not the same as unbelief, and a doubting believer is still a believer. Bring the doubt into the open: name it, ask a pastor or a mature friend, read what thoughtful Christians have written on the question. Keep reading the Gospels themselves, because Christ is his own best evidence. And keep using the means of grace, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, while the question is being answered. Many believers find that a doubt honestly faced leaves their faith firmer than it was before.

In everyday life. Take one thing you believe about Christ and ask how you know it. If the honest answer is that you have always been told so, that is where Theophilus was, and God thought it worth a whole Gospel to move him past it. Spend this week looking into one such question, perhaps how you know Jesus rose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From verse 5 Luke moves into a world full of the Old Testament. Zechariah is a priest, Elizabeth a daughter of Aaron; both are righteous and blameless, and she is barren, like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah before her.

The announcement comes in the middle of an ordinary rota: Zechariah has been chosen by lot for the once-in-a-lifetime incense offering, while the people pray outside (vv. 8–10). Gabriel, last seen in Daniel, promises a son who will be filled with the Spirit from the womb and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Malachi 4:5–6). Zechariah asks how he can know, and offers his age as the evidence against it. The silence that follows is discipline and mercy together, with a limit written into it. Elizabeth conceives, hides herself for five months, and her first recorded words are about God: he has looked on her and taken away her reproach.
verseByVerse.theology:
The barren wombs of Scripture are a recurring picture of human inability and God’s sufficiency. The child of promise is always a child who could not have been born by human power, and the pattern runs from Sarah’s son to the virgin’s: salvation belongs to the LORD.

Gabriel’s description of John’s work picks up the last words of the Old Testament prophets, the promise of Elijah (Malachi 4:5–6). And the long silence ends not with a king or an army but with an old priest’s vision at the incense altar.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah’s theology was correct, and his trust in the moment was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs, and when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence. That gap between what we confess and what we trust is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about faith, and God met it not with contempt but with a season of silence spent with nothing but his word.

Elizabeth’s five months of seclusion (v. 24) show another wisdom: a gift this size sometimes needs to be received quietly before it is announced.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The style changes. The polished Greek of the prologue stops, and the next sentence could have come out of the book of Judges. From here to the end of chapter 2 Luke writes a Greek full of Hebrew idiom, because the story of Jesus continues the story of Israel. Our English Old Testament ends with Malachi’s promise of Elijah coming (Malachi 4:5–6); this Gospel begins with the birth of the one who comes in Elijah’s spirit (v. 17).

In the days of Herod. Herod the Great ruled the Jewish land as Rome’s client king from 37 to 4 BC. He was an Idumean (Edomite), not a son of David, a builder of vast ambition (the temple included), and a paranoid tyrant who murdered his wife and three of his sons. Luke names that throne in his first narrative sentence so that nobody mistakes what kind of night it was when the light came. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born before then, probably around 6–5 BC (our calendar, calculated in the sixth century, is a few years out).

Two kings in one chapter. Luke’s first sentence names a king, and before the chapter is out an angel names another. Herod held the throne of Judea by Rome’s favour, without a drop of David’s blood. To Mary, Gabriel will say that the Lord God will give her son the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (vv. 32–33). One is the king Israel had, the other the King God had promised. Herod built a temple to make his name great; the true King will be carried into it as a baby (2:22–38). Herod’s kingdom was divided among his sons as soon as he died. The kingdom of David’s son has no end.

Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. Zechariah means the LORD remembers, which is what this chapter is about (vv. 54, 72). There were several thousand priests in Jesus’ day, organised since David’s time into twenty-four divisions; Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). Each division served in the temple for a week, twice a year, and all served at the great feasts.

The daughters of Aaron. Elizabeth was also of priestly descent, priestly on both sides, which was considered a special blessing. Her name (Elisheba) means my God is an oath, or my God is fullness; Aaron’s wife had the same name (Exodus 6:23). Put the two names together and you have the chapter in miniature: the LORD remembers, and my God has sworn an oath. Zechariah will sing exactly that, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham (v. 73).

Righteous before God, walking blamelessly. Before God: not just in the eyes of men. Blameless? Luke knew the same Scriptures that say none is righteous, no, not one (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:10–12). He is not contradicting them. This is covenant language, the verdict given of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and of Job (Job 1:1). Not sinless; Zechariah will doubt (v. 20). It means that when they sinned they brought the sacrifice God had appointed, and that a neighbour could point at nothing in their lives. It is a standard an ordinary believer can actually be held to. While Herod built his palaces in blood, God was watching an old couple in the hill country, and he wrote their names in his book as righteous. No tyrant’s throne can hide his faithful ones from his eyes.

Were they saved by their blamelessness? No. Their righteousness before God was the righteousness of faith, the same by which Abraham believed the LORD and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). They looked forward to the promised redemption, offered the sacrifices that pointed to it, and lived out their trust in obedience. Their blameless walk was the fruit of grace, not the price of it. That is why the word is a comfort and not a threat: God does not require you to be sinless to be called righteous. He counts you righteous in Christ, and then works in you a life that can, by his grace, be honestly called blameless.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC. The priests were organised in twenty-four divisions, each serving in the temple for a week at a time; Abijah’s was the eighth.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stage it properly. Children were seen as God’s blessing (Psalm 127:3–5). They are old now. There is a room in that house that was going to be for a child. There were the early years of quiet confidence, then the years of remedies and of prayers with a shape to them, then the year, and every couple who has walked this road can name it, when they stopped saying when and started saying if, and then stopped saying anything at all. Elizabeth has held other people’s babies for decades and handed them back. And in first-century Judea childlessness was a public verdict as well as a private grief: a barren woman walked through the market under a rumour that God had looked at her and turned away. Elizabeth’s own word for it, when it is lifted, is oneidos: disgrace, the thing people say about you (v. 25).

Because Elizabeth was barren. The Bible’s great births often begin with barrenness: Sarah (Genesis 18), Rebekah, Rachel, Samson’s mother (Judges 13) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1). In each case, God opened the womb to give a child who would play a key part in his purposes, making sure that when the child arrived nobody could mistake where he came from. And both were advanced in years, as Abraham and Sarah were (Genesis 18:11). Humanly, it was impossible.

From a barren womb to a virgin’s. The line of closed wombs is not a string of separate miracles. It is a road, and this verse stands near its end. Six months later the same angel will go to a girl in Nazareth with a greater impossibility, and he will point her to this very house (v. 36). Every barren womb God opened prepared the way for the day when a child would come who had no human father at all, because he was not merely a gift to the line of Adam but God’s own Son entering it. Sarah’s son carried the promise. Mary’s Son is the promise. Elizabeth stands at the hinge between them, the last of the barren mothers and the sign given to the virgin.

Said carefully. Elizabeth conceived, and so did Hannah and Sarah. Thousands of women just as righteous, who prayed just as long, did not. It would be a cruelty to read this verse as a pattern with your name in it: hold on faithfully and the answer will come.

The circumstance is not the verdict. The silence of God is not the absence of God. Luke has just recorded that these two were righteous before God, so the barrenness was not a punishment. The village had read the evidence and got the sentence exactly backwards. And the reason for their waiting was not in them at all: the forerunner of the Messiah could not be born until the Messiah was six months away. For all those years the reason for their sorrow was a reason that had not happened yet.

So what may a childless couple take from this? Not a promise that you will conceive; God has not made that promise, and anyone who makes it for him is unkind. Take this instead: your childlessness is not God’s verdict on you, and it is not a punishment. He sees the grief, the empty room, the conversations that change direction when you come in. Your life is not second-class in his kingdom; some of the most fruitful servants in Scripture had no children, and our Lord himself had none. You may pray honestly for a child, use wise medical help, consider adoption, and weep. And you may know that the God who held Elizabeth’s sorrow for all those years is holding yours, with purposes that may be stored far ahead of you.

And for those around them? Be careful with your words. Do not ask young couples when they are going to have children. Do not offer formulas or stories of friends who conceived after they relaxed. Remember the childless on Mother’s Day and Father’s Day, and at the dedication of babies. Include them in the life of families in the church, not as spare helpers but as brothers and sisters. And never, by look or word, become the village that passed a sentence on Elizabeth.
verseByVerse.note: Barrenness was a deep sorrow and often a social shame. Scripture’s great births often begin with a barren woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was chosen by lot. There were thousands of priests and exactly one incense altar, and the duties of each day were assigned by lot. The highest honour was to pass alone into the Holy Place and burn incense at the golden altar in front of the veil. Later Jewish tradition records that a man once chosen was taken out of the draw: once in a lifetime, and many never did. This was Zechariah’s once, at the end of a lifetime of faithful and unremarkable service. The lot is not chance: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). God chose this day, this man.

To burn incense. The temple here is the sanctuary building itself (naos), which only priests could enter. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar inside the Holy Place (Exodus 30:7–8), so that the fragrant smoke rose before the curtain that hid the Most Holy Place. Incense was a picture of prayer rising to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).

At the hour of incense. Probably the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m.: a crowd in a courtyard praying, and one old man alone in the smoke, on the settled understanding that God does not answer out loud any more. Zechariah went to work that morning knowing it was the biggest day of his career and having no idea it was the biggest day in four centuries.

Where God chose to interrupt. Not at a revival meeting, but at the appointed duty, taken in its turn, by a man whose name had come out of a container. The routine is not the opposite of the encounter. In this chapter it is the address.

The curtain he stood before. Zechariah stood alone at the golden altar with one curtain between him and the Most Holy Place, a curtain he would never pass and only the high priest could, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Luke will bring us back to that curtain at the end. When Jesus hung on the cross, from the sixth hour to the ninth hour there was darkness, and the curtain of the temple was torn in two (23:44–45). The ninth hour was the afternoon hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). Generations of priests had burned incense before that veil, and the people had prayed outside it. What they were waiting for was the death that would tear it. Zechariah stood once in a lifetime before the curtain; our great High Priest has passed through it for ever, and lives always to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25; 10:19–22). There is no draw to win and no once in a lifetime. The way into the holy place is open.

Does God still direct things through chance? Yes, in the sense that nothing is chance to him. The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession say that God orders all things, including what seem to us accidents, by his providence (Westminster 5.2; 1689 5.2). That does not mean we should make decisions by drawing lots or opening the Bible at random; after Pentecost the apostles are never again recorded casting lots, because the Spirit and the Scriptures guide the church. It does mean that the shuffle of your week, the job allocation, the seat on the train, the person next to you at the hospital, is not random. You may walk into it expecting God to be there.

In everyday life. Go to the shift, the school run, the weekly meeting, the Sunday service, expecting nothing dramatic and everything from God. And pray with God’s people: the crowd in the courtyard was part of the answer.
verseByVerse.note: With so many priests, the honour of offering incense in the holy place came to few, perhaps once in a lifetime. It was offered morning and evening while the people prayed outside.

parallels.desc: let my prayer be counted as incense

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel of the Lord. The silence is broken. Jews of the time spoke of a long age, stretching back to Malachi, in which prophets had ceased to appear among them (1 Maccabees 9:27). Zechariah was in the middle of a fixed liturgy, in a room he had never stood in before, and when he raised his eyes somebody was there.

On the right side of the altar. The right side was the side of favour, and the detail says the visitor was not passing through. He was waiting. Zechariah had been chosen by lot that morning. The messenger had been at that altar by appointment.

Fear fell upon him. Fear before divine visitation is a recurring note in Luke (1:29–30, 65; 2:9; 5:8–10; 8:37). Again and again an angel has to begin by saying do not be afraid, because it is necessary. Daniel fell on his face in terror when Gabriel, the very angel who now stands before Zechariah, came near him (Daniel 8:17). These are not nervous men. A creature made of dust and carrying a conscience cannot meet the unfallen without discovering what he is: in the presence of someone who has never sinned, a sinner sees his own sin with nothing to hide behind. Fear here is not a failure of faith. It is accurate perception arriving all at once.

The thing the equipment was for. Zechariah has spent his life inside the machinery of holiness: the courses, the lots, the incense, the curtain, all designed to manage the distance between a holy God and a people who could not survive him without a go-between and a sacrifice. Now a messenger from God’s presence stands in the room, and he has come to say that what the machinery was for is on its way. Within the year the forerunner will be born, and behind him the Lord himself, come in a body of flesh (vv. 17, 35). The fear that fell on Zechariah is answered in Luke by Christ. When Peter fell at his knees and said, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord, Jesus said to him: do not be afraid (5:8–10). The holy one came near so that sinners could stand in his presence and live.

Do angels still appear today? Scripture does not slam the door: some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2), and they are sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). But look at the shape of every appearance in the Bible. Nobody summons one. Nobody has a method. They arrive on God’s errand, say what they were sent to say, and go. And see what they are for. Not to be looked at, but to carry a message. Since the message of the gospel is now complete and written down, we should not expect angels to bring new revelation, and we should test anyone who claims one has (Galatians 1:8). Angels serve us still, mostly unseen. From the moment Gabriel opens his mouth, he is no longer the interesting thing in the room.
verseByVerse.note: The altar of incense stood just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid. The first words of God’s messengers to frightened people throughout Luke (1:30; 2:10; 5:10; 8:50; 12:7, 32). God does not appear in order to destroy.

Your prayer has been heard. Which prayer? The text never says. Zechariah is an old man. His wife is long past childbearing. Whatever he had once prayed about a son, he had very likely stopped praying it years ago.

Two answers, both true. The first is that the prayers of twenty and thirty and forty years ago were heard when they were prayed. The answer was scheduled for a date that had everything to do with a second child six months behind this one. The second is probably nearer. The priest at the incense altar prayed for Israel: for the redemption of Jerusalem, for the coming of the Lord to his temple, for the end of the silence. And the answer he is handed is a son, because the son is how the nation gets its answer. Both readings say the same thing about God: he does not lose requests, and when he answers, he often answers on a scale that makes the request look like a rough draft.

The answer behind the answer. John is not the end of the answer. He is its first word. The prayer at the incense altar was for the Lord to come to his people, and Gabriel’s reply is a herald whose whole life will say: he is coming, and he is right behind me. Before the year is out the old priest will sing that God has visited and redeemed his people and raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David (vv. 68–69). He asked for the redemption of Israel. God answered with his own Son.

Heard is not the same as granted. Gabriel does not say your prayer has been granted. He says it has been heard. Paul asked three times and was told no, and the no was itself the answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What this verse forbids is the conclusion the silence keeps pressing: that the request fell into a room with nobody in it. God has never once not been listening. He has often not yet been speaking.

The setting for the jewel. Had Elizabeth conceived at thirty, the child would have been a comfort to his parents. Because she conceived in old age, the child was a sign to a nation. That does not explain anybody else’s waiting; most waiting gets no explanation this side of the grave. It is evidence that the category exists.

Call his name John. God names him, not the father. John (Yôḥānān) means the LORD has been gracious, or the LORD has shown favour. The name is the message.

Should I keep praying for something I have prayed about for years? Yes, unless God has plainly closed the door, as he did for Paul, or the thing itself has become impossible or wrong. Jesus told a parable precisely so that his people would always pray and not lose heart (18:1). Keep praying, but let the prayer grow: bring the request, and also the grief, the questions and your submission to his will, as Jesus did in Gethsemane. Many long prayers end not with the thing asked for but with a heart reshaped to want God more than the thing. Either way, the prayer was heard.
verseByVerse.note: John means “the LORD has been gracious.”

parallels.desc: Sarah will bear you a son

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joy and gladness. Joy is a theme of Luke’s Gospel from beginning (2:10) to end, when the disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy (24:52). Gladness here is exultation, a joy that cannot keep still.

Many will rejoice. Elizabeth’s neighbours will rejoice at the birth (v. 58), but Gabriel is looking well past the village: this child’s arrival is a public event.

Great before the Lord. Not great in the world’s eyes: John will be beheaded in Herod’s prison (9:9; Mark 6:21–28). Jesus said no one born of women is greater than John (7:28). And of Jesus, the angel will say simply “he will be great” (v. 32), with no qualification. John is great before the Lord; Jesus is the Lord before whom John is great.

No wine or strong drink. Like the rule for a Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a vow (Numbers 6:1–4), though Gabriel says nothing of the uncut hair. Samson and Samuel were Nazirites from birth (Judges 13:4–5; 1 Samuel 1:11). But a Nazirite took the vow himself, or a parent dedicated a child, as Hannah did. Here God imposes it before the boy exists. The consecration is not the family’s offering to God. It is God’s claim staked on a child not yet conceived.

Does this make total abstinence the higher path? No, and Luke himself blocks that road. A few chapters on, Jesus says that John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and they said he had a demon, and the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and a drunkard (7:33–34). The same Bible that gives John’s austerity gives Christ at a wedding in Cana where the wine ran out (John 2:1–11). John’s abstinence is a uniform, not a law. It marks him as the wilderness prophet, the man standing outside the system and calling the system to repent. A believer who abstains is free to, and many do for good reasons: their own weakness, a family history, a brother who struggles. A believer who drinks in moderation is not a lesser Christian. Drunkenness is always sin. And anyone using this verse to grade another man’s holiness should notice who the abstainer’s Master turned out to be.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. Instead of being filled with wine, he will be filled with the Spirit (compare Ephesians 5:18). From before birth, set apart by God, as Jeremiah was known and consecrated before he was formed (Jeremiah 1:5), and as the Servant was called from the womb (Isaiah 49:1). Luke means John’s equipping for his office rather than a doctrine of infant conversion, and it becomes visible later in this chapter when he leaps in the womb as Mary arrives with the unborn Jesus (v. 41). The boldness the crowds would later meet at the Jordan was not a strong temperament but God’s gift (compare v. 80).

What does this say about the unborn? An unborn child can be filled with the Spirit. The child in the womb is a person, known and called by God. John was filled with the Spirit before he was born, and in v. 41 he leaps in Elizabeth’s womb at the coming of the Lord. Scripture speaks of the unborn as persons whom God knows and forms (Psalm 139:13–16; Jeremiah 1:5). These verses are not a full argument on their own, but they fit the whole biblical witness that life in the womb is human life, made in God’s image, and so is to be protected. And see the direction of grace: before John could believe, refuse or want anything at all, God had already begun.

And for parents who have lost a child before birth? God knew that child, formed that child and loved that child, and the child’s life was real and is not lost to him. Grieve it as the death of a person, because it was. Scripture gives good hope for those who die in infancy: David said of his dead baby, I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (1689 10.3; Westminster 10.3). Believing parents may rest that child in the hands of a merciful God. The word elect is not there to cast a shadow over your child: many Reformed pastors have held that all who die in infancy are among the elect, and the God to whom your child has gone is kinder than our fears.

In everyday life. Pray for the unborn children you know. And measure greatness the way Gabriel did: a faithful, unseen life is measured in heaven, not on the feed.
verseByVerse.note: No wine or strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, someone set apart to God.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will turn many. John’s work is repentance, turning back to God (3:3). Not to a programme, a party or a temple, but to God himself.

He will go before him. Before whom? Grammatically, before the Lord their God of the previous line. John goes before the Lord God himself, and the one who comes after John is Jesus. Malachi had promised a messenger to prepare the way, and then: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). Isaiah’s voice in the wilderness prepares the way of the LORD, and makes straight a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and Luke will apply it to John and Jesus (3:4–6). When John finally stood aside, it was not for a greater prophet. It was for God come in the flesh.

In the spirit and power of Elijah. Elijah confronted a wicked king and queen (1 Kings 18–21); John will confront Herod and Herodias (3:19–20).

Was John Elijah or not? Keep Gabriel’s exact wording in mind, because a reader with an open Bible will hit a puzzle here. When the priests came out and asked John point-blank, Are you Elijah?, he answered flatly, I am not (John 1:21). Yet Jesus said of that same man, he is Elijah who is to come (Matthew 11:14). They are not contradicting each other; they are answering two different questions. John denies what his questioners meant: that he was the Tishbite himself, returned in person from heaven. Jesus affirms what Malachi meant: that the promised forerunner had come at last, in the spirit and power of Elijah, exactly as Gabriel says here. The prophecy was never that a man would come back. It was that a ministry would come again: the same blunt voice, the same rough clothing, the same summons to a nation to turn round before the LORD arrives. And it gives no support to reincarnation, which Scripture rules out (Hebrews 9:27).

The hearts of the fathers. Gabriel is quoting the closing words of Malachi, the last of the prophets and the last page of our English Old Testament (Malachi 4:5–6): Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers.

The kitchen table. God announces the greatest turning point in the history of the world, and among the first effects named is that fathers will turn towards their children. Where a nation goes cold towards God, the cold shows first at the kitchen table, and where God returns, so does the thaw. Revival that leaves a family exactly as it was is not the revival Malachi promised.

The wisdom of the just. Turning rebels to the understanding and way of life of the righteous. Repentance is not only feeling sorry; it is a change of mind that becomes a change of path.

A people prepared. As Isaiah 40:3 foretold (3:4–6). Everything about John exists to get a people ready for somebody else. He is the road, not the city.

What if the relationship cannot be mended? Sometimes the other person refuses, or is dead, or is dangerous. Repentance asks you to do what lies with you (Romans 12:18): drop the grudge before God, confess your own part, make the approach if it is safe and wise, and keep the door open. It does not ask you to put yourself or your children back under abuse, and reconciliation with an abuser needs genuine repentance on his side, proven over time, with wise help. Where the other person will not come, you can still forgive in your heart and leave the matter with God. The turning of hearts begins with yours.

In everyday life. The Father has turned his heart toward you in Christ. If there is a relationship your repentance needs to mend, do one concrete thing this week: a phone call, a letter, an apology without excuses, a meal.

For worship. The God who closed the prophets with a promise reopened history by keeping it, word for word. And the deepest turning of a father’s heart was never Zechariah’s or ours. It was his own. Jesus would tell of a father who saw his son a long way off, felt compassion, and ran (15:20). That is the Father the forerunner went before: a God whose heart is turned toward rebellious children, who sent his Son to bring them home.

parallels.desc: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How shall I know this? Every reader stops here, and the question is always the same. Why is Zechariah struck dumb for asking, when Mary asks what looks like the same question sixteen verses later and is answered kindly? Gideon laid out a fleece twice (Judges 6:36–40); Abraham asked how he could know, in almost these words, and was given a covenant ceremony instead of a rebuke (Genesis 15:8). But Zechariah had an angel of God standing in front of him, in the temple, with the incense still rising, telling him what God would do, and still asked for proof.

For I am an old man. He looks at the circumstances, not at God. He knows about Abraham and Sarah, but he cannot believe it for himself. He is not asking Gabriel to explain; he is explaining to Gabriel. Mary’s question (v. 34) is how, not whether. Gabriel’s own diagnosis two verses later says precisely this: because you did not believe my words.

The sign God was already giving. Zechariah wanted a sign to prove the promise, and he could not see that the promise was the beginning of the sign. In Luke, God’s answer to how shall I know keeps turning out to be his Son. The shepherds will be told: this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (2:12). And when a later crowd demands proof, Jesus will refuse them every sign but one, the sign of Jonah (11:29–30), his own rising from the dead. Zechariah asked for something he could hold. Within the year God would put the answer in human arms.

Does God strike down those who doubt? No. Read what the Bible actually contains. The psalmists shout at God for whole psalms, and the shouting is in the Scriptures. Job argues for thirty chapters and is vindicated over his tidier friends. A father cries I believe; help my unbelief, and gets his son back the same hour (Mark 9:24). Thomas demands to put his hand in the wound and is offered the wound (John 20:27). God is not brittle. He has never once been rattled by an honest question. What happened to Zechariah is not the punishment of doubt. It is the granting of a request. He asked for a sign, and he got one, and it was himself. He wanted evidence he could hold. God gave him nine months of it, attached to his own face. It is one of the oldest mercies in Scripture that God so often gives us exactly what we asked for, in the form we would never have chosen. Gabriel does name the cause, because you did not believe (v. 20), so it was discipline too; but it was a father’s discipline, with an end date, given to a man God had already called righteous.

So what is the difference between honest doubt and unbelief? Honest doubt brings its struggle to God and wants to believe; it says help my unbelief. Unbelief has already weighed God’s word against something else and decided the something else is more reliable. The first is a weak faith asking for help; the second is a verdict against God. You can tell which you are in by what you do with the question: whether you take it to God and his word, or use it as a reason to stay away. If you are worried that your doubts mean you have no faith, the very worry is often a sign that you want to trust him.

In everyday life. Listen for your own little for: I cannot be forgiven for that, for I have done it too often; God cannot use me, for I am too old. Each one weighs his word against your record. Turn the sentence round, and put his faithfulness after the for.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am Gabriel. He does not argue biology with the old priest. He gives his name and his post. Gabriel (God is my strength, or man of God) appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel (8:16; 9:21), where he came to a man in exile with a message about how long the waiting would be: the seventy weeks decreed for Daniel’s people, and at the end of them an Anointed One (Daniel 9:24–27). Gabriel is the angel of the countdown. A priest who knew Daniel is being told by the messenger who announced the clock that the clock has run out, and he asks him for a sign.

I stand in the presence of God. It is a courtier’s phrase: the words he brings have just come out of the throne room. To weigh his words against a doctor’s estimate is not caution. It is a category error.

This good news. The verb (euangelisasthai) is the one from which gospel and evangelise come. The gospel begins here, in an old man’s ear, beside an altar. The next time an angel uses the word, it is to say: I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (2:10–11). Daniel’s countdown ended in an Anointed One, and here the messenger of the countdown brings the first news of him. The good news is never only that God has done something. It is that God has sent someone.

You will be silent and unable to speak. The sign he asked for, and a discipline. He could not believe the word, so he will not be able to speak a word. Verse 62 suggests he could not hear either. A priest whose work runs on words is stripped of the one faculty his office depends on. It was also a mercy: nine months is exactly the time it takes to watch a promise you refused to believe come true in your own house.

Until the day. There is a limit written into the sentence, and the end date is the fulfilment. God does not put him in the dark and leave him there. He puts him in the dark until the light he refused to believe in comes into the room.

Fulfilled in their time. Gabriel is entirely untroubled. The word will be fulfilled, not because Zechariah came round, but because God said it. Unbelief only robs the doubter of joy. The promises of God do not draw their strength from the faith of the person who hears them, which is why people whose faith is thin can lean on them.

Does God discipline his children today? Yes, and Hebrews says it is a mark of sonship, not rejection: the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). But be careful how you read your circumstances. Not every hardship is discipline for a particular sin; Elizabeth’s barrenness was not. Where God does discipline, it is a Father training a child, never a judge punishing a criminal, because the punishment for our sin fell on Christ. Discipline always has a purpose and a limit, as Zechariah’s did. If you suspect a trouble is God’s correction, do not despair and do not dig for hidden reasons. Confess what you know is wrong, and trust the Father to bring you through to the day of fulfilment.
verseByVerse.note: Gabriel appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people were waiting. Luke takes the camera outside for three verses. The incense offering did not take long, and the priest normally came out quickly and pronounced the priestly blessing over the people from the temple steps. A long delay was worrying: a priest who offended God could die in the Holy Place (Leviticus 16:2, 13).

He was unable to speak to them. The priest could not give the blessing, some of the oldest words in Israel’s worship: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace (Numbers 6:24–26). The blessing the waiting crowd expected never came.

The blessing on its way. On the day God finally spoke, the man appointed to bless Israel was struck dumb, because the LORD was about to make his face shine upon them in a way no formula could carry. The blessing was not cancelled. It was on its way in person. At the very end of Luke’s Gospel, Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples (24:50–51), the blessing the priest could not give. Luke has bookended his whole Gospel with it: a priest who cannot bless, and a Priest who blesses as he ascends. He was carried into heaven still blessing them, and he has never lowered his hands. Every believer now lives under the raised hands of the risen Priest.

He had seen a vision. They could not know what, but they knew God had done something in that room. And Zechariah did not leave early. He served out the rest of his days in silence, doing everything that did not require a voice, with the greatest news of his life locked inside him. Obedience is largely what a person keeps doing after the moment of glory has passed and he is back on the roster with nothing to show for it.
verseByVerse.note: The people waited for the priest to come out and pronounce the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kept herself hidden. We are not told why. She is an old woman in a village where everyone has known for decades that she cannot have children. She waits until the God who did it is the only possible explanation, and only then lets herself be seen. The sixth month will be when Gabriel comes to Mary (v. 26), and her pregnancy will be Mary’s sign (v. 36).

Not every mercy needs announcing. Some works of God are still soft when they happen, and a crowd that handles them roughly can damage them. The instinct to publish everything immediately is not faith. Sometimes it is a hunger to be seen to be blessed, to have the room’s approval at last. Elizabeth had lived for decades under the village’s verdict, and she did not rush to win it back. God’s look was enough for her.

Thus the Lord has done for me. Her first words are praise, and pure theology: not a word about herself. The Lord did it; the Lord looked.

He looked on me. With favour, with grace. It is the look of Exodus, when God saw the affliction of his people in Egypt and came down to do something about it (Exodus 3:7–8): not casual noticing but the look that ends in action. He saw Hagar in the desert, Israel in Egypt and Elizabeth in the hill country, and he has looked on us in Christ, who bore our reproach outside the gate so that we might never be put to shame.

My reproach. Rachel said the same: God has taken away my reproach (Genesis 30:23). And see what she says was taken away. Not the barrenness: the reproach, oneidos, the thing people said. What God took away was not only a medical condition. It was a sentence a whole village had passed on her, and which she had heard them pass. Yet the only verdict Scripture records about her is the one in verse 6, and it had read righteous before God the whole time.

What about shame that God has not yet removed? Some shame is the echo of other people’s cruelty, like Elizabeth’s; some is the right sting of our own sin. Christ deals with both. For our sin, he bore the shame of the cross, despising it (Hebrews 12:2), so that the guilt is gone and the shame no longer defines us. For the shame others put on us, he gives a verdict that outweighs theirs. You may still feel it, and the feeling may take years to fade. But the feeling is not the verdict. In Christ, God has looked on you with favour, and those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed (Psalm 34:5).

In everyday life. Watch your words about others: never be the voice whose verdict someone has to live under for years.

parallels.desc: Rachel: God has taken away my reproach

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six months later Gabriel is sent again, not to a priest in the temple but to a betrothed girl in Nazareth. The gospel moves from the centre to the edges, and that is Luke’s whole Gospel in miniature.

Mary is greeted as favoured: one on whom God’s grace has freely fallen. Roman Catholic teaching has built on this greeting the doctrines of her immaculate conception and sinlessness; the Reformed reading takes it as God’s gracious choice of her, and Mary settles it herself when she calls God her Saviour (v. 47).

Gabriel then makes four claims about her son, each higher than the last: he will be great, he will be called the Son of the Most High, he will receive the throne of his father David, and his kingdom will have no end (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Daniel 7:14). Mary asks how, not whether, and is told that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, as the cloud of God’s presence covered the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). Her answer, let it be to me according to your word, is surrender that is also worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gabriel joins two lines of promise in one child: the covenant with David, of a son whose throne would be established for ever, and Daniel’s vision of one who receives an everlasting dominion.

The conception by the Holy Spirit shows that the incarnation is God’s act, not a human achievement. The child is not a demigod, partly divine and partly human, but fully human and at the same time the eternal Son of God: two natures in one person, as the church has always confessed. Gabriel does not explain the mystery. He announces it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary says yes without knowing how it will happen or what it will cost. Faith is not the feeling that everything will be easy; it is placing yourself in the hands of the God who has spoken.

And the greatest conversation in this chapter took place not in a palace or a sanctuary but in the house of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of. No person and no place is too small to be where God’s grace arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast. Six months later Gabriel is sent again, and Luke means the reader to feel the drop. The first annunciation was in the temple, to a priest in the middle of the liturgy, about a child born to a barren woman. The second is in a village in despised Galilee, to a girl with no title or office, about a child born to a virgin. The first is wonderful; the second is greater. And the date is the sixth month of Elizabeth’s pregnancy: Luke dates the coming of the Son of God by the swelling of an old woman’s body in the hill country.

Nazareth. A small, obscure village in the hills of lower Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in the rabbinic lists of Galilean towns. Archaeology suggests a few hundred people on a ridge off the main road. Hence Nathanael’s question, Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46).

To a virgin. Parthenos, a young unmarried woman who has not had sexual relations. Luke makes this unmistakable: he says virgin twice in this verse, and Mary herself says she has not known a man (v. 34). This echoes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:23).

Betrothed. Jewish marriage had two stages. Betrothal was a binding agreement, often made when the girl was in her early teens: the couple were legally husband and wife, and breaking it required a divorce (Matthew 1:19). But they did not yet live together; about a year later came the wedding. So Mary is legally bound to Joseph and still living at home, which is exactly the condition in which a pregnancy is a catastrophe.

Of the house of David. Joseph was a descendant of King David, and as Jesus’ legal father he gave him the legal right to David’s throne (3:23–31; Matthew 1:1–16). In Israel a legal son, named and received by his father, was a true heir.

The Son comes round the back. Luke’s whole Gospel is in this contrast: shepherds before scholars, a Samaritan before a priest, a tax collector before a Pharisee, a dying thief before the men who arranged the cross. And it begins with the Son of God himself. The heir of David’s throne does not come in at the palace gate. He comes round the back, through a girl nobody had heard of. Isaiah had said he would grow up like a young plant, like a root out of dry ground, with no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2). The King chose the low door, so that no one would ever be too low to reach him. The Lord of glory is not impressed by what impresses us, and that is the best news the overlooked have ever heard. If you live somewhere nobody has heard of, in a church of thirty people, you are standing on exactly the kind of ground God likes to choose. Enthroned above every name, he still answers to Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee. Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; the couple did not yet live together.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greetings. Chaire, the ordinary Greek greeting, literally rejoice. There may be an echo of the prophets’ calls to the daughter of Zion to sing and rejoice, because the King of Israel, the LORD, is in her midst (Zephaniah 3:14–17; Zechariah 9:9). Nobody else in the Bible is greeted with the title that follows it.

O favored one. Kecharitōmenē, from charis, grace. Its form is a perfect passive participle: something was done to her, and the result of it stands. The plainest English is: you who have been graced. Somebody else is the actor here. The same verb is used of all believers in Ephesians 1:6: his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us (literally graced us) in the Beloved.

Textual note: blessed are you among women. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add blessed are you among women to Gabriel’s greeting here; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. The words are certainly Luke’s, but they belong to Elizabeth (v. 42).

Where Christians differ: full of grace. The Latin Vulgate translated the word gratia plena, full of grace, giving the familiar Hail Mary, full of grace. Roman Catholic teaching has understood Mary as filled with grace from her conception, and so preserved from original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), as remaining sinless all her life, and as one who can dispense grace to others and may be prayed to. Mary is the most highly favoured woman who ever lived; the Reformers said so without embarrassment. This commentary’s view: the Greek word means one who has been shown favour, not one who is a source of grace. Grace, by definition, is not owed and not earned; the greeting tells you that Mary received something, which is exactly what a woman needing nothing could not do. Mary was a sinner saved by grace, who calls God my Saviour (v. 47). Only the drowning have any use for a lifeboat. She is to be honoured as the most blessed of women, the mother of our Lord, and a model of faith and obedience (v. 45). But she is not to be prayed to, and she does not dispense grace. Grace comes from God alone, through Christ alone.

The Lord is with you. The promise given to the great servants of God when he called them: Moses, Joshua, Gideon (Judges 6:12), Jeremiah.

Nearer than she knew. Every servant who heard those words before heard them as a promise of help: God would go with Moses to Pharaoh and with Gideon against Midian. To Mary they are about to become literal. Within weeks the Lord will be with her in her own body, and her relative Elizabeth will greet the unborn child as my Lord (v. 43). The God who had promised to dwell among his people chose first to dwell beneath one girl’s heart. That is the favour: not that Mary was raised up to God, but that God came down to her. All the favour any of us will ever receive flows from the Son Mary carried, and none of it flows through anyone but him. He is the fountain, and we are all, Mary first among us, cups held out to be filled.

Greatly troubled. Not by the angel (as Zechariah was), but by his words. Gabriel has not yet mentioned a child, and in her humility she cannot see why God’s favour should rest on her.

Tried to discern. She thought it through (dielogizeto). Mary is thoughtful (2:19, 51). The first thing Luke tells us about her mind is that it went to work.

If God favours me, why is my life so hard? Because his favour is not a promise of ease but of himself, which is a far better thing to be given and a far heavier thing to carry. Mary was the most favoured woman in history, and her favour brought scandal, poverty, exile and a sword through her soul at the cross. Being the favoured one of God bought Mary a pregnancy nobody would believe, a fiancé who nearly divorced her (Matthew 1:19), a birth among animals, a son whose neighbours tried to throw him off a cliff, and an old man in the temple telling her that a sword would pierce through her own soul. Hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn his favour; often it is the very road his favour takes. Look at what the favour was for: Christ came to her and through her. In your hard place, the question is not whether God has stopped favouring you, but what he is bringing to you, and through you, in it. And the Lord is with you is said to every believer (Matthew 28:20).

In everyday life. If you are in Christ, you too have been graced (Ephesians 1:6). When the day goes badly, do not read it as a change in his face towards you. Say it over to yourself: I have been graced, and the Lord is with me.

parallels.desc: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valour”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found favor. It is the phrase used of Noah in a world God had already decided to flood: Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8). A man does not find what he produced himself.

Conceive and bear a son. The words echo Isaiah 7:14: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. Matthew makes it explicit (Matthew 1:22–23). And the mechanics are ordinary: the eternal Son enters the world through nine months of nausea and backache. God did not arrange a dignified entrance. He arranged a real one.

Did Isaiah really say virgin? The Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14, ʿalmah, means a young woman of marriageable age, who would be expected to be a virgin; the Greek translation of the Old Testament, made long before Jesus, rendered it virgin (parthenos). Matthew quotes it in that form (Matthew 1:23). Matthew and Luke both say plainly that Mary conceived without a man (v. 34), so the question of the word does not touch the fact. And the sign Isaiah promised was meant to be a wonder, a child who would be called God with us.

The hinge of the Bible. From the promise in Eden that a woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), through the covenant sworn to Abraham, through the throne promised to David, through the prophet who said the virgin shall conceive and to us a child is born, the entire weight of it comes down on one sentence spoken to a girl in Galilee.

Call his name Jesus. The Greek form of Joshua (Yeshua), meaning the LORD saves, or the LORD is salvation. Matthew gives the meaning: for he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). Joshua led Israel into the promised land; Jesus brings his people into God’s eternal rest (Hebrews 4:8–10). The child is not called the LORD reigns or the LORD judges, which would have been true. He is called the LORD saves. And the naming is done before he is conceived: the rescue was decided before the rescuer had a body. Joshua bore the name as a hope; this child bears it as a fact. Luke will let us hear the name thrown back at him on the cross: he saved others; let him save himself (23:35). He would not, and that is the glory of the name. He kept it by refusing to save himself, so that he could save a dying thief beside him that same afternoon, and every sinner since who has called on him. When you sin today, do not hide from him; go to him by name.

Saves from what? First and most deeply, from our sins: from their guilt, which he carried in our place on the cross, bearing the punishment we deserved; from their power, which his Spirit breaks in us; and finally from their presence, when he returns. He also saves from everything sin has brought: death, the fear of death, and the judgment to come. People often want a Jesus who rescues them from loneliness, debt or anxiety, and he cares about all of those. But the name points to the root. If he saves you from your sins, everything else is on its way to being put right.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will be great. John was to be great before the Lord (v. 15); the measuring rod was named because John needed one. Jesus is simply great, without qualification, because there is nothing to measure him against. This is the language used of God himself: Great is the LORD (Psalm 48:1).

Son of the Most High. The Most High (Hypsistos) is a name for God (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 91:1). Called in Hebrew idiom means will be, and be recognised as. Israel’s kings were spoken of as God’s sons by adoption at their coronation (Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14). This one is the Son before anybody crowns him.

The throne of his father David. The fulfilment of God’s covenant with David, made a thousand years earlier: I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever; I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son (2 Samuel 7:12–16; also Psalm 89; Isaiah 9:6–7). The last Davidic king had been dragged off to Babylon six centuries before. The promise is not dead. It was waiting for the right heir.

The house of Jacob. Jacob was renamed Israel; the house of Jacob is God’s people. And it now includes all who belong to Christ by faith, Jew and Gentile: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29; 6:16).

No end. Here the language stops being merely royal. Daniel had watched one like a son of man come to the Ancient of Days and receive an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14); Isaiah had promised a child of the increase of whose government there will be no end (Isaiah 9:6–7). No merely human king ever gets that sentence, for the plain reason that human kings die. Thrones have risen and fallen, Herod’s and Caesar’s among them, and his has not moved.

Where Christians differ: has the throne been given yet? A reader will fairly ask whether this has happened. Jesus never sat on a throne in Jerusalem. Israel is not restored as a kingdom. Sincere Christians who love the same Bible answer this differently. Many, including teachers a reader may know and value, such as John MacArthur, hold that the promise is literal and still ahead: Christ will reign in Jerusalem over a restored Israel for a thousand years after his return (the premillennial view), and Gabriel’s words will be fulfilled as plainly as they were spoken. Others, in the Reformed tradition, hold that the reign began at the resurrection (the amillennial view, which reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of the present age), when God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority (Ephesians 1:20–21), and point out that Peter said as much at Pentecost: God had sworn to David to set one of his descendants on his throne, and this Jesus God raised up and exalted (Acts 2:30–36). This commentary’s view: the second reading is the more likely, since Peter applies David’s throne to the risen and ascended Christ: the promise is being fulfilled now. Gabriel’s kingdom is not an earthly, political kingdom confined to a thousand years, but an everlasting one. He reigns now at God’s right hand, gathering his people from every nation, and will reign for ever when he returns to make all things new. And both readings agree on everything Gabriel actually says here: that the throne is his, that the kingdom is real, and that it has no end. Whatever else is still to come, no future is coming in which he is not King.

If Jesus reigns now, why is the world such a mess? Because his reign, for now, is carried on in the way he chose: by his word and Spirit, gathering and ruling a people, while he patiently delays the final judgment so that more may repent (2 Peter 3:9). Psalm 110 shows the King seated at God’s right hand in the midst of his enemies, until they are made his footstool. So the evil you see is real but not sovereign; it is the rebellion of a defeated enemy on borrowed time. Christ is already Lord of every power (Matthew 28:18), and the day is fixed when every knee will bow. You live in the middle: the King has come, and the King is coming.

parallels.desc: on the throne of David, no end
a kingdom that shall not be destroyed

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said to the angel, 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since I am a virgin. Literally since I do not know a man, the Hebrew idiom for sexual relations that runs right back to Genesis 4:1. And the tense is present: that is not my situation. She is betrothed, and the obvious answer would have been: you will be married within the year. She understands the angel to mean that she will conceive now, before her marriage to Joseph.

Same words, opposite postures. Zechariah asked how shall I know this? and then produced his evidence, for I am an old man, which is not a question but a rebuttal. Mary asks how will this be? and produces nothing at all. The difference is not the intelligence of the question but the direction it faces. One is asking God to justify himself; the other is asking God to explain himself, and God does not refuse the second; Gabriel does not rebuke her.

What will people say? There is something else in her question that ought to be said out loud, because it is easy to miss underneath the theology. She does not ask what will people say? That question was coming, and it was going to cost her more than anyone else in this chapter. A betrothed girl visibly pregnant had, under the law, put herself within reach of stoning (Deuteronomy 22:23–24); at best she faced a quiet divorce and a lifetime of whispering. It simply is not what she asks first. Her mind goes to God’s method before it goes to her own reputation, and she has perhaps ten seconds in which to think.
