The answer moved into her. Mary’s question is the first question ever asked about the incarnation, and the answer to it is the incarnation. Gabriel does not reply with a method. He replies with God (v. 35). Her virginity is not an obstacle the plan must work round. It is the plan. This child needs no human father because he already has a Father, and he does not begin in Nazareth; he comes from above and takes his flesh from her. A son of Adam by ordinary descent could save no one. Mary’s how is answered by who.

What it does not mean. Not, as Augustine argued, that Mary had taken a vow of lifelong virginity. Nothing in the text suggests a vow; she was betrothed to be married in the normal way, and her question is about conceiving now. (See Luke 2:7 on whether Mary had other children.)

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit will come upon you. The answer to how: by the direct creative power of God, not by any human father. As the Spirit hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), the Spirit will bring about a new creation in Mary’s womb. Jesus is the beginning of the new humanity, the second Adam (3:38; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

Overshadow. The word (episkiasei) is not a euphemism. It is temple language: the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud that settled on the tabernacle so that even Moses could not go in, because the glory of the LORD filled it (Exodus 40:35), and the word for the cloud on the mountain of transfiguration (9:34). Mary is being told, in the only vocabulary Israel possessed for it, that she is about to become the place where God dwells: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, literally tabernacled (John 1:14).

Did it really happen, or is it a legend? A modern reader deserves the blunt question put plainly. First, Luke means it literally. The word is parthenos, and Mary’s own question settles the sense: she is betrothed, and says she has not known a man. This is a claim about biology, made in a culture that knew perfectly well where babies come from. Second, it does not read like legend. The pagan tales sometimes offered as parallels, a god taking a mortal woman, a hero fathered by Zeus, are lurid couplings producing half-divine hybrids. This is their opposite: no union, no partner, a quiet overshadowing, and a wholly human child. Some suggest the story grew out of Isaiah 7:14, but Jews of the time did not expect a virgin-born Messiah, so the prophecy is more likely to have been noticed after the event than to have created it. And nobody inventing a Messiah’s origin would have chosen this one, because it left Mary a betrothed girl visibly pregnant before her wedding. That was not a badge of honour but a scandal she would carry, and her son with her: years later men would sneer at him in public, we were not born of sexual immorality (John 8:41). Legends are built to impress. This account cost the family its reputation, and the Gospels record it soberly anyway, because it was true.

Why it matters. Not as a conjuring trick to prove he was special, but because of who was being born. The virgin conception, which Matthew and Luke both teach independently and the historic creeds confess, is how the eternal Son took a real human nature, born of woman (Galatians 4:4), without becoming one more son of Adam by ordinary descent, an heir of Adam’s ruined line. He was truly one of us, a body that tired and a mind that learned (2:52), yet without sin, holy from conception. Take away the miracle and you do not have a simpler Christ. You have a different one.

Called holy. Holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). A lamb with a blemish could not be offered, and a Saviour with sin of his own could not bear ours.

The Son of God. Not because the Spirit was his father in a physical sense, as pagan myths told of gods fathering children. The eternal Son, who already existed (John 1:1–14; Philippians 2:6–7), took human nature in Mary’s womb by the Spirit’s power. The conception does not make him the Son; it is the way the Son became man.

Does it matter if a Christian doubts the virgin birth? Yes, more than people think. A believer who is confused about it is not thereby lost, and should be taught patiently. But to deny it is to deny the plain testimony of two Gospels and the faith of the whole church, and it loosens the doctrine of who Christ is. If Scripture is wrong here, where it speaks so plainly, on what ground do we trust it about the resurrection? And the miracle carries the gospel: our salvation began not with human effort but with God coming down. Hold it gladly. It is not an embarrassment to be explained away but a glory to be adored.

For worship. The Word by whom everything that exists was made became an embryo. The Son who had no beginning acquired a birthday. He who fills heaven and earth was, for a season, a few millimetres long, in the dark, under a girl’s heart, in a Galilean hill town. Angels long to look into this (1 Peter 1:12). The God who began your salvation without any human help will finish it.
verseByVerse.note: “Overshadow” recalls the cloud of God’s presence overshadowing the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: the cloud settled on the tent

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your relative Elizabeth. A sign, offered without being asked for, which Mary could go and see for herself (v. 39). The man who demanded evidence got silence, and the girl who demanded nothing got a relative six months pregnant. Relative (syngenis) is a general word; Luke does not say how they were related.

Her who was called barren. Luke lets the village nickname be heard. That is what Elizabeth had been called for years, and Gabriel repeats it in the same breath as the news that it is finished.

Nothing will be impossible. What is translated nothing is literally no rhēma. The word can mean a thing or matter, as the Hebrew word behind it can, but its root sense is a spoken word, and Luke uses it two verses later of what God has said (v. 38). No word God speaks will fail to do what it was sent to do. And Gabriel is very nearly quoting what the LORD said to Abraham when Sarah laughed behind the tent door: Is anything too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). Jesus will say the same of salvation: what is impossible with man is possible with God (18:27).

A signature, not a blank cheque. This verse gets written on cards and handed to families in hospital corridors, and heard as a promise that the outcome they are desperate for is available if only they believe hard enough. Then the outcome does not come, and a grieving person concludes either that God let them down or that their faith was too small. Both conclusions are false. The verse is not a blank cheque but a signature under what God has already put in writing. What is guaranteed here is stronger: not that everything we want is possible, but that nothing God has promised can fail. No word of God has ever fallen to the ground. He spoke to Abraham, and Isaac came; to Elizabeth, and John came; to Mary, and the Son of God came.

The impossible thing at the centre. Elizabeth is the lesser wonder, offered to hold up faith in the greater. An old woman bearing a child is something God had done before, for Sarah. A virgin bearing the Son of God had never been done and never will be again. Luke’s Gospel will end with another of the same kind, when women at a tomb hear: why do you seek the living among the dead? (24:5). All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

So what has God put in writing? If the request you are carrying is not among the things God has promised, that is not the end of the matter. Look hard at the list of things he has written down: that he will never leave you nor forsake you; that nothing in all creation can separate you from his love; that he works all things together for good for those who love him; that he will finish what he began in you; that he will raise your body on the last day (John 6:40; Romans 8:28, 38–39; Philippians 1:6; Hebrews 13:5). Not one of those is negotiable, and not one of them depends on the strength of your grip. Pray boldly for the healing, the job, the child, the prodigal, because God is able. Rest your weight on the promises, because God is faithful.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.' And the angel departed from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant of the Lord. The word (doulē) is literally slave, a female bond-servant, the feminine of doulos. It is not modesty but a legal category: somebody with no right of refusal, whose time and body and future belong to another. Hannah used the same word of herself (1 Samuel 1:11).

The cost. Count what she agrees to in that half-second. An unmarried pregnant girl in a village of a few hundred people, where everyone would do the arithmetic, faced suspicion that might follow her for life. She might lose Joseph: Matthew tells us his mind was made up to divorce her before an angel changed it (Matthew 1:19–20). Under the law, she could in principle face death for adultery (Deuteronomy 22:20–24). Her explanation will be that an angel came. She said yes anyway.

Let it be. A single word, genoito, and its form in Greek is the mood of wishing: not a shrug of resignation but a reaching towards. Her response is the opposite of Zechariah’s, and Elizabeth will praise her for exactly this: blessed is she who believed (v. 45). The shape of it is the shape of every real obedience: a yes to a future she cannot see. Faith is not the confident feeling that things will turn out comfortably. It is the decision to trust the character of the one who is speaking, at the moment his word has made everything harder.

Room for the woman’s offspring. There was another woman once, and another word asking to be believed. Eve weighed God’s word against the fruit in front of her and reached out her hand. But Mary is not the one who undoes Eden. Her yes makes room for the one who will. In the garden God had promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), and Luke will trace this child’s line back through David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God (3:38). The second Adam is being given a body. The eternal Son said to the Father, Behold, I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7), and took the body Mary’s yes made room for. A woman’s unbelief let the ruin in; a woman’s faith opens the door, and through it comes the Son who will bear the curse and end it.

What if I cannot say yes to God about something? Be honest with him about it; he knows already. Tell him what you fear, what it will cost and why you are holding back. Then look at the one asking. Mary said yes not because the road looked easy but because she trusted the character of the God who spoke. Ask him for the will to obey, because it is God who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13). Take the next step you can see, even a small one. And remember that the perfect yes was spoken by her Son in Gethsemane: not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). Your yes rests on his.

In everyday life. Make Mary’s words your own prayer today: I am the Lord’s servant; let it be to me according to your word. Say it over the part of your life you have been keeping back from him, and then do the first thing obedience requires.

parallels.desc: let your servant find favour in your eyes

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary goes with haste to the hill country, to the one person who might understand: another woman visited by grace in a way that makes no human sense. At the sound of her greeting the child in Elizabeth’s womb leaps.

Filled with the Spirit, Elizabeth blesses Mary and her child and asks why the mother of my Lord should come to her: the first confession of Jesus as Lord in Luke, using the title Israel’s Scriptures give to God himself. And the section ends with a beatitude about faith (v. 45). What the Spirit commends in Mary is her trust, which sets her against Zechariah, who heard the same angel and did not believe.
verseByVerse.theology:
John’s leap is recognition and worship before birth. With Jeremiah 1:5 and John’s filling with the Spirit from the womb, it shows that God’s grace goes before us, calling and shaping before we can respond. It is not an argument for conscious faith in infants. It is a sign that God’s sovereign grace comes first.

Elizabeth’s blessing places Mary in the line of women through whom God worked deliverance (Judges 5:24). But the child she carries is the Saviour of the world, and verse 45 keeps even that from becoming a cult of the mother: the Spirit singles out not her body but her believing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary does not work through her news alone. She goes to someone who can understand. Grace is not meant to be received in isolation, and an isolated believer is a believer at risk.

Elizabeth, six months into her own miracle, is still astonished to be visited. And there is no trace in her of comparison with the younger woman whose portion is plainly larger than her own.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
With haste. Mary does not sit down to process. She packs, eager to see the sign (v. 36), and goes to the one other person on earth who will not think she has lost her mind.

The hill country. The highlands around Jerusalem; tradition names Ein Karem. From Nazareth it was a journey of 80–100 miles (130–160 km), four or five days on foot, in the first weeks of a pregnancy, by a girl probably in her mid-teens.

Grace looks for company. Grace that has just landed on a person is heavy, and the first thing it looks for is somebody else who has been under the same weight. This is a good deal of what the church is for, and it is why an isolated believer is a believer at risk. Look around your church for the person carrying something only another believer could understand, and make the journey to them.

The baby leaped in her womb. The verb skirtaō is the one the Greek Old Testament uses of hills skipping like rams (Psalm 114:4) and of the twins struggling inside Rebekah (Genesis 25:22). John, filled with the Spirit from the womb (v. 15), recognises the presence of his Lord, himself an unborn child perhaps only weeks after conception. There may be an echo, too, of David leaping and dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:16): the ark was the place of God’s presence, and the presence has come to the hill country of Judah again, in a girl.

The first to recognise him. The baby leaps first, and the mother’s prophecy comes second. Apart from Mary, the first person in Luke’s story to recognise Jesus Christ was an unborn child who could not see or reason. John’s entire ministry will consist of pointing away from himself towards somebody else. He began it before he was born, in the dark, at the sound of a voice. Which is a fair picture of how anybody comes to recognise him: by the Spirit, before we understand. The presence of Christ makes the unborn leap, the old prophesy and the young sing. Wherever he comes, even hidden, even small, joy breaks out, because he is the Lord, and the Spirit will not let him go unhonoured.

The unborn. Luke, a physician, calls that child brephos, the same word he uses of the newborn Jesus lying in the manger (2:12, 16), and of the infants people brought to Jesus to be touched (18:15). One word, three stages, no seam anywhere.

Does this mean an unborn baby can have faith? Luke is describing something unique: John’s Spirit-given recognition of the Lord as part of his special calling as forerunner. It is not a general rule about all unborn children. But it does show that God is not limited by age or understanding, that the Spirit can work in a person before birth, and that the unborn are persons with whom God deals. That is why believing parents may pray for their children from the womb, and why the Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, speak of elect infants being regenerated by the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (1689 10.3; Westminster 10.3).
verseByVerse.note: The hill country of Judea was the highland around Jerusalem, some 80 miles or more from Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: and she exclaimed with a loud cry, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A loud cry. Elizabeth does not greet Mary. She shouts, overtaken by the Holy Spirit in her own hallway.

Blessed are you among women. The construction is a Hebrew superlative: most blessed of all women, because of the child she carries. Jael was praised in similar words for delivering Israel (Judges 5:24). Mary will bear the Deliverer.

The fruit of your womb. Mary’s honour comes from her child. Elizabeth blesses Mary, then moves immediately past her to the child, and returns to Mary only to commend her faith (v. 45). Almost every word after this is about him.

And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? This is the first human confession of Jesus as Lord in Luke’s Gospel, and it is made by a pregnant old woman in a village house about an embryo she cannot see. “Lord” (kyrios) can mean simply master or sir, but it is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s own name, and Luke has used it of God again and again in this chapter. On the lips of a woman filled with the Spirit it is not a courtesy title. Elizabeth is not saying the mother of somebody important. Like David speaking of my Lord (Psalm 110:1), she is confessing that the child inside her young relative is her Lord in the fullest sense.

The elder bows. Elizabeth is the elder by decades, a daughter of Aaron, six months into a miracle of her own; Mary is a girl from Galilee. By every human measure the seniority runs one way, and Elizabeth’s first instinct is to humble herself, because Mary’s child is her Lord.

No trace of comparison. That can be harder to find than a miracle. Two people are blessed at the same moment, unequally, and the one with the smaller share is the one who is delighted. The Spirit filled Elizabeth, and what came out was joy at another woman’s greater portion. Her son will say the same thing thirty years later: he must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Where Christians differ: Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus (AD 431) gave Mary the title Theotokos, God-bearer or Mother of God. It was meant as a statement about Christ: the one Mary bore is truly God, one person, not two, not a man who later became divine. Protestants have generally accepted the doctrine while being wary of the title, because it has been used to exalt Mary. This commentary’s view: the doctrine is true and important: the child in Mary’s womb was the eternal Son of God made man, Elizabeth’s Lord. But it does not mean that Mary is the source of his deity, or that she should be honoured above other believers. Mother of my Lord is the biblical phrase, and Mary’s honour is always derived from her Son. The title, rightly used, says something about him.

How do I stop envying a fellow Christian? Start where Elizabeth started: with the Lord, not the comparison. Her eyes were on the child, and so the difference in gifts did not matter. Envy grows when we measure our share against someone else’s; it shrinks when we remember that every gift, theirs and ours, is grace we never deserved. Thank God aloud, specifically, for the thing in your brother or sister that you envy. Then serve them in it. And remember the body: their greater gift is given for your good as well (1 Corinthians 12:26).

For worship. Elizabeth called an unborn child my Lord, and she was right. He was Lord in the womb, Lord in the manger, Lord on the cross and Lord on the throne. He still comes hidden, in a word read and bread broken, and the same Spirit still opens eyes to know him.

parallels.desc: most blessed of women be Jael
how can the ark of the LORD come to me?

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaped for joy. This is the Spirit’s interpretation, not a mother’s fond guess. The word (agalliasei) is exultation, the joy of the messianic age. The joy promised in v. 14 has already begun.

Blessed is she who believed. The first beatitude in Luke’s Gospel. Not Mary’s purity, not her lineage, not her womb, which Elizabeth has already blessed: what the Holy Spirit singles out in the mother of the Lord is that she believed.

The chapter’s whole argument. Her faith is the contrast with Zechariah’s unbelief (v. 20), spoken in the house where her husband still sat silent. One does not believe, and is silenced. One believes, and is blessed. The whole Gospel will turn on this: the word of God comes, and everything depends on whether it is received.

Blessed rather. Later a woman in a crowd calls out to Jesus, Blessed is the womb that bore you, very close to what Elizabeth says here. And Jesus answers her: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it (11:27–28). He is not disowning his mother. He is redirecting the blessing onto the thing his mother actually did, which stands open to anybody.

A fulfillment. See when she believed: not once the pregnancy showed or Joseph came round. Mary believed that there would be a fulfilment: future, unseen, and about to make her life extremely difficult. Faith is not the conclusion reached once the evidence is safely in. It is trust extended across the gap while the evidence is still on its way.

What was spoken was about him. What had been spoken to Mary from the Lord was a promise about her Son. Luke closes his Gospel on the same note, from the other side. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus calls two disciples slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken, and beginning with Moses and all the Prophets he interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:25–27). Mary believed before a word of it had come true; the disciples struggled to believe after all of it had. Both were brought to the same place: every word God has spoken leads to Jesus.

Is my faith strong enough to make me blessed? The blessing does not rest on the size of your faith but on the faithfulness of the one you trust. Mary was blessed because she believed God’s word, and the power was in the word, not in her believing. A trembling hand that holds Christ receives all of Christ. If your faith is weak, take it to the word: read the promise again, pray it back to God, and ask him to strengthen what he has begun. Weak faith in a strong Saviour saves; strong faith in anything else does not.

parallels.desc: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–56 — Mary's Song of Praise: The Magnificat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary’s song, the Magnificat (from its first word in Latin), is modelled closely on Hannah’s prayer (1 Samuel 2:1–10).

The song moves from what God has done for Mary (vv. 46–50) to what he does in the world (vv. 51–55): scattering the proud, bringing down the mighty, exalting the humble, filling the hungry and sending the rich away empty. Mary sings in the prophetic past, because what God will do in her Son is certain. It is not a call to revolution, since every verb has God as its subject, but the song of a God who chooses what the world counts weak (1 Corinthians 1:27). And it ends with Abraham (vv. 54–55): the reversals are God keeping an old appointment.

Then Luke notes simply that Mary stayed about three months and went home (v. 56), to a village that could count and a fiancé who would resolve to divorce her.
verseByVerse.theology:
Speaking of future events in the past tense is the language of prophetic certainty: Isaiah 53 tells the Servant’s suffering and vindication as done, centuries before either happened.

God looked on Mary’s humble estate, not despite it but by choice. The same pattern runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem. The reason is not that the lowly are better people. It is that a grace which chooses them cannot be mistaken for a reward for merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship for many centuries, in the church’s evening prayer and in settings by composers such as Monteverdi and Bach.

It announces a King whose reign will outlast every empire and whose justice will overturn every injustice. A church that sings it knows how the story ends, and lives accordingly: not grasping for power, not trusting in the mighty, not filling itself with the world’s goods, but walking with the God who lifts up the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Magnificat. Mary’s song is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin (magnifies). It is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and the Psalms: something like fifteen allusions in ten verses. When a girl who has hidden Scripture in her heart is put under sudden pressure, what comes out is what was already in. The song has four movements: what God has done for Mary (vv. 46–49), his character (v. 50), what he does in the world (vv. 51–53), and what he has done for Israel (vv. 54–55).

Textual note: Mary or Elizabeth? Nearly all manuscripts say that Mary spoke these words; a few early Latin witnesses name Elizabeth. The song fits Mary: the lowly servant (v. 48) and the God who has done great things for her (v. 49).

My soul magnifies the Lord. The word (megalynei) means makes great, declares the greatness of. God cannot be made greater than he is, so think of two lenses. A microscope makes something small appear larger than it is. A telescope lets something unimaginably vast appear nearer its true size. Worship is never the first. Mary is not inflating God. She is bringing him close enough to be seen as he actually is, and everything else, including her own alarming circumstances, takes its proper proportions the moment he does. Her soul goes out of itself and grows larger by looking at somebody else, and the one she looks at is not an idea but a rescuer with a name, who has been at this work since Eden, who has never yet abandoned a promise, and who at that moment was small enough to be carried under a girl’s ribs and great enough to hold the heavens together. There is no danger of magnifying him too far. The whole of eternity will not be long enough to get him into proportion. What do you magnify by habit: the problem, the person who wronged you? Turn the telescope round.

God my Savior. Mary needed a Saviour. Here, in the second line of her own song, with the Holy Spirit upon her, she calls God my Saviour: not the Saviour, in general, but mine. A person who needs no rescue does not use that word. Roman Catholic teaching answers that Mary was saved by being kept from sin rather than rescued out of it; but nothing in the text hints at that distinction, and Scripture says that all have sinned (Romans 3:23). She rejoiced in the God who saves sinners (Habakkuk 3:18). She is the first of a very long line of people who had nothing to bring and were given everything.

The Saviour she carried. A few months later an angel will tell shepherds: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (2:11). The God Mary calls her Saviour is about to be born of her as a Saviour, and the child she carries is the only way her own sins will ever be dealt with. Mary gave him his human life, and he would give his life for hers.

How do I magnify the Lord when I do not feel like it? Mary’s song did not come from nowhere; it came from Scripture she had already stored up. So fill yourself with God’s words, especially the Psalms, so that they are there when you need them. Then begin with what you know, not what you feel: tell God who he is and what he has done in Christ, aloud if you can. Feelings often follow truth spoken in faith. And sing with the church. On days when you cannot sing, let the congregation sing for you. Praise is not pretending that things are fine; it is seeing God as he really is, which is always the truest thing in the room.
verseByVerse.note: Mary’s song, known as the Magnificat, is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The humble estate of his servant. The word (tapeinōsin) means lowliness, low social position, the state of counting for nothing. Mary is not describing her humility as a virtue. She is describing her social altitude, which was ground level. And looked on is a deliberate turning of the head. Hannah prayed: if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant (1 Samuel 1:11).

God’s settled method. Not the impressive brothers but the boy left out in the field with the sheep. Not the priest but the girl. God looks in the direction nobody else is looking. Paul states it in so many words: God chose what is low and despised in the world, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

The lowliness he took. The God who looked on Mary’s humble estate did more than look. Her Son would take that estate as his own. Paul says he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:7–8). Luke quotes Isaiah over the suffering Servant with the very noun Mary uses here: in his humiliation justice was denied him (Acts 8:33). The lowliness Mary sang about from below, her Son entered from above. He went lower than Nazareth, lower than the manger, down to a criminal’s death, so that the lowest of the low could be lifted with him.

All generations will call me blessed. A prophecy that has come true: not that she will be worshipped, but honoured as the one God blessed. Protestants have often been so anxious about what has been built on Mary that they have quietly declined to obey a plain sentence of Scripture. A church that never calls Mary blessed is not being careful; it is disagreeing with the text. So call her blessed, gladly.

Great things for me. She gives the reason in the very next breath, and the reason is not herself. That is the difference between honouring Mary and praying to her: a mirror is not honoured by being stared at, but by being looked along, to the light it is turned towards.

Should Christians pray to Mary or ask her to intercede? No. Generations call her blessed because God chose her; she herself calls God my Saviour (v. 47). Scripture gives one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom every believer may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:14–16). Prayers addressed to Mary, as in the Hail Mary, give her a role Scripture never gives. We honour her best by sharing her faith: let it be to me according to your word (v. 38).

Holy is his name. God’s name is God himself, as he has revealed himself: set apart, utterly pure, majestic. Holy and awesome is his name (Psalm 111:9). The holiness that could have consumed us has instead bent down and looked on us with favour. Mary has just said that the greatest thing which ever happened to a human being happened to her, and her sentence ends by getting out of the way.

In everyday life. When someone praises you this week, do what Mary did: in the very next breath, give the reason, and the reason is him.

parallels.desc: look on the affliction of your servant
holy and awesome is his name

verseByVerse.quote: And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mercy. The turning point of the song. Everything before it is about Mary; everything after it is about the world. And the joint between them is mercy (eleos), the Greek Old Testament’s usual word for the Hebrew ḥesed, God’s steadfast, covenant love: not pity felt at a distance but the love that has bound itself and will not walk away (Exodus 34:6–7). Mary is saying that what has happened to her is not an exception. It is a sample.

Those who fear him. Few phrases do more damage when misheard. To fear God is not to be terrified of him, but to revere him, take him seriously, trust and obey him. It is entirely compatible with running to him; a God small enough not to be feared would be too small to be worth reaching.

From generation to generation. Psalm 103:17: But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him. A young girl is singing about grandchildren she will never meet. The promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself (Acts 2:39).

Mercy with a face. Within months Zechariah will sing of the same mercy and name its coming: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high (v. 78). The covenant love that bound itself to Abraham was never only an attitude in heaven. It was on its way to earth in a person. In Christ the mercy of God has hands that touch lepers, a voice that tells a sinful woman her sins are forgiven (7:48), and a body given for us.

What about my child or grandchild who has walked away? Take hold of this verse in prayer. The mercy that reached Mary in Nazareth had been travelling towards her since Abraham. It does not lose speed with distance, and it does not require the previous generation to have finished the job. Nothing in this verse guarantees a particular grandchild; it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise, because every person must come to Christ by his own faith, and God’s mercy is his to give. What it does say is what kind of God is being prayed to: one whose stated habit is to keep turning up in a family long after the people who first prayed for it are dead. So keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open, and live the gospel in front of them.

In everyday life. If you are afraid of God in the wrong way, as a judge waiting to catch you out, bring that fear to the cross, where his anger against your sin was spent on Christ. Then learn the right fear: the awe that makes you careful with his name, honest in your work and quick to run to him.

parallels.desc: the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him

verseByVerse.quote: He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The past tense. He has scattered, he has brought down, he has exalted, he has filled, he has sent away. All the verbs are in the past tense (the Greek aorist), and none of it has visibly happened. This is the prophetic past: when God has spoken, the outcome is so certain that it can be reported as history, as Isaiah described the Servant’s suffering and vindication seven centuries before a nail was driven (Isaiah 53). And Mary can sing it for one reason: the thing that guarantees the reversal is already inside her. From where she is standing the war is over. What remains is the clearing up.

Strength with his arm. God’s arm is a picture of his power in action, especially at the exodus: with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Deuteronomy 26:8; Isaiah 51:9; 52:10). And Isaiah asks, to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? (Isaiah 53:1), and answers with the suffering Servant. The arm of the LORD, in the end, is a crucified man.

The thoughts of their hearts. The proud plan in their hearts, and God scatters their plans, as at Babel (Genesis 11). Mary locates the pride not first in palaces but in the heart: the quiet conviction that I am the author of my own life and need nothing from God, which can wear religious clothes as easily as royal ones. Luke will show a Pharisee standing in the temple thanking God that he is not like other men, and going home unjustified (18:11–14). Pride is the sin of anyone who comes to God with something to show.

Brought down the mighty. The great reversal. Hannah sang: The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts (1 Samuel 2:7–8). This is a major theme of Luke: the humble exalted and the exalted humbled (14:11; 18:14), blessings on the poor and woes on the rich (6:20–26). Herod sits on his throne; Mary’s son will lie in a manger. No throne is safe from him, and no beggar is beyond him.

Filled the hungry. Psalm 107:9. Hunger here is both physical and spiritual: those who know their need, and hunger for God (6:21; Matthew 5:6). The rich are those who are self-satisfied and need nothing from God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25).

The line most readers would rather skip. The rich sent away empty is uncomfortable, because most people reading this are, by any measure the world has ever used, the rich. And Luke refuses to let us spiritualise it away. But the mechanism is exact. Both go home with what they arrived with room for. Nobody is turned away at the door for owning things. They are sent away empty because they came full, and a full man cannot be filled. Money is dangerous not because God objects to it, but because it is the most efficient device ever invented for producing the sensation of not needing anything. Whatever we reach for first when the ground moves is, in practice, the thing being trusted.

What it does not mean. Not a call for revolution, as some have read it. Every one of the verbs has God as its subject, and the way he is doing it at this moment is by placing himself inside a poor girl in an occupied province. The overthrow is real, and there is no army in it. Nor does it mean that all poor people are saved and all rich people lost. But it does show that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), that he cares about the poor and the oppressed, and that his kingdom overturns the world’s values. These are real social realities as well as spiritual ones, and the church should reflect them.

So what should a comfortable Christian do with this? Not feel vaguely guilty and carry on. First, come to God hungry: confess that nothing you own can save you, and ask him to fill you with Christ. Second, hold your money with an open hand: give generously, regularly and sacrificially, especially to the poor and to the work of the gospel (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Third, notice the lowly around you, the poor, the elderly, the overlooked, and treat them as God does. Wealth is not a sin, but it is a test, and the question is whether it has become the thing you trust.

parallels.desc: he brings low and he exalts

verseByVerse.quote: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has helped. Mary’s song ends where the story of salvation began, reaching back past David and Moses to Abraham. Isaiah 41:8–9: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham. The verb means to take hold of someone in order to help, like a hand under the elbow of a man who is going down.

In remembrance of his mercy. When God remembers, it never means that something had slipped his mind. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant, and heard the groaning in Egypt (Exodus 2:24). Remembering, in the Bible, is a promise coming due, and Zechariah, whose name means the LORD remembers (v. 5), will sing the same (v. 72).

To Abraham and to his offspring. God’s promise to Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). It was made to a childless man, roughly two thousand years before this song.

The offspring the oath was about. The help God sends Israel is not a policy. It is a child. Paul notices that the promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, singular, and says: who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Mary sings of Abraham’s offspring with Abraham’s offspring under her heart. Luke will show the two halves of the promise meeting in one pair of arms, when old Simeon takes the baby in the temple and calls him a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel (2:32). Help for Israel and blessing for all the families of the earth were never two promises. They were one Son.

An old appointment. So the reversals she has just sung are not God changing his policy, or finally losing patience with the powerful. They are God keeping an old appointment: covenant faithfulness arriving in a world arranged the wrong way up.

Does God still have promises for the Jewish people? Christians who love the Scriptures disagree on the details, especially in reading Romans 11. All agree on what Mary sings here: that God has kept his promise to Abraham in Christ, Abraham’s offspring, and that the gospel is to the Jew first (Romans 1:16). Many in the Reformed tradition, from the Puritans onward, have also expected a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end (Romans 11:25–26). What no Christian may say is that God has forgotten Israel, or that the Jewish people can be saved apart from their Messiah. The mercy Mary praised is offered to them in her Son, and we should pray and work for it.

For worship. Two thousand years is a long time to hold a sentence steady. The family that carried the promise sold a brother into slavery, worshipped a calf, split in two and went into exile. The line thinned until it ran through a village builder and a girl from Nazareth. And not one syllable of what God said to Abraham was ever withdrawn. He had bound himself by an oath, to a man long dead, about descendants not yet born, and he kept it, because that is what he is like. The promises that now include us rest on the same oath.

parallels.desc: Israel, my servant, offspring of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About three months. Until near the time of John’s birth, since Elizabeth was in her sixth month when Mary arrived (v. 36). Whether Mary stayed for the birth Luke does not say; he rounds off her part of the story first, as he often does.

Returned to her home. To Nazareth, around three months pregnant and soon to begin showing, to a village where everyone can count. The one other person on earth who would believe her is now eighty miles behind her.

What happened next. Matthew tells us that Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly (Matthew 1:19), and it took an angel in a dream to stop him. Mary walked home to a fiancé who had every reason to conclude she had betrayed him, and to a village that would agree with him.

Nobody warned her. Gabriel told her about the child, the kingdom, the Spirit and her relative. He said nothing about the whispering, or the look on Joseph’s face. She found out the way everybody finds out: by arriving. The mother of the Lord did not get an easier road on account of who she was carrying. She got the ordinary road, walked in the ordinary way, with heaven inside her and nobody able to tell.

The shame he shared from the womb. The child under her heart was walking that road with her, already sharing the suspicion that fell on her. He began his human life under a cloud he had not earned, and he ended it under a sentence he had not earned, numbered with the transgressors (22:37). From the first months of his life the Lord of glory was content to be misjudged, so that those who are rightly judged might be cleared.

Why does God not tell us what obedience will cost? Because he wants us to trust him, not the plan. If we knew every hard thing in advance, we would lean on our own preparations; instead he gives us enough light for the next step and promises to be with us on the road. Jesus did tell his disciples to count the cost (14:28), so we are not to follow blindly. But the details usually come as we go. What God does tell us in advance is the end: that he will never leave us, and that he will bring us home.

In everyday life. Mary had three months with Elizabeth before she faced Nazareth. If you are about to walk back into something hard, find your Elizabeth first; and if you are the mature believer, make room for the younger one who needs you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–66 — The Birth of John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke gives John’s birth one verse and moves at once to the naming. On the eighth day, at the circumcision, the family assumes the boy will be called Zechariah. Elizabeth says he will be called John; Zechariah writes on a tablet: his name is John. At once his mouth is opened, blessing God.

The order matters. His silence lifts not when he privately makes up his mind but when he publicly acts on Gabriel’s word, putting God’s choice above his family’s expectation. The neighbours are filled with fear, and all who hear lay these things up in their hearts, as Mary will (2:19, 51): not understanding everything yet, but refusing to let go of what they have received.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question everyone asks, what then will this child be, is answered by the rest of Luke and Acts. John will be the voice in the wilderness, the greatest among those born of women (7:28), the last of the prophets and the hinge between the old covenant and the new.

And the whole district shares in the response, rejoicing, wondering and remembering. In Luke the gospel is never only a private matter between one person and God; its effects spread through families and neighbourhoods.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah went into the temple with correct theology and too little trust. He comes out of nine months of silence writing God’s word on a tablet before he says a word of his own. The discipline has done its work.

The neighbours’ fear is the awe that God’s nearness produces, and their instinct to lay it up in their hearts is the right response to grace we do not yet understand: not instant explanation, but faithful keeping until understanding comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She bore a son. Exactly as the angel said. The house has been silent for nine months. Now there is a baby crying in it.

Great mercy. Literally that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, the same verb as Mary’s my soul magnifies (v. 46). Luke records the neighbours’ theology rather than their congratulations. They do not call it luck. They name the one who did it, and so should we when we tell of another’s blessing.

They rejoiced with her. The angel had promised that many would rejoice at his birth (v. 14), and here is the first instalment: a house full of neighbours. Hold that against verse 25: the reproach she named, the thing people said, has become the thing people celebrate. Nothing about her has changed except that God acted. He turns reproach into celebration, and he does it in front of the very people who passed the verdict. His mercy is never small and never private: it spills over, and those who stand near it are made glad.

A village’s joy, then the world’s. This is the herald’s birth, and the joy it brings is the size of a hill-country village. Six months later another birth will be announced, not by neighbours passing the word but by an angel in the night sky: I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people (2:10). John’s birth fills a house; Jesus’ birth fills the heavens with a multitude praising God. The joy at John is real, but it is a lamp lit before the dawn.

What if people have misjudged me and never changed their minds? Then you are in good company: the prophets, the apostles and our Lord himself were misjudged to the end of their lives on earth. Do what you can to put things right, honestly and humbly, especially if there is some truth in what is said. Then leave your reputation with God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Paul said it is a very small thing to be judged by any human court; it is the Lord who judges me (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). On the last day every hidden thing will be brought to light, and if you are in Christ, the verdict will be the one already given: no condemnation.

parallels.desc: everyone who hears will laugh over me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered, 'No; he shall be called John.' And they said to her, 'None of your relatives is called by this name.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day. Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign God gave to Abraham (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). The forerunner of the new covenant begins his life marked with the sign of the old one.

The Lord under his own law. Eight days after his own birth, Jesus will lie where John lies here, and receive the same sign and his name (2:21). The one who gave the covenant to Abraham submitted to its mark. Paul gives the reason: God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). From his eighth day the Son was keeping, for his people, the law they had broken. John is circumcised because he is a son of Abraham. Jesus is circumcised because he came to be the obedient son of Abraham that none of Abraham’s other sons had been.

Does circumcision here support infant baptism? Paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers), whose godliness and learning we honour, argue that baptism has replaced circumcision as the covenant sign and should likewise be given to the infants of believers. This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that baptism belongs to those who profess repentance and faith. Circumcision marked physical descent within the old covenant people, which included believers and unbelievers alike. The new covenant people are those who know the Lord, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), born not of blood but of God (John 1:13), and the New Testament shows baptism following faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12). The true counterpart of circumcision is the circumcision of the heart by the Spirit (Colossians 2:11–12). Both sides agree that children of believers are to be brought up in the faith and prayed for from birth.

After his father. Naming at circumcision seems to have been customary, and naming a son after his father or grandfather was common.

No; he shall be called John. His mother answers as flatly as a sentence can be put. How does Elizabeth know the name? Luke does not say. What he does record is that the woman with no standing at all in that discussion contradicted her entire family, in public, on the strength of a word from God, and did not soften it.

None of your relatives. The room’s response is not theological. It is social: not the name is wrong but the name is not ours. It is the oldest objection in religion and the least examined: we have never done it that way. But John belongs not to his family’s line, but to God’s purpose. God names his servants, and his name for this child was grace. He has always been the God who does a new thing, and the new thing is always mercy.

The pressure of people who mean well. It is not persecution. It is a room full of people she loves, all of whom think she is making a mistake, and all of whom mean well. That is far harder to withstand than hostility, and it is the form most believers actually meet. She had nothing to appeal to except what God had said. It was enough, and she held it alone until somebody put a writing tablet into her husband’s hands.

Is tradition always wrong then? No. Elizabeth was keeping the tradition of circumcision on the eighth day, gladly, because God had commanded it. Family customs and church traditions are often good gifts, carrying the wisdom of those who went before. The question is what has authority. Where a custom simply expresses love and order, honour it. Where it contradicts what God has said, God’s word wins, however much you love the people who hold the custom. Scripture alone binds the conscience, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both say (Westminster 20.2; 1689 21.2). And when you have to break with a custom, do it with the same firmness and the same love Elizabeth showed: no sneering, no lecture, just a clear no and a reason.

In everyday life. Name the area where people who love you are quietly pulling you away from what God has said: how you handle money, whom you marry, how you raise your children. Hold to the word, and keep loving the room.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the name was often given then.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, 'His name is John.' And they all wondered. And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made signs. Signs, not questions. Zechariah’s condition in verse 22 is described with the word kōphos, which covers both an inability to speak and an inability to hear (Mark 7:32). So Zechariah may have spent nine months unable to hear his wife’s voice, with nothing in his head but the sentence Gabriel had spoken.

A writing tablet. A wooden board coated with wax, written on with a stylus. His name is John: not his name shall be, which is what Elizabeth said, but his name is. He is not casting a vote. He is reporting a fact settled nine months earlier, by a word he had not believed and now obeys exactly.

Immediately his mouth was opened. And they all wondered: husband and wife, who could not have consulted each other in words in front of them, agreed. Look at when his voice comes back. Not when he privately came round, not at the birth, but immediately after he wrote the name: at the point of public, irreversible obedience.

Blessing God. His first words after nine months of silence were praise: not an explanation, not a complaint about the discipline. The doubter has become a worshipper (vv. 68–79).

The first loosened tongue. Isaiah had said that when God came to save, the ears of the deaf would be unstopped and the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:4–6). When John, in prison, sends to ask Jesus whether he is the one who is to come, Jesus answers with that list: the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear (7:22). The first mute tongue opened in this story belongs to John’s own father. The age of the Messiah begins in that house with a loosened tongue blessing God.

Does God always lift discipline when we obey? God’s discipline always has a purpose and a limit, and he delights to restore. Very often, as here, the turning point comes when we stop arguing and obey. But do not make it a formula, as though obedience were a coin that buys an end to hardship. Some consequences of sin remain in this life even after repentance: David was forgiven, and his child still died. What is always lifted at once is the barrier between you and God: when you confess, he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). The relationship is restored immediately, and the rest is in a Father’s wise hands.

In everyday life. Is there a step of obedience you have agreed with privately but never taken publicly: a confession to make, a baptism to ask for? Write the name on the tablet.

For worship. Zechariah was silent for his own unbelief. Another would be silent for ours. Luke tells us how the Ethiopian read it: like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth (Acts 8:32). The Lamb of God stood before Herod and made no answer (23:9), and because he held his peace under judgment, mouths like Zechariah’s are opened in blessing, and the dumb are taught to sing. He bought our songs with his silence.
verseByVerse.note: A writing tablet was a wooden board coated with wax.

verseByVerse.quote: And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, 'What then will this child be?' For the hand of the Lord was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear came on all. Awe at the evident work of God, the reaction that fell on Zechariah in the temple, now spread across a district. Luke will record it again and again (5:8–9; 7:16; 8:25). A God who can be discussed comfortably has usually not turned up yet.

Laid them up in their hearts. The news spread through all the hill country of Judea, and some would remember it thirty years later, when John appeared preaching in the wilderness. This is one of Luke’s signature motifs (2:19, 51).

Keeping what you cannot yet explain. Something happens with God’s fingerprints on it and no available explanation. Luke’s neighbours neither force a meaning onto it nor shrug it off. They carry it, unexplained, and wait. Some of what God does is only legible years later, and the people who can read it then are the ones who kept it.

What then will this child be? The question everyone asked. It hangs over the hill country, unanswered, for thirty years. Luke will answer it, but not yet: the greatest of the prophets, and the forerunner of the Lord.

The question behind the question. Luke’s Gospel is full of people asking who someone is, and this is only the first. When John is grown, crowds will wonder whether he might be the Christ, and he will say: he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie (3:15–16). Then the question moves to Jesus. Who is this, that he commands even winds and water? (8:25). Who do you say that I am? (9:20). What John will be can only be answered by who Jesus is.

The hand of the Lord. God’s power and favour were on him from the beginning (Acts 11:21). When it is with someone, it means God has taken hold of a life for a purpose of his own (Ezra 7:6). Pray for the children you know, by name, that it would be with them.

How do I lay things up in my heart in practice? Write them down. Keep a simple record of answered prayers, providences you could not explain, verses that came alive at a particular time. Tell them to your family. Return to them when you are discouraged, as Israel was told to remember the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). And resist the urge to tie every event to a neat lesson. It is enough to say: God was in this, and I do not yet see why. The meaning often arrives years later, and the record lets you see it when it does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zechariah’s song, the Benedictus (from its first word in Latin, blessed), is praise and prophecy, not explanation. Its first half (vv. 68–75) is about the Messiah: the God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people, raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and remembered the oath he swore to Abraham, so that his people might serve him without fear all their days. Its second half (vv. 76–79) is about John, who will go before the Lord to prepare his ways.

Verse 77 is the key to the whole song, and it answers the question a modern reader raises at verse 71. Rome was never overthrown, and Jerusalem fell within a lifetime. But Zechariah defines the salvation he means: knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins. And he ends with the image of a sunrise from on high, the great light dawning on a people in darkness (Isaiah 9:2; Malachi 4:2), to guide their feet into the way of peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Benedictus draws three lines of promise together in the two children of this chapter: the covenant with David (vv. 69–70), the oath sworn to Abraham (vv. 73–75), and the prophetic promise of a forerunner going before the Lord (vv. 76–77). God is keeping them specifically, in the births of two real children at a datable moment in history.

And the purpose of that salvation is stated plainly in verses 74–75. Salvation is not merely rescue; it is freedom for a life of worship, serving God in holiness and righteousness, without the fear that guilt produces, because his people have been freely saved.
verseByVerse.examples:
When Zechariah opens his mouth at last, he says nothing in his own defence and nothing against the relatives who doubted. He speaks entirely about God. Seasons of enforced silence, when we are made to listen rather than speak, can be like that: what finally comes out is truer than what we said before.

The chapter ends with John growing strong in spirit and living in the wilderness until his public appearance (v. 80). Moses, Elijah and Paul all had their seasons in the wilderness, and so did the Lord himself. The wilderness is not the failure of the plan. It is where the messenger is formed, and it cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Benedictus. Zechariah’s song is called the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin (blessed). It has two halves: praise for what God has done through the Messiah of David’s line (vv. 68–75), and a prophecy about John’s role (vv. 76–79). Zechariah, a priest, praises God first for the Messiah, not for his own son.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. The priest who doubted now speaks as a prophet. He does not describe what he saw. He preaches.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. A traditional Jewish blessing; it is how the Psalms bless God (Psalm 41:13; 72:18; 106:48), and Zechariah the priest has said the words thousands of times. He has never once said them about this.

He has visited. The word (epeskepsato) means come to look after, care for: not a social call but God coming to see about his people with the intention of acting, as when he had seen the affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:16; 4:31). God himself has come to his people, in the person of Jesus (7:16; 19:44).

Redeemed his people. Literally made redemption (lytrōsis): release by payment of a price, the buying back of a slave or a prisoner. The exodus was God’s great act of redemption in the Old Testament (Exodus 6:6). Now God has acted to bring a greater redemption, which Jesus will accomplish by giving his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Again the past tense: it is as good as done, though the Messiah is not yet born.

Four hundred years of quiet. From Malachi to Gabriel is roughly four centuries without a prophet. The temple was defiled, cleansed, and rebuilt in marble by a murderer, and heaven said nothing. Generations prayed and died without hearing a word. And then, in the ordinary rotation of a village priest’s week of service, he came. He had not been waiting for Israel to improve, because Israel had not improved. The silence was never abandonment; it was an appointment being kept from the other end of it.

Redeemed from what, and at what price? From slavery to sin and from the condemnation it deserves. We were not merely lost; we were held, under the curse of the law and the sentence of death. The price was not silver or gold but the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19). He took our place and bore the penalty we owed, so that we might go free. That is why a Christian is not his own: he was bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Redemption is both a release and a change of owner.

In everyday life. If God feels silent in your life, keep praying and serving in the ordinary rotation of your week. And when you notice his visiting, say aloud what Zechariah said: blessed be the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah’s song, known as the Benedictus, celebrates God’s faithfulness in terms of the Old Testament promises.

parallels.desc: blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
he sent redemption to his people

verseByVerse.quote: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A horn of salvation. A horn was a symbol of strength that acts, like the horns of a wild ox (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:10). David called the LORD my rock and the horn of my salvation (Psalm 18:2). And Zechariah is almost certainly echoing one text: There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed (Psalm 132:17). The rescue God has raised up is not an idea or a message. It is a power, and it is in David’s house.

In the house of his servant David. Zechariah was from Aaron’s line, but he praises God for the king from David’s line, not the priest from his own. Mary’s child, not yet born, is the horn.

By the mouth of his holy prophets. The salvation arriving is the one the prophets described for centuries (Acts 3:21): God has not improvised.

Saved from our enemies. Psalm 106:10. Zechariah would have thought first of the Romans. But Rome could not touch the thing that would still have been wrong with Israel on the morning after Rome fell. He did not rescue his people by breaking Rome but by breaking death, and every enemy that could have destroyed us lies under his feet.

Was Zechariah wrong about the enemies? Rome was not overthrown. Israel was not liberated. About seventy-five years after this song Jerusalem was burned and the temple pulled down stone from stone. Zechariah is speaking, Luke says, filled with the Holy Spirit, so the question deserves a straight answer. Two things answer it, and the second is much the stronger. The first is that Zechariah is repeating the language of the covenant promises, and covenant language about enemies runs deeper than any particular empire. The enemies Scripture finally names are not Roman. They are sin, death and the devil, and a Gospel that ends at an empty tomb has something to say about all three. But the better answer comes from Zechariah himself, six verses later. He defines the salvation he is singing about in so many words: to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins (v. 77). That is his own gloss on his own prophecy. The rescue he means is not from an occupying army. It is from guilt. The old priest who had spent his life killing animals for other people’s sins is announcing that the sins themselves are about to be dealt with.

Does Christ also save me from people who hate me? Not always from their hostility in this life; he told his disciples they would be hated for his name (21:17). But he saves you from their power to harm you finally. They can take your job, your reputation, even your life, and they cannot touch your soul or separate you from God’s love (12:4–7; Romans 8:35–39). Meanwhile he commands you to love them and pray for them (6:27–28), because the same horn of salvation that rescued you can rescue them. Your real enemies, sin, death and the devil, he has already defeated.

In everyday life. Name the enemy that feels strongest this week, the temptation, the fear, the accusation, and set it beside the empty tomb.
verseByVerse.note: A horn was a symbol of strength, like a bull’s horns.

parallels.desc: I will make a horn to sprout for David

verseByVerse.quote: to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mercy promised. God’s covenant love, promised long ago: you will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old (Micah 7:20). Zechariah now reaches back past David to Abraham, and names the guarantee.

His holy covenant. God remembers his covenant: not that he had forgotten, but that he now acts on it (Exodus 2:24; Psalm 105:8–9). Zechariah’s name, the LORD remembers, is fulfilled; and Elizabeth’s name contains the word oath.

The oath. Genesis records one occasion on which God, in so many words, swore an oath to Abraham. It came on a mountain, after a knife had been raised over a bound boy and a hand had stopped it: By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, I will surely bless you, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Genesis 22:16–18). God swore by himself (Hebrews 6:13–18). The promise Zechariah is standing on cannot fail without God failing.

The mountain and the hill. See what happened on that mountain and what did not. Abraham was spared his son. The ram was in the thicket, and the father walked down the hill with the boy beside him. When the promise sworn there finally came due, the Father who swore it climbed a hill outside Jerusalem with his own Son, and there was no ram, and he did not spare him (Romans 8:32).

Serve him without fear. Salvation is being got out in order to be free for something, and the something is worship, as Israel was freed from Egypt to worship God (Exodus 4:23). The verb (latreuein) is the word for priestly service, the temple word, and Zechariah, a priest, applies it to the whole people.

The cringe goes. A great many believers serve God with a low, constant dread running underneath everything: of not having done enough, of a God who is quietly disappointed, of the sin that keeps coming back. That is not the arrangement. Zechariah puts deliverance first and service second. The fear has to be dealt with before the serving can begin, and God deals with it himself. Perfect love casts out fear, for fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The reverent awe of verse 50 stays. The cringe goes.

All our days. Holiness toward God and righteousness toward others (Ephesians 4:24; Titus 2:11–14), and all our days means all of them, not only the good ones.

How do I get rid of the dread? Not by trying harder to deserve God’s approval, which only feeds it. Go back to the order of the verse: delivered first, then serving. Look at the cross, where the punishment you fear was borne in full by Christ; there is nothing left for you to pay. Remind yourself that you are a son, not a hired hand: you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). Confess sin quickly and specifically, and take God at his word when he forgives. Then serve because you are accepted, not in order to be. The dread may linger as a habit of mind; answer it each time with the gospel.

In everyday life. Take the task you are dreading because you might not do it well enough for God. You will not do it perfectly; Christ served perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19). So do it as a forgiven child doing something for his Father, in the strength of the Spirit he has given you.

parallels.desc: the covenant he made with Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, child. For eight verses Zechariah has sung about somebody else’s son. Now he turns to his own, eight days old.

Prophet of the Most High. Jesus will be called Son of the Most High (v. 32); John is the prophet of the Most High. A great title, but not the greatest, and a father holding his miracle baby is making the ranking without a trace of ambition.

To prepare his ways. Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 laid together again (v. 17). In both prophets the one whose way is being prepared is the LORD himself, and Zechariah applies it to the child in Mary’s womb. The LORD whose way Isaiah cried out to prepare walked out of a Nazareth workshop, and the forgiveness John announced was paid for in full by the One he announced.

Knowledge of salvation. Not to save them himself, but to tell them what salvation is and where it is found: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29). Preaching does not create the salvation. It carries the news of it.

In the forgiveness of their sins. Here is what the Benedictus has meant all along: not first freedom from Rome, but forgiveness of sins. John will preach a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (3:3). Jesus will send his disciples to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (24:47). That is the standard by which every claim to be preaching the gospel can be measured.

The truth about ourselves. John’s method, when he came to preach, was not what most people expect of a herald of good news. He told people the truth about themselves. You cannot hand a man the knowledge of forgiveness while he is convinced there is nothing to forgive. So when you speak of the gospel, do not leave out the part about sin; without it, forgiveness sounds like an answer to a question nobody asked.

How do I know my sins are forgiven? Not by a feeling, though feelings of peace often come, but by God’s promise to everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Christ. If you have come to him confessing your sin and relying on his death for you, he has forgiven you, completely, because he is faithful to his word and just to the blood of his Son (1 John 1:9). Forgiveness is not a probation; it is a verdict. Your sins are not filed away to be brought out later; they are removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). When you sin again, as you will, come again. The fountain does not run dry.

parallels.desc: a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins

verseByVerse.quote: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tender mercy. The Greek is splanchna eleous: literally the bowels of mercy, the inner organs, the seat of the deepest emotions, compassion felt physically. Its verb is used of Jesus when he sees the widow of Nain walking behind her son’s body out of the town gate (7:13). The reason given here for the whole plan of redemption is not God’s justice or his glory, though both are true. It is that something in God moved. That does not mean his holiness has softened or his justice been set aside. It means the holy God, who will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7), was moved to find a way to be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The mercy is tender because it is costly.

The sunrise from on high. The word (anatolē) carries two meanings at once, both of which this priest knew. It is the ordinary word for the dawn. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses to translate Branch, a title for the Messiah, the promised shoot from David’s stump: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). Zechariah picks the one word that says dawn and David’s heir in the same breath. For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:2).

In darkness and the shadow of death. Isaiah 9:2: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone. Isaiah wrote this of Galilee of the nations (Isaiah 9:1), where Jesus would minister. And Isaiah 42:6–7 and 49:6 speak of the servant as a light for the nations: the light is for Gentiles too (2:32).

Those who sit. Not those who walk in darkness, or search in it. Those who sit: the posture of somebody who has stopped moving, because there is nowhere to go and no way of seeing the way there. Anyone who has sat with someone six weeks after the funeral, when the visitors have stopped coming, or lain awake at four in the morning with a diagnosis, knows that position exactly. The Bible’s picture of humanity apart from God is not a traveller who has taken a wrong turning. It is somebody who has sat down in the dark.

Nobody helps the sun come up. Nothing whatever is contributed by the people sitting in the valley. The light arrives from above, on its own schedule, whether or not anyone below is ready, and when it comes, the same people who could not find the path can suddenly see the whole country. That is what grace is. Not a lamp handed to a man so that he can go looking. A sunrise.

The way of peace. Peace (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is the fullness of well-being that comes from being right with God: peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. The angels will sing of it at Jesus’ birth (2:14).

What if I am a Christian and still sitting in darkness? It happens, and Scripture does not hide it: Isaiah speaks of one who fears the LORD and walks in darkness and has no light, and tells him to trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isaiah 50:10). Darkness in a believer’s feelings is not the same as being outside the light. The sun has risen whether or not clouds cover it today. Keep to the means of grace, tell a pastor or trusted friend, and seek medical help if the darkness is depression; that is not a lack of faith. And wait for him, as those who watch for the morning (Psalm 130:6). He has never failed to bring it.

In everyday life. Someone you know is sitting in the dark this week, grieving, depressed, far from God. You cannot make the sun rise for them, but you can sit with them, pray for them and tell them that the light is coming from above.

For worship. Centuries of night, and a world sitting in the shadow of death since a garden gate closed behind it. And then over the eastern rim, without one hand raised anywhere to help it: the Dayspring himself, the Branch of David, to set our feet in the way of peace. He rose then. He has not set since.

parallels.desc: the sun of righteousness shall rise
light on those in the land of deep darkness

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, thirty years. Luke has spent the rest of the chapter on little more than a year, and now he covers three decades in a sentence and moves on.
