Grew and became strong in spirit. Similar words are used of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:21, 26) and of Jesus (2:40, 52): growth in body and in spirit, by the Spirit with whom he was filled.

In the wilderness. The wilderness of Judea, between the hill country and the Dead Sea: limestone ridges and dry gorges, almost waterless. The wilderness was where Israel had been formed, where Elijah had fled, and where the prophets had said God would make a way (Isaiah 40:3). The son of a priest had a hereditary right to serve in the temple, in the rota his own father had drawn the lot in. He never took it up.

Was John connected with Qumran? Some have suggested that John was raised by the Essene community at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, who took in boys and also lived in the wilderness and quoted Isaiah 40:3; this is possible but unproved. Luke says nothing of it, and John’s message, a call to all Israel to repent and a baptism given once, was quite unlike the separatist community’s repeated washings. He was in the wilderness because God was preparing him there.

Until the day. About thirty years later (3:1–2). The greatest man born of women, by Christ’s own reckoning, spent thirty of his thirty-odd years doing, so far as the record goes, nothing whatever.

The waiting room. That is a hard verse for anybody whose life feels like a waiting room: the years that count for nothing on any visible ledger, the training never used, the gifts nobody has asked for. Luke’s summary says thirty such years were not lost. The plain speech that could not be bought, the ability to look a king in the face and tell him the truth about his marriage: that is what the desert does to a man.

Formed for one sentence. Everything the desert made of John, it made for the sake of someone else. Thirty years of formation produced a voice, and the voice had one message: one who is mightier than I is coming (3:16). The wilderness that shaped him is the same wilderness into which Jesus will be led by the Spirit for forty days (4:1–2), not to be prepared to point, but to stand where Israel fell and win. John’s hidden years made a herald; Jesus’ hidden years (2:52) made ready the Lamb. When John finally appeared to Israel, the first thing he did with all that the desert had given him was step aside for Christ.

What if my wilderness never ends in public ministry? Then it was still not wasted. Most of God’s servants never have a public appearance to Israel; their whole life is the hidden part, and God counts it. The point of John’s desert was not that it led to fame but that God was with him in it and forming him for whatever he had appointed. Your hidden years may be preparing you for a single conversation, a child raised in the faith, a quiet faithfulness that holds a church together, or simply for heaven. Nothing done for God in obscurity is lost (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 15:58).

In the flow. Luke has built this chapter in pairs: two announcements, two mothers, two songs. This verse parks John in the wilderness so that the stage is clear for the birth of Jesus. A sentence almost the same will close Jesus’ childhood (2:40).

parallels.desc: the word of God came to John in the wilderness

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Luke 2 is perhaps the most familiar story in the world, and so the one most easily heard without being noticed. Luke means its details to astonish: the emperor of Rome issues a decree that fulfils a prophecy he has never read; the Son of God is born where animals feed; the armies of heaven appear not to priests or rulers but to shepherds, near the bottom of Jewish society. The incarnation is not a dignified event.

The chapter moves through four scenes: the birth in Bethlehem (vv. 1–7), the angels and the shepherds (vv. 8–20), the presentation in the temple with Simeon and Anna (vv. 21–40), and the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple (vv. 41–52). They show three things about the child: he is born in David’s line, as Scripture promised; those filled with the Spirit recognise him as the one Israel has waited for, and as a light for the nations; and from his earliest years he knows himself as the Son of his Father, whose claim comes before every other. And already the shadow of the cross falls across the chapter, in Simeon’s word about a sword.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of Jesus begins with a decree from Caesar Augustus, the most powerful man in the world, hailed as saviour, lord and bringer of peace, and Luke never raises his voice to point out the contrast.

Augustus orders a tax registration; God uses it to bring a Galilean couple to Bethlehem, where Micah had said Israel’s ruler would be born (Micah 5:2). God works through the harsh machinery of politics, and he does not remove the cost. Then, in a crowded house with no room to spare, the Son of God is laid in a feeding trough.
verseByVerse.theology: Augustus commanded armies and moved millions with a decree. The child in the manger would command no army, spend his public life in a minor province and die as a criminal. Yet it is the child whose kingdom has no end. From the first chapter Luke asks his reader to see that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary and Joseph did not choose to travel to Bethlehem at the end of a pregnancy; the Roman state imposed it, and in the imposition God’s plan was carried out. The Christian living in circumstances he did not choose is living in the same pattern. And the manger has comforted every believer who has felt overlooked or without a place: the Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation, and no circumstance is too humble for God to be present in it.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 2 tells of the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the announcement to shepherds by an army of angels, the presentation of the infant in the temple where Simeon and Anna recognise him, and the one story we have of his boyhood, when at twelve he stayed behind in his Father’s house. The whole chapter holds two things together: the glory of who this child is, Saviour, Christ the Lord, God’s salvation, a light for the nations, and the lowliness of how he came, in a feeding trough, to a poor family, under the law, growing up unseen in Nazareth.

Caesar Augustus. Octavian, the great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar, who ended a century of Rome’s civil wars and became the first Roman emperor, ruling from 27 BC to AD 14. The Senate gave him the title Augustus, revered one, and he was styled divi filius, son of the deified one. He was hailed in inscriptions as saviour and lord, and a famous decree in Asia Minor called his birthday the beginning of the good news (euangelia) for the world. Every one of those words is about to be given to somebody else in this chapter, by an angel over a field of sheep: good news, a Saviour, a Lord, and peace (vv. 10–14). One of these men issued a decree that moved the world. The other could not yet hold up his own head.

That all the world should be registered. “All the world” (oikoumenē) means the Roman Empire. A census was taken for taxation and military purposes.

How providence works. Augustus wants a tax register. God wants a Galilean couple in Bethlehem, because Micah had said that the ruler of Israel would come from there. The most powerful man on earth signs an order, and without the least idea what he is doing, he serves a prophecy he has never read. God governs history by means of people who are convinced they are governing it themselves. He turned the census of the most powerful man on earth into a road for a pregnant girl, so that a seven-hundred-year-old promise would land in the right town on the right night.

When Quirinius was governor. A well-known historical puzzle, and the difficulty is real. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius is known to have been governor of Syria from AD 6, when he conducted a census in Judea after it came under direct Roman rule; Luke himself mentions the revolt of Judas the Galilean that it provoked (Acts 5:37). But Jesus was born before Herod died, usually dated 4 BC. On the face of it Luke is a decade out. Quirinius may have held an earlier office in the region during which an earlier census began. Or the Greek may be read, as the ESV footnote allows, as: this was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria, distinguishing it from the famous later census. That is the simplest answer.

Did Luke make a mistake? Weigh this before concluding that he blundered. Luke plainly knew about the AD 6 census, since he reports its consequences himself, so he is hardly the man to have muddled it with another. He was a careful historian (1:3), and where this writer can be checked he has generally proved accurate, getting a mass of shifting local titles right where a careless man would have stumbled. Such a man has earned the benefit of the doubt at the one point where our own records happen to be thin. The puzzle is not settled, but it is not a proof of error, and honesty serves better here than invented certainty.

For worship. Augustus wanted every name in his empire written on a list, and he never knew that the Name above every name was about to be written on it. The Lord of heaven and earth let himself be counted as one more subject of Rome, a line in a tax ledger. Caesar’s titles have crumbled into museum stones. The child entered on his list is Saviour and Lord for ever, and he writes the names of his own people in heaven, where no empire can strike them out (10:20).
verseByVerse.note: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14. The ESV notes that verse 2 can also be read “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria” — the dating of this census is debated.

parallels.desc: the revolt “in the days of the census”

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each to his own town. The town of his family’s origin, or where he held property; an Egyptian census edict from AD 104 similarly required people to return to their home districts.

The road was not shortened. From Nazareth to Bethlehem is probably four or five days on foot for people who are not pregnant. Mary is in the last stage of a first pregnancy. Every mile of it was ordered by a man in Rome who wanted his revenue figures. The Christmas story is often told as though God arranged a gentle providence for the holy family. He arranged a tax census, a long walk, and an overcrowded town, and he did not remove one inch of the road to spare the mother of his Son. Nor did he spare his Son the greater road that lay ahead.

The city of David. Bethlehem, about five miles (8 km) south of Jerusalem, was David’s home town (1 Samuel 16:1; 17:12). The name means house of bread: the Bread of Life is born there (John 6:35). Micah had prophesied: But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Micah 5:2).

Of the house and lineage of David. Jesus’ legal descent from David came through Joseph (1:27). A thousand years earlier a shepherd boy had been anointed in that town (1 Samuel 16:1–13); six centuries earlier the line had been carried to Babylon; and now David’s family walks back into its ancestral town to be counted as taxpayers of a foreign empire. The dynasty had come to this.

The shoot from the stump comes home. Yet God had sworn to David that a son of his would sit on a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; 1:32–33). The house of David looked like a stump. Isaiah had said a shoot would come up from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1), and here it is, carried home inside his mother to be born where David was anointed. Joseph brings him the legal right; God brings him the throne.

His betrothed. Still betrothed: Matthew tells us Joseph had taken her as his wife but had no union with her until the child was born (Matthew 1:24–25). Luke’s wording is a witness’s exactness: this is how their situation looked to everyone who saw them on that road, in a culture where everybody counted the months. Whatever else her yes to the angel cost (1:38), it went on costing all the way to Bethlehem, and the cost was not glorious: tiredness, and dust, and about ninety miles (145 km) of road.

What about my life being pushed around by other people’s decisions? This is worth remembering by anybody whose life is currently being moved about by decisions taken in rooms they will never enter: a restructure, a policy, a landlord, a letter from an office. Being inside God’s will has never meant being outside other people’s decisions. Joseph and Mary were in the exact centre of the plan of God and were also, at the same moment, two more names on a Roman list. You may appeal, object or plan around the decision where that is right. But you need not believe that the people in the room are the ones in control. Your Father is, and he can turn their decree into your road.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth to Bethlehem is a journey of roughly 80–90 miles.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She gave birth to her firstborn son. While they were there: we do not know how long they had been in Bethlehem, and the tradition that she gave birth on the night they arrived is not in the text. The most important birth in history is recorded in a handful of words, with no adjectives. “Firstborn” carries the meaning of legal rights and of being consecrated to God (v. 23; Exodus 13:2). And Christ is the firstborn of all creation and the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:15, 18). There firstborn does not mean the first thing God made but first in rank, for all things were created through him and for him (Colossians 1:16).

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Luke could have written her son. That he writes her firstborn son is, on the plainest reading, the ordinary way of speaking of a woman’s first child, and it naturally implies others came after, though it does not require it. Read it alongside Matthew’s note that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth (Matthew 1:25), and alongside the four brothers named later in the Gospels, and their sisters (Matthew 13:55–56; Mark 6:3). Rome and the Orthodox East, and some of the Reformers too, read it differently, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life and that the brothers were cousins or Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. The word alone does not settle the argument: firstborn was also a legal term for the son who opened the womb and carried the firstborn’s rights, which is exactly the status that sends this family to the temple fifteen verses later. This commentary’s view: the natural reading is the right one, and nothing in Scripture requires straining past it: Mary and Joseph went on to have a family in the ordinary way. Nor is anything precious lost by taking it plainly. Mary’s honour never rested on what happened after Bethlehem. It rests on the virgin conception, on the child she bore, and on the faith with which she received him.

And wrapped him in swaddling cloths. Strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn, to keep the limbs straight and warm. Not a sign of poverty: it is what every mother in that world did, and Luke says Mary did it herself; he mentions no midwife. He was not neglected (Ezekiel 16:4). This is a real infant, with real limbs that need binding.

And laid him in a manger. A feeding trough for animals, perhaps of stone or wood. Luke says it three times in ten verses, which is his way of underlining. The one who would say I am the bread of life was laid, on the first night, in the box the animals ate out of. The tradition of a stable or a cave comes from the manger; many houses had an area at the lower end where animals were kept at night.

No place in the inn. “Inn” (katalyma) is not the word for a commercial inn; that is pandocheion, which Luke uses in the parable of the good Samaritan (10:34). Katalyma means a lodging place or guest room, the same word as the upper room of the Last Supper (22:11). The likeliest picture is not a hard-faced innkeeper but a crowded family house in Bethlehem, its one guest room already taken, perhaps by other relatives in town for the census, and a couple put in the lower part of the house where the animals were brought in at night. Nobody turned them away; there simply was no room. It was the first sign of the welcome the world would give him all his life, which John sums up in a sentence: his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Does it matter whether it was an inn or a guest room? Not to the gospel, but it helps us read honestly. The popular picture of a cruel innkeeper is not in the text, and preaching against him misses the point. Luke’s emphasis is not on someone’s unkindness but on God’s chosen lowliness: the Son of God did not merely suffer rejection at the door of an inn; he entered the world at the bottom of an ordinary crowded house, among the animals. It also means the Christmas story is closer to home than we thought. He came into the kind of overcrowded, makeshift family arrangement many people know.

For worship. The Word by whom all things were made is lying in straw in a back room in an overcrowded village, and nobody in the world is aware of it but two tired parents and, soon, a few shepherds. He who upholds the universe by the word of his power is being held up by his mother, because he cannot hold his own head. There is no distance in the universe like the distance he came, and he came all of it.
verseByVerse.note: Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. A manger is a feeding trough. The word for “inn” can mean a guest room — the same word used for the upper room in 22:11.

parallels.desc: though he was rich, he became poor

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth is announced not to the emperor, the high priest or the scholars, but to shepherds at work in a field at night, men whose testimony counted for little. To them the glory of the Lord appears, unseen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple.

The angel names the child Saviour, Christ and Lord, and gives the strangest of signs: a baby in a feeding trough. The shepherds go with haste, find everything as they were told, tell everyone, and go back to their sheep praising God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is the first instance of the great reversal that runs through Luke: the humble are lifted up, and those the world dismisses are the ones God honours.

Luke is also careful about how the news is received. The neighbours wondered, a word he never confuses with faith. Mary, in the same room, treasured and pondered what she heard (v. 19), and the contrast is the point.
verseByVerse.examples: The shepherds go at once, and then become the first to announce the Saviour’s birth, with nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen. That is still the pattern of Christian witness: not credentials or eloquence, but people who have met Christ and tell what God has said about him.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shepherds out in the field. The choice of company is deliberate. Shepherds were humble working men, not the gentle figures of the Christmas card, and near the bottom of Jewish society; the work made ritual purity practically impossible. Some later rabbinic writings looked down on them as unreliable, even listing herdsmen with tax collectors as men whose testimony was not accepted in court.

The announcement goes to a night shift. Not the emperor whose decree opened the chapter, nor the high priest a few miles away in Jerusalem. The news comes first to men with no standing, no purity and no legal credibility, because the news is precisely that God’s grace is not distributed on the basis of any of those things. And David, the shepherd king, was from Bethlehem; Jesus is the good shepherd (John 10:11).

Keeping watch by night. Taking turns to guard against thieves and wild animals: not a spiritual retreat, but work, at an hour when everybody with a choice is in bed.

What does this do to the date of Christmas? Flocks were kept in the open from spring to autumn, and sometimes all year in the milder Judean climate, so Luke’s detail does not fix the season. The date of 25 December was chosen by the church centuries later; we do not know the time of year, and no doctrine hangs on it. Christians may gladly celebrate the birth of Christ on that day, as long as they do not mistake a tradition for a command. What Luke does tell us is the hour, night, and he means it, because the whole chapter is about a light arriving in the dark.

The glory of the Lord. The shining brightness of God’s presence, which filled the tabernacle so Moses could not enter and settled on the temple so the priests could not stand (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). Scripture records no return of that glory to Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple and go out to the mountain east of the city before the exile (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Six centuries later it comes back in a field, to men who could not have gone into the temple courts without a wash. God did not wait for his people to climb up to him; he brought the weight of his presence down to the bottom of the social ladder, in the dark. That is the gospel before a word of it is spoken: the holy God has come to the unclean, and come to save.

Why the glory came back tonight. The glory returns on this night and no other because the Lord of the glory has just been born a few fields away. The light around the shepherds is the reflection; its source is lying in a feeding trough. John would write that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14), and Paul that God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). What Israel once met in a cloud over a tent it would now meet in a face. The glory had not merely come back to visit. It had come to live in a man.

In everyday life. If you work nights, care for animals, clean offices or drive the early bus, you are in exactly the company God chose for the first announcement of his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear not. Again, the first word is comfort; before any content, the terror is addressed. God knows exactly what his presence does to people, and he never leaves them standing in it.

I bring you good news. One verb in Greek, euangelizomai, the verb from which comes gospel. This is the gospel. The noun was imperial vocabulary for the dispatch announcing a victory or an heir, and heaven puts it in the mouth of an angel over a sheep field.

Great joy for all the people. “The people” (laos) usually means Israel in Luke, but the joy will spread beyond (v. 32), and Luke will spend twenty-two more chapters showing what all means: a Samaritan, a centurion, a sinful woman, a tax collector, a thief on a cross.

This day. “Today” (sēmeron) is a key word in Luke: today this Scripture has been fulfilled (4:21); today salvation has come to this house (19:9); today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). The gospel is never a rumour about the distant past or a hope for the vague future. It is today.

A Saviour. The title the empire gave to Augustus. This is the true Saviour, who saves from sin (Matthew 1:21; Acts 5:31). It is the only place in Matthew, Mark and Luke where Jesus is given the title Saviour (John has it once, 4:42).

Saved from what? A modern reader may say he does not need a Saviour, only a little help and a better year. The angel’s word assumes what the whole Bible says plainly: our deepest trouble is not our circumstances but our guilt before a holy God, and no improvement in circumstances touches it (Romans 3:23). Augustus could end a war and build a road. He could not forgive one sin or open one grave. That is why heaven announces a Saviour and not an adviser. The person who feels no need of one is not the exception to this verse; he is the reason for it.

Who is Christ the Lord. Three titles in one breath, and two of them were being claimed for Caesar Augustus that year. “Christ”: the Anointed One, the promised king from David’s line. “Lord” (Kyrios): the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name. Caesar took that title too; only one of the two was entitled to it. This exact phrase, Christ the Lord, appears only here in the New Testament. A newborn baby is the Saviour, the Messiah, and the Lord God. The empire had its saviour and its lord, and he died in his bed at Nola like any other man. Ours was laid in a feeding trough, nailed to a cross, raised from the tomb, and he reigns.

Joy for a hard December. Good news of great joy is a hard sentence to be handed in a hard season. For some, Christmas is mainly an empty chair. So notice that the angel does not command anyone to feel joyful. He reports an event: unto you is born this day. A joy that depends on the state of your heart will go down with your heart. A joy that rests on a birth that has already occurred, in a place you could walk to, cannot be taken away by grief; it can only be temporarily hidden by it.

So what do I do if I cannot feel the joy this year? Do not fake it, and do not conclude that you have lost your faith. Let the joy rest where the angel put it: on the fact that a Saviour has been born for you. Go to church anyway, and let others sing the words you cannot. Tell a friend or pastor how hard it is. Weep if you need to; Jesus wept at a grave. Read the angel’s words slowly, and say them back to God: this is true, even tonight. The feeling may come later, or not this year. The fact does not depend on it, and he will carry you until it returns.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah; “Lord” was the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

parallels.desc: he will save his people from their sins
to us a child is born
the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sign for you. Again and again in Scripture, when God gives a sign, the sign is remarkable: a burning bush, a fleece, a shadow going backwards on a sundial. Here the sign is a baby in a feeding trough.

Swaddling cloths and a manger. The cloths were normal. Every baby in Bethlehem was wrapped that way; they say he is completely human, and nothing about him looked other than ordinary. There was no halo. The manger was not normal, and in a village the size of Bethlehem it was enough: they were given no street and no name, and there would almost certainly be only one.

The sign is the opposite of what you would expect. That is the sign: his lowliness. Kings are found in palaces. This King is found in the place the animals eat from. It also exposes us. Part of every human heart still measures worth by impressiveness, and would have walked past a feeding trough on the way to the palace. God put his Son where the impressive would not look, so that he would be found by those who had stopped trusting in their own standing. And it meant the shepherds could come. They would not have been allowed into a palace; they could go into a place with animals.

A sign, not a scene. There is a way of asking for a sign which is really asking for a scene: something loud enough to end the possibility of doubt. God gave one here, and it could be walked past by anybody not told what to look for. The pattern has not changed. What God offers his people is not usually a blaze in the sky but a set of appointed ordinary things: bread, wine, water, a book, a gathering of unimpressive people. The world looks at that and sees a feeding trough. Faith looks at the same feeding trough and sees exactly what it was told it would find.

Should I ask God for a sign? Not as a condition of believing what he has already said. The shepherds were given a sign by God; they did not demand one. Jesus refused to perform signs for those who wanted proof on their own terms (11:29). We have something better than they had: the full record of his life, death and resurrection in Scripture. In making decisions, ask God for wisdom (James 1:5), study his word, seek counsel and pray; do not lay out fleeces as a test. And look for him where he has promised to be found: in his word, his people and his ordinances.

For worship. The God who could have lit the whole sky over Bethlehem chose to be recognised by a feeding trough, so that shepherds could find his Son and the proud would walk past. At the end of this Gospel Luke uses almost the same words again: the body of Jesus is wrapped in a linen shroud and laid in a tomb where no one had yet been laid (23:53). Wrapped and laid at his coming, wrapped and laid at his dying, and both times the lowliness was the sign. Blessed are the eyes that see the glory of God lying there.

parallels.desc: the LORD himself will give you a sign

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A multitude of the heavenly host. “Host” (stratia) means an army: the massed host of heaven (1 Kings 22:19), drawn up over a field outside a village. The armies of heaven have come not to fight but to announce peace. Luke does not say they sang; he says they were praising God and saying.

Glory to God in the highest. In Latin, Gloria in excelsis Deo, sung in Christian worship for centuries. Heaven’s first response is not relief or wonder at the mechanism. It is glory given to God: this birth is not chiefly about us. It is about him.

And on earth peace. Peace with God, reconciliation, the end of hostility between the holy God and rebellious humanity (Ephesians 2:14–17), and the shalom that flows from it. Not the political peace of the Pax Romana, which lasted as long as the legions did. Not the absence of conflict either: the child in the trough will say plainly that he did not come to bring that sort (12:51). It is the ending of a war between heaven and earth, the peace Christ makes by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). Glory in the highest, and peace at the bottom: the angels sing at both ends, because the God who is glorified in the highest heaven has just made peace at the lowest point of the world.

Among those with whom he is pleased. Literally among men of his good pleasure (en anthrōpois eudokias). “His good pleasure” is God’s: those on whom God’s favour rests, whom he has chosen in his grace; Ephesians 1:5 and 9 use the same word for God’s choosing will. The peace is not for those who are good enough to please God, but for those whom God has chosen to favour. Scripture’s word for this is election: before the world began, God freely chose a people for himself and set his love on them, for reasons found in his mercy and not in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). It does not make the angels’ news less glad. It means the peace rests on God’s will, which does not change, rather than on ours, which does.

Textual note. The King James Version, following later manuscripts, reads: on earth peace, good will toward men. The difference is one letter in Greek (eudokia or eudokias). One family of manuscripts has eudokia, good will, standing on its own as a third item; the other has eudokias, of good pleasure, attached to the men. The earliest and best manuscripts have eudokias, giving the ESV’s reading. The old reading is familiar from carols, but the better text points to God’s good pleasure.

A warmer reading, not a colder one. The old reading makes the announcement a general benevolence broadcast over the earth; the better text makes it a specific grant to particular people. That is not colder but warmer. A goodwill announced to everybody in general is a goodwill guaranteed to nobody in particular. What the angels announce is peace that has an owner’s name on it, resting not on how the recipients turn out but on the good pleasure of God, which is the one foundation that does not move.

How do I know if God’s good pleasure rests on me? Not by peering into the hidden counsels of God, but by looking at the Son he has given. The gospel is offered freely to everyone: whoever comes to him, he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have come to Christ, trusting him and turning from your sin, that is the evidence that God’s favour rests on you, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is not a locked door to worry about; it is the reason the door was opened to you. If you are not sure you have come, come now. The peace is for all who believe.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV’s “among those with whom he is pleased” follows the better manuscripts; older translations read “good will toward men.”

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us go over to Bethlehem. The sky closes, and the shepherds say the only sensible thing. “Thing” is literally word (rhēma), meaning both the event and the message. They act on the word at once. They do not doubt like Zechariah, but obey like Mary.

Which the Lord has made known to us. There is no debate about whether the vision was genuine, no waiting for daylight. And they get the theology exactly right in passing. They do not say the angel told them; they say the Lord did. A messenger is a mouth and not a source.

And they went with haste. Leaving their flocks. The phrase has been used once already in this Gospel, of Mary going up to the hill country (1:39). Luke reserves it for people whose response to a word from God is to start moving.

The interval where faith dies. The gap between hearing something from God and acting on it is where a great deal of faith quietly dies. Faith rarely dies there by a decision to disobey. It dies of delay: a thing is weighed, put off until the season is better, and then no longer feels urgent. What is remarkable about these men is not their piety. It is that the interval was about ten seconds long.

Just as they were told. They walked into a crowded house in the middle of the night with a story that must have sounded insane, and there in the animals’ quarters was precisely what they had been told they would find. That is the reward of obedience in this story: not a further revelation, but confirmation of the one they already had.

They found the message lying in a manger. The angels had given them a message: a Saviour, Christ the Lord. When they arrived, the message was a baby. That is the peculiar glory of the gospel. Its content is not finally an idea to be weighed but a person to be found; all the promises of God, as Paul says, find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). They went home having seen him. And the Lord who made known to them where the Christ could be found still makes him known, through the word read and preached, so that people who were never in Bethlehem may come to him today. He has never yet sent anyone to look for Christ and let them come back empty.

But is it not wise to wait and think before acting? Yes, about many decisions; Scripture commends counsel and care (Proverbs 15:22). But where God has spoken plainly, waiting is usually a polite form of not obeying. You do not need to pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, to come to Christ, or to be baptised as a believer; he has already said. Think hard about how; do not linger over whether. And with the call of the gospel itself, delay is the most dangerous thing of all: now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made known the saying. Nobody commissioned these men to tell anyone. But having looked, they told everyone. The shepherds became the first evangelists. Men whose word counted for little were God’s first witnesses to the birth of Christ, as women would be to the resurrection.

Concerning this child. Look at what they told. Not their experience: not the light, or the fear, or how the sky had looked, but what had been said about him: that he was the Saviour, the Christ, the Lord. Every true witness since has had the same subject. The child was the news, and he still is. The message they carried has outlived the empire that despised them: a Saviour is born, and he is Christ the Lord.

And all who heard it wondered. “Wondered” (ethaumasan): were amazed. Wondering is not believing. Crowds marvel at Jesus all through this Gospel, and marvelling saves nobody.

Amazed, and nothing more. It is entirely possible to be moved by this story every December for fifty years and to remain exactly where those neighbours were: amazed, and nothing more. Wonder is a doorway, and it is a good one; Luke never sneers at it. But a doorway is for walking through. Mary, Luke goes on to say, did something different with the same news: she treasured it and pondered it, and the difference is the whole point.

What should I say when I tell someone about Jesus? Start with him, not with yourself. Your story matters as a witness to what he has done, but the heart of it is the message: who Jesus is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he calls everyone to turn and trust him. Say it simply, as the shepherds did. You do not need answers to every objection; you can say, I do not know, but I know this. And do not be discouraged if people only wonder. Your task is to tell; it is the Spirit’s work to turn wonder into faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary treasured up all these things. The but is doing real work: everybody else in the room wondered; Mary went deeper. “Treasured up” (synetērei): kept carefully, held on to, the way a person stores something valuable rather than leaving it out. This is probably one of Luke’s hints at his source: who else could have told him these things, but Mary herself (1:2–3)?

Pondering them in her heart. “Pondering” (symballousa): literally throwing together, putting together, comparing, thinking through, seeking the meaning. This is not vague reverie. She has an angel’s announcement, a relative’s prophecy, a birth among animals, and shepherds at midnight with a story about an army in the sky. She lays the pieces alongside each other and keeps turning them. She did not understand everything (v. 50), but she reflected on it.

A believer’s inner method. Like the hill-country neighbours (1:66), Mary neither forces a meaning onto what she cannot explain nor lets it go. She keeps a record of what God has done and said, and carries an unresolved thing without abandoning it or pretending it is resolved.

The child at the centre of the pieces. Every piece Mary was turning over concerned one person. The angel had called him the Son of the Most High, whose kingdom would have no end (1:32–33). The shepherds had heard him called Saviour and Lord. And she had just wrapped him in cloths and laid him where the animals ate. Mary was among the first on earth to hold together, in one heart, the pieces of what the church would spend centuries learning to confess: that the baby she nursed was her Lord, truly man and truly God, one person. She could not yet see how. She did not let go of either half.

What does Christian meditation look like? It is not emptying the mind, as in Eastern practices, but filling it with God’s word and turning it over. Take a short passage, read it slowly several times, and ask: what does this say about God? About Christ? About me? What does it command, promise or warn? Connect it to other things you know of Scripture, as Mary connected the angel’s words with the shepherds’ story. Then turn it into prayer and praise. Ten unhurried minutes on a few verses will often do more than an hour of skimming. Psalm 1 calls the man blessed who meditates on God’s law day and night.

For worship. Twelve years later Luke says the same of her again (2:51). The God who gave her the pieces did not leave her holding them for ever. After the cross and the empty tomb Luke shows her among the disciples in the upper room, praying with those who now knew who her son was (Acts 1:14). The child she had pondered in the straw was the risen Lord she worshipped. He is patient with his ponderers, and he gives them, in his time, the whole picture, which is himself.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the shepherds returned. To their flocks, to their ordinary work. Their circumstances were the same; they were not. Luke does not record that any of them left their trade. The shepherds went home in the dark, singing, to a job nobody respected, which is very nearly a definition of the Christian life.

Glorifying and praising God. They join the angels’ song (v. 14). The night did not deliver them from the ordinary; it went with them into it. Everybody who has come down from a mountaintop knows the temptation to conclude that the real thing was up there. The shepherds’ testimony is the opposite. The glory came to them at work, in the middle of a shift, and sent them back to the same sheep praising.

The angels left, and the child stayed. Why could they go back praising? Because what they had seen was not a vision that faded with the light. The angels went back into heaven (v. 15); the child stayed. The glory had not visited a hillside and withdrawn, as it once withdrew from the temple in Ezekiel’s day. It had taken flesh, and would die for the sins of men like them. Their ordinary work was now done in a world where God was with them in a man. That is still the Christian’s footing on a Monday: not the memory of a high moment, but a living Lord who is present in the ordinary because he once entered it.

As it had been told them. Heard (from the angel) and seen (the child): everything matched. The word came; they acted on it; they found it exactly as promised. A decree was signed in Rome, a prophecy was kept in Bethlehem, an announcement was made in a field, and every part of it fitted.

Should a new believer leave his job to serve God? Usually not. Paul told the Corinthians that each should remain in the condition in which he was called, and serve God there (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). God calls some to leave their nets and preach, and the church should test such a call. But most believers glorify God by going back to the sheep: doing their ordinary work honestly, well and joyfully, for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23). The question is not whether your job is spiritual enough, but whether you do it with praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In the presentation the old covenant meets the new. Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem to do what the law required: the mother’s purification and the presentation of the firstborn (Leviticus 12:1–8; Exodus 13:2, 12–15). They bring the offering of the poor, two birds instead of a lamb.

Simeon, righteous and devout, has been promised by the Spirit that he will not die before he sees the Lord’s Christ. He takes the child in his arms and sings that he has seen God’s salvation, a light for the Gentiles. Then the shadow falls: the child will cause the fall and rising of many, and a sword will pierce Mary’s soul. Anna, a widow of great age from the tribe of Asher, is the second witness, and she speaks of him to all who are waiting. The section closes with the return to Nazareth and one sentence for the whole of his childhood.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon’s light for the Gentiles fulfils Isaiah’s Servant Songs (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6) and is the seed of the Gentile mission in Acts.

Simeon also says that the child will reveal the thoughts of many hearts. Jesus does not leave people neutral: he is the stone laid in the road (Isaiah 8:14), and how people respond to him shows what was already in them.
verseByVerse.examples: Simeon shows a death well prepared for: not resignation, but the release of a watchman who has seen what he waited for. His peace rests only on the salvation he saw, and the believer who has taken hold of it may face death on the same terms. Anna shows long faithfulness. Her decades of prayer were not a waiting room for her ministry but the making of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was circumcised. On the eighth day, as the law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), like John (1:59). Eight days old, and the first blood he ever shed was shed in obedience to the law he had written. Circumcision marked a boy as belonging to the covenant people, under its promises and under its obligations.

In the flow. John’s naming set the whole hill country talking (1:59–66); Jesus’ naming passes in half a verse, because the greater child came more quietly. The verse also starts a thread Luke will pull all through the chapter: everything is done as the law required (vv. 22–24, 27, 39).

Under the law, all the way down. The Son of God enters his own creation and, before he is nine days old, is cut with a knife in submission to a requirement he himself laid down. He steps under it, all the way down: born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). There was no way to redeem people who were under something except by getting under it with them.

He was called Jesus. The LORD saves (1:31). It was a common enough name, and that is part of the point. The name over the cross would be an ordinary name from an unremarkable town.

The name given by the angel. Mary and Joseph obeyed exactly; it was settled before there was anything to name.

The knife and the name. On the same day the child is cut into the covenant, he is given the name that says how the covenant will finally be kept. The knife and the name arrive together, and they will arrive together again at the end: the blood and the saving, the wound and the rescue, in the same event.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law for us? Because we have not kept it, and God’s law still stands. Christ did two things for his people. He bore the penalty for our disobedience on the cross, and he lived the perfect obedience we owed, from the eighth day to the last. Both are counted to everyone who trusts him: our sins to him, his righteousness to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why a believer can stand before God not merely pardoned but accepted as righteous. Paul’s word for it is justification: God’s verdict that a sinner stands righteous in his sight, given not for anything the sinner has done but because Christ’s obedience and death are reckoned to his account (Romans 4:5). Your record before God is not your week; it is his life.

For worship. Jesus does nothing in this verse; it is done to him. He is carried, held, named and cut. The first thing the Saviour ever did about our salvation, he did by being handed over to somebody else’s hands, and the last thing he did about it, he did the same way. The Lord of the law became its subject, so that its subjects might become sons.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time came for their purification. Luke combines two separate requirements of the law into one visit. After giving birth to a son, a mother was ceremonially unclean for forty days, and then brought a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove for a sin offering (Leviticus 12:1–8). This was never a statement that childbirth was sinful; unclean did not mean dirty or guilty. It meant she could not, for that time, touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary (Leviticus 12:4).

Why their purification? A reader with Leviticus open will trip over the pronoun. The law prescribes purification for the mother alone. The child needs none; Joseph needs none. Luke is probably describing the family’s observance as a whole, the household going up together to discharge what the law laid on them, so that the pronoun covers the journey rather than the rite. It may include Joseph, or the family, or simply be loose phrasing. Some later copies smoothed it to her, which is why the King James Version reads her purification; but their is the harder and better-attested wording, and a copyist is far likelier to have tidied a difficulty than to have created one.

To present him to the Lord. Every firstborn son belonged to God, because God had spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover, when the firstborn of Egypt were not (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). The firstborn had to be redeemed, bought back, by a payment of five shekels to a priest (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke does not mention the payment, but speaks of presenting him, as Hannah presented Samuel (1 Samuel 1:22–28): the firstborn handed over to the Lord, who will himself pay a much larger price.

Nothing to be purified from. Of every person in the temple courts that day, this forty-day-old child is the one with nothing whatever to be purified from. He is brought in anyway, counted in with the rest, like any other son of Israel.

A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8): Mary and Joseph could not afford a lamb. The King of heaven and earth was raised by people who could not afford the standard offering. Anyone who has ever stood at a counter and taken the smaller thing because the larger one was out of reach has stood where Mary stood that morning, and the child she was carrying grew up in that house on purpose.

Was Mary a sinner? The law required a mother to bring a sin offering after childbirth (Leviticus 12:6–8), and Mary brought it, as every mother did. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was preserved from all sin. But Mary herself calls God my Saviour (1:47), and Scripture says all have sinned (Romans 3:23) with the single exception of her Son. She shared the common need of all people for a Saviour, and obeyed the law that provided for it. She too was a sinner needing atonement, and her atonement was in her arms.

Does Jesus understand money worries? Yes, from the inside. He grew up in a house that counted coins, worked with his hands for a living, later had nowhere to lay his head, and depended on the gifts of others (8:3; 9:58). He is not a distant Lord who cannot sympathise. Bring your bills, your fears about the rent and your shame about being poor to him in prayer; he knows the counter where you take the cheaper thing. And if you are not poor, remember that the Lord himself was raised by people who chose the two birds. Look out for those in your church who are choosing them now.

For worship. She could not afford a lamb, and she was carrying the Lamb of God (John 1:29). The God who asked a lamb of every mother in Israel provided the one Lamb for every sinner, and laid him first in the arms of a poor girl holding two birds. The birds were offered that day and forgotten. The Lamb grew up, walked back into the same courts, and offered himself once for all, so that no mother and no sinner need ever bring another.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. He is not said to be a priest; he is an ordinary godly man, and his words in verse 29 imply he was old. He was righteous, the word used of Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6), and devout (eulabēs), careful and reverent toward God.

Waiting for the consolation of Israel. “Consolation” (paraklēsin): comfort, encouragement. The phrase comes from the great turn in Isaiah: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isaiah 40:1), the announcement that the exile is over and God is coming back to his people. Simeon is waiting for God to keep a specific promise in a specific book, one of the faithful remnant (Romans 11:5) with Anna (v. 38) and Joseph of Arimathea (23:51).

The comfort was coming as a child. Isaiah’s comfort was never going to be a better political season. Its heart was that God himself would come: Behold your God (Isaiah 40:9). Luke will quote that same chapter when John the Baptist appears (3:4–6). So the consolation Simeon waited for was not an event but a person, the Lord’s own Christ, and when he came, he was small enough to hold. Every promise of comfort in the prophets had been travelling toward this child, and every comfort the church has known since has flowed from him.

And the Holy Spirit was upon him. Three times in three verses Luke mentions the Spirit in connection with Simeon (vv. 25, 26, 27): upon him, revealing to him, moving him into the temple. The silence is not merely broken but flooded.

The Lord’s Christ. A personal promise. “The Lord’s Christ”: the Messiah who belongs to God, God’s anointed one (Psalm 2:2). We are not told when that promise was given. Simeon may have carried it for decades, with no way of proving it to anybody, no date attached, and a body that was running out of time.

The promise not yet kept. That is a position a good many older believers know from the inside: the thing God once made you sure of, which has still not happened, and which you have long since stopped mentioning to people because of the way they look at you. Simeon’s promise was kept. It was kept at the last possible end of a long life, in a place he had walked through a thousand times, on a morning that began like every other. And the reason he did not miss him, when he finally came in through the gate in the arms of a poor couple carrying two pigeons, is that he had spent his whole life learning what to look for.

Should I expect personal promises from God like Simeon’s? Simeon lived at a unique moment, when the Spirit was announcing the Messiah’s arrival, and his revelation was part of that. Today God speaks to us through his completed word, and its promises are ours in Christ: they are more sure than any private impression (2 Peter 1:19). Be careful about treating a strong feeling as a promise from God; many have been badly hurt by doing so. But the shape of Simeon’s life is ours: we too are waiting, for Christ’s return, on the strength of God’s word, and that promise will be kept as surely as his was.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the Spirit. Simeon did not merely decide to go to the temple that morning; he was led at exactly the right moment, on a day when the courts were full of people.

The arithmetic of that morning. The temple complex covered something like thirty-five acres, and Mary and Joseph had come to do a small, ordinary thing that dozens of families did every week. So far as Luke tells us, Simeon had a promise, not a description. Out of all that crowd the old man walks straight to the right child. Most of the appointments God keeps look like that from the inside: no sense of a scene being staged, only a providence arranging a meeting for longer than anyone present has been alive.

He took him up in his arms. Here is the old covenant, in the person of a man near the end of his life, standing in the temple, and it reaches out and takes the new covenant into its arms. Everything the sacrifices had been pointing at is now a warm weight in an old man’s hands. The whole system is holding the thing it was built to announce, and the thing it was built to announce is going to make the system unnecessary.

And blessed God. Not a speech to the crowd, nor an announcement to the priests. The first response of a man who has just received what he waited a lifetime for is to turn away from the gift and speak to the Giver. When God gives you a good gift, speak about it to him first.

How can I know the Spirit is leading me? The Spirit leads above all through the Scriptures he inspired, and he never leads contrary to them. He also guides through godly counsel, through providence, and through desires he shapes in a heart soaked in his word, as Simeon’s was. Most of his leading is not felt as a dramatic impulse at the time; it is seen afterwards, when you notice that you were in the right place. So do not wait for a sensation before you act. Walk in obedience to what is written, pray for guidance, and trust that he is ordering your steps even when you cannot feel it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Nunc Dimittis. Simeon’s song is called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin (now you dismiss). It has been sung at evening services for something like fifteen hundred years.

Letting your servant depart. “Lord” here is not the usual kyrios but despotēs, Master, the word a slave used of his owner; and servant is doulos, the slave himself. “Depart” (apolyeis): release, discharge, as a watchman is relieved at the end of his shift. Simeon had been on watch for the Messiah. He is not saying he wants to die. He is saying his watch is over and he may go off duty. A man who has seen Christ is ready to die.

My eyes have seen your salvation. The promise has been kept. Simeon looks at a forty-day-old baby and does not say he has seen the one who will bring salvation. He says he has seen salvation itself, in his arms. Salvation is not a thing or a system. It is a person. All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God (Isaiah 52:10).

A light for the Gentiles. This is where the song opens out. Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, where the LORD says it is too small a thing for the Servant merely to restore Israel: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. In the temple of Israel, a devout old Jewish man announces that this Jewish baby is salvation for the Gentiles, before Jesus has spoken a word. This is the theme of Luke and Acts: the gospel goes from Jerusalem to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8; 13:47, where Paul quotes the same verse). Every Gentile who has ever come to Christ came in through a door that Simeon saw standing open.

And for glory to your people Israel. The Messiah is Israel’s greatest glory, the one in whom all her history and hope are fulfilled: from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (Romans 9:5).

A death well prepared for. Simeon is the picture of a death well prepared for, and notice what it does not depend on. Not on achievement: we are told nothing about what he accomplished. He can go because my eyes have seen your salvation. There is a whole doctrine of contentment in an old man who holds the Christ and says: that will do. His peace rests entirely on something outside himself which he has laid hold of. Nobody now will hold the infant Christ in the temple. But the salvation Simeon saw with his eyes is the same salvation offered to faith, and the man or woman who has taken hold of it has exactly what Simeon had, and may be discharged on exactly the same terms.

What happens to a believer at death? Depart in peace is exactly right. The believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory to pass through, because Christ has already made full purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3), and no sleep of the soul in between: the dying thief was promised, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). The body rests in the grave until Christ returns and raises it in glory (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). So a Christian may face death as Simeon did, not with bravado but with peace, because his watch is over and his Master is calling him home.

In everyday life. If you have seen Christ by faith, you can face death in peace. Pray Simeon’s prayer at the end of the day. Every night’s sleep is a small rehearsal of the last one; go to it in the same peace.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father. Luke calls Joseph Jesus’ father, as Mary does (v. 48). Luke has spent a chapter and a half establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father (3:23: as was supposed), yet Joseph is his father in every way that a life is lived: he named him, presented him, taught him a trade, and raised him.

Marvelled. Even after angels and shepherds they were amazed, perhaps especially by the words about the Gentiles. They had not exhausted this. There was more in the child than they had grasped, and they knew it.

Never exhausted. If the mother of Jesus, with Gabriel’s words still ringing, could be astonished by something a stranger said about her own son, then the ordinary experience of finding that Christ keeps exceeding your account of him is not a sign of immaturity. It is a sign of accuracy. Those who knew him best were still being astonished by him, and the saints in glory will be astonished for ever. There is no bottom to his riches and no edge to his glory.

A word for stepfathers and adoptive fathers. Any man raising a child who is not his by blood may take heart here. The Son of God was brought up by one, and Scripture calls that man his father without a footnote. The work you do in naming, providing, teaching and protecting is real fatherhood in God’s eyes. And it is a picture of the gospel itself: God adopts sons who were not his by nature, and is not ashamed to be called their Father.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Simeon blessed them. Simeon has blessed God; now he blesses the parents. He does not bless Jesus; the child is the source of blessing. Then he turns to Mary alone, perhaps because Joseph would not live to see what follows.

Appointed for the fall and rising. Now a darker note. The word is appointed: placed there on purpose. And note the order: fall first, then rising. Jesus will divide Israel. Some will fall because of him, stumbling over him; others will rise, be raised up, through faith in him. He is the stone that some stumble over and others build on (Isaiah 8:14–15; 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–8). The child is a stone laid in the middle of Israel’s road, and it is not possible to walk past him without either tripping over him or standing on him. No one can be neutral toward him.

And for a sign that is opposed. A sign spoken against. Simeon does not say the child will meet some opposition; he says that being contradicted is part of what the sign is. Anyone who has hoped that a sufficiently winsome presentation of Christ would stop people objecting to him has hoped for something Simeon ruled out in the temple courts before Jesus could speak.

And a sword will pierce through your own soul also. The word for sword is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for Goliath’s weapon. She will suffer deep grief. Her son will be rejected and misunderstood, even by his own family (Mark 3:21; John 7:5). And John tells us she stood by the cross and watched him die (John 19:25), and there was nothing whatever she could do.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. That purpose clause explains the rest. Jesus reveals what is in people’s hearts. How people respond to him exposes what they really are (5:22; 6:8; John 3:19–21). He does not merely divide people; he shows what was already there. The reaction to Jesus is a reading of the person reacting.

In the flow. Until now every voice in Luke 1 and 2 has spoken of joy. This verse is the first shadow. From here Luke’s Gospel shows both halves of Simeon’s word coming true: tax collectors and sinners rising, while his own town tries to throw him off a cliff (4:28–29) and the leaders plot his death. At the cross the two halves meet in two men crucified beside him, one mocking and one asking to be remembered (23:39–43).

When a child suffers. This is a word spoken to a mother about her son, and it should be handled as one. There are parents reading this who have watched a child suffer and could do nothing: an illness, an addiction, a court, a coffin. It does not answer to the usual comforts, because the helplessness is the whole of it. Two things stand in this verse for such a reader. The first is that Mary was told in advance, some thirty years in advance, and it did not make it easier; God does not seem to think forewarning is the same as sparing. The second is heavier and better. The sword went through her because the nails went through him, and he was there by appointment, and what looked from the foot of that cross like the end of everything was the hour the whole world had been waiting for since Eden. The grief was real. It was not the last word about the grief.

Why do people react so strongly to Jesus? Because he does not allow neutrality. He claims to be Lord and Saviour, and that claim either draws a person to him or offends him. People can be polite about religion in general, but Jesus puts his finger on the heart: our pride, our self-righteousness, our love of sin. So do not be surprised when friends are hostile, and do not water down the gospel to avoid offence. Pray for them, love them, and remember that some who stumble over him today may rise through him tomorrow. Paul himself first opposed the sign.

For worship. The child in Simeon’s arms was appointed for a cross, and the sword that pierced his mother’s soul was the shadow of the spear that, as John records, pierced his side. God did not spare his Son, nor the mother who loved him, because he was determined to spare us. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and all who rest their weight on him will never be put to shame.

parallels.desc: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man and a woman. The law required two witnesses for a matter to be established (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides them: an old man, and now an old woman. Luke often pairs a man and a woman.

A prophetess. Like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah in the Old Testament (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9). God gave prophecy to men and women at the dawn of the gospel, as Joel had promised (Acts 2:17).

Does Anna show that women should prophesy or preach today? Anna’s gift belongs to the time when God was making his new work known, before the Scriptures were complete; it is not a pattern for new revelation today, since the canon is closed and the foundational gifts have ceased. And her ministry was in the temple courts, speaking to those who came, not in leading the worship of Israel, which belonged to the priests.
