The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while honouring women’s gifts in countless ways. What Anna does show is that a godly woman’s prayer and witness are precious to God, and that she may and should speak of Christ to everyone who will listen. Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, hold that prophecy continues today, and some read Paul on women in the church differently. We hold our view because the apostles and prophets were the church’s once-laid foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and because Paul grounds his instruction in creation rather than in custom (1 Timothy 2:13); and we gladly own those who differ as brothers and sisters in Christ.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. Luke gives Anna a genealogy, which is unusual for a woman in an ancient text. Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, grace, the name of Samuel’s mother, whose prayer Mary echoed (1:46–55). Phanuel is the same name as Peniel, face of God, where Jacob wrestled with God (Genesis 32:30).

Of the tribe of Asher. One of the northern tribes of Israel, carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and popularly written off as lost. Here is a daughter of Asher at the presentation of the Messiah. The lost tribes were not lost to God. Whatever else the exile did, it did not lose anybody God intended to keep.

Seven years, then a widow. Probably married young, and widowed young; or, as the ESV footnote has it, a widow for eighty-four years, which with seven years of marriage from girlhood would make her over a hundred. Either way, a very long widowhood. Widows were among the most vulnerable people in Israel. Anna did not remarry, but devoted herself to God: she who is truly a widow has set her hope on God and continues in prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5).

Night and day. Decades of fasting and prayer in a temple that had grown corrupt, with no congregation, no title and, so far as anyone could tell, no answers. She kept praying anyway.

At that very hour. Not that day; that hour. She walks into the right court at the right moment after perhaps sixty years or more of showing up, and begins to give thanks, literally to confess, acknowledge, praise.

To all who were waiting. “Redemption” (1:68): the liberation God had promised: the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem (Isaiah 52:9). There was a circle of faithful people waiting, and Anna told them all: he has come. She was one of the first to preach Christ, and her long years there meant she knew who those people were.

The redemption of Jerusalem was a child. That is a staggering thing to say about a baby six weeks old. Luke lets the phrase echo to the end of his Gospel. On the road to Emmaus two disciples say, with the light gone out of them, we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel (24:21). Anna was right, and so were they; they had not yet understood how it would be done. Jerusalem would be redeemed not by a sword but by this child’s own blood, shed outside its walls, and sealed by his rising on the third day. The risen Lord himself would open the Scriptures to them and show that this was the way it had to be (24:26–27).

For the one whose life looks like the long years. There are believers who have prayed for a marriage, a child, a church, a country, for decades, and have watched nothing move. It is easy to conclude that the years were the waste. Anna’s years were not the waiting room for her ministry. They were the making of it: they produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family’s arms when the priests around her saw a queue. The single hour was the harvest. The decades were the field.

Should Christians fast today? Yes, as a voluntary help to prayer that earns nothing: Jesus assumed his disciples would fast after he was taken from them (5:35). (See Matthew 4:2 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. If you are older, alone or widowed, your prayers are not the leftovers of a life; they may be its centre. And if you are younger, find the Annas of your church and ask them to pray for you.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything according to the Law. Luke closes the infancy narrative with obedience to the law (vv. 22, 23, 24, 27, 39): the Saviour came from an obedient, devout Jewish home.

Do Luke and Matthew contradict each other? This is the sharpest question in the two birth narratives, and it is better faced than stepped over. Matthew has the magi arriving, the flight into Egypt, Herod’s killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and only after Herod’s death the settling in Nazareth. Luke moves from the temple courts to Nazareth in a single sentence, as though nothing came between. But look at what Luke’s sentence actually claims. He says they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord: he is closing the temple business, not publishing the next morning’s itinerary. And Matthew leaves exactly the room Luke needs. The magi come to a house (Matthew 2:11), not to a stable; and Herod kills the boys two years old or under, reckoning by what the magi had told him (Matthew 2:16), which places their visit months and possibly more than a year after the night of the manger. So a sequence holds both accounts without strain: the birth, circumcision on the eighth day, presentation on the fortieth, a settled stay in Bethlehem, the magi, Egypt, Herod’s death, and the return north. And it is Matthew who supplies the reason for the very move Luke reports here without explaining it: they went to Nazareth rather than back to Bethlehem because Archelaus was now reigning in Judea and Joseph was afraid to go there (Matthew 2:22). Not every step of the timing can now be fixed, but nothing in either account rules out the other.

Two witnesses, not competitors. Matthew writes from Joseph’s side, with Judea’s danger in view; Luke writes from Mary’s side, with the temple’s faithfulness in view. Luke is not concealing Egypt. He told us at the outset that he had sifted his material and arranged it (1:3), and no witness who selects is thereby lying about what he leaves out.

The child grew. Jesus grew as a normal child. His humanity was real: he learned to walk, to talk, to read, and in his human mind he was not born knowing everything, but was filled with wisdom as he grew (v. 52). Luke uses very nearly the same words of John at 1:80.

And the favour of God was upon him. “Favor” (charis): grace. God’s delight rested on him, not as a reward earned, but as the settled delight of a Father in his Son. The Son of God spent the greater part of his earthly life doing nothing that anybody thought worth writing down, and the Father’s favour rested on every day of it. He sanctified ordinary life by living it.

Did Jesus do miracles as a child? No. The Gospels say nothing of it, and John tells us that the water made wine at Cana was the first of his signs (John 2:11). The stories of a wonder-working boy come from later legends, not from Scripture. That silence is itself a teaching: the eternal Son lived for thirty years as an ordinary village boy and working man, without display, pleasing his Father in hidden obedience. His ordinary years were not a delay before the real work; they were part of the perfect life he lived for us.

In everyday life. If your days are made of school runs, spreadsheets and meals, you are walking a road the Son of God walked for longer than any other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the only story of Jesus’ childhood in the four Gospels, and in it he does no miracle at all. At twelve, at the Passover, he stays behind in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions. After three days of searching, his first recorded words answer his mother: he must be in his Father’s house. Then he goes home to Nazareth and is submissive to his parents for years to come.
verseByVerse.theology: The word must (dei) runs through Luke and Acts for the necessity of God’s plan: the Son of Man must suffer and must rise (9:22; 24:7). Here Jesus uses it for the first time. Yet his going home in obedience (v. 51) answers anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be above ordinary duty. And he truly grows in wisdom and stature (v. 52): the incarnation was never a costume, but a real human life lived from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples: For the second time in the chapter Mary holds on to what she does not understand (vv. 19, 51). And the hidden years in Nazareth show how God usually forms his people: slowly, in ordinary work and family life, long before any public work begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only story of Jesus’ boyhood. The four Gospels tell us nothing of Jesus between infancy and about thirty, except this one episode. Later legends are full of tales of the boy Jesus making clay birds fly. The canonical Gospels record one incident, and in it the boy does nothing miraculous at all. He asks questions in a temple and goes home and does as he is told.

In the flow. Until now others have spoken about Jesus. Here, for the first time, he speaks for himself, and his first words are about his Father (v. 49). The next time we meet him he is about thirty, at the Jordan, and the Father’s voice from heaven calls him my beloved Son (3:22). Here the Son says my Father; there the Father says my Son.

Every year at the Passover. The law required every Jewish man to go to the sanctuary for three feasts each year: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Women were not required to go, but Mary did. A devout family, and a poor one: the journey costs a working man the better part of two weeks every spring.

The Lamb at the Passover. And it is Passover, which Luke has not chosen at random. This is the feast of the lamb whose blood on the doorposts meant the destroyer passed over the house. The Lamb of God is twelve years old and has come up to keep it. He will come up to keep it again, and the last time he does, he will take the bread in his hands at that meal and say something no one had ever said about it before. He lived inside the story of redemption before he finished it.

Twelve years old. In Jewish practice, as later written down in the Mishnah, a boy of thirteen became a son of the commandment, responsible to keep the law himself; the formal bar mitzvah ceremony came later still, and how fixed the age was in Jesus’ day we cannot be sure. So this is the threshold of his responsible life, the moment Luke chooses to show him, once, before drawing the curtain again for eighteen more years.

They went up according to custom. Families travelled together in large caravans for safety and company.

How can a family make worship a habit today? Begin with the Lord’s Day: be in church with your children every week, not when it suits, so that gathering with God’s people is simply what your family does. Add something simple at home: a short Bible reading and prayer at a meal, a psalm or hymn, praying for one another by name. Let children see you read Scripture and pray on your own. Talk about the sermon on the way home. Jesus grew up in a household where the rhythm of worship was fixed and costly, and he learned it there. Children notice what their parents treat as non-negotiable.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the feast was ended. Passover and Unleavened Bread lasted eight days. Some pilgrims may have left after the first two days; Jesus’ parents stayed for the whole feast.

The boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Deliberately, as his answer shows (v. 49). Not disobedience: his parents had not told him to stay with them, and assumed he was with the group. A twelve-year-old in that culture had considerable independence.

Supposing him to be in the group. In a caravan of extended family a twelve-year-old could plausibly have been with any party, and each parent may have thought he was with the other. It was not neglect.

They went a day’s journey. About 20 miles (30 km). Then, at the evening camp, the horrible widening circle, the same question asked of one face after another; and a day’s walk back to a city full of Passover crowds.

When God seems lost. This passage has the shape of an ordinary Christian trouble. There are seasons when a person who has known God for years cannot find him. Prayer goes flat, and nothing is there. Look at what Mary and Joseph did. They did not press on to Nazareth hoping he would turn up. They went back to the last place they had him, and they kept looking until they found him. And see where he turned out to be: not lost at all, not hiding, not withdrawn in displeasure. He was in his Father’s house, exactly where he had always been, and it was they who had walked a day’s journey in the wrong direction. The searching is a going back, not a going further on: back to the word, back to the last thing he actually said. He is never as far as our fear supposes. He is where he said he would be, and he waits there to be found.

Can a Christian lose Christ? Not in the sense of losing salvation. Those whom the Father has given him, no one will snatch out of his hand (John 10:28–29), and the Westminster Confession teaches that true believers can neither totally nor finally fall from grace (Westminster 17.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). But a believer can lose the sense of his presence, through sin, neglect or a trial God sends, and it can last a long time (Westminster 18.4; 1689 18.4). The remedy is the one in this passage: do not assume, go back. Return to his word, confess what you know is wrong, come to the Lord’s Table, keep company with his people, and keep seeking. He has not moved.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days. Probably one day out, one day back, and a day searching. The echo is fair: the next time Mary’s son is lost to her, it will be in the same city, at the same feast, and after the third day he will be found again, alive, and still about his Father’s business, and the grief of those days will be immeasurably worse.

Sitting among the teachers. Probably in the colonnades of the temple courts, where the teachers of the law sat with their pupils, especially during and after the feasts. The picture is not a boy lecturing the professors. He is sitting among them, the posture of a student, listening and asking questions, which was how Jewish teaching worked. And yet his questions showed remarkable insight.

Amazed at his understanding. “Understanding” (synesei): insight, intelligence. He is holding his own with Israel’s teachers, in the temple, at twelve. Some twenty years later, the teachers in this same temple would be astonished, and then furious, at his answers (20:26, 40).

Remarkable, and learning. Two things here must be held together. His understanding is genuinely remarkable, something the teachers cannot account for. And he is learning: the eternal Son is a boy with a real human mind that has to be taught, by ordinary teachers, out of the Scriptures. He took no shortcut that is closed to us: he came to know the Scriptures by sitting where they are taught, listening and asking, and he did it perfectly.

Is it all right to ask questions in church? Yes, and Jesus did. Ask your pastor about the sermon, join a Bible study where questions are welcome, ask older believers how they understand a hard passage. Good questions come from humility, a desire to understand and obey, not from a wish to catch someone out or to show off. And when you are the one being asked, do not be afraid of saying, I do not know; let us look it up together. A church where nobody asks questions is usually a church where nobody is listening.

For worship. The Wisdom of God sat among the teachers as a learner. He who gave the law to Moses listened to men explain it, and asked them questions about his own word. There is no humility like his. And in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), opened to everyone who comes to learn from him.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son, why have you treated us so? The natural reproach of a frightened, relieved mother. That is not a serene woman. That is a mother at the end of three days, and Luke does not clean it up. She is not asking for information; she is asking the question every frightened parent asks the moment the fear turns to relief, which is how could you do this to us.

Honest before God. The mother of the Lord speaks sharply to the Son of God, and the Bible reports it without correcting her tone. There is a whole permission in that for people who have been taught that honesty with God must first be made polite.

In great distress. “Distress” (odynōmenoi): anguish, pain, a foretaste of the sword Simeon said would pierce her soul (v. 35).

Why were you looking for me? Then the first recorded words of Jesus in this Gospel, the first words of his that anybody wrote down, and they are a question answering a question. Not rudeness, but surprise. Why search everywhere? You should have known where I would be.

Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? These are Jesus’ first recorded words, and they are full of meaning. “My Father”: Mary said your father, meaning Joseph; Jesus says my Father, meaning God. At twelve, he is aware of his unique relationship to God as his Father. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the word Jesus will use of his destiny of suffering. Luke will use it again and again across his two volumes for the compulsion of God’s plan: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), must rise on the third day (24:7), the Scripture must be fulfilled in him (22:37; 24:26). Here it appears for the first time, on the lips of a twelve-year-old, and everything that follows in Luke and Acts is the working out of it. Even as a boy, he knows he is under his Father’s purpose. That does not mean he was pushed along against his will. It means the Father’s plan made his road certain, and the Son gladly made it his own: no one takes my life from me, he would say, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

In my Father’s house, or about my Father’s business? Literally in the things of my Father, which can mean his Father’s house, the temple, or his Father’s affairs, his Father’s business, as the King James has it. If your Bible reads about my Father’s business, nothing is wrong. The Greek will carry either sense, and both meanings fit; the two are not rivals, since the house is where the business is done.

Did Jesus sin by worrying his parents? A careful reader is entitled to ask. He is under the fifth commandment like every other Jewish boy, and he has just caused his parents three days of anguish. If he broke that commandment, the whole gospel comes apart, because a Saviour who needs saving cannot save anybody. He did not, and the answer is in his own reply. He had not run away, and he had not been forbidden to stay. He had done nothing his parents told him not to do; he had assumed, and his words say he expected them to assume it too, that when the caravan left, everyone would know where the son of this family would be. His did you not know is not insolence. It is genuine surprise that after twelve years they had to be told. Causing someone distress is not always a sin; the sin would have been disobedience or disregard, and there was neither.

A prior claim. Mary said your father and I. He answers by naming a different Father. He is not disowning Joseph, whom he will go home and obey for years to come. He is telling his mother, once, and then not again for a very long time, that there is a prior claim on him, and that she of all people had the means to know it. The boy in the temple who said my Father now brings many sons to glory, and is not ashamed to call them his brothers.
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not understand. Luke could have left that out. A writer building a legend would more likely have had the parents nod wisely; instead he records that the two people closest to Jesus on earth heard him explain himself and did not follow it. Mary is not portrayed as all-knowing; she too had to learn.

Take the measure of what they knew. Gabriel, the shepherds, Simeon, Anna: if anyone had the material to understand, it was these two. The mystery of who Jesus was, and what his relationship to his Father meant, was too great to take in at once.

Understanding comes in instalments. The mother of Jesus had more evidence than any of us will ever have, and there were things he said that went straight past her. Understanding, in Scripture, is not the entry fee for faith. It is one of the things faith is given, in instalments, over a long time, and usually later than we would like.

Two ways with what we do not understand. There is a way of handling what we do not understand that quietly disposes of it, filed under things that will make sense one day and never returned to. And there is Mary’s way (v. 51), which is to put it somewhere safe and go on carrying it. She was still carrying this one twenty years later, when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began, at last, to make sense.

Not understood until he opened it. Luke uses almost the same words again of the Twelve. When Jesus tells them that he must be delivered up and suffer, they did not understand this saying (9:45; 18:34). The sayings of Jesus about his Father and his road were too large for the people who loved him best, until the evening of the resurrection, when the risen Lord opened their minds to understand the Scriptures and showed them that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day (24:45–46). They are opened by Jesus himself, from the cross and the empty tomb.

What should I do with a passage I cannot understand? Do not throw it away and do not force it. Read it in its context, compare it with clearer passages on the same subject, since Scripture interprets Scripture (the Westminster Confession 1.9; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.9), and ask for help from a good commentary or a pastor. If it still will not open, put it on the shelf with a note and keep reading. The things necessary for salvation are plain in Scripture (Westminster 1.7; 1689 1.7); harder things can wait. Many believers find that a passage that baffled them for years suddenly opens in a hard season, because they kept it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Submissive to them. The boy who has just spoken of a Father greater than Joseph gets up, walks home, and puts himself under the authority of a village builder and a poor woman for some eighteen years more. “Submissive” (hypotassomenos): not a single act of compliance but a settled condition, sustained into his manhood, working as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). His awareness of his heavenly Father did not lead him to despise his earthly parents.

Higher calling, nearer duty. There is no contradiction between verse 49 and verse 51, and the pairing is the whole point. Being about his Father’s business, for a twelve-year-old in Nazareth, meant obeying his mother. Anyone who has ever used a sense of higher calling as a reason for neglecting a plain nearer duty has the shape of this passage exactly backwards.

His mother treasured up all these things. The second time in this chapter, with the same verb as at verse 19. She still does not understand it, and she still will not let it go.

Increased in wisdom. Growth in understanding. In his human nature, Jesus really learned and developed: although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8).

How can God increase in wisdom? That phrase deserves a pause, because it is one of the sharpest windows in the New Testament onto who Jesus is, and a thoughtful reader is right to stop at it. How can the eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), increase in wisdom? Did he not already know everything? The answer is the mystery the church has confessed from the beginning: in the one person of the Son there are two whole natures, divine and human, and they are not blurred into a third thing (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). According to his divine nature he knew all things and never learned anything. According to his human nature he really was a boy in Nazareth who had to learn his letters, memorise the Scriptures, listen to the teachers, and grow, mind and body together, as every child grows. The verse is not loose language. It is the exact truth about him. He did not merely appear to be a developing child; he was one. This is the same reality met from the other side in his own confession that he did not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32): all-knowing as God, genuinely limited as man, in the one undivided person.

In stature, and in favor. Stature may also mean years, or maturity. The words were used of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26): loved by God and by people. A whole development: intellectual, physical, spiritual and social, covering silently the hidden years of work, family, synagogue and prayer.

Why it matters. The Lord his people follow was once twelve, and once seven; he knows growing up from the inside, and what it is to learn slowly. Bring your child’s struggles, and your own memories of growing up, to one who has been there.

What if my parents are not godly or ask me to do wrong? Honour them still: speak respectfully, help them, care for them in age. But obedience to parents is always in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1), and God’s command comes first. If a parent tells you to sin, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and say so as gently as you can. If a parent is abusive, you are not required to submit to harm; tell a trusted adult, a pastor or the authorities, and get safe. Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph because they were godly and asked nothing against his Father’s will. Your obedience, like his, is first to the Father.

In everyday life. If you are a child or a teenager, Jesus obeyed his parents perfectly for you, and his Spirit in you will help you honour yours. At any age, ask which of his four kinds of growth is being neglected in your life this year, and take one step in it.

For worship. He did not play at being human. He became it, and lived it out through eighteen unrecorded years in a hill town, so that a fully human life could be offered to the Father with nothing missing. Every year of it was obedience, and every year of it was for us.

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man
