3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 begins the story Luke has been preparing since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52), and now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. Luke dates the moment as carefully as any ancient historian: this happened, and it can be placed.

John is the voice of Isaiah 40, the signpost and not the destination. He calls Israel to repent and be baptised, tells the crowds that descent from Abraham will not shelter them from the coming judgment, and shows what repentance looks like in ordinary work. Then he points to one mightier than himself, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.

The chapter ends with the baptism of Jesus, where the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks, and with a genealogy that runs back past David and Abraham to Adam. Jesus is not only Israel’s King; he is the son of Adam, come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry by naming the powers of the day, and the word of God comes to none of them. It comes to John, the son of a village priest, in the wilderness.

John calls God’s own people to a baptism of repentance, as if Israel itself needed converting, knocks away the claim that descent from Abraham is enough, and gives the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers each a concrete answer; none is told to leave his work.

Then he points away from himself to the one coming after him, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire, and Luke calls the whole of this preaching good news (v. 18). The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison: the herald is silenced just as the King steps forward.
verseByVerse.theology:
John’s saying that God can raise children for Abraham from stones does not abolish the covenant with Abraham; it shows what that covenant always meant. As Paul argues in Galatians 3 and Romans 4, Abraham’s true children are those who share his faith. The people of God are marked by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism with the Spirit and fire holds together two sides of one coming. The Spirit brings the new heart Ezekiel promised; the fire purifies those who receive the Messiah and consumes the chaff that refuses him.
verseByVerse.examples:
John’s three answers show that repentance is not only a feeling but a change of direction that can be seen. For the crowd it meant sharing a spare tunic and food; for the tax collector, honest accounts; for the soldier, no threats and no false charges. For two of the three it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real cost.

John also took his message to the palace, where it was dangerous, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 3 brings us from the hidden years to the public stage. John preaches a baptism of repentance, shows ordinary people what repentance looks like at the wardrobe, the tax table and the barracks, and turns every eye to one mightier, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire. Then Jesus steps into the river among sinners, the Father speaks, and a genealogy runs back to Adam: this is the Saviour of the whole human race, the second Adam come to undo what the first Adam did.

Luke the historian. Luke dates John’s ministry the way ancient historians dated great events, with a list of rulers: seven names, in strict order of precedence, one emperor, one governor, three tetrarchs, two high priests. Then the sentence turns and the word of God goes past every one of them, and lands on a man in a desert whom nobody had put on any list.

The fifteenth year of Tiberius. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14. His fifteenth year was about AD 28–29, depending on how the years were counted. Jesus’ ministry began shortly after. Pilate was prefect from AD 26 to 36.

Herod tetrarch of Galilee. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. A tetrarch was a minor ruler under Rome. He would imprison and behead John (v. 20; 9:9). His brother Philip, another son of Herod the Great, ruled the territory north-east of Galilee from 4 BC to AD 34, and rebuilt Caesarea Philippi.

And Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. A region north-west of Damascus. For a long time this name was used to convict Luke of carelessness: the only Lysanias known was a king executed in 36 BC, sixty years too early. Then an inscription found near Damascus, from the reign of Tiberius, names a Lysanias as tetrarch: a later Lysanias, holding exactly the office Luke assigns him, in exactly the period Luke places him. Luke was right.

Luke can be checked. This is not an isolated rescue, though not every question is closed (the census under Quirinius in chapter 2 is still debated). Again and again, a detail in Luke once called a blunder has turned out to be precise: the city officials of Thessalonica, whom he calls politarchs (Acts 17:6), the proconsul of Cyprus (Acts 13:7), the chief man of Malta (Acts 28:7). He has earned the right to be believed: he is reporting something that happened, at a time that could have been marked on a Roman calendar.

Annas and Caiaphas. There was officially one high priest. Annas held the office from AD 6 to 15, when the Romans deposed him. But he remained the power behind the office; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (AD 18–36) held it after him. Jews may have regarded Annas as still the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life.

The court that would try the King. Many of these names will meet Jesus at the end. Pilate will sentence him (23:24). Herod Antipas will mock him and send him back in a splendid robe (23:11). The high priest’s house will hold him on the night of his arrest (22:54; John 18:13). Luke names, at the opening of the ministry, the very men before whom it will close. The word that passed them by was preparing the way of the one they would crucify, and whom God would raise and seat above every ruler on that list.

The word of God came to John. The standard formula for the call of a prophet: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:2), to Hosea, to Joel, to Jonah. For centuries no prophet had been called in those words. Not in Rome, not in Jerusalem, not in the palace or the temple, but in the wilderness, to the son of a country priest, as it once came to Moses at the back of the desert, Elijah at a brook and Amos among the sycamore figs.

Does God still speak like this today? Not by calling new prophets with new words to add to Scripture. John was the last prophet of the old order, and the word of God came to its fullness in Christ, who is God’s final word (Hebrews 1:1–2). That word is now written, complete and sufficient (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). But God still speaks it, through the Scriptures read and preached, and he still bypasses the powerful to do it. The word that came to John in the wilderness comes to you when you open your Bible, and it has the same authority. Many faithful Christians believe prophecy continues in the church today, though nearly all agree that nothing may be added to Scripture; we believe such revelatory gifts belonged to the laying of the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and we gladly own those who differ as brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

parallels.desc: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah in the days of…

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into all the region around the Jordan. The Jordan valley, north of the Dead Sea. A place of crossing: Israel had entered the promised land by crossing the Jordan under Joshua, out of forty years in the wilderness (Joshua 3). John stands at that same river calling the nation to come out and start again, as if the whole history since had to be wound back and begun once more from the crossing.

Proclaiming a baptism of repentance. A baptism that expressed repentance. “Repentance” (metanoia) means a change of mind leading to a change of life: turning from sin to God. It is not primarily an emotion. A man can weep over his sin all night and repent of nothing; a man can turn round with a dry face and have repented completely. The test is not how sorry you felt but which way you are now facing.

Whom he baptised. Jews were used to ritual washings for purification, and Gentiles who converted to Judaism were probably baptised, the washing by which a pagan entered the covenant people. The startling thing was not that John baptised, but whom he baptised: Jews, God’s own people, called to be baptised like Gentiles. That said something scandalous out loud: being born inside the covenant was not enough; Israel itself needed converting.

For the forgiveness of sins. John promised forgiveness to those who truly repented. Not that the water itself forgave, but that it was the sign of a repentance God would honour. And John’s baptism pointed forward to the one who would actually win forgiveness, by his death (1:77; 24:47).

Did John’s baptism itself forgive sins? No. Forgiveness came from God to those who repented; the washing was the sign of their turning. John’s baptism prepared for the Christ, and those who had received it were later baptised in the name of Jesus (Acts 19:4–5). Christian baptism, too, does not forgive by the water; it is the sign of a forgiveness received by faith, which is why it belongs to those who have repented and believed (Acts 2:38, 41). The water is precious as a sign, and nothing in it saves. Many faithful Christians baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise to families, as circumcision was; we hold that the New Testament pattern is repentance and faith first, and we honour them as brothers and sisters who trust the same Saviour.

As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah 40:3–5. Isaiah 40 begins the second half of Isaiah, the great prophecies of comfort and return from exile: Comfort, comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1). John is the voice crying in the wilderness, the herald of the King.

Prepare the way of the Lord. The image behind it is a road gang. When a king was to visit a region, men went ahead to make the road passable: filling holes, cutting through ridges, straightening the route so the royal party could come through. In Isaiah, it is the LORD God himself who is coming, to lead his people home. John prepares for Jesus, so Jesus is the Lord God who is coming. John is the road crew, and what he is levelling is the ground in front of a nation’s heart.

In the flow. At John’s birth his father sang that the child would go before the Lord to give his people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins (1:76–77). Here is the grown man doing exactly that, and Luke will end his Gospel with the same two words, repentance and forgiveness of sins, proclaimed to all nations (24:47). John’s message is the first form of the gospel.

How do I know if I have really repented? Look at the direction, not the feelings. Have you come to see your sin as an offence against God, not merely as a mistake or an embarrassment? Have you turned to him for mercy in Christ, rather than trying to make up for it yourself? And are you, by his grace, setting yourself against that sin, even if you still stumble? Real repentance is not perfection; it is a changed direction that keeps turning back to God each time you fall. If you find you still love the sin and have no wish to leave it, ask God to grant you repentance (2 Timothy 2:25). He gives what he commands. And if you both love the sin and hate it, that tug of war is not proof that you have never repented; it is the fight the Spirit himself starts in every believer (Galatians 5:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every valley filled. A landscape made passable: valleys come up, mountains come down, and everybody walks at the same height. It is the reversal Mary sang of (1:52).

Nobody arrives on the level he was standing on. The person crushed flat by failure or shame is lifted; the person built up high on competence and being right is brought down. Both are necessary, and the ones who find it hardest are not usually the ones in the valley.

The crooked made straight. Crooked lives made straight, like the tax collectors and soldiers who come to John. Every honest person knows something in themselves answering to it: the habit of self-protection, the small dishonesty that has been there so long it feels structural. Isaiah says the road crew has been sent for that too.

All flesh. Here is why Luke kept quoting. Matthew and Mark quote only the first verse of Isaiah’s passage; Luke, writing with the whole world in view, goes on two more verses to reach this line, because it is his great theme. “All flesh” means all humanity, Gentiles as well as Jews, the note already sounded in Simeon’s song (2:30–32); Acts ends with this salvation sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

What it does not mean. It does not say all flesh shall be saved, but that all flesh shall see the salvation of God: a promise about the reach of the announcement, not the response to it, and John goes straight on to show that seeing and receiving are not the same. Salvation is through faith in Christ, and that is why the announcement must go to all flesh.

What about people who have never heard? They are not saved by their ignorance, and they are not condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are condemned for their sin against the light they had (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12). That is exactly why this verse matters. God has determined that all flesh shall see his salvation, and he has given his church the task of showing it to them (Romans 10:13–15). The right response to the question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore to the crowds. These are not his enemies. They are the crowds that came out to be baptised by him, people who walked into the desert to repent, and this is how he greets them. Matthew says he addressed this to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7); Luke applies it to the crowds, many of whom had perhaps come because it was the thing to do.

You brood of vipers. When a fire swept through the dry scrub, the snakes would come racing out ahead of the flames. John looks at a crowd streaming down to the river and says: you look like the wildlife leaving a fire. They were running from judgment without any change of nature.

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? It is sarcastic: did you think a dip in the river would be enough to escape God’s judgment? (See Matthew 3:7 for the fuller answer.)

Why so hard on people doing the right thing? Because he can see what they have come for. There is a way of pursuing religion which is entirely about damage limitation: getting into the water, getting the ritual done, getting the insurance in place, and changing nothing whatever. A man may be perfectly sincere in wanting to escape the consequences of his sin and have no interest at all in leaving it. John will not baptise that. His terms follow at once: fruit that matches repentance.

What is the wrath of God? A modern reader may find it harder than the snakes, and it needs saying plainly, because it is regularly caricatured. The wrath of God is not divine temper. It is not God losing control, or taking offence, or reacting badly. It is the settled, holy, entirely just opposition of God to everything that ruins what he has made. And it is worth asking honestly what the alternative would be. A God who looked at cruelty and abuse and betrayal and felt nothing would not be a kinder God; he would be a moral vacancy. We do not admire that in people. We do not call a man good because he can watch a child harmed and remain unmoved. The wrath of God is the shadow cast by the love of God: it exists because he cares, infinitely, about what is being done to his world and to the people in it.

Should a Christian fear God’s wrath? Not as one still under it. If you are in Christ, the wrath your sins deserved fell on him; he propitiated it, turned it away by bearing it himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). So a believer fears God with reverence and awe, but not with the terror of a condemned man. If you are not in Christ, the fear is a mercy: it is God’s warning while there is still time to flee to the only shelter.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fruits in keeping with repentance. Fruits that match: not a general improvement. True repentance shows itself in a changed life, as a healthy tree by its fruit (6:43–45), something visible and appropriate to the thing repented of; John gives three worked examples so that nobody can pretend the demand was vague. Paul preached the same: that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (Acts 26:20).

Fruit is evidence, not payment. This is where an anxious believer can get badly hurt. Fruit is evidence of repentance; it is not the cause of it, and it is not what earns anything. A tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples. But the fruit is how you can tell. And no one’s fruit is ever without blemish: it is Christ’s perfect obedience, counted as ours, that makes our imperfect fruit acceptable to God for his sake (Philippians 3:9).

What if I look at my life and see so little fruit? There is a kind of self-examination that is faithful and a kind that is corrosive, and the difference is where it looks for the answer. The corrosive kind stands under the tree counting, gets a number it does not like, and concludes it is not really a Christian. The faithful kind notices the shortage and goes back to the root. John’s whole ministry was about turning people to God, and a man frightened by his own lack of fruit is a man in the exact condition John was preaching for. So do not despair; go back to Christ, abide in him, and ask for his Spirit. Fruit grows from the vine, not from anxiety (John 15:5). And ask a trusted believer what they see; others often see fruit that we cannot.

We have Abraham as our father. This was the answer everybody had ready: descent from Abraham, circumcision, membership of the covenant people. Some later rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of hell to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you.

From these stones. He is probably pointing; the Jordan valley is full of stones. There may be a pun in Aramaic between children (banayya) and stones (abnayya). The God who made Isaac out of a dead womb can make a son of Abraham out of a rock. And he will: Gentiles, as dead to God as stones, will become Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7, 29). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12).

Abraham’s one true offspring. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and that offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16, 29): people become Abraham’s children by being joined to his Son, the one tree in all Israel that bore every fruit God looked for. The axe is aimed at every root but his.

The modern credentials. They are not hard to name. Christian parents. Baptism, whether as an infant or as a believer. Membership of a good church. Thirty years in the same pew. Every one of these is a genuine mercy, and not one of them is the thing itself. A man may be inside all of it and still have never once turned round.

The axe is laid to the root. Not the branches: the root. This is not pruning. And even now means the blade is already resting against the wood, with the axeman standing there; the fire is God’s judgment. Jesus would later tell of a fruitless fig tree given one last year to bear (13:6–9).

Then is a Christian upbringing worthless? Far from it. It is one of the greatest privileges a person can have: hearing the gospel from childhood, seeing faith lived, being prayed for daily (2 Timothy 3:15). But privilege is not the same as possession. Every child of believing parents must personally repent and trust Christ, and every one may. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you have done more than inherit the vocabulary. If you are a parent, do not assume your children are saved because they are yours; pray for them, teach them, and call them to Christ.

For worship. God does not need any of us, and he chooses us anyway. He who can raise children for Abraham from the stones of the Jordan raised us, dead as stones, and made us his children. The axe was laid at the root of every tree, and on the way to the cross Jesus called himself the green wood (23:31): the one living tree that deserved no fire took the blow, so that dead wood might be joined to him and live.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we do? It is the right question, the one the preaching was for (Acts 2:37; 16:30). They do not argue with him; nobody points out that he has just called them snakes. The crowd hears that the axe is at the root and asks the only sensible thing a man can ask in that position. Three groups ask the same question (vv. 10, 12, 14), and only Luke records this section.

The most surprising answer. Here is the last of the prophets, with the crowds of Israel in front of him and the whole weight of the old covenant behind him, asked point-blank what repentance requires. He does not say: come to the temple. He does not say: fast, pray, keep the feasts, tithe, study. He says: share.

Two tunics. The tunic was the basic garment worn next to the skin. Many poor people probably had only one; a second was a luxury. So the instruction is not sell everything and it is not give until you are destitute. It is startlingly modest and startlingly concrete: if you have two and somebody near you has none, that is what the second one is for. (1 John 3:17–18).

Whose is the second coat? Which lands somewhere very specific for a modern reader, because the honest arithmetic is uncomfortable. Almost nobody reading this owns two tunics. We own thirty, in a wardrobe, several of which have not been worn in two years. And John’s test is not what percentage we give away; it is whether the surplus is understood to be ours or understood to be for somebody. That is the shift he is asking for, and it is a shift of ownership before it is a shift of behaviour. The person who thinks of the second coat as their property, from which generosity is an occasional deduction, will always give a little and feel good about it. The person who thinks of the second coat as already belonging to whoever has none will simply hand it over, and will not think of it as generosity at all.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by giving things away. Nor a political programme of enforced equality. Nor that it is wrong to own more than one of anything, or to save for the future (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). But a heart that has truly turned to God will turn toward the needy.

The one who was stripped of everything. John asks for the second tunic. The one whose way he prepares would give far more. Paul grounds all Christian giving in exactly this: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:8–9). At the cross the soldiers cast lots for his garments (23:34): the Lord of all was stripped of the last thing he had. People who have seen what Christ gave do not need to be argued into handing over a coat.

So how much should I give? Scripture gives no fixed percentage for the new covenant, but it gives principles. Give first to the Lord’s work through your local church, regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously and cheerfully, not reluctantly (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Many believers find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep your eyes open, as John says, for the person near you who has none: the brother out of work, the neighbour with an empty fridge. Generosity starts with what is in front of you.
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tax collectors also came to be baptized. Jews working the Roman revenue system. The right to collect tolls and customs was commonly sold to the highest bidder, who paid in advance and collected what he could, keeping the surplus; the system invited extortion. To his neighbours a tax collector was a traitor and a thief with legal protection. Yet they came to John, and later to Jesus (5:27–32; 15:1; 19:1–10), and they call John Teacher, a courtesy the crowds did not bother with.

No more than you are authorized. John does not tell them to quit. Here is a profession soaked in injustice, tied to a pagan empire, and the prophet’s instruction is: do the job honestly. The state has the right to taxes (20:25; Romans 13:6–7). Repentance does not usually mean leaving your calling, but living differently in it.

What it cost. The profit was in the margin. John is telling these men to accept a permanent drop in income for a clear conscience, alongside colleagues who will do better out of not doing the same. That is far harder than resigning. Resigning is over in a day. This is every day.

Friend of tax collectors. John sends these men back to the tax table honest. The one he was preparing for would go further: he would sit down at their tables and be called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). Zacchaeus is not told to repay anyone; he is found and welcomed, and the repayment pours out of him unasked (19:8). John could describe the fruit. Jesus is the one who makes the tree new, because the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

Should I leave a job in a compromised industry? There is a persistent instinct that real repentance ought to mean leaving: leaving the industry, the firm, the compromised environment, and that staying is a failure of nerve. Sometimes leaving is right, and Scripture knows of work that cannot be done honestly at all: if your job requires you to lie, cheat, or take part in what God forbids, you must obey God rather than men. But John’s answer to a room full of men in a corrupt trade was to send them back into it clean. Ask whether you can do this work without sinning. If you can, stay and be the honest one, at whatever cost. If you cannot, seek counsel, pray, and plan your way out.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers also asked him. Their question has a small word in it that changes the tone: and we? They want to know whether there is anything for men like them. These are probably Jewish soldiers in Herod’s service, or police who protected the tax collectors, with power, weapons and poor pay, and the temptations that go with them.

Threats and false accusation. “Extort by threats” is literally shake down; “false accusation” is sykophantēsēte, to accuse falsely, to blackmail. A soldier could report a man, the report would be believed, and the man would pay to make it go away.

Content with your wages. The root of their sins was discontent and greed. Contentment is the cure (Philippians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5).

Contentment turns rules into freedom. Why does a soldier lean on people? Because his pay is poor and there is money to be had. Deal with the extortion by prohibition alone and you have a man permanently resentful, obeying with clenched teeth. Deal with it by contentment and the temptation loses its handle. Contentment is not a temperament; Paul learned it in prison. It is something acquired, slowly, by people who have found something they cannot lose and have begun to reckon everything else against it.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. John does not tell the soldiers to leave the army, but to be honest and content in it, and held to justice: no abuse of power, no cruelty. (See Romans 13:4 for the fuller answer.)

Three answers, all at the wallet. Asked in the desert what repentance looks like, the last prophet of the old covenant answered three times, to the crowd, the tax men and the soldiers, at the wallet. Not because money is the worst of sins, but because it is the place where a man’s actual convictions are recorded, in figures, whether or not he agrees with them.

A centurion at the cross. Luke keeps soldiers in view to the end of his Gospel. Soldiers mock Jesus on the cross (23:36–37). The one man who had all power refused to use it for himself, and when he died, the centurion in charge praised God and said, Certainly this man was innocent (23:47). John told soldiers to stop taking by force. Jesus showed a soldier what power is for: laid down, to save others.

How do I learn contentment? Paul calls it a secret he learned (Philippians 4:12), so it can be learned. Start by giving thanks, specifically and daily, for what you have; gratitude starves discontent. Notice the comparisons that feed it, the adverts, the feeds, the friend’s new house, and starve them. Remember what you cannot lose: Christ has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, and that is the reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5). And give some away; generosity loosens money’s grip. Contentment does not mean you may never seek a better wage, but that your peace does not depend on getting it.

In everyday life. List the small powers you hold, over a child, an employee, a customer, a spouse, and ask whether any of them is being used to get what you want at someone else’s cost.
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In expectation. Messianic hope was intense, and here was a prophet like Elijah.

Whether he might be the Christ. It is not an unreasonable guess. John could have had it, not by seizing anything, merely by not correcting them, letting the question hang. He did not let it hang for a sentence.

I baptize you with water. John’s baptism was only water, an outward sign. Water can wash a man’s skin and leave his heart untouched, and John knows it.

But he who is mightier than I is coming. John points away from himself. Throughout his ministry, he made himself small, to make Christ great: He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals and washing his feet was the job of the lowest slave. Later rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher except untie his sandals. The greatest of the prophets (7:28) considers himself unworthy to be the Messiah’s slave. That is not a poor self-image; it is arithmetic. And it set him free. A man who needs the crowd’s admiration will always be tempted to keep a little of it for himself. John could give all of it away, because his joy was somewhere else: in the voice of the bridegroom, as he would put it (John 3:29).

In the flow. After the three questions of verses 10–14, the question underneath surfaces: is John the answer? What people need is someone who can change them from the inside, and John cannot.

The Holy Spirit and fire. John’s baptism was outward; the Messiah’s will be inward, a drenching in God himself, as Ezekiel and Joel promised (Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28–29). John can put a man under the water; only God can put the Spirit inside him. Fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–4). To be baptised with the Spirit is to have God himself come to live inside you, so that the change reaches the place water cannot: a new heart that begins to love God, trust Christ and turn from sin (Romans 5:5; 8:9).

What does and fire mean? Some take it as the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), others as a refining of believers. “Fire” has a double meaning: purifying fire for those who repent (Malachi 3:2–3), and the fire of judgment for those who do not (v. 17). The more likely reading is that it is one baptism with two outcomes, as John’s picture of the winnowing fork goes on to show: the Spirit for those who repent, and fire, the fire of judgment, for the chaff. One baptism of Spirit and fire: purifying the wheat, burning the chaff. John announces a Messiah who will both save and judge.

Where Christians differ: the baptism of the Spirit. Pentecostal teaching holds that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues. They point to Acts, where the Samaritans and the Ephesian disciples received the Spirit after believing (Acts 8:14–17; 19:1–7), and to the disciples themselves at Pentecost. Sincere Christians differ here, and many who hold that view love Christ better than most of us. This commentary’s view: in the New Testament, all believers are baptised by the Spirit into Christ at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9). Those moments in Acts were the special occasions on which the gospel crossed new frontiers, and Pentecost was the unique, once-for-all outpouring at the beginning of the new age. Peter, explaining to the Jerusalem church what happened at Cornelius’s house, applies John’s words to that household the moment they believed, saying God gave them the same gift as he gave to us when we believed (Acts 11:16–17). Paul says plainly that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, and that anyone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ. Every Christian has it. Believers are commanded to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), but not to seek a second baptism. That is not a reason to want less of the Spirit’s work; it is the ground for asking for more of it, out of security rather than out of fear.

I have been told I lack the baptism of the Spirit. What now? If you trust in Christ, you have the Spirit; you could not call Jesus Lord without him (1 Corinthians 12:3). You are not a second-class Christian waiting for a missing experience. Many believers have spent years anxious about this, and the anxiety itself is not from God. Thank him that you are already joined to Christ by his Spirit. Then ask, as Jesus told us to ask (11:13), for more of the Spirit’s work: more love, more holiness, more boldness, more joy. Seek him through the means he has given, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship, rather than through a particular sensation.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His winnowing fork is in his hand. After threshing, grain was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel, on a threshing floor open to the wind. The heavy grain fell back onto the floor; the light chaff blew away, and was swept up and burned. The tool does not create the difference between wheat and chaff. It reveals it. And the fork is already in his hand: not fetched when needed, held.

The wheat into his barn. The repentant, the true people of God, will be gathered safely. This is the first thing named: the purpose of a harvest is the grain. The whole operation exists for the barn.

The chaff he will burn. There is no way to soften that and no honest reason to try. The unrepentant will be judged, with fire that cannot be put out (Mark 9:43, 48). It comes more often and more plainly from the mouth of Jesus himself. The Messiah is not only Saviour but Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31).

Where Christians differ: is hell conscious and eternal? Some evangelicals hold, as John Stott tentatively did, that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the picture of chaff burned up and to words like destroy (Matthew 10:28). This commentary’s view: the mainstream of the church has not read it that way, and the words of Christ are hard to bend in that direction. The fire here is unquenchable, and Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46); the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11). The punishment is conscious and unending (the Westminster Confession 33.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.2). What is not in dispute among any who take the text seriously is the reality of the judgment and the finality of it. Those who hold the other view are brothers and sisters in Christ, wrestling honestly with the same texts.

How can this be good news? Luke goes straight on to call all of this preaching good news (v. 18). How can it be? Because the alternative to a God who separates is a God who does not care what happens to his world, who lets the cruelty and the abuse and the lies go into the barn along with everything else, for ever. A universe with no final sorting is a universe where nothing is ever put right. The fire is terrible; a harvest with no fire in it would be a harvest with no justice in it.

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy and just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is God giving people, justly, what their sin deserves and what they have chosen: a life without him, for ever. But the same God has done everything needed to save: he sent his Son to bear that very judgment in the place of all who trust him. No one goes to hell who wanted Christ and was refused. If the doctrine troubles you, let it drive you to Christ, and to pray and speak for those who do not know him. It troubled the apostles too, and it made them preachers.

For worship. The winnower is announced beforehand by a man standing in a river with the water still running. Nobody has to be chaff; that is why he is shouting. The Judge with the fork in his hand is the Saviour who went into the fire for his wheat, and he will not lose one grain of it.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many other exhortations. Luke gives us the shape of months of preaching, not the transcript.

He preached good news to the people. “Preached good news” (euēngelizeto): evangelised. He called the congregation a nest of snakes, knocked away their one credential, and finished with a fire that cannot be put out, and Luke calls it good news.

One thing, not two. The hard parts of preaching are not the price of admission for the comfort. Luke does not see two things there. He sees one, and he calls all of it gospel, because the bad news makes the good news necessary and precious. A gospel without warning of judgment is not the gospel. If the axe really is at the root, then a man who tells you so is not being harsh; he is being kind at some personal cost, and the man who assures you the tree is fine is not being kind at all. Nobody thanks a watchman who saw the sword coming and kept quiet (Ezekiel 33:6).

Good news because of who was coming. What made John’s warnings good news was the one they announced. The axe was at the root, but the mightier one was at the door, and he was coming to baptise with the Spirit, to gather his wheat, and to save. John evangelised by pointing; Jesus would evangelise by arriving (4:18; 16:16). The gospel John preached to the ordinary people of Judea was, in the end, a name.

How do I warn someone without driving them away? Let them see that you are warning them because you love them, not because you enjoy it or want to win. Speak about sin and judgment as one who stands under the same need, never from above. Be honest and plain, but gentle and patient (2 Timothy 2:24–26). Do not stop at the warning: always point to Christ, the way of escape, in the same breath. Choose your moment and listen first. And remember that it is the Spirit who convicts; your part is to be faithful and kind.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reproved for Herodias. Luke closes John’s story before Jesus’ begins, in two verses with a great deal held back. Herodias had been married to Herod’s half-brother (called Philip in Mark 6:17; not the tetrarch Philip of v. 1). She was also Herod’s niece. To marry her he divorced his own wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, an insult that would eventually cost him a war. The marriage broke God’s law: you shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John told Herod to his face that it was unlawful (Mark 6:18). A prophet confronting a king, like Nathan with David.

He did not have to. John’s ministry was at the Jordan, among crowds who came to him. Nobody required him to address the tetrarch’s marriage. He could have preached repentance to Judea for years without ever mentioning the palace, and he might have died an old man. He went to the one man in the country who could have him killed, and told him the truth about his private life.

All the evil things. It was not one sermon about one marriage. John kept at it, across the whole range of the man’s conduct, and Mark tells us something Luke leaves out, that Herod was greatly perplexed by him and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:20). It is possible to enjoy sermons for years and keep the one thing they keep naming. Herod could bear to hear about his sin; what he could not bear was to give up Herodias. A man who will not let go of his idol will in the end silence whoever names it.

Added this to them all. Instead of repenting, he silenced the preacher. A door shut, and the voice is gone from the story. Josephus tells us John was imprisoned in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Herod later had him beheaded (9:9; Mark 6:17–29).

Faithfulness is not always repaid here. John did exactly what he was sent to do, without flinching, without ambition, without ever diverting the crowd’s admiration onto himself. And he finished in a cell, executed at a birthday feast because a girl danced well and her mother held a grudge. His reward was not in this life, and Jesus would say of him that among those born of women none is greater (7:28).

Luke’s order. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, before Jesus’ baptism (v. 21), though it happened later. He rounds off John’s story so that the stage is clear: John decreases; Jesus increases.

The forerunner goes first into the dark. John goes before Jesus even here. The same Herod who shut John’s mouth will hear of Jesus and say, John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? (9:9). When at last they meet, Jesus will give him no answer at all (23:9). The prison at Machaerus is the first shadow of the cross. The one whose sandals John was not worthy to untie would follow his herald into the hands of wicked men, not because he could not escape them, but because he had come to die for sinners, Herod’s kind and John’s.

Should Christians speak out about the sins of public figures? Sometimes, yes. John did, and so did Nathan and Elijah. Church leaders have a duty to declare God’s law plainly, including to the powerful, and Christians may rightly say that what a ruler does is wrong. But notice John’s manner: he spoke to Herod, not merely about him; he was moved by the law of God, not by party politics; and he paid for it himself. Speak truth about public sin without gossip, without glee, and without forgetting the sins nearer home. And pray for rulers, including the ones you must oppose (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

In everyday life. Who last told you a hard truth about yourself? Did you thank them, or shut the door? Silencing the one who names your sin only adds to it, while the Christ they point you to stands ready to forgive.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells the baptism itself almost as an aside. What he dwells on is what happened while Jesus was praying: the heavens opened, the Spirit came down like a dove, and the Father spoke.

Jesus had nothing to repent of, yet he went into the water of repentance with the people he came to save, as their representative. The Father’s words join Psalm 2:7 with Isaiah 42:1: Jesus is both the King who will reign and the Servant who will suffer.
verseByVerse.theology: The Father declares his delight in the Son before Jesus has preached a sermon or done a miracle. That pleasure is not a reward for performance; it is the love the Father has had for the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24). Those who are in Christ share that standing: not earned, not provisional, but given.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus prays at his baptism, and Luke shows him praying at every great turning point after it. Prayer is not a technique that makes the heavens open; it is the posture of the Son who depends wholly on his Father. And at the Jordan the three persons of the Trinity are present together and distinct: the doctrine is not a puzzle invented by later councils, but the church’s attempt to describe what happened here.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the people were baptized. Two details are Luke’s alone. The first: he puts Jesus in among the crowd, one of the people. He does not describe the baptism itself; what interests him is where Jesus was standing: in the same river, with the same crowd, receiving the same sign. The second is that he was praying.

Jesus also. What is the one man with nothing to repent of doing in the water of repentance? Matthew records John’s objection, and Jesus’ answer: let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15). He is not there because he needs what the water means. He took his place among the sinners he came to save, on the first day of his public life.

The opening move of the great exchange. What begins in the Jordan will be finished on a hill where he takes the sinners’ death. He is numbered with the transgressors from the Jordan to the cross (Isaiah 53:12; Luke 22:37). He takes the place of sinners, with their guilt and their punishment, and they are given his place: his righteousness, which means his perfect record of doing right, and his welcome with the Father. God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

And was praying. Only Luke notes this, and it is the first appearance of something he will do all the way through. Prayer marks every turning point of Jesus’ life in Luke: here, before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter’s confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28–29), in Gethsemane and on the cross. The prayer does not cause the heavens to open, as though it were a technique. It is the posture of a Son who does nothing out of his own resources.

The heavens were opened. As Isaiah prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). The barrier between heaven and earth is opened. God is about to speak.

Does Jesus’ baptism mean I should be baptised? Yes, though for a different reason. He was baptised to identify with sinners; we are baptised as sinners who have been joined to him, to show that we have died and risen with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). He commanded his disciples to baptise those who become disciples (Matthew 28:19), and the New Testament pattern is that those who believe are baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). If you trust Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It is not what saves you, but it is the obedience of the saved, and the Lord who stepped into the Jordan for you asks it of you. Christians who baptise infants read the covenant signs differently and are dear brothers and sisters; the pattern of Acts, faith and then baptism, is why we ask believers for it.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Trinity. All three persons of the Godhead are present in one sentence. The Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends. One of the clearest revelations of the Trinity in Scripture: one God, three persons, each distinct and each active.

And the Holy Spirit descended on him. Anointing him for his ministry. He has been the Christ, the Anointed One, from his birth (2:11); now he is publicly anointed with the Spirit (4:18; Acts 10:38). To anoint is to set apart and equip for a task. It does not mean he became divine at the Jordan. It means that, as a man, he was publicly commissioned and filled with power for his work as Prophet, Priest and King. Isaiah had foretold it: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

In bodily form, like a dove. Only Luke says in bodily form: a visible appearance, not a private impression. Why a dove? A dove came back to Noah over a drowned world, and the judgment was over (Genesis 8:8–12); and at the beginning the Spirit hovered over the face of the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again: a new creation begins.

You are my beloved Son. The voice weaves two Scriptures together, and the combination is the programme of the ministry about to start. You are my Son is Psalm 2:7, the coronation psalm of the Davidic king. “Beloved” may also echo Genesis 22:2, Isaac, Abraham’s beloved only son, who was to be sacrificed.

With you I am well pleased. Isaiah 42:1: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The opening of the first Servant Song; the later songs show the same Servant crushed for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). In one sentence the Father declares Jesus to be both the Son-King and the suffering Servant: the throne and the cross, laid on him together.

In the flow. The word Son ties the next chapter and a half together: the Father’s verdict (v. 22), Adam, the son of God (v. 38), the devil’s If you are the Son of God (4:3, 9), and Nazareth’s Is not this Joseph’s son? (4:22). Whatever Satan suggests and the neighbours assume, heaven has already said who he is.

Did Jesus become the Son of God at his baptism? No. He was the Son from eternity, and Luke has already said that the child to be born would be called the Son of God (1:35). Some ancient manuscripts here read today I have begotten you, which some took to mean he was adopted as Son at the Jordan; the better text reads with you I am well pleased. The baptism was the public anointing of the Son for his work, not his becoming Son.

For believers. The Father pleased with him before the first sermon or healing is pleased with us in him, not because of our performance, but because of his (Ephesians 1:6): not earned, not provisional, not reviewed annually. You do not work in order to be loved. You are loved, and then you work.

How can God be pleased with me when I keep failing? Because his pleasure in you rests on Christ, not on your record. When God looks at a believer, he sees him clothed in the righteousness of his Son, and he delights in him as he delights in his Son. Your failures grieve him, as a father is grieved, and he will discipline you for your good. But they do not change his verdict, because it was never based on you. So when you fail, do not hide from him; run to him, confess, and hear again over your head what he said over his Son’s: beloved. That is not licence to sin; it is the only soil in which real obedience grows.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke’s genealogy differs from Matthew’s in three ways: it runs backwards, from Jesus to Adam; it comes after the baptism rather than before the birth; and it goes past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God. Matthew presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel’s story; Luke, writing with the world in view, presents him as the answer to the human story.

The two lists also differ in many names between David and Joseph. Several explanations have been offered, and both Gospels trace Jesus to David. The list runs through a family history with foreigners, deception and disgrace in it, which God did not clean up first, and ends with the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.theology: By tracing Jesus to Adam, Luke shows that his humanity is one with that of every person who has ever lived: he entered the human story with real ancestors and a real history. Luke lays the foundation for Paul’s contrast (Romans 5:12–21): Jesus’ story is the answer to Adam’s.
verseByVerse.examples: Readers often skip genealogies, but this one is the gospel in miniature. Salvation came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding and sometimes scandalous history of real families, most of whom had no idea what they were part of. A Jesus who was only divine could not represent us; a Jesus who was only human would have no righteousness to give. The son of Adam who is the Son of God is the Saviour we need.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age. Luke says about thirty, which is exactly what a careful historian writes when he does not have the precise date. Thirty was the age for public service: Levites at the sanctuary (Numbers 4:3), David on the throne (2 Samuel 5:4). Eighteen years of that life had gone by since the last thing Luke recorded, and not one line of them survives.

As was supposed. Luke guards the virgin birth. He has spent two chapters establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father, and he will not now quietly contradict himself. Jesus was Joseph’s son by law, by household, by trade and by every register in Galilee; not by blood.

Why the genealogy is here. Matthew puts his genealogy at the very beginning, tracing Jesus forward from Abraham, to show that he is the son of Abraham and of David, the Jewish Messiah (Matthew 1:1–17). Luke places his after the baptism, just before the temptation, and traces it backward all the way to Adam, the son of God (v. 38). The voice from heaven has just called Jesus my Son. The genealogy shows him as the true Son, the new Adam, who will succeed where Adam failed, as the temptation (4:1–13) immediately shows.

The son of Heli. Set Luke’s list beside Matthew’s, and from David onwards they do not match. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob (Matthew 1:16). Matthew comes down through Solomon and the kings; Luke through Nathan, another of David’s sons, through names that appear nowhere in the royal chronicles.

Why do the two genealogies differ? Christians have answered this in three main ways. One: Luke gives Mary’s line, and Heli was Mary’s father, Joseph being reckoned son of Heli as his son-in-law. That fits Luke’s careful as was supposed and his close interest in Mary through chapters 1 and 2, though it must be granted that Luke writes son of Heli and not father of Mary. Two: Matthew gives the royal, legal line of succession through Solomon, and Luke the physical descent of Joseph through Nathan. Three: levirate marriage, the law by which a man who died childless had offspring raised up to his name by his brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so that one man could have a legal father and a biological father under two names. The ancient historian Julius Africanus (about AD 220) gave this explanation, saying it came from Jesus’ own family relatives. Each answer carries a difficulty. Genealogies in that world were kept to make a point, not to satisfy a modern registrar, and these two evangelists are making different points. The more likely answer is that Matthew traces Joseph’s legal line through Solomon, the royal line, while Luke traces the physical line through Nathan, probably Mary’s, with Heli as Joseph’s father-in-law. Any of these is possible, and both Gospels trace Jesus to David: legally through Joseph, and by blood through his mother. The difference does real work rather than real damage: the crown comes down one branch of David’s family, and the blood, most likely, down another, and they meet in him. We cannot now be sure which explanation is right, and believers may hold both lists true while leaving that question open.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Names we do not know. From Joseph back to David, Luke names men who appear nowhere else in Scripture. Maath, Naggai, Esli, Josech: no stories, no deeds. Ordinary people, faithful or unfaithful, in whose line God was working toward the birth of his Son.

The son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Apart from Nathan and David at the end, only two names in the whole stretch surface elsewhere. Zerubbabel led a return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, and laid the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2). Both genealogies include him and his father Shealtiel, perhaps because the two lines crossed there.

The son of Nathan, the son of David. Luke’s line runs through Nathan, a son of David by Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14); Matthew’s runs through Solomon, the line with the legal right to the throne, and also the line of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), Solomon’s descendant, of whom the LORD said that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:30). A curse lies across the royal succession.

The crown and the blood. Luke’s line runs through a son who never reigned and so never came under that word. On one common reading, Jesus, physically descended through Nathan, escapes the curse while inheriting the legal right to the throne through Joseph. However the details are explained, both lines meet in David, and the two lists agree on everything that matters.

God kept their names. History has kept nothing about these men except that they existed, married, and had a son. God kept their names. Not one of them lived to see the point of his own place in the list, and every one of them was necessary, because the Son of God came through their houses.

Does an ordinary, unremembered life matter to God? Yes, more than we can see. Most believers will leave no mark on history: no book, no building, no name on a plaque. But God records what the world forgets. He numbers the hairs of your head (12:7), writes the names of his people in the book of life (Philippians 4:3), and remembers a cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). A faithful marriage, children raised in the faith, honest work, prayers for a grandchild: these are the links through which he has always carried his purposes. You may never see what your place in the line was for. He does.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesse, Obed, Boaz. Now the names begin to be recognisable. This is the line of the book of Ruth, its last page (Ruth 4:18–22), and it is worth remembering what stands behind it. Boaz married Ruth, a Moabite widow, a foreigner, from a people the law had barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). The line of the Messiah runs directly through a woman who by birth had no right to be anywhere near it. Luke does not name her, but she is there. God’s plan included Gentiles from the beginning.

The son of Perez, the son of Judah. Here the list goes somewhere most family trees would rather not. Perez was born to Judah by Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law, whom Judah failed to provide for and then took for a prostitute at a roadside without recognising her (Genesis 38). It is one of the ugliest chapters in Genesis, and that is where the line runs. Jacob had prophesied that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10).

Jacob, Isaac, Abraham. The patriarchs, to whom God made the promises (Genesis 12:1–3). Jacob the deceiver; Isaac, born when his parents were long past hope of a child; Abraham, who twice passed his wife off as his sister to save his own skin, and who was given the promise anyway. Matthew begins here; Luke goes further back, to Terah and Nahor, Abraham’s father and grandfather, who lived beyond the Euphrates and served other gods (Joshua 24:2). God called Abraham out of a pagan family.

He did not clean it up first. Without a word of commentary, this stretch says that God brought his Son into the world through a family history containing deception, prostitution, foreignness, cowardice, idolatry and long stretches of nothing at all. He ran the line of the promise straight through Judah’s roadside and Ruth’s Moab, and had it read aloud in public for two thousand years. The family did not have to be made clean first, because the child at the end of it would make it clean. The Son of God took a family tree full of sin so that he could carry the sin itself: him who knew no sin God made to be sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). The one born of Judah and Tamar’s line is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), and the Lamb who was slain to ransom people from every tribe.

What about my family history? There is a mercy in that which is easy to miss. A family history is one of the things people are least able to change and most often ashamed of: the divorce, the addiction, the prison sentence, the abuse, the generations who never knew God. Luke is quietly reporting that the Saviour of the world has one too, and that God is not embarrassed by it, and did not require it to be respectable before he would work through it. Your family’s past does not decide your future in Christ. Patterns can be broken by grace (Ezekiel 18:14–17). Grieve what was wrong, forgive what you can, seek help where you need it, and begin a new line of faithfulness. God has done it before.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beyond Abraham. The line runs back past Abraham and the flood to the first man, and then one step further. Matthew stops at Abraham; Luke keeps going, and the difference is the whole shape of his Gospel. Jesus is not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of the whole human race. This fits Luke’s great theme: all flesh shall see the salvation of God (v. 6).

The son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad. A note for the reader with Genesis open. This Cainan (v. 36) is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, which runs Arphaxad, then Shelah, but appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which Luke and his readers used. Whether the Greek preserves a dropped name or a copyist’s eye slipped cannot be settled. Ancient genealogies could skip generations, since son of can mean descendant of; Matthew does so openly.

Noah, Enoch, Seth. Noah, through whom the human race was preserved through the flood, narrowed to one boat. Enoch, who walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24). Seth, born after Abel was murdered and Cain went out from God’s presence; in his days people began to call upon the name of the LORD (Genesis 4:26).

The son of Adam, the son of God. The climax. Adam had no human father; he was created directly by God, and so called God’s son. Jesus also had no human father; he is the eternal Son of God made man. Now the reason for placing the genealogy after the baptism is plain. At verse 22 a voice from heaven said You are my beloved Son. At verse 38 the list arrives at the same title from the other end. The Son declared at the Jordan is traced back, through seventy generations of ordinary and disgraceful and forgotten people, to Adam, and past Adam to God.

One of us. That is the point of every name in the list. He did not appear in human form as a visitor wearing the costume of our race; he entered the human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history, all the way back to the beginning. What Adam ruined, he is now inside, as one of us, related by blood to every person who has ever lived.

The last Adam. Adam, the first son of God, failed the test in a garden and plunged humanity into sin and death. Jesus, the true Son of God, is about to be tested in the wilderness (4:1–13), and will succeed. Where the first Adam was made and failed, the second Adam has come and will not. He is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49). To be the head of a humanity means that what he does counts for all who belong to him. Adam’s one disobedience brought condemnation on everyone in him; Christ’s obedience, shown first in the wilderness and finished on the cross, brings a right standing with God and life to everyone joined to him by faith (Romans 5:18–19).

Does it matter whether Adam was a real man? Yes. Luke places Adam in the same list as David and Abraham, as a real ancestor, and Paul’s whole argument in Romans 5 depends on one man’s sin bringing death and one man’s obedience bringing life. If there was no first Adam, the parallel with the last Adam loses its footing. Christians discuss many questions about Genesis and science, and should do so humbly. But the Bible’s teaching that all humanity descends from one man created by God, who fell, and that Christ came as the second head of a redeemed humanity, is part of the gospel itself.

For worship. Two men stand at the head of the human race, and the list between them is a chain of dust returning to dust, from a garden to a river in Judea. At the end of it, with the Spirit resting on him and his Father’s voice still in the air, stands the one who came to break it: the last Adam, who would go down into the dust himself and come up on the third day with a new humanity in him.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam — Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup> Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>9</sup> Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” <sup>10</sup> And the crowds asked him, “What then shall we do?” <sup>11</sup> And he answered them, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.” <sup>12</sup> Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” <sup>13</sup> And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” <sup>14</sup> Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.” <sup>15</sup> As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, <sup>16</sup> John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>17</sup> His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>18</sup> So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people. <sup>19</sup> But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, <sup>20</sup> added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. <sup>21</sup> Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened, <sup>22</sup> and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>23</sup> Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, <sup>24</sup> the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, <sup>25</sup> the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, <sup>26</sup> the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, <sup>27</sup> the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, <sup>28</sup> the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, <sup>29</sup> the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, <sup>30</sup> the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, <sup>31</sup> the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, <sup>32</sup> the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, <sup>33</sup> the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, <sup>34</sup> the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, <sup>35</sup> the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, <sup>36</sup> the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, <sup>37</sup> the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, <sup>38</sup> the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is a chapter of beginnings and confrontations. The Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing, where Israel failed and where Israel’s true representative does not. In the Nazareth synagogue he reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture is fulfilled in their hearing, and the town that marvelled at him tries to throw him off a cliff. In Capernaum his healings and exorcisms show in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

Each of the devil’s three offers (bread, power, protection) is a short cut around the path of obedience that leads to the cross, and Jesus refuses each with the word of Scripture. The Nazareth sermon is Luke’s statement of the mission: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, the year of the Lord’s favour. Two stories from Israel’s own Scriptures, a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general, show how far that favour can reach, and the congregation cannot bear it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Father has just said “You are my beloved Son”, and the devil’s challenge begins, “If you are the Son of God”. The wilderness tests that sonship: will he use divine power for his own relief, take the world’s kingdoms by the world’s methods, or force the Father to prove his care?

The three assaults echo Israel’s wilderness failures: hunger and grumbling (Exodus 16), the golden calf (Exodus 32), and testing God at Massah (Exodus 17:1–7). Where Israel failed, Jesus stands, by means every Israelite had: the word of God, believed and obeyed. The section ends with a phrase Luke means us to remember: the devil departed “until an opportune time.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation shows Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of plenty and fell; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness, starving, and stands. What the first Adam lost, the second wins back (Romans 5), not by raw divine force but by trusting the word of God.

The devil’s departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) points to the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3). At the cross the temptations return almost word for word: save yourself; if you are the Christ. What looks like Satan’s victory there is his defeat, because the Son who refused every short cut in the desert walked the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus’ weapon against every temptation is Scripture, remembered and spoken with precision. He reaches for nothing unavailable to ordinary disciples. A Christian who has stored up Scripture has the weapon he used.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, with a clause removed: the dangerous misuse of Scripture is the plausible one, and the safeguard is knowing what God is doing across the whole book.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 4 shows the Son of God beginning his work, and the whole chapter is about the power of his word: Scripture against every temptation in the wilderness, Isaiah’s promise declared fulfilled at Nazareth, and in Capernaum a word that silences a demon, rebukes a fever and heals a street at sunset. Who is he? The obedient Son and the anointed King, come to set captives free.

The setting. The genealogy has just ended with Adam, the son of God (3:38), and now the new Son of God faces the test the first Adam failed. Adam was tested in a garden, with every tree but one to eat from, and fell; Jesus is tested in a wilderness, starving, and stands. He is also the true Israel, God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), which failed its forty years of testing. The story of the human race and of Israel is being lived again, by one man, and this time to the end.

Full of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan (3:22) now leads him into a desert, not away from God but deeper into the Father’s purpose. Being full of the Spirit does not mean being spared temptation; it means being equipped for it.

Led by the Spirit in the wilderness. Temptation was not an accident or a defeat; it was part of God’s plan. It was probably the wilderness of Judea, the landscape of Israel’s failure and of the scapegoat sent away carrying sin (Leviticus 16:10). The Son goes out into it of his own will, led by the Spirit, because that is where the battle has to be fought.

For forty days. The number is not decorative. Israel was forty years in the wilderness and failed there (Deuteronomy 8:2); Moses was forty days on the mountain without bread (Exodus 34:28). Jesus goes where Israel went, on Israel’s terms, and does what Israel could not do.

Being tempted by the devil. The tense suggests continuous temptation throughout the forty days, coming to a head at the end. The devil (diabolos, the slanderer) is a real, personal being, the enemy of God and of man, and the temptations he pressed on this real man were real.
