He was hungry. Forty days without food takes a body to the edge of what it can survive. The attack comes at the point of greatest physical weakness, which is where such attacks generally come.

If God tempts no one, why does the Spirit lead Jesus into temptation? A difficulty sits in the very first line, and a thoughtful reader should not step over it. James says plainly that God himself tempts no one (James 1:13). The knot loosens once you see that one Greek word (peirasmos) covers two things English keeps apart. It can mean a test, a trial meant to prove and strengthen, the way God tested Abraham on the mountain (Genesis 22:1) and tested Israel forty years to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). And it can mean a temptation, an enticement whose whole aim is to make a person fall. The two can occupy the very same moment while pulling in opposite directions. From the Father’s side this is a test: the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to prove and display an obedience the world would need to see. From the devil’s side the identical event is a temptation: every word out of his mouth is designed to make Jesus fall. God ordains the testing; Satan supplies the enticing. They share the same forty days, and God never does the second.

Then what am I asking when I pray, lead us not into temptation? Not that God might otherwise tempt us. When God leads you into hard testing he is never trying to make you sin (James 1:13); he is proving a faith he fully intends to carry through, and he has bound himself to provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). The prayer is the prayer of people who know their own weakness and ask the Father to keep the test from ever becoming a fall: to spare them trials they could not bear, and to hold them in the ones he sends. The sinless Son did not need to pray it for himself. We do, every day.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? This commentary’s view: being God, he could not sin, yet the temptation was real and fully felt: a strong bridge cannot fall, but the weight on it is real. (See Matthew 4:1 for the fuller answer.)

Is being tempted a sin? No, and this settles a question that torments sensitive believers. Jesus was tempted, really tempted, by a real enemy, at real cost, and he was without sin. The pull itself is not the fall. If it were, the Lord who was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), could not be our Saviour. What becomes sin is welcoming the thought, entertaining it, turning it over with pleasure, and acting on it (James 1:14–15). So when an ugly thought arrives uninvited, do not conclude that you are a hypocrite. Turn from it, at once, to the one who faced the same and stood. Feeling the pull is the battlefield, not the defeat.

In everyday life. Expect temptation especially when you are weak: tired, hungry, lonely, ill, or just after a high point. Prepare for that hour beforehand, with Scripture already in your memory and someone you can be honest with. And do not read the hard season as a sign that God has left you. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, and he will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are the Son of God. The Greek form takes the claim for granted for the sake of argument. The devil is proposing that a Son with a Father like that ought not to be this hungry, and that if the Father is not going to do something about it, the Son should. The temptation is: use your sonship for yourself, to meet your own needs independently of your Father.

Command this stone to become bread. There is nothing wrong with bread. He will make it for five thousand people (9:10–17). The temptation is not to a bad thing. It is to a good thing, taken by the wrong hand at the wrong moment. To do it now, for himself, at Satan’s suggestion, would be to step out of dependence on his Father, who had led him into the wilderness to hunger. He would not use his divine power to avoid the human condition he came to share (Philippians 2:7).

The shape of temptation. Temptation rarely opens by suggesting that God does not exist. It opens by suggesting that God is not looking after you, and that you had better see to yourself. In the garden the serpent did the same: has God really said? He is keeping something good from you. The lie is always about the Father’s heart.

It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture, three times. He does not argue with Satan; he answers from the written word, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and stops. His weapon was available to every person in Israel and is available now. If Jesus needed Scripture to resist temptation, how much more do we; and the Spirit who filled him now lives in us to wield it.

Man shall not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3, and the context is the whole point. Moses reminded Israel that God let them hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna, to teach them that life comes from every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. Israel was hungry, grumbled, and demanded. Jesus is hungrier, and quotes the lesson Israel refused to learn, in the same desert, about the same God. His food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

Does this mean physical needs do not matter? No. Jesus did not despise bread; he fed the hungry and taught us to pray for daily bread (11:3). The verse says not by bread alone. Bread keeps the body alive for a time; God keeps the whole person alive for ever, and it is God who gives the bread in the first place. The point is order and dependence. A real need is not to be met by stepping outside the Father’s will, because the Father who gives the command is also the one who gives the food. If a choice ever comes between obeying God and getting what you need, the need is safer in his hands than in yours.

In everyday life. A real need will meet a wrong way of meeting it: money by a small dishonesty on an expense claim; comfort from a bottle or a screen at the end of a hard day; affection from someone else’s spouse who seems to understand you. The need is genuine; the offer is a way of feeding yourself that does not go through the Father’s hand. This is not a call to neglect ordinary provision; most of the time the Father feeds us through ordinary means. The question underneath is always: is he going to look after me, or had I better see to it myself?

For worship. The Son of God went hungry so that hungry people could be fed with the bread that does not perish. He would not turn one stone into bread for himself, and on the last night he took bread and broke it and said, this is my body, given for you. The one who refused to feed himself in the desert makes himself the food of his people. Everything he would not take for himself, he gives to us.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order. Matthew has the temple second and the kingdoms last (Matthew 4:1–11). Luke strings his scenes with and, and makes no claim about sequence. He ends with Jerusalem and the temple because Jerusalem is the goal of his whole Gospel, which began in the temple and will end there (9:51; 24:53). The order is a signpost, not a clock.

In a moment of time. No mountain is mentioned, and the phrase suggests a vision rather than an ordinary view. Every empire, every capital, every throne, laid out in an instant.

Delivered to me. Is he lying? If the claim were simply false the temptation would have no force, and Jesus does not treat it as false. He disputes the price, not the ownership. Jesus himself calls Satan the ruler of this world (John 12:31), and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). Since Adam’s fall, humanity has been under his dominion.

Delivered by whom? Look at the word he uses: handed over. Not seized, not created, not owned outright, but held on licence from someone who can revoke it. The devil is a usurper administering territory that was never his, on a lease he did not write and cannot extend. Ultimately all authority belongs to God, who gives the kingdom of men to whom he will (Daniel 4:17), and Satan is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). His claim is partly true, and it is far smaller than it sounds.

It will all be yours. This is the subtlest of the three, because what he offers is not something Jesus should not want. The kingdoms of the world are exactly what the Father has already promised him: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). The devil is offering him his own inheritance by a short cut: the nations without Gethsemane, the crown without the cross, at a price that looks small. It is the same temptation Peter would put to him, and Jesus would answer him as he answers Satan here (Mark 8:32–33).

In everyday life. This temptation is the right thing by a wrong route: church growth built on a softened gospel; the promotion gained by the quiet betrayal of a colleague; the peace in a family bought by pretending an offence never happened. It does not mean every success is suspect; to want a church to grow is not bowing to Satan. The question is what you are willing to bow to in order to get it.

Does Satan really control the world, so that Christians should withdraw from it? No. His power is real but borrowed, limited and already broken. The earth is the LORD’s, and everything in it (Psalm 24:1). Satan blinds minds and holds people captive (2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Timothy 2:26), and Christians must not be naive about him. But Jesus came to bind the strong man and plunder his house (11:21–22), and after the resurrection he declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So Christians do not retreat from the world as enemy territory; they go into it as the King’s ambassadors, doing their work, raising their families and serving their neighbours under a better Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s; Luke ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his whole Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written. Jesus does not argue about who owns the kingdoms or on what terms. He goes straight past the whole question to the one word that decides it: worship.

Deuteronomy 6:13. Again the setting matters. It comes just after the Shema, where Moses warns Israel about what will happen when they enter the land and find themselves suddenly comfortable: cities they did not build, wells they did not dig, vineyards they did not plant (Deuteronomy 6:10–12). The danger is not persecution; it is prosperity. Israel repeatedly bowed to idols for the sake of prosperity and security; Jesus will not.

Only. The word only is not in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13, but it is in some copies of the Greek Old Testament, and it is implied by the whole passage, which goes straight on: you shall not go after other gods (Deuteronomy 6:14–15). There is no room for divided worship. Worship is not divisible. A man who worships two things worships neither; he simply has one master he admits to and one he obeys. No servant can serve two masters (16:13).

Jesus, who is God, worships God. This does not mean there are two gods, or that the Son is less divine than the Father. The eternal Son, equal with the Father, took a true human nature, and in that nature he lived the life of worship that every human being owes to God and none of us has given. He will receive all the kingdoms, but from the Father’s hand, through obedience and the cross (Philippians 2:8–11).

The hinge of all three. The first was about bread, the third will be about proof, but underneath every one of them is the same question: who is God here? Every temptation comes down to that, however small the surface of it looks. Behind the extra glass or the figure adjusted on the form is a quiet transfer of allegiance: something other than God trusted to deliver what only God can give. So the test is usually taken not in the moment of crisis but beforehand, in the settled question of what a person actually worships when nothing is happening. Jesus came into that wilderness with the answer already fixed, and the devil found nothing in him to negotiate with (John 14:30).

How do I know what I actually worship? Ask yourself not, what do I say I believe? But: what is the thing whose loss would make life feel unliveable? What do I daydream about when my mind is free? What do I spend money on without thinking, and what makes me angry when it is threatened? Whatever answers those questions is being worshipped, whether or not it has ever been called by that name. The answer may be a good thing: a child, a marriage, health, a reputation, a career. Good things become idols not by being loved but by being loved in God’s place. The cure is not to love them less but to love God more, and to bring them to him with open hands, to the one who would not bow for a world and who holds them, and you, more safely than you can.

For worship. He would not bow, so that we might be set free from bowing to everything else. He is the only man who ever gave God the whole of his worship, and he did it as our representative: our worship is divided and cold; his was single and burning, and in him the Father counts it ours.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took him to Jerusalem. The third assault moves to the holy city, and it comes with a Bible verse; whether in a vision or physically, Luke does not say.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (little wing) was a high point of the temple complex, probably where the walls stood high above the valley; Josephus said looking down made you dizzy. This is not a private test. It is a proposal for a public one.

Throw yourself down. Prove your sonship; force God to act. A rescue in front of the temple crowds would be a sign from heaven, the very thing his enemies would demand (11:16). The temptation is not to doubt the promise, but to use it: to manufacture a crisis that obliges God to act, and call the manufacturing faith. It is the most religious of the three, and the only one that comes with chapter and verse.

For it is written. Twice Jesus has answered from Scripture. Now the devil quotes it too, and accurately.

He will command his angels concerning you. Psalm 91:11–12, a genuine promise. Nothing is invented, but something has been left out: the psalm promises angels to guard you in all your ways, and that is the point he hides (Matthew 4:6 drops the clause altogether). God guards his people in the paths they walk in obedience to him. Jumping off a building to see whether he will catch you is not one of your ways. And the psalm goes on: you will tread on the lion and the adder (Psalm 91:13), the serpent Jesus is about to defeat. The devil quoted the verse just before his own sentence.

How Scripture is nearly always misused. Not by inventing a verse; anyone can check an invented verse. By quoting a true one with the qualifying clause removed, or the occasion changed, or the covenant context stripped off. That is the strongest argument there is for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. The man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. The man who knows what God is doing in Scripture as a whole can hear a true verse being used against its own purpose and say so.

How do I read a promise in context? Ask four plain questions. Who is speaking, and to whom? What does the rest of the paragraph and chapter say? Is the promise for a particular person and occasion, or for all God’s people? And does my reading agree with the rest of Scripture, and with the way Jesus and the apostles used it? Psalm 91 promises real protection to those who trust God, and Christians may lean on it in danger. It does not promise that a believer will never suffer, since the same Bible shows faithful people imprisoned and killed (Hebrews 11:36–38). It promises that nothing will touch them outside their Father’s will, and that in the end no harm will undo them.

For worship. He stood at the top of the temple and would not jump, and some years later he stood at the bottom of a hill outside the city and let them lift him up on a cross. He refused to throw himself down to make his Father prove his love; instead he gave himself up to prove his Father’s love to us. The angels who would have caught him at the temple were held back at Calvary. There was no rescue for him, so that there would be rescue for us.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is said. Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture. The devil had a text; Jesus has the Bible.

Deuteronomy 6:16. Moses finishes the sentence with the place name that explains it: as you tested him at Massah. At Massah (Exodus 17) Israel is thirsty, and instead of asking, they quarrel and demand. The question they put is recorded because it is the question underneath all such demands: is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:7).

What testing God is. It is not asking him for something. Scripture is full of people asking, urgently and repeatedly, and God never once objects. It is making his response the condition of believing him. Trust says: he is good, and I will do what he has told me to do, and leave the outcome with him. Testing says: I will construct a circumstance that forces his hand, and I will read the result as a verdict on whether he loves me.

How it happens without our noticing. It is the bargain made silently at two in the morning: if this scan comes back clear, I will know he is with me. It is the resignation handed in without a plan, filed under stepping out in faith. And it is the terrible weight that settles when the scan is not clear, because a verdict was attached to it that God never agreed to. He does not owe us a demonstration.

The Rock at Massah. Massah has a sequel that makes this answer shine. When Israel tested the LORD there, God did not strike the people. He told Moses to strike the rock, and said that he himself would stand before Moses on it, and water came out for the people to drink (Exodus 17:6). Paul says that the Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). The Son in this desert is the Lord whom Israel tested at Massah, and he will be the struck Rock. At the cross the blow falls on him, not on the people who quarrelled, and out of him flows the living water (John 7:37–39).

But God says through Malachi, put me to the test, and Gideon asked for signs. Yes (Malachi 3:10; Judges 6:36–40). Testing God in the forbidden sense means demanding that he prove himself on our terms, as Israel did at Massah and as Satan urged Jesus to do. Malachi’s call is God inviting his people to trust a promise he has made. Gideon’s fleece was a weak man’s request that God graciously answered; it is not a pattern for seeking guidance, now that God has spoken in his word.

Then how do I seek guidance without laying a fleece? Begin with what God has already said: is the choice in front of you commanded, forbidden, or left free by Scripture? If it is left free, pray for wisdom, which God promises to give (James 1:5). Think it through honestly; ask the counsel of mature Christians who know you; weigh your gifts, your responsibilities and the open doors in front of you; and then decide, trusting that God rules even your mistakes. You do not need a sign in the sky. A Christian who has prayed, consulted Scripture and sought counsel, and then chooses between two good paths, is not out of God’s will whichever he takes.

Is it wrong to ask God for evidence? No. God does not ask for blind faith. Luke wrote his Gospel so that his reader might have certainty (1:4), and the risen Christ gave his disciples many proofs that he was alive (Acts 1:3). What Jesus refuses here is something else: setting the terms on which God must perform before we will trust him. The sceptic who says, if God is real let him do this for me now, and the believer who says, if he loves me he will do this by Friday, are making the same demand. God has given evidence enough in Christ, above all in his resurrection. The question is whether we will come to it on his terms or insist on our own.

In everyday life. Trust God in the path of obedience, without taking reckless risks and expecting him to bail you out: refusing a treatment your doctor urges because God must heal you without it, or spending money you do not have because God will provide. But a missionary going to a dangerous place, or a believer losing her job for refusing to lie, is not presumption but faith. The difference is not the size of the risk. It is whether God asked you to do it.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the devil had ended every temptation. Every kind: the arsenal was emptied. The three temptations cover the whole range: appetite, power, presumption. Many readers have heard in them John’s list, the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16), and the three pulls Eve felt when she saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and to be desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Where Eve took the fruit, the last Adam met all three, each at its strongest, and gave the enemy nothing. The devil departed from him, beaten: the first proof that the devil, resisted, flees (James 4:7). We fight a beaten foe, under a Captain who has never lost.

Until an opportune time. The enemy withdraws to wait, and Luke means this as a signal. The next time Satan moves openly against Jesus in this Gospel is as the Passover draws near: then Satan entered into Judas (22:3). This is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). The opportune time was Gethsemane and the cross, and there the temptations came back in almost their original shapes: save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews (23:35–39).

The victory is real, and it is not yet final. That is a fact about the Christian life as well. A believer who fought a sin through and prayed it through may find it standing in the doorway again eighteen months later, and conclude that the earlier victory was not real or that nothing has changed. The verse says something different. A returning temptation is not evidence that the last resistance was fraudulent. It is evidence that the war is longer than the battle.

The opportune time is the hour of exhaustion. He chose the end of forty days without food, and later the last night, in the dark, when the friends were asleep. That is a good reason to be more careful, not less, when you are tired, and no reason at all to conclude, when it comes, that you have gone backwards.

If Jesus defeated Satan here, why does the devil still trouble me? Because his defeat comes in stages. Here, in the wilderness, he was beaten in single combat. At the cross he was disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). At Christ’s return he will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the second and the third: the enemy is defeated and doomed but still active, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and fights on in the hills. He can tempt and accuse and harass you, but he cannot condemn you, and he cannot take you out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28).

parallels.desc: your hour, and the power of darkness

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns in the power of the Spirit and comes to Nazareth, where he grew up. In the synagogue he reads Isaiah 61, a Jubilee text, and announces that it is fulfilled today. He stops in the middle of a sentence, before “the day of vengeance of our God”: the favour has come, and the reckoning waits for his return.

The congregation admires him and dismisses him in the same breath. Then he tells two stories from their own Scriptures in which the blessing passes by Israel to an outsider, and they drive him to the brow of the hill to throw him off, and he passes through the midst of them, because the hour and place of his death are not theirs to choose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Jubilee was Israel’s built-in rehearsal of release: the trumpet, the cancelled debt, the freed slave, the restored land. Jesus announces the real one: the debt of sin cancelled, captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. Nazareth wanted a Messiah who would bless Israel and defeat its enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies. Every generation of the church is tempted to resent grace when it reaches people who had been written off.
verseByVerse.examples:
In Luke the gospel is always a present-tense announcement: salvation arrives today, at a particular address, in the hearing of particular people (2:11; 19:9; 23:43).

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched, because his hour has not come. And the scene warns about familiarity: Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus, and could not receive him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the power of the Spirit. He went into the wilderness full of the Spirit; he comes out in power. The testing did not drain the anointing; it proved it. Luke stresses throughout that Jesus’ ministry is empowered by the Spirit (v. 18; Acts 10:38).

To Galilee. The northern region, where most of his ministry will take place (4:14–9:50). Between the wilderness and Nazareth there is a period of ministry Luke does not narrate. John’s Gospel probably fills in some of it, with the wedding at Cana and the first visit to Jerusalem (John 1–4), and Luke simply notes that word was spreading.

A report about him. Jesus will shortly refer to things he did at Capernaum that Luke has not yet described (v. 23): an orderly account (1:3) is arranged to be followed, not clocked to the day.

And he taught in their synagogues. Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer and for the reading and teaching of Scripture, in every Jewish town. They probably began during the exile. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak, and Jesus, and later Paul, used them for preaching (Acts 13:15). The gospel began its journey in the ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary people.

Being glorified by all. At first, universal acclaim. Fifteen verses later his own village tries to throw him off a cliff (v. 29), and Luke sets the two side by side deliberately. The early approval is real, and it is worth almost nothing, because it has not yet been tested by anything he actually came to say. The second shout, in Jerusalem, would be the first one finally tested. Here is a Saviour who cannot be flattered into silence or frightened into retreat, who knew exactly what the cheering was worth, and loved them anyway.

Is it wrong to want to be liked? No. Wanting the good opinion of others is natural, and Scripture commends a good name (Proverbs 22:1). Jesus himself grew in favour with God and man (2:52), and elders must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). What is dangerous is needing it: letting the crowd’s approval decide what you say, or measuring your faithfulness by your popularity. Be glad when people think well of you, and do not lean on it; in the beloved Son you already have the Father’s approval, and need not buy the crowd’s. The approval that will last is the one you will hear at the end: well done, good and faithful servant.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The programme of the ministry. Luke places this scene at the start of the Galilean ministry as a kind of manifesto, setting out what Jesus came to do. Mark and Matthew record a similar rejection at Nazareth later (Mark 6:1–6; Matthew 13:53–58). Luke may have brought it forward for its meaning, or it may be a different visit. Verse 23 implies that Jesus had already worked in Capernaum.

Nazareth. His home town, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, where everyone knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3).

As was his custom. Week after week, for most of his life, the Son of God walked to a small building in an unremarkable village and sat through the service. A synagogue in Nazareth meant a handful of families, the same faces, and teaching that was probably very ordinary indeed. It was not instruction he needed. He went anyway, every week, including, on this particular Sabbath, to a congregation that would try to kill him that same day. The Lord of the Sabbath kept the Sabbath, born under the law he had given, and he is himself the rest every Sabbath had been waiting for (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). If the sinless Son worshipped with God’s people every week, how much more we, who now draw near by his blood (Hebrews 10:19–25).

What if my church is weak, or the preaching is thin? That is a quiet rebuke to a very common piece of modern reasoning: that a person who is not being fed, or who finds the preaching thin, or who has outgrown the place, is thereby excused. Jesus had better grounds for that argument than anyone who has ever used it, and he did not use it. Go, and go as a giver as well as a receiver: to pray with others, to sing, to encourage the person next to you, to hear God’s word read even if the sermon is poor. If a church has abandoned the gospel itself, that is a different matter, and you may need to find one that preaches Christ. But dullness, weakness and ordinary faces are not reasons to stay at home. They are the setting in which Jesus worshipped for thirty years.

And he stood up to read. A service included the Shema, prayers, readings from the Law and the Prophets, and a sermon. Readers stood to read Scripture, out of respect, and sat to teach, and a visiting teacher could be asked to do both.

He unrolled the scroll and found the place. Whether or not it was the appointed reading, he was handed the book he had inspired, and he found the sentence about himself, because the whole book is about him.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.

parallels.desc: Paul invited to speak after the readings

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The passage. Isaiah 61:1–2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6, to set at liberty those who are oppressed. Luke quotes largely from the Greek Old Testament and weaves the two passages together, and the effect is to sharpen the note of release. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add to heal the brokenhearted; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. In Isaiah the speaker is the Lord’s anointed, announcing return from exile. Jesus claims it as his own job description, and every clause names something the following chapters will contain.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. The man on whom the Spirit came at the Jordan (3:22) reads out the passage about the man on whom the Spirit rests. Father, Son and Spirit are all in the first line: the Spirit of the Lord, upon me.

Because he has anointed me. Anointed (echrisen) is the verb behind Christ, and its Hebrew equivalent is behind Messiah. He is anointed not with oil but with the Spirit (Acts 10:38), reading his own title aloud.

To proclaim good news to the poor. The poor (ptōchois) are the destitute, the needy, and in the Old Testament especially the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 66:2). The gospel comes first to those who know they have nothing (6:20; 7:22). Luke’s Gospel will be full of them, from shepherds to a widow with two small coins. Both material and spiritual poverty are in view.

To proclaim liberty to the captives. Liberty (aphesis) is the same word Luke uses for forgiveness (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). Forgiveness is a release: God cancels the debt, and the guilty go free as a prisoner walks out of an open cell (Colossians 2:13–14). Jesus sets free those bound by sin, by Satan and by disease (13:16).

And recovering of sight to the blind. From the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 61:1, where the Hebrew has the opening of the prison to those who are bound. Jesus will heal the physically blind (7:21; 18:35–43), and open the eyes of the spiritually blind (Acts 26:18).

To set at liberty those who are oppressed. Isaiah 58:6. The oppressed are the crushed, the broken, those bruised under a weight they cannot lift.

To proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour. The phrase echoes the Jubilee of Leviticus 25:8–55: the fiftieth year, when the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, debts were cancelled, slaves walked free, and land sold off in hard times went back to the family that had lost it. He stands up in a village synagogue and says the real one has arrived.

Where he stopped. Isaiah’s sentence does not end where Jesus ends it. The prophet went on: and the day of vengeance of our God (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus breaks off in the middle of a line, and the silence speaks. His first coming is for salvation; the day of vengeance is still to come, at his return (21:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Every year since that morning, including this one, is the length of that unread half sentence: the year of favour is still open (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Are these promises literal or spiritual? The question is badly put, and Luke will not let it be answered either way alone. Actual blind men receive actual sight in this Gospel; actual poor people are actually fed. And the same Gospel says that the deepest poverty is a man who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich towards God (12:21), and that the worst blindness is in people whose eyes work perfectly. Both are meant. A Christianity that spiritualises every one of these clauses has stopped doing what Jesus did; a Christianity that keeps them all material has stopped saying what he said.

So is the church meant to fight poverty or preach the gospel? Both, in their order. The church’s distinctive task, which no one else will do, is to proclaim Christ and the forgiveness of sins (24:47). But the people who hear that message are given new hearts, and new hearts love their neighbours with food, money, time and justice (1 John 3:17; James 2:15–16). Mercy to the poor is not a substitute for the gospel and not an optional extra to it; it is what the gospel produces. A congregation that preaches release and ignores the widow down the road has misheard the sermon at Nazareth.

In everyday life. Think of yourself in the list first: you were the poor man, the captive, the blind and the crushed, and he came for you. Then look at those still there: the colleague trapped in a habit, the lonely neighbour, the family at church who cannot pay a bill. Bring them the news and bring them help. The Jubilee has begun in Christ, and it will be complete only when he comes again.

For worship. Here is the trumpet of the true Jubilee, sounding in a village synagogue. The one who stopped reading in the middle of the verse is the one holding the year of favour open. The day of vengeance is coming; but first he came to bear the vengeance himself, so that for everyone who comes to him, the day of favour will never end.
verseByVerse.note: “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next words, “the day of vengeance of our God.”

parallels.desc: to let the oppressed go free

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The attendant. The synagogue official who looked after the scrolls. Luke slows the film: three ordinary actions, one at a time, and then a silence.

And sat down. Sitting was the posture for teaching. The room knows a sermon is coming.

A sermon of one sentence. There may have been more (Luke says he began to say), but this is the whole of it in one line. Prophets said, thus says the LORD. This man reads a seven-hundred-year-old prophecy about a Spirit-anointed liberator and says: that is about me, and it is happening now, in this room. He did not come to explain the prophecy. He came to be it.

There are only three possible responses. Either the man is deluded, or he is lying, or the year of the Lord’s favour has just begun in a small village. Being impressed is not one of the options. The one thing that cannot be done with such a sentence is to admire the delivery, which is precisely what the congregation is about to attempt.

Today. The word is sēmeron, and it is one of Luke’s. Born this day (2:11); today salvation has come to this house (19:9); today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). Luke will not let salvation be filed under history or postponed to the future; it keeps arriving in the present tense, at a particular address. It is fulfilled in the hearing of a room that is about to reject him. The today does not depend on the response. It depends on who has just sat down. And it is addressed to you: whatever burden you are carrying, the release he announced is not for some future day when you are better; it is offered now, in your hearing.

How is the whole Old Testament about Jesus? Not that every verse is a hidden prediction, but that the whole story is heading towards him. Its promises are fulfilled in him (2 Corinthians 1:20); its sacrifices, priests and temple are pictures of what he would do; its kings and prophets point to the King and Prophet who would come; and its failures show why he was needed. After his resurrection he took the disciples through Moses and all the prophets and showed them the things concerning himself (24:27, 44). So when you read the Old Testament, ask not only what it meant then but where it leads: what does this show me of the Christ who was coming?
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

parallels.desc: everything written about me must be fulfilled

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all spoke well of him. Or bore witness to him. At first, admiration, as the neighbours wondered after the shepherds came (2:18). Wonder is not faith. It is what a person feels when something has been genuinely interesting and nothing has yet been decided.

Gracious words. Literally words of grace. Grace is God’s favour freely given to the undeserving. Grace is poured upon your lips, sang the psalmist of the King (Psalm 45:2). But he has just announced that the Jubilee has arrived in their village, and the congregation is appraising the performance.

And they said, Is not this Joseph’s son? The turning point. The compliment and the problem arrive in the same breath, and the second sentence cancels the first. At first the question is not hostile. It is the sound of a small community being pleasantly astonished by one of its own. They knew him at nine. They knew the family, the trade, the house, the brothers and sisters. They have watched him buy timber. And that is exactly the difficulty. It is not open unbelief; it is a settled framework into which the claim will not fit. They do not disbelieve the sermon so much as find the preacher already accounted for. He has been categorised, filed under people we know, and there is no category above it. Familiarity made it impossible for them to accept that God was at work in someone so ordinary. They did not know, as Luke’s readers do (3:23), that he was not really Joseph’s son. And Matthew and Mark record that they took offence at him (Matthew 13:57; Mark 6:3).

Whose son is he? Luke has already given the reader the answer the synagogue lacked. Jesus was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph (3:23), and the angel had told Mary that the child would be called holy, the Son of God, and given the throne of his father David (1:32, 35). So the question is half right. He is Joseph’s son legally, and through that line the heir of David’s throne. He is not Joseph’s son in nature, for he is the Son of the Most High, the one the Father had just called beloved over the Jordan (3:22). That is why the words were gracious: they came from the Word who had become flesh, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

The particular danger of everyone who has grown up near the things of God. Familiarity does not usually produce hostility. It produces a mild, unthreatened appreciation. The person who has heard the Christmas story every year since infancy has an account of Jesus in place before he ever hears a sermon, and the account is not wrong so much as too small, and it has the enormous advantage of never requiring anything. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus Christ, and it was the town where, Mark tells us, he could do few mighty works (Mark 6:5). The people who received him were very often those with no prior file: a Roman officer, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector up a tree, a dying criminal. And God still often speaks through people we think we have already filed.

I grew up in church. How do I stop Jesus becoming familiar? Familiarity itself is not the enemy; it is a great privilege to have known the gospel from childhood. The danger is assuming you already know what a passage says before you have read it. So read the Gospels slowly, as if for the first time, and ask what surprises you. Read them in a different translation. Notice the reactions of people who met him for the first time, and ask why you do not react the same way. Above all, pray: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Only the Spirit can make the old story new, and he loves to do it.

For worship. He grew up among them so quietly that they could not believe he was more than the carpenter. That is the glory of the incarnation: the eternal Son was so truly man that his neighbours mistook him for an ordinary one. He is always larger, kinder and holier than our file on him.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Physician, heal yourself. Jesus answers the question they have not asked out loud. The proverb here means: prove yourself; do for your own people what you did elsewhere. They wanted signs, not faith. On the cross they will throw the same taunt: he saved others; let him save himself (23:35).

Capernaum. Luke has not yet told us about anything at Capernaum. That comes eight verses later (vv. 31–41). Luke has set the Nazareth visit at the head of the ministry, ahead of Capernaum stories that had already happened, because it explains everything that follows: why Jesus is based at Capernaum and not at home, why the message goes to outsiders, and how it will end.

Is this the same visit as Matthew 13 and Mark 6? Matthew and Mark record a rejection at Nazareth much later (Matthew 13:54–58; Mark 6:1–6). Whether that is this visit told in its chronological place, or a second visit to a town that had not changed its mind, cannot be settled from the evidence; the details differ enough to allow either. What is certain is that Luke knew what he was doing when he put it first, and that none of the Gospels claims to give a diary.

The demand underneath. They want a miracle, and they want it on grounds of local loyalty. The claim underneath is one of entitlement: we knew you first, so we have first call. He has just come from forty days of refusing exactly this, and the wilderness is still on his clothes.

No prophet is acceptable in his hometown. Acceptable (dektos) is the same word as favour in the year of the Lord’s favour (v. 19). Jesus proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord, but he himself is not acceptable to his own. He is placing himself in a line of prophets consistently rejected by their own people and killed by the people who had the Scriptures (Jeremiah 11:21; Acts 7:52). He would be despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3), so that we, who had rejected him, might be accepted in the Beloved.

Why would God not do a miracle for people who asked for one? Because they were not asking in faith; they were setting terms. Jesus never refused anyone who came to him in need and trust: the leper, the centurion, the blind beggar. What he refused was the demand for proof as a condition of believing, the very thing he had refused the devil, and later called the mark of an evil generation (11:29). A sign given to people who have already decided what they will accept does not produce faith; it produces spectators. When God seems silent to your prayers, it is not because he is withholding favours from those who have not earned them, but sometimes because he is drawing you from wanting a display to wanting him.

In everyday life. If those closest to you are least willing to hear the gospel from you, you are in good company: the brother who still sees you as a teenager, the parents who smile at your faith as a phase. Jesus went on loving the town that refused him; let your life speak over years. But their resistance is not always the prophet’s rejection; sometimes they are rightly put off by our pride, preachiness or inconsistency. Before you comfort yourself with this verse, ask honestly whether the offence is the gospel or you.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two examples from Israel’s history. Jesus chose the two stories that turn admiration into a lynch mob, both about Elijah and Elisha, and both about God going somewhere nobody expected.

Many widows. During the famine God sent in Ahab’s time (1 Kings 17–18), Israelite widows were starving in every village. Jesus gives three years and six months, as James 5:17 does; 1 Kings 18:1 probably counts from a different point.

Only to Zarephath. 1 Kings 17:8–24. Zarephath was a Gentile town near Sidon, Jezebel’s home country. God sent his prophet past all the widows of Israel to a foreign widow, fed her through the famine with a jar of flour that did not run out, and raised her son from death.

Only Naaman the Syrian. 2 Kings 5. Syria (Aram) was the enemy. Naaman commanded the army that raided Israel’s borders. He was healed when he humbled himself and washed seven times in the Jordan, and Israel’s lepers were not.

The point. Both stories are in their own Bible, and together they say something the congregation understands perfectly: the fact that the blessing is near you does not mean it is for you, and God has a settled habit of taking it past his own people to somebody they despise. This is the story of Luke and Acts in miniature (Acts 13:46; 28:28).

Grace is grace. To them this is worse than an insult. He is not saying they are unworthy and Gentiles are worthy. He is saying that grace is not owed to anyone, and so may land wherever God pleases; no one can put him in his debt by birth or religious upbringing (Romans 11:35). The Nazareth congregation’s rage is the exact rage of the elder brother in Luke 15, and of the workers hired at dawn who grumbled that the latecomers were paid the same (Matthew 20:11–12). It is what religious people feel when they discover that the thing they thought they had earned is a gift.

A greater prophet than Elijah. Luke goes on to show what kind of prophet is standing in front of them. At Nain Jesus raises a widow’s only son and gives him to his mother, the very words used of Elijah at Zarephath (7:15; 1 Kings 17:23); and the one cleansed leper who gives thanks is a foreigner like Naaman (17:15–18). Elijah and Elisha each reached an outsider, and Israel remembered it as a startling exception. Jesus is the prophet in whom that mercy stops being an exception and becomes the plan: a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32).

Is it unfair of God to bless some and pass by others? Fairness would mean everyone receiving what they deserve, and none of us wants that, because all of us deserve condemnation (Romans 3:23; 6:23). No widow in Israel had a claim on Elijah, and no leper had a right to be healed. That God shows mercy to any is grace; that he chooses where to show it is his right as God (Romans 9:15–16). The question that should astonish us is not why he passed by some but why he came to anyone at all. And the stories prove the door is open to the most unlikely: if a Sidonian widow and an enemy general were welcomed, no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

In everyday life. There is probably some category of person you have quietly written off: a nationality, a lifestyle, a political tribe, an individual with a name. Would you find it hard to be glad if God saved them tomorrow? Whoever came to mind is your Naaman, and Naaman is the one the story is about. Pray for that person this week, and thank God that his grace reached outsiders, including you.
verseByVerse.note: Both of these beneficiaries were Gentiles. Zarephath lay on the coast near Sidon.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All in the synagogue were filled with wrath. Six verses ago the same room was speaking well of him, and nothing has happened in between except two Bible stories. What turned a congregation into a mob was the suggestion that God’s grace is free: free enough to go to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general and past the people who had the Scriptures. The same reaction met Paul when he mentioned the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

They drove him out. This is a Sabbath, and these are worshippers fresh from a service in which the Scriptures were read. The men marching have known him since he was a boy. There was no trial. This is a village losing its temper so completely that it means to kill.

The brow of the hill. Nazareth sits on a hillside, with steep drops nearby, and the plan was to throw him down the cliff. It foreshadows the cross. And the devil had just suggested he throw himself down from a height. He refused to do it for the devil, and he will not let them do it to him.

Passing through their midst. Perhaps by his sheer authority, perhaps by a miracle; Luke does not say. He does not vanish or call for angels. He simply walks through the middle of them and leaves. Whatever happened there, the reason it happened is the one the Gospels give again and again: his hour had not yet come (John 7:30; 8:59). He cannot be killed early, or in the wrong place: he would die in Jerusalem, not Nazareth (13:33; John 10:18). His death is something he has come to do, for the very people who were shouting at him. He was never the victim of the crowd. He was always its Saviour.

The pattern of the whole Gospel. Grace offered, rejected by his own, and going on to others: the first congregation Jesus preached to tried to murder him, and he walked away and kept preaching. It is a fair warning to anyone who imagines that faithful preaching is chiefly a matter of being well received.

How can religious people become so violent? Because religion without grace makes people possessive of God. When a person’s standing rests on his heritage, his correctness or his good record, anything that suggests God might welcome outsiders on the same terms feels like theft. The more he has invested in his own goodness, the angrier he becomes. That is why the people who most wanted Jesus dead were not the irreligious but the devout. The cure is not less seriousness about God but a deeper knowledge of our own need. A person who knows he was saved by grace alone cannot be furious when grace saves somebody else. So when someone with a worse past than yours is welcomed and blessed and it irritates you, recognise the voice of Nazareth in your own heart, and go back to the grace that welcomed you.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth is built on a hillside with steep drops nearby.

parallels.desc: Jesus hid himself and went out

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth, which rejected him, Jesus goes to Capernaum, which becomes his base. In what appears to be a single Sabbath he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon’s mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a crowd brought to his door.

The first person in the crowds to name him aloud is a demon, and its knowledge saves it nothing: the demons believe and shudder (James 2:19). Jesus silences it and casts it out with one sentence, the same word of authority that rebukes the fever. At sunset, when the Sabbath ended and the sick could be carried, he lays his hands on every one of them. Then at dawn he refuses to be kept: he was sent to announce a kingdom, and he goes to the next town.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “the Holy One of God” appears elsewhere in the New Testament, outside this scene and its parallel (Mark 1:24), only on Peter’s lips (John 6:69). The demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually, and it does it no good: knowing who Jesus is without submitting to him is not faith.

The divine must appears again, the necessity that took him to the temple at twelve. And here is Luke’s first mention of the kingdom of God: not a place or a programme but God’s rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King, which is why its arrival looks like demons evicted, bodies mended and the poor given news.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon’s terror is the correct reading of what the kingdom means for the powers of darkness. Every healing, exorcism and act of forgiveness in the Gospels is territory changing hands, and a church that prays for the sick, names fear, guilt and lies for what they are, and proclaims forgiveness in Jesus’ name is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to keep Jesus local, the property of one congregation or tradition, is always well meant, and he always refuses it. He came not to be kept but to be followed to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Mark. From here Luke follows Mark’s account closely (Mark 1:21–39), with his own touches. The section that follows is one long day: a sermon, an exorcism, a healing in a house, a whole town at the door at sunset, and a departure at dawn.

Down to Capernaum. Down: from the hills of Nazareth to the lakeside, about 700 feet (200 m) below sea level. Rejected at home, he moves to a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, on the trade road, larger and more mixed than Nazareth, with a customs post (5:27) and a centurion (7:2). It became his base (Matthew 4:13). The town that received him got him; the town that had him from childhood lost him.

His word possessed authority. The word is exousia, and it is the key to everything that follows in this chapter. It means the right to act, backed by the power to do it. A scribe taught by citation: Rabbi Hillel said this, Rabbi Shammai said that. Jesus quotes Scripture constantly but never props himself on a rabbi, and he will shortly be saying, I say to you, in a way no scribe on earth would have dared (6:27). The difference is this: the scribes passed on what others had said about God’s word; Jesus spoke as the one whose word it is.

The same authority in the sermon and the exorcism. In four verses the crowd will use the word again: with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits (v. 36). Luke puts the sermon and the exorcism in the same paragraph so that nobody separates them. The word that breaks a demonic hold and the word that is read on a Sunday morning are one word, and the reason preaching is worth anything at all is that it carries it.

In the flow. Nazareth heard the programme and would not have it; Capernaum now sees it carried out (v. 18). The word one town drove out is the word that sets another town free.

Does a sermon today carry that authority? Only as far as it faithfully says what Scripture says. A preacher has no authority of his own; his opinions, illustrations and jokes carry none. But when he opens the Bible and explains truly what God has said, the word he speaks is the word of God, and the hearer is dealing with Christ, not merely with a man (1 Thessalonians 2:13). That is why you should test every sermon by the Bible (Acts 17:11), and why, when it passes the test, you should receive it not as advice to consider but as the Lord’s word to obey, from the voice that sets captives free and gives what it asks.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rescue in church. The first miracle Luke records in the public ministry is not a healing. It is a rescue, in the synagogue, on the Sabbath. A man has sat there, perhaps for years, with an unclean spirit, and perhaps nobody knew, until the presence of Jesus made it impossible to stay hidden. A religious setting is no proof of a clean one, and the arrival of Christ does not create trouble so much as reveal it.

A man who had the spirit of an unclean demon. Luke, writing for Gentiles, for whom demon could mean a neutral spirit, adds unclean: an evil spirit.

What is a demon, and does this still happen? A modern reader has no framework for any of this, so the plain question has to be faced. Scripture gives less than curiosity would like and enough to go on. Demons are personal, created, spiritual beings in rebellion against God, angels who fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). They are not equal and opposite to God; they are creatures, and Luke will shortly show one obeying a single command. They are not the explanation of ordinary sin, ordinary illness or ordinary sorrow: Luke, a physician, carefully distinguishes the demonised from the sick a few verses on (vv. 40–41). And they are real. The New Testament does not treat them as a first-century way of describing epilepsy. Does it happen now? Scripture never suggests the enemy has gone out of business, missionaries in many parts of the world report encounters they cannot explain any other way, and a person in the modern West is far likelier to be destroyed by respectable idolatry than by anything dramatic. Both errors are real: to see a demon behind every difficulty, and to have quietly stopped believing in the enemy at all. The second is much the commoner, and it suits him better.

What have you to do with us. The cry opens with Ha!, or perhaps, leave us alone! The question is a Hebrew idiom: what do we have in common? (1 Kings 17:18). Us: the demon speaks for all the demons, because the kingdom of God has invaded their territory.

Have you come to destroy us? Yes: they know their end is coming (Matthew 8:29; 1 John 3:8). (See Mark 1:24 for the fuller answer.)

The Holy One of God. The first in the crowds to name him aloud is a demon. The Holy One of God: set apart by God, sinless, belonging to God (1:35). And it is this holiness the demon cannot bear. It shrieks because absolute purity has walked into the room; it may also be trying to gain power by naming him, as ancient magic believed. And it saves them nothing. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to have him are two entirely different things.

Could a Christian be held like the man in the synagogue? No. The man in Capernaum sat among the worshippers, perhaps for years, but sitting in a synagogue is not the same as belonging to Christ. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The New Testament never describes a believer possessed, nor tells believers to cast demons out of one another. Christians can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist the devil (James 4:7) with the armour God gives (Ephesians 6:10–18); but they cannot be owned by a demon. Some Christians speak of believers being oppressed or harassed by evil spirits, and that is a real distinction; what Scripture rules out is a demon taking possession of one who belongs to Christ.

Then what is the difference between my faith and the demon’s knowledge? The demon knows who Jesus is and hates him. Saving faith knows who he is and trusts him: it agrees that what God says about Christ is true, and it rests on him, personally, for forgiveness and life (the Westminster Confession 14.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2). The demon says, have you come to destroy us? Faith says, you have come to save me. The test is not whether you can recite the creed, but whether you want him: whether you come to him, lean on him, and would rather have him than anything else. A frightened believer who clings to Christ has what this demon, for all its accurate theology, can never have.
verseByVerse.note: “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus rebuked him. Two commands follow.

Be silent. Literally, be muzzled. The demon has said nothing false, and he shuts it up, as he will again six verses later. He will not accept testimony from unclean spirits, however accurate: the messenger discredits the message, and an early identification would force the ministry into the wrong shape. But mostly because truth spoken by an enemy in terror is not witness. Witness comes from people who have been rescued and love him, and by the end of Luke’s second volume there will be thousands of them.

And come out of him! That is the whole exorcism: no ritual, no formula, no appeal to other authorities. Jewish exorcists of the period used elaborate techniques. Jesus uses one sentence, and it is finished.

Having done him no harm. A detail only Luke, the physician, records. The demon threw the man down on its way out, and Luke, as if checking him over, reports that he was unhurt. It is the note of someone who cared what happened to the person and not only to the story.

What is this word? Or, what is this message? Both his teaching and his command. The crowd’s reaction is exactly right. They do not ask what technique he used or where he trained. They ask about the word. They have grasped the connection Luke has been drawing since verse 32: the authority in the teaching and the authority over the spirits are one thing.

For with authority and power. Authority (exousia) is the right to command; power (dynamis) is the ability to enforce it. Jesus has both, and Luke often pairs them (9:1). Men may have authority without power, like a king in exile, or power without authority, like a thief with a gun. Jesus has the right and the might, perfectly joined.

They come out! The kingdom of God has come, and Satan’s power is being broken (11:20). The strong man’s house is entered by someone stronger, and there is no struggle in the doorway (11:21–22).

Should Christians today try to cast out demons? The New Testament never gives believers a technique of exorcism, and Jesus’ authority here was his own. The apostles cast out demons in his name as signs of the kingdom, and what is now laid on every Christian is to resist the devil, firm in faith (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9), to put on the armour of God, and to pray. Where someone seems genuinely oppressed by evil, the right response is not drama but the gospel: patient prayer, the word of God, the elders of the church, and wise care, including medical care where illness may be part of the picture. The power is in Christ’s name and word, not in a ritual.

For worship. Everything that holds a human being, the powers of darkness and death itself, is under orders it did not choose to take, from a voice that made it. He speaks once, and what has held a man for years lets go and goes out, and the man sits up unharmed on the floor of a village synagogue. There has never been a rival. There has only ever been a King, and a rebellion that had not yet been told it was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon’s house. The authority that silenced a demon in public now walks into somebody’s kitchen. Simon has not yet been formally called in Luke (5:1–11), another mark of arrangement rather than chronology; he must already have known Jesus before the boat scene.

Simon’s mother-in-law. The leader of the apostles was a married man (1 Corinthians 9:5).

Ill with a high fever. Luke, the doctor, grades the fever. Only he says high; Greek physicians distinguished great and small fevers.

They appealed to him. She did not ask. Somebody else did: a household asking on behalf of a woman too ill to ask for herself. That is intercession, and it is a comfort to anyone who has ever sat by a bed with nothing to offer but a request.

He rebuked the fever. The same verb as for the demon (v. 35) and the storm (8:24): he rebuked it. Not that the fever was demonic: it is the same sovereign word applied to a different enemy. Jesus confronts illness as an enemy, part of the disorder sin has brought into the world, and he has authority over every power that harms.

Immediately she rose. Complete healing, with none of the weakness that usually follows a high fever, and her first act with a restored body is to feed the people in her house. Serve (diēkonei) is the word for ministry. That is the shape of the thing all through Luke: what is received is not kept.

Why does God heal some people and not others? A chapter of instant healings will be read by somebody who has prayed for years and buried the person anyway. Luke is not describing the normal experience of God’s people, and he never says he is. Paul left a co-worker ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and had a thorn he asked three times to have removed, and it was not (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). What these days in Capernaum show is not a policy but a person: what he is like, what he will finally do, and what has already begun. Every fever he rebuked came back eventually and every person he healed later died. These are signs of the morning, not the noon. If your prayer was not answered with healing, it was not because you lacked faith or God lacked love. The full healing is still coming, at the resurrection (Revelation 21:4).

Does Christ still heal like this today? God still hears and answers prayer for the sick, sometimes with healing, often through ordinary means. But the healing miracles of Jesus and the apostles were signs that confirmed who he was and what they preached (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Many Christians believe the gift of healing continues; the more likely reading is that such sign gifts belonged to that foundational period. The reason is that Hebrews speaks of these signs as confirming the message to the first hearers, in the past tense, and Paul calls them the signs of an apostle; the instant, complete healings of the Gospels and Acts do not appear as a regular gift in later church life. Brothers and sisters who believe the gift continues are faithful Christians who love the same Lord, and we agree that God still heals in answer to prayer; we differ on whether he gives healing as a gift to particular people. The church prays for the sick (James 5:14–15) and leaves the outcome to God.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, notes that it was a high fever. Simon (Peter) was married.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the sun was setting. Luke gives the hour because it explains the crowd. The Sabbath ended at sundown, and carrying a burden, a sick relative on a mat, counted as work under the rules about carrying burdens (Jeremiah 17:21). So the moment the sun is down the doors open all along the street.

On every one of them. Only Luke says he laid his hands on each one. A word over the crowd would have taken four seconds. He touched them one at a time, after a day that had begun in the synagogue, for hours, into the night.

The untouched. Some of those he touched had not been touched by anybody for years; some conditions made a person ceremonially unclean, and left them alone. That is not efficiency. It is what he is like, and there is no one so far gone, so long untouched, or so far down the line that he stops before he gets there.

He would not allow them to speak. Luke links Son of God and the Christ. As in the synagogue, he will not be announced by demons (11:15), and the popular idea of Messiah was political; he would reveal himself in his own way, culminating in the cross.

Does Jesus still notice individuals, when millions pray to him? Yes, and this verse is the proof. He is not a crowd manager. He laid his hands on every one of them, and he has not changed (Hebrews 13:8). As the risen Lord he knows his sheep by name (John 10:3), and because he is God, his attention is not divided: he is not less present to you because he is also present to someone else. When you pray, you are not a number in a queue. You are one person, known completely, with his full attention.

In everyday life. Bring the people you love to him in prayer, one face at a time. And in a busy week, choose one person who is easy to overlook, the housebound neighbour, the elderly member who no longer comes, the colleague nobody eats with, and give them your full attention, unhurried, for an hour.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown; only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A desolate place. After a night like that, the first thing he does is leave. Luke does not say here what he went to do; Mark, telling the same morning, says he went to pray (Mark 1:35). It is the pattern Luke established at the Jordan (3:21), and it happens not in a crisis but the morning after the most successful day of his ministry so far, with the town at his feet. Success has its own temptation: to begin living from the crowd’s need of us rather than from the Father’s love for us. Jesus went to his Father before the crowd could set the agenda.

They would have kept him. This is Capernaum at its best, not hostility. Nazareth drove him out; Capernaum tried to hold him in. Both wanted him on their own terms. He goes anyway.

I must. There is the must again, dei, the divine necessity that first appeared on the lips of a twelve-year-old in the temple (2:49) and will drive him all the way to Jerusalem. And it is attached, not to healing, but to preaching. The healings are real, and they are not the mission; they are the announcement made visible. Bodies healed die again. The word of the kingdom gives eternal life.

The kingdom of God. Its first mention in Luke: not a place or a programme, but God’s reign, his rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King, to save and to judge. Which is why its arrival looks like this: demons evicted, bodies mended, the poor given news, debts cancelled. Wherever he goes, the territory changes hands.

Sent for this purpose. Sent by the Father, for more than one town. The desire to keep him is always well meant. He was not sent to be kept. He was sent to be followed, to the next town.

In the flow. I was sent picks up the Nazareth reading (v. 18), and the programme cannot be held in one place: the word keeps moving outward, town after town, until it is preached openly in Rome (Acts 28:31).

Is it wrong to want our church to keep what God is doing? Not to be thankful and to want it to continue. What is wrong is to turn blessing inward, as though God’s work existed for us. A church blessed with gifted people, money and growth should ask not only how to keep them but where to send them: planting another congregation, supporting missionaries, releasing its best people to go. The church in Antioch, at the height of its blessing, sent away two of its leading teachers (Acts 13:1–3). Healthy churches give away what they have been given.

In everyday life. Do not let good things crowd out the main thing: the Christian worker so busy meeting needs that the gospel is never spoken; the parent so busy with activities that the children never hear about Christ at home. And when a week goes well, take time alone with God before the next demand arrives, as he did.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preaching. One sentence closes the chapter and widens the frame. The tense means he kept on preaching: a summary of an extended period of ministry.

Judea or Galilee? A reader with an older translation may find Galilee here instead, and the difference is a genuine textual one. The manuscripts divide: some, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read Galilee, but the best manuscripts read Judea, which is also the harder reading. That is generally the stronger claim, since a copyist is far likelier to smooth a difficulty than to create one. Everything in this chapter has happened in Galilee, and Mark 1:39 has Galilee, so Judea looks like a slip and would have invited correction. But Luke uses Judea elsewhere for the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee, rather than the southern province alone (1:5; 6:17; 7:17; 23:5; Acts 10:37). On that usage there is little difficulty. He is saying that the preaching spread throughout the Jewish land.

Why put the sentence here. The chapter began with one man alone in a desert and ends with a preaching circuit across a nation, synagogue by synagogue, exactly as he said (v. 43).

In the synagogues. The same institution whose Nazareth branch had just tried to kill him. He did not abandon the synagogue because a synagogue rejected him. He went to the next one. If a door has closed on you somewhere, as Nazareth closed on him, do not conclude that God has finished with you.

Does a textual difference like this mean we cannot trust the Bible? No. Differences between manuscripts are real, and honest translations tell you about them in footnotes. But the great majority are tiny matters of spelling or word order, and no doctrine of the faith rests on a doubtful reading alone. Here, whichever word Luke wrote, the meaning is the same: Jesus preached throughout the land. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can recover what was written with remarkable confidence. God has kept his word.

For worship. The trumpet of the Jubilee had sounded in one village and been shouted down. So he took it to the rest, and he has never stopped taking it to the next town. In the wilderness and the synagogue, the cliff edge and the kitchen, the queue at sunset and the empty place at dawn, he was the same: the Son who would not bow, the King whose word cannot be resisted, the Saviour whose hands reached every one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Galilee. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days.
