And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes of people meeting Jesus: a miraculous catch that brings a fisherman to his knees; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; a paralysed man whose friends would not be stopped by a crowd; a tax collector called from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens the chapter’s deepest question, whether what Jesus brings can be contained in the old forms. It cannot. New wine needs new wineskins.

Luke gives the fullest account of how Peter, James and John came to follow. They met someone who exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust at the same moment, and Peter’s “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is answered not by departure but by a calling. And the closing dispute explains the rest: the bridegroom is present, and forms built for a world still waiting for him cannot hold him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the shore of the lake of Gennesaret, after a night of catching nothing, Simon lends Jesus his boat as a pulpit and then, against all his experience, lets down the nets again: “at your word I will let down the nets.” The catch nearly sinks two boats.

The miracle is about the person who commanded the fish. Simon falls at his knees in the language of Isaiah (Isaiah 6:5): this is what happens when a creature with a conscience meets holiness. Jesus neither agrees nor dismisses; he commissions, and the calling never rested on Simon’s worthiness. They leave everything, the catch of their lives included, and follow him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The catch authenticates the call. Before inviting Simon to follow, Jesus shows, in the very place where Simon’s competence is greatest, that the one who commands the fish is the one who made them.

Catching men describes a rescue: the verb means to take alive. And the shape of the morning is the shape of every conversion: Christ comes first, a sinner is left with nothing to stand on, confesses it, and is called anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simon’s obedience is not blind: he states the futility plainly, and obeys because the one who commands can be trusted.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade; Luke’s own Gospel sends several people home. But everyone who follows has a moment when something must be left on the beach, and it is very often the thing that had only just started going well.

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 5 shows the authority of Jesus reaching into ordinary lives and calling them to himself: a fisherman made a fisher of men, a leper touched, a paralysed man forgiven, a tax collector called from his booth, and new wine the old wineskins cannot hold. Here is the Lord whose holiness makes sinners tremble and whose grace makes them follow.

The setting. Only Luke tells the story of the great catch. Matthew and Mark record the call of these four men in a few brisk lines: Jesus walks past, says follow me, and they go (Matthew 4:18–22; Mark 1:16–20). Luke gives a whole morning, and plainly not their first meeting (4:38–39; John 1:35–42). So the call is a deepening: an introduction at the Jordan, an acquaintance in Capernaum, and then this morning, when acquaintance becomes the leaving of everything.

To hear the word of God. Luke introduces the first disciples through a sermon, not a miracle. The word of God is Luke’s phrase for Jesus’ preaching, and the crowd is hungry for it.

In the flow. Jesus has just said he must preach in other towns (4:43). Chapter 5 shows what that preaching does: it gathers people, the company who will one day be his witnesses (24:48), and it starts with a sermon and a fisherman.

The lake of Gennesaret. Luke’s precise name for the Sea of Galilee, from the fertile plain of Gennesaret on its north-western shore. Luke, who knew the Mediterranean, does not call a lake 13 miles long a sea.

Washing their nets. The last job of a night shift, done by people who want to go home: working boat owners at the end of a wasted night (v. 5), and a teacher climbs into the boat and asks for a favour.

Simon’s boat. Jesus borrows what belongs to Simon, as a first step in claiming Simon himself. Jesus enters their exhaustion and their disappointment before he asks anything of them, and he asks for something small before he asks for everything. He borrows our small things to give us great ones.

From the boat. A natural pulpit. Water carries sound, and a boat pushed out a few yards turns a beach into an auditorium. Before he is called, he is made to hear.

How does God usually call people? Most people are called the way Simon was: not all at once, but finally. A few Christians can name the hour they first believed; many cannot, and came to Christ over months or years, through a Christian home, a friend, a church, a slow dawning, and then a moment when it became their own. Both are real conversions. What matters is not whether you can date it but whether you are now following him. If your story is gradual, do not doubt it for that reason. God was at work in every stage, as he was with Simon at the Jordan, in his house, and in his boat.
verseByVerse.note: The lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee. Nets were washed and mended after a night’s fishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put out into the deep. Simon has fished this lake all his working life. Net fishing was done at night, and he has just worked the whole of it for nothing. It is now morning, the worst time. And a carpenter from an inland village is telling a fisherman how to fish. Your nets is plural: the whole crew is to do it.

Master. Simon states the professional reality plainly, and he is right. Master (epistatēs), a word Luke alone uses, means someone in charge. It is a real title, and it is not yet Lord. Three verses from now it will be. He knows enough to obey; he does not yet know who he is obeying. That is where most obedience begins.

At your word. Simon does not say he now expects fish, or has felt an inner assurance. He gives exactly one reason: at your word. This is faith: not blind, but faith in a word, from a person he had begun to trust. It is not the disappearance of the objection. It is the objection stated honestly, and then the obedience anyway, because of who is speaking.

Whose word it was. Simon did not yet know it, but the word he leaned on was the word that had made the lake. By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and he spoke and it came to be (Psalm 33:6, 9). Simon’s faith was small and his reasons thin; the one he trusted was neither. Faith does not save by its size but by its object, and a fisherman’s grudging at your word, spoken to the Creator, was enough to fill two boats.

The cost of obedience. Letting clean nets down again means hours more work, in front of a crowd who know it will not work. Simon is not risking his life. He is risking looking a fool, which for most people is harder.

Does this mean I should obey any impression that comes to me? No. Simon obeyed a word spoken audibly by Jesus himself. For us, Christ’s word is Scripture, and that is where we must look for his commands (2 Timothy 3:16–17). A strong feeling or an inner voice is not the same thing, and should be tested by the Bible and by wise counsel, not obeyed as if it were the voice of Christ. But where Scripture does speak, to forgive, to give, to be honest, to keep a vow, to tell someone the gospel, Simon is our pattern: obey, even when experience says it will not work.

In everyday life. Where does Christ’s word tell you to do something that seems pointless by your own experience? Forgiving the relative who has never changed; going on praying for a child who shows no sign of interest. Say with Simon: at your word, I will. Your obedience will be halting, as Simon’s was, yet the Father accepts it for the sake of the Son whose obedience never faltered and is counted yours.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night; daytime in deep water was the wrong time and place.

parallels.desc: a night of nothing, then a great catch

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They enclosed a large number of fish. Luke does not describe the fish arriving; he describes the equipment failing. Psalm 8 says God put all things under the feet of the son of man, even the fish of the sea, and Hebrews sees that psalm fulfilled in Jesus (Psalm 8:6–8; Hebrews 2:8–9). In this boat the fish of the sea are doing as he says.

And their nets were breaking. Literally, were beginning to break: the miracle reported by men trying to cope with it.

Their partners. James and John (v. 10): a small fishing business. Even both crews together barely coped, and the catches God gives are still usually too big for one boat.

So that they began to sink. That excess is the message. A moderate catch could have been put down to luck; this cannot be absorbed into anybody’s experience. It is a picture of the harvest of people that the gospel would bring (v. 10; Acts 2:41).

In his own trade. Jesus demonstrates his authority not in a synagogue but in their own trade, at the point where their competence was greatest and had just failed. In front of him is someone the fish obey.

The same lake at the end. After the resurrection, on the same lake, a voice from the shore says, cast the net on the right side, and the net comes up full and unbroken (John 21:6, 11). Simon’s story begins and ends with a catch he did not earn, from a word he did not expect, in water he had already worked all night for nothing.

Will obeying Christ always bring visible success? No. Here obedience brought a spectacular catch, but Scripture is full of faithful people whose obedience brought prison, loss or apparent failure: Jeremiah preached for some forty years and was largely ignored; Paul was beaten and imprisoned. The promise is not that obedience is always rewarded with results we can measure, but that it is never wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58). God sometimes gives the overflowing net to show what he can do; more often he asks us to keep letting down the nets and trust him with what comes up.

parallels.desc: the net full of large fish

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fell down at Jesus’ knees. Luke calls him Simon Peter, the only time before 6:14, as if to mark the moment. He does not count the fish or ask how it was done. He goes down on his knees in a sinking boat full of the largest catch of his life.

Depart from me. A surprising response to a miracle of blessing. Nothing has been said about sin; there has only been a boatload of fish. And the fish have told him something about the man in the stern that his conscience cannot survive standing next to. It was a blessing, not a rebuke, that broke Simon open: God’s kindness leads to repentance (Romans 2:4).

The oldest pattern in Scripture. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up and the first word out of him is: woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts! (Isaiah 6:5). Job meets God and repents in dust and ashes (Job 42:5–6). Not one of them is told to feel this way. It is what happens when a creature with a conscience gets close to holiness. And holiness is not first a rule but what God is: utterly pure, utterly other, a blazing goodness no sinner can see and live (Exodus 33:20). Conviction of sin is the beginning of true discipleship.

O Lord. Three verses ago he said Master. Now he says Lord. The word could mean no more than sir, but on his knees, in a sinking boat, it carries the weight of the title Israel’s Scriptures give to God himself. He has understood the one thing that matters: the gap between himself and this man is not the ordinary gap between two men.

The shame that wants to be left alone. Some shame does not want to be forgiven so much as to be left alone: that finds the nearness of God unbearable and would genuinely prefer distance to exposure. Simon means it. He is right about himself and wrong about what to do with it. He is a sinful man. That is the accurate diagnosis, and it is the reason Jesus got into the boat.

I feel more sinful now than before I was a Christian. Is something wrong? Usually, something is right. Growing in grace means seeing God more clearly, and the clearer the light, the more dust you see in the room. Paul near the end of his life called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). A deepening sense of sin is not a sign that you are going backwards, provided it drives you to Christ and not away from him. The danger is not feeling your sin but concluding, as Simon did for a moment, that you must keep your distance. The right response to seeing your sin is the one Simon made next: to stay at Jesus’ knees and hear him say, do not be afraid.

For worship. Simon asked the Holy One to leave his boat, and the Holy One stayed. His holiness is not the kind that keeps its distance from the unclean; it came all the way down to stand among them, and would go further still, to bear Simon’s sins in his own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The nearness Simon dreaded was the very nearness that saved him.

parallels.desc: woe is me, for I am lost

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John. With Simon, they became the inner three, present at the raising of Jairus’ daughter and on the mountain of transfiguration (8:51; 9:28).

Do not be afraid. Gabriel said it to Zechariah and Mary, the angel to the shepherds (1:13, 30; 2:10). The encounter with holiness always produces the fear, and the answer to the fear is always the same word. And he does not argue with the diagnosis: He answers it with grace. A sinful man is exactly the kind of man he calls. He declines to leave, and gives the man a job. Grace does not deny the sin; it outbids it.

Catching men. From now on is a phrase Luke reserves for hinges. The word for catching is zōgreō, to take alive, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle rather than killing them (Numbers 31:18). Fishing, after all, is not good news for the fish; the net means death. This net means the opposite. Simon will pull people out alive, out of the water that was drowning them.

The same trade, reversed. Nothing of who he is gets discarded; the patience and the nerve are taken up and turned round. The first great haul comes on a morning in Jerusalem when about three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41).

They left everything. Only Luke, telling this morning, says everything, and everything includes the fish: the catch of a lifetime, enough money to change a family’s year, left with the boats and the nets. Jesus was worth more. This is what following him means (14:33; 18:28).

Must every Christian leave his job to follow Jesus? No. Not everyone is called to leave a trade; Luke’s own Gospel is full of people sent home (8:39). Most Christians follow Christ as fishermen, nurses, accountants and parents, and serve him in that calling (1 Corinthians 7:17, 20). What every follower must leave is the claim of anything else to be first. Everyone who follows Christ has a moment where something has to be left on the beach, and it is usually the thing that had just started going well. For some it is a job; for others an ambition, a relationship, a habit, a way of spending money, or the right to run their own life.

Is every Christian meant to be catching people? Yes, though not all in the same way. The Twelve were called to a unique apostolic office, and some are called to preach. But every believer is part of a church that is sent into the world with the gospel (Matthew 28:19–20), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). For most that means praying for people by name, living so that faith is visible, inviting friends to hear the gospel, and speaking of Christ when the door opens. You catch people alive by bringing them to the one who saves; you do not have to do the saving.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man “full of leprosy”, an advanced case, comes to Jesus. The law put such a man outside the camp, crying out that he was unclean, cut off from worship and from touch, though he had done nothing to earn it (Leviticus 13:45–46). He is sure of Jesus’ power and unsure only of his will.

Jesus touches him. A word would have done; the hand is the miracle inside the miracle. Here holiness runs the other way. Then Jesus sends the man to the priest (Leviticus 14), because the priest’s verdict was his way back to his family and town. The instruction to tell no one fails at once, and as the crowds grow, Jesus keeps withdrawing to desolate places to pray.
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch is the incarnation in a single gesture. The Son of God did not keep his distance from our condition; he entered it and gave his own wholeness to the sufferer, a picture of the exchange in 2 Corinthians 5:21: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”

The leper’s “if you will” is the question of everyone who suspects that God may not want them, or that their case is too far gone. The answer is not merely that he can. It is “I will”: his desire to cleanse is as certain as his power.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus’ withdrawal to pray as his popularity grew (v. 16) was a habit, not an episode. Fruitfulness was his reason to pray more, not less, because the demands it creates can be carried only in communion with the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man full of leprosy. Only Luke, the physician, says full: an advanced case. Leprosy in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at) covers a range of chronic, disfiguring skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy (Hansen’s disease). A person with it was ceremonially unclean, had to wear torn clothes and cry out, unclean, unclean, to warn people away. He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). No one could touch him without becoming unclean themselves.

A living death. No home, no synagogue, no temple, no work. Very likely nobody has touched him in years, and he was not necessarily being punished for anything; the condition simply put him outside. And here he is in one of the cities, breaking every convention to get to Jesus.

If you will, you can. Both halves matter. You can is not a request but a statement: he has no doubt about the power. If you will is where the uncertainty is, and it is not doubt so much as the absence of any claim. He does not bargain. He puts the whole thing in the other man’s hands and leaves it there. And clean means not just healed but restored: to God’s people, to worship, to his own family.

The shape of real petition. He expects everything, but he knows he cannot command it, and can only trust the character of the one he is asking. Underneath it is a fear many carry: not, is God able? but, is God willing, for someone like me?

Am I God, to make alive? The leper’s you can is a larger confession than he may have known. When Naaman arrived in Samaria asking to be cured, the king of Israel tore his clothes and said, am I God, to kill and to make alive? (2 Kings 5:7). Later rabbis spoke of a leper as one counted dead, and of his cure as like raising the dead. Israel had no remedy for it, only a law to diagnose it and a camp to keep it outside. So a man who kneels to Jesus and says, Lord, you can, is ascribing to him what the Old Testament reserves for God. He is right. The one in front of him is the Lord who kills and makes alive, come in person to the place where the law could only say unclean.

Should I add if it is your will to every prayer? It depends on what you are asking. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess (1 John 1:9), wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), or the Spirit to his children (11:13), you need not pray if you will; he has told you he wills it. Where he has not promised, healing, a job, a spouse, a particular outcome, it is right to ask boldly and add, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). That is not weak faith. It is trust in a Father who knows better than we do.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He touched him. This is the miracle inside the miracle. A word would have been enough (7:7). Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee that nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Holiness is contagious in him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean. Here it runs the other way: Jesus is not defiled by the leper; the leper is cleansed by Jesus. The holiness is the stronger thing, and it moves outward. Here is the incarnation in a single gesture, and the exchange Paul describes: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). He takes what is ours; we receive what is his.

I will; be clean. The answer to his question. Two words in Greek, answering the exact thing the man was unsure of: not, I can, but I will. His will and his power are one.

Immediately. Skin diseased for years made whole in a moment. A sign that the Messiah had come: the lepers are cleansed (7:22).

A picture of salvation. Sin is like leprosy: it defiles, isolates, spreads and kills, and no human remedy can cure it. Years of exclusion had taught this man to expect a no. What he got was a hand on the skin nobody would touch, and a word with not a hair’s breadth of hesitation in it.

Does I will mean that God always wills to heal every sick person who asks in faith? No. This healing was a sign that the kingdom had come in Jesus. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and was told, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every prayer for healing is rightly prayed as the leper prayed, if you will. And if healing does not come, his will towards you is no less kind; the same Lord who touched the leper has promised a body that will never fall ill again.

What does it mean for me that Jesus touched the leper? It means there is nothing about you that makes him recoil. People who carry deep shame, from abuse suffered, from sin committed, from a body or a mind that does not work as it should, often feel untouchable, as if God would keep his distance if he really knew. This verse says otherwise. He comes nearest to what we hide. Bring him the thing you are most ashamed of, by name, in prayer; and if you can, tell a mature Christian, so that you hear his welcome spoken aloud. And then become his hand to others: notice who in your church or street is untouched, and go near.

For worship. For years no one had touched him, and the first hand to rest on his skin again was the hand that had made it: no reluctance, no recoil, only, I will. The will that went out to the leper is the same will that held him to the cross, where the clean one was numbered with the transgressors so that the unclean could be clean for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two instructions that seem to cancel each other. Tell no one, and go and show yourself to the priest. They do not cancel. The second is a legal procedure, not a publicity campaign, and it is the thing the man most needs.

He charged him to tell no one. A restraint Jesus imposes repeatedly in Galilee. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate, which is exactly what happens anyway (v. 15).

Go and show yourself to the priest. Leviticus 14 lays down the week-long ritual by which a healed leper is examined, declared clean and restored; without it he cannot re-enter the town or his family’s house. So Jesus heals the disease in a second and then sends the man through the process to heal everything else the disease had done to him, because he needs to be received back by his community. Grace does not despise process. The Lord who cleanses the heart in an instant patiently walks us back into every relationship that sin had broken.

The shadow and the substance. The law could examine a leper and pronounce him clean; it could never make him clean. Jesus gives the healing, and then sends the man to the procedure, the shadow bowing to the substance it had been drawn from (Hebrews 10:1).

For a proof to them. The phrase carries an edge. Since leprosy was rarely if ever cured, a priest had to declare clean a man who had been full of it. The establishment that would shortly decide Jesus was a blasphemer had been handed, by its own procedure, a public proof of what he could do.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because before the cross a reputation as a wonder worker would have drawn crowds wanting a political Messiah; after the resurrection the command is the opposite (Matthew 28:19). (See Matthew 12:16 for the fuller answer.)

In everyday life. The man was cleansed first and sent to the priest after: obedience follows the gift, and still has to be walked out. A person converted from fraud still needs to pay back what he took; a believer restored after a fall still needs the patient rebuilding of trust. The cleansing is his gift, complete; the process is for restoring the life around it.

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report went abroad. The instruction to keep quiet has failed. Mark tells us the man disobeyed and spread the news everywhere (Mark 1:45).

To hear and to be healed. To hear comes first, then to be healed, and Luke does not sneer at them. They want the word and they want their bodies mended, which is a perfectly reasonable pair of things to want.

But he would withdraw. The tense means it was his habit: the busier it got, the more he went away.

It inverts the usual assumption. In a growing ministry prayer seems a luxury. Jesus treats fruitfulness as a reason to pray more, not less.

The danger of crowds. The pressure of an admiring crowd, to be what they want and believe their estimate of you, is not resisted by good intentions. He met it by leaving. He took his sense of who he was from his Father’s voice, you are my beloved Son (3:22), not from theirs, and that is the only place where anyone is safe from the crowd.

Why did the Son of God need to pray? Because he was truly man, living in dependence on his Father, and because prayer is the communion of the Son with the Father, not a sign of lack. Hebrews says he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7). He did not pray because something was missing in him as God. As a true man he lived each day by trusting his Father, and he showed us what a human life lived wholly towards God looks like.

I am too busy to pray much. What do I do? Begin by being honest that busyness is the reason to pray more, not the excuse to pray less. Then be practical. Choose a fixed time, even fifteen minutes, before the day’s demands begin, and guard it as you would a meeting with your employer. Find a place, as he did: a room, a car parked before work, a walk. Use Scripture to guide your prayers, a psalm or the Lord’s Prayer, so that you are not left staring at a blank wall. And pray in the gaps, briefly and often, through the day (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Small, regular prayer will do more than occasional heroic efforts.

For worship. The one through whom all things were made went out alone to speak with his Father, and he still prays now: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He has never once grown too busy to pray for his own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Here the religious authorities appear in Luke for the first time: Pharisees and teachers of the law from Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem, seated, as if for an inspection. Four friends, blocked by the crowd, take the roof apart and lower a paralysed man in front of him, and Luke calls it faith: their faith, for the man himself says nothing and is simply carried.

Jesus forgives the man’s sins first. The scribes are right that only God can forgive sins, and wrong about the man in front of them. So Jesus does the thing that can be checked, the healing, as evidence for the claim that cannot: “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing shows the priority of Luke’s Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. Jesus removes the paralysis too, and he does not suggest it was caused by the man’s sin (compare John 9:3). But he deals first with what would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

He never disputes the scribes’ premise that forgiveness belongs to God alone; he acts on it, under the title of Daniel’s Son of Man (Daniel 7:13–14).
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends show what serious intercession looks like: not eloquence or technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish for somebody else.

And the faith Jesus saw was theirs. There are seasons of grief, depression, shame or exhaustion when a believer cannot get himself into the room, and somebody else has to do the carrying. This passage says the carrying counts.

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and teachers of the law. The religious authorities appear in Luke’s narrative for the first time, and they are sitting down. Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes (v. 21), experts in the law of Moses. They have come from every village and from Jerusalem: the gathering has the shape of an inspection. The conflict that will run through the Gospel begins here.

In the flow. Here begins a run of five scenes (5:17–6:11) in which Jesus’ authority meets the religious leaders: over sin, the company he keeps, fasting, and twice over the Sabbath. Each time the question underneath is, who is this?, and each time the opposition hardens (6:11).

Who were the Pharisees? A movement of devout laymen, numbering over six thousand in Herod’s day, according to Josephus, who were zealous to keep the law of Moses in every detail of daily life, and who added a large body of oral tradition to guard it. They tithed even their herbs, fasted twice a week, and kept strict rules about purity, food and the Sabbath. Ordinary people respected them as the most serious believers in Israel. Their fault was not that they cared about God’s law, which was good, but that they trusted in their own keeping of it and looked down on others (18:9). Paul had been one (Philippians 3:5), and some came to faith (Acts 15:5).

The power of the Lord. Luke states it before anything happens, like a stage direction. The Lord here means God. Jesus’ healing power was the power of God, by the Spirit (4:14), the Anointed One of the Nazareth reading at work (4:18, 21). The power of God is resting on the man the experts have come to examine, and not on them.

Carried. Outside, while the inspection proceeds, men are carrying a friend on a mat; Mark says four (Mark 2:3). Somebody had to decide it was worth a day, and carry a paralysed body through the streets, slowly and in public, to a house so full that there was no way in.

Seeking to bring him in. They did not see the crowd and go home. The man on the mat has not said a word and will not say one in the whole passage. Everything that is about to happen to him happens because other people would not give up on getting him in front of Jesus.

How do I carry someone to Jesus today? First, in prayer: name them before God, regularly and specifically, for years if need be. Then in friendship: time, practical help, meals, lifts, honest conversation. Bring them where Jesus is spoken of, to church, to a Bible study, to a Christian friend who can answer their questions, and when the moment comes, tell them plainly about him yourself. Carry them together with others, as these four did; it is too heavy a load for one person. And remember that your task is to bring them, not to heal them. That is his part.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes, experts in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No way in. The crowd was an obstacle, as crowds often are to those who need Jesus most (18:39; 19:3).

They went up on the roof. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside stair. Familiarity has made this scene charming, and it was not: a grown man on a stretcher, and a roof over a room packed with religious dignitaries, which they begin taking apart.

Through the tiles. Dust and debris must have come down on the heads of the seated Pharisees, and somebody’s property is being damaged with no evidence that anybody asked the owner. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order, and Luke, in the next verse, calls it faith. The friends did not have better theology than the men in the room; they had a friend they refused to leave outside.

Tiles or clay? One small detail draws the charge that Luke did not know Palestine. Mark says the men dug through the roof (Mark 2:4), which fits an ordinary Galilean house of beams, branches and packed clay; Luke says through the tiles. But tiled roofs were the normal Greek and Roman construction and had appeared in the towns of the region, and in any case Luke is writing for readers across the empire, who would picture a roof the moment he named its material. He is translating the scene into terms they could picture. Two writers describing the same hole for readers on different sides of the Mediterranean is not a contradiction. Either way, they made a hole in someone’s roof.

Into the midst before Jesus. Every effort in the scene ends at one spot: in front of Jesus, not the teachers from Jerusalem, who had the seats and the learning and no power to heal. Luke keeps moving the helpless to that same place (7:38; 17:16; 23:42). Faith is not particular about the route; it is certain about the destination, because there is no one else to bring a paralysed man to. Peter will say it in Jerusalem: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

The man who could do nothing. His entire contribution was to lie there. Luke he says Jesus saw their faith, and the man’s part in the sentence is as the thing being carried. People do get carried. There are seasons when a believer cannot pray, cannot come, cannot generate any momentum whatever, through grief, depression, exhaustion or shame, and the honest truth is that they will not get themselves into the room. Somebody else has to do the carrying, and the carrying counts.

I am the one who cannot pray right now. Am I failing? No. There are seasons of illness, grief and darkness when a Christian can hardly pray at all, and Scripture does not condemn him for it. The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26), Christ intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34), and God gives brothers and sisters to carry us. Let them. Tell one or two trusted friends that you are struggling and ask them to pray for you. Keep coming to church if you can, even if you only sit there. You are not less a Christian because you are on the mat for now.

In everyday life. Be persistent and creative in love: when the friend says no to church for the third time, try a meal at home; when a sick member cannot come, take the service to them. But creative love is not a licence to manipulate people, to trick them into a meeting, or to pressure them until they give in. The men broke a roof, not a person’s will. Bring people to Jesus; do not drag them.

For worship. Four men broke open a roof to bring their friend down to Jesus; he had broken open heaven to come down to us. He came by a lower road than any outside stair, to lie where the helpless lie: in a manger, at last in a borrowed tomb. We were the man on the mat, unable to move one muscle towards him, and he is the friend who would not leave us outside. Every rescue that ever ended at his feet began with his own descent.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek readers knew; Mark describes digging through a roof of packed earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he saw their faith. A hole in the roof is faith made visible. Our faith and prayers can matter for others.

Man, your sins are forgiven you. Nobody in that room expected that sentence. Jesus deals first, deliberately, with the deeper problem. The perfect tense means: your sins have been forgiven, and stand forgiven.

Was the man’s paralysis caused by his sin? Not necessarily, and the passage must be handled carefully because it can be heard cruelly. Jesus is not saying the paralysis does not matter; he removes it. He is not suggesting it was caused by the man’s sin; he says nothing of the kind here. Some Jews believed sickness was always caused by sin. Sometimes it is (John 5:14), though not always, and Jesus explicitly denies that reasoning about the man born blind (John 9:2–3). What he is doing is treating the deeper condition first, in a man who had not come about it and may not have known he had it. If you are ill, do not assume God is punishing you for something. All sickness belongs to a fallen world; your particular illness may have no link to any particular sin at all.

The deeper need. A man who is healed and unforgiven has been given a working body and a few more decades, and the account is still open. The greatest need of every person is forgiveness, and to be forgiven by God is to have the debt your sins have run up against him cancelled, not hidden. He does not bring it up again, now or at the judgment: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12).

Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Blasphemy is speaking against God, or claiming what belongs to him alone. The penalty was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). And notice where the charge is made: inwardly. They began to question, Luke says; they had not yet spoken it aloud (v. 22).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? Their theology is correct. Entirely correct. All sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). A person can forgive a wrong done to himself, but only God can forgive sins against God. That is not a Pharisaic invention; it is the plain teaching of the Old Testament: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25). Any faithful Jew in that room would have said the same. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the major premise right: only God forgives sins. They have the observation right: this man has just forgiven sins. And instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy. If Jesus is not God, he is a blasphemer. And Jesus does not leave them to take his word for it: in the next breath he offers evidence the whole room can check (v. 24). All through Luke, the people who reject Jesus are rarely those who understand him least; they are usually those who have grasped exactly what he is claiming.

Can someone else’s faith save a person? No. Luke does not say the paralysed man lacked faith, and the friends’ faith brought him to Jesus, which is what faith on behalf of others can do. We may carry others to Christ in prayer and witness, but each person must come to him in his own faith.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus perceived their thoughts. Jesus answers the argument going on inside their heads, and it is the LORD who sees and searches the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). It is another sign pointing to who he is.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk? The question is sharper than it looks, and the answer is not the obvious one. Which is easier to say? Plainly the first. Anyone can announce that a man’s sins are forgiven, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. Saying rise and walk to a paralysed man is the dangerous sentence: in three seconds everyone in the room will know whether it worked. In another sense, forgiveness is far harder, because it is a divine act, and would cost Jesus his life. Jesus will now do the visible, harder-to-say thing, to prove the invisible one.

That you may know. Jesus does the checkable one, and says why: a visible miracle as the credential for an invisible one. That is the logic of miracle throughout the Gospels. A Jesus who heals bodies and cannot deal with guilt would be a remarkable physician and no use at all at the end.

The Son of Man. Jesus’ most frequent name for himself, used here for the first time in Luke. It can sound modest; it was not. He is drawing on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man is given an everlasting dominion. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, choosing that title while forgiving sins was not a retreat from the claim. It was the claim, doubled.

On earth. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven, by God, at the appointed time and through the appointed sacrifices. Jesus says the authority is here, at ground level, in a crowded house in Capernaum, exercised by a man they can see. The thing the whole temple system existed to deal with has walked into a room and dealt with it, in one sentence, freely, for a man who did not ask.

Rise. Three commands, impossible for a paralysed man. The word of Jesus gives the power to obey, as his Spirit now does in us (Ezekiel 36:27). As Augustine prayed, give what you command, and command what you will.

How can I know my sins are really forgiven, when I cannot see it? By the same logic Jesus used here. You cannot see forgiveness, but you can see the one who grants it, and he has given you evidence enough: his miracles, his death, and above all his resurrection, by which God declared his sacrifice accepted (Romans 4:25). Your forgiveness does not rest on your feelings, which rise and fall, but on his word: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (Acts 10:43). If you have come to him trusting him, you are forgiven, as surely as that man walked. Feelings of guilt may linger; take them to his promise, not his promise to your feelings.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rose up before them. Luke lingers on the bed. The bed that had carried him, he now carried, out through the doorway they could not get him in by, past the seated dignitaries.

Glorifying God. Only Luke records his praise. Jesus sent him home. There was probably a house somewhere in Capernaum where a family had been carrying this man for years, and that evening he walked in on his own feet, carrying the mat, to tell them what God had done.

Amazement. Now the crowd too glorifies God, with awe, not admiration of a technique: all of them, which in that room includes the delegation from Jerusalem.

Extraordinary things. The word is paradoxa: things contrary to expectation. And the thing most contrary to expectation was not finally the walking man. It was that God’s own prerogative had been exercised, out loud, by a man on earth. The paradox would deepen. The one with authority to forgive would be counted a blasphemer, crucified and raised on the third day, so that forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). The crowd saw the first page of it.

Amazed and unchanged. Luke does not say they believed; he says they were amazed and afraid, and by chapter 6 the scribes and Pharisees among them will be watching him to accuse him (6:7). Amazement is not faith. The man who went home with the mat had been forgiven; the men who went home with an anecdote had only been impressed.

For worship. The four friends came for a pair of working legs and went home with a forgiven friend. And that street in Capernaum, loud with praise, is a foretaste of the morning when the lame will leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6), every mat will be rolled up for the last time, and the whole forgiven company will glorify God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and calls him with two words. To every devout passer-by Levi was beyond the pale, and unlike the fishermen, he could never go back to his booth.

His first act as a disciple is a great feast for the only people he knows, tax collectors and others, with Jesus in the middle. The Pharisees and their scribes complain to the disciples, and theirs is a serious question, since to share a table was to declare acceptance. Jesus answers with a doctor’s logic: the sick need a physician, and he came to call sinners to repentance. Everyone in that house was sick; the difference lay in what they knew about themselves.
verseByVerse.theology:
Levi is Matthew (Matthew 9:9): the kingdom comes to the most unexpected people.

Jesus’ saying about calling not the righteous but sinners does not divide humanity into those who need him and those who do not, for “none is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). It describes two self-assessments. Much of the Pharisees’ theology was sound; their trouble was their self-knowledge. They could not be called to repentance because they did not believe they needed it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi’s banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace: no method, just a house, his friends, and Jesus in the same room.

The wish to keep the table clean rests on a real principle, that holiness is kept by separation. What it has not reckoned with is a holiness that travels outward, as it did at the leper’s skin. Jesus’ table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tax collector named Levi. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); he had both names, as Simon was also Peter and Saul was also Paul. Levi probably collected tolls for Herod Antipas on goods passing along the trade route through Capernaum.

Sitting at the tax booth. At work, in the place of his sin. To everyone walking past Levi is a collaborator, a thief with legal protection (see 3:12), and, in many eyes, ritually unclean from contact with Gentiles. And he was very probably rich.

Follow me. No preliminaries, no probation. Nothing in Levi’s life made the call reasonable; the call made Levi. It is the voice that had just said rise to a paralysed man (v. 24), and it works the same way: the command carries the power to obey it. The Son of Man who has authority on earth to forgive sins spends it on him, in public, at the booth.

Leaving everything. The same phrase as at verse 11, and for Levi it costs differently. The fishermen could go back to their boats (John 21:3); there is no going back to a tax booth once you have walked away from one. Money had been Levi’s security, and his compensation for everyone’s contempt. When Christ called, it lost its grip in a moment, because something greater had taken its place. That is how idols usually fall: not by being argued down, but by being outshone.

The man who wrote it down. The man rising from that booth is the man the church has long believed wrote the Gospel that opens the New Testament, and only its apostle list calls him Matthew the tax collector (Matthew 10:3), as though he never got over it.

What did Levi do about the money he had taken? Luke does not tell us, but Zacchaeus, another tax collector, shows what repentance looked like for such a man: he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid anyone he had defrauded fourfold (19:8). Following Christ does not wipe out our obligations to people we have wronged. Grace forgives the sin before God freely and completely; it also makes us want to put right what we can. If you have cheated someone, the gospel does not ask you to earn forgiveness by repaying, but it will lead you, gladly, to repay.

In everyday life. No one is beyond Christ’s call. Picture the person you consider least likely to become a Christian. Levi was that man in Capernaum. Pray for them as for a future disciple.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew’s Gospel calls Levi “Matthew.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great feast. Levi’s first act as a disciple is to throw a party. He has no theology yet; he has a house and a contact list.

A large company. Luke’s polite way of describing the social world a man in that trade moved in. He fills the room with the only people he knows, the outcasts, and puts Jesus in the middle of it. It is not a strategy. It is a man who has been given something and wants the people he cares about to meet the one who gave it.

Reclining at table with them. To recline at a man’s table was to declare peace with him, to accept him, to be publicly associated with him. It was closer to a signed statement than to a meal.

They grumbled. The word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8). And they complain, not to Jesus, but round him to his disciples. It is an old form of religious criticism: raise it with the followers, where it will do most damage and cost least.

Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? The objection is worth understanding rather than dismissing. The Pharisees kept themselves separate from sinners: those who did not keep the law as they interpreted it, and the openly immoral. Eating with them would make you unclean. The Pharisees are not complaining about the menu; they are asking a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God, and by their own logic they are entirely right to ask it. Their premise is that holiness is preserved by separation: that you keep clean by keeping away. It is not a stupid premise. It is much of the book of Leviticus, and it had kept Israel identifiable through centuries of pressure. What they have not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round. Luke has just shown it, and they had no category for it: a hand stretched out to a leper, and the cleanness travelling from the toucher to the touched (5:13). To the Pharisees, holiness meant separation from sinners. For Jesus, it meant going to them. The charge will come again (7:34; 15:2; 19:7).

But does the Bible not tell us to avoid bad company? Yes: bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), and we are not to walk in the counsel of the wicked (Psalm 1:1). The difference is the direction of influence and the purpose of the friendship. Jesus ate with sinners as their physician, and he was never drawn into their sin; they were drawn to him. Paul says Christians must not keep close company with someone who calls himself a brother and lives in open sin, but he does not mean the immoral of this world, or you would need to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). So be a friend to unbelievers, with open doors and real love; but if a friendship is pulling you into sin rather than you drawing them to Christ, step back.

In everyday life. Levi’s method is open to anyone: a meal, a house, and the people you already know. Invite a neighbour and a Christian friend to dinner together; open your home at Christmas to someone who would otherwise be alone. He receives sinners and eats with them (15:2), and every one of us is at his table only because he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A physician. A proverb nobody can disagree with. A doctor found among the sick is not compromising his profession; he is doing it. He does not catch their disease; he heals it. So the question, why do you eat with sinners?, answers itself the moment you know what he came for.

I have not come to call the righteous. The word is ironic. Jesus is not conceding that the Pharisees are righteous: none is righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10, quoting the Psalms). He is using their own self-description back at them.

Everyone in the house is sick. The difference between the two groups at Levi’s dinner is not their condition but what they know about themselves. The tax collectors are aware of it; the men in the doorway are not. And a man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor however available the doctor makes himself. The Pharisees were disciplined and orthodox, and their diagnosis of themselves was wrong in the one direction that refuses treatment. It takes God himself to open such eyes, as he later opened the eyes of a Pharisee named Saul, who came to count all his religious gain as loss for Christ (Acts 9:18; Philippians 3:4–9).

But sinners to repentance. Only Luke adds to repentance. Repentance is a turning round: coming to agree with God about your sin, and leaving it to come to him (Acts 26:20). The table at Levi’s house is a doctor’s visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease. Grace receives sinners and changes them.

Does that mean Jesus accepts me as I am? Yes, and he will not leave you as you are. He receives anyone who comes to him, however sinful, without first requiring that he be cleaned up; the leper came full of leprosy, and Levi came straight from the booth. That is why you need not wait until you are better to come. But the same Jesus calls you to repentance, and his acceptance is the beginning of a new life, not a seal of approval on the old one. You come as you are; you do not stay as you are. Both halves are love.

For worship. The Great Physician makes house calls, and he goes to the worst cases first, because he loved the diseased. His remedy is costly as no earthly doctor’s ever was: by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). He has never yet lost a patient who put himself in his hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Asked why his disciples do not fast like John’s disciples and the Pharisees, Jesus answers with two images and an observation. The bridegroom image is a claim about identity: in the Old Testament the bridegroom of Israel is God himself (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19). Fasting at a wedding is not more serious; it is out of time. Then the shadow: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days”, the first hint of the cross in Jesus’ own teaching in Luke.

The garment and the wineskins press the point. What Jesus brings is not a patch on the old system but its fulfilment, and the old forms, though God gave them, were never designed to hold it. The last saying describes a palate: people settled in the old say it is good enough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language places Jesus where the prophets place the LORD, and Revelation carries the image to the end: the marriage supper of the Lamb and the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride (Revelation 19:7–9; 21:2).

Verse 39 describes people content with something genuinely good, the law and the tradition God gave, in the presence of something better. They had not chosen something bad, and that is what made their position so dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom’s presence is the reason for Christian joy, and the resurrection confirmed it. Christian fasting is the fast of people who have known him, live between his going and his return, and want him back: not a technique for getting God’s attention, but a body saying what the heart already knows.

The wineskins test every tradition honestly. Not, is this old? Age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life? The wine is always the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They fast often. The third complaint of the section, and the observation is accurate. The law commanded only one yearly fast (Leviticus 16:29), but Pharisees fasted twice a week (18:12), and John’s followers were austere, and their teacher was in prison.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? He answers with a wedding. A Jewish wedding feast could last up to a week and was a time of joy, and later Jewish writings say that wedding guests were excused from certain religious duties, including fasting. Fasting expressed mourning, sorrow and longing. The point is not that fasting is wrong. It is that fasting at a wedding is absurd. It is not more serious; it is out of time. While Jesus is here, the time of longing is over.

The bridegroom. The image does much more than settle a dispute about diet. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God. Your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5); as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isaiah 62:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19–20). So when Jesus says the bridegroom is present, he is placing himself where the Old Testament places God (compare John 3:29). The messianic wedding feast has begun.

Taken away. Then the shadow. A bridegroom does not leave his own wedding feast; the word suggests a removal by force (Isaiah 53:8). This is the first hint of the cross in Jesus’ own teaching in Luke, and nobody at that table could have understood it.

Then they will fast. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Fasting is right for Christians now, as we long for his return. But it is no longer a mark of mourning without hope, nor a means of earning favour.

Should Christians fast, and how? Jesus plainly assumes it: they will fast in those days, and those days are these. But it is not the fast of the men asking the question. It is the fast of people who have known the bridegroom, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God’s attention. A body saying what the heart already knows. In practice, fasting means going without food, or some meals, for a set time in order to give that time to prayer: before a big decision, in a time of repentance, in grief, or in longing for God’s work. Do it quietly, not for show (Matthew 6:16–18). Begin modestly, with one meal; take medical advice if you have a health condition; and never treat it as earning anything from God. And do not make your own pattern of fasting a rule for others, or look down on Christians who do not fast as you do: that is exactly the error of the men who asked the question.

For worship. The bridegroom of Israel came in person and sat down at a feast, knowing he would be snatched away to a cross for his bride, to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Our fasting now is the longing of a bride whose bridegroom has gone ahead, and our feasting the foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement. A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable. Three short parables (vv. 36–39) explain why Jesus’ disciples do not follow the old patterns.

A new garment. Luke’s version is sharper than the others. Matthew and Mark speak of unshrunk cloth on an old garment (Mark 2:21); Luke has a man cutting up a new garment to patch an old one. The loss is doubled.

The point. Has Jesus come to repair Judaism, the same religion with better preaching and fresh material sewn over the worn places? No. What he brings is entirely new: the kingdom of God, and the new covenant that he will seal in his own blood (22:20). It cannot be stitched onto the old ways of fasting and rule-keeping without ruining both. The gospel is not a supplement to religion; it is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The old garment was not bad. God gave it, and Jesus honours it: he sends the leper to the priest and goes to the synagogue weekly. It is not being criticised. It is being finished with, because what it was for has come.

How the saying is abused. The saying is abused in both directions. Some use it to junk the creeds and twenty centuries of the church’s thinking. But the newness in this parable is not new ideas. It is the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, which is the oldest thing there is. Others treat every inherited practice as a doctrine, which is the Pharisees’ error exactly. What is genuinely new is a person, a covenant sealed in his blood, and a Spirit poured out on ordinary people.

In everyday life. Do not treat Jesus as a patch on your old life: church added to the week but the business kept dishonest, prayer added to the marriage but the temper unchecked. Becoming new does not mean discarding your family, culture or honest gifts; Christ takes them up and makes them his.

For worship. He did not come to tailor a patch for a worn religion. He came with a whole new garment, and he cut it from his own life: the righteousness he wove in years of perfect obedience, given entire to people who had nothing to wear but rags, the robe of righteousness Isaiah sang of in the chapter Jesus read at Nazareth (Isaiah 61:10). Now he wraps sinners from head to foot in what he alone has made, and not one thread of it is theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wineskins. The same point, with a better image. New wine is still fermenting and expanding. A new goatskin stretched with it; an old one was set hard.

Both are lost. This is not a saying about how the old is expendable. It is a warning that forcing new life into hardened forms wastes the life and wrecks the form.

Fresh wineskins. Must (blēteon): it is necessary. (Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and both are preserved; the earliest do not.) The point is not that novelty is good. It is that living things expand, and whatever contains them has to be able to give. That was true of the first Christian generation in the most literal way. Within thirty years the gospel had gone to Gentiles with no food laws, no temple and no priesthood, told that the whole apparatus had been a shadow of what had now come (Colossians 2:17). Not because the shadow was false, but because the substance had arrived.

How do I tell a wineskin from the wine in my own church? Ask whether a thing is commanded in Scripture or chosen by people. The gospel, the preaching of the word, prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the ordering of the church and the moral law are given by God; they are the wine and must not move. The time of the service, the style of music, the order of worship, the building, the translation used, are human choices, wineskins; they may be good and well loved, and they may be changed when they no longer carry the life. Not, is this old? Age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown? What must never move is the wine. Everything else is leather.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only Luke adds this saying. A wry comment on human nature, often misread.

Old wine. Old wine is smooth; new wine is raw. People used to the old will not even try the new. He is not commending old wine. He is describing a palate.

The old is good. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read better, but the best read good: the old is good enough. Why change? Having settled into something, we will always find a reason not to change. And the old is good, which is what makes it so hard to leave.

The point. This is why the Pharisees and many others reject him. Their problem was never that they had chosen something bad. They had something genuinely good, a law given by God, real discipline, real Scripture, and they were comfortable in it, and it had made the arrival of something better feel like a disturbance rather than a fulfilment.

The new wine was standing in front of them. What they refused to taste was not a recipe but a person. The bridegroom was at the table (v. 34), and the one of whom Moses and all the prophets had written was reclining at Levi’s feast (24:27). Their old wine was good because it had come from him, and it had been laid down for this very day. To prefer it to him was to prefer the promise to the one who kept it. The old covenant was never meant to be held against Christ; it was meant to make Israel thirsty for him.

A dangerous spiritual position. It requires a good thing to settle into. Levi could be reached in two words; the men outside had spent a lifetime acquiring a taste that made the new wine unpalatable. If you fear this describes you, take heart: the truly comfortable rarely worry about being comfortable, and the Lord who reached Levi in two words is well able to reach a settled heart. Honest questions about Jesus are another matter, and Luke wrote his Gospel to answer them (1:1–4).

In the flow. This saying closes the chapter and explains it. A fisherman, a leper, a paralysed man and a tax collector have tasted the new wine, while the experts objected; the Sabbath scenes that follow (6:1–11) show the same palate at work. The dividing line runs not between the religious and the irreligious but between those who know they need what Jesus brings and those who are content without him.

Does this mean tradition is bad and new is always better? No. Jesus is not saying that whatever is new is from God; many novelties in the church’s history have been errors. The new wine is not a new idea but himself, the fulfilment of everything the old covenant promised. And Scripture tells us to hold fast to the traditions of the apostles (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The warning is against a heart so settled in its religion that it no longer needs Christ, or cannot hear him when he does not taste like what it is used to.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke adds this saying — a wry comment on those content with the old ways.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth.
