And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Chapter 6 holds Luke’s counterpart to Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount: shorter, sharper, and close to it without being identical. Before the sermon come two Sabbath controversies and the choosing of the Twelve, and they raise the question the sermon assumes: by what authority does Jesus say what is lawful, and what kind of people does that authority gather? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) describes life under the reign of God.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) reverse the world’s values: the poor, the hungry and the weeping are blessed; the rich, the full and the laughing are warned. Poverty is not made a virtue, nor comfort a sin, but God’s blessing runs towards those the world has left behind, and challenges those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from him.

The heart of the sermon (vv. 27–45), love your enemies, do not judge, bear good fruit, rests on the character of God: love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. The house on the rock closes it with a warning: hearing these words is not enough, and only the life built on Christ, hearing and doing what he says, will stand when the storm comes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

In the first, the objection is not theft (Deuteronomy 23:25) but the day: by the scribes’ rules, plucking was reaping. Jesus answers from 1 Samuel 21, where David, God’s anointed king, rejected and on the run, ate the holy bread with his men, and concludes: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath, a claim to stand where the Lawgiver stands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath was God’s own institution, rooted in creation (Genesis 2:2–3), set in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8–11), and named the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel (Exodus 31:12–17). To call himself its lord is to claim authority over God’s own covenant sign, one of the clearest claims to deity in the first three Gospels. And this lordship is for giving rest, not abolishing it.
verseByVerse.examples: The grain-field complaint shows what happens when a law loses touch with what it was for. The Sabbath was given as a gift: rest for working people, and a sign of trust that God would provide. Layer on layer of rules had turned it into a burden. Jesus does not abolish the day; he frees it from what had buried it. The same drift can happen in any church, with no bad motives.

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 6 shows the Lord of the Sabbath forming a new people and teaching them how to live. In two Sabbath conflicts Jesus claims authority over God’s own law, and his enemies begin to plot. He answers with a night of prayer and the choice of twelve apostles, a new Israel gathered around himself. Then, on a level place, he preaches the life of his kingdom: mercy received from the Father, and mercy given to everyone else.

The Sabbath controversies. Two conflicts over the Sabbath (vv. 1–11) follow the conflicts over forgiveness, table company and fasting in chapter 5. The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest (Exodus 20:8–11), was one of the great marks of Jewish identity, along with circumcision and the food laws. The KJV’s on the second sabbath after the first (v. 1) follows later manuscripts; the earliest simply say on a Sabbath, so most modern Bibles omit the phrase.

Rubbing them in their hands. It is the most ordinary thing in the chapter, and it starts a fight that ends at a cross. Only Luke mentions the rubbing, to remove the husks. Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field while walking through was explicitly allowed by the law: you may pluck the ears with your hand (Deuteronomy 23:25).

Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? The objection was not theft but the day. By the Pharisees’ rules, plucking was reaping, and rubbing was threshing and winnowing. Which sounds absurd until you understand where the reasoning came from, and it is worth being fair to them, because caricature makes the passage useless. The fourth commandment forbids work on the Sabbath and does not define work. So the rabbis, trying to obey, drew up definitions, and reaping and threshing were among them. And around those definitions they built what they called a fence: additional restrictions, so that a man would stop well short of the actual line and never break the commandment by accident. The Mishnah’s tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters. None of that began in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people who had watched their nation go into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment (Jeremiah 17:27).

A gift turned into an audit. But a day of rest and delight (Isaiah 58:13), given to relieve working people, had acquired a body of case law that only the leisured could master. The drift needs no bad motives, only this: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule, and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of what the thing was for. And underneath the rules a quieter danger grows. A man who can keep every category of labour can begin to feel that he has kept God, and then the rules stop guarding a gift and become a scoreboard, with his own name near the top and other people’s further down.

Is it wrong to have church rules and customs that the Bible does not command? No. Every church needs some ordered customs: a time for the service, an order of worship, a way of receiving members. Wise guidelines can protect good things, such as a family deciding to keep Sunday free of sport so that they can worship together. The error comes when a human rule is treated as God’s law, binding other people’s consciences (Mark 7:8), or when the rule is kept at the expense of the very people it was meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we choose it? If we chose it, hold it gladly and lightly, and never let it stand between a hungry person and bread.

He answers for his men. The charge is laid against the disciples, but it is aimed at the one they follow: in Mark’s telling the Pharisees put it to Jesus himself (Mark 2:24), and in Luke it is Jesus who answers (v. 3). He does not leave them to defend themselves; he steps between his hungry friends and their accusers and takes the question onto himself. That is the shape of his whole work. When the accuser speaks against his people, it is Christ who answers: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is Christ Jesus who died, who was raised, who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you not read. Put to men whose life’s work was reading. The episode is 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came with a handful of men and no food to the priest Ahimelech at Nob, where the tabernacle then probably stood, and asked for bread. The only bread was the holy bread.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on a golden table in the Holy Place before the Lord each Sabbath, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The argument. Scripture records without a word of censure that David, God’s anointed king, not yet on his throne, and his men ate the holy bread in a time of need. If David could do that, the Son of David and his followers can do much more. Jesus is not saying that rules do not matter or that hunger dissolves the law, but that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and its ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. He appeals to Scripture, against a reading of it: God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 12:7).

Why David? There is a further thing in the choice of story, and the men listening would have felt it. Of all the possible precedents he reaches for the one about God’s anointed king, on the run, rejected, with his own small band of followers, doing something the authorities would call unlawful. The parallel is not accidental and it is not subtle. Here is another anointed king, gathering another company, being told by the officials of the day that what he does is not lawful. If David’s men could eat, so can his. Which means the argument is not chiefly about corn at all. It is about who this is, and Jesus is about to say so out loud: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

Does this mean I may break God’s commands when I am in need? No. The holy bread was a ceremonial law, about the use of sacred objects, and it was always meant to serve life. God’s moral law, do not steal, do not lie, do not commit adultery, is never set aside for convenience or need; David did wrong when he lied to the priest in this same chapter (1 Samuel 21:2). The lesson is not that hunger excuses sin, but that God’s law is kind, and that its outward ceremonies were never meant to be used against the hungry and the suffering.

For worship. David had to ask a priest for the holy bread, handed out through a door he could not enter. The Son of David asks no one. He is himself the Presence before whom those twelve loaves were laid. And at the last he is the bread: on the night he was betrayed he took bread, broke it, and gave his own body to his apostles. What only priests could eat at Nob, he gives to every hungry sinner who comes to him.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord of the Sabbath. Among the largest claims Jesus ever made. The Sabbath was no custom that could be rearranged. God instituted it at creation (Genesis 2:2–3), spoke it from the mountain in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:8–11), and named it the sign of his covenant with Israel for ever (Exodus 31:17). There is no institution in Judaism more directly God’s than this one. And a Galilean carpenter says he is its lord.

No soft reading. To be lord of the Sabbath is to have authority over God’s own law, to determine its meaning and use. He does not say the Sabbath is unimportant, or that his disciples were within the rabbinic rules after all. A man may say the Sabbath has been misunderstood. Only its author can say he is its lord. Mark adds: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man. The figure of Daniel 7:13–14, who receives everlasting dominion: it sounds humble in English; it was not. So the quarrel over a handful of grain has arrived at the question the whole Gospel is about: not, what may be done on the Sabbath? but, who is this? The Pharisees are quite right to be alarmed. A man who says this is either speaking blasphemy or telling the truth, and Luke sets that choice squarely before his reader.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians must keep Saturday. Many Reformed and Puritan Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8 and the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday, the “Christian Sabbath”, to be kept by resting from work and recreation and devoting the day to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, is the church’s day of gathering for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and it is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The Westminster and 1689 view, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

Lord in order to give rest. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest but to give it back: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The day pictured God’s rest after his finished work, and Israel’s rest from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). In Christ that rest is given in full. He rested in the tomb on the seventh day and rose on the first, and whoever trusts him stops working to earn God’s favour, because Christ has finished the work (Hebrews 4:10). We do not work towards our rest; we begin from it.

So how should I spend Sunday? Begin with gathering: the Lord’s Day is first of all the day his people meet to hear his word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper, and that should be the fixed point around which the day is arranged. Then rest: make room for what refreshes body and soul, family, a walk, a meal with others, visiting the lonely, reading. Christians who hold the stricter Sabbath view will set aside work and ordinary recreation for the whole day, and they are to be respected for it; others will use more freedom. Whichever conviction you hold, do not judge the brother who differs (Romans 14:5–6), and do not let the day become either a burden or just another day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second controversy concerns a man whose working hand was withered, and critics watching to find a charge. Jesus’ question, whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, removes the neutral ground they stood on: to be able to relieve suffering and decline is itself a choice. Then Jesus heals with a word, and the response is fury, the first plotting against him in Luke.
verseByVerse.theology: The fury of verse 11 begins the road that ends at the cross. It is theological as much as moral: Jesus has claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their reading of it, and refused to be intimidated. Either he is a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided, and these Sabbath disputes are the opening moves of the conflict that leads to Calvary.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man is told to stand up in the middle, in front of everyone, with his disability on display, and he does. A need kept hidden at the edge of the church is often a need left unmet.

And the Christian life often follows the order of this healing: the command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength comes in the obeying, from the Lord who gives what he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. A different Sabbath, the same question, and this time Jesus’ critics are watching him, not his men. The run of conflicts that began at 5:17 reaches its height here, and ends with the first plotting against him (v. 11).

Right hand. Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand: the working hand. In a manual economy that is not an inconvenience; it is the end of a man’s ability to earn. Withered means shrunken, paralysed.

Watched him. The word means spied on. They are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. The man’s hand is of no interest to them except as evidence. Religion that has stopped serving God and started defending itself can sit in a service, look at a suffering man, and see an opportunity. By the rabbis’ rule, healing counted as work, and was allowed on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand could wait until tomorrow.

He knew their thoughts. As at 5:22. Only God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10). So he walks into the trap knowing it is a trap. He could protect himself by doing nothing until sundown. He will not buy his own safety with this man’s withered hand. Here, in one small room, is the whole pattern of his ministry: he sees exactly what mercy will cost him, and he chooses mercy, all the way to the cross.

Stand in the middle. He could have healed the man quietly afterwards. Instead he puts him in the centre of the room, in full view of his critics. The man has probably spent years managing a disability from the edge of the room, and he now stands in the middle of it with his hand exposed and a row of officials staring. Some help cannot be received privately.

Should I deliberately provoke people who oppose me? No. Jesus did not seek conflict for its own sake; he sought the man’s good and the truth, and refused to let fear of critics hide either. Christians are to live peaceably with all, as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and to answer opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). What this verse forbids is the opposite fault: doing good only when no critic is watching, or abandoning what is right because someone is waiting to accuse you. Be quiet where quietness serves; be open where hiding would mean failing someone.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To do good or to do harm. They came prepared for a different argument: healing is work, this condition is not life-threatening, and a hand withered for years can wait until sundown, which, on their own terms, is reasonable. Jesus refuses the terms. He reframes the question: not, is healing work?, but, what is the Sabbath for? By pairing doing good with its opposite he removes the middle ground they were standing on. There is no neutral square marked, wait until tomorrow. To fail to do good when you can is to do harm.

To save life or to destroy it? Life (psychē) can also mean soul. And the irony: Jesus is doing good on the Sabbath, while his critics are plotting to destroy him on the Sabbath (v. 11).

Stricter, not laxer. Their rule asked what may be avoided. His asks what may be done, and a day designed by a God who never stops sustaining his creation cannot be a day for withholding mercy.

Looking around at them all. A long, searching look. Mark says with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). In that silence they have already answered.

Stretch out your hand. Jesus did no work that could be charged: no touch, no medicine, just a word. And the word asks the one thing this man cannot do; it is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first, so that he could then obey. He is told to do the impossible thing, and in the doing of it he discovers it is possible. That is very often the order: the command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. Forgive, he says, to a heart that cannot; love your enemy, to a will that refuses; and the one who commands is the one who gives (Philippians 2:12–13).

But I cannot obey. What do I do with a command I have no strength to keep? Do what the man did: try, in dependence on Christ. Do not wait until you feel able; you may never feel able. Ask him for help, and then take the first small step he commands: the first sentence of the apology, the first prayer for your enemy, the first refusal of the old habit. God works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13), and very often his strength is felt only in the moving. If you fail, confess it, receive his forgiveness, and stretch out your hand again tomorrow.

For worship. He did not touch the hand. He spoke, as he spoke on the first day of the world, and it was so, because the one standing in that synagogue is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He saved life on the Sabbath while they sat counting how to destroy it, and in the end he let them destroy his, so that withered sinners might live.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Filled with fury. The word (anoias) means senselessness, folly: a rage that has stopped thinking. And it is the response to a man’s hand being made whole. A disabled man in their own congregation can work again, and the reaction of the religious leadership is not joy but a plot.

What they might do to Jesus. Mark says they began to plot with the Herodians how to destroy him (Mark 3:6). Luke’s wording is milder at this stage, but the direction is clear. From here the shadow does not lift.

Why such rage? Not because they were unusually wicked men. Because he had made their position untenable in public, and they were not willing to revise it. Fury is what a framework does when it has been exposed and its owners have decided to keep it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were. So the mind goes past the argument to the arguer. If the position cannot be defended, remove the man who exposed it.

An ordinary mechanism. It happens in churches and families, wherever somebody has said something true that cannot be answered, and the response is not to weigh it but to discredit the person who said it. The fury feels like conviction from the inside. It is nearly always the sound of a defence that has run out.

Hated for doing good. Here, for the first time, the leaders of Israel begin to plan against him, and the cause is not any wrong he did but the good. He is the one man who has ever lived without sin, and the nearer his goodness comes to sinners, the more it is resented, because light exposes (John 3:19–20). Yet he does not withdraw his goodness to save himself. He goes on healing the people who will cry for his death, and he dies for enemies (Romans 5:10). The fury in this room is the first shadow of the cross, and he walks towards it of his own will.

How do I know whether my anger is righteous? Righteous anger is anger at what grieves God, for the sake of others, and it stays under control and seeks good. Jesus was angry in this very scene (Mark 3:5), grieved at hardness of heart, and he healed the man. Sinful anger is usually about me: my position, my pride, my being shown up, and it seeks to hurt. Ask: what exactly am I angry about? Would God be angry at it? Does my anger make me want to help someone, or to win? Be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26); and if you find you are furious with someone who has told you the truth, stop and listen before you speak.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
After the first plot against him, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve.

From the wider band of disciples he chooses twelve, a number no Jew could hear by accident: Israel had twelve tribes. He is gathering a renewed people of God, and he names these men apostles, sent ones.

The list is a study in unlikely company: Peter, who had begged Jesus to leave him; Matthew the tax collector; Simon the Zealot; men of whom we know nothing but their names. And it ends with Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are sent ones, commissioned witnesses, and their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus is the foundation of the church’s preaching: the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20).

Judas, chosen with the others after that night, is a weight the reader may not set down. Being chosen for an office is not the same as being saved, and nearness to Christ is no protection on its own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Not every decision needs a night of prayer, but the decisions that shape God’s people belong first to the Father, and leaders, elders and appointment committees may fairly ask whether they have prayed as seriously as the decision deserves.

And the Twelve rebuke churches divided along political lines. If a former agent of the revenue and a man called the Zealot could share a purse for three years, the divisions that keep Christians out of the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
All night in prayer. Luke has just recorded the first plot against him. The next thing he records, and only he records it, is a night on a hillside, alone, from dark to first light. It is the longest of Luke’s prayers (3:21; 5:16), before the largest decision of his ministry so far. What he said we are not told. What Luke gives us is the proportion: a whole night, for twelve men, and Judas among them.

Chose from them twelve. Two stages, and the wording matters. He called the disciples, a larger group of followers (Luke will mention seventy-two later, 10:1, where some manuscripts read seventy), and from them he chose an inner circle. Twelve is not a convenient number: Israel had twelve tribes, and a Jew could not hear it accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is reconstituting the people of God around himself, and a man does not lay the foundations of Israel unless he is entitled to. At the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them the names of these men (Revelation 21:14).

Apostles. Apostle (apostolos) means one who is sent, an envoy, an authorised representative. They would be sent with his authority to preach (9:1–2), and after his resurrection, to be his witnesses to the world (24:48; Acts 1:8).

The apostles’ unique role. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22), commissioned directly by him, and laid the foundation of the church through their teaching, which we have in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). The New Testament also uses the word loosely of messengers (2 Corinthians 8:23), but no one now can be an eyewitness of the risen Lord, so the foundation is not laid again.

Two decisions. The men who decide he must be destroyed made their decision in fury, after a service. His was made alone, on a mountain, after a night of asking his Father, and it is the one that is still standing.

If Jesus prayed all night and still chose Judas, did his prayer fail? No. Jesus chose Judas knowingly: did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil (John 6:70). Prayer is not a way of getting a guarantee that everything will go smoothly; it is submitting our choices to the Father’s will, and the Father’s will included the betrayal, through which the Scriptures would be fulfilled and the world redeemed (Acts 2:23). So when you pray before a decision and it later brings pain, do not conclude that you missed God’s guidance. He may have led you exactly where he meant to, for purposes you cannot yet see.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four lists. The Twelve are listed four times in the New Testament (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). The order varies, but Peter is always first, and in the three Gospel lists Judas Iscariot is always last (Acts, written after his death, names only eleven). They fall into three groups of four, each headed by the same name (Peter, Philip, James son of Alphaeus).

Peter. Peter (Petros, Aramaic Kēphas) means rock (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). This is the fisherman who once begged Jesus to depart from him because he was a sinful man (5:8).

The one who gives new names. In Scripture it is God who renames: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, each name a promise of what God would make of the man. Jesus does the same thing with the same authority. He calls Simon a rock before there is anything rock-like about him, and the rest of Luke’s two books show him keeping his word: the man who denies him three times by a fire in a courtyard stands up at Pentecost and preaches Christ to the city that crucified him. The list of the Twelve is a list of what Christ does with people. He takes them as they are, and names them for what his grace will make them.

Andrew his brother. Who first brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:40–42).

James and John. Sons of Zebedee, fishermen (5:10). James was the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John, by early church tradition, wrote the Gospel, letters and Revelation.

Philip, and Bartholomew. Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Bartholomew (son of Tolmai) is probably the Nathanael of John 1:45–51, since he is paired with Philip.

Matthew. The tax collector at the booth in chapter 5, whom Luke calls Levi (5:27); Matthew’s own Gospel names the man at the booth Matthew (Matthew 9:9). A man who took money from his own people on behalf of the ruling power.

Thomas. The twin (John 11:16), remembered for his doubt and his great confession: my Lord and my God! (John 20:28).

James the son of Alphaeus. Possibly James the younger (Mark 15:40). Of him the Gospels record nothing but a name, and several of the Twelve are almost unknown. They gave their lives to this, and history kept only that they were chosen.

The Zealot. Zealot may mean zealous for the law, or a member of the nationalist movement that wanted to overthrow Rome by force. Whatever precise stage the movement had reached by this date, the label meant a man of fierce conviction.

Enemies at one table. So in one company of twelve, Jesus may have put a former agent of the revenue and a man who believed such agents were traitors. In ordinary life these two would not have shared a road, let alone a purse. Whatever holds a church together, it is not political agreement, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be. If Matthew and Simon could eat from the same bag, the divisions that make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

Judas the son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark; the same man with two names. Also called Judas (not Iscariot) in John 14:22.

Who became a traitor. Luke’s terrible parenthesis. He was not chosen as a traitor, but became one. He heard and saw everything they did, was sent out with power like the rest, and held the money bag (John 12:6). It should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time: outward closeness to Jesus is no guarantee of a true heart.

Could I become a Judas? Can a true Christian fall away? A true believer cannot finally be lost; those whom Christ has given eternal life will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28–29). Judas was never a true believer, though he looked like one; Jesus called him a devil while he walked with the Twelve (John 6:70), John tells us that Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), and Jesus said he was lost so that Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12). So the warning is not meant to terrify true believers but to wake up false ones. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is itself a good sign: Judas felt remorse, but he never turned to Christ for mercy (Matthew 27:3–5). Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and run to Christ; no one who comes to him is cast out (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon begins with blessings spoken straight to the disciples, blessed are you, and Luke pairs them with woes Matthew does not include: the poor and the rich, the hungry and the full, those who weep and those who laugh.

Luke says simply poor, where Matthew says poor in spirit, and neither is safe alone. The kingdom belongs to those who have nothing to trust but God, and the poor usually know it first.

The woes are the prophets’ cry of grief, not a curse: those who have received their consolation have been paid already. The last beatitude is about what the disciples suffer for Christ, and the command attached is not endurance but leaping for joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes express the great reversal Mary sang of: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty (1:51–53).

And the reversal is anchored in Christ, who entered the conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the one who was made poor so that we might be made rich. The woes are mercy raising its voice, a warning to the comfortable before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples: The beatitudes comfort those who suffer, and they also search everyone else: in which column do you stand? The woes need honest application, because by the world’s measures most readers of this commentary are among the rich. Jesus commands leaping joy under persecution, the joy of people who know how the story ends: the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us (Romans 8:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sermon on the Plain. What follows (vv. 20–49) is Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon, shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), with less about the Jewish law and four woes Matthew does not have. Jesus has just been rejected by the guardians of the old ways (v. 11) and has chosen the foundation of a renewed Israel (vv. 12–16); now he tells that new people how to live, and ends with two houses (vv. 46–49), so that no one can treat it as a fine speech and nothing more.

One sermon or two? Luke says Jesus came down and stood on a level place; Matthew says he went up on the mountain and sat down (Matthew 5:1). What follows in each has obvious overlap, beatitudes, love of enemies, judge not, the tree and its fruit, the two builders at the end, and equally obvious differences. Matthew runs to three chapters where Luke runs to thirty verses; Luke adds four woes Matthew does not have; Matthew includes long stretches on the law, prayer and fasting that Luke places elsewhere. Both answers have been held by careful readers, and neither damages anything. Some take them as the same occasion from different angles: the phrase Luke uses need not mean flat ground at the foot of a hill; it can as easily mean a plateau or a shelf on the hillside. Others take them as two occasions, which is simply what travelling preachers do. Jesus spent perhaps three years saying these things village by village, and no teacher says a thing once. Either way the words are his, and the differences are not contradictions but the ordinary shape of a real ministry. The same voice is speaking in both, and it is asking for the same life.

He came down with them. Some readers hear an echo of Moses coming down from the mountain with the law. Here it is the law of the kingdom.

Tyre and Sidon. Jews from the religious heartland, and people from the pagan cities of the Phoenician coast, the country Elijah was sent to (4:26). Luke’s map is already the map of Acts: a foretaste of the gospel to all nations.

Power came out from him. The power of God (5:17) flows from him (8:46); healing is not a technique he applies. So the sermon is not addressed to a neutral audience. Many in earshot have just seen the demonised freed and the sick made well. When he says, blessed are you who are poor, he is saying it to people who have already had evidence.

Is the Sermon on the Plain a way to be saved, or a way to live? A way to live, for those who are being saved. It is addressed to disciples (v. 20), people who have already come to him, and it begins not with commands but with blessings: the kingdom is given before anything is asked. Its demands are real and searching, and no one keeps them perfectly; they show us how far we fall short and drive us to Christ, who kept them for us. But they are also the actual shape of the new life he gives. We do not obey this sermon in order to be accepted; we obey it because we have been, and because the one who preached it lives in us by his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Beatitudes. Luke gives four blessings (vv. 20–23) and four matching woes (vv. 24–26). Matthew gives eight or nine blessings (depending on how they are counted) and no woes (Matthew 5:3–12). Luke’s are in the second person (you), spoken to disciples while he looks at them, though the crowd hears, to actual people whose circumstances everyone standing there could see; Matthew’s in the third (those who).

Blessed. Makarioi: not happy in a shallow sense, but fortunate, in a good position before God, approved by him. It is God’s verdict, not a feeling (Psalm 1:1).

Poor. Luke’s word, ptōchoi, means destitute: a beggar, who depends entirely on what others give. Many of Jesus’ disciples were literally poor, having left everything (5:11, 28). But in the Old Testament, the poor were also the humble, who had no one to depend on but God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2).

Luke and Matthew together. Matthew’s blessed are the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3) and Luke’s flat blessed are you who are poor sound like different sentences. They hold two ends of one truth, and neither end is safe alone. Take Luke without Matthew and you get the error that poverty itself saves, as though an empty purse were a ticket. Take Matthew without Luke and you get the more respectable error: poor in spirit quietly spiritualised into a humble feeling entertained by comfortable people whose lives stay precisely as they were. Matthew names the poverty God blesses: the poverty of a man who knows he has nothing to bring. Luke names where such people are usually found. It is far easier to know you have nothing when you actually have nothing, because money is extraordinarily good at hiding from us the emptiness we all have before him.

Yours is the kingdom. Present tense: it is yours now (12:32). The kingdom of God is God’s saving rule through his King. To have it is to live under that rule now, forgiven, cared for and belonging to him, and to inherit his new world when it comes in full (22:29–30).

Good news to the poor. At Nazareth Jesus had read Isaiah and claimed it: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18). Now he does it. This beatitude is not a wise man’s observation about poverty; it is the Messiah’s announcement. That is why he can say yours is, not yours will be: the King is present. The poor are blessed not because their poverty is a virtue but because the King has come to them first, and given himself.

I am not poor. Is this beatitude for me? Yes, if you come the way the poor come. Before God every one of us is destitute: we have nothing to offer him that is not already his, and no righteousness of our own (Isaiah 64:6). The comfortable Christian must learn by grace what the poor man often knows by experience: that he lives entirely on what God gives. So hold your possessions as a steward, not an owner; receive salvation as a beggar, not a customer; and let your money flow towards the poor, so that it does not wall you off from them or from God. The kingdom is given to empty hands, whatever is in the bank.

Where it applies: An elderly widow in your church lives on very little, and trusts Christ. Do not pity her as one who has missed out. She is rich in the kingdom, and you may learn more from her than she from you.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks poverty in itself makes a person right with God, or that the poor need no help since they are blessed already. The same Lord commands us to open our hands to them (1 John 3:17).

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hungry now. Only Luke has the now. He means real hunger, people who did not eat enough yesterday, though Matthew shows the hunger for righteousness too (Matthew 5:6). Mary sang: he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53). Hunger is not a virtue, and Jesus never says it is. What he says is that the condition which the world reads as God’s absence is, in his accounting, the condition of people who are about to be filled.

You shall be satisfied. At the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15; Isaiah 25:6), and in a measure even now. The word means filled right up, and the filling is not a metaphor. There is a table at the end of this book, and the guest list was drawn up from the streets and lanes (14:21).

You who weep now. Those who grieve over suffering, over their own sin, and over the world’s rebellion against God (Matthew 5:4). He does not tell them to stop, or suggest that the tears are a failure of faith. He lets the weeping stand and puts a date on it.

You shall laugh. God will wipe away every tear (Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 21:4). And the promised end is not relief or resignation but laughter, a startling word for the far side of grief: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy (Psalm 126:5).

Who is speaking. The kingdom reverses present conditions, and this is not a technique for feeling better. It is a claim about how the story ends, made by the only person entitled to make it. The one who promises to fill the hungry had gone forty days without food in a desert (4:2). The one who promises laughter to the weeping wept himself at a friend’s grave (John 11:35) and over Jerusalem (19:41). He is not calling out advice from the dry ground. He has been in the water.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve? No. Jesus blesses those who weep; he does not rebuke them. Paul does not tell the grieving Thessalonians to stop, only not to grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love continuing after loss, and the psalms are full of honest lament. You do not have to pretend to be fine, or hurry yourself out of sorrow to prove your faith. Bring your tears to God; he keeps count of them (Psalm 56:8). The promise is not that you will stop feeling the loss tomorrow, but that the one who is with you in the weeping will one day turn it into laughter.

Where it applies: A friend has lost her husband, and three months on she is still crying in church. Do not tell her it is time to move on, or that a strong Christian would be rejoicing by now. Sit with her, let her weep, and remind her gently that Jesus calls her blessed, and that the morning is coming.

Where it would be wrong: A neighbour has no food in the house, and you tell him he is blessed and will be satisfied in the kingdom, and leave it there (James 2:15–16). Bring the promise and the groceries.

For worship. On the evening of the first Easter, Luke tells us, the frightened disciples saw their Lord alive, and they disbelieved for joy (24:41). Then he asked for something to eat, and ate broiled fish in front of them. That room is this beatitude coming true in miniature: weeping turned to a joy too large to believe, and a table where the risen Christ himself sits down to eat. The now is real, but it is not long.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hate, exclude, revile. The only beatitude about what will happen to the disciples because they follow him, and its four verbs escalate. Hatred: the inward turn. Exclusion: being cut off from synagogue, family and community (John 9:22; 16:2). Reviling: insult to the face. Spurning your name as evil: your name, or the name Christian, treated as a curse (1 Peter 4:14–16). A complete social death.

On account of the Son of Man! Not for being obnoxious, but for Christ’s sake. The clause is narrow on purpose: there is no promise for the Christian excluded for being rude, or hated for opinions that have nothing to do with Christ. Suffering for wrongdoing has no blessing (1 Peter 4:15).

Leap for joy. Not endure; not bear it patiently. Leap, like a lamb in spring, or like John in the womb (1:41, the same word), on the very day they lose their standing, their livelihood and their families. The apostles did exactly this: they left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

Your reward is great. Not that we earn heaven by suffering, but that God honours faithfulness. The joy is about the accounting. Something is being stored where none of this can reach it.

So their fathers did to the prophets. Exclusion is company: the prophets were treated like this, and are now honoured, their tombs built, by the descendants of the men who threw them out (11:47–51; 13:34).

The landing is certain. What makes this command sane rather than cruel is the phrase on account of the Son of Man. It binds the sufferer to Christ so closely that what is done to the one is done to the other. Years later, when Saul of Tarsus was hunting Christians from house to house, the risen Lord stopped him on the road with a question: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The disciple who is thrown out for his name is never thrown out alone. He is held by the one whose name it is, the Son of Man who has received everlasting dominion, and the reward is with him.

How can I rejoice when it hurts? Rejoicing here does not mean pretending it does not hurt, or enjoying pain. It means looking past the hurt to what it means and where it leads. It means you belong to Christ; it means you stand with the prophets; it means a reward is being kept for you that no one can take. Paul could be sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Begin by thanking God, honestly, even through tears, that you were counted worthy to share a little of his Son’s rejection. Then pray for those who wronged you (v. 28). Joy usually follows the thanks rather than coming before it.

Where it applies: You are left out of a family group chat because you became a Christian. Do not answer with bitterness. Rejoice: you are in the company of the prophets.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe. Only Luke records these woes. Woe (ouai) is the prophets’ cry of grief and warning (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1). Not a curse, and not a wish for harm, but a lament: how terrible for you. It is the sound a man makes looking at people walking towards a cliff.

You who are rich. Not that wealth is sinful in itself. But wealth tends to make people self-sufficient, satisfied with this world, and blind to their need of God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25).

You have received. Received (apechete) is a business word, used on receipts: paid in full. It is not that the rich are excluded, but that they have already collected. Abraham said the same to the rich man: you in your lifetime received your good things (16:25).

Your consolation. The word is the one Luke used of old Simeon, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel (2:25), and found it when he took the infant Jesus in his arms. Israel’s consolation was a person. That gives the woe its edge. The rich are not condemned for having comfort but for having settled for a comfort that is not him. They have drawn their consolation in advance, in things, and feel no need of the one who stands in front of them as God’s comfort in flesh. Simeon was content to die once he had held Christ. The rich man in this verse can hold everything except Christ, and calls it enough.

Full now, laughing now. Each woe is the exact mirror of a blessing, and each turns on the same now: those satisfied with this world’s goods, who feel no spiritual hunger; and not innocent laughter, but the careless laughter of those who do not take God or sin or suffering seriously (James 4:9).

Most of us are rich. By any measure the world has ever used, most readers of this commentary are among the rich. The danger is not enjoying good things but being consoled by them, until the kingdom sounds like an optional extra for people whose lives are not working. A man who has been paid already does not come to collect. Christ, who made us rich by his poverty, is the consolation that does not run out.

How rich is too rich? Scripture sets no figure, and the question usually hides a hope of being just under the line. The better questions are these. Am I trusting my money for security instead of God (1 Timothy 6:17)? Could I give a large part of it away without feeling that my life was gone? Is my giving generous, regular and costly, or the leftovers? Do I know any poor people by name? Is my spending shaped by love for others or by keeping up with those around me? If those answers trouble you, the remedy is not guilt but generosity: begin giving more, and more joyfully, and let money become a servant again.

Where it would be wrong: You look down on wealthy Christians, or feel guilty over every good meal. Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia were wealthy and faithful (Genesis 13:2; Matthew 27:57; Acts 16:14–15); the rich are told not to hope in riches but to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

For worship. The woes are spoken with grief, by the Lord who would later weep over Jerusalem (19:41). And he took the woe on himself. He who was rich became hungry, mourned, and on the cross looked for comforters and found none (Psalm 69:20), so that people who had settled for a receipt might be given a river. He tells us where the cliff is because he would rather we came home.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all people speak well of you. Aimed squarely at anyone who speaks for God. A faithful witness to Christ will always offend some (v. 22). If everyone is speaking well of you, either you have said nothing worth opposing, or you have said what people wanted to hear.

The false prophets. One pattern showed even from the outside: their reception. The true prophets were nearly always unwelcome: Micaiah was hated because he never prophesied good concerning the king (1 Kings 22:8). The false prophets had access, standing and a hearing at court, because they told people what they wanted. Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).

When all spoke well of him. Luke has already shown us this verse lived out, by Jesus himself. In the synagogue at Nazareth, after he read Isaiah, all spoke well of him and marvelled at his gracious words (4:22). He went on to say what they did not want to hear: that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed a Syrian, and soon the congregation that had praised him was driving him to the edge of a cliff (4:24–29). He gave up the good opinion of his home town rather than shave a word off the truth.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should try to be unpopular, or that being well thought of is always wrong (Acts 2:47; 1 Timothy 3:7). A man who has made himself unpleasant may console himself that he is being persecuted when he is only being avoided; this woe carries the limit of verse 22. And Luke will shortly commend a centurion whom the Jewish elders of his town warmly praised (7:4–5).

The temptation to shave the corners off. What the verse forbids is the pursuit of universal approval by someone who is meant to be carrying a message: finding the version of the truth that will not cost anything with this person, in this room. It works, and it is precisely what the false prophets did.

How do I speak the truth without being needlessly offensive? Separate the offence of the message from the offence of the messenger. The cross will offend some people whatever you do (1 Corinthians 1:23); your tone, timing and manner should offend no one. So speak when asked, or when love requires it, rather than at every opportunity. Listen first, and understand the person. Say the hard thing kindly, briefly and without contempt, and be honest about your own need of grace. Let your speech be gracious, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6). If people still object, let it be to Christ, not to you.

For worship. He lost the praise of his home town in one sermon and of his nation in one week, and he never bought it back with a softer word, nor ever spoke an unkind one. What he sought was the voice that had spoken over the Jordan: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). Men may speak ill of us; God has spoken well of us in his Son, and that verdict is never revised.

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Love your enemies is among the hardest commands in the New Testament, and it comes in four rising forms: love, do good, bless, pray. None of them is a verb of feeling. Jesus commands treatment, not warm emotion.

The ground of the command is not the enemy’s worth but the character of God, who is kind to the ungrateful and the evil, so that a disciple who loves an enemy is showing a family likeness.

The cheek, the cloak, the beggar and the goods taken (vv. 29–30) concern personal insult and personal loss: what is forbidden is retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. They have never been a command to stay within reach of violence (see on v. 29). The section ends with the summary: be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is what God has already done for his own: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies.

Matthew’s be perfect (Matthew 5:48) becomes in Luke be merciful: in a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy. And the order cannot be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. The sentence begins with your Father, addressed to people who are already his.
verseByVerse.examples:
This command lies behind the church’s martyrs (Stephen died praying for his killers, Acts 7:60), its peacemakers, and its reconciliations. It is also easily shrunk into being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, when the real test is the person who still wishes us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31), stated positively, sends us towards the other person at our own cost, guided by how we would want to be treated.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say to you who hear. Jesus turns back to his disciples, and before the hardest thing in the sermon he marks off the people who are actually listening.

Love your enemies. The heart of the sermon. The love Jesus means (agapē) is not a feeling of liking, but a commitment to seek someone’s good, whatever they deserve.

Four commands, and one who kept them. Love is shown in action, in four rising steps: love (attitude), do good (deeds), bless (words), pray (prayer). Jesus kept all four towards his own enemies within a single night and day. He met the betrayer’s kiss with a question meant to wake him (22:48); he did good to one of them, touching and healing the ear a disciple had cut off (22:51); when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23); and from the cross he prayed: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34); some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though most modern Bibles keep it. The sermon on the level place is his own life, described in advance.

The enemy is real. Hating, cursing, abusing (epēreazontōn, mistreat, harass): Jesus is not talking about a colleague who irritates you, but somebody who wishes you harm and is acting on it.

The commands escalate in cost. None of the four is a verb of feeling: he commands treatment, and the command does not wait for the emotion to arrive. Do good is an action, which can be done at a distance and without much of yourself. Bless requires words, and words about a person come out of somewhere. Pray for is the hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long: it is very difficult to keep asking God to be good to somebody and go on hating them. Nobody arrives at loving an enemy by working on their feelings. It generally goes the other way round: an act, then a word, then a prayer, and somewhere in the third the heart begins to move.

Does this forbid self-defence, military service or the state’s use of force? Jesus is speaking of personal retaliation and the way his disciples treat those who wrong them. The state’s sword is a different matter, given by God to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and a Christian may serve in it (3:14). Protecting the weak from harm is not hating an enemy.

Is it not weak, or even unjust, to love people who are doing evil? No. Loving an enemy is not approving what he does, or pretending it is fine. It is refusing to become his mirror. It takes far more strength to do good to someone who is cursing you than to curse him back. And it does not give up on justice; it leaves justice with God, who says, vengeance is mine, I will repay (Romans 12:19). The Christian can afford to love his enemy because he trusts the Judge. And the one who gave the command kept it first, on the cross, for us.

What it does not mean. This is not a command to pretend nothing happened; forgiveness in Scripture never requires the pretence that the wrong was not a wrong. Nor is it a command to remain within reach of harm (see v. 29). What is forbidden is the natural, satisfying, entirely human project of returning what was given.

Where it would be wrong: A former friend’s lie online accuses you of a crime, or will lose you your job. Loving an enemy does not mean letting a damaging falsehood stand. Correct it calmly and truthfully, and if need be ask the platform or the law to deal with it, as Paul defended himself against false charges (Acts 24:10–21).

For worship. We were not neutral strangers to him but enemies, hostile in mind and doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21), and he did not wait for us to soften. He loved first, and his love turned enemies into children. Now by his Spirit he is making that likeness in us. There is no enemy of yours so hard to love as you were to him.

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The other cheek. Four illustrations, each the opposite of the reflex. A slap on the cheek was more an insult than an injury, a contemptuous blow; Jewish law treated it under fines for damaged honour rather than damaged bodies. So to offer the other cheek is not to invite a beating. It is to refuse the humiliation on its own terms: to decline to be drawn into the exchange the insult was designed to start. Absorb the wrong rather than escalate it (1 Peter 3:9).

Cloak and tunic. The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one. Put people before possessions, give readily, and hold goods loosely, not living for recompense.

He gave his back to those who strike. Isaiah’s Servant said it centuries before: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isaiah 50:6). Luke records the fulfilment. The men guarding Jesus blindfolded him, struck him and mocked him (22:63–64), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). He did not hit back, and he did not demand them back. Yet this was not weakness. He was holding still for a purpose, bearing an insult that was owed to us, with his face set towards finishing it. The disciple who turns the other cheek is walking a short way down a road his Lord walked to the end.

What this verse does not say to the abused. Something must be said plainly here, because few verses in the Bible have been so cruelly misused. Turn the other cheek has been quoted to battered wives, to abused children, to the bullied and the trafficked, to tell them Christ requires them to stay and keep absorbing the blows. He requires no such thing, and it is a wickedness to say he does. Look again at what he is describing: an insult to a man’s honour, and a coat taken by force. This is about personal affront and personal loss, the wound to pride and pocket that makes us itch to hit back and stand on our rights. What is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. He is not handing a violent man a licence, and he is not telling his victim to hold still. Jesus himself walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29–30). Paul invoked his Roman citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37; 22:25) and let the believers lower him over a wall in a basket rather than be murdered (Acts 9:25). And the same love that will not retaliate for itself is fiercely bound to protect the weak, sometimes from the very person harming them.

If you are being harmed, hear this clearly. Getting to safety is not a failure of this verse. Removing yourself or a child from a violent home, calling for help, telling your pastor or elders, insisting that the law do its work: none of that is retaliation, and none of it is forbidden here. A church that tells an abused person to go back and submit to the abuse has disobeyed Christ, not obeyed him. What dies in these verses is the right to hit back for your own honour. Not the duty to keep the defenceless, including yourself, out of the reach of evil.

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Some (Anabaptists, Quakers, Tolstoy) take these words literally and absolutely: Christians may never use force, serve in the army or police, go to court, or defend themselves, and their costly witness to peace deserves respect. This commentary’s view: these commands govern personal relationships and the disciple’s heart: no personal revenge, no retaliation for insult, generosity rather than grasping. They do not abolish the God-given role of the state to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), nor the duty to protect others, nor all legal redress (Paul appealed to Caesar, Acts 25:11). Jesus himself, when struck, did not offer the other cheek literally but protested the injustice (John 18:22–23). The principle is: never repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Giving to everyone who asks is to be exercised with wisdom, for their real good (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

Must I give to every beggar, even if the money will be misused? Jesus commands an open hand, a readiness to give rather than an instinct to refuse. He does not forbid discernment. Paul says that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10), and the church cared carefully for genuine need (1 Timothy 5:3–16). Sometimes the most loving gift is food rather than cash, or time rather than money. What this verse rules out is the closed hand.

Wrong to let it go: Your house is burgled, or your employer stops paying your wages. Jesus forbids personal revenge and a grasping heart, not justice through proper means. Report the burglary; pursue your wages, for withholding a worker’s pay is a sin God hears (James 5:4).

For worship. They stripped him of everything, and he let it go. To beggars who came with nothing he gave not a coin but himself. To sinners standing naked in their guilt he gave his own robe: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10). The Lord who was stripped is the Lord who clothes.
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Golden Rule. The engine of everything around it. Others had stated it negatively: Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, is reported in the Talmud to have said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Confucius and others said similar things. Jesus states it positively, which is much more demanding.

Why positive matters. The negative form can be kept by a man who does nothing at all. The positive form requires imagining what you would want in that person’s position, and then doing it, at your own cost. Consider the enemy who struck you: the negative rule permits you to leave him alone, which is very nearly what you wanted to do anyway. The positive rule asks what you would want if you were him, and sends you towards him.

As you wish. Jesus does not ask you to work out a theory of the good. He tells you to use the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks: how you would like to be treated, with kindness, patience, respect, generosity and forgiveness, and to apply it in the other direction. Not as a self-interested bargain, treating others well so that they will treat you well: the motive is love, not return (v. 35).

He did not imagine our place; he took it. The rule asks for imagination: picture yourself where the other person stands, and act on what you see. The Son of God did not need to imagine. He came and stood there. He was made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17), hungry, tired, misunderstood and tempted, so that he knows from the inside what we need and sympathises with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15). In Matthew this rule is the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 7:12), which he came to fulfil. Here is the fulfilment: one life in which this sentence was never once broken, towards friend or enemy. We break it daily; his unbroken obedience is counted as ours who trust him (Romans 5:19), and he exchanged places with us, treated as his enemies deserved so that they might be treated as he deserves.

What if what I would want is not good for me? The rule assumes a sensible, honest wish, not every passing desire. A man who wishes others would let him drink himself to death has not found a licence to supply someone else’s addiction. The rule is about the kind of treatment any reasonable person wants: honesty, fairness, patience, help in need, the benefit of the doubt, forgiveness, respect. Under all our particular wishes is the deeper wish to be truly loved, and true love sometimes says no. Ask, therefore, not only what you would like but what you would be grateful for in ten years’ time.

Where it applies: You would want your manager to tell you plainly, but kindly, where your work falls short. Do that in your next review of someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What benefit is that to you? Three questions, all the same shape, and each one dismantles a way of feeling good about yourself. Benefit (charis) is the word for grace, credit, thanks. What Jesus is asking, quite literally, is: what grace is there in that? And the answer is none, because grace by definition is unearned, and love returned for love is a transaction that has been earned.

The sting. Love, favours, credit: the three main forms of human exchange, and even sinners, the openly disreputable, manage them. Reciprocity requires no faith, no Spirit, no change of heart, and it is very good at looking like generosity. None of it is wrong, and all of it would happen anyway. The question is whether there is anything in your life that self-interest could not have produced.

Ten healed, and one came back. Jesus never asked this of his disciples without living it first. Luke will tell of ten lepers who cried to him for mercy and were all made clean, and of only one, a Samaritan, who turned back to give thanks (17:15–18). Jesus knew that would happen, and he healed the ten. He gave anyway, because his kindness was never an investment waiting for a return. Every Christian is living on a loan that was never called in.

Is it wrong to enjoy friendships where love is returned? Not at all. Mutual love is one of God’s best gifts, and Jesus had close friends himself (John 11:5; 15:15). Marriage, family and Christian fellowship are meant to be full of love given and received. The point is not to despise reciprocal love but to refuse to stop there. Enjoy your friends with thanks; and then look beyond them, to the person who will never return your kindness, and love them as well.

Where it applies: A single mother in your church cannot cover this month’s bills. Lend her what she needs, without setting a date, and be ready never to see it again.

Where it would be wrong: A relative wants you to co-sign a loan you could not repay, or keeps borrowing to cover gambling. Lending that feeds a destructive habit, or puts your own family at risk, is not love (1 Timothy 5:8). Help in ways that actually help.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expecting nothing in return. The three commands again, with the reciprocity stripped out: lending with the expectation of repayment removed, which amounts to giving with paperwork. In a society without banks, lending to the poor was a major act of charity.

Does this forbid charging interest or expecting repayment? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and Jesus goes further: when lending to someone in need, be ready to lose it. That is different from ordinary business lending and investment, which the Bible does not condemn. The heart of the command is generosity to the needy, even the ungrateful.

Your reward will be great. God will repay (14:14). The disciple stops expecting it from the debtor and starts expecting it from God: the money is transferred to a different account.

Sons of the Most High. This is the real payment. In Hebrew idiom, to be called the son of something is to bear its character (sons of thunder, son of encouragement). To be a son of the Most High is to be recognisably like him.

The Son of the Most High. Luke has used this title once before, of one person. The angel told Mary that her child would be great and would be called the Son of the Most High (1:32). Now Jesus promises his disciples a share in the name. That is the gospel in a phrase. There is one Son of the Most High by nature, and he brings many sons to glory by grace (Hebrews 2:10), so that God is our Father because he is first his. And the family likeness is his likeness: those who belong to him are being conformed to the image of the Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

Kind to the ungrateful and the evil. What theologians call common grace: the goodness God shows to all people, in life, rain, food, family, beauty. It does not save, but it is real kindness from a God who owes rebels nothing, to people who never once acknowledge where it came from. He sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). And beyond all common grace, he gave his Son for enemies (Romans 5:8).

The family resemblance. So the command to love enemies is not a height set for spiritual athletes. It describes the family likeness.

Is it wrong to want a reward from God? No. Jesus offers it here as a motive, and Hebrews says that whoever would draw near to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is wanting the wrong reward, or wanting it from the wrong person: doing good to be admired, or to put others in our debt. The reward Jesus promises is God himself, his approval, and the joy of being like him, and these are rewards only a child would want. It is like a son who wants to please his father, not a hired hand bargaining for wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful. The summary of verses 27–35. Merciful (oiktirmones) means compassionate, full of pity, feeling for others in their need and acting to help. Matthew has: you therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). Luke shows that the perfection of God is seen above all in his mercy.

What mercy is. Mercy is not being nice. It is not tolerance, and it is not the belief that the offence was minor. Here, in a section about enemies, it is what happens when someone deserves one thing and is given another; it presupposes a real debt, and then declines to collect it. You cannot forgive someone who has not injured you; you can only be pleasant to them. The command therefore requires that the injury be named as an injury, and then not paid back. Any account of forgiveness that begins by minimising what happened has skipped the only step that makes mercy possible.

As your Father is merciful. God is the Father of mercies (2 Corinthians 1:3), merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). The standard is not other people, but God himself. Not as much as you can manage, nor proportionate to the offence: which is why this command can never be marked complete.

The tender mercy of our God. What does the Father’s mercy look like? Zechariah sang that the coming of the Messiah was because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high (1:78). The Father’s mercy has a face. It touched a leper, ate with tax collectors, and called a man with a withered hand into the middle of the room. To be merciful as your Father is merciful is, in practice, to watch the Son, because whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9).

Why it is not crushing. The sentence begins with your Father. It is addressed to people who are already in the family, who have already received exactly the treatment they are being told to give. The mercy comes first, from him, at the cross, unearned and unasked: he did not shrink our debt but laid the whole of it on his Son. The command comes second, and it is not, be merciful in order to become his, but, you have seen how your Father behaves: do it like that. Nothing in this section is possible for someone who has not been on the receiving end of it. Everything in it becomes possible, slowly, for someone who has.

Does being merciful mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy gives up the right to personal revenge and the desire to see someone suffer; it does not abolish justice or wise protection. A parent can forgive a child and still apply a consequence; a church can forgive a man who stole from it and still not give him the accounts; a victim can forgive an abuser and still give evidence in court. God himself is merciful and just. What mercy refuses is the grudge, the gloating, the long memory kept like a weapon, and it always leaves room for the person to be restored.

Where it applies: Your teenage son crashes the car after you told him to be careful. He is shaken and ashamed. Before you list the cost, put your arm round him; then, together, work out how he will help put it right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
