The teaching on judging (vv. 37–42) and on fruit (vv. 43–45) is about how we assess others and ourselves. Judge not cannot mean that no moral assessment is ever allowed, since Jesus goes on to tell us to see clearly to remove a brother’s speck and to know a tree by its fruit. What is forbidden is condemnation: pronouncing a final verdict on a person, which belongs to the one Judge.

The blind guide and the log in the eye correct the order, not the duty: first deal with your own sin, then help your brother. And the tree and its fruit show where conduct comes from: out of the overflow of the heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of verse 38 runs through both testaments (Matthew 7:2; Romans 2:1; James 2:13). It is not karma but a reflection of God’s character, who shows himself merciful to the merciful (Psalm 18:25). Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has not understood what grace is.

The hypocrite of verse 42 is not a conscious fraud. He genuinely does not see the log, like the blind guide of verse 39 who is sure he knows the way. That is why we need Christ to show us ourselves.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log and the speck apply to every relationship with authority in it: parents and children, elders and members, employers and staff. Position does not give the right to speak into another life; honest self-examination does.

Verse 40 matters for anyone choosing whom to learn from: formation works, and we become like the one we follow. Verse 45 is a searching test of speech, but speech cannot be fixed by monitoring alone. The heart must be changed, and only Christ by his Spirit changes it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge not. Four commands, each with a consequence attached. Judge not is perhaps the most quoted saying of Jesus in the modern world, and usually quoted wrongly, to mean that no one may ever assess anyone’s conduct. It is not a ban on all judgment. Jesus tells us to recognise trees by their fruit (vv. 43–44), to rebuke a brother who sins (17:3), and to take the log out of our own eye so that we can see clearly to take out a brother’s speck (v. 42). What Jesus forbids is a censorious, self-righteous spirit, that judges others harshly while excusing oneself, assumes the worst, and takes God’s place as judge (Romans 2:1; James 4:11–12).

The judge’s seat. There is a difference between, that was a lie, and, he is a liar; between assessing what a person did and delivering a summary of what they are. The first is often required of us. The second requires access to information, motives, history, what a person was given to work with, what they have resisted, that no human being has. To pronounce a final verdict on a person is a work that belongs to a court, and there is only one.

The Judge who says judge not. The man who says these words is the one who will sit in that court. The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). He forbids us the judge’s seat as its rightful occupant, telling us to get down from his chair. And the measure he promises to use is the measure he himself brings into the world: not the level scoop of strict desert, but the heaped and overflowing measure of a Saviour who came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17).

Forgive and give. Forgive (apolyete) means release, let go: the mark of those God has forgiven (11:4).

Good measure. From the grain market: grain poured into the lap, a fold of the robe held out as a bag. A generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle the grain, and heaped it until it overflowed: a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous. God gives like that. He gave his Son, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32).

The measure you use. Harsh judgment brings harsh judgment; generous mercy brings generous mercy (James 2:13). That is not karma, nor do we earn salvation by forgiving or giving. It is a description of how the same person meets God at both ends: the one who has understood mercy well enough to give it is the one who will know what to do with it when it comes.

Is this a promise that giving money will bring financial return? No. The context is mercy, not judging, forgiving and generosity, and the measure returned is God’s generosity in kind. Paul says that whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6), but the harvest he means is righteousness and thanksgiving, not wealth (2 Corinthians 9:10–11).

If I struggle to forgive, does that mean God will not forgive me? No, not if you are struggling. The verse describes the settled heart of a forgiven person, not a test that a single hard battle can fail. Forgiveness of a deep wound is often a long road, chosen again and again, and God is patient with those who are walking it. What Jesus warns against is the heart that refuses to forgive at all, that holds the grudge and wants it held, because such a heart shows it has never understood its own forgiveness (Matthew 18:32–35). If you want to forgive but cannot yet feel it, ask God for help, decide not to take revenge, pray for the person, and keep going.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can a blind man lead a blind man? Two short sayings, placed straight after the warning against judging, because they explain it. It is a joke with a knife in it. The picture is obviously absurd, and the audience would have laughed, and then stopped laughing, because they knew who it was aimed at. A judgmental person is blind to his own faults (vv. 41–42), and cannot guide others. Jesus applied this especially to the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14), who claimed to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19). The men who had been watching him in the synagogue, hoping to build a charge out of a withered hand, were the recognised guides of Israel.

Will they not both fall into a pit? Teacher and follower alike come to ruin. Note that the blind guide is sincere. Nobody in the parable is lying. He genuinely believes he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain. A guide who knew he was blind would stop. Choose your teachers carefully. And if you teach, make sure you can see.

Fully trained. The word (katērtismenos) is used of mending nets (Mark 1:19). Formation works: a trained disciple ends up resembling the one who trained him, and the ceiling of what you will become is set by the person you are following, whether or not you intend it.

Whose voice is forming you? The first practical question is about intake. Not whose books are on the shelf, but whose sentences come out of your mouth when you are tired: the preacher you always listen to, the writer whose tone you have absorbed, the friend whose judgment you find yourself repeating, the voices on your phone every evening. You are going to end up like them. That is not a warning against having teachers; it is an argument for choosing them deliberately.

A warning to anyone who teaches. You are reproducing yourself, including the parts you would rather not pass on. Parents, Sunday school teachers, pastors and mentors teach most by what they are.

The one teacher worth becoming like. The sermon’s own answer to the whole problem is a person rather than a syllabus. Follow Jesus, and you will become like him: merciful, non-judgmental, loving even enemies. God has predestined his people to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29).

How do I tell whether a teacher can see? Test what he teaches by Scripture (Acts 17:11): does he say what the Bible says, all of it, including the parts that are unwelcome? Look at what he says about Christ, whether he exalts him as Lord and Saviour or uses him for something else. Look at his life, his humility, his honesty about money and power, his treatment of people who cannot help him (1 Timothy 3:1–7). And look at his followers: do they become more like Christ, more loving, more holy, more humble, or more like the teacher, proud and quarrelsome? A teacher who can see will point away from himself.

Where it would be wrong: You decide no human teacher can be trusted and read the Bible only on your own terms. Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church for our good (Ephesians 4:11–13). The answer to blind guides is not no guides but faithful ones, tested by Scripture.

For worship. Here is the one Teacher who sees perfectly, who never led anyone into a pit, and whose every disciple, fully trained, will be like him: when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). He mends us as a fisherman mends a torn net, patiently, knot by knot, until we are whole.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The speck and the log. A comic exaggeration from the carpenter’s workshop: a speck of sawdust against a beam of timber, and the log is often the sin of judging itself. Our moral vision has astonishing resolution at range and is useless up close. We detect an evasion in another person’s tone with real precision, and walk about with structural failures of our own that everybody else can see.

You hypocrite. An actor, pretending to a righteousness he does not have. But in ordinary English a hypocrite is a conscious fraud, and the picture Jesus draws is of somebody who genuinely does not see the log. His is a failure of self-knowledge so complete that he is entirely sincere, which is more frightening, not less. The comfort is that what we cannot see alone, Christ is willing to show us, and he shows it to heal, not to shame.

First the log. Self-examination comes before correction of others. But the speck is still to come out: what is corrected is the order. Once you have dealt with your own sin, you are able, and responsible, to help your brother, gently (Galatians 6:1). This passage is often quoted to mean that nobody may ever say anything to anybody; Jesus assumes Christians are meant to help each other see. Humility makes correction gentle; it does not make it silent.

The look that removed the speck. Only one man has ever stood with no log in his eye, and Luke shows us how he deals with a brother’s fault. In the high priest’s courtyard, as Peter denied him the third time and the rooster crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter (22:61). No speech, no list. Peter went out and wept bitterly; it broke him, and it began his mending, and on the third day the word went round among the disciples: the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (24:34). He sees the whole of our fault, and looks at us in a way that heals.

The qualification is honest sight, not moral superiority. Before speaking, ask what this conversation would cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

How do I find the log, if I cannot see it? Ask for help from outside, because the log is by definition in the eye you are using. Ask God: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). Read Scripture slowly and let it read you. Ask a spouse or close friend, and mean it: what do you see in me that I do not? Notice what irritates you most in others, because it is often a reflection of your own. And when you find the log, do not merely regret it; confess it, and ask the person you have wronged to forgive you.

Where it applies: Before you speak to your teenager about time on the phone, look honestly at your own.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No good tree bears bad fruit. The sermon shifts from conduct to cause. What a person does flows from what he is: the fruit does not determine the tree; it reveals it. This is not a demand to try harder, for a tree does not decide what fruit to bear. So the question this raises is not, what should I be producing? But, what am I?

Known by its own fruit. You can tell a person, and a teacher, by the fruit of their life (Matthew 7:15–20). This is right judgment, the discernment Jesus approves.

The abundance of the heart. The heart is a treasury: whatever has been put in over the years is what comes out. Speech is what spills over when the container is full and no longer being watched (James 3:10–12): what comes out when I am tired, when the phone call has gone badly, and what I say about people who are not in the room. Jesus says it is a straight readout of the treasury.

The implication. To change the fruit, the tree must be changed. Outward reform cannot produce good fruit from a bad heart. A person needs a new heart, which only God can give (Ezekiel 36:26): not a new personality but new desires at the root: God takes away a heart that loves sin and resents him, and gives one that loves him and wants what he wants (Ezekiel 36:27). Monitoring your speech alone produces a careful hypocrite. What has to change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

What overflowed on the cross. One heart held nothing but good, and Luke lets us hear what came out of it under the worst pressure. Nailed up and mocked, his mouth spoke: Father, forgive them (23:34, a prayer some early manuscripts lack). To a dying thief: truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). And at the last: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). That was the overflow: mercy, promise and trust.

One bad word does not prove a bad heart. A tree’s fruit is a pattern over seasons, not one morning’s crop, in yourself or in a friend who once lost his temper badly. Every Christian says things they hate having said.

Then how is the treasury restocked? By God, through ordinary means he has given. The Spirit gives the new heart in the new birth, and then fills it over a lifetime as we take in his word: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16). So fill your mind with Scripture, read and memorised; with prayer; with the worship and teaching of the church; with good books and good friends; and starve what feeds the old heart, the gossip, the bitterness, the screen that leaves you worse. Whatever you think about, dwell on what is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely (Philippians 4:8). Slowly, the overflow changes.

Where it applies: You notice that whenever a certain colleague’s name comes up, you make a cutting remark. That is fruit, and it is telling you something about the root. Confess the resentment to God, pray for her blessing, and say one good thing about her this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses and one storm. It is introduced by the question that makes the parable necessary: why call him Lord and not do what he says? Kyrios means the master whose word settles the matter, so to call him Lord while ignoring his words is a contradiction.

Both builders hear and build; the difference is underground. The same flood strikes both houses: one stands, the other falls at once.

The rock is not a set of principles. It is the one whose words these are. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology: The fallen house sets the sermon in the light of final judgment. Its commands describe the life that will stand on the day every life is tested, possible only through the new heart the kingdom gives. The question of verse 46 is not an attack on assurance; it asks whether what we say about Christ matches what we do with what he says.
verseByVerse.examples:
The two builders mark the difference between a faith that is only heard and a faith that is lived. Every generation of the church has members who have heard much and built little.

Digging deep is unglamorous: prayer and Scripture, honest fellowship, obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood or approval but Christ. The way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, Lord. He does not suggest they are insincere. The doubling is the language of warmth, even fervour. The problem is not coldness.

And not do what I tell you? A contradiction. A lord is someone you obey. The word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter. To call a man Lord and then decide independently what to do with his instructions is not merely a moral failure but a contradiction in terms. It is like calling someone your employer and never coming in. To call Jesus Lord and ignore his commands is hypocrisy. Words of worship without obedience are empty (Matthew 7:21–23; James 1:22). The test of whether Jesus is really your Lord is whether you do what he says, including everything in this sermon: love your enemies, don’t judge, give.

What I tell you. The prophets said, thus says the LORD, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus points to himself: my words (v. 47), but I say to you (v. 27). He claims for his own commands the place that belongs to the commands of God, and he makes a man’s eternal safety hang on whether he does them. Kyrios could mean simply sir, but in the Greek Old Testament it stood for the divine name. Some say the church later put such claims in his mouth, but they run through every strand of the Gospels, and Luke says he wrote from what eyewitnesses handed down (1:1–4). If he said them, either he is mistaken about himself on a scale no prophet ever was, or he is the LORD speaking.

He asks why. The question is put as a genuine question. There is an answer, and every honest Christian knows roughly what it is: because the saying is warm and the doing is expensive; because the language of discipleship costs nothing and its substance costs everything; because one can love the person of Jesus in a general way and have quietly arranged one’s life so that nothing he said in this chapter applies.

Why it comes exactly here. Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, give and expect nothing back, do not condemn, take the log out of your own eye: every command in this sermon is checkable, and none of them can be done by admiring it. Nor has any disciple ever done them perfectly. One man kept this sermon whole, becoming obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8), and for those who are his, his obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19), so their faltering obedience is accepted for his sake. And the Spirit he gives is the power that makes it real in them.

Does this mean I am not saved if I fail to obey? No. The verse is not an attack on assurance and it is not a demand for perfection. Every Christian fails to do all that Jesus says, every day, and the same Lord taught us to pray, forgive us our debts. The question is the direction of a life: whether you call him Lord and are trying, however falteringly, to do what he says, grieving when you fail and getting up again; or whether you call him Lord and have no intention of letting it change anything. The first is a weak disciple. The second is not a disciple at all. If you are troubled by your failures, that trouble is itself a sign that he is your Lord.

Where it applies: You sing with real feeling on Sunday that Jesus is Lord of all, and on Monday you are still refusing to speak to your brother over an inheritance. This week, ring him, and begin the conversation Jesus told you to have.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of being a Lord, Lord hypocrite that you stop singing, praying aloud or calling him Lord at all until your obedience is better. Jesus does not tell you to stop confessing him; he tells you to obey the one you confess. Keep calling him Lord, and let him make the words true.

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two builders. Everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen. Both builders come to him. Both hear his words. Both build houses. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them. And Luke follows the sermon at once with a Gentile centurion who builds everything on Jesus’ word, trusting him to heal without even coming to the house (7:1–10): a living picture of a house built on the rock.

Dug deep. Only Luke says dug deep: hard work, through the soil to the bedrock. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

The rock in the rest of Scripture. The text defines the rock as Jesus’ words heard and done (v. 47), and the rest of Scripture shows why that is not a gospel of self-effort. God was the rock of his people (Psalm 18:2), and Isaiah promised a tested stone laid in Zion, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16), which the apostles identify as Christ (1 Peter 2:4–6; 1 Corinthians 3:11). So the rock is not our obedience considered on its own. It is Christ himself, the Lord whose words these are. To dig deep is to come to him, hear him and do what he says; obedience is how a life rests its whole weight on him, and it is that resting, not the effort, that holds the house up.

When a flood arose. Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season. The same stream broke against both: the obedient are not protected from trouble. What differs is what happens next.

Well built. The KJV reads, for it was founded upon a rock, following later manuscripts; the earliest have well built, and the point is much the same. The flood can be almost anything: bereavement, a diagnosis, a betrayal, persecution, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, death, and finally the judgment of God. Jesus does not specify, and the vagueness is the point. Something always comes.

Without a foundation. He has heard the same sermon; the difference is not in hearing but in doing. His way is easier, quicker, and in fair weather it looks just the same.

Immediately it fell. Luke’s immediately is grim. There is no gradual subsidence, no chance to shore it up. The first serious pressure and it is over, and the wreckage is described as great, because a life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works. Jesus’ words begin with blessing for the poor and with the Father’s mercy (vv. 20, 36), so doing them starts with receiving mercy, not earning it. But true faith in Christ shows itself in obedience. Faith that does not obey is not saving faith (James 2:17).

How do I know whether I have dug deep? Look not at the outside of the house but at what you lean on when the water rises. When trouble comes, do you go to Christ, pray, open his word, and keep doing what he says, even through tears? Or does faith evaporate, and you reach for something else to hold you up? Look too at the ordinary weeks: is there a pattern, however imperfect, of hearing his words and doing them, in forgiveness, honesty, generosity, love for enemies? If you find you have built on sand, it is not too late while the sun is shining. Come to him now, hear him, and begin to dig.

For worship. Both men heard the sermon. Only one of them built on the man who preached it. And that man went down into the flood himself. The waters of God’s judgment broke over him at the cross, and he did not give way; the grave closed over him, and on the third day he rose. He is the rock the deluge could not move, and when the last storm breaks over the whole world, not one house that stands on him will fall, because he cannot.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season.

6.text: <sup>1</sup> On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. <sup>2</sup> But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?” <sup>3</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup> how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>6</sup> On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. <sup>7</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. <sup>8</sup> But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come and stand here.” And he rose and stood there. <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to them, “I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?” <sup>10</sup> And after looking around at them all he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” And he did so, and his hand was restored. <sup>11</sup> But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. <sup>12</sup> In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. <sup>13</sup> And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles: <sup>14</sup> Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, <sup>15</sup> and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, <sup>16</sup> and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. <sup>17</sup> And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, <sup>18</sup> who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. <sup>19</sup> And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all. <sup>20</sup> And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. <sup>21</sup> “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. <sup>22</sup> “Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! <sup>23</sup> Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets. <sup>24</sup> “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. <sup>25</sup> “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. <sup>26</sup> “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets. <sup>27</sup> “But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, <sup>28</sup> bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. <sup>29</sup> To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. <sup>30</sup> Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. <sup>31</sup> And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. <sup>32</sup> “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. <sup>33</sup> And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. <sup>34</sup> And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. <sup>35</sup> But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. <sup>36</sup> Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful. <sup>37</sup> “Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; <sup>38</sup> give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.” <sup>39</sup> He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? <sup>40</sup> A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. <sup>41</sup> Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>42</sup> How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye. <sup>43</sup> “For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, <sup>44</sup> for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. <sup>45</sup> The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. <sup>46</sup> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? <sup>47</sup> Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: <sup>48</sup> he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. <sup>49</sup> But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is four scenes in which the grace of God turns up at the edges of what respectable religion thought possible. A Roman officer sends word about his dying servant; a widow’s dead son is raised at Nain; John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus is really the one; and a woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus’ feet at a Pharisee’s table. In every scene the expected is reversed.

At the centre stands John’s question and Jesus’ answer (vv. 18–35). Jesus replies not with an argument but with what the messengers saw, the works Isaiah said would mark God’s coming to save.

The chapter ends at Simon’s house (vv. 36–50), where the parable of the two debtors shows the order of the gospel: forgiveness comes first, and love follows. The woman’s love is the evidence of her forgiveness, not its price, and her faith is what saved her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The centurion is the first Gentile whose faith Luke records Jesus commending, and in the strongest terms. The local face of the occupying power, he has built the town’s synagogue and valued a dying slave.

The elders plead his merit: he is worthy. He sends word that he is not, and asks only for a word from Jesus, reasoning from his own place under authority that sickness is under Jesus’ orders.

This is the faith the church has lived on ever since: the word of Christ, spoken at a distance, by one whose authority is not limited by where his feet are.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Maker. Jesus marvels at him, one of only two places in the Gospels where he is said to marvel; the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth (Mark 6:6). In one person the Son has two natures: as God he knows all things, and as man he truly met this soldier and was truly moved.
verseByVerse.examples: By every outward measure the centurion is among the most impressive people in the story, and he is the one who says he is not worthy. That is not false modesty but an accurate sense of whom he is asking. Ordinary work had taught him true things about God. And he never came in person, yet received all he asked: Christ’s word is not limited by distance, which is why Christians pray for people on the other side of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 7 is four scenes, and in every one the kingdom of God turns up where respectable religion did not expect it. A Gentile officer asks Jesus only to speak, and Jesus finds no such faith in Israel. At the gate of Nain a funeral meets the Lord of life, and a widow is handed back her only son. From prison John the Baptist asks whether Jesus really is the one, and Jesus answers with the evidence Isaiah promised. At a Pharisee’s dinner a sinful woman weeps on his feet and hears that her sins are forgiven. Jesus is the Lord whose word heals at a distance, raises the dead and forgives sins, and the friend of sinners.

A house built on his word. The sermon closed with a man who built his house on the words of Jesus, and the very next thing Luke shows us is a Gentile who rests his whole household on one sentence from the Lord’s mouth: say the word. The words just preached are the words of the one whose speech heals at a distance and raises the dead. That is why a life can be built on them.

A centurion. A centurion commanded about a hundred men: a career soldier, promoted on competence, the rank at which the empire actually worked. This Gentile probably served Herod Antipas, whose forces were organised on the Roman model: the local face of foreign power. Nearly every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (23:47; Acts 10:1–2), and Luke delights in showing that the soldiers of the empire were not beyond the reach of grace.

A servant, highly valued. The word is doulos, a slave (in verse 7, pais, boy, perhaps the affection of a household). Highly valued means dear to him: not the vocabulary of a man protecting an asset. A Roman writer on farming could call a slave a tool that speaks. Few would have expected an officer to go looking for a Jewish miracle-worker on a slave’s behalf.

The first evidence of his character. A man of considerable power, and the first evidence of his character is not his religion but how he treats somebody who could not have made him do anything. Kindness to the powerless is one of the first places the reality of faith shows.

Why does Jesus not condemn slavery? Slavery in the Roman world was not the same as race-based chattel slavery, but it was still a system of ownership, and the Bible never praises it. Scripture regulates it and undermines it from within: masters are told they too have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9), Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and enslavers are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). The gospel’s teaching that every person is made in God’s image, and that slave and free are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28), is what, in the long run, did much to bring slavery down. Christians were not always faithful to it, and some defended slavery from the Bible; but the leading abolitionists argued from these same truths. Jesus heals this slave without first lecturing his owner, because the man in front of him is dying; but the very fact that he goes treats the slave as a person worth the journey.

Was the centurion a believer already? Not in the full sense, because the gospel of the cross and resurrection had not yet been preached. But he had plainly turned from the gods of Rome towards the God of Israel (v. 5), and he is about to show a faith in Jesus that Jesus himself calls extraordinary. Luke presents him the way he presents Cornelius in Acts 10: a Gentile whom God was already drawing, who responds to the light he has and is given more. That is how God usually works. Nobody comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and the drawing often begins long before the person can name what is happening.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders of the Jews. Probably not timidity. A Gentile officer of the occupying army approaching a Jewish teacher directly would embarrass him before his own people, so he uses the one channel that costs Jesus nothing.

He is worthy. Their word is axios, and their evidence a track record: he loves us, he built us something. It is a case built on merit, which is how human beings naturally think about who deserves help, and the centurion is about to contradict every word of it.

He loves our nation. He was probably one of the God-fearers, Gentiles drawn to the God of Israel and synagogue worship without becoming full converts (Acts 10:2; 13:16).

Built us our synagogue. An extraordinary act of respect towards a conquered people’s God. At Capernaum today the remains of a white limestone synagogue from about the fourth century stand on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and it may well be that the stones the centurion paid for are still there.

Only one is worthy. The elders say he is worthy. He himself will say he is not worthy (v. 6). The difference is between two whole religions: God approached on the strength of a record, or on the strength of his own goodness. There is one person of whom heaven says, worthy are you (Revelation 5:9), the Lamb who was slain, and every sinner who is welcomed by God is welcomed on his worthiness, not his own. Christians do not bring God their synagogues, but a righteousness that is not their own but comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). The centurion, without yet knowing the cross, stood in exactly the right place: unworthy, and asking.

One man or messengers? Matthew tells this same story and has the centurion come to Jesus and speak directly, with no elders and no friends in sight (Matthew 8:5–13). A reader who notices will want to know which it was. The likeliest answer is that this is how people have always reported such things, then and now. We say a king built a palace when he had it built, or that a firm wrote to us when a clerk typed the letter; what a man does through those he authorises to speak for him is credited to the man. Matthew, writing tightly, gives the centurion’s own words and leaves out the machinery of how they travelled. Luke, who told us he had carefully followed what the eyewitnesses handed down (1:2–3), keeps the machinery, and the extra detail sharpens Matthew’s point rather than softening it. The man is so persuaded he has no standing before Jesus that he will not even present himself. He sends others to say he is not worthy to come.

So do good works count for nothing? They count for a great deal before people, and nothing as a claim on God. The centurion’s generosity was real and good; it gave him friends who would speak for him, and it showed what his faith was already doing in him. But it did not put Jesus in his debt, and he knew it. Good works are the fruit of a heart that loves God and its neighbour, and they adorn the gospel (Titus 2:10). What they can never be is a bargaining chip. The moment we bring them to God as a reason he should help us, we have joined the elders and left the centurion.
verseByVerse.note: Luke tells us he sent elders; Matthew compresses the story as if he came himself. Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went with them. No enquiry into the man’s religion: a Jewish teacher sets off towards a Gentile officer’s house because a servant is dying.

Not worthy. The elders said he is worthy; he says, through his friends, that he is not (hikanos, sufficient, fit). A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house (Acts 10:28), and the centurion spares Jesus the difficulty. But it is more than tact. He has understood what the men who built his case had not: that nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Say the word. He asks for nothing except a sentence. He does not need a touch, a ritual, a visit, or a sight of the patient. He believes it firmly enough to stop the healer on the road and tell him not to bother coming.

The faith the church lives on. This is the faith the church has lived on ever since. What is available is exactly what he asked for and got: the word, spoken at a distance, by someone whose authority is not limited by where his feet are. Every prayer for a child at university or a friend in hospital in another city, every sermon trusted to do its work in a heart, rests on what this soldier worked out in Capernaum.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to come close? No. The centurion is not teaching that we should keep Jesus at arm’s length; he is teaching that we do not need to see or feel him for his word to work. Jesus does come close to his people: he promises to make his home with those who love him (John 14:23) and to be with them always (Matthew 28:20). The point is that his nearness does not depend on our sensations. On the days you feel nothing, his word is exactly as powerful as on the days you feel everything.

For worship. The centurion’s words have entered Christian worship, and been said before the Lord’s Supper for centuries: Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof; but only say the word. We are not worthy, and he has come anyway, not only under our roof but into our flesh, and he has spoken the word over us that no illness and no death can disobey.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set under authority. He does not say, I am a man with authority, but set under authority, and only then mentions the men beneath him. His orders are obeyed not because he is impressive but because when he speaks, Rome speaks. His authority is real precisely because it is derived, and it operates entirely through words, at whatever distance the words can travel.

The reasoning. If my word, backed by Caesar, is obeyed by soldiers and slaves, then your word, backed by God, is obeyed by sickness and death. Illness is under orders. The centurion grasped what even the disciples were slow to understand: that Jesus’ word is the word of God, which does what it says and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11).

A soldier taught by his job. As far as Luke tells us, he worked it out from his life in the army, and he was right: creation obeys its Maker more reliably than a legionary obeys Rome. There is something in that for anybody who has ever felt their ordinary working life to be spiritually irrelevant. One of the clearest theologians in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and his job had helped to teach him.

Does under authority mean Jesus is less than God? No. The centurion was reasoning from what he knew, and he had it exactly right as far as it went: Jesus does speak with the Father’s authority, because the Son came to do the Father’s will (John 5:19, 30). But the eternal Son, equal with the Father, came to do his will in the work of salvation, not as a lesser being. The centurion saw that Jesus’ word carries God’s authority; the rest of the New Testament shows that it carries it because he is God the Son, the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The soldier’s analogy was humble and true, and the truth was even greater than his analogy.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are most afraid of this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the conversation, and say to yourself plainly: this too is under orders. That does not mean he will always order it away; it means nothing reaches you that he has not permitted, and nothing stays one hour longer than he allows. He upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), and he uses that authority to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He marveled at him. Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to marvel (also Matthew 8:10), and they are exact opposites. Here he marvels at a Gentile’s faith. At Nazareth he marvelled at the unbelief of the people who had watched him grow up (Mark 6:6). He was surprised, both times, in the same direction: faith turning up where nobody expected it, and refused where everybody did.

How can the Son of God be surprised? The question is worth facing rather than dodging, and the answer is the one Luke gave at 2:52, where Jesus grew in wisdom. In the one person of the Son there are two whole natures. According to his divine nature he knows everything and learns nothing. According to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man, on that road, and was genuinely moved by what he heard. Jesus was truly human and could be astonished. The wonder is real. He was not acting.

Not even in Israel. He says it to the crowd: a deliberate lesson to a Jewish audience, who with the law, the prophets and the promises should have had the greatest faith. It is the point that emptied the synagogue at Nazareth (4:25–27), and a foretaste of the Gentile mission in Acts (Acts 10–11; 28:28), and Matthew adds the saying about many coming from east and west to sit at table with Abraham (Matthew 8:11).

What faith did Jesus commend? Not the man’s generosity, though it was real. Not his humility, though it was accurate. What Jesus names as faith is his confidence that the word of Christ is sufficient: that nothing further is required, no presence, no procedure, no leverage. Faith in the Bible is not a feeling of certainty or a force we generate. It is trust in a person, resting on what he has said. The centurion’s faith was great not because he felt strongly but because he saw clearly how great Jesus is.

They found the servant well. Jesus never saw him, and nobody saw the healing happen: the messengers walked in afterwards and found him up. The other clear healing at a distance in the first three Gospels is also of a Gentile (Mark 7:24–30). The Gentiles receive the blessing of Christ without seeing him, as believers have ever since (John 20:29), and that is often how it looks from inside a Christian’s life. The word goes out, nothing visible happens where you are standing, and you come home and find that something has.

If I have great faith, will God always heal? No. The centurion’s faith was great, but the healing came from Jesus’ will and word, not from the size of the faith. Faith is not a lever that forces God’s hand. Paul, whose faith no one doubts, prayed three times for his own thorn to be removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). We are to pray boldly for healing, and God often gives it. But when he does not, it is not proof that we believed too little. It means he has a better purpose, and his grace will be sufficient.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
At the gate of Nain two crowds meet: the one following Jesus, and a funeral coming out. The dead man is a widow’s only son, her last protection.

Nobody asks Jesus for anything. The Lord saw her and had compassion on her, touched the bier (Numbers 19:11), and with one sentence gave the son back to his mother, in almost the words used of Elijah at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:23).

The crowd calls him a great prophet and says that God has visited his people. Both are true, and the second is truer than they know.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising at Nain is a sign that points forward. The young man would die again; what the miracle shows is Christ’s authority over death itself, which reaches its fullness in his own resurrection and will be seen when the dead hear the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25–29).

The echo of Elijah (4:26) shows Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophets, not one more of them: Elijah cried out to the LORD; Jesus simply speaks.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus’ compassion for the widow came before she asked anything. Compassion begins with seeing, and a Christian may pray to notice the people Christ notices.

His do not weep was no rebuke of grief; he wept himself at a friend’s tomb. He could say it because he was about to remove the reason, and one day he will say it to all his people (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A town called Nain. A village about 6 miles (10 km) south-east of Nazareth, on the slope of the hill of Moreh. Only Luke records this miracle, and Nain is near Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37), and far to the north-west, at Zarephath, Elijah had raised a widow’s only son (1 Kings 17:17–24). The crowd will draw the connection (v. 16).

At the gate. Two processions meet at a gate: one crowd following the Lord of life into the town, the other following a corpse out of it, and one of them is going to have to give way. Burial usually took place on the day of death, outside the town; the body was wrapped and carried on an open bier, with mourners, probably flute players and wailing women.

Three closing doors. A man who had died, past every remedy; the only son of his mother; and she was a widow: that is the one that finishes her.

What those facts meant. A woman’s security then ran through a man: father, husband, son. She has buried the husband and is burying the son. So she is not only a mother in the worst grief there is, but from that morning facing destitution, with no one to protect her in court, walking behind the body of the last person who stood between her and the road.

Nobody asks. No centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart. Nobody in that funeral is looking for him. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief. The God who is a father to the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5) was walking into Nain in human flesh.

Did Jesus plan to meet her? Luke does not say he went to Nain because of the funeral, but the whole Gospel teaches that the Son did nothing by chance and that his Father governs every hour. Whether Jesus knew in advance or not, his Father did, and the timing that brought him to that gate at that moment was no accident. That is worth remembering in your own life. The meetings that change everything often look like coincidence from the inside.
verseByVerse.note: Nain was a village south-east of Nazareth, near Shunem, where Elisha raised a widow’s son. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lord saw her. Here, for the first time, Luke himself as narrator calls Jesus the Lord, at the gate of Nain, in front of a bier, at the very moment Jesus is about to show his power over death.

He saw her. Two crowds, a body and a great deal of noise, and what he saw was the woman. You do not have to be the loudest voice in the room for him to notice you.

He had compassion. The verb, esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs, is something deep, involuntary and physical, the word used of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33). No one asked him; this is pure grace. And it is what Zechariah had sung about God himself: the tender mercy of our God, by which the sunrise would visit us from on high (1:78).

Do not weep. From anybody else, said at a graveside to a woman who has lost her only child, those words would be an outrage. He is not telling her grief is inappropriate; he wept himself at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35). He is telling her to stop because he is about to remove the reason. Nobody else may say it. He may, and one day, to all his people, he will, when he wipes away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).

So should Christians not grieve? Christians grieve, and should. Jesus wept, Paul speaks of sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27), and the Psalms are full of lament. What Scripture forbids is not grief but grief without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Do not say do not weep to a grieving friend; only Christ has the right to say it. What you can say is what he has promised: that death is not the end for those who are his, and that the day is coming when there will be no more mourning. Weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and hold the hope for them until they can hold it themselves.

For worship. He looked at a mother following her only son to the grave, and he knew what lay ahead of him. Simeon had told his own mother that a sword would pierce her soul (2:35). And the Father in heaven would give up his only Son, not to be handed back at a gate, but to be given for us. The compassion that turned over inside him at Nain is the compassion of the God who did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32). He sees every widow still.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He touched the bier. Under the law, contact with a corpse made a man unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–16), one of the strongest defilements in the law of Moses, and a passing teacher had no need to touch it. He put his hand on it, and, exactly as with the leper two chapters earlier (5:13), the traffic runs the other way. Jesus is not defiled by death; death is undone by him.

I say to you, arise. He speaks to a dead man, on his own authority. There is no prayer here. Elijah stretched himself on the widow’s son three times and cried out to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21); Elisha prayed and lay on the Shunammite’s son (2 Kings 4:33–35). The prophets prayed, and God raised. Jesus gives an instruction, because he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

Sat up and began to speak. Luke, the physician, records it in two plain stages. He does not tell us what the young man said. Later legends of raisings often supplied a report from the other side; Luke supplies nothing.

Jesus gave him to his mother. The point of the whole scene: the miracle was for her, and her future with him. The words are almost exactly those of 1 Kings 17:23, he delivered him to his mother, and Luke surely meant the echo. Here the Lord of the prophets says a single sentence, and hands a son back to his mother, and walks on into the town.

What it shows. It was a sign of the final resurrection, when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29). He who laid his hand on a bier let himself be laid in a tomb, and came out on the third day holding the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Since that morning, every funeral of his people is walking towards a resurrection.

Could he only have been unconscious? A sceptic may suggest it, but Luke’s account gives it little room. He calls him a man who had died, his mother and a whole town were mourning him, and people who lived with death at close quarters were seized with fear at what they saw. A man in a faint does not sit up and speak at a stranger’s command at the very moment the command is given. In the end the question is not whether a physician could explain the scene, but who it was who spoke. Luke’s answer is the empty tomb: the Lord who raised this young man was himself raised, and his resurrection is the warrant for all the rest (24:6–7).

Why did Jesus raise some and not others? He did not empty every graveyard he passed. The raisings in the Gospels (this young man, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus) were signs, pointing to who he is and to what he will do on the last day. They were not the final answer to death; the young man of Nain died again. The final answer came at the empty tomb, where Jesus himself rose never to die again, the firstfruits of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). If you have buried someone you loved who trusted Christ, he has not passed them by. Their raising has been kept for the morning when it will be permanent.
verseByVerse.note: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day. Touching it made a person unclean.

parallels.desc: he gave him to his mother

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear seized them all. Holy awe, Luke’s consistent report of what the presence of God does to sinful creatures (2:9; 5:8, 26). And then praise, in two acclamations.

A great prophet has arisen among us! Anybody who knew 1 Kings 17 would reach for Elijah, and perhaps for the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). It is correct, and not enough: Elijah prayed; this man gave an order. Jesus is more than a prophet.

God has visited his people! This one is larger than the crowd knows. The verb is the one Zechariah used in his song: he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68, 78). It means God coming to see about his people with intent to act. They mean God has taken notice of them again; in truth God has arrived in person and is walking through their gate.

Incomplete theology, sound instinct. They knew they had seen God do something, not yet who had done it, and Luke does not despise the partial recognition. You do not need a complete theology to say: I have seen God do something.

Through the whole of Judea. Judea here probably means the whole Jewish land, not only the southern province (4:44). The news travelled far enough to reach John the Baptist in Herod’s prison.

In the flow. A great prophet sets the question for the rest of the chapter: John asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come (vv. 18–19); Simon decides he cannot be a prophet at all (v. 39); the guests ask who this is who even forgives sins (v. 49). Scene by scene, Luke is leading his reader from prophet to Lord.

Is calling Jesus a prophet enough? It is true but incomplete. Jesus is a prophet, the greatest of them, the one Moses foretold (Acts 3:22). But many today are happy to call him a great prophet or a great teacher precisely to avoid calling him Lord and God. Luke will not let us stop there. The crowd at Nain said more than they knew; we are meant to say all of it. If Jesus is only a prophet, he cannot forgive sins (v. 49), and he cannot raise you on the last day. He is God come to visit his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John, imprisoned by Herod (3:19–20), sends two disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come. His question shows that doubt is not proof a faith was never real.

Jesus first heals many in front of the messengers, then sends them back with what they have seen and heard, in the words of Isaiah’s promises (Isaiah 26:19; 29:18; 35:5–6; 61:1). Everything John was promised is coming, but not everything is coming yet.

Only after the messengers leave does Jesus praise John to the crowd: no reed, no courtier, but a prophet and more, the messenger of Malachi 3:1. The section ends with the children in the marketplace: John was called demon-possessed and Jesus a glutton, and objections that contradict each other were never the real reason.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus treats John’s doubt with complete respect. He does not rebuke it; he answers it with evidence, and then honours John in public.

The saying about the least in the kingdom concerns place in the history of redemption, not personal holiness. The least believer now lives on the far side of the cross, with a finished redemption and the indwelling Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples:
John’s question is the question of a believer whose expectations have not been met. Jesus’ answer points him to what has actually happened, and that is still the help for faith under pressure: the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, the witnesses to the risen Christ.

And he sent his doubt to Jesus. The children in the marketplace warn against a habit of always having a new objection, so that nothing God sends ever gets us up.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these things. A centurion’s servant healed at a word, a dead man sitting up at a town gate. And John is in prison for confronting Herod Antipas (3:19–20), in the fortress of Machaerus, according to Josephus, beyond the Dead Sea. He has probably been there for months, and he will not come out.

The one who is to come. A way of speaking of the Messiah (ho erchomenos), drawn from texts like Psalm 118:26 and Malachi 3:1. John himself had used it: he had said that one mightier than he was coming (3:16).

Or shall we look for another? Take in who is asking. This is the man who leapt in his mother’s womb at the sound of Mary’s voice (1:41). Who was filled with the Spirit before he was born. Who baptised Jesus and saw the Spirit come down like a dove. Who had pointed at this very man as the Lamb of God (John 1:29). That man is now asking whether he got it wrong.

Why did John doubt? Several things may be going on, and it is honest to say we cannot be certain which. He may be asking for his disciples’ sake rather than his own. More likely he is struggling with the shape of it. He had preached a Messiah who would come with the axe at the root and the winnowing fork in his hand, and with the fire of judgment (3:9, 17). What he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties with sinners, and no fire at all. And John was in prison, and the Messiah was supposed to proclaim liberty to the captives (4:18). Jesus did not fit his expectations. Or he may simply be in the darkness that a cell and a death sentence can bring on anybody. Even the greatest of the prophets had moments of doubt.

What it does not mean. Not that John lost his faith. If the greatest born of women could come to the edge of this question, doubt is not proof that a faith was never real; it is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight. And he sends it to Jesus, as Luke tells twice over (v. 20).

The Lamb John had named. The answer to John’s question lay in his own earlier words: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). A lamb does not come swinging an axe. It comes to be offered. The fire and the winnowing fork John preached were real, and the day of judgment will come, but the Messiah would first stand under that judgment himself. John was puzzled because the Coming One was not yet doing what he had foretold. He was doing something greater first: walking towards the cross where the fire would fall on him, so that it need never fall on those who trust him.

Was John sinning when he doubted? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Unbelief refuses to trust God; doubt is a believer struggling to hold on while something does not make sense. Scripture is full of believers who asked God hard questions: the psalmists (Psalm 13; 73), Habakkuk, Job, and here John. What they did not do was walk away from God; they took their questions to him. Doubt becomes dangerous when it is nursed in private, fed by resentment, and never brought to Christ and his word. Brought to him, it is very often the road to a stronger faith. Jesus did not rebuke John for asking. He answered him. And John sent his question to the right place: not to the crowds or to his own fears, but to Jesus himself.

For worship. The Lord did not leave his forerunner alone in the dark. He is the Servant Isaiah promised, who does not snap the reed that is already bent or snuff out the wick that has burned low (Isaiah 42:3). He does not scold his sheep for crying out in the night; he answers.
verseByVerse.note: John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that hour. Only Luke records it: before Jesus answers a word, he works, while John’s messengers watch. They are given first not an argument but evidence.

Diseases and plagues and evil spirits. Luke, the physician, distinguishes them: diseases; plagues (mastigōn, scourges), severe afflictions; and evil spirits, not collapsed into the medical ones.

Sight to the blind. Given their own clause, because sight to the blind is what Isaiah returns to again and again, and no first-century physician could do it. Bestowed (echarisato) means gave as a gift, from charis, grace.

The method. The same method Jesus will use after the empty tomb, showing his hands and feet. A man in a cell has asked whether his life’s work was pointed at the right person, and the reply is not, trust me, but what his own messengers saw that afternoon: checkable, specific, and matching a text John had known since boyhood. That is how Christ handles honest doubt. He does not scold it, and he does not ask for a leap in the dark. He points at what has actually happened.

Where is the evidence for me? You were not standing there that afternoon. But you have the same evidence John received, written down from what eyewitnesses handed on, so that you may have certainty (1:2–4). You have the empty tomb and the witnesses to the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You have the fulfilled prophecies. You have two thousand years of changed lives, and very likely some in your own church. And if you are a believer, you have the work of Christ in you: a love for him you once did not have. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust resting on what God has done in history.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What you have seen and heard. Not, tell John I am the Messiah, and no rebuke: a list of observable facts, and the list is a quotation.

Isaiah’s promises. Jesus answers in the language of Isaiah’s promises about the coming of God to save: Isaiah 35:5–6 (the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer); Isaiah 29:18 (the deaf shall hear); Isaiah 26:19 (your dead shall live); Isaiah 61:1 (good news to the poor), which Jesus read at Nazareth (4:18). John had built his ministry on Isaiah 40:3. Jesus is saying: you know what the prophets said would happen when he came. Yes, I am the one.

Lepers and the dead. Isaiah’s lists of signs never mention lepers, and only Isaiah 26:19 speaks of the dead living; Jesus adds both from his own works (5:12–13; 7:11–15), and they are greater still. The inclusion of lepers is its own argument: Scripture records no leper cleansed between Naaman in Elisha’s day (4:27) and Jesus.

Good news to the poor. The climax of the list, placed after raising the dead, perhaps as the greatest sign. A dead body raised will die again; a soul raised by the gospel lives for ever.

Where he stopped. As at Nazareth, Jesus leaves out the vengeance. Isaiah 35:4 says your God will come with vengeance; Isaiah 61:2 goes on to the day of vengeance of our God. The judgment John expected will come, but not yet. This is the time of grace, the day of vengeance held back so that sinners could be gathered in. Everything John was promised is coming; not everything is coming yet.

Not offended by me. The beatitude is unmistakably meant for the man in the cell. Offended (skandalisthē) means caused to stumble, tripped up by something in the road. It is a gentle word and an honest one, and it names John’s actual difficulty without embarrassing him: do not stumble because I am not the kind of Messiah you expected.

Where believers stumble. This is where a great many believers stumble: not that Christ has failed to do what he said, but that he has not done it in the order or on the timetable we assumed: the healing that did not come, the prodigal who has not come home. He offers John not an explanation but the evidence, and a blessing for the man who can hold on when the answer is smaller than the question. And John, so far as the record goes, held on, and died in that cell, and was right all along.

Why did Jesus not get John out of prison? We are not told, and the silence is part of the lesson. Jesus could have opened the doors of Machaerus with a word, as he would later send an angel to open a prison for Peter (Acts 12). He did not. John was beheaded (Mark 6:27). Faithfulness to Christ does not guarantee rescue in this life, and the gospel of the kingdom is not a promise of comfort now. What Jesus gave John was not freedom but the assurance that he had not been wrong, and a blessing on his faith. Some believers are delivered from the lions; others die by the sword, and Scripture honours them both (Hebrews 11:33–38).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John’s messengers had gone. A quiet kindness: Jesus waits until the men are out of earshot, and then defends John to a crowd that might have thought less of him for his question.

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds along the Jordan bent whichever way the air moved, but John was no man to go with whatever was blowing: he rebuked a king and went to prison for it. (See Matthew 11:7–8 for the fuller answer.)

A man dressed in soft clothing? John wore camel’s hair (Mark 1:6), and the men in splendid clothing are in kings’ courts, which is where John is now, in a cell beneath one. (See Matthew 11:7–8 for the fuller answer.)

A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. The first two questions expected the answer no. This one expects yes, and then gets more than it asked for. John stood in the line of the great prophets, the first in centuries to call the whole nation to repentance. And what is more than a prophet? A prophet speaks of what is coming. John was the only one who could point with a finger and say: that man. Every other prophet in Israel’s history described a horizon; John stood at the edge of it and named the person walking over. And there is a second thing that made him more: the prophets foretold the Messiah, and John was himself foretold, as the messenger sent ahead of the Lord (Malachi 3:1).

Did Jesus think less of John for doubting? No, and this passage is the proof. Jesus answered John’s question privately and then praised him publicly. The very doubt we might have used against him, Jesus did not mention to the crowd at all. That is how the Lord treats his struggling servants: he deals gently with the weakness, and honours the faithfulness. If you have been through a season of doubt, you need not fear that Christ has written you off. He judges a life by its direction and its faithfulness, not by its worst night in prison.

In everyday life. When someone is absent, and the conversation turns to their weakness, speak of their faithfulness, not their worst moment, as Jesus did of John.

For worship. He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). John never heard what Jesus said about him that day, but it stands in Scripture for ever, and so it is with all his people. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who speaks for us when we cannot hear it.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written. Malachi 3:1, combined with Exodus 23:20. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. The messenger goes ahead of the LORD, who is coming to his temple.

Before your face. Jesus quotes it with the pronouns changed: before your face, your way before you. Now God speaks to the Messiah about the forerunner who prepares his way. The one whose way is prepared, in Malachi, is the God of Israel, and Jesus applies the text to himself without comment. John prepares the way for the Lord, and the Lord is Jesus.

None is greater than John. Not greater than the prophets: greater than anybody. Not Abraham, Moses or Elijah had a higher place in God’s purposes than the man in Herod’s cell wondering whether he had been wrong. He stood at the turning point of history. The prophets saw Christ from afar; John saw him and pointed.

The least in the kingdom. Not a demotion of John: greater not in character but in privilege, which side of the cross a person stands on. John belonged to the age of promise and stood at its threshold. He announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

What the least believer has. The least believer after the cross and resurrection has what John did not yet have: an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, the forgiveness of sins actually purchased, and the Holy Spirit indwelling in the fullness of the new covenant. Not because he is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at. John was filled with the Spirit from the womb; but the least believer now receives the Spirit as the Spirit of the crucified and risen Christ, poured out because Jesus has been glorified (John 7:39), living in him for good and teaching him to call God Abba, Father, through a Son whose work is finished (Romans 8:15–16). Do not treat as ordinary what John died longing to see (1 Peter 1:10–12).

Is John in heaven, then? Yes. Being least in the kingdom or greater than John is not about who is saved. John was a man of faith, filled with the Spirit from the womb, and he is among those who will sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of God (13:28). Old Testament believers were saved by faith in the promised Christ, just as we are saved by faith in the Christ who has come (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). The difference Jesus speaks of is one of privilege and clarity, not of salvation: we know the name, the cross and the empty tomb that John died before seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the tax collectors too. Luke’s parenthesis explains how the crowd took Jesus’ words about John, one group having said yes to God in the water and the other no, and so sets out in advance the two people at Simon’s dinner (vv. 36–50). Luke singles out the tax collectors: the men notorious for extortion heard John, agreed with God about themselves, and went into the water.

They declared God just. Literally, they justified God. To acknowledge that he is in the right about you: when he says you need washing he is not exaggerating. And when God justifies a sinner, the same word runs the other way, which is the heart of the gospel. When God justifies, he pronounces a verdict from the bench: the sinner is not made sinless overnight, but pardoned and accepted, because our sin was counted to Christ and his righteousness is counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21).
