Rejected the purpose of God. Lawyers (nomikoi) were experts in the law of Moses, and the purpose of God (boulē) here is the call to repent. They rejected it for themselves: entirely orthodox about God’s purposes, they declined to be included. They thought they were righteous and did not need to repent (5:32). Baptism was the public sign of agreeing with God about your sin, and they would not be seen to need it.

Can God’s purpose be rejected? A reader who has been taught the sovereignty of God will feel a difficulty here, and it is worth facing rather than stepping round. Does this verse make his plan subject to a committee vote in Jerusalem? It does not, and Luke of all writers is the last person who thought so. This is the man who will record that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). The eternal purpose of God went forward exactly as decreed, and these men were not consulted. What they rejected was the purpose of God for themselves: the good and gracious call held out to them in John’s preaching, the invitation to repent and be washed. God’s call, as it comes to people in preaching, can be refused. They were offered it, and they would not have it, and the refusal was entirely their own. And God’s plan was not delayed by a single day. That is where the mystery sits in Scripture, and where it is left: God is sovereign, and people are responsible, and both are true.

The water Jesus entered. When all the people were being baptised by John, Jesus too was baptised (3:21). The sinless Son of God went down into the same river as the tax collectors, standing with sinners in the water of repentance he did not need, because he had come to be numbered with them. John’s baptism always pointed past itself, to Jesus (Acts 19:4), so the purpose the lawyers refused was, in the end, Christ himself, and the water they would not be seen in was water the Lord had already entered for them.

How do I justify God? By agreeing with him about yourself. When his word says you have sinned, you do not argue, minimise or compare yourself with others; you say, Lord, you are right. That is what confession is: saying the same thing as God (1 John 1:9). David did it after his adultery: you are justified in your words and blameless in your judgment (Psalm 51:4). The wonderful paradox is that those who justify God are justified by him, freely, through faith in Christ. Those who justify themselves, like the lawyer in 10:29, find that their own verdict is the one God will not accept.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation. The people of this generation means especially the religious leaders who rejected both John and Jesus, and Jesus reaches for a scene everybody would have recognised.

Children in the marketplace. Children in the square played at weddings and funerals. Whichever game is proposed, the second group sits there, sulky and contrary: the person who cannot be pleased, and is never wrong, because the objection simply changes.

Two tunes. Readers differ over which group of children stands for this generation: the ones calling out their complaints, or the ones who will not join in. The sentence works either way, because the sting is the same: whatever tune is played, the same people stay sitting down. John came with the dirge: fasting, camel’s hair, judgment, repentance. Jesus came with the flute: feasts, tax collectors, wine, a wedding. The response to both was the same, dressed up in two different objections.

The bridegroom’s music. The flute was wedding music, and Jesus had already said whose wedding it was. When he was asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered: can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? (5:34). The joy around him was the celebration of the Bridegroom’s arrival (Hosea 2:19), and to refuse to dance at that wedding is to refuse him. And he would sing the dirge too. As he came near Jerusalem he wept over the city, because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:41–44). He played both tunes himself, and wept when neither was answered.

Not confined to Pharisees. A very common condition: always, sincerely, weighing an objection: the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; the church is too formal, or too casual; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one is a fanatic. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated, and the reasons contradict each other. The God who kept playing for that generation is patient still (2 Peter 3:9), and gives grace to get up.

But is it wrong to criticise a church or a preacher? Not in itself. Scripture tells us to test everything (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). A church can be genuinely unfaithful, and a sermon can be genuinely wrong. The question this parable puts is not whether you ever disagree, but what your criticisms are doing. Do they lead you to a better obedience, a more faithful church, a deeper engagement with God’s word? Or do they keep you safely seated, so that nothing ever reaches you? Discernment moves a person towards God; this kind of objection keeps him at a distance.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eating no bread and drinking no wine. John was an ascetic, fasting, living on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6). His austerity was commanded before he was born (1:15): the funeral song, a call to mourn for sin.

He has a demon. Too strict. The verdict on John was not that he was mistaken but that he was possessed: a fanatic, not right in the head. Nobody argues with an ascetic; they diagnose him.

Eating and drinking. At feasts, with sinners (5:29): the wedding music, the joy of the kingdom. He went to Levi’s house full of tax collectors, and he is about to go to a Pharisee’s.

A glutton and a drunkard. Too loose. The charge echoes Deuteronomy 21:20, where a rebellious son who was a glutton and a drunkard was to be stoned. It was not a joke; it was an accusation with a death sentence attached.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant as an insult, and it happens to be one of the truest descriptions of him anyone produced in his lifetime. He is the friend of sinners. That is the gospel. They said it to shame him, and it is the hope of every person who has ever come to him ashamed. In the end he was numbered with the transgressors (22:37) and laid down his life for his friends (John 15:13).

The point. Two ministries, both from God, both rejected for mutually exclusive reasons: too severe, too relaxed. Which is the proof that the reasons were never the reason. People who do not want God’s message will always find an excuse to reject the messenger.

Wisdom is justified by all her children. The language of verse 29 again. Wisdom, in the Old Testament, is God’s own wisdom personified, calling in the streets and being ignored (Proverbs 1:20–33). Here she is vindicated, and the vindication comes from her children: the people who actually responded, the tax collectors who went into the water, and the sinners who left his table forgiven. You cannot argue a generation out of an objection that was never about the evidence. You can only produce the children.

Did Jesus approve of sin by eating with sinners? No. He ate with sinners as a physician goes among the sick (5:31–32), not to share the disease but to heal it. He was the friend of sinners, not the friend of sin. His company changed people: Levi left his tax booth, Zacchaeus gave back fourfold, the woman in the next scene left forgiven. Following him means going where sinners are, welcoming them warmly, and eating with them, while never pretending that sin does not matter. The church that keeps sinners at a distance has forgotten its Lord; the church that tells them sin is harmless has forgotten why he came.

In everyday life. Who are the tax collectors and sinners in your world, the people your church crowd might be embarrassed to be seen with? Invite one of them for a meal this month, and remember that you were once at that table too.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus accepts a Pharisee’s invitation, and at the semi-public meal a woman known in the town as a sinner comes in, weeps on his feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them with perfume.

Simon concludes silently that Jesus cannot be a prophet, or he would know what sort of woman she is. Jesus answers with the parable of two debtors, sets Simon’s missing courtesies, no water, no kiss, no oil, beside what she has done, declares her sins forgiven, and tells her that her faith has saved her. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the two debtors is the key to the scene. Forgiveness is the cause and love the effect. Verse 47 is often misread, and the passage corrects it: the parable puts cancellation first, her sins were already forgiven, and Jesus names her faith, not her love, as what saved her. Her love is the evidence of her forgiveness, as wet ground is evidence of rain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman gives everything she has left, because what she has received is worth more than all of it.

Simon is not a bad man. He is careful and serious, and he has never seen the size of his own debt, so he cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. A church helps people most when it helps them see both how much they owed and how freely Christ has forgiven it.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom’s children. Jesus has just been called a friend of sinners, and said wisdom is justified by her children. Luke now shows both: the friend of sinners, and a sinner who responds to wisdom.

A Pharisee’s invitation. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as with tax collectors (11:37; 14:1). This Pharisee, Simon (v. 40), was curious, perhaps wanting to evaluate this new prophet.

Reclined at table. At a formal dinner, guests lay on low couches arranged around a low table, propped on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them, away from the food. So a woman could stand behind him at his feet without reaching the table. Such dinners were semi-public, and uninvited townspeople could stand round the walls to watch: that is how she gets in.

A woman of the city, who was a sinner. Luke tells us almost nothing: no name, no history. Applied to a woman and stated as her public identity, sinner most likely means she was known for sexual immorality, perhaps as a prostitute, though Luke does not say. It was very likely the only thing about her anybody in the room could have told you.

Was this woman Mary Magdalene? No. Luke gives no name, and Mary Magdalene is introduced only in the next chapter, as one from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2), with nothing to link her to this story. The identification came much later, chiefly through a sermon of Gregory the Great in the sixth century, and it has no ground in Scripture. Mary Magdalene deserves to be remembered as what the Gospels say she was: a woman set free by Jesus, who supported his ministry, stood by the cross, and was the first to see him risen.

Is this the same anointing as the one at Bethany? Probably not (Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9; John 12:1–8). This one happens in Galilee, earlier in the ministry, in a Pharisee’s house, by a woman known as a sinner, and the point is forgiveness. The other is at Bethany days before the cross, by Mary of Bethany, and the point is his burial. That the host in both is called Simon is no difficulty: it was one of the commonest names in the land, and the New Testament alone has several men called Simon.

She came because he was there. She came on purpose, at great risk of humiliation, into the last house in town where a woman like her would be welcome, and Luke gives one reason: she learned that he was there. Whatever she had heard him say or seen him do, it had persuaded her that this man would not drive her out, even in a Pharisee’s house. That is the pull of Christ on the guilty. The Pharisees’ holiness made sinners keep their distance; his holiness drew them in. His presence made the coldest room in town the one place she had to be (15:1). And she brought an alabaster flask of perfume: she had already worked out what she was going to do before she got there.

Should a church welcome people like her? Yes, and gladly. If a woman known for sexual sin walked into your church on Sunday, the question is whether she would meet Simon or Jesus. Welcoming her does not mean pretending her past does not matter or that sin is harmless; Jesus is about to speak of her sins as many. It means receiving her as he did: with dignity, without flinching, and with the good news that her sins can be forgiven. Most people who have lived as she lived already know they are sinners. What they do not yet know is that there is a friend of sinners.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so a woman could stand at his feet. Doors were often open at such meals and onlookers could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At his feet, weeping. A run of actions in one sentence, and every one a scandal. Standing behind him at his feet: the lowest place in the room. Weeping: nothing has yet happened; whatever this is, it started before she arrived. They are tears of repentance and of gratitude, which suggests she had already met Jesus, or heard him preach, and received forgiveness (v. 47). Enough of them to wash the dust off a man’s feet.

The hair of her head. A respectable Jewish woman did not unbind her hair in public; later rabbinic discussion treats it as grounds for divorce. She takes down her hair in a Pharisee’s dining room, in front of his guests, and uses it as a towel.

Kissed his feet. And kept on kissing them: Jesus will say she has not ceased (v. 45). The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, the part a slave washed. Perfume on the feet, not the head, which is where you anoint a guest of honour: she takes the lowest place, as one who did not think herself worthy to anoint his head.

He did not stop her. Kissing the feet was homage, given to a benefactor or a king, and Jesus lets it go on and on. When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up at once: stand up; I too am a man (Acts 10:26). When John fell at an angel’s feet, the angel forbade it and said, worship God (Revelation 19:10). Jesus does not say either thing. He receives it, and then defends it to the host. He is the Lord, and the forgiveness she is weeping over came from him, so the gratitude belongs at his feet.

What she is not doing. She is not performing; there is no sign she is aware of the audience at all, and she asks for nothing. She is not trying to earn something: the debt was cancelled first, and this is what came after. She spends what is left of her dignity, in public, on a man’s feet, because she has been forgiven, and there is nothing else she can think of to do with it.

Do I have to be emotional to love Jesus? No. Tears are not the measure of love, and some of the deepest Christians are quiet people who rarely cry. What this woman shows is not a temperament but a direction: everything she had, poured out on Christ, with no thought for what it cost or who was watching. A reserved believer can love like that in his own way: in costly giving, in obedience nobody sees, in standing with Christ when it is embarrassing. The question is not whether you weep, but whether anything you have is held back from him.

In everyday life. What is your alabaster flask: the thing of value you have been keeping back? It may be money, time, reputation, or a plan for your life. Love that knows it has been forgiven is extravagant, and does not calculate who will notice.

For worship. The feet she washed with her tears would carry him to the cross for her, and after his rising he would show them to his friends: see my hands and my feet, that it is I myself (24:39). She poured out perfume; he poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to himself. Simon is far too well brought up for a scene at his own table; the objection happens behind his face. Some manuscripts read the prophet. The people had said Jesus was a great prophet (v. 16). Simon now concludes he is not.

Who and what sort of woman. Simon is not a fool. A prophet has supernatural knowledge; a prophet who knew what she was would not let her touch him, because touching a sinner would make him unclean; this man is letting her touch him; therefore either he does not know, or he does not care, and either way he is not a prophet. Simon thinks holiness means separation from sinners. What he cannot conceive is a third possibility: that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Who and what sort: she is, in his mind, a type before she is a person. Underneath the logic is something every religious person can feel. If my standing with God rests on my being better than her, then a welcome for her threatens me. That is why grace offends the respectable before it offends anyone else: it takes away the distance they have worked so hard to keep, and puts them on the same floor as the sinner.

Jesus answering. Jesus replies to an unspoken thought (5:22; 6:8): Simon wanted to know whether this man had prophetic knowledge, and has just had a demonstration without noticing. Simon is the one who does not know what sort of woman she is, or what sort of man he himself is.

I have something to say to you. He uses the man’s name and asks permission to speak: no humiliation in front of the guests, a courtesy Simon had not extended to him. Teacher is respectful, and a good deal less than Lord, which is what the centurion called him in verse 6 without ever having met him.

Is it wrong to be wary of people with a bad reputation? Not always. Scripture warns against bad company (1 Corinthians 15:33), and wisdom takes care, especially where there is danger to others. Simon’s error was not caution but contempt. He saw a category and not a person; he assumed she could not change; and he assumed that his own holiness depended on keeping her at a distance. Jesus’ holiness is the kind that touches the unclean and makes it clean. Be careful with sin, especially your own, but never write a person off as a type.
verseByVerse.note: Simon was a common name; this Pharisee is not Simon the leper of Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two debtors. Four sentences, and it dismantles the room, told to make Simon judge himself, as Nathan made David judge himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

Five hundred denarii, and fifty. A denarius was a day’s wage: more than a year and a half’s wages, and about two months’. Both are real debts. And sin is a debt to God (11:4; Matthew 6:12): we owed God love with all our heart, and trust and thanks every day of our lives, and every day we have kept back part of it. Nothing we do tomorrow can pay for yesterday, because tomorrow’s obedience is owed already (17:10).

They could not pay. Both were bankrupt. This is the point Simon misses: he is a debtor too. The difference in the size of the debts made no difference whatever to the outcome, because fifty denarii a man does not have is as unpayable as five hundred.

He cancelled the debt of both. Entirely the lender’s act; nobody negotiated. Cancelled (echarisato) means forgave freely, as a gift: the same verb Luke used of sight given to the blind (v. 21). He graced them both.

Now which of them will love him more? Love is the response to forgiveness, in proportion to the sense of how much has been forgiven. Simon answers, the one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt, with a small hedge that gives him away: he can see that the answer is going somewhere he will not enjoy. You have judged rightly, says Jesus, and Simon has condemned himself.

Which way round. The hinge of the scene, regularly got backwards. The cancelling comes first and the loving after, in proportion to how much was cancelled: love is the effect, grace the cause. So the question the parable leaves hanging over Simon’s dining table is not, who is the better person? It is: how big do you think your debt was? Simon is not being told that he is unforgiven. He is being told that his estimate of what he owed is the reason his welcome was so cool.

Who paid the debt? The lender in the parable simply cancels. But a cancelled debt is never free; someone absorbs the loss. The rest of the New Testament tells us who did. God did not wave our debt away as though justice did not matter. He nailed the record of debt that stood against us to the cross (Colossians 2:14), where Christ paid it in full. That is why forgiveness can be completely free to us and completely just in God: it was free because it cost him everything (Romans 3:24–26).

Am I the fifty-denarii debtor? If you have lived a fairly respectable life, you may feel that the woman’s debt was larger than yours. In terms of what people could see, perhaps it was. But the parable’s point is that both debtors were equally unable to pay, and both needed the same free cancellation. And anyone who looks honestly at his own heart before a holy God, at the pride, the coldness, the years of ingratitude, soon stops feeling like the small debtor. The Christians who love Christ most are usually not those with the most lurid past, but those who see most clearly what they were saved from.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; five hundred denarii was more than a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning toward the woman. Jesus turns to face her for the first time, since she has been behind him throughout, and he speaks to Simon. So she hears every word of what follows with his eyes on her.

Do you see this woman? Simon saw only a sinner. He had seen nothing but a category; he looked at her and read a file. Jesus asks him to look again, and then tells him what is actually there: a forgiven woman pouring out love.

Three contrasts. Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting, and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to an honoured guest. None was legally required, and scholars debate how strictly they were expected; but water for a guest’s feet goes back to Abraham’s tent (Genesis 18:4), and a host who meant to honour his guest would offer them. Simon omitted every one of them. Against each omission, Jesus sets what she did, and every one of hers is enormously larger: tears for water, kisses on the feet for a kiss of welcome, costly ointment for ordinary olive oil.

Not an oversight. Three courtesies are hardly all forgotten by accident. Simon wanted Jesus at his table and was not prepared to honour him at it, and everyone would have registered the slight. The one who thought he had nothing much to be forgiven gave nothing much.

He came to his own. What makes the omissions so sad is who the guest was. Simon thought he was hosting a teacher of doubtful credentials, not the Lord who had healed at a distance and raised the dead. The one who made the water was given none for his feet. John says it of his whole coming: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). And the woman at his feet is the other half of it: to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12). The same Lord, cold-shouldered at Simon’s table, would later wash his own disciples’ feet (John 13:5).

What does it look like to give Jesus the minimum today? It looks like a Christian life run on courtesies: attending, but not worshipping; reading a chapter, but not listening; giving what will not be missed; mentioning Christ only where it is safe. None of it is scandalous, and that is the point. Simon broke no law. Jesus’ diagnosis is not that we try harder, but that we look again at how much we owe him. Coolness towards Christ is cured not by guilt, but by grace seen more clearly.
verseByVerse.note: Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to a guest.

parallels.desc: let a little water be brought, and wash your feet
you anoint my head with oil

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which are many. Jesus does not deny that her sins are many. He declares them forgiven. Are forgiven (apheōntai) is a perfect tense: an action completed in the past whose result stands in the present. Her sins have been forgiven and remain forgiven. That happened before she entered the house. It is why she came in.

For she loved much. Read quickly, it sounds as though her love bought the forgiveness, and that reading has a long history. It cannot be right, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself. First, it reverses the parable Jesus has just told and Simon has just agreed with: the debt is cancelled and then the loving follows. Second, the tense: her sins have already been forgiven. Third, three verses later he tells her plainly what saved her, and it is not her love: your faith has saved you.

The lender at the table. In the story the debtors love the lender; in the room the woman pours out her love on Jesus. So the man reclining at Simon’s table is the creditor. Her sins were debts owed to God, and the one she owes her love to is the one sitting in front of her. That is why he can say, on his own authority, I tell you, her sins are forgiven, and why nobody in the room misses the claim (v. 49). He is not a prophet passing on news of God’s pardon. He is the one whose pardon it is, and before long he will pay the debt himself.

The for of evidence. So what does for mean? It is the for of evidence, not of cause: her sins have been forgiven, as you can see from her great love. We use it constantly: it rained last night, for the ground is wet. Nobody thinks the wet ground made it rain. The wet ground is how you know.

Where Christians differ: love and forgiveness. Some Roman Catholic interpreters, following the Latin, have taken this verse to mean that her love (as an act of contrition and charity) merited or brought about her forgiveness; many Catholic scholars today read the order as the parable gives it. This commentary’s view: the parable (vv. 41–43) makes the order plain: forgiveness first, love second. Jesus will tell her that her faith, not her love, has saved her (v. 50). We are forgiven by grace through faith, and love is the fruit.

He who is forgiven little. Aimed at Simon. Not that Simon’s sins were few, but that he thought they were. Feeling little need of forgiveness, he felt little love. The causation runs the same way: Simon’s cold hospitality was evidence of Simon’s small sense of debt, exactly as her tears were evidence of her large one. Self-righteousness kills love.

Why it matters. If love earns forgiveness, then every anxious believer must ask whether they have loved enough, and the honest answer is always no. If love is the evidence of forgiveness, the question changes entirely, and the way to love more is not to squeeze harder but to look longer at what you have actually been forgiven. That forgiveness stands in the perfect tense over our lives, and no later failure can reach back and undo it.

My love for Jesus feels small, so am I really forgiven? Your forgiveness rests on Christ’s work and God’s promise, not on the size of your love. If you have come to Christ in faith, your sins are forgiven, however weak your love feels today. But a small love is a call to look again, not to despair. Love for Christ grows as we see more of our sin and more of his grace, and both are the Spirit’s work. Pray for eyes to see. Read the cross accounts slowly. Come to the Lord’s Table remembering what the bread and wine mean. Love is not manufactured; it is kindled.
verseByVerse.note: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price, as the parable shows.

parallels.desc: we love because he first loved us

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your sins are forgiven. He has been speaking about her to Simon. Now he turns and speaks to her, and it is the first time anyone in the scene has addressed her at all.

Why say it out loud? She already knew. The thing was settled before she came through the door, and her tears were the evidence of it. So why say it? Because she needed to hear it said, in that room, in front of those people. A woman who may have spent years as the town’s byword had just knelt at the feet of a rabbi at a Pharisee’s dinner party, and the whole room was watching to see what he would do with her. He tells her, where everyone can hear, that her sins are gone. It is an assurance of what was already true. She had been condemned by the town; now she is declared forgiven by the Lord, in front of the Pharisees.

Assurance spoken. There is a great deal of pastoral practice in that. Assurance is not merely a private transaction with God. People need to be told, in words, on the authority of Christ, that their sins are forgiven: which is a good part of what preaching, and the gospel spoken over a struggling friend, and the Lord’s Table are for.

Who is this, who even forgives sins? The same question as at the paralytic’s healing (5:21), and it is the right question. Only God can forgive sins committed against God; everyone at that table knew it. They have understood the claim perfectly and, once again, drawn no conclusion from it. The question hangs over the Gospel: who is he? He is the one who forgives sins, because he is God, and because he will pay the debt himself on the cross. And what Jesus does with the murmur is nothing. He does not turn to defend himself or argue the point. He has one more thing to say, and it is not to them.

Your faith has saved you. Not her love, not her tears, not her perfume: her faith. Faith is the empty hand that receives forgiveness. The same word is used when Jesus heals (8:48), but nobody in this room is ill: it is her whole standing before God that has been put right. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root: the trust that got her through a door she had no business entering, to the feet of a man she believed would not throw her out. And she was right about him. That is all her faith consisted of, and it was enough.

Go in peace. Literally, go into peace: into a new life of peace with God and wholeness, the Hebrew blessing shalom. She came weeping; she leaves in peace.

In the flow. The chapter ends where it began, with faith: the centurion trusted Jesus’ word for a dying body (v. 9), this woman for her sins (v. 50), and the second is the greater gift. The question of Nain and of Simon’s heart is answered: he is the Lord who forgives.

Can a pastor say your sins are forgiven? Only Christ forgives sins in his own right. But a minister of the gospel, or any Christian, may and should declare God’s forgiveness to those who repent and believe, because God has promised it. When Jesus gave the apostles authority to declare sins forgiven (John 20:23), it was the authority to proclaim his forgiveness, not to dispense it on their own account. When a Christian friend says to you, on the basis of God’s word, if you confess your sins he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), that is the voice of Christ reaching you through his people. There is no priest standing between you and God, and no purgatory to pay off what remains: Christ’s forgiveness is complete. Roman Catholic Christians understand absolution and purgatory differently, and many of them love Christ sincerely; the reason for this answer is that by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).

What if I have done something worse than she did? There is no sin that Christ cannot forgive for anyone who comes to him in repentance and faith. Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, a blasphemer and persecutor, and said he was shown mercy precisely as an example to everyone who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Whatever is in your past, the question is not its size but where you take it. Bring it to the feet of Christ, as she did. He has never once turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).

For worship. She came in with no name in the record, no standing, no argument and no words, into a room full of men who despised her, and put everything she had left on the feet of Christ. He did not flinch. He received it, defended her to the man whose house it was, told her out loud that she was forgiven, and sent her out through the same door in peace. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that welcome, and there is not one now.

parallels.desc: who can forgive sins but God alone?

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is about hearing the word of God, and about the one whose word it is. The parable of the sower, the lamp on its stand, and Jesus’ saying that his family are those who hear the word of God and do it all press the same question: how are you hearing? Then four miracles show whose word this is. Jesus stills a storm, frees a man held by a legion of demons, heals a woman who had bled for twelve years, and raises Jairus’s daughter from the dead. Nature, the powers of darkness, long sickness and death itself all obey him.

The chapter opens with the women who travelled with Jesus and paid for the mission out of their own means (vv. 1–3). Luke names them.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the key to the rest. The seed is the word; the soils are the hearers. It warns that much of the sowing will come to nothing, and promises a harvest in those who hold the word fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus travels through towns and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, and with him go the Twelve and a group of women he had healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, and adds that many others provided for them out of their own money.

A rabbi’s travelling company did not include women, and Jesus’ practice exposed him to the charge his enemies were already making (7:34). He did it anyway. Each woman is described by what he had done for her: the company around him is made up of the rescued.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus’ practice fits his whole ministry, which welcomed those the religious leaders shut out, and it looks ahead to the honoured place of women in the church (Acts 2:17–18; Galatians 3:28).

Luke sets these women just before the parable of the soils. Here is a company in whom the word took root and bore fruit, and their fruit was that they gave what they had to keep the sowing going. They are also at the cross when the Twelve have scattered (23:49) and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1–11): when the testimony mattered most, they were the witnesses.
verseByVerse.examples:
These women are the New Testament’s first clear picture of money put to work for the gospel. They did not only believe; they paid for the mission, and kept paying. Paul’s teaching on giving (2 Corinthians 8–9; Philippians 4:14–19) grows from the same root: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it.

They did not preach in the synagogues, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and the freedom to travel, and they put both under the mission for years without asking anyone to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 8 is about hearing, and about the one whose word must be heard. The seed is the word of God, and only the honest heart that holds it fast bears fruit; then four scenes show why his word deserves such hearing. The disciples’ question hangs over the chapter: who then is this? The Lord of Psalm 107 is in the boat.

Through cities and villages. Luke gives the shape of the ministry in a sentence: town after town, on foot, saying the same thing. This was his main work, as he had said (4:43): I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

Proclaiming the good news. Two verbs. Proclaiming (kēryssōn) is the word for a herald making a public announcement in the king’s name. Bringing the good news (euangelizomenos) is the verb behind our word gospel. He is announcing something that has happened: the King has come, and his reign has begun. What does the kingdom of God mean? Not a territory on a map but a reign: God himself stepping in as King to put right what sin and Satan have ruined. That is why, wherever Jesus goes, demons leave and the sick get up; as he says later, if it is by the finger of God that he casts out demons, the kingdom of God has come upon them (11:20).

The herald who is the news. A herald announces another man’s king and then steps aside. This herald cannot step aside, because the kingdom he proclaims has arrived in his own person: where he goes the sick are healed and the bound are freed, and the reign of God is seen walking a Galilean road. The Twelve are the beginning of a renewed Israel (22:30). The women are the first spoils of his war on the strong man (11:21–22). Luke draws the procession like a king’s train after a victory, except that every captive in it is a captive set free, walking beside the one who freed them.

And the twelve were with him. Learning by being with him (Mark 3:14). The Twelve were trained less by lectures than by company: they watched him, walked with him, and heard the same message preached in a hundred villages until it was in their bones.

And also some women. Only Luke tells us this in the middle of the Galilean ministry (Mark mentions it only at the cross, Mark 15:41), and it was remarkable in its culture. Rabbis had disciples, and disciples were men; one rabbi, in a saying preserved in later rabbinic writings, said it was better to burn the words of the law than to teach them to a woman. A travelling teacher whose company included women invited exactly the accusation his enemies had already made, that he was a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Every one of them is described by what was done for her, not by what she brought. Like the woman of 7:36–50, they follow because of what he did for them. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising. It is a collection of the rescued.

Mary, called Magdalene. Then a name, and it needs rescuing from centuries of misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, south of Capernaum, and the surname simply says where she was from. She watched at the cross (Mark 15:40; compare 23:49), saw the burial (23:55), was at the tomb on the third morning (24:10), and was the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:11–18).

From whom seven demons had gone out. A severe case of possession, perhaps over a long time. Seven speaks of complete bondage, and of complete deliverance. It is affliction, not scandal, and it is the only thing Scripture ever says about her past.

What it does not mean. Nothing in Scripture says Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. She is not the woman who wept at Jesus’ feet a few verses earlier, who is deliberately left unnamed; the two stories simply stand side by side, and that is what first invited people to merge them. Then a sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century identified Mary with the sinful woman of 7:37 and with Mary of Bethany, and fixed the idea in the Western imagination for a thousand years. Luke introduces her here as a new character, freed from demons, not from immorality.

Why does it matter who Mary Magdalene was? Because the truth honours both Christ and her. The legend turned her into a symbol of sexual sin repented, and in doing so it obscured what the Gospels actually say: that she was set free from a terrible bondage, that she gave her money and her life to Jesus, that she stayed at the cross, and that the risen Lord appeared first to her and sent her to tell the apostles. That is a greater story than the legend. And it is a warning to all of us: tradition, however old and beautiful, must always be tested by Scripture.

For worship. Seven demons once held Mary of Magdala, and not one of them could keep her when he spoke. Before long death could not keep him either, and the first person he showed himself to on the morning of his victory was this woman: the strongest bondage broken, and a woman once owned by darkness sent to announce the light to the apostles. What has he freed you from? Name it, and let it lead to devotion, as it did for Mary. Glory to the Lord who wins his battles for the bound, and then lets the freed carry the news.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joanna, wife of Chuza. Herod is Herod Antipas, and Chuza was his steward (epitropos), a high official over the royal household or estates: he managed the finances of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell and would have his head brought in on a platter. Joanna is a court wife, with status, money and a husband employed by the enemy, and she is walking round Galilee with an itinerant preacher from Nazareth. Luke does not tell us what conversations that produced at home.

Fed by those he feeds. The verb Luke uses for these women is the one Jesus will use of himself at the Last Supper: I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). Here the Servant of the Lord lets himself be served. He who in the next chapter will break five loaves for five thousand eats bread that Joanna paid for. The Word made flesh needed a meal and a bed, and took them gratefully from people he had healed, and so turned their giving into fellowship with himself.

The gospel in Herod’s house. Acts 13:1 mentions Manaen, brought up with Herod, among the leaders at Antioch; and Paul sends greetings from the saints of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22). Joanna is named again at the empty tomb (24:10), so whatever it cost her, she was still there at the end. Perhaps she was one of Luke’s sources for the inside story of Herod (9:7–9; 23:8–12).

And Susanna, and many others. A name with no story at all, and then a crowd of women whose names nobody wrote down. But she was known to Jesus, and her name is in Scripture for ever.

Who provided for them out of their means. Provided (diēkonoun) means served, ministered, the root behind our word deacon, and the tense is continuous: they kept on providing, out of their own money. Thirteen men walked from village to village, eating every day and sleeping somewhere every night for months on end, with no visible income, and Luke tells us in half a verse where much of the money came from. The Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ was funded, in large part, by women, as Lydia and others would fund Paul’s (Acts 16:14–15).

Is giving money really ministry, or just a lesser support role? It is ministry, in the full sense of the word. Luke uses the same verb for these women that the New Testament uses for the service of deacons and for Christ’s own service (22:27). Paul calls the Philippians’ gift to him a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Not everyone is called to preach, but everyone who belongs to Christ is called to serve, and putting your money under the gospel is one of the plainest ways to do it. The preacher in the pulpit and the giver in the pew are partners in the same work (Philippians 1:5).

How much should I give to Christ’s work? These women kept on providing out of their own means, and Luke records no amount, only the habit and the love behind it. The New Testament does not set a fixed percentage, but it gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, in keeping with how God has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, because whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly (2 Corinthians 9:6). Give cheerfully, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the work of the gospel in your own church, which supports those who teach you (Galatians 6:6), and then beyond it. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. The real question is not what is the least I can give, but what does this gift say about where my treasure is (12:34)?
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower explains why the same word meets such different responses, and why the disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. Jesus tells it to a great crowd (vv. 4–8), then explains it privately (vv. 9–15), with a hard word in between about why he teaches in parables.

That hard word quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, the hardening that follows a persistent refusal of God’s word. It is a judgment on people who have already refused what they were given; yet a parable is also a door held ajar for anyone who, like the disciples, comes back and asks.

The seed is the word of God; what differs is the ground. The parable is not a rigid classification of people but a mirror, and every hearer is invited to look into it.
verseByVerse.theology:
In Mark, Jesus asks how the disciples will understand any of the parables if they do not understand this one (Mark 4:13). It sets the pattern for all his teaching: the response to the word decides everything.

The seed does not change, and neither does the generous hand that scatters it. What varies is the heart. The good soil is an honest and good heart: not a morally superior heart, but one that lets the word say what it says without bargaining, even when the diagnosis is unflattering. And the last word is patience.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable puts one question to every hearer: not whether you have heard the gospel, but what has happened to the word in you.

The rock soil has troubled sincere believers, and should be handled with care. It describes someone who fell away, not someone who is struggling and worried about it, and what God begins he finishes (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28). The remedy is not to inspect your own roots but to go deeper, in the quiet habits nobody sees, before the dry season comes.

The thorns are the soil to watch most closely in a comfortable life, because nothing seems wrong. Cares, riches and pleasures are not sins in themselves, and that is why the choking is so hard to notice until the harvest shows a stalk with nothing ripe on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Luke has just shown two hearers at one dinner: a Pharisee who heard nothing, and a forgiven woman who loved much (7:36–50). Now Jesus explains why the same word meets such different hearts, in a section on hearing (8:4–21) that ends with his true family, those who hear the word of God and do it.

A great crowd. People are coming from town after town, and this is the moment Jesus chooses to tell a story in which three of the four soils yield nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds, and preparing his disciples for the years ahead and for every century since.

A sower went out. Every listener had watched it done. In that farming, it seems, sowing often came before ploughing: a man walked the field with a bag at his hip, flinging seed in wide arcs, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed really did fall everywhere, on the path, on thin soil over limestone, into corners where last year’s thorns were still rooted. The same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

Along the path. Footpaths ran through and around the fields, packed hard by generations of feet. The seed could not sink in. Only Luke adds that it was trampled underfoot, the detail of a careful reporter: before the birds even arrive, the ordinary traffic of ordinary life has walked over it, and then, lying on the surface, it is easy picking. Nothing has gone wrong with the seed; the surface would not let it in.

The sower is not named. Jesus identifies the seed (v. 11) and all four soils, and about the man with the bag he says nothing at all. That silence is a mercy to everyone who has ever tried to sow anything. The variable is the ground, not the preacher’s skill, and the sower cannot manufacture soil.

The sower telling the story. Jesus does not name the sower, but the scene does. The first man with the bag is standing in front of this crowd, telling them what his own preaching will meet: hearts packed hard, hearts shallow, hearts already crowded. He knows most of the great crowd will drift away, and he sows anyway, because the seed is his Father’s word and the harvest is his Father’s business. The Son of God did not ration the word to the promising; somewhere among the paths and rocks were hearts his Father had prepared.

So does it not matter how we share the gospel? It matters, but not in the way we fear. We should speak clearly, kindly and wisely (Colossians 4:5–6), and Paul worked hard to remove needless obstacles (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). But the parable lifts from us the burden of thinking the harvest depends on our skill. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Your job is to scatter the seed faithfully and widely; the soil is in God’s hands. That frees you to share Christ without manipulation, and without despair when most people do not respond.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some fell on the rock. This is not bare stone. Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil, and to a man walking the field it looks like the rest. Seed goes in, germinates fast, precisely because the shallow soil warms quickly, and comes up before anything else in the field. Then the sun comes, and the roots find rock instead of water. Only Luke mentions moisture: no depth, no water, no life. The fastest growth in the field is the first to die.

And some fell among thorns. Here nothing seems wrong. The soil is good, the seed goes in, the plant grows, and so does everything else. The thorns were not planted; their roots were already there from last year, unseen. They do not attack the wheat. They grow at the same time, for the same water and light, faster and stronger. Choked: slow death by competition, while the crop is still standing.

A hundredfold. Deep, clean, prepared ground. A hundred grains for one is an enormous return, far beyond what a farmer in that country would normally expect (compare Genesis 26:12, where Isaac reaped a hundredfold because the LORD blessed him). The figure is deliberately extravagant: the yield of the fourth soil more than covers everything lost on the other three.

Ears to hear. Luke says he called out, raising his voice over the crowd at the end. Everyone has ears; not everyone truly hears, and hearing in the Bible means listening, understanding and obeying. A man who hears the parable of the soils and never asks which soil he is has not yet really heard it.

Ears for his voice. Whose voice is calling out over the crowd? In the Old Testament the summons to hear belongs to God: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4); incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live (Isaiah 55:3). The prophets said, thus says the LORD, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus raises his voice and points the summons at his own words, as though hearing him and hearing God were the same thing. The Father settles it from the cloud: This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (9:35).

Can a person change from one soil to another? Yes, by the grace of God. The parable describes how people respond to the word at a given time, not a fixed caste they are born into. Hard ground can be broken up; God promises to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). Many Christians can look back on years when the word bounced off them, or sprang up and died, before God finally made the soil good. That is why we keep sowing, and why we keep praying for those who have heard and not yet believed.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples asked. They do not assume they have understood; they come back and ask, and that asking is the parable enacted. The crowd heard a story about farming and went home; these men heard the same story and pressed for more. What separates them is not superior insight (Mark records Jesus telling them they had not understood it either, Mark 4:13). It is that they came back.

To you it has been given. Note the passive: understanding the kingdom is not achieved by intelligence but given by God (10:21; Matthew 16:17).

The secrets of the kingdom. Secrets (mystēria) are truths once hidden and now revealed by God: above all, that the kingdom has come in Jesus, in an unexpected form, like a seed, and not yet like a harvest (Ephesians 3:3–6).

The secret is a person. The secret is not a key for decoding stories but a person, sitting with them and explaining his own parables: no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). The Twelve are not sharper than the crowd; they are closer to him, and the one who is himself the mystery of the kingdom opens it to those who stay and ask. And John tells us Isaiah said these words because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41): the Lord high and lifted up of Isaiah 6, whose holiness made the prophet cry out that he was lost, is the teacher answering fishermen’s questions.

So that seeing they may not see. One of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be softened. Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9–10: the commission God gave Isaiah after the vision of the throne, telling him in advance that his preaching would harden a rebellious people. Luke, unlike Mark, leaves out the end of the quotation (lest they turn and be forgiven), perhaps because he holds it back for the end of Acts (Acts 28:26–27).

Does God then deliberately blind people? Three things have to be held together. First, this is a judgment, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given. Isaiah’s commission comes after generations of ignored prophets, and Luke has already shown us a Nazareth that tried to kill Jesus and experts plotting against him. The parables are a form of judgment on those who have already rejected the truth. They hear the stories without understanding, because they do not want to. To those who reject the light, more light is withheld (v. 18). Second, a parable is not merely a veil. It is also a door held ajar. It hides the thing from the casual and rewards the man who comes back and asks, which is precisely what has just happened in verse 9. The same story that closed the crowd’s ears opened these men’s, and the difference was whether they returned. Third, this is mercy as well as judgment. To be told plainly and to reject it plainly is a far more terrible position than to be told in a story you did not follow. A parable leaves the door open longer than a sermon does.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to keep people from salvation. For the hard-hearted, parables confirm their blindness: the same sun melts wax and hardens clay. Nor can it excuse one’s own dullness. The remedy is in verse 9: they asked.

If understanding is given, why do some get it and others not? Scripture answers with two truths and does not let us drop either. Understanding is God’s gift, given freely to whom he wills, so that no one may boast (Matthew 11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 4:7). And those who do not understand are not innocent victims; they are people who love the darkness and will not come to the light (John 3:19). God never blinds a willing seeker. If you want to understand, that wanting is itself the beginning of the gift, and the promise stands: ask, and it will be given; seek, and you will find (11:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed is the word of God. That identification settles a great deal. The seed is the gospel message, not the preacher or his technique, and it is the same seed in all four soils. Its power is in the seed, not the sower (Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 Peter 1:23). The sower is first Jesus, and then everyone who spreads his word.

The devil comes. The birds are the devil. This is not only a psychological account of inattention. Something intelligent and hostile is at work in the moment between hearing and believing, and its strategy is remarkably modest. It does not need to refute the word. It only needs to remove it before it goes in: by distraction, by doubt, by forgetfulness, by the next thing that comes along. The god of this world has blinded the minds of those who do not believe (2 Corinthians 4:4).

Believe and be saved. Only Luke adds this. That is what is at stake in a distracted hour. Faith comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17); Satan’s strategy is to stop the hearing from taking root.

The one the devil could not rob. Luke’s readers have already watched the devil try this once. In the wilderness he came to Jesus with the same aim, to pry the word of God loose from a hungry man (4:1–13). Three times he tried, and three times Jesus answered, it is written, and the word stayed where it was. What every heart on the path loses, the Son of Man held, and not for himself only. Within this chapter he will drive out a legion, and at the cross he would disarm the powers, so that the enemy who snatches seed from the path has met one he cannot rob, and those who belong to Christ are kept by the stronger hand.

What a footpath is. A footpath is not naturally hard ground. It is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get in, and the traffic that packed it was perfectly innocent. That is the danger of a life with no quiet in it. The word arrives on Sunday, and by the time the car is out of the car park there has been a conversation, a screen, a plan for the afternoon, and it is gone, and nobody did anything wrong.

Can the devil take the word from a Christian? He can steal a particular sermon from a believer’s attention, and he often does. But he cannot snatch a true believer out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28), because the word that saves has been planted by the Spirit, who keeps what he has begun. The path in this parable describes those in whom the word never went in at all. For the Christian, the warning is practical: guard the moment after hearing. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

In everyday life. You are kept by the one the devil could not rob, so guard the moment after hearing. Next Sunday, before you speak to anyone after the sermon, take two minutes to name to God the one thing he said to you, and on the drive home talk about it instead of the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Receive it with joy. This soil has hurt sensitive consciences, so it must be handled carefully. The response is real as far as it goes: they receive it with joy, and the joy is not called false. But joy alone is not proof of genuine faith.

But these have no root. No depth: the word has not gone down into their heart and will. Root is the part nobody can see, and it only shows up in a drought. Only Luke says they believe for a while: a real but temporary belief, of the mind and the feelings, but not a heart transformed by God.

And in time of testing fall away. Testing (peirasmos) is the same word as at 4:13: trial, or temptation, the two senses English keeps apart and Greek does not. Matthew says, when tribulation or persecution arises (Matthew 13:21). Fall away (aphistantai) means depart, apostatise.

I have prayed for you. Testing is the word Luke uses again for the hour that came on the Twelve. On the night of his arrest Jesus told them to pray that they might not enter into temptation (22:40), and before it he told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift them like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (22:31–32). Peter fell that night, and fell hard. Yet he did not fall away, because the root of his faith was not his own resolve but the prayer of his Lord. The Father always hears the Son (John 11:42), and that is the deepest difference between the rock and the good soil: the Son of God prays for his own, and he always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25).

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians (Christians who follow the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius, and Wesleyan Methodists after him) take this as a believer who loses salvation, and many of them hold the view out of a deep reverence for the Bible’s warnings. This commentary’s view: the parable describes a faith that was never rooted, never the saving faith of the good soil. Its fruit never came. Scripture teaches that those whom God truly saves he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and that those who fall away permanently show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). This is the perseverance of the saints. But the warning is real: God keeps his people through warnings like this one, not in spite of them. Examine yourselves.

Is this me? Have I lost my salvation? The question presses on any believer who has ever gone through a bad season, and three things need saying, in this order. First, the passage is not describing someone who is struggling. It describes someone who fell away, who is no longer there. A person worried about this verse is by definition still asking the question, which is not what the rock soil does. Second, Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes. Paul was sure that the one who began a good work in the Philippians would carry it on to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John’s own comment on those who left is not that they lost something but that they went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The rock soil is not a Christian who was lost; it is a plant that never had root. Third, and this is the pastoral point, the remedy is never endless introspection. Staring at your own root system is exactly what a plant cannot do. What can be done is to go deeper: to put the word somewhere it can reach water, in the unspectacular disciplines that nobody sees, before the drought arrives. Because it will. The sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather. And a dry season is not falling away: doubt, grief and even depression have brought many of God’s dearest children to cry out, why are you cast down, O my soul? (Psalm 42:5), and they were still his, still asking, still reaching for water.

How do I put down roots? Roots grow in hidden places and over time. Read the Bible daily, not for information only but to meet God. Pray, especially when you do not feel like it. Sit under faithful preaching week by week, and come to the Lord’s Table. Join yourself to a church where people know you well enough to notice if you wither. Learn the great truths of the faith, so that when trouble comes you know what God has promised. And obey what you already know, because obedience is how the word goes down from the head into the will. None of it is dramatic. All of it is how God keeps his people.

In everyday life. If you are a new Christian full of joy, thank God for the joy and give your attention to the roots. If you are leading others, do not measure a conversion by its excitement; walk with new believers through their first drought.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the thorns. This is the most dangerous soil, because it is the only one where nothing appears to be wrong. The man is still in the field, still green. What is happening is gradual and invisible until harvest, when it turns out there is nothing on the stalk.

Choked as they go. There is no decision and no turning point. It happens over a decade, in the course of getting on with life, and the verb is strangled, slowly.

Cares, riches and pleasures. Not one of the three thorns is in itself a sin. Cares: anxieties, worries about daily life, the future, money, health, a difficult child, an ageing parent, a job that may not last (12:22–31; 21:34). Riches: not theft, simply having things and the work of keeping them, and the love of money and possessions that so easily grows from it (12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). Pleasures of life: only Luke adds this. Not vice, but the innocent pleasures of an ordinary life, good things that crowd out God.

The thorns are legitimate things. In a comfortable country the word is choked almost entirely by legitimate things, which is why it is so hard to see. A man being strangled by an obvious sin usually knows it. A man being strangled by his mortgage, his hobbies and his family’s diary has nothing to repent of that he can name. Underneath, each thorn is a rival saviour. Worry quietly assumes that everything depends on me; riches promise a security God never promised through them; pleasures offer a happiness only he can give. The thorns grow wherever the heart has begun to trust them instead of him.

Their fruit does not mature. Not, they bear no fruit at all. There is growth, perhaps even the beginning of fruit, but it never ripens. No one can serve two masters (16:13).

The one thing necessary. Luke shows the remedy for the thorns in a home in Bethany. Martha, whom Jesus calls anxious and troubled about many things (the same word as the cares of this verse), is busy with good work for Jesus; Mary sits at his feet listening to his word, and Jesus says that one thing is necessary, and that Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her (10:38–42). The thorns are not beaten by more effort. They are outgrown by a greater love. When Christ himself is the treasure, cares lose their grip, riches become tools, and pleasures become thanksgivings.

Are the thorn-soil hearers saved? The seed is choked and brings no fruit to maturity, and in the parable only the good soil bears a crop. The more likely reading is that they never truly believed: a faith that bears no fruit at all is not saving faith (compare John 15:2, 6). Some Christians read them as believers who are saved but fruitless. But a true believer may struggle with worries and riches and still bear fruit; the warning is not to let them choke the word.

Is it wrong to enjoy the good things of life? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and food, friendship, marriage, work and rest are his gifts. The thorns are not the pleasures themselves but the place they take. A pleasure becomes a thorn when it takes the time, the attention and the love that belong to God, when it becomes the thing you cannot give up. The test is not whether you enjoy things, but whether you could enjoy them less for Christ’s sake, and whether they lead you to thank him or to forget him.

In everyday life. Ask not what sins you are fighting but what has quietly become non-negotiable in your week. Thorns are not planted; they are simply left. Pull one out this week: cancel the thing that always crowds out prayer, give away what has begun to own you, or hand a named worry to God.

For worship. In his presence there is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures for evermore (Psalm 16:11); the pleasures that choke are thin and brief beside that. The cares that strangle us he bids us throw on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7), and he knows their weight: the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head and carried a world’s sin, and his heart was never once divided. Every fruit of his obedience came to full ripeness, and that undivided obedience is counted to people whose hearts are divided still. Blessed be the Lord who was never choked, and who is untangling us.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold it fast. Every mark here is unspectacular. Hearing the word: the same word, from the same sower, that fell on all the other ground. Hold it fast (katechousin): keep it, grip it, refuse to let it go. It is active, because things get taken. Mary treasured the word (2:19). The good hearer hangs on to it.

In an honest and good heart. Only Luke has this phrase (kalē kai agathē), which in Greek described a person of fine and noble character, and Jesus fills it with new content.
