The heart he commends is the honest one: open to God, not managing an impression, letting the word say what it says without negotiating. That is the one mark of good soil anybody can test in himself: when the word says something I do not like, do I let it stand?

Where does a good heart come from? Such a heart is itself God’s gift; he prepares the soil. The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what Paul said (Acts 16:14). No one is good soil by nature. Since the fall, every human heart is path, rock or thorns until God breaks it up and makes it new (Jeremiah 17:9; Ezekiel 36:26). If your heart has received the word and held it fast, give God the glory. And if you long for a better heart, ask him for it. That longing is already his work.

And bear fruit with patience. The last word is patience (hypomonē): endurance, steadfastness under pressure, the opposite of the rocky ground (v. 13). The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is never praised for speed at all.

The ear that was never closed. There has been one hearer whose heart was wholly honest and good. Isaiah heard the Servant of the Lord say that morning by morning God wakened his ear to hear as one who is taught, and that he was not rebellious and did not turn back (Isaiah 50:4–5). Jesus held his Father’s word fast through the whole of his life, in Gethsemane and on the cross, and bore fruit with endurance to the end. And the good soil in his people comes from him. The heart that receives the word is the new heart of the new covenant (Ezekiel 36:26), made in his blood (22:20). And the patience in which it bears fruit is the endurance of the one who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

What is the fruit? The fruit is a changed life: the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience and good works (Colossians 1:10); and, in God’s time, others brought to faith. It is not measured by size or fame. A hundredfold in the parable is the same seed reproduced, and the fruit of the word in you is Christlikeness. Do not compare your harvest with someone else’s; Jesus speaks elsewhere of a hundredfold, sixty and thirty, and all of it is good soil (Matthew 13:23).

In everyday life. The patience is the Spirit’s fruit in you, not a grit you must manufacture. Choose one verse from Sunday’s sermon and carry it with you all week: write it down, repeat it, pray it. That is what holding fast looks like in an ordinary week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two short teachings apply the parable. The lamp saying guards against a wrong conclusion: the disciples have been let into the secrets of the kingdom, but not to keep them to themselves. What is now hidden will come to light: a promise for the gospel, and a solemn word for anyone hiding something.

Take care then how you hear gathers up the section. To the one who has, more will be given: understanding grows as it is used and withers when it is not, and Luke alone warns that even what a man thinks he has can be taken away.

Then Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive, and he says that his family are those who hear the word of God and do it. This is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15 given a family name.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying applies the parable to the disciples’ own calling. The secrets of the kingdom were given to them (v. 10) to be made known, not kept: the word is the lamp, and the world they will be sent into is the stand.

The family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already shown of Mary. She is not demoted; she is the first member of this family, the woman who said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38). The brothers who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5) later came in by the same door (Acts 1:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
A family made by hearing and doing the word is the root of the church’s fellowship across every natural division. The first churches drew Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women into one household, and every congregation is meant to be that kind of family still.

Take care then how you hear becomes a practical question: not what was preached, but what was done with it between Sunday and Tuesday. And the warning about what a man thinks he has is aimed at the person who is sure he is fine.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lighting a lamp. The saying is placed here on purpose. A disciple let into the secrets of the kingdom could easily conclude that they are his to keep. The lamp saying shuts that down. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick, holding perhaps an hour or two of light, and you light it to give light, not to hide it.

Or puts it under a bed. The two absurdities are exact. A jar over it would smother it for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed would set the house on fire. Both destroy the light while pretending to keep it.

On a stand. Not so that the lamp may be admired, but so that those who enter from outside can see (11:33; Matthew 5:14–16). The secrets of the kingdom were given to the disciples (v. 10) to be put where strangers can see by them.

A light for the Gentiles. The lamp has a name in Luke. When old Simeon took the baby in his arms in the temple, he called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32). The light hidden for now in parables and in a house in Galilee is Christ himself, and the stand it was always meant for is the world. After the resurrection repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:47). The ones who enter from outside are the nations, coming in to see by him. The disciples are not the light. They are the household that must not cover it.

Nothing is hidden. This cuts two ways. Forward, it is a promise: the truth of the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will be fully revealed, and the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house. Luke is writing the second volume that proves it.

Nor is anything secret. The sentence has a second edge. Everything hidden in human hearts will be exposed at the judgment (12:2–3; 1 Corinthians 4:5). There is no permanently private life. For anyone hiding something, that is terrifying. For anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off, it is a deep comfort.

What if I have something hidden? Bring it into the light now, before God, and where needed before those you have wronged. The light that will one day expose everything is the same light in which there is forgiveness: if we walk in the light, the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). What is confessed to God is covered by Christ, and it will not be held against you on that day. The secrets that destroy are the ones we keep. A Christian has nothing to fear from the final light, because everything shameful in his life has already been dealt with at the cross.

In everyday life. The light is Christ, already lit; your part is not to cover him. Find the one place in your week where no one knows you are a Christian, at work, at the gym, among a set of friends, and ask what it would look like this week to take the jar off.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care then how you hear. Not what you hear but how: with an honest heart, holding it fast, obeying it. The four soils were not four kinds of seed. Hearing is a moral act, with consequences.

To the one who has. Read at speed, it sounds like a cruelty: the rich get richer. It describes how understanding behaves: capacity grows by use. A man who acts on what he has understood finds more opened to him; the next thing is intelligible because the last one was obeyed.

From the one who has not. A man who receives and does nothing loses even the ability to receive, not by an arbitrary penalty but by atrophy. Neglected truth is lost.

Even what he thinks that he has. Luke alone has this sharp phrase; Mark says simply what he has. Luke’s version is more disturbing: the man’s holdings were never what he supposed. He has been carrying a receipt for something that is not in the vault. That is the rock soil and the thorn soil: both would have said they had it, and the discovery came at the worst moment, in the drought and at the harvest. And there is a mercy in being told now, while he can still come and ask.

More will be given. What is the more? In Luke it is Christ himself, opened ever more fully. The disciples who listen so slowly in this chapter keep listening, and at the end the risen Lord walks with two of them and, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:27). And the one from whom even what he thinks he has is taken is the man who has the Scriptures without him. The scribes knew every line and refused to come to the one they were about (John 5:39–40).

What does good listening look like on a Sunday? Come prepared: pray before the service that God would speak, and come rested enough to listen. Listen expecting God, not merely a speaker, to address you (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Have your Bible open and test what you hear by it (Acts 17:11). Listen for yourself before you listen for others: what is this saying to me? Afterwards, talk about it, and decide on one thing to do. And keep listening when the preacher is not gifted; the seed is the word, not the sower.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers. Luke mentions the brothers without explanation; Mark names four of them, James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mentions sisters as well (Mark 6:3). John tells us plainly what they thought of him at this stage: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). They came to faith only after the resurrection (Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7).

Why had they come? Luke is discreet; Mark is not, and records that his family set out to seize him, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31–35). Whatever exactly is happening at the edge of this crowd, it is not a social visit, and they cannot even reach him because of the crowd.

My mother and my brothers. Read carefully, this is not a put-down of his mother. He does not say he has no mother and brothers, and he does not refuse to see them. He loved his mother, and from the cross he provided for her (John 19:26–27). What he does is redefine the family, in public, at the very moment the claim of blood was pressed on him. A new family has come into being, bound not by blood but by obedience to God’s word.

The good soil with a family name. This is the good soil of verse 15 given a family name, and almost word for word the two builders at the end of the sermon (6:47–49).

Not a rejection of Mary. It is an inclusion of everybody else on the terms Mary met first. The woman who said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38), is the founding member of the family, and even her blessedness lies chiefly in hearing and keeping God’s word (11:27–28).

The family he makes. Who has the right to say who his mother is? Only someone who can make a family by his word. Jesus is founding a household around himself, and its centre is his person. The brothers who thought him mad are later found among the praying disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14), in the family by hearing, like everyone else. Their blood tie gave them no head start; grace is the only door he has ever opened. So doing the word is not the entrance fee into the family; it is the family likeness. A child does not obey in order to become a child, but a child who truly hears his father begins to look like him (James 1:22–25).

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children, Jesus’ half-brothers (compare 2:7, where Jesus is her firstborn son; Mark 6:3). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, read them as cousins, since the Hebrew and Aramaic word for brother can be broad, or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage; some early Protestants, Luther and Zwingli among them, also thought Mary remained a virgin, and the view is held out of reverence for her. But Scripture never suggests either reading, and the plain one is the more likely.

Does following Jesus mean neglecting my family? No. Scripture commands us to honour father and mother (Ephesians 6:2) and says that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus himself cared for his mother to the end. What this passage teaches is priority, not neglect: when family claims and Christ’s claims collide, Christ comes first (14:26). For many believers, especially converts from other faiths, that collision is painful and real. For them the promise is precious: they gain, in the church, mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold (Mark 10:29–30).

In everyday life. Grace has made you Jesus’ family, and hearing and doing God’s word is its likeness. You will never do it perfectly, but your elder Brother did his Father’s will perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours. Who in your church has no family nearby, or a family that has rejected them for Christ? Invite them to your table this month. And if your own relatives do not yet believe, keep loving them as Jesus loved his brothers: patiently, until the day they too may come in.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus himself tells the disciples to cross the lake, so it is obedience that puts them in the storm. He falls asleep in the stern, and experienced fishermen conclude they are about to drown.

Jesus rebukes the wind and the waves with the verb Luke used of a demon and a fever (4:35, 39). He does not pray; he commands. Then he asks where their faith is, which assumes they had some and had mislaid it. They are more frightened after the calm than during the storm, and they ask the question the chapter is built around: who then is this?
verseByVerse.theology:
In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea: he stills the storm and hushes the waves (Psalm 107:29; compare Psalm 89:9; Job 38:8–11). The disciples’ question has one answer, and Luke leaves it hanging until Peter’s confession (9:20).

The sleep matters as much as the stilling. He sleeps in peace, trusting his Father; the one who will tell his disciples not to be anxious (12:22) is at rest in a sinking boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and are still terrified. That is an honest picture of discipleship: knowing who he is in general is not the same as trusting him in a particular crisis. In a crisis, faith is more often mislaid than lost.

The story is less about their failure than about the one in the boat with them. He did not scold them for waking him; he stilled the storm, and then asked where their faith had gone, to help them grow.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four miracles. Having taught the disciples how to hear, Luke now shows, in four miracles over nature, demons, disease and death (8:22–56), who it is they are hearing.

Let us go across. The trip was not the disciples’ idea and it was not a detour. They are in that boat, in that weather, because Jesus told them to get in and where to go. He intended them to reach the other side. The storm was not the result of some failure; obedience put them there.

As they sailed he fell asleep. This is the only time the Gospels tell us that Jesus slept, and Luke puts it with a doctor’s plainness: as they sailed, he dropped off. A day of preaching to crowds lies behind it. The Son of Man who will soon say he has nowhere to lay his head (9:58) finds a place in the stern of a fishing boat; Mark adds that it was on the cushion (Mark 4:38). It is the incarnation, doing what a body does. And he sleeps in peace, trusting his Father: in peace I will both lie down and sleep (Psalm 4:8).

A windstorm came down. Came down: the geography explains it. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling down to the water from the heights to the east. Cold air drops into the warm basin without warning, and the small, shallow lake goes from flat to dangerous in minutes.

In danger. Luke states the professional verdict plainly, and the men making it include four commercial fishermen who had worked this water all their lives. They have concluded they are going to drown. Sometimes fear is simply an accurate reading of the instruments.

If I am obeying God, why am I in a storm? Because obedience does not exempt us from storms; sometimes it leads us into them. The disciples were exactly where Jesus told them to be. Paul was shipwrecked on a voyage God had appointed (Acts 27). A storm is not proof that you have taken a wrong turn. It may be the very path on which Christ means to show you who he is. The question is not whether storms will come, but who is in the boat with you.

For worship. He slept in the storm because he was truly man; he stilled it because he was truly God. The Word made flesh grew tired and slept in a fishing boat, sharing our weakness; he knows what exhaustion is. And the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4); even asleep in the stern, the Son of God had never stopped holding the sea.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Master, Master, we are perishing! The doubled address is the sound of men shaking somebody awake. Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s, where they say: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). And their verdict is in the present tense: not, we are going to drown, but we are perishing; it is happening.

They wake him. Underneath the panic, they do one right thing. Some instinct sent them to the back of the boat and not only to the oars. It is not much of a faith, but it is pointed in exactly the right direction, which is very often what faith looks like at three in the morning.

He rebuked the wind. The verb is rebuked, and Luke has used it before in this Gospel: of the demon in the synagogue (4:35), and of Peter’s mother-in-law’s fever (4:39). Jesus speaks to the storm as a master to a disobedient servant. And there is no prayer, as a prophet would have prayed; he speaks to the weather in the imperative.

A calm. Instantly, a dead flat calm. When a wind drops, the swell normally runs on for hours. Here the water goes flat in the same instant. What they had asked for was rescue. What they got was a demonstration.

Jesus does what God does. In the Scriptures these men learned as boys, exactly one person speaks to the sea like that. The LORD rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry (Psalm 106:9); at his rebuke the waters fled (Psalm 104:7); he shut in the sea with doors and said, thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:8–11). The same rebuke has silenced a demon and a fever and now the sea, because the one rebuking is Lord over every kind of disorder, in a soul, in a body, in the world itself. The one who does that is in the stern of their boat, and they had just woken him up.

Will Jesus always calm my storm? Not always in the way we ask. Sometimes he stills the storm; sometimes he stills his child in the storm, and carries him through it; sometimes he brings him home through it. Paul’s thorn was not removed, and many martyrs were not rescued. But this story shows what is always true: nothing in your storm is beyond his command, and you are never in the boat alone. Cry out to him, as the disciples did. He hears, and whatever he does, he will bring you to the other side he promised.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where is your faith? The question is gentler than it looks in English. He does not say, why have you no faith? He asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some, and that it was mislaid rather than absent. That is the ordinary condition of most believers in most crises, and there is comfort in seeing it named without contempt. The question is not an accusation but a search: where did you put it?

What he is not rebuking. Not their fear of the storm, nor their waking him. What has gone missing is the conclusion they should have drawn from what they had already seen. His word, let us go to the other side, should have been enough. They had watched him command a demon and a fever with a word, and a dead man sit up at a town gate. The storm did not find them ignorant; it found them not applying what they knew.

Afraid, and they marveled. They were more frightened after the storm stopped than during it. The wind had merely threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. This is what happens whenever sinful people find themselves close to the holy. Isaiah saw the Lord and cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); Peter, in a boat on this same lake, fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man (5:8). The fear in the boat is not a failure of faith. It is the right response of creatures when God comes near.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him? There it is: the question this whole Gospel exists to answer, asked out loud for the first time by the men closest to him, sitting in a wet boat on a flat sea. They do not answer it. Luke leaves it hanging, and he will leave it hanging until the next chapter, when Peter finally says it (9:20). But these men had very likely known Psalm 107 since childhood: then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress; he made the storm be still (Psalm 107:28–29). They are with the Lord himself.

Is fear always wrong for a Christian? No. There is a fear that is simply realism, and a fear that is reverence. The disciples’ first fear (of drowning) was natural; their second fear (of him) was the beginning of wisdom. What Jesus questions is not the feeling of fear but faith gone missing: forgetting who is in the boat. The answer to sinful fear is not to stop feeling, but to fear God more. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). The psalmist is afraid and trusting in the same breath.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore, in Gentile country east of the lake, a man held by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet. He has lost his clothes, his home among the living and his very self.

The demons know exactly who Jesus is, and all they do is beg. Jesus lets them go into a herd of pigs, and the herd rushes into the lake: the destruction is the demons’ doing, and it shows what had been living in the man. The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind and sitting at Jesus’ feet, and they ask Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with him and is sent home instead, to tell what God has done for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This deliverance happens in Gentile territory, to a Gentile man: the kingdom of God does not stop at Israel’s borders. He is the Gentile counterpart of the man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33), freed by the same word.

The restored man sits at Jesus’ feet, where a disciple sits (10:39; Acts 22:3). He has not merely been emptied; the ground has been given to a new Master.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople are a warning about valuing what we can count over what we cannot control. A madman in the tombs could be chained; the power that set him free could not be managed, and they asked it to go.

The man’s request to follow, and Jesus’ refusal, is a call many believers know: go back to the people who knew you before. It is a harder road than the boat, and his testimony there was one no stranger could give.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The country of the Gerasenes. This is Gentile territory: the region of the Decapolis, east of the lake, Greek-speaking, with pigs on the hillsides, which tells you at once that no Jewish community is farming here. Luke explains opposite Galilee for readers who did not know the geography.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? Manuscripts vary, and the likeliest answer is that the spot was Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi), where the hills drop sharply to the shore, while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. (See Mark 5:1 for the fuller answer.)

One man or two? The second is the number. Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matthew 8:28). Neither denies the other. Matthew adds a second man; he does not subtract one. Where a pair is involved and only one does the talking and only one is left with a story to tell, a writer naturally follows him. Mark and Luke keep the camera on the man who spoke, who was called Legion, who begged to come along and was sent home instead. The same thing happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

No clothes. Only Luke mentions the nakedness: the loss of the most basic mark of human dignity, and for a long time it was his settled condition.

Among the tombs. No house: no address, no household, no place at anybody’s table. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside, in a Jewish frame the last word in uncleanness, and in any frame a man living among the dead because the living will not have him. Here is Satan’s work: degradation, isolation, uncleanness, death.

Liberty to the captives. At Nazareth Jesus read that he was anointed to proclaim liberty to the captives (4:18), then reminded his hometown that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed Naaman the Syrian (4:25–27), and they tried to throw him off a cliff. Here he acts out that sermon: he crosses a storm to a Gentile shore and goes straight to the most bound man on it. It is the mission of Acts in miniature, a generation early.

Was this man demon-possessed, or mentally ill? Luke, a physician, distinguishes healings from exorcisms (4:40–41), and this man’s condition had a demonic cause: the demons speak and are cast out into the pigs. Possession is real, and the New Testament does not say it has ceased. But most mental illness has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Christians should neither see demons behind every illness nor deny that the devil works. And the modern assumption that nothing personal and evil stands behind the darkness of the world is itself a belief, not a finding; Luke the doctor knew the difference between a fever and a demon, and he records both.

Could a believer end up like the man from the tombs? No. That man was owned until Jesus stepped off the boat; once Christ claims a person, the ownership has changed hands for good. The Holy Spirit dwells in every believer (1 Corinthians 6:19), who is sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13) and has been rescued from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). A house cannot have two owners. A Christian can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and is told to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but never to fear being taken over by him. The one who lives in you is greater than the one who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In everyday life. No one is too far gone, too degraded, too unclean for Jesus to reach. Every town has someone everyone has given up on: the addict, the man who sleeps rough, the relative no one mentions. Jesus crossed a stormy lake for a man like that. Pray for that person, and ask what step of love you could take. Use the help God gives through doctors and counsellors, and bring the bondages no programme has broken to the one before whom every bondage gives way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He fell down before him. The demon recognises its master and submits: the posture of worship, forced out of an enemy.

What have you to do with me? The opening phrase is a stock formula of confrontation, literally what to me and to you?, the ancient equivalent of what do you want with me? The same words came out of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:34).

Jesus, Son of the Most High God. Son of the Most High is the title Gabriel used to Mary (1:32). Most High God is a title often used by or to Gentiles for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17). The demons know exactly who Jesus is.

I beg you, do not torment me. This is the first of four times in this scene that begging happens, and three of them come from the demons. The powers of darkness spend the whole passage pleading. And they know there is a schedule; Matthew records them saying it: have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29).

The Judge has come as Deliverer. Why do the demons speak of torment? Because they know who will judge them. The Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), and the demons recognise the Judge before the court has sat; this carpenter is the one appointed to judge the living and the dead (Acts 10:42). But the Judge has come first as Deliverer. He will bear judgment himself at the cross, for sinners, not for demons, and on this beach he spends his authority not on sentencing the man’s captors but on freeing their captive.

Chains and shackles. Luke adds a case history, as a doctor would: for many a time it had seized him. The town had tried chains and guards, again and again, to manage a man it could not help.

Driven into the desert. The demon drove him, as a herdsman drives cattle, and each failed restraint sent him further out. Chains can stop a man harming anybody; they cannot give him back his mind.

Should Christians fear demons? No. This passage is written to cure that fear. The demons are the ones who are terrified; they fall down, beg, and know their doom. Christ has disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Christians should take the devil seriously, be watchful and resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). But they should never be fascinated by him or afraid of him. The right response to the dark powers is not fear of them, but trust in the one before whom they tremble.

For worship. Heaven named him Son of the Most High before he was born, and now hell names him the same on a Gentile beach. Heaven and hell agree on who he is; only men argue. What the demons confess in terror the redeemed will confess in joy (Philippians 2:10–11), and the one before whom darkness trembles is the one under whose wings his people shelter.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then asked him, What is your name? It is the only question Jesus asks in the whole encounter, and it is worth asking why he asks it. Not for information. Perhaps to bring the man to awareness of his condition, or to expose the extent of the possession. But perhaps the simplest reason is the deepest: a name is what a person has, and this man has not been addressed as a person in years. The town called him a danger; the tombs were his address. Jesus asks him who he is.

Legion. The answer is horrifying on two counts. A Roman legion numbered about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. Whether the number is literal or a way of saying an army, a legion is not a crowd. It is an occupying force: organised, under orders, in possession of ground, and in the Decapolis people had watched them march.

For many demons had entered him. And the second horror is who answers: the question was put to the man, and the occupation speaks. He has been so comprehensively taken over that when asked for his own name he gives theirs. There is no I left to reply.

The real occupation. Israel longed for a Messiah who would drive the legions out of the land. Jesus meets a legion on this beach, and it is not Roman. Here is the occupation that really held the human race, and here is the King who really breaks it, not with a sword but with a word. Zechariah had sung of salvation from our enemies (1:71), and on a Gentile shore Luke shows how deep those enemies went and how complete the rescue would be.

Not into the abyss. Only Luke mentions the abyss (abyssos), the deep: in the Greek Old Testament it renders the waters of Genesis 1, and in later Jewish writing and in Revelation it is the bottomless pit, the prison of rebel spirits before their final judgment (Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–2; 20:1–3). They know he can send them there, and from verse 27 to verse 31 there is no struggle, only begging.

Why did Jesus not send them to the abyss at once? Because the time of their final judgment had not yet come (Matthew 8:29). Christ has defeated Satan decisively at the cross, but the final sentence will be carried out at his return, when the devil and his angels are thrown into the lake of fire (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Until then, evil is real but bound and limited, able to do only what God permits (Job 1:12). We live between the victory and the final execution of judgment, which is why we must still resist the devil, and why we can do so with confidence.

In everyday life. You have a name, given by him. Whatever has defined you, the addiction, the diagnosis, the failure, the label others have put on you, it is not who you are in Christ. He calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A herd of pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7). Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13).

His permission. Even demons need Jesus’ permission.

Who does the drowning. Jesus does not command the pigs into the lake. He grants a request, and it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death, doing to a herd in a moment what they had been doing to one man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them.

Into the lake. It showed visibly that the demons had left the man, and how many there were, and what they had wanted to do to him. The town had been looking at a naked man in the tombs and calling it madness. Now they have a hillside of evidence. And unclean spirits went with unclean animals into the deep.

The arithmetic. Sceptics point to the drowned herd as proof that Jesus cared nothing for livelihoods or animals. The loss was real, and the objection deserves an answer. One human being, made in the image of God, somebody’s son, is pulled out of a living death; a herd of pigs is lost. He will say in this Gospel that a man is worth more than many sparrows (12:7), and the scale holds here. This is not carelessness of animals; a righteous man regards the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). It is a judgment that one man was worth the loss. And the ruined herd forced the district to a decision it could no longer avoid: it put a price on the table.

What a man is worth to him. The town weighed the man against the herd and found the herd heavier. Jesus weighed them the other way, and the cross shows how far his scale tips. One man’s freedom cost the owners a herd of pigs; the freedom of all his people cost the Son of God his own life. You were ransomed, Peter writes, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). Nobody values a human being as highly as the one who paid for him. Ask where your own spending of time and money shows that you value things more than people.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What had happened. Every term answers something in verse 27. He had worn no clothes: he is clothed. He had lived among the tombs, driven into the desert: he is sitting. He had been out of his mind: he is in his right mind.

Sitting at the feet of Jesus. Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple. It is where Mary of Bethany will sit (10:39), and where Paul says he sat under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). He has not simply been emptied; he has been re-seated. That matters, because a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24–26).

Clothed, and in his right mind. No longer naked (v. 27); someone had given him clothes, perhaps from among the disciples. In his right mind is sōphronounta: sober, self-possessed, sane, at peace.

Healed. Healed (esōthē) is literally saved. The salvation is of the whole man: body, mind and soul. Luke uses the word that will run through the rest of the chapter.

They asked him to depart. This is the real indictment of the passage. The man they had chained and finally left in the graveyard is sitting in his right mind, and they want the man who did it to leave. Luke names one reason and implies another. The stated one is fear, for they were seized with great fear: something has come that they cannot manage, and that is more unsettling than a madman, because a madman can at least be chained. The unstated one is the hillside, and the herd in the lake that somebody has to account for. They preferred their pigs, their peace and their way of life to the presence of Jesus. Many still ask him to leave for the same reasons.

He returned. Jesus does not argue with the request, or press, or stay to reason with them. He came a long way across a dangerous lake for one man, and when the district asked him to go, he went. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

Can someone ask Jesus to leave for good? Jesus is patient, and he came back to the Decapolis later, where crowds received him (Mark 7:31–37). But this passage is a warning not to presume. The Gerasenes had one visit and sent him away. Scripture warns against hardening your heart today (Hebrews 3:15), because the day of opportunity does not last for ever. If you sense Christ calling you and you are inclined to send him off because he is disturbing or costly, do not wait. He may not cross the lake again on your timetable. But if you fear you have already sent him away for good, take heart from the fear itself: the Gerasenes were glad to see him go, and you are not. He has never yet turned away anyone who comes to him (John 6:37).

For worship. Look at the man at his feet: clothed, quiet, in his right mind. Christ does not tidy the surface; he gives a man back himself and a place at his feet. The same Lord would one day be led out of Jerusalem to a cross, and answer by praying for those who put him there (23:34). There is a patience in Christ that outlasts our refusals, and the man at his feet is what that patience makes of anyone it will not give up.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begged to be with him. This is the fourth begging in the passage, and the first from a human being. The demons begged three times; now the man begs to go with him, as the redeemed long to be with their Redeemer. And it is the only request in the scene that is refused.

A reasonable request. His neighbours had just told Jesus to leave. Every person in that district knew what he had been; there is no starting again in a place like that. The boat was leaving with twelve men who had left everything to follow, and he wanted a place among them.

Return to your home. But Jesus sent him away, with two commands, and both cost him something. Not everyone is called to leave home; some are called to stay and witness where they are. Return to your home: to relatives who had watched him deteriorate, to a town that had chained him and then given up. That is a harder road than the boat.

Declare how much God has done. He is not sent to argue or to explain the kingdom of God; he has had perhaps an hour’s instruction. He is sent to tell what happened to him, and he becomes, in effect, the first missionary to the Gentiles of the Decapolis. In Jewish territory Jesus often told people to keep quiet (8:56); here, where messianic excitement was less of a danger and where Jesus himself was not staying, he sends the man to tell. Anyone who has felt disqualified from speaking should notice: he had no training and no theology, only a before and an after that a whole district had witnessed.

How much Jesus had done. He was told to speak about God. He spoke about Jesus. Luke sets the two sentences side by side without comment, because what Jesus did, God did. He is the one the demons called Son of the Most High God (v. 28). And Mark adds that everyone marvelled (Mark 5:20). When Jesus later returned to the Decapolis, people brought the sick to him (Mark 7:31–37), perhaps in part the fruit of this man’s testimony.

How do I know whether to stay or go? Most Christians are called, like this man, to serve Christ where they already are: in their family, their street, their workplace. Some are called to leave for the gospel, and the church should test and send them gladly (Acts 13:1–3). Wanting to be with Jesus is right; but being with Jesus is not only a matter of geography. He goes with those he sends. If you are unsure, ask what doors God has opened, seek the counsel of your church, and remember that home is often the hardest and most fruitful mission field there is.

What should I say when I tell people about Jesus? Start where this man started: with what the Lord has done for you. Winning the argument is not your assignment. Tell honestly what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now (1 Peter 3:15). Then point beyond yourself to him: who he is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he receives all who come to him. Your story opens the door; his story is the message.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke folds one story inside another. Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, falls at Jesus’ feet in the road because his only daughter, about twelve, is dying. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years, as long as the girl has lived, touches the fringe of Jesus’ garment from behind and is healed at once.

Jesus stops the whole procession to find her. He brings her to tell the whole story in public and calls her daughter. While he is still speaking, word comes that Jairus’s daughter has died. Jesus tells him not to fear but only believe. In the house he takes the girl by the hand, her spirit returns, and he tells them to give her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
Each story interprets the other: the delay has not exhausted Jesus’ power or his compassion, and the messenger’s too late is not too late for the Lord of life.

When Jesus says she is not dead but sleeping, he is not correcting the diagnosis. Luke, a doctor, makes clear she was dead. Jesus is changing what death means for those who belong to him: it is a sleep from which he will wake them (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15; John 11:11).

The fringe she touched was probably the tassel of Numbers 15:38–40, worn as a reminder of God’s commandments. Some have linked it with Malachi 4:2, where the sun of righteousness rises with healing in its wings, since the Hebrew word for wings can mean the corners of a garment.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman came when every other resource was gone. Her faith was confused in its theology, secretive in its method and frightened in its execution, and Jesus called it faith and commended it aloud.

Jairus did everything right, and then came the delay and the news that it was over. Many lives feel like that. Only believe is not a demand to produce enough faith to raise the dead; that reading crushes the bereaved. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, to keep hold of the one standing beside him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd welcomed him. One shore had just asked him to leave; the other has been waiting for the boat to come back.

Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue. Luke gives us his name and his office, and both matter. A ruler of the synagogue was not a priest but a lay official: the man who organised the services, invited readers and preachers, cared for the building, and carried a good deal of the community’s respect. In a Galilean town he was somebody, and close to the circles that have been watching Jesus with growing hostility since chapter 5 (5:17); Luke will later show a synagogue ruler indignant at a Sabbath healing (13:14).

Falling at Jesus’ feet. He goes down in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is, and his position is gone in a second. Suffering does that, and it is not always a cruelty: it strips away the calculations we cannot ordinarily get past. Jairus did not come because his theology changed. He came because his daughter was dying and there was nowhere else.

At his feet, three times. Luke keeps putting people in the same place. The freed man sat at the feet of Jesus (v. 35); Jairus falls at his feet (v. 41); the healed woman will fall down before him (v. 47). A Gentile madman, a synagogue ruler and an unclean woman, as different as three people in Galilee could be, all end up on the same ground. These are the feet of the Lord, and the kneeling begins among the desperate, long before the proud get there.

An only daughter. Only Luke says only, as with the widow’s son at Nain (7:12) and the boy of 9:38: he notices the depth of grief when an only child is lost. About twelve, in that culture, is the edge of womanhood, when a girl might soon be betrothed; she has had exactly one childhood, and it is ending. And twelve links her with the woman who had been ill for twelve years (v. 43): the girl had lived as long as the woman had suffered.

The people pressed around him. Pressed (synepnigon) means crushed, nearly suffocated. It is the same word as the thorns that choked the seed (v. 14).

What if I only come to Jesus because I am desperate? Then you are in good company. Jairus came because his daughter was dying; the woman with the twelve-year bleeding came because every doctor had failed; the prodigal came home because he was starving. Jesus never once asked anyone whether their motives were pure enough before he helped them. Need is not a bad reason to come to Christ; it is the usual one. What matters is not why you first came, but that you came to him, and that you stay. Many who came to him for a healing found the Healer.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve years. Luke interrupts himself: Jesus is on his way to a dying child, and the narrative stops for a woman nobody has noticed. Jairus’s daughter has been alive for twelve years; this woman has been losing her life for as long. It was probably continuous menstrual bleeding.

What those twelve years cost. It was far more than a medical condition. Under the law, a woman with a chronic discharge was in continuing ritual uncleanness, and anything she lay or sat on, and anyone who touched those things, became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Twelve years unable to worship at the temple, twelve years cut off from normal contact, twelve years in which every human touch carried a consequence for the other person. If she was married when it began, she may well not be married now. And it is not her fault. She has done nothing.

All her living on physicians. Some manuscripts omit these words. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching, but he is gentler than Mark, who adds that she had suffered much under many physicians and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that she could not be healed by anyone.

She came up behind him. Secretly, and it had to be. She is ceremonially unclean in a dense crowd, touching a rabbi, and by the law as she understood it her touch would defile him.

The fringe of his garment. The fringe (kraspedon) is the tassel the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their cloaks, to remind them of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). It is the furthest edge of him that a person crouching in a crowd could reach. Some believed the tassels of a holy man had power (Matthew 14:36). Her faith was mixed with superstition, but it was faith in Jesus.

Immediately. Luke’s verb means literally that it stood still, and some think it a doctor’s word for a flow stopping. And once again the traffic runs the other way: instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his healing passed to her.

Does Jesus accept a faith that is mixed with superstition? Yes, if it is reaching for him. Her understanding was confused; she thought the power was in the tassel. But Jesus did not wait for her theology to be corrected before he healed her. He honoured the faith, and then, in front of the crowd, he corrected the theology: it was not the cloth but your faith in me. That is how he still deals with new and weak believers. A trembling, half-informed faith in Christ saves; a well-informed faith in anything else does not. And he will not leave a weak faith where he found it.

In everyday life. If you have exhausted every other remedy, and spent all you had, come to him now, even if all you can manage is the edge of the garment. And remember the person in your church who has been sick or isolated for years.

For worship. Under the law, the unclean defiled the clean; in Christ, the clean cleanses the unclean. He took our uncleanness upon himself at the cross, bearing our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), so that power and wholeness could flow out from him to all who reach for him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said, Who was it that touched me? He is on his way to a dying child and he stops the whole procession to ask a question he already knows the answer to. Jesus knew. He wanted her to come forward, for her own sake.

The crowds are pressing. Everyone denied it, presumably even the woman herself at first, and then Peter spoke up. His exasperation was reasonable: everyone is touching you.

Power has gone out. He distinguishes between the crowd’s pressing and this touch, and the distinction is the point. Many touched him; one touched him in faith. Power (dynamis) is the power of God, flowing from him, and Luke has used it before of the healing that flowed from him (5:17; 6:19). Something went out of him, and he felt it go.

Why stop? Now the real question. He knows what happened. She has what she came for. The child is dying up the road and every second matters. He stops because a healing is not the same as a person, and he has not come for transactions. She had tried to take the gift and remain invisible, which is entirely understandable for a woman in her position, and it would have left her exactly as she was in every way except the physical. Still unspoken of. Still, as far as her town was concerned, unclean. Still nobody’s daughter. He will not let her have it that way. He is going to bring her to say it out loud, in front of everyone, and then he is going to say something to her that she can carry for the rest of her life, and he holds up a dying child’s father in the road while he does it.

Does power going out of him mean Jesus has limited power? No. Jesus is fully God, and his divine power is infinite. The phrase tells us that the healing was a real act of his, consciously given, not a magic that leaked from his clothes without his knowledge. He perceived it because he is the source of it. It also reminds us that his healing was personal and costly: he did not dispense blessings like a machine. Every mercy we receive from Christ is given by him, knowingly, to us.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
She came trembling. She came when she saw that hiding had failed, and she is shaking, not because she doubted the healing but because of what she has done: an unclean woman has touched a rabbi in public and taken something without asking, in front of a crowd and a synagogue ruler.

In the presence of all. Only Luke has this phrase. Twelve years of it, out loud, to a street full of strangers.

Why did Jesus make her do this? So that everyone would know she was clean. That is the confession he stopped the procession to get, and it is worth seeing why it was worth the delay. Her healing had been secret; her restoration had to be public. Her testimony is now on the public record. Everyone in that crowd has heard, from her own mouth, that she is well, which means she can go back to worship, and into her family’s kitchen, and into ordinary human contact, and nobody can say otherwise. After twelve years of exclusion, the whole town could now accept her. And so she would know that she had been healed not by magic but by Jesus, through faith. He did not merely stop the bleeding. He put her back into the community, and he did it by bringing her to speak.

Daughter. Luke shows Jesus bringing the excluded back into Abraham’s family with a single word. He will call a woman bent double for eighteen years a daughter of Abraham (13:16), and a despised tax collector a son of Abraham (19:9). Here, for a woman nobody could touch for twelve years, the word is simply daughter, spoken as his own claim on her.

Your faith has made you well. Made you well (sesōken) means has saved you, body and soul. And he is careful about what her faith did, and what it did not. It did not manufacture the power; that came out of him. Her faith was simply the hand that reached.

Go in peace. As to the sinful woman (7:50). Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything put back in its right place. She came for one thing and he gave her the lot: her body, her standing, her place among people, and a name to be called by.

Do I have to tell people what Jesus has done for me? Not necessarily in a crowded street, but Christ does call his people to confess him openly. With the heart one believes, and with the mouth one confesses (Romans 10:10). For a believer, that confession is made in baptism, which is the public declaration that you belong to Christ, and then in a life of speaking of him. It is not a test you must pass to be saved; it is what Christ draws out of those he has saved, for their own good and for others. Like this woman, you may tremble. He will meet you there with peace.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking. The timing is unbearable, and Luke means it to be. Jairus had come while there was still time; then the crowd slowed them, and Jesus would not move on until the woman had told her whole story, and while she was telling it his daughter died. From where Jairus stood, it must have looked as though the delay killed her. That has to be said plainly, because it is what many lives feel like, and a pious hurry past it is worthless. But he had a greater purpose.

Do not trouble the Teacher. A teacher can heal the sick, but not raise the dead. The advice is kindly meant and entirely rational: the man is being gently told to let the poor rabbi get on.

Do not fear; only believe. Jesus answers at once, before the message can take root. In Mark the verb means keep on believing (Mark 5:36); Luke gives it as a single plain command: believe. Jesus is not telling him to generate enough faith to raise the dead; that reading crushes bereaved people, and it is not what the sentence says. He is telling a man who has just been told it is over to keep holding on to the person standing next to him for another ten minutes. And the woman’s healing was for Jairus as much as for her: he has just watched, at his own cost, what this man does for someone who had run out of options.

And she will be well. Only Luke adds this. Well (sōthēsetai) means saved, the same word as verse 48. It is the promise of Jesus, given after the worst news, not before it.

Why does God seem to delay when I pray? Scripture never pretends that God’s delays are easy; the psalms cry, how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). But the story of Jairus, like that of Lazarus (John 11:6, 15), shows that his delays are never neglect. He was not too late for Jairus; he was exactly on time for a greater miracle. Your waiting may be for something God means to do that is greater than what you asked. That does not mean every prayer is answered as Jairus’s was. It means the one who makes you wait is the same one who loves you, and he has never once been late for his own purposes.

For worship. Death sends its messengers to every house: it is over, do not trouble him any more. Only one voice has answered them and been proved right. He went himself into the house of death, and on the third morning the women were asked why they sought the living among the dead (24:5). Because he lives, his word to Jairus is his word at every believer’s graveside,: do not fear; only believe. And when you are the one bringing bad news to someone, bring Christ’s word with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and John and James. The inner three, who will also be on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:28) and, in Mark’s account, in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33), see him raise the dead, see him in glory, and see him on his face in the dirt. And, tenderly, the parents are included, because this is their daughter and not a demonstration.

Weeping and mourning. The house is full of noise: family and, it seems, professional mourners; Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). Mourning (ekoptonto) means beating their breasts. According to a later rabbinic rule, even a poor family was expected to provide flute players and at least one wailing woman.

Not dead but sleeping. This is sometimes used to argue that she was never dead, only in a coma. That cannot be what Luke, a doctor, means. The messenger reported a death. The professional mourners had arrived, and they did not come for the unconscious. Luke’s own next sentence says the crowd knew she was dead. And when she revives, Luke writes that her spirit returned (v. 55), which is not the language of waking from a faint. He is not correcting a diagnosis. He is changing a category. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and in his vocabulary that is now what death is: temporary, from which he can wake her. That is exactly how the New Testament will go on to speak of believers who die: those who have fallen asleep (John 11:11–14; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). It is a claim about who is standing in the room.

They laughed at him. Scornful laughter. Luke’s phrasing is careful and it is not kind to them: they laughed, knowing. It is derision from people who were right about the facts, and they had every reason. Within minutes, the girl they had come to mourn got up and walked.

Does sleeping mean that the dead are unconscious? No. Jesus means that her death is not final; she will wake. The word describes the body awaiting resurrection, not the soul. Those who die in the Lord are with him at once, conscious and at rest (23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory: the believer’s soul goes immediately into the presence of Christ, and the body sleeps in the grave until he raises it on the last day (Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

In everyday life. When you stand at the grave of a believer, grieve, but with hope, and use his word: she is not dead but sleeping. It is not a euphemism; it is a promise. And if people laugh at your hope, do not be surprised. They laughed at him.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But taking her by the hand. As with the leper and the bier at Nain, he touches what the law says will defile him (Numbers 19:11), and death gives way.

Child, arise. The word is a family word. Mark preserves it in Aramaic, Talitha cumi (Mark 5:41), the kind of phrase a mother might use in the morning: little girl, get up. The greatest power in the universe is exercised in the tone of voice used to wake a child for school.

And her spirit returned. Only Luke says this. Her spirit had left her body at death (23:46; Acts 7:59), and came back: a clear statement that she had been dead, and that the human spirit lives on after death. And she got up at once.

Something to eat. This is the sentence that gives the passage away, and it is not the kind of detail a legend-maker tends to add. The room must be beyond speech, and the first instruction the Son of God gives, having conquered death in a bedroom in Galilee, is: get her something to eat. She was really alive, in a real body, and hungry. After the resurrection Jesus himself would eat to show he was not a ghost (24:41–43). The one who commands the wind and the abyss and the grave is also the one who notices that nobody has thought about her supper. After the great moments, someone has to think about the meal: be the one who notices.

Can a thinking person believe this really happened? The mourners are the first to tell us that dead girls do not get up; they laughed because they knew it. The real question is not whether death normally wins, but whether God exists and has come among us in Jesus. If he has, and if Jesus himself rose from the dead, then one girl raised in Galilee is no strain at all. Luke, a careful doctor, tells us he investigated everything from the beginning and wrote from those who were eyewitnesses (1:1–4), and details like the supper are the kind legends seldom bother to invent. He wrote within living memory of these events, while people who had been in Galilee could still be asked. The deeper reluctance is often not the evidence but the cost: if this happened, Jesus has a claim on my life.

Tell no one. Everyone would know she was alive, but they were not to spread the story. He is not asking them to keep a secret so much as refusing to be turned into a spectacle, and Luke has recorded the same instruction before (5:14).

In the flow. This raising closes the four miracles of 8:22–56 at the deepest point, death itself, and answers the disciples’ question, who then is this? Chapter 9 presses it until Peter says that he is the Christ of God (9:20). And a girl raised to die again points ahead to the one who will rise, never to die again (24:6; Romans 6:9).

Why tell these parents to tell no one, when he told the Gerasene to declare it? The Gerasene lived in Gentile territory, where Jesus was not staying and where no crowd was waiting for a Jewish king. Here in Galilee, news of a girl raised from the dead would bring crowds wanting a wonder-worker or a political Messiah, and Jesus’ hour had not yet come. He was not hiding his glory; he was guarding his mission. The full truth of who he is could only be told rightly after the cross and resurrection, and then it was to be told to the ends of the earth.

Will Jesus raise my loved one who has died in him? Yes. This girl was raised to die again; what Christ promises his people is far greater. On the last day, all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (John 5:28–29), and those who belong to him will be raised imperishable, in bodies like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). The same hand that took this girl’s will take theirs. Meanwhile, their spirits are with him. Grieve for them, but grieve as one who knows that the Lord who says arise has never yet been disobeyed.

For worship. The hand that took a dead girl’s fingers in a Galilean bedroom was itself nailed to a cross, laid still in a tomb and raised on the third day, and it holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). One word from him on the last day will call every sleeping believer out of the dust, and the Lord who remembered a hungry girl’s supper will sit them down at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Almighty over the grave, and thinking of our hunger: that is our Lord.

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the turning point of Luke’s Gospel. Up to here Jesus has preached, healed and gathered disciples in Galilee; from 9:51 he is on the road to Jerusalem and the cross.

The hinge is verse 51: Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem, as Isaiah’s Servant set his face like a flint (Isaiah 50:7). Just before it, on the mountain, Moses and Elijah speak with him of his departure, his exodos, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. The cross is not a defeat but a new exodus, the deliverance all of Israel’s history had been moving towards.

The chapter holds glory and the cross together. Peter confesses the Christ of God, and at once Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, and that whoever follows him takes up his cross daily. The cross is the road to the glory, and the glory shows what the cross accomplishes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus gives the Twelve his own power and authority over demons and diseases and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom and to heal. They are to take nothing for the road and to depend on those who receive them, staying in the first house that takes them in. Where a town refuses them, they shake its dust from their feet as a solemn warning.

Then the news reaches Herod, who has beheaded John and is perplexed. The theories he hears, John raised, Elijah, one of the old prophets, are all too small. His question, who is this?, is the right one, and the tragedy is that he only ever wanted to see a sign (23:8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
An apostle is one who is sent. The authority the Twelve carry is the authority Jesus has used since chapter 4, lent to them for their errand, and Acts will show the same word going on through his people.

It is given to men who will soon argue about greatness, fail to cast out a demon and want to burn a Samaritan village. He does not wait until they are ready. And the errand keeps word and deed together. Healing without the message withholds the reason for it; the message without any deed announces a kingdom that seems to change nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Taking nothing for the road is not a travel policy for every age (22:35–36) but a lesson in dependence: the messengers carry nothing that would make them independent of the people they are sent to. Staying in the first house guards the message too: once a messenger’s comfort depends on his host, his message is for sale.
