Herod is a warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be interested in Jesus for years and never come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 9 is the turning point of the Gospel, and Herod asks the question the whole chapter answers: who is this? Jesus feeds five thousand, taking, blessing, breaking and giving, as he will at the Last Supper and at Emmaus; Peter confesses him the Christ of God; the Father says, this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him. Below the mountain the disciples fail, argue about greatness and want fire on a Samaritan village, and nothing may come before following him.

The setting. Chapter 9 is the climax of the Galilean ministry, ending with Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51).

He called the twelve together. Chosen in 6:13 and trained by being with him through chapters 6–8, they are now sent.

Power and authority. Two words, and they are not the same. Power (dynamis) is the capacity, the ability to do the thing. Authority (exousia) is the right to do it. A man may have one without the other: a burglar has the power to open your door and no authority; a magistrate has the authority to arrest and may not have the strength. The Twelve are given both, and earned neither.

Power that is his to give. No prophet could hand on power as his own. When Elisha asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit, Elijah could only say that he had asked a hard thing, which God alone could grant (2 Kings 2:9–10). Jesus calls twelve men together and gives them power and authority over all demons, simply because it is his to give. No mere servant of God could make that claim. What he lends here for a short mission in Galilee he will pour out from his throne as power from on high (24:49).

Demons and diseases. What Luke has shown Jesus doing since chapter 4 (4:31–41), the same two categories kept carefully distinct, is now delegated. And look who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), want to burn a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready. He never has.

He sent them out. The verb is apesteilen, the root of our word apostle: one who is sent. The title says nothing about the man’s qualities and everything about his commission; an apostle is not a rank but an errand.

To proclaim and to heal. And the errand has two halves, held together: word and work, announcement and demonstration. The healings confirmed the message that the kingdom had come. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.

Does this authority belong to the church today? It was given to the Twelve for their mission, and its signs confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many Christians believe it continues. The more likely reading is that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic age, while the commission to proclaim the kingdom goes on for every generation. The church still prays for the sick and resists the devil, but does not claim the apostles’ authority.

So does God still heal? Yes. God heals today, often through medicine and sometimes beyond it, in answer to the prayers of his people (James 5:14–15). What has ceased, on the reading this commentary takes, is not God’s power or his willingness to answer prayer, but the gift given to particular people to heal at will as a sign authenticating new revelation. Christians who see it differently are brothers to be loved, not opponents. Either way, pray for the sick in faith, use the doctors God has given, and leave the outcome in his hands.

In everyday life. If you have felt unqualified to do anything for God, notice that the Twelve were unqualified too, and that whatever he calls you to, he equips you for. Take the task in front of you this week, the conversation, the class, the visit, and go, depending on him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take nothing for your journey. Five items: staff, bag, bread, money and a second tunic, which between them cover security, supply and comfort. He takes all five away. They are to travel light, depending entirely on God’s provision through the hospitality of those who receive them.

No staff. Mark says take only a staff (Mark 6:8). Perhaps Mark means take the one you have, while Luke and Matthew mean do not acquire another. The point is the same: no extra provisions. None of the explanations is certain, but both accounts fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Nor bread, nor money. They were not to beg, but to receive what God provided. Sent to preach the kingdom of God with no food and no money, every one of them will be hungry within a day and dependent on somebody who has not yet heard the message.

Whatever house you enter, stay there. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. The rule forbids trading up. A messenger who moves to better lodgings has begun to be paid, and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale. It is also simply a matter of not humiliating the first family who took him in.

What it does not mean. These orders were never meant to bind every missionary for ever: later Jesus told the same men to take a moneybag and knapsack (22:35–36). They fit this short, urgent mission in Galilee. What remains is the posture: urgency, simplicity, contentment and dependence on God.

Sent as he was sent. The list strips the apostles down to the shape of their Lord’s own life. He had no house and would soon say that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (9:58); he was supported by the gifts of others (8:3); he went from village to village trusting his Father for the day’s bread. So the message of a King who became poor is carried by men who are visibly poor, and their emptiness puts his fullness on display. And when he asked them later whether they had lacked anything, they said, nothing (22:35).

Should churches pay their ministers and missionaries? Yes. Jesus’ instruction assumes that those who receive the message will provide for the messenger, and he says elsewhere that the labourer deserves his wages (10:7). Paul argues the same at length (1 Corinthians 9:3–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). What this passage guards against is the minister whose comfort shapes his message. A church should pay its pastor and support its missionaries generously, so that they are free from anxiety; and those who serve should be content, and never preach for gain (1 Peter 5:2).

In everyday life. Ask what in your life is extra equipment against the possibility that God will not come through: the savings you trust more than him, the back-up plan that makes obedience unnecessary. And if someone shows you hospitality this week, receive it graciously and do not compare it with what others might have given.
verseByVerse.note: The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies; a second tunic was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wherever they do not receive you. Rejection is not treated as a possibility to be prayed against but as a certainty to be prepared for: men with power over demons are told that some towns will simply not have them.

Shake off the dust from your feet. The gesture was known: Jews coming home from Gentile lands are said to have shaken the dust of pagan roads from their feet before entering the holy land. Used of Jewish villages, it is startling. A town of Israelites that refuses the kingdom of God is treated as though it stood outside the land; the boundary of God’s people now runs not round the nation but round the message, and the town is left to God’s judgment. Acts shows it repeated: Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off against Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51), and at Corinth Paul shook out his garments (Acts 18:6).

As a testimony against them. A warning, and a witness at the judgment (10:10–16). Their responsibility has been discharged; the town is accountable.

The Lord who weeps over the town. The command to shake off the dust comes from the Lord who will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:41–44). He is not careless about the towns that refuse; he grieves over them more than his messengers ever will. But he is also their Judge, and refusing his messengers is refusing him: the one who rejects you rejects me, he will say, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me (10:16). A village that shuts its door on twelve Galileans has shut it on the Son of God.

What it does not mean. Not a gesture of personal contempt or revenge. It is not a curse; it is a solemn warning, which might still bring them to repentance.

Two wrong instincts. With people who do not want to hear, two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing, as though a refusal were a problem of technique, until the gospel has become an irritation; or to shrug and conclude it never mattered. The dust does neither. It takes the refusal with complete seriousness, and then leaves without bitterness for the next village, because the responsibility has changed hands.

So should I stop talking to my unbelieving friend about Christ? Not necessarily, and almost never from the relationship. The disciples were passing through towns on a short mission; most of us live alongside the same people for years. What changes, after a clear refusal, is usually the method, not the love. Stop pressing an argument he has heard and declined. Keep being his friend, keep praying for him, live the gospel in front of him, and be ready to speak again when he asks or when God opens a door (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15). And remember that a refusal today is not a verdict for ever. Many who once shut the door have later opened it.

In everyday life. You are responsible to tell the gospel faithfully, not to make people accept it. If you have been carrying guilt for someone who has heard and refused, hand the weight back to him. Your part was to tell them; his part is the heart.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They departed. They obeyed. One verse covers the whole mission: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere.

What is not here. No account of how it felt to set out with no money, no debate about the instructions, no description of the first house or the first refusal or the first demon. The orders to take nothing were not an ideal held up for admiration but the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Preaching the gospel. Evangelising (euangelizomenoi), Luke’s favourite word. The proclamation is named first, as in verse 2 and at 4:43, where Jesus said preaching was what he was sent for.

Healing everywhere. Everywhere is emphatic, at the end of the sentence. They did not concentrate on the promising places.

His work in their hands. Luke opens his second volume by calling this Gospel an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1), as though Acts were what he went on doing, from heaven, through his servants. The healings in these villages were his healings; the Twelve were the hands. That is why their success can be told in a sentence.

What if my service for God feels ordinary and unseen? Then you are in exactly the place the Twelve were. Most of what God does through his people is never written up. Paul says that each one’s work will be revealed on the day (1 Corinthians 3:13), and Jesus promises that even a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). God sees the ordinary faithfulness: the Sunday school class taught for twenty years, the elderly neighbour visited weekly, the prayer list kept. The summary will come later, written by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod the tetrarch heard. The news of the mission reaches the palace. This is Antipas, the son of Herod the Great who held Galilee and Perea (3:1). Tetrarch is a lesser title; he wanted to be called king and Rome never allowed it. And he was perplexed (diēporei): thoroughly at a loss, unable to find a way through.

John had been raised from the dead. The three theories, which the disciples will report again (v. 19), are all serious ones; Elijah was the forerunner Malachi promised. All of them high, none of them right: every one puts Jesus in the prophetic tradition, and every one is too small.

John I beheaded. Luke does not tell the story of John’s death, which Mark tells at length (Mark 6:17–29). He records only Herod’s own confession, three words of autobiography that are the three he would least want quoted. Not, John was executed; John I beheaded. Whatever else this man is, he is not lying to himself about what he did, and if Mark’s account is any guide, he was haunted by it (Mark 6:16).

Greater than John, greater than Elijah. Jesus is not John come back; John said that one mightier than he was coming, the strap of whose sandals he was not worthy to untie (3:16). He is not Elijah; Elijah’s promised return had already come in the spirit and power of John (1:17). He is not one of the old prophets; they spoke the word of the LORD, and he is the one of whom the Father will say, this is my Son, my Chosen One (9:35). Herod had killed the greatest man born of women (7:28), and still had not met the one John came to announce.

But who is this about whom I hear such things? It is the right question, the great question of the chapter and of the Gospel. It is the question the disciples asked in the boat (8:25), and it has just been asked, correctly and urgently, by a murderer in a palace. Herod asks it; the disciples will answer it (v. 20); the Father will declare it (v. 35).

He sought to see him. There is the tragedy. Herod wanted to see Jesus out of curiosity, not faith, and eventually he gets what he asked for. At the trial Luke tells us Herod was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him (23:8). And Jesus does not answer him a word (23:9). Herod is the only person in Luke’s account of the trials to whom Jesus says nothing at all.

Why did Jesus not answer Herod? Because Herod had already had his answer and refused it. He had heard John preach, and liked to listen to him (Mark 6:20), and then killed him rather than lose face. He had heard about Jesus for years and never come to him. What he wanted at the trial was a show, not a Saviour. Jesus’ silence was a judgment: there comes a point where more words would only be entertainment. That is a solemn warning to anyone who treats Christ as a subject of interest rather than a Lord to be obeyed. Seek him while he may be found (Isaiah 55:6).

In everyday life. If you have been interested in Christ for a long time, ask the harder question: what am I going to do about the answer? Jesus still receives anyone who comes to him today.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Luke records that he later saw Jesus at his trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Twelve return, and Jesus takes them away to rest near Bethsaida. The crowds find out and get there first, and Luke alone says that Jesus welcomed them.

The disciples sensibly suggest sending the crowd away to find food and lodging. Jesus tells them to feed the people themselves. They have five loaves and two fish, and they are right that it cannot be done. He has the crowd sit in groups of about fifty, blesses and breaks the loaves, and gives them to the disciples to set before the people. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of pieces are left over.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding recalls Israel in the wilderness: a hungry people in a desolate place, ordered companies as under Moses (Exodus 18:25), and bread from God. But Jesus does not pray for bread from heaven as Moses did; he breaks it with his own hands. It also looks forward to the feast Isaiah promised, when the LORD spreads a banquet for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6–9), and the Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of that table.

The four verbs, took, blessed, broke and gave, return at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus (24:30–31). The baskets left over show that his kingdom does not give minimum rations.
verseByVerse.examples:
Sending people away is the reasonable answer in many situations: the need beyond a church’s strength, the person whose troubles are more than anyone can carry. It is not wickedness. The question is whether the need has been brought to Jesus before anyone decides.

The loaves really are too little; the point is not to be optimistic about them but to put them in his hands anyway. The same scene teaches that guarding time for rest is right, as Jesus did, but that the plan is not the master when real need is standing in front of us.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On their return. They report back to him, because every ministry is answerable to the Lord who gave it.

He withdrew apart. For rest, and private teaching. Mark gives Jesus’ own words: they were to come away to a desolate place and rest a while (Mark 6:31).

To a town called Bethsaida. Bethsaida lay at the top of the lake, near where the Jordan runs in, in Philip’s territory and beyond Herod’s reach. The feeding took place in a deserted place near it (v. 12).

The crowds followed. The rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out where the boat is going; Mark says they got there first.

He welcomed them. Only Luke says this. Welcomed means received gladly: not tolerated, not endured. He met the people who had wrecked his plan as though they had been invited.

Those who had need of healing. Word and deed again, until the day is nearly over (v. 12).

The rhythm and the need. This should not be flattened into a lesson about being available at all times. Jesus withdraws constantly (5:16; 6:12). The rhythm is real and he defends it, right up to the moment when the need is standing in front of him, and then the rhythm gives way, every time.

So should I never protect my rest? You should protect it; Jesus did. Rest is God’s gift and command, and a worker who never stops will soon have nothing to give. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when the thing you had properly and prayerfully arranged is taken from you by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests. Guard your time in the ordinary run of things. When the need is genuine and in front of you, let love decide, and trust God to give you the rest you missed another way.

For worship. The Lord who invites the weary to come to him and find rest (Matthew 11:28) was himself weary, and gave up his rest to welcome a crowd. Every one of us who has come to him has come uninvited, at an inconvenient time, and been received gladly. His welcome is the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (Matthew 14; Mark 6; John 6).

The day began to wear away. The light is going, and with it the margin: a crowd of thousands, in open country, several hours from anywhere, with night coming.

Send the crowd away. A reasonable suggestion: they are right about everything except one thing. This is not hard-heartedness but twelve men taking responsibility for a practical problem their teacher appears not to have noticed. John tells us Jesus himself already knew what he would do (John 6:6).

A desolate place. A wilderness, and Israel had been here before. Can God spread a table in the wilderness? was the people’s question in the desert, asked in unbelief (Psalm 78:19), and the answer was manna every morning for forty years (Exodus 16). Now the question returns from twelve tired men, and the God who answered it then is standing in front of them in a human body. Moses prayed and God sent bread; Jesus will take the bread into his own hands.

Experience has a short half-life. These men have only just come back from a mission in which they cast out demons and healed the sick with nothing in their pockets. Now their instinct is to count resources and organise a dispersal. Experience of God’s provision fades quickly in all of us.

Is it ever right to say no to a need? Yes. No church and no Christian can meet every need, and Jesus himself sometimes moved on when crowds wanted more (4:42–43). Wisdom, limits, and referring people to others better placed to help are not unbelief. The question this passage puts is whether we have brought the need to Jesus before we decided. Sometimes, after prayer, the answer is that this is not ours to carry. Sometimes he hands it back to us and says, you give them something. The sin is not in saying no, but in leaving him out of the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You give them something to eat. You is emphatic. He hands the problem back, and there is no possible reading on which the Twelve can obey in their own strength. They had just been out preaching and healing in his power; could they not trust him for this?

Five loaves and two fish. Their answer is the inventory. John tells us they came from a boy, and were barley loaves, the bread of the poor (John 6:9): with small dried or pickled fish. It is one packed lunch.

Unless we are to go and buy. There is an edge in that clause. Mark supplies the figure they were working with: two hundred denarii, about two-thirds of a labourer’s annual wage (Mark 6:37), and John adds that even that would not give each of them a little (John 6:7). They have costed it. It cannot be done.

They are right. Here the disciples are simply accurate: no amount of faith changes that sum, and Jesus never suggests otherwise. The command is not to be optimistic about the bread but to put it in his hands anyway. Our inadequacy is the starting point for his sufficiency, and nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

Greater than Elisha. A man once brought Elisha twenty loaves of barley, and the prophet said, give them to the men to eat; his servant answered, how can I set this before a hundred men? And the word of the LORD was that they would eat and have some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). The echo is plain: an order to give, an objection about numbers, and food left over. But Elisha fed a hundred with twenty loaves on a word from the LORD. Jesus feeds five thousand men with five, and the word is his own.

What if what I have really is too little? It is too little, and that is not the problem: the question is never whether it is enough, but whether you will put it into his hands (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). (See Mark 6:38 for the fuller answer.)

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About five thousand men. Men (andres); Matthew adds, besides women and children (Matthew 14:21). The real number in that field was perhaps fifteen or twenty thousand people in all.

Groups of about fifty. Consider what that commits the Twelve to: organising thousands, in failing light, into a hundred companies, with five loaves in a bag and no explanation. They have to seat the whole crowd before they know there is anything to serve. The word is literally reclining, as at a banquet.

And they did so. The disciples obeyed before they saw how it would work: obedience with no visible warrant.

Why groups of fifty? Two reasons suggest themselves, and both are in the text. The practical one is distribution. A crowd of thousands cannot be fed by twelve men passing baskets through a mob; it can be fed by twelve men working a hundred defined companies, each one a manageable size, in order, with nobody missed. The other is older. When Israel came out of Egypt and was fed in the wilderness, Moses organised the people in ordered companies, with chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens, to govern and judge them (Exodus 18:21, 25). A crowd in a desolate place, arranged in fifties, about to be fed by God, is not an image any Jew would fail to recognise. Jesus is the new Moses, feeding the new Israel in the wilderness, and he is greater than Moses, because Moses did not make the manna.

A picture of the church. He did not feed a mass. He fed people in groups small enough to see each other’s faces, sharing out of the same basket: an early picture in this Gospel of what the church would turn out to look like.

Why does God ask me to obey before I see how it will work? Because that is what faith is. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen (Hebrews 11:1). Abraham went out not knowing where he was going (Hebrews 11:8). If God always showed us the outcome first, we would be trusting the outcome, not him. He gives enough light for the next step, and the next step is usually something ordinary: seating people on the grass. Do that, and leave the bread to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the five loaves. Four verbs follow: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave, as a Jewish head of household did at the start of a meal. Jesus looked up to heaven, to his Father, the giver of every gift. He is the host of this meal.

He broke and gave. Luke will use these four verbs twice more. At the Last Supper Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them (22:19). And on the first Easter evening, at a table in a village house, the stranger who had walked seven miles with two downcast disciples took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened and they recognised him (24:30–31). The hands on this hillside are the hands they would know again.

No moment of multiplying. He gives thanks over the actual, insufficient five, and it is in the breaking and the giving that there turns out to be more. There is no moment at which the pile visibly grows; it simply does not run out.

To set before the crowd. He could have handed it out himself. Instead the bread goes from his hands into theirs, and from theirs to the people, so that the men who had said send them away spend the next hour walking up and down a hillside giving away food they did not have. This is the pattern of ministry: we receive from Christ and give to others. We do not make the bread; we hand it out.

Is the feeding the Lord’s Supper? No, but it points towards it. The feeding was a meal in the wilderness for a crowd; the Supper is the ordinance Christ gave his church, a remembrance of his death and a means of grace in which, by faith, believers feed on him spiritually (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–26; 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; Westminster Confession 29.7). Luke uses the same four actions so that we see the connection: the one who fed the five thousand is the one who gives himself as the bread of life (John 6:35). When you come to his Table, you come to the same host, and he still takes, blesses, breaks and gives.

In everyday life. Give thanks before it is enough. Before your next meal, before your next week of work, before you face a need too big for you, take what you have, look up, and thank God for it. Then hand it on. Everything you have to give others has come first from his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All ate and were satisfied. All: down to the last group of fifty at the far edge of the field. Were satisfied (echortasthēsan) is a strong word. It was used of animals grazed to the full, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the satisfaction God gives: I will satisfy her poor with bread (Psalm 132:15); he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things (Psalm 107:9). They were fed until they had had enough.

Twelve baskets of broken pieces. Twelve baskets: not twelve crumbs, but kophinoi, the stiff wicker baskets a traveller carried. There was more at the end than at the beginning. Twelve is the number of the tribes: enough for all Israel. And it is the number of the men who had said it could not be done: one basket each, carried back by the very people who had costed it and said no. Each of them walked off the field holding the evidence.

Nothing wasted. The one who had just fed thousands out of a boy’s lunch had the leftovers gathered (John 6:12). Extravagance and carefulness sit in the same paragraph without the slightest tension.

Was it really a miracle? Some explain the feeding as a sharing miracle, the crowd moved by the boy’s example to bring out food they had hidden. But all four Gospels record it as a miracle; the disciples distributed food from five loaves and two fish; and twelve baskets of fragments were left over. Jesus himself later recalled it as something he had done (Mark 8:19). The point is that he is the one who feeds his people in the wilderness.

The meaning. John tells us that the next day Jesus explained: I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The miracle points to Jesus himself, who gives himself to satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. And it is a foretaste of the messianic banquet, when people will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29; 14:15). It is the feast the LORD spreads for all peoples, where he swallows up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). A hillside full of satisfied people is a small, real sample of that table.

In the flow. Luke goes straight from the baskets to Peter’s confession, leaving out the long stretch of Mark between (Mark 6:45–8:26), so that Herod’s question, who is this? (v. 9), is followed first by a sign and then by an answer (v. 20).

Why am I not satisfied, if Christ satisfies? Many Christians feel a restlessness that seems to contradict this verse. Part of the answer is that we often try to feed on other things while hungry for him, and they do not fill. Part is that our satisfaction in Christ is real now but not yet complete; we taste, and long for more (1 Peter 2:3). Even the hunger is a gift, a sign that we were made for him. Come back to him: in his word, in prayer, at his Table, among his people. And wait for the day when we shall hunger no more (Revelation 7:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and out of that prayer comes the question the whole Gospel is about. The crowds give the same answers Herod heard. Then Jesus asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers: the Christ of God.

At once Jesus tells them to keep it quiet, because in Galilee Messiah meant a king who would raise an army against Rome. Then he says what kind of Christ he is: the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the nation’s leaders, be killed, and on the third day be raised.

He tells everyone the cost of following: deny yourself, take up your cross daily, and follow me. The section ends with a promise that some standing there will see the kingdom of God before they die.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter’s confession is right, and Jesus at once fills the title with its true meaning: the Christ of God is the suffering, dying and rising Son of Man. That title comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days.

The word must (dei) marks God’s plan. The cross is not an accident or a failure of the mission; it is the appointment, and Jesus never speaks of his death without his rising.

The promise that some would see the kingdom before they died was kept, first, eight days later, when three of them saw the Son of Man in glory on the mountain, and then in the resurrection and at Pentecost, within the lifetime of those who heard it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke’s word daily brings the cross into an ordinary week. It is not reserved for martyrs; it is the everyday refusal to let self rule. And self-denial must be guarded from twisting: it is not self-hatred, nor the erasing of a personality God made, but the dethroning of self as the final judge of every decision.

The question about gaining the whole world is set at the highest price on purpose: if the trade fails there, it fails at every lower price. And most Western believers are tempted not to renounce Christ but to be embarrassed by him and his words, which is why the warning speaks of shame.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praying alone. Praying alone, with the disciples there: Jesus was in prayer and they were nearby. Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi, Mark 8:27), and he alone tells us Jesus was praying. Luke puts Jesus at prayer at turning point after turning point in the story (3:21; 6:12). The most important question in the book comes up out of a conversation with the Father.

Who do the crowds say that I am? The answers are the same three that reached Herod’s court a few verses earlier (vv. 7–8): John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. The crowds are not hostile and they are not stupid. Every one of those answers is respectful, and every one puts him in the prophetic line: a great man in a great tradition. And every one is wrong in the same way. They are all attempts to fit him into a category that already exists. The modern answers are much the same: a great moral teacher, a prophet, a spiritual genius. They are compliments, and they are all too small, because no mere teacher accepts what Jesus is about to accept, to be confessed as God’s own Anointed.

But who do you say that I am? You is emphatic. The Greek puts the pronoun first and hard: you, what do you say? It is the pivot of the Gospel, and it cannot be answered by a survey. Everything up to this point has been evidence; the question is what has been made of it. It is the question every person must answer.

The Christ of God. Christos is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed: the one Israel had been promised since David, the king who would come. Kings and priests were anointed with oil to show that God had set them apart (1 Samuel 16:13); to call Jesus the Christ of God is to say that God has appointed him to rule and to save his people (2:26; 23:35). Peter has stopped putting him in the line of the prophets and named him as the one the whole line was pointing at. Matthew records the fuller confession and Jesus’ blessing (Matthew 16:16–19).

Right word, wrong picture. The confession is correct, and Luke moves straight past it, because being right about the title is not the same as understanding it. Peter has the correct word and, as the other Gospels show, the wrong picture. In Mark’s account, within moments of getting it right he is arguing with it (Mark 8:32). That is most people’s first real confession: the word is true, and the content arrives later, and usually costs something.

How did Peter know? Matthew tells us Jesus’ answer: flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 16:17). Peter did not reason his way to the confession by being cleverer than the crowds. He had seen the same evidence, and God opened his eyes. That is still how anyone comes to say Jesus is Lord: only by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). If you can say it from the heart, it is the gift of God, and you have reason to give thanks rather than to be proud.

What if I am not sure what I believe about Jesus? Then do what Peter did: stay close to him and look at the evidence. Read one of the Gospels through, asking at every page who this is. Pray honestly, even if your prayer is, if you are there, show me. Speak to a Christian you trust. Jesus did not ask the question to shame his disciples but to bring them to the answer, and he has not stopped asking it. The crowds had opinions; Peter had a confession. The difference is not cleverness but coming close.
verseByVerse.note: Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi) but notes that Jesus was praying. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell this to no one. Two forceful verbs. Why silence a true confession? Because for many in Galilee in that decade, Messiah meant something specific and largely political: a son of David who would raise an army, break Rome, and restore the kingdom. John’s Gospel records a crowd trying to make him king by force after the feeding (John 6:15). A public messianic claim would have started a movement he had not come to lead. So the word is held back until it can carry the meaning he gives it in the very next sentence.

The Son of Man. Having accepted the name Christ, he at once calls himself the Son of Man, his own preferred title and not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying a human being. Its background is Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure who comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Luke lets the two sides of the title meet at the trial: the Son of Man who must suffer here tells the council that from now on he will be seated at the right hand of the power of God (22:69). The title of glory is the name of the one who goes to the cross.

Must suffer many things. The first passion prediction, immediately after the confession: yes, I am the Christ, but the Christ must suffer. Must (dei) is divine necessity, the plan of God written in Scripture (24:26, 44–46). Luke uses it at every hinge of this Gospel: a boy in the temple who must be in his Father’s house (2:49), a preacher who must go to the next town (4:43), and now this. The cross is not a plan that went wrong. It is the appointment.

Rejected by the elders. Together they formed the Sanhedrin, the council of the nation: not Rome, but the men who had the Scriptures.

Killed, and raised. Death and resurrection together, in the same sentence, the first time of telling, and again at 18:31–33. The disciples will still be devastated, and Luke will tell us why: they did not understand it (v. 45), and they were afraid to ask.

Luke’s omission. Luke does not record Peter’s rebuke and Jesus’ get behind me, Satan (Mark 8:32–33). Perhaps to spare Peter, or to keep the focus on the teaching.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners. God’s justice required that sin be punished, and his love purposed to save; at the cross both were satisfied, when the Son of Man bore in his own body the penalty his people deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 1 Peter 2:24). The must is not fate imposed on Jesus from outside. It is the eternal plan of the Father, Son and Spirit, written in Scripture, which the Son freely embraced: no one, he said, takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). So the cross is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling victim. The Judge, in the person of his own Son, takes the penalty he himself requires, and that is why it is both just and astonishing love (1 John 4:10).

In everyday life. Check the picture of Jesus you carry around. Is it a Christ who exists to make your life go well, or the Christ of God who must suffer and calls you to follow? When suffering comes, it is not proof that he has failed you. It is the road he walked first.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to all. What follows is not advanced material for the Twelve but the terms of entry, said to all. If anyone would come after me: would means wants to, wills to. It is a choice, and three clauses follow.

Let him deny himself. This is regularly misheard. It is not deny himself things, giving up sugar or television, but deny himself: say no to self as the centre and master of life. The verb is aparneomai, and Luke uses it again of Peter in the courtyard, in the warning that he would deny Jesus and in his remembering it (22:34, 61). To deny the self is to say about your own claims what Peter said about Jesus: I do not know him. And this can be twisted into something poisonous, so it must be guarded. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to. In practice: when what I want and what Christ says pull in different directions, his word decides, and I let it, even when no one would ever know (Galatians 2:20).

And take up his cross. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution, and everyone hearing this had seen it. The phrase meant one thing: a man going to his death. So the image is not merely bear your hardships; a difficult marriage or a chronic illness is real, and Scripture says much about it, but it is not this. To take it up is to accept rejection, shame and even death for Jesus’ sake.

Daily. Only Luke adds daily (compare Matthew 16:24; Mark 8:34). A cross is carried once; Luke takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, so it is not reserved for martyrs. The cross is a way of life: dying to self in a thousand daily choices, for Christ.

And follow me. To Jerusalem, to the cross, and beyond. Self-denial and the cross are not the goal; he is. The point of putting the self down is to walk after him.

Behind Jesus. Luke gives this saying a picture later in his Gospel. On the road to Golgotha the soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene and laid the cross on him, to carry it behind Jesus (23:26). It is this verse made visible. But look at the order of the procession. Jesus goes first, to the place where the real dying is done, and the cross Simon carried was the one on which Jesus, not Simon, would die. Every disciple’s daily cross is carried behind that one, on a road whose end has already been reached by the one in front.

Whoever would save his life. Life (psychē) here is the self, the whole person. A life organised round its own preservation, guarded against every cost of following Jesus, is being lost in the very act of being protected.

Whoever loses his life. There is no third option on offer, and the man who declines to choose has chosen.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by self-denial; only Christ’s cross atones. And not seeking suffering for its own sake. But the life that belongs to Christ takes the shape of his cross.

Does this mean I cannot enjoy anything? No. Self-denial in this sense is not the rejection of God’s good gifts; God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). It is the refusal to let the self be king over them. A Christian may enjoy a meal, a holiday, a career, a marriage, and enjoy them more than others, because he receives them from God’s hand and is ready to give them up if Christ asks. What he may not do is make any of them his master. The question is not, do I have good things? but, who rules over them?

In everyday life. What does taking up your cross today look like? Name one way you can say no to yourself for Christ’s sake: telling the truth when a lie would protect you, or serving someone who will not thank you. Small crosses, carried daily in the strength of the Spirit who raised Jesus, are how the self is dethroned; and on the days you drop yours, the cross that saves you is still his.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Only Luke adds “daily.”

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What does it profit. A commercial question, in commercial words: profit, gains, forfeits. And he sets the price at the extreme: the whole world, on one side of the scale.

And loses or forfeits himself? Against it he sets one item: himself. Luke says himself, where Mark says his soul. The self, the whole person: not the soul as some detachable religious component, but the man, the self who was going to enjoy all that. Nothing in the world is worth losing yourself for. And the point is that the trade is not merely bad; it is incoherent. The buyer has purchased everything and disposed of the only person who could have had it.

Worth more than the world. Luke’s readers have seen this trade offered once before. When the devil took Jesus up and showed him every kingdom of the world in an instant, he offered the lot for one act of worship (4:5–7). He would not gain the world by losing his obedience; he would gain it by losing his life. Now he is the heir of all things, holding by the cross what Satan offered without it. The one who tells us not to make the trade is the one who refused it for us, and who is himself worth more than everything on the other side of the scale.

The prices people actually pay. If the trade fails at the maximum price, it fails at every price below it, and the prices most people actually pay are small: a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

Ashamed of me and my words. He chose shame rather than denies or rejects, because the pressure on disciples was often not violence but scorn. Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ. A great many are embarrassed by him, and by the words particularly, which is what he specifies: me and my words. It is one thing to hold a private faith and quite another to be the person at the table who believes what he said about sin, or judgment, or himself.

When he comes in his glory. Measure for measure: at the judgment, Jesus will disown those who disowned him (12:8–9).

A threefold glory. His own, his Father’s, and the angels’. Jesus claims to share the Father’s glory: the one about to be rejected will return as the glorious Judge, and the man whose association is now a social liability will arrive in a company like that.

If I have sometimes been ashamed of Jesus, will he disown me? This verse describes a settled refusal to own him, not a moment of weakness. Peter denied him three times and was restored (22:61–62; John 21:15–19). Paul says if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful (2 Timothy 2:12–13). The answer to shame is not despair but to turn back to him, as Peter did. And if this verse troubles you, the trouble itself is a good sign: those who are settled in being ashamed of him are not usually grieved by it.

In everyday life. Where are you tempted to be ashamed of Jesus? What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father. He was not ashamed of us: he endured the cross, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2). Next time the conversation turns, ask God for courage to say one true sentence about him.

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some standing here. Sceptics have built a case on this sentence. Jesus told the people in front of him that some of them would still be alive when the kingdom of God arrived. They all died. Therefore, it is said, he was mistaken.

Until they see the kingdom. Luke leaves out Mark’s come with power (Mark 9:1), making it simpler: they will see the kingdom. Three answers are given. The weakest takes it as the second coming and strains the words. The second, much better, takes the kingdom to mean what Luke consistently means: the reign of God breaking in. On that reading the promise was kept within the hearers’ lifetime: in the resurrection, at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and as the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome.

The answer eight days later. But the strongest answer is the one Luke himself supplies straight away: about eight days after these sayings Jesus took Peter and John and James up the mountain (v. 28). All three of the first Gospels put the transfiguration immediately after this promise. The fulfilment begins there, a preview of the kingdom, and continues in the resurrection, the ascension, Pentecost and the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, all within the lifetime of some of them.

A mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them all to pick up a cross. Then he lets three men see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. That is how it still works. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

Is the kingdom here now, or still to come? Both. The kingdom of God came with Jesus: in his works, his death and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit, God’s reign broke into the world, and every believer has been transferred into it (Colossians 1:13). But it has not yet come in its fullness; that awaits Christ’s return in glory, when every enemy will be put under his feet and the dead raised (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). We live between the two: citizens of a kingdom that is real now and will be visible then. That is why Christians can be joyful and longing at the same time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days later Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray, and while he prays his face is changed and his clothing becomes dazzling white.

Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, appear in glory and speak with him about his departure, his exodos, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter offers to build three tents, not knowing what he is saying. A cloud overshadows them, the cloud of God’s presence, and the Father’s voice says, this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him. When the cloud lifts, Jesus is alone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration shows who Jesus is and what his kingdom will be. The disciples do not see a form he puts on and takes off but the radiance of who he always is, for a few minutes no longer veiled by his humanity. John says the same: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah speak with him about the cross, the greater exodus to which everything they did had pointed. Some manuscripts read my Beloved at verse 35, but my Chosen One is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is Isaiah’s title for the Servant (Isaiah 42:1). And the one command in the scene, listen to him, is aimed at men who for eight days had refused what he said about his suffering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter’s tents show a familiar temptation: to hold on to a moment of glory and try to preserve it. The glory was given for the road down, and the road down is where most Christian work is done.

The response the Father asks for is not to build but to listen. The Christian life does not depend on spectacular experiences, though God in mercy gives some; it depends on hearing the Son in Scripture. And the timing is a kindness. Jesus had just told them to take up a cross, and then let three of them see what lay beyond it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About eight days after. Luke ties it to the confession and the first prediction of the cross. Matthew and Mark say after six days; Luke’s about marks a rough count, and a week counted with its first and last days included covers the same span.

Peter and John and James. The inner three (8:51): the same three who were in the room when Jairus’s daughter was raised, and the same three who, in Mark’s account, are taken deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). They see him in glory and they see him in anguish, and the second scene is unintelligible without the first.

Up on the mountain to pray. Only Luke says why he went: not to be transfigured, but to pray, and it happened while he was praying, as the voice at the baptism came while he was praying (3:21–22).

The appearance of his face was altered. Mark and Matthew use metemorphōthē: he was transfigured, the word behind metamorphosis. Luke, writing for Greek readers used to stories of gods changing shape, perhaps avoids it for that reason, and describes what was seen. Matthew says his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). As Moses’ face shone after being with God (Exodus 34:29–35); but Moses reflected a borrowed glory, and Jesus’ glory was his own, shining from within.

Not added, but uncovered. And his clothing became dazzling white (exastraptōn), flashing like lightning. Nothing was added to him; the covering came off something that was there all along. In the communion of the Son with the Father on that mountain, the glory broke through the surface.

Where did the glory come from? From who he is. Jesus is the eternal Son, the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature (Hebrews 1:3). In becoming man he did not stop being God; he veiled his glory in our flesh (Philippians 2:6–7; John 1:14). On the mountain the veil was drawn back for a moment. It is also a preview of the glory he would enter after his suffering (24:26), and of the glorified body that believers will one day share, when he transforms our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

In everyday life. You will not shine like the sun, but prayer, with your eyes on him in his word, is where the Spirit changes us, usually so slowly that only others notice: a temper a little shorter-lived, a fear a little quieter, a face turned more often towards him.

For worship. The carpenter from Nazareth is the Lord of glory. He did not keep it shining. He let the veil fall back, walked down the hill and went to Jerusalem, where the face that shone was blindfolded and struck (22:63–64), as he had said it would be spat upon (18:32). That is the wonder: not only that the glory was there, but that he hid it for us, until the morning it could shine unhidden and draw us, beholding him, into the same likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Elijah. Moses, who gave the law; Elijah, first among the prophets: the whole Old Testament, standing on a hillside. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (24:27, 44). Both were expected before the end (Malachi 4:4–5).

Both met God on a mountain. Both had met God on a mountain, Moses at Sinai and Elijah at Horeb, the same mountain, and each was hidden in a cleft or a cave while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22; 1 Kings 19:9–13). Moses asked to see God’s glory and was shown only his back; Elijah, in despair, was met not in wind or fire but in a low whisper. Now they appear in glory, standing in the light, talking with him.

His departure. Only Luke tells us what they talked about, and his word is startling: exodos, exodus. Moses led the first exodus; now the word is applied, in his hearing, to a death in Jerusalem. Jesus will lead a new and greater exodus, through his death, resurrection and ascension, freeing his people from slavery to sin and death and bringing them home to God. That is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven before it happens: a deliverance out of a slavery deeper than Egypt’s. What is slavery to sin? Jesus said that everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34): sin is not only something we do but a master we cannot sack, holding us under guilt and death. The exodus at Jerusalem breaks that master’s grip, so that the Son sets us free indeed (John 8:36). The word also means death, departure from life (2 Peter 1:15).

To accomplish at Jerusalem. Accomplish (plēroun) means to fulfil, complete. His death is not something that will happen to him, but a work he will finish. Jerusalem is the goal of the whole Gospel (v. 51; 13:33).

How did the disciples know who Moses and Elijah were? The text does not say; most likely it was given with the vision itself, or by what they heard them say. This is not a precedent for contact with the dead (compare 16:27–31). It was a unique revelation of the glorified state of God’s people and of the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to Christ’s departure.

Does this show the dead are conscious? It shows that Moses and Elijah were alive with God, centuries after they left the earth, and that they knew and cared about the work of Christ. That fits the rest of Scripture: God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (20:38), and those who die in the Lord are with him at once (23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep. But Scripture forbids us to seek contact with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). This was God’s doing, once, on a holy mountain, for his Son’s sake.

For worship. Moses and Elijah are in glory, and they are not talking about glory. With the light of heaven on them, what they discuss is Calvary. And for a believer, death too is an exodus, a departure out of bondage into the presence of God. The greatest of the saints in heaven are absorbed in the cross. So shall we be, for ever: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus — his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heavy with sleep. They almost missed it, and only Luke records it. The Son of God is shining, and the disciples are struggling to stay awake. Luke tells us the same thing in Gethsemane, where Jesus finds them sleeping for sorrow (22:45). There is no rebuke here. It is simply what men are like.

They saw his glory. Luke is careful to say so, because the testimony rests on these men. Peter himself would later write: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, and we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18).

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters, probably with the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, a feast that looked forward to God dwelling with his people. Luke notes that Peter speaks as Moses and Elijah are parting from Jesus: the tents are a way of making them stay. Peter’s instinct is to keep this foretaste of the kingdom, and the proposal goes wrong twice. Three tents make three equals, Jesus level with Moses and Elijah; and a camp on the mountain means no road to Jerusalem, where the exodus they had just been discussing was to be accomplished. The answer, when it comes from the cloud, leaves Jesus standing alone.

Not knowing what he said. Candid and gentle: Peter does what people do in the presence of something overwhelming, which is to talk, and to propose a project.

The tent God had already pitched. Peter offers to make a dwelling for Jesus, and does not see that Jesus is the dwelling. John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, using the verb for pitching a tent, and adds, we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The Feast of Booths looked forward to God living among his people; on this mountain the fulfilment is standing in front of Peter, shining. The tent of meeting has come in person, and the glory Peter wanted to shelter is the glory that shelters Peter.

Why can we not stay on the mountain? Because the glory was given for the road, not instead of it. Christians have high moments: a conference, a season of revival, a time of deep closeness to God in prayer. They are real gifts. But they are not meant to be housed and preserved, and trying to recreate them leads to disappointment or worse. The way to the final glory runs through Jerusalem: through faithful ordinary obedience, through suffering, through the cross. The mountain strengthens you for that; it does not excuse you from it. And one day there will be a dwelling that does not end, when God himself makes his home with his people (Revelation 21:3).

In everyday life. If you are living on the memory of a past spiritual high, thank God for it, and then ask what obedience he is calling you to in the valley this week. And if your prayers often fight sleep, take comfort: so did Peter’s. Keep coming.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud overshadowed them. Peter is interrupted mid-sentence. The cloud is not weather but the cloud of God’s presence, the cloud of Sinai and of the tabernacle (Exodus 24:15–18; 40:34–35), unseen in Israel for centuries. Luke’s verb is the one he used at the annunciation: the power of the Most High will overshadow you (1:35). And only Luke says they entered the cloud, and were afraid as they did: everything Israel knew said that men do not walk into that and come out.

A voice out of the cloud. At the baptism the words were spoken to Jesus himself (3:22); on the mountain they are spoken to the three disciples, about him. This is my Son: not one of three, but the Son, the answer to Peter’s three tents.

My Chosen One. Some manuscripts read my Beloved, as in Mark, and the KJV and NKJV follow them (my beloved Son). Chosen One is very likely what Luke wrote, the harder reading a copyist would smooth. It echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God presents his servant, whom he upholds, his chosen, in whom his soul delights. Jesus is the chosen Servant of the Lord, who will suffer (Isaiah 53). The rulers will mock this very title at the cross: if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One (23:35).

Listen to him! The only command in the scene: not look, not build, but listen. It echoes Deuteronomy 18:15: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, and it is to him you shall listen. Jesus is that prophet, greater than Moses. And the command is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one thing he said: that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed and be raised. Listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross.

Jesus was found alone. The cloud lifts, and there is one figure, not three. The Law and the Prophets have stepped back, and what is left standing in the ordinary light is a man they are going to follow down the hill to Jerusalem.

They kept silent. Why did they tell no one? Jesus ordered them to tell no one until he had risen (Mark 9:9). Before the cross, the glory they had seen would only have fed the wrong hopes.

How do I listen to him today? Through his word. The voice on the mountain turned the three from Moses and Elijah to Jesus alone, and Scripture does the same. The Son who spoke on earth now speaks through the Scriptures his Spirit inspired (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16). There is no need for a new voice from a cloud, and we should not seek one; the canon is closed, and Scripture is sufficient. Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words usually agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it, and that shared conviction matters more than the disagreement. Listen when you read the Bible, slowly and with prayer. Listen when it is faithfully preached. Listen especially to the parts you would rather not hear, as the three needed to hear about the cross. And listen in order to obey, for hearing in the Bible always means doing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen
my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only son is seized by a spirit, and the disciples who stayed below have failed to help. Jesus grieves over a faithless generation, then says, bring your son here. He rebukes the spirit, heals the boy and gives him back to his father, and everyone is astonished at the majesty of God.

While the crowd marvels, Jesus tells the disciples again that he will be handed over. They do not understand, and are afraid to ask. Instead they argue about which of them is greatest, and Jesus sets a child beside him. Then John reports that they tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name, because he was not one of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples’ failure, after their success in verses 1–6, shows that the authority they had been given was never their own. It came from Jesus and depended on trust in him; Matthew records Jesus naming their little faith (Matthew 17:20).

The second prediction contains a bitter play on words: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men. And Luke’s note that the meaning was concealed holds two things together: a hiddenness God appointed until the resurrection (24:16, 45), and a hiddenness the disciples chose, as their argument about greatness shows.

The saying that whoever is not against you is for you seems to clash with 11:23. But there the subject is a man’s own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground; here it is one servant’s judgment of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another man doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child beside Jesus challenges any measure of greatness by influence, platform or numbers. The test of a man is not how he treats those above him but how he treats those who can never do him any good.

The father’s report that the disciples could not help is an honest record of failure, and a comfort of a hard kind: the church’s work has always included things that did not work. And John’s complaint that the man did not follow with us names an instinct every group knows: treating the edge of our circle as the edge of the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Down from the mountain. From glory to need, and it is the contrast Moses walked into. He came down Sinai carrying the words of God and found the people round a golden calf (Exodus 32). Jesus comes down with the voice of the Father still in the disciples’ ears, and finds a boy in convulsions and a ministry that has failed. That descent is where nearly all Christian work is done: the next morning at the bottom of the hill, among people with a problem that will not wait.

Look at my son. A father, shouting over a crowd, does not ask for a miracle; he asks Jesus to look at the boy. Look at means look upon with favour and compassion. He has stopped expecting anything and is asking for attention.

The God who looks. The father asks for what the desperate have always asked of God: look. Hannah prayed that the LORD would look on the affliction of his servant (1 Samuel 1:11), and Luke’s verb here is the very one Mary used when she sang that God had looked on the humble estate of his servant (1:48). The father asks it of Jesus to his face, which is what the incarnation has made possible: the God who looks down from heaven has come close enough to be stopped on a hillside and asked to turn his eyes on one boy, and he does.

My only child. Once more Luke alone has the word only, as with the widow’s only son at Nain (7:12), Jairus’s only daughter (8:42). No other children, and in that world no future for the family either.

A father in a crowd. He is not a disciple, and Luke does not tell us his name: a father who has lived for years with a child destroyed in front of him at unpredictable intervals, and who has come to a preacher’s followers and been let down. Anybody who has cared for a severely ill or disabled child will recognise the exhaustion in the request.

Does God see my child? Yes. The God who saw Hagar’s son crying under a bush in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17), and who looked on this boy through the eyes of his Son, sees every child and every parent. If you are caring for a child who is ill, disabled or far from God, you may feel unseen by everyone, including the church. Jesus is not like the crowd. Bring your child to him in prayer, as this father did, even if all you can manage is, Lord, look at my son. And ask your church family for help; they are meant to carry this with you (Galatians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A spirit seizes him. The father’s description is clinical: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, and then the flattened exhaustion afterwards. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the cause was demonic (v. 42). It shatters him (syntribon: crushes, bruises, breaks), and even between seizures it will hardly let him go. Satan’s aim is destruction.

Ill or possessed? So was this boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that sits the sharper question people actually mean: were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil? The answer comes from Luke himself, and it is worth having, because he is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and his Gospel is full of his clinical eye: the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the high fever (4:38), the sweat like drops of blood (22:44; those verses are missing from some early manuscripts, but the other examples stand without them). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart. He writes that they brought Jesus those who were sick with various diseases, and that demons also came out of many (4:40–41). He describes a crowd who came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits who were cured (6:17–18): two groups, named separately, in a single breath. Jesus himself speaks the same way: I cast out demons and perform cures (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that. Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this particular boy something else was behind them.

Two errors. Luke’s care rules out two harmful errors. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy: a cruelty this Gospel forbids by the plain fact that its author lists sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil’s grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second is the fashionable error, that demon was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose properly. But in two verses’ time Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

But they could not. The honest report of a ministry failure, by the man it failed. The nine disciples who stayed below had failed, though Jesus had given them authority over all demons (v. 1). These men came back earlier full of what they had done (v. 10), and it was real. Here, at the bottom of the mountain, with a father watching, nothing worked.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? Jesus calls it faithlessness (v. 41), and in Mark he adds that this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer (Mark 9:29; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add and fasting, but the earliest do not). The authority they had been given was real, but it was derived, and they had stopped depending on the one who gave it.

What his servants could not do. The failure throws the whole weight of the scene onto one person: the nine had real authority, and it failed, and the father’s hope now rests on Jesus alone. Every gift Christ gives his people remains his gift, and never becomes a power they own. What cannot fail in this story is not the ministry but the Master.

What should I do when the church fails someone? Admit it honestly, as this father’s words force the disciples to. Churches and Christians do fail people: in counsel, in care, in prayer, in noticing. The answer is not to pretend otherwise, nor to give up on Christ because his people failed. The father did the right thing: when the disciples could not help, he took his son to Jesus himself. If you have been let down by Christians, do not let their failure keep you from the Lord. And if you are the one who failed, take it back to him in prayer, and learn dependence.

In everyday life. Past success is no guarantee of present power. Every work of God needs fresh dependence on him. Do not walk into this week on the strength of last week’s fruit. Pray before you begin, every time.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
O faithless and twisted generation. One of the sharpest things Jesus says in this Gospel, and it is not aimed at the father, who came and told the truth, but at a generation: the crowd, the disciples, the whole scene at the foot of the mountain. Twisted (diestrammenē) means perverse, crooked: the word Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5).

How long am I to be with you and bear with you? The tone is not simply anger. It is the sound of a man carrying something heavy: the weariness of the holy Son among unbelievers. He has come down from the light of his Father’s presence into a valley where nothing works, and he says so.

Bring your son here. Then, without pausing, compassion: the exasperation is not the last word. He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy. He does not make the father’s help conditional on the crowd improving.

Its last attack. The thing is at its worst in the final seconds before it is finished, as anyone knows who has watched a besetting sin or a long oppression flare up hardest just as ground is being taken.

Gave him back to his father. Luke tells it more briefly than Mark, but ends on this: he gave him back to his father, almost the phrase used at Nain, where he gave him to his mother (7:15). Luke will not let a miracle be reported as an event when it can be reported as a gift.

The majesty of God. Majesty (megaleiotēti) means greatness, magnificence. The crowd saw God’s greatness in what Jesus did, the word used of the transfiguration (2 Peter 1:16): the majesty seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley.

Does Jesus lose patience with me? He grieves over unbelief, and he says so; we should not pretend he is indifferent to it. But look at what he does with his weariness: he says, bring your son here. His patience is not endless in the sense that sin does not matter to him; it is endless in the sense that he goes on bearing with his people until he has finished his work in them. The same Lord who sighed over a faithless generation went to the cross for it. If you fear you have exhausted his patience, the very fear shows his Spirit is still at work. Bring your need to him.

For worship. The splendour that shone beside Moses and Elijah stooped to lift a broken boy into his father’s arms. That is the greatness of our God: not only that he rules the universe, but that he hands sons back to fathers, and at the cost of his own Son is bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
