The second passion prediction. While everyone was marvelling at his power (v. 43), Jesus speaks of his weakness. The timing is the point: at the height of the crowd’s enthusiasm he tells his disciples something that will spoil it, so that they are not swept up in it.

Let these words sink into your ears. Literally, put these words into your ears. He is not making an announcement; he is asking them to store something they will need later and cannot use yet.

Delivered into the hands of men. One word here is new. Delivered (paradidosthai) means handed over, betrayed. It is the word that will be used of Judas throughout the passion, and the word Isaiah’s Greek text uses of the Servant who was handed over because of their sins (Isaiah 53:12). And there is a bitter play on words: the Son of Man into the hands of men. The one who heals by his hands will be handed into human hands.

Concealed from them. They did not understand, because they could not reconcile a suffering Messiah with what they believed. Only Luke adds that it was concealed. By whom? The passive is probably deliberate, and two things are true at once. There is a hiddenness that God appoints, not as punishment, but because the time for understanding had not yet come: Luke says the same of the Emmaus pair, whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16), until they were opened after the resurrection (24:31, 45). And there is a hiddenness the disciples make for themselves, for Luke shows straight afterwards what they were thinking about instead: which of them was greatest.

Afraid to ask. The human half: they were afraid, very likely of the answer. Not-understanding can be genuinely stuck, or it can have grasped enough to know it does not want the rest. They had understood more than they wanted to (Mark 8:32).

Why would God hide the meaning from them? For a time, and for their good. They could not yet bear the full truth of the cross, and they would understand it only in the light of the resurrection, when the risen Christ opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). God’s timing in revelation is wise. There are things in his word you may not understand yet, and some will become clear only through later experience, or in glory. That is no excuse for not asking; the disciples’ fear was their own fault. But it is a comfort when understanding is slow. He will finish teaching you.

In everyday life. The question that most needs asking is often the one nobody will raise, because everyone suspects what the answer will cost. Ask it, in prayer and to people who know the Scriptures.

For worship. The hands that had just lifted a broken boy would be handed over into the hands of men, and he told his friends so while the crowd was still marvelling. He was not caught by the cross; he walked toward it with open eyes. We understand now what they could not: that the handing over was love, that the Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and that the one men handed over now holds us, and will not hand us over to anyone.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of them was the greatest. He has just told them he is going to be handed over and killed, and what fills the silence is an argument about rank. Luke sets the two side by side without comment. The same argument will arise at the Last Supper (22:24).

What were they arguing about? The timing suggests an answer. Three of them had just been up a mountain and come back different, and would not say why (v. 36). Peter had been the one to name him the Christ. The nine had not managed to cast out the demon. Perhaps the choice of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy, or the failure of the nine. There was material for a dispute, and it was fresh. So this is not a general failing of ambitious men. It is what happened in the hours after the glory, among people who had been let in on something, which is precisely where this particular sin lives. Nobody argues about greatness who has not first been given something.

The reasoning of their hearts. Luke does not say they told him. He knew what they were thinking (5:22; 6:8): the argument was in their hearts, and he could see it. This is the one who knew what was in man (John 2:25) reading the inner life of twelve people at once, including the parts they would not have admitted to each other.

A child by his side. He does not answer the argument or lecture them on humility. He takes a child (paidion, a young one, small enough to be taken) and stands the child beside himself, in the place of honour. The picture is the argument: twelve grown men are ranking themselves, and he places beside himself the one person present with no rank whatsoever.

Is it wrong to want to do well? No. Paul tells us to excel, to work heartily, to aim for the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24; Colossians 3:23). Ambition for God’s glory and for the good of others is a virtue. What Jesus exposes here is the desire to be thought greater than others: comparison, rank, the need to be ahead. The test is simple. Can you rejoice when someone else is honoured, chosen, or more fruitful than you (Romans 12:15)? Do you want to be great, or do you want Christ to be great? Pride hides easily in spiritual success, so watch especially after God has blessed you.

In everyday life. Your place beside Christ is a gift no one can outrank. Notice this week when you mentally rank yourself against someone: a colleague, a fellow church member, a sibling. Confess it to God plainly, and then do something to honour the person you were measuring yourself against.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Receives this child. A first-century child was loved, but in law and society had no standing and no capacity to confer honour on anybody. Receives is the language of hospitality: to welcome, to take somebody in. So the question here is not, who is willing to be like a child? (that comes at 18:17), but: who will you make room for, when the person can do nothing for you?

Him who sent me. The child stands for Christ, and Christ for the Father who sent him, so that the person with the least standing in the room is joined, in two links, to the throne of God. It is a claim about where Christ has chosen to be found (compare 14:21). The welcome of the least is the shape of God’s own hospitality.

The one who is great. He does not abolish greatness; he inverts the measurement. Not the one who seeks to be great, but the one who becomes small: who welcomes the unimportant and serves without seeking recognition (22:26–27).

Making it concrete. Everyone is attentive upwards. The test is how a man treats the people who cannot advance him or repay him. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching. Whatever is being said to them is being said to Christ, and whatever is being given them is going to the Father.

Does this mean children’s work in the church matters? Very much. Those who welcome, teach and care for children in Christ’s name are receiving Christ himself, though their work is often unseen and rarely thanked. The crèche rota and the Sunday school are not lesser ministries for those not gifted enough to preach. And the principle reaches further: the disabled, the elderly with dementia, the newcomer who does not fit, the person with nothing to give. A church’s greatness is measured by how it receives those who can do nothing for it.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
We saw someone. Nobody had asked John anything. Jesus has just said the least is the greatest, and John immediately produces an incident in which the disciples enforced a boundary.

What John reports. The man was casting out demons successfully, where the disciples had just failed (v. 40). And he was doing it in your name: not in his own, not as a rival, but under the authority of Jesus.

He does not follow with us. The only ground for stopping him is John’s own: not one of our group. Not, he does not follow you. Us. The same pride as the argument about greatness, now as group pride.

Not against you. The correction is immediate and generous. Anyone genuinely working in Jesus’ name against Satan is on the same side. What is being corrected is a thoroughly religious instinct: the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition.

The name that does the work. When Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp, outside the circle at the tent, Joshua begged Moses to stop them, and Moses answered that he wished all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29). John plays Joshua here. But the power at work is not Moses’ spirit shared out; it is Jesus’ own name. The name, not the group, does the work, and the name belongs to him.

Against or with? A reader will notice that Jesus says something apparently opposite two chapters later: whoever is not with me is against me (11:23). The two are not in conflict, and the difference is in the pronouns. There, the subject is a man’s own relation to Christ, and there is no neutral ground: no one is uncommitted where he is concerned. Here, the subject is one servant’s judgment of another, and the presumption runs the other way. So this verse is a rule for how to view others, and 11:23 is a test for oneself. About my own standing before Christ, assume nothing. About another man doing good in his name, assume the best. Do not exclude genuine fellow workers; but you yourself must be wholly with Christ.

In the flow. In a few verses the disciples fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), argue about greatness (v. 46), try to stop an outsider (v. 49), and will soon want fire on a Samaritan village (v. 54): men who have just been shown the glory of Christ are absorbed in their own standing. In the very next verse Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51). The road to the cross is the answer to their pride, and he travels it first.

What it does not mean. Using the name of Jesus does not make a man a true believer, and this is no licence to treat doctrine as unimportant (Matthew 7:22–23; Acts 19:13–16; Galatians 1:8). The issue here is group loyalty, not the truth of the gospel. That is a long way from saying it does not matter what anyone believes.

How do I tell a fellow worker from a false teacher? Ask what he says about Christ and the gospel, not whether he belongs to your group. Does he confess Jesus as Lord and God, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith, not by works (Galatians 1:6–9)? Does his life and teaching honour Christ? Where those are present, rejoice in his work, even if he baptises differently, governs his church differently or sings different songs. Where the gospel itself is denied, the name of Jesus is being used, not served, and love requires us to say so.

In everyday life. Rejoice when Christ is served by believers outside your own circle. Pick out a church in your town that is not yours but preaches Christ faithfully, and pray for it this week. And watch for the moment when you are more pleased that your group succeeds than that Christ is honoured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With verse 51 the Galilean ministry ends and the long journey to Jerusalem begins; it runs to 19:44. Jesus sets his face to go there, knowing what waits for him.

A Samaritan village refuses him because he is heading for Jerusalem, and James and John want to call down fire, as Elijah once did. Jesus rebukes them, not the village, and they go on elsewhere. Within a few years Samaria would receive the gospel with joy (Acts 8:5–8).

Three short encounters close the chapter. One man offers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. A second is called and asks first to bury his father. A third asks first to say goodbye at home, and hears that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke gives ten chapters to the journey, and the journey is a picture of discipleship: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, and so to the cross.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead is one of the most startling sayings in the Gospels, because burying a father was a sacred duty. It does not abolish family duty. It refuses one word, first, and only the Lord of the commandments may claim a place ahead of father and mother. Fit for the kingdom speaks of usefulness for the work, not of whether a man can be saved.

And the fire James and John wanted is answered by the direction Jesus is walking. He does not destroy those who refuse him; he goes to the sacrifice that will bring even Samaritans to him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The three would-be followers show three ways of not following. The first has not counted the cost. The second and third both say first, and there will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient; it is because these things are reasonable that they postpone everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of them decided; the question passes to the reader. And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly: the one who called people to follow had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards his death, and he told them so before they began.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The journey to Jerusalem. Here Luke’s Gospel turns its face to the cross: his long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins, running to 19:44, ten chapters. Everything from here on happens on a road with one destination, and much of Luke’s unique material is here: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus.

For him to be taken up. When the days drew near is literally, when the days were being fulfilled: time is running out on purpose, and it is being counted. Taken up (analēmpsis) is a noun used nowhere else in the New Testament. It reaches past the cross to the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22): the death, the rising, and the going home to the Father, in one word.

He set his face. The phrase is Hebrew in shape, and Luke repeats it in the next breath. In the prophets, to set one’s face is the posture of a man sent with a hard commission: Ezekiel was told to set his face toward Jerusalem and preach against its sanctuaries (Ezekiel 21:2). Above all it is the Servant’s resolve in Isaiah, who sets his face like a flint in the same breath as he gives his back to those who strike and does not hide his face from spitting (Isaiah 50:6–7). So the face turned to Jerusalem already knows what waits there. He is not swept toward the cross by events. He turns and starts walking.

Messengers ahead of him. To arrange food and lodging. The direct route from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria; some Jews went round it, adding days, though Josephus says Galilean pilgrims usually took the direct road. Jesus goes straight through.

A village of the Samaritans. The Samaritans descended from northern Israelites who intermarried with peoples settled there after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). Their Scriptures were the five books of Moses alone, and their holy mountain was Gerizim, not Jerusalem (John 4:20). The hostility was ancient and mutual.

They did not receive him. He was going to worship at the temple they rejected, and Samaritans were often hostile to Jewish pilgrims passing through. So the refusal is not personal. And there is an irony in it: what he is rejected for, at the very start of the journey to the cross, is going to the cross.

Did Jesus know everything that would happen in Jerusalem? Yes. He had already told the disciples twice (vv. 22, 44), and he would tell them again in detail: he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon (18:31–33). He did not go to Jerusalem hoping for the best. He went as the Lamb who knew the altar. That is what makes his resolve so overwhelming. Every step south was taken with full knowledge, and every step was chosen. He was not a victim of circumstances but the willing Saviour.

In everyday life. Is there a hard thing God has made clear you must do? His face was set for you first, and his Spirit steadies yours: set your face. Do not wait for it to become easy. And when obedience costs you a welcome somewhere, remember that it cost him a bed at the start of the road.
verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John. Jesus called them Boanerges, Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17). Here we see why.

Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? They ask permission. They do not act. There is even a kind of deference in it, do you want us to?, which makes the request more disturbing rather than less, because they genuinely expect the answer might be yes. Their precedent is scriptural. Elijah, in this same region, called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent by the king of Samaria to arrest him (2 Kings 1:9–16). These two have recently come down a mountain where they saw Elijah in glory. And they had been given power (v. 1). Why not use it? They are not making it up; they are reasoning from the Bible, and reasoning badly. Because the situation is not the same at all. Elijah faced armed men sent by an idolatrous king to seize a prophet. James and John are facing a village that declined to provide beds.

He rebuked them. Luke records no word to the village at all; the rebuke goes to the disciples. This is not the time for judgment, but for grace. The day of vengeance has not yet come (4:19).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add as Elijah did, and others add Jesus’ words: you do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them. These are probably not original, but they capture the meaning. They are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and the modern versions put them in a footnote, which is why one Bible may be shorter than another at exactly this point. Two things are worth saying, and they pull in opposite directions. The words are almost certainly not what Luke wrote: a scribe appears to have supplied the content of a rebuke Luke deliberately left unstated, and once written in a margin it moved into the text. But the sentence that was added is entirely true, and it is true from Luke’s own pages. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10) is in this Gospel in Jesus’ own words. And within one chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed the theology exactly right. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.

Another village. No fire, no argument, no curse. They walked on.

The fire that did come. And Jesus would later send his gospel to Samaria (Acts 1:8), where it would be received with great joy (Acts 8:5–8, 14–17), and John himself would go there with Peter to lay hands on Samaritan believers so they would receive the Holy Spirit. Something did come down on Samaria from heaven, not fire but the Holy Spirit. The man who wanted to burn a Samaritan village lived to pray for Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

Will God never judge, then? He will. The day of vengeance is real, and Jesus himself speaks of it often (17:26–30; 21:22). Those who finally reject him will face God’s just and eternal judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). But judgment belongs to God, not to us, and it belongs to the last day, not to this one. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Our task is to warn, to plead and to pray, never to wish destruction on those who reject us. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Romans 12:19).

In everyday life. When people reject you or the gospel, resist the desire for revenge: the Lord who could have sent fire on you sent the gospel instead. When you enjoy imagining the downfall of someone who has mocked your faith or hurt you, turn the thought into a prayer for them. And be careful of using Bible verses to justify the anger you already feel.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three would-be followers. Three short encounters on the road (vv. 57–62) cover between them most of the ways a person fails to follow.

Wherever you go. Nobody called this man. He volunteers everything, sincerely, perhaps impulsively. Matthew tells us he was a scribe (Matthew 8:19), used to attaching himself to a teacher. Does he know where Jesus is going? To Jerusalem, to the cross.

Foxes have holes. Not a refusal but a disclosure: Jesus does not take advantage of enthusiasm. The comparison is exact and slightly bitter: the animals of the land he made have somewhere to sleep.

Nowhere to lay his head. Jesus had left his home in Nazareth, and had just been refused lodging in Samaria. The man has said wherever you go on a road where the last village would not have him. Following him means giving up security and comfort. Count the cost first (14:28).

What a comfortable church needs to hear. A certain kind of preaching promises that coming to Christ secures a settled, prosperous life. The one making this offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he told the volunteer so before he signed. Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided; the question is left standing for the reader.

Must every Christian give up their home? No. Jesus’ own followers included people with houses, like Martha (10:38), and Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Jesus was not laying down a rule that disciples must be homeless, but telling a volunteer the truth about the road. What every disciple must do is hold home, comfort and security loosely, ready to lose them if following Christ requires it, as many believers around the world do today. A Christian may have a home; he may not make it his foundation. The question is whether you would still follow if it cost you the house.

In everyday life. Before you make a large promise to God, count what it may cost, and then make it anyway, leaning on his grace rather than your enthusiasm. And if you are helping someone come to faith, tell them honestly about the road.

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow me. This one is called, with the same two words that were said to Levi at the tax booth (5:27), and, as Mark tells it, to fishermen at a lakeside (Mark 1:17).

Let me first bury my father. The most reasonable sentence in the chapter. Burying a father was a sacred duty in Judaism, so important that, according to later Jewish writings, it overrode other religious obligations, like reciting the Shema. A son who did not bury his father had failed at the commandment to honour him.

Was the father already dead? In that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest. If the father had just died, he would be burying him that day, at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. More likely, his father was still alive and the man meant: let me wait until my father dies, and I have my inheritance and have fulfilled my family duty, perhaps years from now. It is not a plea for three days off. It is a request for an indefinite postponement, a few years, perhaps many, until the duty is discharged and the inheritance settled and the man is free to go with nothing owing. Either way, he puts something else first. That is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin. He is refusing one word, and the word is first.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead. A deliberately paradoxical saying: let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. The village will manage the funeral. It cannot manage the proclamation. The kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family duty.

Go and proclaim. The commission is the reason for the severity: he is not told to abandon his family for no purpose, but given an urgent one.

The Lord who has the right to come first. Only God may claim a place ahead of father and mother. The fifth commandment stands under the first, and here Jesus claims the place of the first: no duty, however sacred, may stand in front of following him. That is the honest answer to the objection that this sounds like a cult leader cutting a man off from his family. From any mere man it would be. The demand is only right if the one making it is God, which is what this chapter has been showing. And the one who claims it honoured his own Father perfectly, all the way to Gethsemane, where he prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). His claim is the call of the Son who first put his Father before his own life.

What it does not mean. This gives no Christian leave to neglect his parents or stay away from funerals. Jesus condemned the Pharisees for using religion to avoid caring for parents (Mark 7:9–13). Whatever you put first is your real lord. And if you have lately buried a parent, nothing here faults your grief or your care: Jesus himself wept at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35).

What if my family really does need me? Then caring for them may be exactly the way you follow Christ. Scripture is clear that providing for your family and honouring your parents are Christian duties (1 Timothy 5:4, 8), and Jesus provided for his own mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). The man in this passage was not caring for his father; he was using his father as a reason to delay obeying Christ. The question to ask is not, do I have family duties?, but, am I using them to avoid something Christ has plainly told me to do? Duty done for Christ is following; duty used against Christ is the first that he refuses.

In everyday life. What do you want to do first, before following Jesus fully? There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish first, which is what makes them so effective. Name your first, and give it to him.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me first say farewell. The third man volunteers like the first and asks for a delay like the second, and his request is the smallest: to go home and say goodbye.

The precedent of Elisha. There is a precedent. When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at the plough, Elisha asked to kiss his father and his mother goodbye, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). He went back, burned his ploughing equipment, and followed. So the man is asking for what the prophet allowed, and this time the answer is no. Jesus demands more than Elijah, because he is more than Elijah.

Hand to the plow. The difference is instructive: Elisha destroyed the plough; this man wants to keep the option of the house. The ancient plough was light and single-handled, steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A ploughman who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment. A divided heart, half looking back to the old life, cannot plough straight for the kingdom. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32). The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

Fit for the kingdom. Fit (euthetos) means suitable, useful, well-placed for a purpose. Not that he cannot be saved, but that half-hearted discipleship is useless for kingdom work.

The three obstacles. Comfort (v. 58), duty (v. 60), and family affection (v. 61). All good things, and none can come before Christ. The first would not count the cost; the second and third both said first. None of them is told he cannot come.

In the flow. The chapter began with the Twelve sent out with nothing (vv. 1–6), turned on who Jesus is (vv. 20, 35), and showed that his followers walk behind him with a cross (vv. 22–23). Now three would-be followers learn what that means: nothing may come before him. The next chapter sends out seventy-two more (10:1; some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read seventy).

Is it wrong to miss my old life? Not in itself. Feelings of loss are human, and Christ is not offended by honest grief over what following him has cost. The danger is the backward look that wants to return: the heart that keeps the old life as an option, in case Christ does not prove worth it. Paul’s remedy was to count everything loss compared with knowing Christ, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:8, 13–14). The cure for looking back is not trying harder not to look, but fixing your eyes on what is ahead: on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2).

In everyday life. Is there an option you are keeping open, a relationship, a habit, a way back, in case following him does not work out? Close it this week, as Elisha burned his plough.

For worship. One man in this chapter put his hand to the plough and never looked back. Through the refusal of a Samaritan village, the failure of his friends and the darkness of the cross, he kept his eyes on Jerusalem until the work was done, and his last word there was a prayer of trust: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). Because he did not turn back, the furrow is cut: his unbroken obedience is counted as ours, and people who have looked back a thousand times are counted fit in him.
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

parallels.desc: Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 holds three scenes. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) widens the mission beyond the Twelve and ends in Jesus’ own joy in the Father. The parable of the good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) answers a lawyer who wants to know how little love he can get away with. And at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) Jesus names the one thing necessary.

The chapter opens the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:44). Together the three scenes show what the kingdom does in the world, what it asks of those who belong to it, and where its life begins: at his feet, receiving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others and sends them in pairs ahead of him, into every town he is about to visit. He tells them to pray for more labourers, warns them that they go as lambs among wolves, and sends them on an urgent mission: travel light, stay where you are welcomed, heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God has come near.

Towns that refuse them hear the same announcement on the way out. The section closes with woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, where most of his works had been done, and with the chain that makes it all so serious: whoever rejects the messengers rejects Christ, and the Father who sent him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 16 governs all Christian mission. An authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him, so there is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want, and it gives no leader shelter from honest criticism.

The woes teach that judgment is weighed by the light received (12:47–48; Romans 2:12–16). Those who stood nearest to Christ are the most exposed if they stay unchanged.
verseByVerse.examples: Chorazin was condemned for mighty works no evangelist wrote down (John 21:25), and Sodom fares better only because nobody ever stood in her streets announcing the kingdom. Even a rejecting town hears the offer one last time, and nearness is not reception. That bites hardest on anyone with a Bible on the shelf and a lifetime of sermons behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Only Luke records the sending of the seventy-two. The Twelve were sent in chapter 9; now a wider circle goes out ahead of Jesus as he sets his face toward Jerusalem. The mission is not only for apostles. Running through the chapter is a single question: what does it mean to have the kingdom of God come near, and what do you do when it is standing at your door?

Seventy or seventy-two? If your Bible says seventy where this one says seventy-two, nothing is wrong and nothing much hangs on it. The manuscripts divide almost evenly, here and again at v. 17, and translators go different ways. Either figure carries the same symbolism, because the Old Testament supplies both. The elders Moses appointed number seventy (Numbers 11:16), but two more were left in the camp and prophesied anyway (Numbers 11:26); and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. A copyist working from either tradition could easily tidy the other toward it. What the number says is the same on both counts. Moses’ seventy were appointed to carry a burden he could not carry alone. Genesis’ seventy are the nations of the world. Twelve for the tribes of Israel; seventy-two for the whole earth. This mission is larger than the Twelve, and it is pointed outward.

Two by two. Not only for company, though that helps on a dark road. Under the law a matter was established by two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and what these men carry is testimony. Pairs are harder to discredit and harder to discourage (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Where he himself was about to go. They are not independent operators but an advance party, like John the Baptist preparing the way, and everywhere they go he is coming behind them. The messenger arrives first, and the Lord follows into the place the message has opened. No believer ever goes anywhere for Christ where Christ is not already on his way.

The harvest is plentiful. Most of us picture evangelism as a thin crop in a resistant field. Jesus says the field is not the problem; it is ready (John 4:35–38). Harvest is also, in the prophets and in John the Baptist’s preaching, a picture of the end (3:17), so the image carries both urgency and hope: the crop is ripe, and ripe crops do not wait.

Pray earnestly. Faced with a shortage of workers, he does not first say go. He says pray, to seventy-two men he is about to send out that very hour. Pray earnestly (deēthēte) means beg, plead. And the one being begged owns the field: the Lord of the harvest, and his harvest. The labour shortage is not finally our problem to solve. It is his, and he has told us how to raise it with him.

The Lord appointed. Luke calls Jesus simply the Lord as the chapter opens. The harvest the Father owns is the harvest the Son has come to gather, and no one goes into it whom he has not first appointed. Mission begins in his choice, not in our enthusiasm.

To send out. The verb (ekballō) is often used for driving out, including the casting out of demons, and here it probably keeps some of its force. Workers often have to be pushed into the harvest, by a God who overcomes their reluctance, rearranges their lives and sometimes uses hardship to get them moving.

What does praying for labourers look like in practice? Name real places and real people: your own church’s need for teachers and youth leaders, a missionary you know, an unreached people group, the street you live on. Pray for the sending of preachers and church planters, but also for ordinary believers in workplaces and families who will speak of Christ there. Pray for your own children and grandchildren to be among those sent, which is harder than it sounds. And hold your hands open while you pray, because the Lord of the harvest may answer by sending you, to the next room or the next continent.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lambs in the midst of wolves. He says it as he sends them, not afterwards. A lamb among wolves is not an underdog with a fighting chance. It is food, and no shepherd ever put one there on purpose, which is exactly what he says he is doing. The whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending: the Shepherd who will lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

The design, not a fault. The vulnerability of the mission is not a fault to be engineered out; it is the design, and it is his own. These men are sent ahead of a Lord who has set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and has twice told them that he must suffer (9:22, 44). The lambs walk the road the Shepherd is walking. A church that has made itself safe, powerful and protected has stepped off his road. The gospel of a crucified Lord has always travelled best in the hands of people who could be hurt.

No moneybag, no knapsack. The list is close to the one given the Twelve (9:3); no sandals probably means no spare pair: no wallet, no bag and no change of shoes for a journey on foot. The point is total dependence on God, shown in the plainest way possible. They will eat because someone feeds them, and they will be fed because God has gone before them into the houses.

Greet no one on the road. An Eastern roadside greeting was often not a nod but an extended exchange of embraces, enquiries after family and business, and invitations to stay. Elisha, sending Gehazi urgently to a dead child, told him not to greet anyone he met on the way (2 Kings 4:29). So it is not a rule about manners but about urgency, for one sweep through the towns he is about to visit: the ordinary courtesies of the road must not eat the daylight.

Does this mean Christian workers today should go without money or supplies? No. These were instructions for one short, urgent mission inside Israel, where hospitality to travelling teachers was expected. Later Jesus deliberately reverses them: now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack (22:35–36), because the situation has changed. Paul travelled with funds, received gifts and sometimes worked with his hands. What carries over is not the packing list but the posture: go in dependence on God, do not let comfort set the terms of obedience, and do not let lesser things crowd out what is urgent.

In everyday life. Take the thing God has plainly given you to do, a conversation you owe a friend, a reconciliation, a call to a lonely relative, and ask what small courtesies, hobbies and screens keep eating the daylight. And if you feel exposed as a Christian at work or at home, remember you were never promised the wolves would be tame. You were promised a Shepherd.
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace be to this house! The greeting is shalom, which never meant merely the absence of trouble. It means wholeness, a life not at war with God or with itself. In the mouth of a man sent by Jesus it is not a pleasantry but the peace the angels sang over Bethlehem (2:14), and the next sentence treats it as something that goes somewhere, settles or does not, and can come back.

A son of peace. “Son of peace” is a Hebrew idiom: a person who belongs to the peace being offered and is ready for it. Where such a person is found, he was prepared before the messengers arrived. Evangelism is not manufacturing interest out of nothing; the work is largely to find the one whose heart God has made ready, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart before Paul finished speaking (Acts 16:14).

It will return to you. Nothing is lost. Like the dove sent out from the ark that found no place to rest and came back to Noah’s hand (Genesis 8:9), a blessing offered to a house that will not have it is not wasted; it comes back to the one who offered it. That is a quiet mercy for every believer who has spoken and been rebuffed and felt they had spent something they could not get back.

Peace to you. The peace belongs to Jesus before it belongs to his messengers. The crowds will shout it as he rides into Jerusalem (19:38), he will weep that the city did not know the things that make for peace (19:42), and on the evening of the resurrection he will stand among frightened disciples and say, Peace to you (24:36). The seventy-two speak a peace they cannot yet explain; one day he will speak it himself, risen, to men who had failed him.

Remain in the same house. The rule is the same as the Twelve’s, and for the same reason: a messenger who trades up for better hospitality has begun to be paid, and a man whose lodging depends on the standing of his host will eventually trim his message to keep it.

The laborer deserves his wages. Paul quotes this saying to Timothy as Scripture, beside the command from Deuteronomy 25:4 not to muzzle an ox (1 Timothy 5:18). So within the apostles’ lifetime a saying of Jesus was set beside the Law of Moses under the single heading the Scripture says. The principle is plain: those who work for the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is not charity; it is wages earned.

Should I give to my church if I am not sure the money is well used? Give, and give gladly, because supporting those who teach you is obedience to Christ, not a favour to an institution (Galatians 6:6). But you are not asked to give blindly. A faithful church is open about its finances, and you may ask how money is spent. If you have real concerns, raise them with the elders, privately and kindly. What you should not do is let vague suspicion become a permanent excuse for keeping back what Jesus says the labourer deserves.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat what is set before you. It sounds like a rule about manners, and it is a great deal more. These Jewish men may have been going into towns where not every kitchen was kept by the purity laws, the daily, physical boundary of the covenant people. Many readers think Luke, writing for a Gentile church, sees where that is going: in his second volume Peter will be told, what God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:14–15), and within days he will be in a Roman centurion’s house. Paul gives the same rule: eat whatever is set before you without raising questions on the ground of conscience (1 Corinthians 10:27).

Receiving the person. There is a plainer point too. To eat what a poor household puts in front of you, without inspecting it, is to accept the person. Anybody who has been served a meal by people who had very little will know that scrutinising it would have been the one unforgivable thing.

Heal the sick. The touch and then the word: not a strategy to earn a hearing and an explanation of it, but one announcement made in two ways. The healings are signs that the King has arrived, and wherever he goes, sickness and death begin to retreat.

Has come near. Not that the kingdom of God will come, but that it has come near. The perfect tense (ēngiken) describes a settled state: it has drawn near and is standing at the door, and 11:20 will say plainly that it has come. God’s kingdom is his rule putting the world right: sin forgiven, sickness healed, the devil’s grip broken. It is near because the King is near: these towns lay on his own route (v. 1), and the healings were his. It is close enough to be reached, and it demands a response.

Is “heal the sick” a command to the church today? It belonged to this particular mission, whose signs confirmed the arrival of the kingdom in Jesus. Many Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, hold that such healing gifts continue, and they should be heard charitably; this commentary takes the view called cessationism, the more likely reading in its judgment, that the sign gifts belonged to that foundational time, when Christ and his apostles were establishing the word (Hebrews 2:3–4). But God still heals. The church still prays for the sick, the elders anointing and praying in faith (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, through medicine and sometimes beyond it. And the heart of the command, the message that the kingdom has come near, goes on until he returns.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go into its streets. He does not tell them to leave quietly but to go out into the public street and make an announcement, the last thing a rejected messenger would naturally want to do.

Even the dust. The gesture is the one the Twelve were given (9:5): the dust a devout Jew shook off at the border on returning from pagan ground. Performed in an Israelite street, it says something grave: that this town has put itself outside, and the line no longer runs where they think it does.

Nevertheless know this. This is almost word for word what they were told to say to the towns that received them (v. 9); the only real difference is the nevertheless. So the last thing a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated, a final warning that is still an invitation. The kingdom came as near to that town as to the village that took the messengers in, and nearness is not the same as reception.

More bearable for Sodom. Sodom is the Bible’s byword for a place beyond saving (Genesis 19), and a Galilean village that declined two travelling preachers will fare worse. Not because hospitality outranks Sodom’s sins, but because Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near, and nobody healed her sick in the market square. These towns had it, in daylight, and preferred not to.

The Judge who held back the fire. The one who speaks of Sodom here was himself refused by a Samaritan village a few verses earlier, and when James and John asked whether they should call fire down on it, he rebuked them (9:52–55). He is not soft on judgment; he claims to know what the last day will hold for every town in Galilee. But he will not bring that day early. He sends the offer instead, because the Judge of that day is first on his way to Jerusalem.

Degrees of judgment. “On that day” is the day of judgment, and its verdict is weighed: there are degrees of punishment according to privilege and knowledge (12:47–48; Matthew 11:22–24; Romans 2:12). Every sentence is just, and sentences differ, because the Judge knows exactly what each person was given.

Is it right for Christians to walk away from people who reject the gospel? The gesture was a solemn act by commissioned messengers on a short, urgent mission, not a licence to write people off. We still warn plainly, and we may move on from those who will not hear when there are others waiting (Acts 13:51; 18:6). But we do not stop praying, and we leave the door open, because Paul himself had once been on the rejecting side. With friends and family, keep loving, keep living the gospel, and speak again when God gives an opening. Judgment belongs to God, not to our frustration.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin! These are among the most severe words in Luke’s Gospel, and they fall not on Rome or the Sanhedrin but on three small towns at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, where he had lived and where most of his ministry so far had happened.

The town with no recorded miracle. Chorazin appears in the New Testament only here and in Matthew 11:21, and not one miracle done there is recorded. Yet Jesus speaks of the mighty works done in you as though everyone knew (John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles that no evangelist thought to write down.

Tyre and Sidon. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy pagan ports, denounced by the prophets for pride and cruelty (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28); a Galilean would have filed them under hopeless. Sackcloth and ashes were the marks of repentance, as when the king of Nineveh came down from his throne (Jonah 3:6). And Jesus says they would have repented, long ago: he knows what people would have done under circumstances they were never given.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. Capernaum was his base, the town he moved to after Nazareth threw him out (4:31), where he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and emptied a street of its sick in one evening. The most privileged town of all. And the language he uses about it is borrowed. It is the taunt Isaiah aimed at the king of Babylon, who said in his heart I will ascend to heaven and was told you are brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:13–15). The most privileged village in Galilee is addressed in the words written for the archetype of proud rebellion. Hades is the Greek name for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead; here it is the place of judgment. Chorazin and Capernaum are ruins today, and even the site of Bethsaida is disputed.

The mighty works done in you. Everything in these woes turns on whose works they were. The miracles of Galilee were the signs Isaiah said would mark God’s own coming to save: the blind seeing, the lame leaping, the deaf hearing (Isaiah 35:4–6), the credentials Jesus pointed John the Baptist to (7:22). Chorazin and Capernaum had watched the Lord arrive in their streets and had gone on as before. The measure of judgment is nearness to Christ himself, and few towns on earth had stood nearer.

If Tyre and Sidon would have repented, why did God not send them these miracles? God gives light as he wills, and owes it to no one: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Romans 9:15–16). We are not told why he chose Galilee and not Phoenicia, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. But we are told enough to stop us accusing him. Those who received more are judged more strictly, and those who had less are judged by what they had. The towns that saw and did not repent are condemned for their own refusal, not for a decree they were trying to obey. The secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29); what is revealed is that the light came, and they would not walk in it.

In everyday life. If you have grown up hearing the gospel, ask honestly whether you have more light than you are walking in. Capernaum’s danger was not open hostility; it was a town that had seen it all and stayed exactly the same. If you ask that because you fear you have grown cold, take heart: Capernaum never asked it. Numbness in grief, illness or depression is not the hardness Jesus condemns here, and a heart that grieves over its own dullness is already being stirred by him.

For worship. These woes are spoken by the one who wept over Jerusalem (19:41), not as a judge glad to be rid of a case but as the one whose love was spurned, and he goes on toward Jerusalem to die for sinners no better than Chorazin. The Lord who weighs light so exactly gave the greatest light of all, himself, and still says to every town and every heart: come.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who hears you hears me. One sentence holds the whole doctrine of Christian mission. Follow it backwards, the direction the authority runs: the Father sends the Son, the Son sends the seventy-two, so what is done to the seventy-two is done to the Son, and to the Father. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked him: why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

The envoy. In the ancient world an authorised envoy carried the standing of the man who sent him; the rabbinic principle was that a man’s representative is as the man himself. Insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king. Jesus puts ordinary men, with no money, no bag and no spare sandals, in that position, and connects them by a direct line to the throne of heaven.

A comfort and a weight. The first is a great comfort. A believer stammering through the gospel to a colleague is not sharing a personal opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The second is a weight. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken, and the person declining is not declining you. That should stop a rejected Christian from taking it as a verdict on himself, and from being casual about what has just happened in the conversation.

The authority of preaching. When the word of God is faithfully preached, Christ himself speaks: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14–17); we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20). The preacher is not the source of the authority, but his message, if true to Scripture, carries Christ’s authority. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) puts it boldly: the preaching of the word of God is the word of God.

What it does not mean. The verse has one limit, or it becomes a tyrant. The chain runs through what the messenger says from Christ, not through everything a messenger happens to want, and it has been used to protect leaders from criticism. A sermon carries Christ’s authority exactly as far as it says what Scripture says, and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against it (Acts 17:11).

How do I tell when a preacher is speaking with Christ’s authority? Open your Bible during the sermon and ask whether the point is actually in the passage. Where it plainly is, receive it as Christ’s word to you, even if it is unwelcome and even if the preacher is not gifted. Where he adds his own views on politics, schooling or methods, weigh them as one man’s wise or unwise counsel. If he contradicts Scripture, speak to him privately, and if necessary to the elders. And do not treat a dull delivery as an excuse: the authority is in the word, not the voice.

For worship. The Father sent the Son, and the Son has never stopped sending. How kind of God, that the voice which called the worlds into being should be willing to be carried by such as us, and should count the welcome given to his smallest messenger as a welcome given to himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two come back amazed that even the demons submitted in Jesus’ name. He tells them what their tour looked like from where he stood: Satan falling like lightning. He confirms their authority and then redirects their joy from what they can do to what has been done for them: their names are written in heaven.

Then, in one of the few places Luke tells us what Jesus felt, he exults in the Holy Spirit and thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children. He claims that only he can make the Father known, and tells his disciples privately how blessed their eyes are.
verseByVerse.theology:
Father, Son and Spirit meet in one sentence at v. 21: the Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father. The joy of God overflows into the mission and into those who share it.

Verses 21–22 are among the highest claims Jesus makes in the first three Gospels: all things handed over, and a knowing of the Father that no one shares except by the Son’s choice. The wise from whom these things are hidden are not scholars as such but the self-sufficient. The dividing line is whether a man will come with empty hands.
verseByVerse.examples:
The register of names in heaven reverses everything the seventy-two were celebrating: the authority varies with the day; the name was written for good, by somebody else, where no enemy can reach. That belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by usefulness.

And verses 23–24 rebuke the boredom of long familiarity. Prophets and kings died longing to see what a Gospel shows us on any ordinary morning.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two returned with joy. Joy is one of Luke’s great themes, from the angels’ good news of great joy (2:10) to the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy after the ascension (24:52). Here it is the joy of men who have seen God at work through their own unremarkable hands.

Even the demons. The word “even” gives them away. They expected the preaching to work, and the healings they had been told to do (v. 9). They did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name. Whatever the exhilaration, they have not confused whose authority it was.

I saw Satan fall. It may look back to the primordial fall of the adversary (Isaiah 14:12 is often read this way), or forward to the cross and the final defeat (Revelation 12:9–11). Or it may describe what has just happened, and the context favours this: they came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins I saw. He is telling them what their tour looked like from where he stood. The kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of Satan (11:20–22), and the decisive blow would fall at the cross, when the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12:31) and the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15).

Like lightning. The image is exact in two ways. Lightning is sudden: not a slow retreat but a fall. And lightning comes down; whatever height the adversary held, he is not holding it.

There is no ordinary Christian work. Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers. And the Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like lightning. There is only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

If Satan is defeated, why is there still so much evil? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. The decisive battle was won at the cross, and his final end in the lake of fire is certain (Revelation 20:10). Between those two points he is like an enemy whose capital has fallen, still dangerous in retreat. He prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), and we are to resist him, firm in faith. But he cannot take back one person Christ has rescued, and every time the gospel is believed, his kingdom shrinks again. We fight from victory, not toward it.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Serpents and scorpions. The language comes from Psalm 91:13: you will tread on the lion and the adder. Serpents and scorpions are biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power, reaching back to the serpent in the garden (Genesis 3:15). The next clause explains it: the enemy is Satan, and the promise is primarily spiritual, authority over the forces of evil.

What it does not mean. Set beside the longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:18; those verses are missing from the earliest manuscripts), this verse has been made the charter of snake-handling churches, where people have died. But Jesus is describing the authority the seventy-two have just exercised over demons, not inviting anyone to pick up vipers. And Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple, and Jesus refused: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (4:9–12). To engineer a danger in order to make God prove a promise is not faith; it is what Jesus called temptation.

Nothing shall hurt you. Read as bodily immunity, the phrase is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2); Stephen was stoned; Paul was beaten and shipwrecked, though he once shook a viper into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will. Luke puts both halves in one breath: some of you they will put to death, but not a hair of your head will perish (21:16–18). The promise is that the enemy cannot finally destroy them: no power can separate them from the love of God (Romans 8:35–39).

Does every believer have this authority over the enemy? The victory over Satan is real and secured (v. 18), and every believer is protected by Christ: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4), and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). We resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word, and he flees (James 4:7). But the particular commission and signs given to the seventy-two belonged to their mission. A Christian does not need special formulas, shouted commands or rituals to be safe. And Jesus himself immediately points them away from the power to the greater thing: their names are written in heaven (v. 20).

In everyday life. If you are troubled by fear of curses, spirits or the occult, or haunted by a dark past, take your stand on Christ’s finished work, renounce any involvement plainly, and pray in his name; you do not need to perform anything.

For worship. He gives authority over serpents because he has already trodden on the serpent. In the wilderness he would not use the promise to save himself; on the cross he would not come down to save himself; and so he saved us. Nothing shall hurt you is a promise only he could make, because he let everything hurt him, and rose.

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rejoice in this. He has just confirmed the authority in the strongest terms, and he does not say the joy was wrong, only that it was aimed at the wrong thing. What they rejoiced in was real, but it is not what a person can stand on.

Why not? Because it is about what they can do. And anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance. There will be a day like the one at the foot of the mountain, where the disciples tried and nothing happened (9:40). There will be seasons when the work does not go. A joy founded on effectiveness is a joy on a schedule, and the schedule is not in your hands. Spiritual power can also feed pride, and there will be some on the last day who say, did we not cast out demons in your name?, and are told, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Power in ministry proves nothing about the heart.

Your names are written in heaven. The perfect tense: they have been written and remain written. The image is a citizen register, the roll of a city listing those who belong to it: the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12). And every feature of it is the reverse of what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent and is not being reviewed. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else. And it is written in heaven, the one place no enemy can reach.

Election. Election is God’s choosing of particular people for himself, an act of love whose reason lies in him, not in them. The names were written early, before the foundation of the world (Revelation 17:8; Ephesians 1:4). Joy rests on grace, not on performance.

Who can read the register? Only someone who has seen it. A few sentences earlier Jesus said I saw Satan fall from heaven (v. 18); now he speaks of what is written in heaven as a man speaks of a room he has lived in. No prophet ever told anyone that his name was entered there. The Son can say it, because he came from the Father and knows the Father’s book, and because he is about to go up to Jerusalem to make the writing good. The seventy-two hear their eternal standing from the lips of the one on whom it rests.

For those who measure themselves by usefulness. This verse belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness: the minister whose sense of standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation, the parent who reads his children’s faith as a report card on his own, the Christian who has been ill for two years and quietly suspects he has become surplus. The thing worth rejoicing in was never the doing. It is a name, already written, in a book they cannot reach and cannot lose.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking at the Christ he has offered to you. The same Lord who told the seventy-two their names were written goes on, a few verses later, to reveal the Father to anyone he chooses (v. 22). Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ alone, your trust is itself the sign of the writing, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The fruit of the Spirit, love for other believers, and a growing hatred of sin confirm it (1 John 3:14). And if you are unsure, do not stare inward: come to him now. Nobody who comes is found missing from the roll.

For worship. Before the seventy-two were born, before the mountains were brought forth, a hand wrote their names, and the names stand in the book of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8), written in his blood and kept by his life. No failure on earth reaches that page, and the God who wrote it does not erase.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Luke stops to tell us what Jesus was feeling, which he seldom does. The verb is ēgalliasato: not quiet contentment but exultation, the verb of Mary’s song, my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour (1:47). And it happens in the Holy Spirit; only Luke mentions the Spirit here. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father: three persons, one delight. And the occasion for it is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

Lord of heaven and earth. Intimacy and sovereignty together. Father is the word of a son at home; Lord of heaven and earth is the title of the King of all things. Jesus holds both in one breath, and teaches us to do the same.

Hidden and revealed. He thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and that has to be faced rather than smoothed. These things are what the seventy-two had just seen: Satan falling, the kingdom arriving, and the identity of the one in whose name it happened. The wise here are the professionally religious, men with the texts, the training and the standing, who have watched all of it and concluded he is a problem. The little children (nēpioi, infants) are fishermen and farmers who could not have argued a point of law. Learning simply supplies one more thing to hold onto, and pride blinds (1 Corinthians 1:18–31).

Your gracious will. “Gracious will” (eudokia) is good pleasure, the word of the angels’ song of peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). Jesus does not merely accept the Father’s arrangement; he is delighted by it. The Lord of heaven and earth owes his light to no one, and the Son bows before that freedom with joy, not with questions.

All things have been handed over. Scholars have long called this passage the Johannine thunderbolt, because it sounds exactly like the fourth Gospel. All things: not some authority in a defined area, but everything, handed over.

No one knows who the Son is. Then a mutual knowing that admits no third party: the Father knows the Son; the Son knows the Father; nobody else knows either except by the Son’s choosing.
