Only God can know God fully. That is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others. It is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door that only he can open.

Anyone to whom the Son chooses. Knowing God is a gift of sovereign grace (John 6:44; 14:6; 17:6). And he opens the door. That is the last clause, and it is why this prayer is joy rather than terror.

Does God, then, choose who will understand? Jesus says so plainly: the Father has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, for such was his gracious will, and the Son reveals the Father to anyone he chooses. The Reformed reading takes these words at face value: understanding is God’s gift, and no one can boast of having worked it out. Christians in the Arminian tradition (named after the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius) read them differently, holding that God’s choosing follows his foreknowledge of who will believe, and they love these words too; but the plainest sense lays the reason in the Father’s gracious will. Yet those who reject Jesus are responsible for it (vv. 13–16), and the invitation is to all: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28), which in Matthew follows these very words. Both are true. If you want to know God, that desire is already the Son at work, so come.

Can people of other religions know God without Christ? They may know that God exists, for creation declares his power (Romans 1:20), and their consciences bear witness. But they do not know him as Father, and they cannot be saved by that knowledge. The saving knowledge of God comes only through the Son: no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). That is not narrowness for its own sake. It is the shape of reality, and it is why the church must go and tell, because the Son is willing to reveal the Father to anyone, from any nation, who comes to him.

For worship. Beneath the noise of the world there is a joy that has never stopped: the Father delighting in the Son, the Son exulting in the Father, the Spirit filling the Son with gladness. For one hour on a Galilean road that joy broke the surface. The Lord of heaven and earth did not need us to complete his happiness. He opened the door anyway, and the gladness of God himself is the house we are brought into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are the eyes! Not blessed are you for being perceptive, but blessed are the eyes, for what happens to be in front of them. The blessing is entirely a matter of where they stand in history, and they did nothing to arrange it.

Many prophets and kings. Put names to that. Abraham, promised that all nations would be blessed through his offspring, died with one son of the promise and a burial plot, yet rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56). David, promised a son whose throne would stand for ever, went to his grave a thousand years before the child was born. Daniel saw one like a son of man receive an everlasting kingdom, and was told to seal the book. They all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). And a group of Galilean labourers had been eating with him.

The boredom of proximity. There is a boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time: the sense that the gospel is a known quantity and the Bible a familiar book. It is not usually unbelief, only the effect of proximity on the extraordinary. Yet we have what even the disciples lacked before the cross: the finished account of the death and the rising, the whole of the Scriptures, and the Spirit given. Daniel was told to seal up his book; ours lies open on the kitchen table.

My eyes have seen your salvation. Luke has already shown us one man at the end of that long line of longing who was allowed to see. Old Simeon took the infant in his arms and said that now he could depart in peace, because his eyes had seen God’s salvation (2:29–30). Salvation was a child he could hold. That is what the blessed eyes of the disciples are looking at: not an experience or a doctrine, but a Person. Everything the prophets and kings strained toward has a face, and it is turned toward these men as he speaks.

Were the Old Testament believers worse off in salvation? No. They were saved by the same Christ, through faith in the promise, as we are through faith in the fulfilment (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). Abraham was justified exactly as a believer is today. What they lacked was not salvation but sight: they saw the dawn from a long way off, and we stand in the morning. Our advantage is in clarity and fullness, which is why it is ours to be more grateful, not more proud.

In the flow. In the very next verse one of the wise and understanding stands up, a lawyer who knows the Scriptures and still asks how to earn life (v. 25), and the prayer of verse 21 comes true in front of the reader.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer stands up to test Jesus with the greatest question there is, how to inherit eternal life, and answers it himself from the law: love God with all you are, and your neighbour as yourself. Jesus agrees that whoever does this will live. The lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asks for the edges of the word neighbour.

Jesus answers with a story. A man lies stripped and half dead on the Jericho road; a priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan, the man the lawyer would least want to admire, stops and pays the cost of saving him. Then Jesus turns the question around: not who is my neighbour, but who proved to be one. The command at the end is not lowered by an inch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus uses the law here as it was meant to be used: not as a ladder to life but as a mirror (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Anyone who kept these two commands perfectly would live, and no one has, apart from the man telling the story. His perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him, and the law then becomes the shape of a grateful life rather than the price of acceptance.

The priest and the Levite are offered no excuse. They were going down, away from the temple, with their duty behind them, and the law they knew commanded help even for an enemy’s fallen animal (Exodus 23:4–5). Its main meaning is Jesus’ own application, go and do likewise, though it also shows the mercy of Christ, who came to us when we were his enemies.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Samaritan’s care is costly and specific: his own bandages, oil, wine and animal, a night of nursing, two days’ wages, and an open promise to pay the rest. Go and do likewise means that kind of schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening mercy, not a feeling or a good intention.

Read honestly, that is unbearable, and that is why it matters who tells the story: the command is addressed to people who have already been lifted out of a ditch (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lawyer stood up. A lawyer here is not an advocate in a court but an expert in the law of Moses, a scribe, whose whole training was in what God had said and what it required. And Luke tells us his motive before he opens his mouth: this is not an enquiry but an examination, in public, of a Galilean teacher with no formal qualifications. He stands, a respectful posture; the purpose is not respectful.

Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? The question is enormous, the most important question there is, and the rich ruler will ask it in the same words (18:18). But the wording gives the man away. What shall I do? The assumption is already in place before the answer arrives: eternal life is a thing achieved by an action, and what he wants is the specification. And there is a second thing buried in it that only shows up on a second reading. He asks what he must do to inherit. An inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes by belonging to a family, and the beneficiary contributes nothing but a relationship. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence and not noticed.

What is written in the Law? How do you read it? Jesus does not answer. He asks two questions back, and both are respectful: this man knows the law, and he is being invited to say so. But the second question is doing something the first is not. What is written asks for the text. How do you read it asks for the man. Two people in a disagreement about Scripture usually have the same words in front of them. What differs is the reading, and a reading is never neutral. It is done by a person, with a history and a set of interests, who wants some things to be true and others not to be. So Jesus has, in a handful of words, moved the examination. The lawyer came to test him on the content of the law. He is about to be tested on what he has been doing with it.

Beginning with Moses. Luke ends his Gospel with the same Teacher on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreting the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures (24:27). The lawyer is about to read Moses accurately and still miss the one standing in front of him, the only man who would ever do what Moses commands. A reading of the law can be correct in every word and still be wrong at the centre.

In the flow. The lawyer’s answer in verse 27 sets out the plan of the rest of the chapter. Love your neighbour is shown on the Jericho road (vv. 30–37); love the Lord your God is shown at Jesus’ feet in Bethany (vv. 38–42). In both, the one who gets it right is the one nobody expected: a Samaritan, and a woman sitting in a student’s place.

What does eternal life mean here? Not simply living for ever, which in one sense everyone will do, in joy or in judgment. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, the life of God’s kingdom, beginning now and completed at the resurrection. Jesus defines it elsewhere: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). So the lawyer is really asking how to belong to God for ever, and the answer will turn out to be a Person, not a performance.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall love the Lord your God. He puts together Deuteronomy 6:5, from the Shema, which every Jew recited daily, and Leviticus 19:18, a single line in a chapter of miscellaneous statutes, and welds them into one command, as Jesus himself did (Mark 12:29–31). He has read the law and seen its spine. And the four terms are not separate compartments but a way of saying all of you, with nothing held back: the affections, the life, the effort, the thinking.

Do this, and you will live. An echo of Leviticus 18:5: if a person does them, he shall live by them. Is Jesus really telling a man he can earn eternal life by keeping the law? Take the sentence at face value and it is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer. It is in the doer, and no such doer has ever lived, apart from the man saying it.

Law and gospel. So Jesus uses the law as it was meant to be used: not as a way to earn life but as a mirror, to convict of sin. Through the law comes knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20); the law was our guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). Its work is to bring a man to the end of himself so that he will look elsewhere. The perfect law demands perfect love because God is holy (Leviticus 19:2). Only one man ever kept it, Jesus, and his perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). God treats those who trust Christ as though Christ’s record were their own, and lays their sin on him (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Watch how well it works. Jesus says do this and you will live, and the lawyer does not say amen and go home. The very next thing he does is start negotiating the terms, desiring to justify himself (v. 29). He has been handed a standard that leaves him nowhere to stand, and rather than fall, he reaches for a definition small enough to survive on. The parable that follows takes his last handhold away.

If no one can keep the law, why should Christians still try to obey it? Because the law that could never save us now describes the life Christ has saved us into. Once we are justified by faith, the same commands become the shape of gratitude, and the Spirit writes them on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). We obey not to be accepted but because we are accepted, and our obedience, though imperfect, is pleasing to the Father for Christ’s sake. The law still shows us our sin daily and sends us back to Christ; and it still shows us the path of love. A Christian does not throw away the map because he has stopped trying to earn the journey.

In everyday life. Because Christ kept these two commands for you, you can afford to measure yourself honestly against them rather than against other people. Have you loved God with all your heart today, or with a corner of it? Where you have not, do not reach for a smaller definition; go back to the one who kept them, and ask him for grace to love a little more today.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor? Luke gives the motive again, and this time the whole chapter turns on it. To justify is to declare someone in the right, as a judge does at the end of a case. Desiring to justify himself: wanting to pronounce that verdict over himself, to come out of this conversation still standing, still right, still able to say that he had done what was required. Self-justification is the instinct of the human heart: to define God’s law in a way we can keep. Jesus will later say to the Pharisees, you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts (16:15). The question that produces one of the world’s best-known stories is asked by a man looking for somewhere to hide.

A clever question. On the surface it sounds like precision, a careful scholar wanting to know the scope of a term. But run it out. If neighbour can be defined, it has edges; if it has edges, there are people outside them; and a man can love everyone inside the line and walk past the rest with a clear conscience. Not whom should I love? but whom am I permitted not to?

A live question. Teachers discussing Leviticus 19:18 leaned on its phrase, the sons of your own people, so neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite; the sect at Qumran made it a rule to love the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness. The instinct presents itself not as wickedness but as realism: nobody can help everybody, so a line has to be drawn. Jesus is about to tell a story in which the line the lawyer most wanted, the racial and religious one, is crossed by the man he least wanted to admire.

The one who could have justified him. Luke uses the same word again a few chapters on. A tax collector who could only beat his breast and ask for mercy went home justified, and the Pharisee who listed his record did not (18:9–14). The lawyer is trying to do for himself the one thing that can only be done for him, and he is trying it in the presence of the one person who can do it. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem to become the righteousness that sinners cannot produce. The man looking for a smaller law is standing beside the Lord who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable of the good Samaritan. Only Luke records it, and it is one of the best-known stories in the world. That familiarity is its danger: a story so famous that its name has become a word for kindness has lost, for most readers, the shock it was built to deliver.

Going down to Jericho. Note what we are not told: no name, no trade, no nationality, no religion. The lawyer asked for a category, and the first thing the story refuses him is a category. The road was notorious: some seventeen miles (27 km), dropping over three thousand feet (900 m) from Jerusalem to Jericho through limestone gorges and blind bends. Jerome, living nearby centuries later, says it was still called the red or bloody ascent.

Stripped and half dead. The details remove the only two things a passer-by could have used to identify him. Clothing told you a man’s nationality and status; speech told you the rest. Naked and silent, he is unclassifiable. He is a human being in a ditch, and there is no way to work out whether he is one of ours.

By chance a priest. Why? Perhaps fear of the robbers; perhaps ritual purity, since contact with a corpse made a priest unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13); perhaps simple indifference. Jesus gives no reasons; excuses do not matter. But he was going down, away from Jerusalem, toward Jericho, where many priests are said to have lived between their weeks of service. His duty was behind him. And the law he was protecting commands a man to help even his enemy’s fallen animal (Exodus 23:4–5).

So likewise a Levite. Levites assisted the priests in the temple: religious, respectable, knowledgeable about the law. Luke adds a phrase for the second man: he came to the place. He got closer. He looked, from nearer, and crossed anyway.

The shape of the story. Stories like this often ran in threes, and after a priest and a Levite the natural third man was an ordinary Israelite: the temple establishment fails and the common man does right. What arrives instead breaks the pattern.

The same road, later. On his last journey Jesus passes through Jericho and climbs this very road toward Jerusalem (18:35–19:28). A blind beggar shouts from the roadside and the crowd tells him to be quiet; Jesus stops and gives him his sight (18:35–43). In Jericho he stops under a tree for a man the whole town had written off (19:1–10). The one telling this story does not pass by on the other side. He stops for the man at the edge of the road, on his way up to die.

Is it always wrong to pass by someone in need? Not every passing by is sin. There are real dangers, prior duties and needs you cannot meet, and sometimes the loving thing is to call for help rather than to stop yourself. A woman alone at night is not commanded to pull over on a dark road. But the priest and Levite had no such reasons that Jesus thought worth mentioning; they simply did not want the cost. The test is honest: am I unable, or merely unwilling? Has God put this person in my path, and is there something I can actually do? If so, the ditch is my business.

In everyday life. Who have you passed by on the other side? The colleague whose marriage is falling apart, the neighbour whose bins have not moved in a week, the widow at church who sits alone. A busy schedule of good things can make a very convenient other side of the road; but the Lord who stopped for a blind beggar on his way to die did not pass you by, and he can make room in your week for them.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a Samaritan. The hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. Samaritans descended from the remnant of the northern kingdom mixed with settlers brought in after the Assyrian conquest; they had their own holy mountain, Gerizim, where their temple had stood until a Jewish army destroyed it, and Jews regarded them as heretics and half-breeds. Within living memory, Josephus says, Samaritans had scattered human bones in the temple courts at Passover. Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and only a chapter earlier a Samaritan village had refused Jesus a bed (9:52–54). This is the man Jesus makes the hero.

He had compassion. All three saw. Only one had compassion. The verb is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs: compassion felt physically. Luke uses it of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and here. The priest and Levite saw and crossed over; he saw and was moved and went to him. The difference is not in the seeing but in what the seeing was allowed to do.

Oil and wine. Jesus itemises the care: bandages from whatever cloth he had, since there is nothing else on that road, and oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, wine to cleanse and oil to soothe, both of them his own travelling supplies, now gone. There may be a quiet irony here: oil and wine were also offerings in the temple the priest had just left. The Samaritan poured them out in the true worship, for I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

On his own animal. So the Samaritan walked, at the pace of an injured man, in robber country, for however many miles remained; and the care at the inn was a night spent nursing a stranger.

Two denarii. In the morning: two denarii, two days’ wages for a labourer, enough to cover board for perhaps a fortnight. Then comes the promise that goes furthest of all, to repay whatever more is spent. Without payment, a penniless guest might have been held as a debtor. He has just written a blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despises him, and bound himself to return.

Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan? From the early church onward (Origen, Augustine), many read the parable as an allegory of salvation: the man is Adam, the robbers are the devil, the priest and Levite are the law and the prophets, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the church, the two denarii the two commandments of love, and the return is the second coming. This commentary’s view: the parable’s primary meaning, given by Jesus himself, is ethical: go and do likewise (v. 37). It answers the lawyer’s question, who is my neighbour?, and reading every detail as a code goes beyond the text. Yet there is a true echo: Christ is the supreme neighbour, who came to us when we were his enemies, half dead in our sins, and gave himself to save us (Romans 5:8–10). The parable both commands love and points to the love that makes it possible, and every Christian’s mercy flows from his.

What if helping someone could be dangerous or be taken advantage of? The Samaritan took a real risk, and love sometimes will. But wisdom is not the enemy of love. He did not hand the man his purse; he paid the innkeeper and arranged care, which is both generous and sensible. You may help through the right channels, involve others, set limits that protect your family, and decline to fund what would harm someone. What love may not do is use prudence as a disguise for indifference. Ask: what would genuinely help this person, and what part of that can I carry?

For worship. The despised Samaritan is the clearest picture in the Gospels of the despised Saviour, despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3), whom they called a Samaritan (John 8:48). Every act of mercy we do is a faint echo of the mercy that found us on the road.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage — two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers? The question has been turned inside out, and that is the parable’s most important move. The lawyer asked, who is my neighbour?, which puts the other person under examination and the questioner safely in the chair. Jesus asks which of the three proved to be a neighbour, which puts the questioner in the road and asks what he did. It is no longer a question about the boundaries of obligation. It is a question about what kind of man is walking past. Neighbourliness is not defined by the other person’s status, but by my compassion.

The one who showed him mercy. He seems unable to say it. The answer is a single word, the Samaritan, and he uses a whole phrase instead. Luke leaves it exposed without comment: a man who has understood the story perfectly and cannot get the word out of his mouth.

You go, and do likewise. And there the parable stops, which is unbearable if you have been reading honestly. Go and be the Samaritan: cross a racial hatred, spend your own money, take on an open-ended liability for a stranger who can never repay you. Anyone who finds that manageable has not understood it. Anyone who has understood it is standing where the lawyer is standing, looking for somewhere to put his feet.

Who is telling the story. Now it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road than the one from Jerusalem to Jericho, to where we were lying, when we were stripped and half dead and in no condition to ask. He bound up the wounds at his own expense. He paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. And he is on the road to Jerusalem as he speaks, to settle the account himself.

Does this mean I must help everyone in need? The parable defines a neighbour as the one who shows mercy to the person in front of him, whoever he is. It does not tell us how to meet every need in the world, nor is it a programme for the state. You cannot help everyone, and God does not ask you to. But it forbids us to decide that someone in real need, whom God has put in our path, is not our concern because of who he is. Begin with the household of faith and those nearest you (Galatians 6:10), and let your circle of mercy keep widening.

Can’t anyone be a good Samaritan without Jesus? Many people who do not believe show striking kindness, and Christians should honour it gladly: it is God’s common goodness at work in his world. But remember the question the parable answers. The lawyer asked what he must do to inherit eternal life, and the standard Jesus sets is mercy without limit, to anyone, every time, from the heart. Nobody, believer or not, has kept that. So the parable does not divide the kind from the unkind. It shows everyone that they need a Neighbour who kept it for them, and a new heart that begins to love like him (Ezekiel 36:26).

Mercy received, then mercy passed on. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy. It is mercy received, and then mercy passed on: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Go and do likewise remains binding. But it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch, and that is why it is good news and not a sentence.

For worship. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the name of the one who showed mercy. God has said it for ever. To his Son, who humbled himself to the point of death on a cross for people who had despised him, he has given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:8–10). The word that stuck in the lawyer’s throat will be on every tongue in heaven, and it will be a name of mercy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a village house (John names it Bethany). Martha, the head of the household, welcomes Jesus and his company and sets about the work of feeding them. Her sister Mary takes a disciple’s place at his feet, a place not normally open to a woman, and listens.

Martha’s good service has become a grievance, and she accuses her sister and finally Jesus of not caring. He answers her tenderly and without lowering the truth: she is anxious about many things, one thing is necessary, and Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken from her.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus does not send Mary back to the kitchen; he defends her right to receive what he is giving, and so welcomes women as full disciples.

The good portion lasts. The dinner is eaten by nightfall; the word Mary takes in is the living and abiding word of God (1 Peter 1:23). What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene does not abolish the tension between doing and receiving; it orders it. Martha’s work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

Many who serve have prayed her prayer, do you not care?, and Jesus does not rebuke the tone; he answers what is underneath it. The cure is not less service but the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The placing. After the parable about doing comes a story about listening: loving neighbour by serving, loving God by hearing his word. Martha and Mary show the balance, and the order.

A village. Luke does not name it. John does: Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1; 12:1–3).

Martha welcomed him. It is her house; Luke says so, which is unusual enough to notice. In a culture where hospitality was a sacred obligation, a travelling teacher with and his disciples, perhaps thirteen or more people, meant a great deal of work, and Martha opened her door to the lot of them. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary sat and listened. Sat at the feet is the posture of a disciple under a rabbi; Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). Women were taught the law as it applied to their duties, and the formal relationship of teacher and student was a male arrangement. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and within minutes he will defend her right to be there. And she listened: the tense means she kept on listening.

At the Lord’s feet. Luke keeps bringing people to this place: a sinful woman weeping (7:38), the freed demoniac clothed and in his right mind (8:35), Jairus (8:41), a healed Samaritan giving thanks (17:16). Mary sits where the forgiven, the rescued and the grateful sit. We know of no rabbi who said that listening to him was the one thing necessary. This Teacher will say it within the hour (v. 42), and only the Lord could say it truly.

Does Mary’s place at Jesus’ feet mean women may hold every office in the church? It means women are full disciples: called to learn, to know the Scriptures deeply and to sit under Christ’s word as fully as any man, which was a revolution in its day. That is the point Luke is making. The question of who may serve as an elder or preach to the gathered church is answered elsewhere, where the New Testament reserves that office to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). This commentary holds that complementarian view (men and women equal in worth, with some roles given differently), because Paul grounds it in creation rather than in local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), and it understands headship as self-giving service, never domination. Many faithful Christians read those passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and they deserve to be heard with respect. Mary’s example rebukes any church that keeps women from learning deeply. It does not settle the eldership question either way.

In everyday life. If you are a woman who has been told, in so many words, that deep study of Scripture is not really for you, know that Jesus defended your seat.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Distracted with much serving. The verb is periespato: pulled away, dragged in different directions; less busy than torn. And what tears her is much serving, diakonia, the word that will become the church’s term for ministry. Her service was good, and necessary. The problem is not that Martha chose work over devotion but what the work has become inside her: it pulled her away from Jesus.

Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? She went up to him and said it, and added: tell her then to help me. Three things in one sentence, each a step further than the last. She interrupts his teaching. She accuses her sister in front of the guests. And, this is the sharp one, she accuses him. Do you not care? That is not a request. It is a charge, and it is levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed into her house. They are almost the words the disciples threw at him in the storm: teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). Anxiety turns into resentment, against others and against God. She has moved from serving him to reproaching him, and the distance between those two things was crossed in an afternoon, in a kitchen, doing a good thing. Then tell her: she does not even ask him to intervene. She tells him what to say. Busy, worried people often judge others who are not as busy.

Not hard on her. It would be easy to be hard on her, and a mistake. Every word of her complaint is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance, and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score. Service can quietly become a way of earning a place, a bid for thanks or for proof that we matter, and then everyone not helping feels like a threat to it. Do you not care? is what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

Is it wrong to complain to God? Not to bring him your distress: the psalms are full of honest lament, how long, O LORD?, and he invites us to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). What Martha shows is the moment honest weariness hardens into accusation, when do you not care is said as a verdict rather than a cry. The cure is to tell him the truth about how you feel, and then to let him tell you the truth about himself. He does care. That is precisely why he will not simply give Martha what she asks.

The guest who serves. Martha thinks the serving in this house runs one way, from her kitchen to his table. At the last supper Jesus will say, I am among you as the one who serves (22:27), and he promises that at his return the master will dress himself for service and wait on his servants at table (12:37). When this Lord comes into a house, he has come chiefly to give, and the first duty of his hosts is to receive.

In everyday life. Busyness has a way of turning into resentment: the sigh as you clear up after the church lunch, the mental list of who never helps. Those are signals, not proofs that you are wrong to serve. Stop, sit down for five minutes with him, and let him take the score card out of your hand.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha, Martha. The doubled name is not impatience. Luke records it at other moments: Simon, Simon (22:31); O Jerusalem, Jerusalem (13:34); Saul, Saul (Acts 9:4). It is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person and is about to say something she needs and will not enjoy. A gentle rebuke, from love.

Anxious and troubled. Two verbs, and neither is busy. Anxious is merimnas, the worry Jesus forbids in 12:22–26 and the root of the cares that choke the word (8:14). Troubled (thorybazē) means agitated, in an uproar. He is diagnosing not her workload but a heart not resting in God.

One thing is necessary. If your Bible has a footnote here, some manuscripts read few things are necessary, or only one; the shorter reading is very likely original, and the sense is unaffected. Not just one dish, but the one thing that matters most: listening to Jesus. David knew it: one thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD (Psalm 27:4). David’s one thing was the LORD himself. Here it is to sit at Jesus’ feet, and he says it without apology, standing where the LORD stands in the psalm.

The good portion. Portion (meris) is a share, used of a helping at table (Genesis 43:34) and of the LORD as his people’s inheritance (Psalm 16:5): Martha is in the kitchen dividing up portions, and Mary has taken the one that matters. And “will not be taken away” is a promise. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall; the word Mary is taking in is permanent.

What it does not mean. This is not a rebuke of practical service; Luke has just praised a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills. Nor is it a recommendation of the monastery over the kitchen. It is a statement about order. Listening to Jesus comes first, and is the source of true service; service without listening becomes anxious and resentful.

With young children, a job and an elderly parent, how can I possibly sit at his feet? The good portion is not measured in hours, and Jesus is not asking a mother of three to keep a monk’s timetable. It is a matter of where your heart rests. Take what you can: ten minutes with a Psalm before the house wakes, a passage read aloud at breakfast, a sermon listened to while you drive, a prayer while you wash up. Guard the Lord’s Day as a time to receive. And let the busy hours themselves be done at his feet, in the sense of being done for him and in dependence on him. Little and real is better than much and anxious.

For worship. The good portion is a Person, and nothing can take him away. The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him (Lamentations 3:24). Meals are eaten and forgotten, but the Lord himself is the inheritance of everyone who sits at his feet, and Mary’s portion is the same one offered to us.

parallels.desc: one thing have I asked of the LORD
the LORD is my chosen portion

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 moves from prayer to conflict. It opens with a disciple’s request to be taught to pray, and Jesus gives the Lord’s Prayer, the parable of the friend at midnight and the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask (vv. 1–13). Then, accused of casting out demons by Beelzebul, he shows that the kingdom of God has arrived, warns that there is no neutral ground, and offers a sign-seeking generation only the sign of Jonah (vv. 14–36). It closes at a Pharisee’s table with six woes against religion that keeps the outside clean and leaves the heart full of greed (vv. 37–54).

The order is not random. Prayer is life with the Father; the conflict shows his kingdom at work in Jesus; and the woes show what religion becomes when the form remains and the Father is not known.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus has been praying, and a disciple asks him to teach them to pray, as John taught his disciples. He gives them a prayer: one word of address, Father, and five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God comes first, then us.

Luke’s form is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13); scribes who prayed Matthew’s form every week filled Luke out to match it, which is why older Bibles print the fuller wording. Nothing was lost, and two forms show that Jesus gave the prayer as a shape for praying, not a formula that only counts when recited syllable-perfect.
verseByVerse.theology:
Father is the revolution in this prayer. Jesus gives his disciples his own word, and with it not a warmer name for the same relationship but the Son’s own relationship, opened to people with no natural claim to it (Romans 8:15).

The first two petitions put God’s honour and God’s reign before every need, and they cannot be prayed at a distance: to ask for his kingdom is to ask for one’s own to end. The request for bread is deliberately small: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The word for in the forgiveness petition must not become a bargain: our forgiving is the evidence that his has landed, and a standing policy, not something done once years ago (Matthew 6:14–15).

And lead us not into temptation is not a fear that God might make us sin (James 1:13). It is the prayer of someone who knows his weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 11 is a chapter about the God who hears and the people who will not: prayer to the Father, a kingdom that has arrived with no neutral ground before it, and religion that cleans the outside and leaves the heart full of greed. The thread through it all is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him as Father.

Jesus was praying. The order matters: he prays, they watch, and then one of them asks. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel: at the baptism (3:21), all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), on the mountain where his face changed (9:28–29). Something about the way this man prayed was different enough that men who had grown up saying prayers several times a day concluded they did not know how.

Lord, teach us to pray. They had watched him still a storm, feed thousands and raise the dead, yet what Luke records a disciple asking to be taught was how to talk to his Father. Prayer must be learned; it does not come naturally to sinners, and the best teacher is the one who prays perfectly.

As John taught his disciples. Teachers and movements had characteristic prayers that marked out what a group was for. Jesus’ disciples want the same from him: a prayer that belongs to them, that expresses who they are as his.

Why does prayer feel so hard? Almost every Christian who has been at it for a while will admit, if pressed honestly, that prayer is the part that never quite settles. It is the first thing to go in a busy week and the last thing to come back. Part of the reason is that prayer is the one Christian activity with no audience and no visible result in the moment; part is that our flesh resists dependence; and part is that the enemy hates it. The answer is not a technique, and it is not more determination. It is what the disciple did here: to say out loud, to the one person who can do anything about it, that he does not know how. Then to start small and keep going, using the words Jesus gives.

For worship. The Son of God, who had the Father’s presence every moment, still went away to pray. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (22:32), and he lives now to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). The one who taught us to pray is praying still, and our stumbling words reach the Father on the strength of his.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s Prayer. Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13), with five petitions to Matthew’s seven; Jesus probably taught it more than once. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, fill Luke’s version out to match Matthew’s; the earliest do not. It is both a prayer to pray and a pattern for all prayer, with God’s concerns first, then ours.

Is this prayer a form to recite or a pattern to follow? Both. Luke says when you pray, say, and Matthew pray then like this (Matthew 6:9). Christians may pray these words together, as the church has done from the beginning, as long as they are prayed from the heart and not as empty repetition (Matthew 6:7). And they shape all our other prayers: praise before petition, God’s glory before our needs, forgiveness alongside bread. A believer who prays only these words has prayed well; a believer who never prays them has missed a gift.

Father. One word, and it was a revolution: simply Father, without our or in heaven. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16); an individual Israelite almost never addresses him so in prayer. Behind Luke’s Greek very probably stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). It is not baby-talk; grown men used it of their fathers. But it is family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of the period prayed to God with it. He hands it to them as the first word.

The Son’s own word, opened to us. Paul says what has happened: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15). Adoption is God taking into his family people who were not his children by nature, and giving them everything a son has: his name, free access to the Father, and a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7). You do not come to God as a servant hoping to be noticed, but as a child who belongs at the table.

What if my earthly father was absent or cruel? Then the word may at first bring pain rather than comfort, and you are not wrong to feel that. But Jesus is not asking you to picture God as your father was. He is showing you what fatherhood was always meant to be, and what your father failed to be. God is the Father from whom every family is named (Ephesians 3:14–15): faithful, patient, never abusive, never absent. Many believers with wounded histories have found that learning to say Father to God slowly heals what an earthly father broke. Begin by reading how Jesus speaks of him, and let that, not your memory, fill the word.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” (hagiasthētō) means treated as holy, honoured. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known: God’s name is God himself as he has revealed himself. Since it cannot be made more holy than it is, the petition asks that he be treated as holy, known and reverenced as what he actually is, first by the one praying and then by everybody else (Ezekiel 36:23). The prayer opens by asking that God’s reputation be honoured in a world that has trampled it, and the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer.

Your kingdom come. The central petition, and the shortest. God’s reign, which has come in Jesus (11:20), is still to come in fullness (22:18). It was the prayer of the early church: Maranatha, our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22). And it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God’s rule to come is to ask for one’s own to end. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

For worship. The God whose name the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy has let us call him Father. It cost the Son everything to open that word to us, and Luke lets us hear him keep hold of it to the end: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). He held on to the word through the darkness of bearing our sin, so that rebels might be brought to the Father’s table and say it after him.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our daily bread. Now the prayer turns to us: bread, forgiveness and protection; body, past and future. The word behind daily is epiousios, so rare that Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it; it may mean for today, or necessary, or for the coming day. The point is daily dependence on God, as Israel gathered manna day by day (Exodus 16:4): enough for today, asked for today, and again tomorrow (Proverbs 30:8).

A daily appointment. Anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all has asked for something this prayer will not give. Manna rotted overnight if it was hoarded (Exodus 16:19–20), not as a punishment but as a daily appointment. “Each day” is only in Luke. And the words are us and our: we pray for others’ bread as well as our own.

Should Christians save and plan, if we pray for daily bread? Yes. Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine; the ant prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8); Paul tells believers to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8). This petition does not forbid savings, insurance or a pension. It forbids trusting them. The man with a full barn still prays for daily bread, because the barn, the health to use it, and the next breath are all from God (12:16–21). Plan wisely, give generously, and pray this prayer as honestly with money in the bank as without it.

Forgive us our sins. Matthew has debts; Luke has sins, probably to make the meaning clear for Gentile readers. We need forgiveness as much as bread, every day. Sin is a debt: the obedience and honour we owe God and have not paid.

For we ourselves forgive. Here Luke keeps the image of debt. The word for in the middle must not become a bargain. God’s forgiveness is not purchased by ours; this same prayer has just called him Father, which no one earns. Our forgiving is the evidence that his has landed: a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot keep a ledger open against his neighbour, and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35). The tense is present and continuing, a standing policy; and everyone means no exceptions.

The one who forgives. The man teaching this petition has already said to a paralysed man, your sins are forgiven, and proved it by making him walk (5:20–24). And at the cross Luke alone records him doing the second half of the line under the greatest wrong ever done: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34). Some early manuscripts lack this prayer, but it is widely accepted as genuine and most Bibles print it.

Does forgiving mean I must trust again or pretend it did not happen? No. Forgiveness means you release the debt: you give up the right to repay, and you hand the case to God, who judges justly (Romans 12:19). It does not mean the wrong was small, that consequences vanish, or that trust is instantly restored. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by changed behaviour. A victim of abuse may forgive and still rightly report the crime, keep away from the abuser and protect others; forgiveness never requires anyone to remain in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated. And if the feelings lag behind, keep praying this prayer; forgiveness is often a decision renewed many times before the heart catches up.

Lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) is the one used of Jesus in the wilderness (4:2), and covers both testing and enticement. God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13); yet trials come under his hand. On the Mount of Olives Jesus will twice tell his disciples to pray that they may not enter into temptation (22:40, 46), and within hours Peter will deny him. So the prayer is: Father, I am weak; do not bring me to a test I cannot bear, or let me fall when tested (1 Corinthians 10:13). Matthew adds: but deliver us from evil.

In everyday life. Name to your Father the particular situation where you know you are weak, the screen late at night, the colleague who provokes you, the shop where you overspend, and pray specifically not to be led there, and then do not walk into it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two pictures follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater. A man with a guest and no bread knocks on a friend’s barred door at midnight, and the friend gets up and gives. How much more the Father. Then come the commands to keep asking, seeking and knocking, and the promise that everyone who asks receives.

That promise raises the honest problem of prayers that were not granted, and Jesus answers it with a father and a child: no father hands his son a snake for a fish or a scorpion for an egg. The Father gives good gifts, and the best of them is the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The promise is not a blank cheque (1 John 5:14; James 4:3), and Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked (22:42). A request refused is not a deaf father; it is a father who saw a snake where the child saw a fish.

Where Matthew has good things (Matthew 7:11), Luke has the Holy Spirit, and so tells us what good things finally means. The best gift the Father has to give is himself.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man at midnight is not asking for himself. He has nothing to set before his guest, which is where everyone stands who has tried to help another person and found himself empty, and it is the reason to knock.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, the gift promised to everyone who asks is God himself, and he cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A friend at midnight. Only Luke records this parable, and to feel it you have to see the house. A Galilean peasant home was often a single room: the family asleep together on a raised platform, and one door barred at night with a heavy beam. Getting up meant waking everyone. Bread was baked in the morning, so by midnight most houses had none, and neighbours knew who had baked.

Nothing to set before him. Hospitality in that culture was a sacred obligation, and many students of village life think a traveller arriving at night was in a sense the whole community’s guest. So the man banging on the door is doing what any neighbour would expect. And the request is modest: three small loaves, enough for one meal, and lend: he will return them.

A friend’s door. And he asks a friend. There is an existing relationship, and he presumes on it at the worst possible hour, which is precisely what friendship is for. That is the picture Jesus chooses for prayer, immediately after teaching them to say Father: not a subject petitioning a distant monarch through the correct channels, but a man in the dark, out of bread, with somebody depending on him, walking round to a house where he knows he will be heard.

Asking for someone else. He is not asking for himself. He wants the bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them, which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty. The parent with a child in trouble, the friend sitting with someone grieving, the Sunday school teacher on Saturday night: I have nothing to set before him. That is not a reason to give up. It is the reason to knock.

You give them something to eat. The disciples had already stood where this man stands. With five thousand hungry people and five loaves, Jesus told them: You give them something to eat (9:13). Then he took the loaves, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd (9:16). That is the shape of all Christian giving: empty hands, a Lord who looks up to his Father, and bread passed on.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not bother me. The excuses are entirely accurate: in a one-room house, unbarring the door and stepping over the children will wake everyone. But I cannot means I will not.

This man is not God. The parable is not a picture of a reluctant deity who has to be worn down. It argues from the lesser to the greater, by contrast: if a reluctant, sleepy neighbour will get up and give, how much more will God, who never slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4).

Because of his impudence. The word is anaideia: shamelessness, and its sense here is argued over. The traditional reading makes it the asker’s: his brazen persistence wins, which fits what follows (v. 9). A second reading gives it to the sleeper, who gets up to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced, and who has tied his own name to keeping his word (Psalm 23:3; Ezekiel 36:22).

Most prayer dies of good manners. What the parable licenses is the boldness of a man banging on a door in the dark because he has nothing and knows where the bread is. It is possible to be so respectful of God that nothing is ever actually asked for, and this parable was told to kill that. We do not have to wear God down. But we should pray with the persistence of someone who knows he has a real need and a friend who can meet it (18:1–8).

Borrowed boldness. Boldness at God’s door is not cheek; it is borrowed. Only the Son has an unbarred right to his Father’s house (2:49), and he hands his disciples his own word for God, Father, as the first word of their prayers. A sinner may knock without shame at midnight for the same reason a son may walk into his father’s house at any hour: the Son has brought him in and stands beside him at the door.

If God already knows what I need and wants to give it, why keep asking? Because prayer is not information for God; it is fellowship with him. He has chosen to work through the prayers of his people, as a father delights to hear his children ask even when he has already bought the gift. Persistent prayer also changes us: it clarifies what we truly want, exposes motives, deepens dependence, and keeps our eyes on him rather than on the problem. And Scripture simply commands it: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). We keep knocking not to change his mind but because he has told us to, and because he is worth talking to.

For worship. The sleeper in the story gave three loaves to save his face. Our Father, who has staked his own name on hearing his children at any hour, gave his own Son to save us, and a giver like that does not grudge bread at midnight.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ask, seek, knock. Three verbs, rising in intensity. Ask: make the request. Seek: search with effort. Knock: stand at a closed door and stay there, as the man in the parable did. The present tense of each suggests keep on, which rules out the reading where a single well-formed request closes the matter. And three promises answer the three verbs: given, found, opened.

For everyone who asks receives. Not a few privileged people, but everyone. Prayer is not reserved for the spiritual elite.

The honest problem. A great many people have read this verse and then buried someone they prayed for, and a Christian who has asked for years for a marriage to be saved or a child to come home may fairly ask what is going on. Three things must be said. First, Scripture never treats this as a blank cheque: if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14); you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly (James 4:3). Second, Jesus himself prayed a prayer that was not granted in the form he asked: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). Third, and this carries the weight, Jesus answers the question himself, at once, with a father and a child (vv. 11–13).

In everyday life. Asking, seeking and knocking are what children do, and no child of this Father is scolded for coming back to the door. And if a prayer you prayed for years has been answered with a no, bring that grief to him honestly as well. Asking again is not unbelief; it is exactly what he told you to do.

For worship. The God who says ask, seek, knock is not hiding behind his door. In Luke the great Seeker is God himself: the shepherd after the lost sheep, the woman sweeping for the lost coin, the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (15:4–10; 19:10). We seek because we were sought first, by a Father who did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? A second argument from the lesser to the greater: from earthly fathers to the heavenly Father. Two pairs, and both are chosen with care. It is often said that a fish and a water snake look roughly alike, and that a pale scorpion with its legs and tail curled in might pass for an egg. What is being described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he wanted and will hurt him. And every parent listening knows the answer instantly. Nobody does that. It is not even a temptation.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew 7:9. It was probably added to match Matthew.

You who are evil. A striking aside, dropped in as an agreed fact. He is talking to ordinary decent parents, and takes it as common ground that they are sinful (Romans 3:10–12). And even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

Is it not harsh to call loving parents evil? Only if evil meant as wicked as possible. Jesus means that even our best love grows from hearts bent away from God and curved in on ourselves: we love our children, and we also love being needed, being proud of them, getting our own way with them. The decent parent and the scoundrel need the same Saviour (Romans 3:23). And the point of the phrase is not to crush parents but to lift our eyes: if love mixed with sin still gives good gifts, think what love without any sin will give.

How much more will the heavenly Father. Here is the answer to the hardest question a praying person meets, why some requests are refused, and it is not a qualification of the promise but a description of who is keeping it. A request denied is not a father who is deaf; it is a father who has seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless. What it does is remove the one conclusion that would be unbearable: that the silence means indifference.

The Holy Spirit. Matthew’s version ends with good things (Matthew 7:11). Luke has the Holy Spirit, and so tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is himself, present in a Person: to dwell in his children, make them holy, help them pray (Romans 8:26) and empower them for witness (Acts 1:8). Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift promised to everyone who asks is God himself, and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

The promise of the Father. Luke follows this promise to its fulfilment. The risen Jesus tells his disciples he is sending the promise of his Father upon them (24:49), and at Pentecost Peter says that Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, has poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). To ask the Father for the Spirit is to ask for what Christ died and rose to give.

If every believer already has the Spirit, why ask? This is not a promise of a second blessing for some Christians, that is, a later, separate experience of the Spirit that only some believers receive, as some traditions teach; many who hold that view love the Spirit deeply, but Luke’s words here do not require it. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). The disciples asking here were living before Pentecost, and the Father was eager to give. We ask now for his ongoing work: to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), for his fruit, and for his help in our weakness. You will never ask for that and be handed a scorpion.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus frees a mute man from a demon, and the crowd marvels. The critics answer in two ways still common today: some say he works by Beelzebul, which concedes that the miracle happened, and others demand a sign from heaven, which postpones a decision while looking reasonable.

Jesus shows that the charge is illogical and inconsistent. His works are the finger of God, and the kingdom has arrived: one stronger has overpowered Satan and is carrying off his goods, which are people. The section ends with two warnings: there is no neutral ground, and a life swept clean but left empty is not safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The returning spirit is a warning against reformation without regeneration: the house is swept, but nobody lives there. The remedy is occupation by the stronger one himself (v. 22).

The saying that whoever is not with him is against him sits beside 9:50 once the pronouns are noticed. About a stranger doing good in Christ’s name, be generous; about your own standing before Christ, assume nothing. Generous outward, rigorous inward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman’s blessing on Jesus’ mother is well meant, and Jesus redirects it: blessedness is hearing the word of God and keeping it, which anyone can do, and Mary is the great example of exactly that (1:38).

And anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things he has stopped doing should turn the swept house into a question: not what have you got rid of, but who lives there now?

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A demon that was mute. Luke’s phrasing is compressed: the demon is named by its effect. Matthew adds that he was blind as well (Matthew 12:22).

In the flow. Jesus has just promised that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask (v. 13). Now Luke shows God’s power at work in Jesus, and religious men calling it the devil’s. The rest of the chapter grows from this one exorcism, and it ends with the scholars of the law lying in wait for him (vv. 53–54).

The people marveled. Wonder, which is not the same as faith and never has been. Then come two responses from the critics, still the two most often made by those who do not want to accept him.

By Beelzebul. The charge concedes a good deal. Nobody disputes that the man is speaking or suggests a trick; the miracle is granted and the source reassigned. Later Jewish polemic kept the same line, calling Jesus a sorcerer rather than denying his deeds (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a).

The name. Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron whom a king of Israel once consulted instead of the LORD (2 Kings 1:2–3); the name means lord of flies, perhaps a Hebrew mockery, and by the first century Beelzebul was a title for the chief of the demons. So the charge is as serious as a charge can be: the power in him is the enemy’s, said of a man who has just given a mute person his voice back.

A tongue set free. Isaiah had said that when God came to save, the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:4–6), and Jesus pointed John the Baptist to such works as his credentials (7:22). The critics are not debating a technique of exorcism. They are deciding what to do with the God of Isaiah’s promise standing in front of them, and they decide to call him the devil.

A sign from heaven. The second response is subtler, and worse: a real sign, from the sky, on their terms. The demand for further evidence, made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable. Luke says they were doing it to test him, which is what Jesus refused, in the wilderness, to do to his Father (4:12).

Is it wrong to want evidence for faith? No. Christianity is not a leap in the dark; God has given abundant evidence, and Luke wrote his Gospel so that Theophilus might have certainty (1:4). The risen Jesus was seen by many witnesses, most of them still alive when Paul wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Honest questions are welcome, and Christians should answer them patiently. What Jesus refuses is the demand that God perform on our terms after he has already spoken. If you are genuinely seeking, read the evidence that exists, the Gospels themselves, and ask God to show you the truth. If you find you would not believe whatever you were shown, the problem is not the evidence.

Was this not simply an illness that ancient people blamed on demons? Luke, a physician (Colossians 4:14), does not blame every illness on demons. He distinguishes healing the sick from casting out demons (4:40–41; 6:18; 13:32), and he records Zechariah struck mute by God with no demon involved (1:20). So when he says this man’s silence came from a demon, he is reporting a real distinction, not a primitive habit of mind. Scripture neither sees a demon behind every illness nor lets us explain the spiritual world away. And the people who were there, hostile witnesses included, did not argue that it was an illness; they argued about whose power cured it.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing their thoughts. Whether or not the charges were said to his face, Jesus answers what is in the room, as Luke keeps noting (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). Solomon confessed that only the LORD knows what is in every human heart (1 Kings 8:39). The man accused of serving the prince of demons answers the thoughts behind the accusation, and shows whose knowledge he has.

A kingdom divided. The first answer: the charge is illogical. He begins with a proposition nobody would dispute, drawn from politics and family life.

And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? The logic is simple and airtight. If the prince of demons is expelling demons, he is dismantling his own operation. No commander destroys his own positions. Something is assumed along the way that is easy to miss under the argument. Jesus takes it as given that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom: organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against (4:5–6). That is a good deal more than most modern readers assume, and he says it in passing as something too obvious to argue.
