And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second answer is inconsistency: Jewish exorcists were active at the time (Acts 19:13–14), and the Pharisees did not call their work satanic. (See Matthew 12:27 for the fuller answer.)

They will be your judges. Your own people’s practice condemns your double standard. An objection not applied consistently is not really the reason; something else is doing the work, and the argument has been assembled afterward to justify a conclusion already reached. That is a hard word for anyone who has built a reason for refusing what he did not want to accept: the reasoning is usually sound. It simply is not what is actually going on.

In everyday life. Look for the double standard in how you weigh other people’s ministries: the church across town whose fruit you dismiss while excusing the same weaknesses in your own, the preacher you criticise for what you praise in your favourite.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The finger of God. Matthew reads by the Spirit of God (Matthew 12:28); Luke keeps the Exodus wording, which would have rung like a bell in that crowd. Pharaoh’s magicians, beaten by the plague of gnats, told Pharaoh: this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19); and the tablets of stone were written with the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). So the phrase carries deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, and Jesus applies it, to men who have just accused him of witchcraft, to what he has done for one mute man. His exorcisms are as clearly God’s work as the plagues of Egypt, and like them they show God liberating his people from a tyrant.

The kingdom of God has come upon you. The verb (ephthasen) is the point: has arrived, has overtaken you. Not merely near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but already here. The kingdom is God reigning, and where the King acts, the reign is present, which is why the evidence for its arrival is not a throne or an army but a man who can suddenly talk. And it has come upon you, the people accusing him. They were standing in it.

Has the kingdom come, or is it still coming? God’s reign has broken in. Satan’s kingdom is being invaded and overthrown. Yet the kingdom has not come in its fullness: we still pray your kingdom come (v. 2), and we still live among sickness, sin and death. This is the already and not yet of the kingdom. It came in the King’s first coming; it grows as the gospel spreads and hearts bow to him; and it will be complete when he returns and every enemy is put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). Every demon driven out by the finger of God was a pledge of the day when the devil himself is thrown down for good (Revelation 20:10).

Where is the kingdom of God today, if not in exorcisms and healings? Wherever Christ reigns. It is present whenever a sinner repents and believes, because that is a captive set free; whenever the word is faithfully preached and the church lives under it; whenever a believer forgives, gives, or resists sin in Christ’s strength. It is not a political programme or a territory, though it will one day fill the earth. Look for it where people bow to Jesus, and pray for it there first.

In everyday life. When you face a temptation that has mastered you for years, remember that the finger of God is stronger than that habit. And when you pray for someone bound by addiction or despair, pray as one who believes the King has already invaded the enemy’s territory.

For worship. The finger that wrote the law on stone and humbled Pharaoh touched a mute man in Galilee, and he spoke. That same power raised Christ from the dead (Ephesians 1:19–20). The tyrant who held the world has met the finger of God, and the finger of God has a human hand.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong man, fully armed. A short parable, and it interprets everything he has just done. The strong man is Satan: not weak or asleep but fully armed, in his own house, guarding property he regards as his. While that arrangement holds, his captives cannot escape by their own strength. The human race was not neutral territory awaiting instruction. It was occupied.

One stronger than he. The stronger one is Jesus: John promised that one mightier than he was coming (3:16), and in Nazareth Jesus announced liberty to the captives (4:18). Attacks: the initiative is not Satan’s. Overcomes: it is not a contest; it is a result. The victory began in the wilderness (4:1–13), continued in the exorcisms, and was won at the cross, where he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14–15).

The armor in which he trusted. The man is not merely beaten but disarmed, and what is removed is also his confidence.

Divides his spoil. The property is not merely recovered but given away. Isaiah said of the Servant: he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12). And the goods in this parable are not gold. The thing carried out of the strong man’s house is a human being who could not speak. Every demon evicted, every sinner forgiven is plunder taken off an armed occupier by someone who walked in and was not stopped.

No struggle recorded. No exorcism in this Gospel is a struggle. He speaks and it is over; the demons do not fight him, they beg (8:28, 31). The strong man never lands a blow, until the cross, where the blow he landed was his own undoing. While men argued about the source of his power, the house of the great occupier stood open, and the goods he had held for the whole of human history were being carried out and handed back.

Can the strong man move back into a believer? No. A believer belongs to Christ and is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19); he has been delivered from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). The strong man cannot move back into a house the stronger one now owns. Christians can certainly be tempted, deceived and oppressed by the devil, and must resist him (Ephesians 6:10–18), but not owned. If you are a believer troubled by dark thoughts or fears, you need not look for an exorcist. Confess any sin, renounce any occult involvement, and stand on what Christ has done.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me. The middle ground is abolished in one sentence. One group accused him of working by Beelzebul; the other wanted a further sign, and would have thought itself open-minded, merely waiting for more evidence. Jesus tells them there is no such position. In the war between Christ and Satan there is no neutral ground.

Whoever does not gather with me. Gather and scatter are harvest words, and Luke has already named the harvest: plentiful, with few labourers (10:2). Scattering does not require malice, only absence. Grain left ungathered is lost whether it was trampled deliberately or simply not picked up.

But did Jesus not say the opposite in 9:50? A reader with a good memory will object. Two chapters ago John reported that they had stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name, and was told: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you (9:50). The two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There, the subject was you: the disciples’ judgment of a stranger. Here the subject is me: a person’s own standing before Christ. And the two run in opposite directions on purpose. About somebody else, doing good in Christ’s name outside your circle: assume the best, and do not stop him. About yourself, in relation to Christ: assume nothing, because neutrality is not on offer. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend the rest of the chapter dismantling.

Is it not narrow to say there is no neutral ground? Everybody draws this line somewhere: a shepherd who says each sheep is either in the fold or out on the hills is not being narrow, only accurate. Jesus can say it because of who he is. If he were one teacher among many, neutrality would be reasonable. But he has just shown himself the stronger one who sets captives free (v. 22), and in front of a rescuer there is no polite middle position. And see whom the saying offends most: not irreligious people, but the respectable men who thought waiting for more evidence was a safe place to stand. The same Jesus who will not allow neutrality welcomes anyone, of any past, who comes to his side.

In everyday life. Ask what you are actually doing for the harvest: praying for the lost by name, supporting gospel work, speaking of Christ when the door opens, welcoming newcomers at church. Sympathetic spectating is not a third option.

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out. A strange little story, a warning that follows the point about neutrality, and one of the most searching things in the chapter. Deliverance from evil is not enough by itself.

Waterless places. Desert places were widely thought to be the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). And note the pronoun the spirit uses when it decides to return: my house. It has been evicted and has not conceded ownership.

Swept and put in order. Everything in that sentence is good news, which is what makes the story so unsettling. This is not a person who relapsed but one whose life visibly improved: the mess dealt with, the habits sorted out. And there is one word missing, which Matthew supplies: empty (Matthew 12:44). Reformed, but not occupied.

Seven other spirits. Seven: complete possession. The house was not merely available. It had been made attractive.

Worse than the first. The warning is aimed at something religion produces in quantity: reformation without regeneration. Reformation is a person changing his habits; regeneration is God giving him new life from within, the new birth without which no one can see the kingdom of God (John 3:3–6). A man gives up the drink, or the affair, or the temper, and everyone says he is better, which makes it harder to see that nobody has moved in. An empty swept house is not a neutral state on the way to something better; it is a vacancy, advertised. It applied to a generation stirred by John and Jesus but never committed to him (Matthew 12:45), and it applies to anyone who makes a fresh start without Christ.

The remedy is occupation. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation, by the one stronger who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (8:35).

Can a Christian be repossessed? No. This parable describes a life cleaned up but left empty, someone reformed but not converted. A believer is not an empty house; the Holy Spirit lives in him, and what Christ has taken he keeps (John 10:28). But the warning is still for church members, because it is possible to sit in church for years, clean and orderly, without ever having received Christ. The question to ask is not whether you have stopped doing bad things, but whether Christ himself lives in you by faith. If you fear that you are that empty house, the fear is itself a hopeful sign, since an empty house does not worry about who lives in it; turn to Christ now, and he will come in.

In everyday life. When you put off an old habit, ask what you are putting on in its place: prayer where there was the screen, generosity where there was grasping, fellowship where there was isolation. And ask the Father for the Spirit he promises to those who ask (v. 13).
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman in the crowd raised her voice. Only Luke records this. It is one of the most human interruptions in the Gospels: in the middle of an argument about demons and kingdoms, a woman shouts a blessing on his mother.

Blessed is the womb! A common way of praising a man in that culture: praise the son by praising the mother who produced him. It is entirely well meant, and it is also true. Elizabeth said something very like it, filled with the Holy Spirit (1:42), and Mary herself sang that all generations would call her blessed (1:48).

Blessed rather. The word menoun means yes, but more than that: a redirection, not a contradiction. Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed. He refuses the assumption under the compliment, that blessedness is physical nearness to him. There is one womb that bore him, and nobody else can have it. What he offers instead is open to the whole crowd: hear the word of God and keep it, which anybody can do, in any century. It is the same point as 8:21.

Mary heard and kept. Mary is the outstanding example of the very thing he commends: let it be to me according to your word (1:38). Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (1:45), and twice Luke tells us she treasured these things in her heart (2:19, 51). What made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

The word of God, from his lips. In Luke the word of God is what Jesus himself speaks (5:1; 8:11). So when he says blessed are those who hear the word of God, he is not pointing away from himself. The woman praised the body that bore him; he points her to the voice that is speaking to her, and the way into Mary’s blessedness is to listen to her Son.

Where Christians differ: devotion to Mary. Roman Catholic and Orthodox devotion gives Mary a unique place of honour and intercession: praying to her, and, in Catholic teaching, calling her Queen of Heaven and Mediatrix (one who shares in bringing Christ’s grace to us). They distinguish this honour from the worship due to God alone, and many of them love Christ deeply; the difference is real, and it can be stated without contempt. This commentary’s view: Jesus himself redirects attention from his mother’s physical role to the blessing of obedience, which she shares with all believers. Mary is rightly called blessed, and is a great example of faith. But she is not to be prayed to or venerated. Christ alone stands between God and men as mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and Mary herself rejoiced in God as her Saviour (1:47).

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
As the crowds grow, Jesus calls them an evil generation for seeking a sign. He refuses evidence on demand to people who have decided what would count, and offers only the sign of Jonah: a prophet given back from the deep, with a call to repent.

Two pagan witnesses will condemn them at the judgment: the queen of the South, who travelled far to hear Solomon, and the men of Nineveh, who repented at Jonah’s preaching. Something greater than both is here. The section closes with sayings about light: the lamp has not been hidden, so the trouble lies in the eye, and the gravest danger is that the light a man steers by is darkness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites answered far smaller light, and judgment is weighed by the light received (10:13–15). It is the well-informed, not the ignorant, whom Nineveh condemns.

The eye sayings are about the heart: in Jewish idiom a bad eye was a grudging, grasping one (Deuteronomy 15:9). The men around Jesus were not short of information; their window was blocked by what they wanted.
verseByVerse.examples:
The warning that the light in you may be darkness is aimed first at religious people, and the cure is to let God search us by his word (Psalm 139:23–24).

The promise after the warning is warm. A life with no part kept dark becomes a lamp, and a lamp is for others.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation is an evil generation. Luke marks the moment carefully: the crowds were increasing, and that is when he said it. Popularity does not impress Jesus; it has never once altered what he told people. This generation is evil because it does not repent, despite seeing God’s works.

It seeks for a sign. They had asked for a sign from heaven (v. 16). He refuses, though he has spent the chapter performing signs: a mute man is standing there talking. What is refused is evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain, as when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul (v. 15).

The sign of Jonah. Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites in two ways, which are not rivals. The first is the man and his message: a foreigner with one sentence of judgment walked into Nineveh, and the city repented in sackcloth (Jonah 3:4–9). They saw no wonder; they heard a word. The second is where he had been: he arrived as a man who had gone down into the deep and been given back after three days (Jonah 1:17). Matthew spells that out (Matthew 12:40); Luke leaves the reader who knows Jonah to see it.

So will the Son of Man be. Luke shows at the end of his Gospel how the sign is given. The risen Jesus tells his disciples that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). That is Jonah’s story raised to its full height. The sign this generation is promised is an empty grave outside Jerusalem and the word that goes out from it to the world, and it is enough.

How was Jesus three days and three nights in the earth if he died on Friday and rose on Sunday? Luke does not use the phrase; it comes in Matthew’s account of the same saying (Matthew 12:40), but readers of Luke often ask it. In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day and night. Esther called for a three-day fast, night and day, and went in to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); an Egyptian had not eaten for three days and three nights and it was the third day (1 Samuel 30:12–13). Friday, Saturday and Sunday make three days. The phrase is an idiom, not a stopwatch, and the first readers would have heard no contradiction.

For worship. The sign of Jonah is mercy all the way down. Jonah went down into the deep because he ran from God; Christ went down into death because he ran toward us, bearing the judgment Nineveh deserved and we deserve. And on the third day he came back, rejoicing, to preach peace to the very city that rejected him.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South. Two witnesses are called, and both are chosen to sting: a pagan queen and a pagan city. The queen of Sheba, probably from south-west Arabia, travelled well over a thousand miles on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody’s God, and said the half had not been told her (1 Kings 10:1–7). She travelled a vast distance to hear Solomon; they had a greater one in their midst and would not listen.

Something greater than Solomon is here. The word is neuter: not someone greater but something greater, which is broader and stranger, the kingdom and the wisdom of God present in the person of Jesus. It is not merely that a better teacher than Solomon has turned up. The wisest man who ever lived is outranked by Wisdom itself, standing in the street. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30), in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

The men of Nineveh. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and deported ten tribes, whose armies were remembered for cruelty long afterward. If a first-century Jew had a byword for a people beyond hope, it was these. They repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there, who had run in the opposite direction, preached judgment with no promise of mercy, and was furious when it worked (Jonah 3:5–10; 4:1).

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. He does not argue for it. He says behold, and leaves it there, and Israel’s prophets pointed away from themselves to the LORD; this one points to himself. If pagans repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at his?

The point. Two Gentiles will condemn Jesus’ generation, and neither had a fraction of its light: Sheba had a rumour, Nineveh one sentence from an unwilling foreigner. The men listening to Jesus have him. Judgment is proportional to light (10:13–15): a pagan queen who crossed deserts for a rumour of wisdom will stand up beside people who could not be troubled to cross a room.

Will the queen of Sheba and the Ninevites be in heaven? Jesus does not say, and we should not speculate beyond him. His point is not their final destiny but their response: they answered far smaller light with seriousness, and that response will expose those who answered the greatest light with indifference. The Ninevites’ repentance was real enough to turn away a temporal judgment (Jonah 3:10). Whether any of them came to saving faith in the God of Israel is known to God. What is certain is that no one is saved apart from the grace of God revealed in Christ, and that we, who have heard him, have no excuse.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lamp on a stand. The saying was used before (8:16), and here it has a different edge. Something greater than Solomon and Jonah is the lamp, and it has not been hidden: it has stood in the middle of Galilee, healing people in daylight. So the problem is not lack of light but lack of sight.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. The lamp on the stand is outside; now there is a lamp inside, the eye. Think of a house with a window: if the window is clear, the house is bright; if it is blocked, the house is dark, however strong the sun outside. Spiritually, the eye is the heart’s ability to perceive God’s truth.

When your eye is healthy. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sincere, undivided, and in the wider usage of the day, generous: a single-minded focus on God. You receive the light and live in it.

When it is bad. “Bad” (ponēros) means evil, diseased. In Jewish idiom an evil eye meant a grudging, envious, tight-fisted disposition (Deuteronomy 15:9; Matthew 20:15). So this is not about eyesight or intellect but about whether a person is undivided and open-handed, or grasping and calculating, and that condition determines what light can get in.

A blocked window. That explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. A person’s capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true, and nobody ever thinks that is happening to him.

How can I tell if my eye is bad? Watch for the things that make Scripture suddenly unclear to you. When a plain passage about money, sex, forgiveness or anger seems strangely complicated, ask whether the difficulty is in the text or in what obeying it would cost. Notice envy, which turns other people’s blessings into grievances, and greed, which makes generosity feel foolish. Then ask God to heal your sight: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). A single eye is not a perfect one; it is one turned wholly toward God and willing to see.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest the light in you be darkness. Few warnings in Luke should trouble a religious person more. A man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. This is the danger that the thing you navigate by is itself darkness: the traveller with a faulty compass, getting further off the harder he tries. Be careful means inspect the instrument. The Pharisees thought they saw (John 9:39–41).

Who is it for? The context answers. Luke goes straight from this saying to a Pharisee’s dinner table and six woes. The men being warned are the most religiously informed people in the country, men who could recite the law, tithed their garden herbs, and had built their whole lives around getting this right. So the people at greatest risk from this verse are not the irreligious. They are the ones with the most exposure: long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two can feel identical.

If I cannot tell from the inside, how can I ever be sure? Not by staring inward, but by letting something outside you test you. Measure yourself by Scripture, not by your feelings or your church’s customs. Invite honest friends to tell you what they see. Look at fruit: does your knowledge make you humbler, kinder and more prayerful, or prouder and colder? And above all, pray as David did: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). The man who asks God to show him his darkness is not the man this verse describes.

Wholly bright. And then, after the warning, the promise, and it is unexpectedly warm. Having no part dark is the condition. Not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut; the whole of it, with nothing held back, no dark corner reserved.

A lamp with its rays. The result is not a person who has achieved something impressive but one who has become useful: someone others can see by.

Having no part dark. Only one life has met that condition in full. His eye was single toward his Father from first to last, and on the mountain, as he prayed, his clothing became dazzling white (9:29). What he offers the Pharisees is not a technique for self-inspection but himself, the light by which every other light is tested.

For worship. The light that searches us is the light that saves us. The Lord who warned that a man’s light may be darkness went himself into the darkness that fell over the whole land as he hung on the cross (23:44), so that people steering by broken compasses might be brought out into his day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal, and he goes. He does not perform the ritual handwashing, a tradition of the elders rather than a command of Moses, and when his host is astonished he answers with the picture of a cup clean outside and full of greed within. The Maker of the outside made the inside too, and the remedy for greed is to give away what was grasped.

Then come six woes, three on the Pharisees and three on the lawyers. Woe is the prophets’ word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict. They tithe herbs and neglect justice and the love of God, love the best seats, are unmarked graves, load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of murdered prophets, and have taken away the key of knowledge. The chapter ends with the scribes and Pharisees lying in wait to catch him in his words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. Jesus does not abolish the small duty, but a measurable duty can be checked off, and justice and the love of God never can.

The heaviest woe is the key of knowledge. The knowledge in question is knowing God, which the Scriptures exist to produce, and the keyholders neither went in nor let others in.
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens woe puts a test to every teacher: does what you say make it easier or harder for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? And the tomb-building woe explains why every generation admires the awkward prophets of the past and finds its own intolerable: a dead prophet requires a subscription, and a live one requires repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Pharisee asked him to dine. Luke records three such meals (7:36; here; 14:1), and at every one the host is challenged. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked, not a man denouncing his enemies from a safe distance but a man eating their food. The word Luke uses means the morning or midday meal.

He reclined at table. Reclining was the posture of a formal meal with guests, so the whole exchange took place in front of the Pharisee’s friends.

He did not first wash. The washing was not hygiene but a purity ritual (Mark 7:3–4), to remove ceremonial defilement picked up in the day. The law of Moses required such washings only of priests handling holy things; this was the tradition of the elders. The Pharisees had applied the priestly standard to everybody, all the time, a serious and in its way admirable ambition: they wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

Deliberate. It may well have been deliberate. His disciples had done the same in front of a delegation from Jerusalem, and he had defended them (Mark 7:1–5). He is not being careless or rude. He is declining, in front of witnesses, to endorse a system, and he is about to explain why.

A guest at every table. In Luke, Jesus is forever at someone’s table: Levi’s (5:29), Simon the Pharisee’s (7:36), Zacchaeus’s (19:5–7). He accepts the Pharisees’ invitations on the same terms as the sinners’, because both need him. And the guest at their tables is the host of a greater one, where people will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29).

Should a Christian accept invitations from people who disapprove of him? Jesus did, again and again, knowing the hostility at the table. Accept them where you can, and be a gracious guest; meals are one of the best places for real conversation. But do not buy peace by pretending to agree with what you believe is wrong. Jesus was courteous enough to come and honest enough to speak. You can be both: thankful for the food, kind to your host, and clear about Christ when the moment comes.
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The outside of the cup. He answers the unspoken criticism with an image from the table in front of him. The Pharisees had detailed rules for washing vessels (Mark 7:4), and rabbinic discussions later written down in the Mishnah debate whether the inside and outside of a cup could be clean or unclean independently. Jesus takes their own debating point and turns it on them.

Full of greed and wickedness. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup. It is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. “Greed” (harpagē) is plunder, rapacity: a startling charge against the most scrupulous men in the country. Something is being taken.

You fools! “Fools” (aphrones) means senseless. The argument is from creation: the same God made the visible and the invisible parts of a man, and he sees the inside (1 Samuel 16:7). A religion that attends to one and not the other has not understood who it is dealing with.

The Maker at the table. The guest asking whether the Maker of the outside did not make the inside also is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He is not guessing at what God sees when he looks into a man; he is looking. And he still stayed for the meal.

If Jesus warns against calling a brother a fool, how can he say it here? There (Matthew 5:22) he forbids the angry insult that despises a person. Here he gives the Lord’s verdict on teachers who ignore the God who made the inside as well as the outside (v. 40), as the prophets did before him. He is the Judge, and he sees hearts; we do not. So we may name folly in what people teach and do, but we must never use contempt as a weapon against a person, and never imagine that our anger shares his perfect knowledge.

Give as alms. A difficult sentence, and translators differ. The likeliest sense is: give the contents of the cup and dish, the food and wealth it stands for, to the poor, instead of grasping them. The inside is full of greed, and the remedy for greed is not scouring the cup but giving away what was grasped (Micah 6:8). A person can be meticulous about religious observance and tight-fisted, and Jesus treats the second as the diagnosis and the first as the cover.

Everything is clean for you. When the heart is right, the ritual rules do not matter. Mark notes that in teaching like this Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

Does this mean that almsgiving cleanses a person? No. The phrase is hard, and has been read as give the contents of your cups as alms or give from within, from the heart. On either reading Jesus is not teaching salvation by charity. He is telling men obsessed with outward purity that a heart turned outward in generous love is what God calls clean. Only the blood of Christ cleanses a sinner before God; but a heart he has cleansed will show it by opening its hands.

In everyday life. The Maker who sees your heart came to give you a new one, so you can afford to look honestly: lay your bank statement alongside your church attendance and ask which one tells the truer story about your heart. Then give something away this week that you would rather keep.

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you Pharisees! Six woes follow, three on the Pharisees (vv. 42–44) and three on the lawyers (vv. 46–52). “Woe” (ouai) is not a curse or an insult. It is the prophets’ word, a cry of lament as much as a verdict: the sound a man makes watching somebody walk toward a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later (19:41), and the woe and the weeping come from the same heart.

Mint and rue. The law required a tithe of the produce of the field (Deuteronomy 14:22–23). It said nothing explicit about a pot of mint by the door. The Pharisees tithed the garden herbs too, counting out every tenth leaf. There is something admirable in that: they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt.

Justice and the love of God. The same men counting mint leaves were failing at the two largest things in the law, the weightier matters (Matthew 23:23). Justice: fair dealing with others, especially the poor. The love of God: loving him with the whole heart. The two great commandments (10:27).

Without neglecting the others. This clause is regularly ignored. Jesus does not abolish the herb-tithing. He says they were right to do it. What he condemns is the trade: the quiet substitution of the small and achievable for the large and demanding.

How the trade happens. Nobody decides to swap justice for mint. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off, and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will run out before he reaches the things that do not. Attendance is countable. Reading plans are countable. Positions on secondary matters are defensible. Whether I am just, and whether I love God, are neither, and they are the two things this verse says were being neglected.

Both, in one life. One man did the weightier matters and the smaller ones together. Jesus kept his Father’s law down to its details, and in the same life proclaimed good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed (4:18), and loved his Father with the whole heart from boyhood to the cross. The Pharisees at this table were looking at what they had neglected, sitting across from them in a body.

Where Christians differ: the tithe today. Some teach that Christians must give a tenth of their income, as a binding law. Others say the tithe belonged to the old covenant, and the New Testament gives no fixed percentage. This commentary’s view: the New Testament does not command a tithe for Christians, but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate, sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Jesus was speaking here to Jews under the law, before the cross. A tenth is a wise starting point, and many will give more. The heart matters more than the percentage, and the point of this verse is the weightier matters: justice and the love of God.

What does justice look like for an ordinary Christian? Paying your workers and your bills fairly and on time. Telling the truth in business, on forms and in references. Refusing to exploit someone’s weakness, ignorance or poverty. Speaking up for the person who is being treated unfairly at work or in church, especially the one with no voice. Treating the cleaner and the director with the same respect. And caring about the poor with your money and your time, not just your opinions (Proverbs 31:8–9). Justice is love in the shape of fairness, and it is checked daily, not annually.

In everyday life. Keep your quiet time, keep your giving, keep your church commitments; and then ask whether anyone you dealt with today was treated unjustly by you, and whether you loved God at your desk as well as in your pew. Often you did not. Then go back to Christ, who kept both for you: his obedience is counted as yours, and your imperfect love is accepted for his sake.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The best seat. The best seat in the synagogue was probably a bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the chest where the scrolls were kept: to sit there was to be seen by everyone, in the act of being religious. And greetings in the marketplaces were the elaborate public respect paid to a recognised teacher in the open square.

The word is love. The seats themselves are not condemned: somebody has to sit at the front. What is diagnosed is an appetite, love of prominence and recognition (Matthew 6:1–5; 23:5–7).

The second audience. A man who loves the front seat has acquired a second audience, and it stands between him and the first. Every act of piety now has two possible payments, and one arrives immediately: they have received their reward (Matthew 6:2). It is a woe and not a scolding because it is self-defeating in a way the man cannot see. He is doing good things and being paid in the wrong currency, and the payment leaves nothing outstanding.

What if I recognise this in myself? Two things are worth saying. The first is that the desire to be well thought of is not curable by pretending not to have it. Public modesty about one’s own achievements is one of the front seats. The second is where the actual remedy lies, and it is not in trying harder to be humble. It is in the fact that a man who already has the approval he most needs stops shopping for the substitute. The prayer Jesus taught begins with the word Father, and a person who has heard that word settle on him has considerably less use for a bench at the front. Practise doing some good things in secret, where only he sees (Matthew 6:4), and let him be enough.

The lowest place. At another Pharisee’s table Jesus tells guests to take the lowest seat, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (14:7–11). He was describing his own road: laid in a manger (2:7), numbered with criminals at the end (22:37). And God has given him the highest place there is.

For worship. Before Jesus had preached a sermon, a voice from heaven said: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). He never needed a greeting in the marketplace, because he had that, and everyone who is in him is wrapped in the same pleasure. Beside that honour every bench at the front of every building on earth is a small thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unmarked graves. Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), barring him from worship, so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover so that pilgrims could go round them (compare Matthew 23:27). An unmarked grave is a grave a man walks straight over, and finds out afterward, if ever.

Deadly in three ways. First, they are graves: whatever is on the surface, the contents are dead. Second, they defile: the self-appointed guardians of purity were in fact sources of defilement to the people they taught. Third, and worst, nobody can tell. The damage is done precisely because they look entirely safe.

Not obvious hypocrites. Obvious hypocrites are much less dangerous, because everybody eventually spots them. This is a description of respected men, whose seriousness about God is genuine and whose lives are outwardly admirable, quietly transmitting something that kills. A young believer takes his cue from the most impressive religious person he knows, and if what that person has is scrupulosity without justice and knowledge without love, that is what he will catch, without any idea that a transfer has taken place.

The one who touched the dead. Under the law, contact with death spread uncleanness to whatever it touched. In Luke, when Jesus is involved, the movement runs the other way. At Nain he came up and touched the bier, and the dead young man sat up and began to speak (7:14–15); in Jairus’s house he took a dead girl by the hand, and her spirit returned (8:54–55). These Pharisees, without knowing it, passed death on to everyone who walked over them. Jesus touches death, and passes on life.

How do I protect myself and my children from unmarked graves? Test every teacher, however respected, by Scripture and by fruit (Matthew 7:15–20; 1 John 4:1). Watch whether a ministry produces love, humility and joy in Christ, or fear, pride and harshness. Be wary of anyone who cannot be questioned. Do not take your whole picture of the Christian life from one impressive person; let your children see many ordinary faithful believers. And where you find real spiritual abuse, name it and bring it into the light; protecting victims always matters more than protecting a reputation.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You insult us also. The lawyers were the experts in the law of Moses, and many of them were Pharisees. Note what he does not say: not that is untrue, but you insult us, which concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, one of the commonest defences against a word that cannot be answered. The interruption does not end it. It doubles it.

Burdens hard to bear. The picture is of pack animals and their drivers. These men had built an elaborate structure of rulings around the law, specifying exactly how each command was to be kept, and the ordinary Israelite was expected to carry it. Peter would later call it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

Not with one of your fingers. Either they found clever ways round their own rules, or, the heavier charge, they did nothing to help others carry them: no interest in whether an ordinary man with a farm and five children could actually do it. Set that against Jesus, who two chapters later lays his hands on a woman bent double for eighteen years and straightens her, and is rebuked for doing it on the Sabbath (13:10–17). The lawyers would not move a finger toward the load. He puts his hands on it.

Does this mean Christian teachers should not preach high standards? No. Jesus set the highest standard of all: be perfect, love your enemies, deny yourself. The difference is that his standards come with grace to keep them and forgiveness for failing them, and he himself carried the heaviest load. The test for anyone who teaches is uncomfortable and simple. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself, and whether he points people to Christ who bears it.

In everyday life. Christ has put his hands on your load; lift a finger for theirs: the young mother overwhelmed by advice, the new believer drowning in expectations, the friend who feels he can never do enough.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You build the tombs of the prophets. Building and beautifying prophets’ tombs was a genuine piety of the period. On the face of it, it is the most respectful thing imaginable, honouring the men their ancestors murdered, and it seemed like repentance. Jesus calls it complicity.

Witnesses who consent. There is a bitter play in it: the fathers put the prophets in the ground, and the sons put up the masonry over them. They honour dead prophets and reject the living one, as their fathers did.

Safely over. Tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. A dead prophet has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living prophet is sitting at their table telling them their religion is an unmarked grave, and they are about to arrange his death. A man who says he would never have joined the mob, while queuing to join this one, has not broken with his fathers. He has simply arrived late.

The pattern in every generation. Every generation of the church admires the reformers, martyrs and awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. The reason is not always hypocrisy. It is that a dead prophet requires a subscription and a live one requires repentance.

Are there prophets today whom we must heed? Not in the sense of new revelation: the prophets and apostles laid the foundation once for all, and the canon of Scripture is closed (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But God still sends faithful preachers and believers who apply his word to us with uncomfortable accuracy: the pastor who preaches on the sin our church tolerates, the friend who tells us the truth. The test is not whether they claim a new word from God, but whether what they say is what Scripture says. When it is, we must not honour the Bible on the shelf while silencing the person reading it to us. Some Christians believe God still gives prophetic words today; most of them agree that nothing said now can add to Scripture or correct it, and that is the point that matters here.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prophets and apostles. The quotation matches no known book exactly. The likeliest explanation is that Jesus is speaking as the Wisdom of God, the one who sent the prophets; Matthew puts the words directly in his mouth, I send you prophets (Matthew 23:34). And note the word apostles: he is looking at the men who will be sent after him, and some will be killed: Stephen (Acts 7:58–60), James (Acts 12:2).

The blood of all the prophets. The generation that rejects the Messiah fills up the measure of all its ancestors’ guilt (Matthew 23:32). It is the climax of a long history of rejection.

From Abel to Zechariah. The two names are the bookends of the Hebrew Bible. Abel is the first murder in Genesis (Genesis 4:8). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court, on the king’s orders, for rebuking the people (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); his is the last murder of a prophet recorded in Chronicles, which stands last in the Hebrew ordering of the books. So from Genesis to Chronicles: from the first page to the last, the whole of the Old Testament. As he died, Zechariah said: may the LORD see and avenge!

Is God punishing men for what their ancestors did? That is the hardest question in the paragraph, and Scripture appears to forbid exactly that. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20); children shall not be put to death because of their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). If this verse meant inherited guilt, it would contradict the law and the prophets outright. It does not, and Jesus has already said why, one verse earlier: you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers (v. 48). Nothing is charged to these men that they have not personally ratified. The guilt is not inherited down a bloodline; it is incurred by choosing, in your own generation and with your own eyes open, to do the identical thing. And there is a reason the reckoning falls here. This is the generation to whom the Son himself has come, the one to whom every murdered prophet was pointing. A long account is closed not because these men are worse than their ancestors but because they have more light than any of them and are about to do worse with it. The judgment is proportional to the privilege, exactly as at Chorazin (10:13–15).

Which Zechariah? Matthew calls this Zechariah the son of Barachiah (Matthew 23:35), while 2 Chronicles 24:20 names his father as Jehoiada. Luke gives no father’s name. Jehoiada may have been his grandfather, or the name may reflect a confusion with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). This is a real difficulty, and believers who hold Scripture true admit that no answer is certain. Either way, Jesus means the last prophet’s murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order, as Abel’s was the first.

Required of this generation. This was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24), within forty years of these words.

What it does not mean. This verse and others like it have been quarried for centuries to justify appalling treatment of Jewish people. But it is addressed not to a nation or a race but to the scribes and lawyers in that room. The speaker is himself a Jew, as are his disciples and every prophet whose blood he invokes, and he will weep over this city rather than gloat over it (19:41). To turn a Jewish prophet’s rebuke of Jewish leaders for killing Jewish prophets into a charge against Jewish people as such is to end up standing exactly where the men being rebuked are standing. Christians owe Jewish people love, gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, and the gospel offered humbly.

In everyday life. Each time you hear a clear word and set it aside, it becomes easier to do again. Name the truth you have been putting off, and, since the blood that speaks pardon still pleads for you, obey it before the week is out.

For worship. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground for vengeance; Zechariah’s prayed that the LORD would see and avenge. There is another blood, shed by this same generation, that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). It cries not for vengeance but for pardon. Father, forgive them, said the one whose blood it was. The account of all the prophets’ blood was settled in full, and for everyone who trusts him it is settled in mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The key of knowledge. The last woe is the heaviest. Behind the door is the knowledge of God: not information about him, but knowing him, which the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders by office. The key is the right understanding of Scripture, which points to Christ (24:27, 44–45; John 5:39), and they have taken it away, locking with their traditions the door God had opened.

You did not enter yourselves. They had the key and never used it. They did not come to Jesus. A lifetime handling the Scriptures of the living God, and they never went in. It is possible in every generation.

You hindered those who were entering. People were already on their way in, and these men got in the way: by burying the law under rulings no ordinary person could carry (v. 46), by making the entry requirements ceremonial rather than moral (v. 39), and by teaching so that God came out looking like the sort of person these men were. That last is the real mechanism. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine. He transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine.

How do I know whether my teaching opens or shuts the door? Ask whether people leave your teaching seeing Christ more clearly, and wanting him more. Ask whether you point to the cross and the empty tomb, or mainly to rules and techniques. Ask whether ordinary, struggling people find in you a way in or a wall. Teach the Bible as a book about Christ, not a manual of performance. And be in the room yourself: the surest way to open the door for others is to be someone who has gone through it and is still delighting in what is inside.

For worship. The lawyers took away the key; Christ turns it. On the evening of his resurrection he opened the Scriptures on the Emmaus road until their hearts burned (24:32), and then opened the minds of the rest to understand them (24:45). No keyholder on earth can lock out a sinner whom he has let in.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To press him hard. The dinner produced not repentance, not even argument, but something colder. “Press him hard” (deinōs enechein) means to be bitterly hostile, and they provoke him to speak, firing questions as a witness is pressed until he says something usable.

Lying in wait. Lying in wait is the vocabulary of an ambush. Respectable men follow a guest out of a house, not to learn anything but to get a sentence they can use, as they will try again in Jerusalem (20:20–26). This is a turning point: from here the opposition is a hunt with a purpose, and it will run without interruption to a trial and a cross.

Truth softens or sets. The word of God had been spoken to these men as clearly as ever, by a guest at their own table, and it hardened them. That is not a failure of the message. Pharaoh’s heart set harder with every plague; Isaiah was told that this people would hear and not understand (Isaiah 6:9–10). The truth is never neutral. It softens or it sets, depending on what it lands on.

In the flow. The scene leads straight into Luke 12, where Jesus’ first words to his disciples are beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, and do not fear those who kill the body (12:1–4). The journey to Jerusalem now has hunters following it, and Jesus walks on toward the cross with his eyes open.

Why does the same word soften some and harden others? Because the word meets hearts in different conditions, and because God in his sovereign mercy opens some hearts (Acts 16:14) and in his justice leaves others to the hardness they have chosen (Romans 9:18). No one who hardens himself can blame God; no one who is softened can boast. The practical lesson is for us: when the word cuts, do not reach for a reason to resent the one who spoke it. Bring the wound to God and ask him to soften you. A heart that asks to be softened is already being softened.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Luke 12 is a sustained call to undivided allegiance in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus moves between a vast crowd and his disciples. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one whose authority reaches beyond death, and then fear nothing, because he counts the hairs of your head. Do not covet or stockpile: the rich fool who planned bigger barns died the night he planned them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom, which the Father is glad to give. Be dressed for action, lamps burning, waiting for a Master who will come home and serve his servants.

The chapter ends at a high pitch. Jesus speaks of a fire he has come to cast and a baptism he must undergo first, and of the division he brings even into families. He rebukes a crowd that can read the weather but not the present time, and calls everyone to settle with God on the road, before they reach the Judge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled, and Jesus turns from the thousands to the handful. His first warning is for people already inside: beware hypocrisy, the playing of a part. It cannot last, because everything hidden will be revealed.

The teaching on fear follows. Those who kill the body have nothing more they can do; the one to fear is God, and the God to be feared is the God who forgets no sparrow. Then the stakes rise: to acknowledge Christ before men is to be acknowledged before the angels of God. The hardest saying of the chapter, the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, is followed at once by the promise that in the hour of trial the same Spirit will give the words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). The one with authority to cast into hell is God, not the devil, and the passage turns on the fact that this same God does not forget a sparrow.

The blasphemy against the Spirit must be read in its context, the charge that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (11:15; Mark 3:30). It is not a word said in a bad moment but the settled, eyes-open decision to call the Spirit’s light darkness, and the fear of having committed it is the disproof.
verseByVerse.examples:
The saying about inner rooms and housetops cuts both ways. Much that is said for Christ is said quietly and seems unrecorded; Jesus says it is heard. But the main force is the warning: what a person is when nobody is watching will be read out.

The confession sayings are not a performance test. Peter denied Jesus three times in public and was restored; what is warned against is a settled refusal to own him. And the promise of words in the hour of trial is not a promise of acquittal: Stephen spoke under it and was stoned.

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 12 is Jesus teaching his disciples how to live in the open before God while the world presses in: no masks, no fear but the fear of God, no hoarding and no anxiety, ready for a Master who will come home and serve his servants, and settled with God today, on the road.

The setting. The teaching follows straight on from a dinner that ended with the Pharisees and lawyers pressing him hard and lying in wait to catch him in something he might say (11:53–54). Most of it is addressed to the disciples, with the crowds listening.

Tens of thousands. Luke’s word is myriads, and people are being walked on: the height of his popularity, with his enemies still at his heels. Yet in the middle of the crush he turns from the thousands to the handful. The first warning is for people already inside, after watching what religion had done to the men at that dinner table.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Leaven was not a sachet of yeast but a lump of dough kept back from the last batch, left to sour, and worked into the new one. It is small, invisible once mixed in, and changes everything it touches (1 Corinthians 5:6). So hypocrisy starts small and spreads through a life and a community. And Luke alone gives Jesus’ own definition: which is hypocrisy. A hypokritēs was a stage actor, speaking his lines from behind a mask. It is not failing to live up to what you believe, which is the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part: pretending to be what you are not.

Nothing is covered up. The argument against hypocrisy here is first practical. He does not say it is wrong, though it is. He says it does not work: the performance has a closing date, and at the judgment everything behind the mask will be public (8:17). That is either a frightening sentence or a liberating one, depending on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The eyes that see through every mask. The one who says this is the one who will do it: when the Lord comes, he will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). Luke has shown him doing it already: he knew the thoughts of the scribes before they spoke (5:22), and read the heart of the Pharisee at whose table a sinful woman wept (7:39–40). So this is the Judge himself telling his friends what his eyes will one day uncover, while there is still time to come out from behind the mask and be forgiven.

If I struggle with sin I have not overcome, am I a hypocrite? No. A hypocrite is not a person who fails; he is a person who pretends. The believer who fights a sin, confesses it to God and perhaps to a trusted friend, and keeps getting up again is not acting a part. He is being honest about a war. Hypocrisy begins when you cultivate an image you know is false: hiding what you are, performing what you are not, and condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The cure is not to stop striving for holiness until you are perfect. It is to walk in the light (1 John 1:7): honest before God, honest with someone, and humble about yourself. And the deepest cure is the gospel itself. Hypocrisy runs on the need to be approved, and a person who knows he is fully known by God and still loved in Christ no longer needs a mask to win approval (Romans 8:33–34).

For worship. The Lord who warns us against masks wore none: what he said in the temple he said in the garden. And he came to save hypocrites, knowing everything behind every mask and loving us still. On the day when all is revealed, those who are in him will not be found out. They were found out long ago, at the cross, and covered.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; here it pictures hypocrisy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inner rooms and the housetops. The private rooms are the inner rooms: the windowless storeroom at the back of a house, the one place where a conversation could not be overheard through a doorway. The housetops were flat, and where the roofs adjoined, a man standing on his could be heard by the whole street; it was where public announcements were made. So: the most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town. What is said in the first will be repeated from the second, and every careless word will be judged (Matthew 12:36).

A double meaning. It cuts both ways. It is an encouragement: the disciples are about to be hauled before synagogues and rulers (v. 11), and much of what they say for Christ will be said quietly, in rooms with no audience. Jesus says it is being heard, and will be preached to the world. But the immediate context is hypocrisy, and the primary force is the warning: everything a man is when nobody is watching, the private appetites, the things said about people not in the room, is going to be read out.

Not done in a corner. The rooms where Jesus taught the Twelve were small: a boat, a house, an upper room. Within weeks of his resurrection what had been said to a handful was proclaimed to thousands, and Paul could tell King Agrippa that none of it had been done in a corner (Acts 26:26). The same law ran the other way at the cross. The bargain to betray him was struck in secret, in the absence of a crowd (22:3–6), and God turned that whispered plot into the most public news in the world, announced from every housetop as the place of mercy.

Will my forgiven sins be broadcast at the judgment? Scripture’s emphasis for believers is that their sins are blotted out, cast into the depths of the sea, remembered no more (Hebrews 8:12; Micah 7:19). Whatever is opened on that day will be opened as the record of grace, not as evidence for condemnation, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The warning here presses hardest on the hidden life that is being kept from God now. Bring it into the light today, in confession, and it will never be used against you.

In everyday life. Speak in private as a child whose Father hears it all: the comment about someone you would never make to their face, the message you would hate to see forwarded. And take courage from the other side of it: the quiet word for Christ to one person, which nobody else heard, has been heard in heaven.
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, my friends. He has not called them that before in this Gospel; it is the only place in the first three Gospels where Jesus addresses his disciples as my friends (compare John 15:14–15). The placing is deliberate. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, preparing them for persecution, and he opens by naming the relationship it is being said inside.

Nothing more that they can do. Hypocrisy very often comes from fear of people, and Jesus addresses the root. He does not say persecution will not come. He says that its worst is death, and there it runs out of resources, because death is not the end and they cannot touch the soul.

Authority to cast into hell. Luke’s word is not merely power but exousia, authority, the lawful right to rule what lies beyond death. Some have taken this to be the devil, but Satan is never handed the keys of anyone’s final destiny, and believers are told to resist him (James 4:7), not to fear him. The one whose authority runs past the grave is God. The word for hell is geenna, Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem: everyone listening could have pointed at it. Jesus uses it of the place of final, conscious punishment.

Fear him. The fear of God drives out the fear of people: do not fear what they fear; the LORD of hosts, him you shall regard as holy, let him be your fear (Isaiah 8:12–13); the fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). And this awe is the beginning of wisdom.

Are Christians meant to be afraid of God? A sensitive reader will stop here. The answer is that this is spoken to my friends, and the two things are not in tension. The fear of God is not cringing terror for his children, but reverent awe of the one who holds all power, including over eternity. What is commanded is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror. And the effect is the exact opposite of paralysis: a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else, because the worst any human power can do to him has been placed in its true proportion. A child can be in awe of his father’s strength and run into his arms in the same moment. That is why the next thing Jesus says is fear not.

The road to Jerusalem. The man who says this is walking to Jerusalem to be killed (9:51), and he lived the sentence before he asked it of anyone. When Pharisees warned him that Herod wanted to kill him, he sent back word that he would go on, today and tomorrow, and finish his course (13:31–33). And when they did their worst, they could kill his body, seal a tomb and post a guard, and after that they had nothing more that they could do. Every tyranny runs on the fear of what can be done to a body; this sentence cuts the supply line, and the friends he warns here are invited to stand where he stands.

How can a God of love have authority to cast into hell? Because love that is not also just would not be good. A God who looked at cruelty, abuse and contempt for himself and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent.
