Jesus, the kindest man who ever lived, speaks more plainly about hell than anyone in Scripture, and he speaks of it here to his friends as a warning, not a threat. Hell is God’s final, just answer to sin that was never brought to him for mercy (Romans 2:5–6). And the same God has opened the way of escape at his own cost, so that no one who flees to his Son will be condemned (John 3:16–18).

In everyday life. Whose opinion do you fear most? Your manager’s, your family’s, the group chat’s? Name the person whose disapproval most shapes what you say about Christ. Then put that fear next to the fear of God, and watch it shrink to its true size.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Two verses after fear him comes fear not, and the bridge between them is a bird nobody wanted. Sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, food for the very poor. Matthew records the price as two sparrows for a penny (Matthew 10:29); Luke says five for two pennies, which suggests that a buyer of four got the fifth thrown in free, the one with no value at all.

Not one of them is forgotten. Including that one. He does not say God feeds them, or watches them, or values them. He says none of them is forgotten, which is the language of memory: the death of a bird thrown in free with a purchase is registered.

The hairs of your head. The perfect tense means the number is known and stands known, a figure that changes daily and is never out of date. Nobody needs to know it. That God does tells you not that the information is important but that the attention is total.

Fear not. The God to be feared (v. 5) is the God who cares. Jesus has not understated the danger: he has just conceded that they can kill you. But even then your body is not outside his care. Nothing happens to you that he does not know and allow, and he works all of it for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The one to be feared and the one who counts the hairs are the same person, and the second fact is what makes the first bearable.

Priced at Calvary. How does a disciple know he is worth more than many sparrows? The sparrow’s value was fixed in the market, a fraction of a penny. Ours was fixed at the cross: you were ransomed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). Our worth is not something we bring to God. It is what he has decided to spend on us, and he spent his Son.

If God cares so closely, why did he let this happen to me? Jesus does not promise that sparrows never fall; Matthew says not one falls to the ground apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29). The promise is not that nothing painful will happen, but that nothing will happen unknown, unnoticed or outside his purpose. You may not see the reason this side of glory, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend the pain is small. It asks you to trust the character of a Father who counts hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who will one day wipe every tear away. Bring the question to him honestly; the psalms give you words for it.

For worship. The fifth bird, thrown in for nothing, is in God’s register. A dying thief, worth less than that to the world that crucified him, said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (23:42), and the Son of God answered with paradise. He has never forgotten one sinner who called on him.
verseByVerse.note: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; Matthew says two for a penny, Luke five for two, as if the fifth came free.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Acknowledges me. The word means confesses, openly declares loyalty; the unusual construction, confesses in me, suggests declaring an allegiance, not merely stating a fact. And the setting for both halves is public: before men, then before the angels of God. There are two courtrooms, and what happens in the second corresponds to what happened in the first.

Before the angels of God. At the judgment Jesus is the judge, and his word, this one belongs to me, decides eternal destiny. The promise is worth as much as the warning: whatever is said for him in a difficult room is said again, by him, in front of the angels. The other half is measure for measure (compare 9:26).

What it does not mean. Not that a single failure means final rejection: Peter denied Jesus three times in public (22:57–62) and was recommissioned on a beach (John 21:15–19). The warning is against a settled refusal to own him over a life, and the warning itself is one of the means God uses to keep us faithful.

The smaller moments. Nor should it be softened into nothing. Very few Western Christians will ever stand in a court; the moments that count are smaller and more frequent: the conversation at work where it would be easier to say nothing, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned. None of those is a courtroom denial. But a man can spend his whole life quietly declining to be identified, and never once decide to.

If I stayed silent when I should have spoken, have I denied Christ? Probably you failed, as Peter did, and the answer is the same as his: go back to the Lord, confess it, and be restored. He looked at Peter, and Peter wept, and that look was mercy (22:61–62). A single silence is not a settled life of denial. But do not leave it there: ask God for the next opportunity, and take it. Often the best repair is simply to go back to the person and say, I wanted to tell you what Christ means to me, and I did not. That is how a failure becomes a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word against the Son of Man. Few verses have caused sincere Christians more terror, and it must be handled slowly. That a word against the Son of Man is forgivable is an extraordinary concession. Men can insult him, mock him, misjudge him, and be forgiven if they repent: Paul once blasphemed Jesus and persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13), and Peter denied him. Both were forgiven.

Spoken against, and praying. Why can a word against the Son of Man be forgiven at all? Because he came to be spoken against: appointed for a sign that is opposed (2:34), called a glutton and a drunkard (7:34), accused of working by Beelzebul (11:15), and from the cross he prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34). The forgiveness held out to his slanderers was bought by the one they slandered. That is also why the other sin is beyond forgiveness: it refuses the Spirit who points to that blood, and there is no other blood to flee to.

Blasphemy against the Spirit. The context unlocks the verse. In Mark and Matthew this saying comes straight after the accusation that Jesus cast out demons by Satan (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32), and Luke has just given us that accusation (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work through Jesus in the open and called it the devil: for they were saying, he has an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30). That is the sin: not a word said in a bad moment, but a deliberate, settled rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, in full knowledge, calling God’s light darkness.

Why can it not be forgiven? Not because God’s grace is insufficient, but because the Spirit is the one who brings people to repentance. His work is to convict of sin and to point to Christ (John 16:8–14). To reject him finally is to cut oneself off from the only way to forgiveness. It is not that someone wants to repent and cannot be forgiven, but that he no longer wants to repent. A man who has finally and permanently refused the Spirit’s work has, by definition, stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. He does not lie awake. He has no interest in the question.

Where Christians differ, and a pastoral word. Some have taught that the unforgivable sin is a specific act, such as suicide or a particular blasphemous word. This commentary’s view: it is not a single act or careless word, but a final, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ. Anyone who is worried that they have committed it has not, because the very worry shows the Spirit is still at work in them. Those who have committed it do not care. And a family grieving a suicide should hear plainly that Scripture nowhere calls that tragedy the unforgivable sin; a true believer who dies in such darkness is still held by Christ, from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28).

The anxiety is the disproof. If you are reading this with your stomach tight, that tightness is not the symptom but the disproof: the Spirit does not trouble hearts he has stopped working on. The unforgivable sin has never once been committed by a person who wanted to be forgiven.

What about blasphemous thoughts that come into my mind against my will? Many tender believers are tormented by sudden, horrible thoughts about God or the Spirit, which they hate even as they arrive. Those thoughts are not the sin Jesus describes; they are temptations or intrusive thoughts, and the distress they cause shows your heart is on God’s side. Do not argue with them endlessly or try to prove you did not mean them. Bring them to Christ, tell him you hate them, and turn your attention to his promises. If they are persistent and consuming, speak to a wise pastor, and do not be ashamed to see a doctor too.

In everyday life. If you know someone haunted by this verse, do not leave them with it: sit with them, read John 6:37 aloud together, and remind them that the door is open.

For worship. Glory to the Spirit who does not give up easily. Fifty days after a Jerusalem crowd called for the death of the Son of Man, he cut men to the heart (Acts 2:23, 36–41), and about three thousand were baptised in the name of the one they had spoken against. The God who warns of the one sin never forgiven has forgiven every sin of everyone who comes to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they bring you. Not if. When. Luke’s second volume shows it again and again: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Stephen before the council (Acts 7), Paul before governors and a king (Acts 24–26). The range covers religious courts and civil ones, Jewish and Gentile, sometimes both at once.

How you should defend yourself. The word for defend yourself (apologēsēsthe) is the root behind apologetics, and in that world a technical term for a courtroom defence speech. A man in the dock had to make one, and men trained for years to do it well. They are told not to worry about it.

In that very hour. The Spirit who is blasphemed by unbelievers (v. 10) helps believers. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly before the council, and they were astonished at uneducated, common men (Acts 4:8–13). Stephen spoke with a wisdom they could not withstand (Acts 6:10).

The Son of Man standing. Stephen made his defence under this promise, and at the end of it he saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56): the one who promised to acknowledge his confessors before the angels (12:8) was on his feet for the first martyr. Later Jesus repeats the promise in his own name: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (21:15). The risen Lord is no spectator at his servants’ trials. He gives the words, and he watches from the throne.

What it does not mean. Two guards. It is not a licence for unprepared preaching. The situation named is arrest and official interrogation, not a man who has not opened his Bible all week and intends to trust the Spirit on Sunday; Paul told Timothy to do his best to present himself to God as one approved, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). And it is not a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen spoke under exactly this promise and was stoned. What is promised is not acquittal but the right words.

The ordinary comfort. The dread of not knowing what to say, at a hospital bedside, in a conversation that has suddenly turned serious, in front of someone hostile, is one of the commonest reasons Christians stay quiet. The promise is not that you will be eloquent. It is that in the hour, and not before it, you will not be alone in the room.

In the flow. The chapter’s first movement began with the mask worn for fear of what people think (v. 1) and ends with the last fear that keeps a disciple quiet. The Father counts the hairs, the Son confesses his own before the angels, and the Spirit gives the words: the whole Trinity stands behind a frightened witness.

In everyday life. Pray for persecuted Christians standing trial today, that the Spirit would give them words; find one name or country and pray for it specifically.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man interrupts teaching about hell and martyrdom, not to ask Jesus to settle a family estate but to tell his brother to divide it: he has already reached his verdict. Jesus refuses to be his arbitrator and warns the whole crowd against all covetousness, including the respectable kind that is sure it is only claiming what it is owed.

The parable of the rich fool follows: the land produced the harvest, the man forgot the Giver and told his soul that grain would satisfy it, and God’s first word to him is Fool.
verseByVerse.theology:
The fool of the Psalms is the one who says in his heart that there is no God (Psalm 14:1): not a philosophy but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist; he simply ran his life without reference to God. His soul, which he addressed as if it were his own, was on loan, and it was called in that night.

The alternative Jesus names is not poverty but being rich toward God: living as one who has received every good thing and uses it for God’s purposes, instead of treating it as one’s own achievement, accountable to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: The man’s problem was not his abundance but his accounting: what began as the land producing became my barns, my grain, my goods. And the question left hanging, whose will they be, is answered by everyone who hears it: somebody else’s.

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell my brother. Jesus has just been talking about hell, martyrdom and the courts, and a man in the crowd wants help with a family estate. In that world it was not unreasonable: rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes, and the law gave the eldest son a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). But he does not ask Jesus to settle the dispute; he says tell my brother. He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? The address is cool, man, not friend, and the refusal is flat. And there is an echo in it of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt: who made you a prince and a judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). Why refuse? Not because the grievance was necessarily unjust; Jesus never enquires. He declines because this is not what he came to do. He did not come to sort out property disputes, but to deal with the heart, and to act as referee over one man’s estate would have made him a hired official in a family quarrel, when he is the Lord of both brothers. The man’s real problem is not his brother, but his greed.

Judge of the living and the dead. The man’s question, who made me a judge, has an answer he did not know: God did. Peter would tell Cornelius that Jesus is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42). He will not sit as arbitrator over one field, because he will one day sit as Judge over both brothers and every field on earth, and he came first to bring them both under a better rule.

In the flow. Jesus has just told his friends not to fear those who can kill the body; this man shows the other thing that rules a heart besides fear, the grip of possessions. From here to verse 34 the chapter turns to money and anxiety.

All covetousness. He refuses the case, diagnoses the plaintiff, and then says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out. Covetousness (pleonexia) is the desire for more, and all covetousness includes the respectable kinds: the legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. The tenth commandment forbids it (Exodus 20:17), and Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). This man may well have been in the right. What Jesus saw was not a wronged brother but a man whose grip had closed.

Is it wrong to seek justice in a money dispute? Not in itself. Scripture values justice, and Paul himself used his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11). There are times when a fair settlement should be sought, especially to protect the vulnerable. But Jesus’ warning cuts close to every inheritance quarrel: ask what is happening in your heart. Is the money worth the brother? Christians should be slow to take one another to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–8), quick to seek reconciliation, and willing, sometimes, to be wronged rather than lose a relationship. Where you must pursue a claim, pursue it without bitterness, and be ready to let go of more than you think you can.

In everyday life. Where this saying applies: the quiet resentment over who got what in a will, the endless browsing for the next upgrade, the sense that a little more would finally be enough. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to shame a widow for seeking what she needs to live, or to tell a poor family that wanting a decent wage is covetous. Greed is the grip, not the need.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land produced. Only Luke records this parable, and the way it opens matters: not a rich man made a fortune, but the land produced. He may have ploughed and sown well, but the harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange (Acts 14:17). Every Israelite knew this; it is why firstfruits were brought to the temple and the edges of the field left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). It is the first thing the man will forget.

He thought to himself. Literally he dialogued with himself: not with God, not with his neighbours, not with the poor. No wife, no labourers who brought the harvest in, and above all no Giver: the whole discussion of an enormous surplus takes place inside one skull.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops? His problem is real. He is not a fraud or an oppressor; the parable gives him no vices at all. He has a genuine logistical difficulty, and the question he asks is the sensible one. A good question, with a wrong answer. The question had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. He could have shared with the poor (3:11); there were poor people within a mile of that farm. And listen to the pronoun: my crops. Everything is mine. In the three verses of his soliloquy he will say I or my again and again, and God will be mentioned by nobody but God.

Twelve baskets left over. Luke has already shown the opposite kind of life in the man telling this story. Before the great decisions of his ministry Jesus went out to talk with his Father (6:12). And in a deserted place he took five loaves and two fish, gave thanks, and fed about five thousand men, with twelve baskets left over (9:17). The rich fool’s surplus went into barns; Jesus’ surplus went into baskets for others.

In everyday life. The pay rise, the bonus, the inheritance, the unexpected refund: before it is absorbed into a larger lifestyle, stop and ask God and someone wise what it is for.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

parallels.desc: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Larger barns. The solution is entirely rational and entirely revealing. There are two things a man can do with a surplus: distribute it or store it. He never considers the first, and he demolishes serviceable buildings to build larger ones. And the ownership has quietly changed: it began as the land producing (v. 16); it is now my barns, my grain, my goods.

To my soul. This is the sentence the parable is built to reach. Having talked to himself for two verses, the man addresses the last available party, his own soul, as if it could be satisfied with grain, and tells it that its needs have been met.

Ample goods. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods: quantity, offered as an answer to a soul. Laid up for many years: a guarantee about a future he does not own. Relax, eat, drink, be merry: real goods, not one of which a soul can live on (compare Isaiah 22:13). He treats the ache of the soul as a supply problem. And it very nearly works: he was content, and he went to bed satisfied.

Something for the soul to eat. The man is right that his soul needs feeding, and wrong about the menu. Jesus never mocks the soul’s hunger; he came to meet it. He tells of a father who kills the fattened calf so that a lost son may eat (15:23), and at the last takes bread and says, This is my body, which is given for you (22:19). The barn-builder says to his soul: you have ample goods laid up. Christ says: I have been given for you. One is a store that will belong to someone else by morning; the other is a gift that death cannot recall.

Was his sin saving and planning ahead? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), and a man who does not provide for his family has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool’s sin was not the barns but the heart: everything was my crops, my barns, my goods, his future taken for granted and God left out. Saving for old age is wise; living as if the savings were your life is folly.

Is it wrong to look forward to retirement? Not at all. Rest after a lifetime of work is a good gift, and age brings real limits. The question is what retirement is for. The rich fool’s plan was to stop being useful and start consuming. A Christian’s later years can be some of his most fruitful: time to pray, to serve the church, to help grandchildren and neighbours, to give generously, to mentor younger believers. Plan for rest, enjoy it with thanks, and keep asking how you can be rich toward God with the time and money you have saved.

For worship. Blessed be the God who made the soul too large for any barn. He has put eternity into man’s heart (Ecclesiastes 3:11), so that no harvest could ever be enough, and then filled the emptiness with himself: whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35).

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fool. The first word God speaks in this parable comes in the same breath as be merry. He is not called wicked but a fool, and in the Bible that is not an insult about intelligence. The fool says in his heart, there is no God (Psalm 14:1): not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer was clever, successful and prudent. He simply made every plan as if God did not exist and as if he would never die. Then God speaks one sentence, and every plan is finished: he rules the calendar we write our plans in (James 4:13–15).

This night. Required (apaitousin) is a financial word: demanded back, as a loan is recalled. The soul he was addressing as his own had been on loan the whole time, and it is being called in tonight. He said many years. God says this night. The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

Into your hands. Set beside this night the night at the end of Luke’s Gospel. The rich fool’s soul is demanded back; he had no say. Jesus, dying, cried out, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (23:46). Nobody collected his life like a debt. He gave it, into a Father’s hands, for fools like this one. And because he did, Stephen under the stones could pray, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59). For those in Christ the night the soul is called in is not a creditor at the door. It is a Son receiving his own.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be? The question is left unanswered, and it lands hard precisely because everyone knows the answer is somebody else’s. He cannot take any of it with him (Psalm 49:16–17; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19; 1 Timothy 6:7). He tore down good barns to build larger ones for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once. Perhaps it went to the very kind of inheritance dispute that began this conversation (v. 13).

Rich toward God. For himself is the diagnosis; rich toward God is the alternative. And the alternative is not poverty: the man was rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to use what you have for him, for his kingdom, for the poor, for eternal treasure (v. 33; 1 Timothy 6:17–19).

What does being rich toward God look like? It begins with knowing God himself as your treasure, and then it shows in how you use everything else. It means giving regularly and generously to the church and to gospel work; caring for the poor and the stranger; being hospitable; supporting family members in need; and holding your possessions as a steward, ready to release them. It also includes being rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:18): time, attention and love spent on others. A poor widow with two small coins can be richer toward God than a millionaire (21:1–4).

Is it not harsh to call a hard-working man a fool? Not when you see what the fault is: it is not hard work, and Jesus finds no fault with his farming. The folly is that he rested everything on the one thing he could not control, the length of his life. That is the heart’s oldest idol: the belief that enough in the barn means I am safe and need no one, not even God. Religious people can build the same barn out of a record of good works. For the man in the story the word came too late. For us, hearing the parable while it is still today, it comes in time, and that is a mercy (2 Corinthians 6:2).
verseByVerse.note: In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God.

parallels.desc: the fool says in his heart, “There is no God”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The therefore ties this to the barns. The rich fool trusted his supplies; the disciples, most of whom had nothing to store, are tempted to worry about them, and underneath the two problems are the same. The needs named are food and clothing, and they are named to people who might go hungry.

Jesus argues from the least regarded creatures: ravens, unclean scavengers that God feeds, and wild flowers that will be burned as fuel within the week. Worry cannot add an hour to life. The alternative is not serenity but a different pursuit, seeking the kingdom, and behind it the tenderest words in the passage, fear not, little flock: the Father is glad to give you the kingdom. The section ends with treasure in heaven and the heart that follows it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity. Ravens still hunt and farmers still plant. What is addressed is anxiety, the energy spent on what worry cannot secure.

O you of little faith is a name Jesus uses only of disciples. It traces ordinary worry to a shortage of trust in a particular Father, without making every anxious believer faithless. The nations, the Gentile world with its gods to be bargained with, had reason to be anxious: if nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better. Against that stands the fact that the Father knows what his children need. They do not have to lobby him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that worry achieves nothing does not cure it. What the argument does is change the question from how to stop worrying to what to trust instead.

The command to sell possessions is not a metaphor, but Luke shows it is a transfer of ownership, not a rule about percentages (19:8–9; Acts 5:4): nothing may be held back from him. And the heart follows the treasure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore. The therefore ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson for the disciples, most of whom had nothing to store, is not store less but worry less. The rich fool trusted his possessions; the poor can be just as preoccupied with them through anxiety. Both try to secure a life by managing supplies.

Your life, your body. Anxious (merimnate) means divided in mind, distracted: Martha’s word (10:41), and the cares that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14). Food and clothing are the two irreducible necessities, and this is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

More than food. If the Creator has already given the great things, a living soul and a body, he is hardly going to withhold the small ones that keep them going. And life is not the sum of what sustains it: a man can have all the food and clothing he needs and be, as the last parable showed, a fool who dies that night.

Consider the ravens. The choice of bird would have registered. Ravens were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers, the least regarded; Matthew says birds of the air (Matthew 6:26), but Luke names the bird nobody wanted. And there is a psalm about exactly this: he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry (Psalm 147:9).

Yet God feeds them. Without a barn between them, unlike the rich fool. If God feeds the birds nobody wants, how much more will he feed his children.

Nowhere to lay his head. The one who says this lived it. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58). He was supported by women who gave out of their means (8:3), and in the wilderness, starving, he refused to turn a stone into bread for himself (4:4). When he tells anxious disciples to consider the ravens, he is not a rich man advising the poor. He is the poorest man in the company, inviting them into the trust he lived in.

What it does not mean. Not that we should stop working or planning. The ravens are set against the rich fool’s barns, not against the farmer’s plough: the birds still go out after their food (compare 2 Thessalonians 3:10). The verse is against the belief that security comes from the size of the reserve.

Is anxiety a sin, then, and is every anxious believer of little faith? Jesus is speaking to worry about food and clothing that springs from not trusting the Father. But some anxiety has roots in the body and the mind, and it is a real illness. Elijah despaired (1 Kings 19:4), the psalmist wrestled with his troubled soul (Psalm 77), and they were not cast off. Seeking help from a doctor or counsellor is not a lack of faith. The command still invites every anxious believer to bring the fear to the Father who knows what we need (v. 30).

In everyday life. Where this saying applies: the late-night spiral about bills you have already planned for, the fear that God will not provide when he always has, the constant checking of a balance that has not changed. Where applying it would be wrong: telling a family with no food to stop worrying instead of helping them. The church is often the Father’s answer to the raven’s cry.
verseByVerse.note: Ravens were unclean birds — yet God feeds them.

parallels.desc: he gives to the young ravens that cry

verseByVerse.quote: And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Having argued from the birds, he argues from the results, and the question is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible, the alert mind doing necessary work, and it feels like preparation. What has it ever produced? The phrase can also be read a single cubit to his stature, about eighteen inches of height (the ESV notes this). Either way, nobody has ever managed it by worrying. If anything, worry shortens life.

If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? And there is the second turn, the sharper one. He calls adding an hour to a life a small thing, and that inverts the whole scale. From where we stand, an extra hour of life is not a small thing at all; it is precisely what a person at a bedside would give everything for. Jesus calls it the little end of the problem, and if a man cannot manage the little end, the anxiety about food and clothing is aimed at something he is even less able to control. Worry is useless. It does not change tomorrow; it only spoils today. And it forgets God, who controls what we cannot.

Clearing the ground. This is not exactly a comfort but a demolition: anxiety is a machine that runs continuously, burns enormous fuel, and produces nothing. That clears the ground for the right question: not how do I stop worrying? but what am I going to trust instead? The answer is not a technique. It is a Father.

When the days drew near. Jesus measured his own life not by hours he could add but by an hour his Father had set. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51); in the garden he prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42); and to the men with swords he said, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). He walked unhurried into the darkest hour there has ever been, because his times were in his Father’s hand, and he calls his friends into that same trust.

What is the difference between worry and responsible concern? Concern looks at a real problem, does what can be done, and then leaves the rest with God. Worry keeps turning the problem over long after anything can be done, and treats the turning as if it were doing something. A parent who books a doctor for a sick child is concerned; a parent who lies awake rehearsing every terrible outcome is worried. Paul’s cure is specific: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6–7). Do the next thing, pray about the rest, and give thanks.

In everyday life. Has worrying ever changed anything? Take the thing you are anxious about and divide it into two lists: what I can do today, and what only God can do. Do the first list. Pray over the second, item by item, and then deliberately give thanks for one thing.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.”

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the lilies. The lilies are probably the wild blooms that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring, anemones perhaps, scarlet and brief. The two activities named are the two halves of a household’s labour: men toiled in the field, women spun thread for cloth. The flowers do neither.

Even Solomon. Solomon is the highest available standard, the king whose court left a foreign queen breathless (1 Kings 10:4–5). And a weed on a hillside beats him: dressed by nobody, and gone in a fortnight.

Thrown into the oven. The detail is deliberately unglamorous. The hillsides dried out, and the stalks were gathered as fuel for a peasant’s clay oven. So God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will be burned within the week to heat somebody’s bread.

O you of little faith. The rebuke is gentle, and it is a rebuke. Little-faith ones is one word, used by Jesus only of disciples; nobody is called little-faith who has none. And the diagnosis is not your circumstances but a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father. That does not make an anxious believer faithless, or turn an illness of the mind into a sin; but underneath most ordinary worry lies a belief about God: that he might forget me, or not care, or not be able. So the deepest cure is knowing him better, because those who know his name put their trust in him (Psalm 9:10).

Greater than Solomon. A chapter earlier Jesus told this crowd that something greater than Solomon is here (11:31). The greater than Solomon was dressed in splendid clothing by Herod’s soldiers to mock him (23:11), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). The King who robes the hillsides went to his death with less covering than a wildflower, and says how much more will he clothe you as the one who would be stripped to keep that promise.

How can little faith grow? Not by staring at your faith, but by looking at God. Faith grows as it feeds on his promises and remembers his past faithfulness. Read the Psalms that recount what he has done. Keep a record of answered prayer. Sit under the preaching of his word. Take small steps of obedience that require trust, and watch him keep his word. And pray as the father of the boy with the unclean spirit did: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not reject that prayer. He answered it.

For worship. The God who paints anemones for a single week has clothed his people in the righteousness of Christ, a garment of salvation that will never wear out or be thrown in the oven.
verseByVerse.note: Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor be worried. The word, meteōrizesthe, was used of a ship tossed on the swell or something suspended in mid-air (it gives English meteor): anxious suspense, unanchored, going wherever the next wave puts you. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise it.

All the nations of the world. The nations is the standard Jewish term for the Gentiles, used here as description, not insult. The pagan world had gods of harvest, weather and household to be managed, none notably fond of you and none reliable, so provision had to be negotiated without end. In that setting anxiety is rational: if nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Your Father knows. Your Father: the name he taught them to pray with (11:2). Knows: so it need not be brought to his attention, and much anxious praying is really lobbying, as though the case had not yet been properly presented. That you need them: the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual. It is not a technique for calming down but a fact about who is in charge of the supply.

Revealed by the Son. What makes the difference between the nations and the little band around Jesus is not that the disciples were cleverer, but that they had been brought to know God as Father. No one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). The anxious pagan could not say your Father. The Son came to make orphans into sons: God sent forth his Son to redeem, so that we might receive adoption as sons and cry, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:4–6). Adoption takes a stranger into God’s family for ever, with a son’s name, access and inheritance, not for any merit but because he is joined to the Son (Galatians 4:7).

If my Father already knows, why pray about my needs? Because he tells us to ask: give us each day our daily bread (11:3). Prayer is not briefing God; it is trusting him out loud. Asking reminds us that every meal is a gift, keeps us dependent, and turns anxiety into conversation. The difference between pagan prayer and Christian prayer is not that one asks and the other does not. It is that the pagan asks in order to persuade a reluctant power, and the Christian asks as a child whose Father already knows and already cares.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. 'Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not seek nothing. He has just said the nations seek after food and drink, and uses the same verb: go after this instead (Matthew adds and his righteousness, Matthew 6:33). The alternative to anxiety is not serenity but a different pursuit, and the man chasing the kingdom grows calmer because his attention has gone somewhere it can get purchase.

Added to you. Food and clothing, as extras: not the object of the deal but not withheld either. It is not a promise that a Christian will never be hungry; Paul knew what it was to be in need (Philippians 4:12). What is promised is that the Father who knows will not forget, not that provision will always look like comfort.

Fear not, little flock. Only Luke records this saying, among the tenderest things Jesus called his disciples. Little flock is an honest name: a small, vulnerable group in an occupied province, like sheep among wolves (10:3). He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is, with all the weight of Psalm 23, of Isaiah 40:11, where he gathers the lambs in his arms, and of Ezekiel 34, where God himself searches for his sheep.

Your Father’s good pleasure. The verb (eudokēsen) means it was his glad decision, the same verb as at the Jordan: with you I am well pleased (3:22). The Father’s delight in his Son and his delight in giving the kingdom to the Son’s little flock are one delight, and at the last supper Jesus tells the Twelve, I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom (22:29). If he gives you the kingdom, will he not give you bread? He who did not spare his own Son, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32).

So what does seeking the kingdom look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks like the day you already have, lived under a different King. At breakfast it is thanking him and asking what he wants of you today. At work it is honest effort and fair dealing, done as for the Lord. At home it is patience with a tired spouse and time for a child. In money it is giving first and spending carefully. When you are wronged it is forgiveness; when you fail it is confession. It also means gathering with his people on the Lord’s Day and sharing Christ when the door opens. It rarely feels dramatic. It is ordinary walking in God’s will, one decision at a time, with his kingdom, not your comfort, as the question you ask first.

In everyday life. Where this saying applies: the choice between a promotion that would swallow your family and church life and a slower path that keeps them; the decision to give before you spend. Where applying it would be wrong: thinking you must leave your job for full-time ministry to really seek the kingdom, or neglecting your family’s needs for a church project. The kingdom is sought in the ordinary calling God has given you.

parallels.desc: he will tend his flock like a shepherd
the kingdom given to the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sell your possessions. The command is not a metaphor, and some early Christians did exactly this (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–37). Does the Lord require every Christian to liquidate everything?

A transfer of ownership. Luke supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half his goods, and salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they still had. And Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on this: while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? (Acts 5:4). So the command is not a rule about percentages but a transfer of ownership: whatever is still in the disciple’s hands is at the Master’s disposal. For one man that means selling the lot, as for the rich ruler whose possessions owned him (18:22); for another an open house or a quietly emptied account. It can never mean a Christian who has drawn a line and considers the rest his own.

Moneybags that do not grow old. Leather purses wore out, and wealth stored as fine clothing could be eaten by moths or stolen. He is not against investment; he is against bad investment. What is given to God and the poor is stored up in heaven (1 Timothy 6:18–19), and treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary: kindness, generosity and faithful work done for Christ.

Where your treasure is. The order is not what anyone expects. We assume the heart chooses and the money follows; he says the heart goes to where the treasure already is. So the affections can be steered: a man who cannot make himself care about something can move his money into it and find, months later, that his heart has followed. And it shows what you actually love, as distinct from what you say you love: not the confession of faith, but the bank statement and the diary.

Where Christ is. Why should the heart want to go there? Because that is where the Lord is: seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1). Treasure in heaven is not a private account in the sky but everything given away for love of him, laid up with the one who gave himself away first. The heart that follows its treasure upward arrives not at a vault but at a person.

How much should I give, and to whom? The New Testament sets no fixed figure, but it asks for regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). Begin with your own church, which feeds you; then the needy around you, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10); then gospel work further afield. Many find a tenth a wise starting point and grow from there. Give in a way that costs you something, plan it rather than leaving it to impulse, and do it quietly. If you are in debt or poverty, give what you can with a glad heart; the widow’s two coins counted most of all.

In the flow. The section began with a man wanting more from his brother (v. 13) and ends with Jesus telling his disciples to give away. A heart whose treasure is in heaven looks for the one who is coming from there, and so the servants waiting for their master come next.

In everyday life. Where this applies: the possession you could not bear to lose, the room full of things you have not used in years. Where applying it would be wrong: selling the family home without your spouse’s agreement, giving away what your children need, or treating a tired single mother’s modest savings as a sin. Hold everything open-handed, and let love, not guilt, decide what goes.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three parables of readiness describe the church living between Christ’s first coming and his return. The servants wait, belts fastened and lamps lit like Israel on the Passover night, for a master returning from a wedding feast at an hour nobody knows. Their readiness comes down to opening the door at once. And the master who finds them awake will tie up his own robe and serve them, as Jesus did at the Last Supper (22:27; John 13:4–5).

The thief changes the colour of the same arrival: what differs is the state of the person inside. Peter asks whether the parable is for the Twelve or for all, and Jesus answers with a parable about a steward set over others: yes, especially you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The master who serves his watching servants overturns every ancient picture of authority, and it is the pattern of Christ’s whole ministry: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45).

The steward (oikonomos) owns nothing and holds the keys; his one named duty is to feed the household at the proper time, the commission Peter later received on a beach (John 21:15–17). His reward is a larger trust, not retirement. And the hidden hour is part of the design: if the time were known, readiness would be put off, as the wicked servant puts it off when he decides his master is delayed.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bad servant’s ruin begins with a private conclusion that his master is delayed; then he turns on the people he was given to feed and to his own appetites.

The two beatings show that judgment has degrees, weighed by what each knew, though ignorance reduces the sentence without producing innocence. And the closing principle falls hardest on the well-taught: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible and years of clear preaching are gifts entrusted, not rewards. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter but an account, and the believer who keeps turning to Christ finds that account settled at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Readiness for Christ’s return. From possessions Jesus turns to his return, and the two are linked: those whose treasure is in heaven are already leaning toward the day it is opened.

Stay dressed for action. Literally let your loins stay girded, as the ESV notes. A long outer robe had to be pulled up and tucked into the belt for running, working or fighting; to be girded was to be unable to lounge. And it has a history: Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened, sandals on and staff in hand (Exodus 12:11), dressed to leave a country that night.

The exodus he accomplished. On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, literally his exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (9:31). The disciples dress like Israel on the Passover night because a greater exodus is under way, and its Lamb is the one speaking (1 Corinthians 5:7). The fastened belt is not the dress of people hoping to be rescued. It is the dress of people whose ransom has been paid and whose departure is certain.

Lamps burning. A lamp kept burning through the dark hours needed somebody awake to trim the wick and top up the oil. Readiness is not achieved once and possessed; it is maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

From the wedding feast. A wedding feast could run for days, and there was no knowing which night the master would come back or at what hour. The servants have no timetable, only a duty that continues regardless.

The door at once. The whole of their readiness reduces to one modest test: not whether they achieved anything impressive in his absence, but whether, when he knocked, somebody on the other side of the door was still expecting him.

What does being ready actually mean? Not living in a constant state of alarm, or giving up ordinary work to watch the sky. It means being a true believer, trusting Christ now, with nothing between you and him that you would be ashamed for him to find. It means keeping short accounts with God and others, confessing sin quickly and putting wrongs right. And it means being about your Master’s business: faithful in the work, the family and the church he has given you. A ready servant may be found asleep in bed at night; what matters is that he is the Master’s, and expecting him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the literal wording, “Let your loins stay girded” — the long robe tucked into the belt for work.

parallels.desc: your belt fastened, ready to leave

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will come and serve them. Nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for this. The master ties up his own robe, the same girding the servants were told to do in v. 35, sits them at his table, and waits on them. That whole society rested on the line between those who recline and those who serve; a master returning at midnight expects his meal (17:7–8). The Truly, I say to you is Jesus flagging that he knows how this sounds.

Picture or promise? Both, and Luke shows it. At the Supper he says it about himself in plain words: who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). And on the same night John records him rising from the meal, tying a towel round himself, and washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), girded, exactly as here. He came not to be served but to serve. So the image is not a flourish. It is what he is like, and it is what he did. The Lord of glory will serve his people at the banquet of the kingdom.

The second watch, or the third. Whether Luke counts the night in Roman four watches or Jewish three, these fall in its depths: the hardest time to stay awake and the least expected time to come. That is where most Christian waiting is done. The first years are rarely the hardest. What is hard is year twenty, in the dark, with no sign of anything, holding a lamp.

Will Christ really serve us in heaven, rather than we serving him? Both. Scripture says his servants will worship him (Revelation 22:3), and we will gladly serve him for ever. But the deepest truth of the kingdom is that he serves us first and always: he feeds us at his table, wipes away our tears, and gives us himself. Our service is only ever a response to his. Heaven is not a place where Christ finally gets the reward of being waited on by us. It is the place where we discover the full extent of how he loves to give.

In everyday life. If you are in the dead middle of a long night, a long illness, a long wait for a prodigal, a long season of dryness, keep your lamp lit for one more hour. Do the next small faithful thing. The Master who is coming is not a harsh inspector but the one who will tie on an apron and serve you.

For worship. The King of kings, before whom angels veil their faces, will tie up his robe and bring the dishes to tired servants who managed to stay awake. He has served us once already, at the cross, with his own body and blood, and the hands that pass the bread at the feast will still bear the marks of that first service.
verseByVerse.note: The second and third watches covered the middle of the night.

parallels.desc: he dressed himself and washed their feet

verseByVerse.quote: But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thief. The register changes completely. A few verses ago the arrival was a master coming home from a wedding; now it is a burglary, and the householder is asleep. Same event, opposite colour, and the difference is entirely in the state of the person inside.

Broken into. Literally dug through: a thief made a hole in a mud-brick wall. The householder is not blamed for sleeping at night; he is caught out because the one thing he needed, the hour, was the one thing unavailable.

An hour you do not expect. Not that Christ is a thief, but that his coming will be as unexpected: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). The image is about the timing, never his character, and no one knows the day (Mark 13:32).

Why the hour is hidden. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled, and everyone would schedule it late, as the servant in the next parable does. The unknowability is the arrangement: it makes readiness a way of living rather than a task done nearer the time. A man who has worked out when the thief is coming has not increased his readiness; he has explained why it can wait. And there is mercy in it: no Christian is asked to be ready later, only now, which is the only thing anybody can actually do.

The time of your visitation. His first coming was already being missed: weeping over Jerusalem, he would say you did not know the time of your visitation (19:44). The city that read the prophets every Sabbath slept through the arrival of its King. But shepherds keeping watch by night heard the news first (2:8–11), and Simeon and Anna were among those waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Lord who came once to a sleeping house and a few watchers is telling his friends now which kind of household to be.

Will Christ come secretly first and take believers away before the end? This commentary holds that he will not. Many earnest believers have been taught that Christ will first remove his church secretly before a great tribulation, and they long for his appearing as sincerely as anyone; this is a difference among brothers, not a test of faith. The New Testament describes one visible, public return of Christ at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, believers are gathered to him, and the world is judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). His coming is unexpected in its timing, like a thief, but not hidden in its manner: every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). That is why the call is simply to be ready, all the time, for the day itself.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said, 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?' And the Lord said, 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? It is a very Petrine question, and Luke keeps it because of what it exposes. What is Peter actually asking? Probably this: is the standard the same for the Twelve as for the crowd, or is there a separate arrangement for us? He has heard a warning about servants and unexpected arrivals, and he wants to know which category he is in.

Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household? Jesus does not answer the question directly. He does something better and more uncomfortable: he tells another parable, and this one is especially for people with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, it does apply especially to you, Peter, but not in the direction the question was hoping. The manager is an oikonomos, a steward, often himself a trusted slave, but one placed over the whole household and its supplies, with authority to run it (16:1). He held the keys and the accounts. He was not the owner of anything, and he could be dismissed. The word is used of church leaders: stewards of the mysteries of God, of whom it is required that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7).

Their portion of food. His one named duty is not to increase the estate, nor to keep order, but to feed the household: Christian leadership as Jesus states it, feeding God’s household with his word, faithfully and at the right time. It is the commission Peter will be given on a beach three times over (John 21:15–17), and hand on to the elders (1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).

Faithful and wise. Faithful: trustworthy with what is not his. Wise: knowing what the household needs and when. A reliable man with no judgment will feed them the wrong thing, and a shrewd one who cannot be trusted will feed himself. And the steward is not asked to produce food from nowhere, only to distribute what the master has provided, on time, to people who are hungry now.

A Son over the house. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Jesus is the steward who never once fed himself from the stores: he taught daily in the temple (19:47), and on his last night, with the cross hours away, he was still setting food before his disciples (22:14–20). Every pastor and parent who feeds others is handing out what he provided, and will answer to him.

If I am not a church leader, is this for me? Yes, in its own measure. Every Christian is a steward of something: a family to feed spiritually as well as physically, a Sunday school class, a friend who looks to you, gifts and money and time (1 Peter 4:10). Parents especially are managers of a household, given the task of feeding their children with God’s word at the proper time. The questions are the same for you as for a pastor: am I faithful with what is not mine, and wise about what the people in my care need now?
verseByVerse.note: A household manager was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So doing. The blessing is not attached to results but to still working faithfully at the thing he was left to do, on the day the master happens to arrive. That removes the metric most people in Christian work quietly measure themselves by: the steward answers not for the size of the household but for whether the food went out on time. The aim is not a heroic finish but an unbroken habit.

A bigger job. The reward for having been trusted with a job is a bigger job: not a pension or an easier post, but more responsibility, permanently (19:17). Faithful servants will share Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12). Scripture gives few details, but it means real work in a renewed creation, every gift used with no sin to spoil it and no death to cut it short (Revelation 22:3–5).

All his possessions. The steward began with no property at all and ends with the run of the estate, all of it entrusted, none of it his by right. That is what being an heir means: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

Are rewards in heaven earned? No. Every reward is grace upon grace: God gives the gifts, the strength to use them, and then rewards the use as if it were ours (1 Corinthians 4:7; 15:10). Salvation itself is never earned; it rests on Christ alone. But Scripture does promise real, differing rewards to faithful servants, and Jesus means us to be encouraged by them. There will be no envy in heaven, because every servant will be full, and every crown will be cast at his feet (Revelation 4:10).

In everyday life. What the Master has given you to do is probably not glamorous: the nappies, the spreadsheet, the hospital visit, the Bible study preparation, the care of an ageing parent. Do today’s portion of it faithfully, and stop measuring yourself by results he has not asked you for.

verseByVerse.quote: But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My master is delayed. Everything that follows comes out of that one sentence, said to himself. No moment of rebellion, no decision to become a tyrant: a private conclusion about a timetable. And it is not even wrong; the master is delayed. What is wrong is what the servant does with an accurate observation. People begin to think he will never come (2 Peter 3:3–4), and live accordingly.

To beat and to get drunk. These are the two directions in which a leader goes bad. He turns on the household: authority given to feed his fellow servants is used to hit them, which in religious office seldom involves fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, discipline that is really about control. And he turns to himself: eat and drink and get drunk echoes the rich fool, and the food he was appointed to distribute (v. 42) goes down his own throat. A man who expects his employer within the hour does not start drinking the cellar.

Cut him in pieces. The phrase is violent, and its exact sense is disputed (possibly cut him off), but the verdict is not. The household is God’s: to mistreat those he has entrusted to you is to sin against him (Ezekiel 34:2–10). He held the keys and the office, and the accounting placed him where he had actually been standing all along.

Is this servant a true believer who loses his salvation? Luke’s own word answers it. He is put with the unfaithful, the apistoi, which also means unbelievers: he ends among the people who never trusted the master, because that is what he was. He is a professing servant, a leader in the household, whose conduct shows he never truly knew his master; Matthew says he is put with the hypocrites (Matthew 24:51). He held office in the household without ever belonging to its Lord, and his treatment of others exposed it. Cut in pieces is a picture of severe judgment, not of a believer’s fall from grace. A true servant may fail and be disciplined, but those who belong to Christ endure to the end because he keeps them.

The Master beaten in his own house. The parable came true against Jesus himself within months. In the high priest’s house his guards blindfolded the Lord of the household and beat him (22:63–64). He did not return the blows; he went on to the cross for servants like them. So the judgment here is the verdict of one who knows in his own body what it is to be struck by those who should have served, and who will not let it stand in his house.

What should a church do about a leader who abuses those in his care? Take it seriously and act, because Jesus does. Abuse of any kind, physical, sexual, emotional or spiritual, must never be tolerated or covered up to protect a ministry’s reputation. Crimes should be reported to the civil authorities; victims should be believed, protected and cared for; and the leader should be removed from office while the matter is examined honestly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). A leader is a servant over the household, never its owner. A church that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable has taken the side of the servant in this parable.

In everyday life. Ask where the long delay has made you careless: in your use of authority at home or work, in your appetites, in what you excuse because judgment feels far away. If you lead anyone, ask the people under you whether you serve them or use them, listen, and bring what you hear to the Master who forgives servants who confess (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knew his master’s will. Deliberate disobedience in full knowledge brings greater judgment.

A light beating. Two servants, the same offence, different sentences, and the difference is what each knew. Judgment has degrees: it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for the Galilean towns that watched him work (10:13–14). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion (Romans 2:12). But the second servant is not acquitted. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence.

Much was given. The passive was given is the reverent way of saying God gave, so every item is a deposit, not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible in your own language, a church down the road, years of clear preaching, health, money, time. Each raises the bar, for teachers above all (James 3:1), and for Christians in wealthy and free countries.

An account, not a shelter. This falls hardest on the well-taught. The man who has heard the gospel plainly for four decades and done nothing about it is not in the safer category; he is nearer the severe beating than the light one. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter. It is an account. The believer who has heard much and, however haltingly, keeps turning to Christ is not that servant; his account was settled at the cross.

Does this mean people who never heard the gospel will be saved by their ignorance? No. The servant who did not know still receives a beating; ignorance lessens judgment but does not remove guilt, because all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). Salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why the church must send preachers. God will judge everyone with perfect fairness, according to what they knew. Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or believe, are in the hands of a merciful God, and we may trust that his elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit. Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on the kindness of the Saviour who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

By his stripes. Both servants deserve a beating, and there is no third servant who does not. The gospel answers not with a lighter sentence but with a substitute. Pilate, finding no guilt in Jesus, still said, I will therefore punish and release him (23:16), and the flogging followed (Mark 15:15). The one who knew his Father’s will perfectly and did all of it took the stripes owed to servants who knew and did not: wounded for our transgressions, so that by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). He did not merely suffer alongside sinners; he stood in their place and bore the penalty, so that it will never be laid on them (1 Peter 2:24).

Should I avoid learning more of the Bible so as to be judged less? That would be to choose darkness so as not to be blamed for it, which is itself a sin against light. The goal is not to know less but to obey what you know. Every truth learned is a gift to be lived, and the same God who requires much gives grace to do it. A believer who keeps learning and keeps obeying, however imperfectly, is not storing up judgment but growing in Christ.

In everyday life. You have been given much, and you will never use it perfectly. Christ did his Father’s will perfectly in your place; his obedience is counted as yours, and for his sake your faltering service is accepted. So name three things you have been given that most of the world has not, and ask of each: what does my Master want me to do with it this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–59 — Fire, Division, and the Urgent Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with three urgent sayings. Jesus longs for the fire he came to cast, the fire of the Spirit and of judgment, but first he must undergo a baptism, the drowning of the cross, and he is pressed until it is accomplished. Pentecost waits on Golgotha.

He brings peace with God, but not the peace of a world where the question of who he is goes unasked, and so he divides even households (Micah 7:6). Last, he turns to the crowd: they read the clouds from the sea and the hot wind from the desert correctly, and will not read the present time. They must settle with God on the road, before they reach the Judge.
verseByVerse.theology:
The distress of 12:50 is not a man hanging back from the cross. Gethsemane shows that the dread was real; this shows what lay under it: he wanted what lay beyond the cross so much that the waiting was torment.

The charge of hypocrisy at 12:56 is precise. The crowd can read evidence and has declined to read it in the one place that matters. And the call to judge for themselves is not an invitation to decide what suits them, since a person can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Proverbs 14:12). It asks why they have not drawn the conclusion already in front of them, and the honest answer is usually that it would cost something.
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying speaks to anyone whose family went cold at their conversion. Jesus said it in advance, which is the mercy in it: when everything was done gently and the fracture came anyway, it is not proof of failure.

Every generation is expert at reading something, markets, politics, a career, and often never asks what God is doing in its own lifetime. And the last penny is an illustration of urgency, not a doctrine of purgatory: settle now, on the road, and know that the settlement is an amnesty bought at the Judge’s own expense (7:41–42; Colossians 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fire on the earth. For two verses Luke lets us hear what it was like inside him. In Scripture fire pictures judgment (3:9, 17), purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and the Holy Spirit: John announced that the Messiah would baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire (3:16), and Acts opens with tongues as of fire resting on the waiting disciples (Acts 2:3). The same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on. Would that it were already kindled is a compressed, awkward exclamation in the Greek: a man wishing out loud.

A baptism. The word means to be plunged, submerged, and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Psalm 42:7). He is talking about his death (Mark 10:38) and calling it a drowning: on the cross he would go under the full weight of God’s holy anger against the sins of his people, as a man goes under a flood, because the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6).

How great is my distress. The word (synechomai) means gripped, hemmed in; Luke uses it of a high fever (4:38) and of an army closing on a city (19:43). It is a glimpse of Jesus’ inner anguish on the road to the cross, anticipating Gethsemane (22:42–44, though verses 43–44 are missing from some early manuscripts; the agony itself is plain in 22:42).

Pentecost waits on Golgotha. Read the two verses together: the fire he longs for cannot be lit until the baptism of Calvary is finished, and he is pressed between them. This is not a man hanging back. He wanted what was on the far side badly enough that the waiting was a torment, because he longed to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

In the flow. Before he returns as Judge, Jesus must be plunged into death at Jerusalem, and that makes the chapter’s warnings urgent. People will divide over him (vv. 51–53), and the crowds must read the times and settle with God while they are still on the road (vv. 54–59).

Does this baptism tell us anything about Christian baptism? Indirectly, yes. Jesus calls his death a baptism, and Paul says that believers are baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). That is why this commentary holds believer’s baptism by immersion: going under the water pictures union with Christ in the death he describes here, and coming up pictures resurrection, and in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers as members of God’s covenant people, much as Israel’s sons were circumcised, see the same union signified in the baptism of infants, and we honour their faith. But the reality behind every baptism is this one, which Jesus endured alone.

For worship. He wanted the cross over, not to escape it but to reach a people set alight by the Spirit he would pour out. He went down into the flood alone, and stands now on its far shore with all whom he carried through. The fire he longed to kindle has never gone out.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? The sentence is meant to shock, not least because the angels announced on earth peace over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14), and Zechariah sang that he would guide our feet into the way of peace (1:79). Both are true. Jesus brings real peace: peace with God, which every human being most needs and cannot manufacture (Romans 5:1), and peace among those who belong to him. What he never promised is the peace of the world, a peace without truth, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked.

Rather division. His coming divides people by their response to him. Simeon said it over the infant: this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and a sword would pierce through his mother’s own soul (2:34–35). The division would cut even his own mother, and he never asks a disciple to stand where he has not stood.
