Five divided. Five is a household: father, mother, son, daughter, and the son’s wife living with them. Three against two, then two against three: the same fracture from both sides, because in a divided house both halves feel like the ones being left.

Every pair in both directions. The source is Micah 7:6, a society coming apart in a time of judgment, where a man’s enemies are the men of his own house. Jesus says it will happen because of loyalty to him. And every pair is named in both directions: there is no suggestion that the believing half will find it easy or behave well.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciple should go looking for a quarrel or leave his family to fend for itself. Paul tells believers to live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and a great deal of family division is caused by Christians being insufferable rather than by Christ. But when others reject Christ, conflict may come, and loyalty to Christ must come first (14:26).

The mercy of a warning. Someone reading this is living inside it. Jesus does not say the division is good. He says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold at his conversion often concludes that he handled it badly. When everything has been done gently and the division comes anyway, it is not evidence of failure. It is the thing he warned about, happening.

How do I love a family that opposes my faith? Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Be the kindest, most helpful person at the family table, and let your life speak before your words. Do not preach at every gathering; do answer honestly when asked. Pray for them faithfully, sometimes for decades. Keep the door open, and refuse bitterness when they mock. Where there is real danger or abuse, you may need distance for safety, and that is not unloving. And remember that God has often used one believer’s patient faithfulness to bring a whole household to Christ (Acts 16:31–34).

Is this not the trouble with religion, that it divides people? Every strong conviction divides, the sceptic’s included. The real question is what a conviction does to those who disagree with it. The Christ who divides is the one who prayed for the men crucifying him (23:34) and told his followers to love their enemies (6:27). A faith whose centre is a man laying down his life for those who rejected him gives no licence to hate anyone, and Christians who have used it that way have betrayed him.

In everyday life. Where this applies: the parent who disowns a child for being baptised, the spouse who mocks every prayer. Where it would be wrong: excusing rudeness or neglect, or cutting off a family that simply finds your faith strange. Ask whether the offence is Christ, or you.

For worship. The Prince of Peace accepted being the cause of division, because the only lasting peace is peace with God. His own family once thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and still he gathers into his family everyone who does his Father’s will. In him the lonely believer has a household that can never be divided.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A cloud rising in the west. He turns to the crowds and begins with the weather. West of Israel is the Mediterranean: cloud building over the sea meant rain, as Elijah’s servant saw from Carmel (1 Kings 18:44).

The south wind. South is the Negev and the desert; a south wind meant scorching heat that could strip a crop in a day. Two signs, two confident readings, and Jesus grants that they are right: their instincts about the sky are reliable and hard-won.

You hypocrites. The charge is precise. They can read evidence and have declined to in the one place it matters, and the selectiveness makes it hypocrisy rather than error. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what is standing in front of him has made a choice, and is pretending it was a limitation.

But why do you not know how to interpret the present time? “The present time” (kairos) is this decisive moment, the time of God’s visitation. And consider what he expects them to have read. Not a secret sign. The whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor being told good news, thousands following, and the religious authorities plotting a death. The Messiah was among them, and he had said so in plain words at Nazareth: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21). Any of it could have been interpreted by a man who reads clouds for a living. But they would not read it, and he will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:44).

Turning it on ourselves. Every generation is expert at reading something: markets, politics, the mood of a culture, a career. And the person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

Does this mean I should try to match news events to Bible prophecy? Not in the way that often happens. Jesus’ point is that the decisive time had already arrived in his own coming, and his hearers were ignoring it. The present time, for us, is the age between his first and second comings: the day of salvation, when the gospel goes to the nations and his return is always near: no one can set the date, though Scripture names things that will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Reading the times means recognising that, and responding with repentance, faith and readiness, rather than building charts of headlines. Discernment is spiritual, not speculative.

In everyday life. Can you read the signs of what God is doing? Take ten minutes and ask: where has God been at work in my life in the last year, in a trial, an answered prayer, a conviction that will not go away? The Spirit who gave you eyes for his Son will teach you to read it.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? One short question, and it assumes a great deal. He has just told them they can read the sky and will not read the times. Now he asks why they do not work it out themselves. You have the evidence; use your own judgment, honestly, and you will see who I am and what you must do. The time for decision is now.

Not for want of a teacher. The resources for the judgment are already in their possession. The verb is the one for reaching a verdict, and for yourselves puts the responsibility where the crowd would least like it. They had spent the chapter asking him to settle things: my inheritance (v. 13), a sign (11:16), whether this parable is for us (v. 41). He hands it back.

What it does not mean. It is not an invitation to make it up: a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Proverbs 14:12; Jeremiah 17:9). The question is narrower and harder: given the evidence you can already read, the conscience you have, the Scriptures you possess, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? Very often, because the conclusion would cost something. The crowd’s problem is not a shortage of light but an unwillingness to act on it.

Who do you say that I am? The verdict Jesus wants them to reach for themselves is a verdict about him. He had put that question to his disciples in private, and Peter answered, The Christ of God (9:20). Nothing of the evidence was hidden from the crowd: they had seen the lame walk and the demons go, heard the poor given good news, and watched the lawyers fail to answer him. The judgment they are declining to make is not about a point of ethics but about a person. And there is a strange mercy in the question. The one who will one day judge them is asking them to judge him first, while a right verdict can still save them.

Should I not rely on my pastor and church to tell me what is right? Listen to them, gratefully: God gives teachers to the church, and you should be humble enough to be taught (Hebrews 13:17). But no teacher can believe for you, repent for you or obey for you. The Bereans checked even Paul against Scripture (Acts 17:11). On the plain things, who Jesus is, what sin is, what he commands, you already know enough to act. Take your questions to your pastor, but do not hide behind them.

In everyday life. Is there a question you keep postponing, whether to be baptised, whether to make things right with someone, whether to give up a known sin, because you are waiting for someone to tell you? You already know, and the Spirit who gives willing hearts will help you. Do it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle on the way. The picture is a lawsuit already in motion: a man walking to court with his accuser, which is how it worked, with a debt he cannot pay and the case certain to go against him. The road is the last stretch of time in which anything can be done. Make an effort is a strong verb: put yourself into it.

Judge, officer, prison. Three handovers in a row, down to debtors’ prison. On the road he is a man who can negotiate. In the courtroom he is a case.

The very last penny. The penny (lepton) was the smallest coin in circulation.

The meaning. In context (vv. 54–57), this is a parable about the coming judgment of God. We are all on our way to court with a debt we cannot pay, and now, on the way, is the time to be reconciled with God through Christ.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. Roman Catholic teaching has sometimes cited this verse in support of purgatory, a place where souls pay for their sins after death before entering heaven. This commentary’s view: the parable is about urgent reconciliation before judgment, not about a process of purification after death. Christ’s one offering has cleared the believer’s account completely (Colossians 2:13–14; Hebrews 10:14), and the believer who dies goes at once to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). For those who reject Christ, the debt can never be paid.

Three reasons the purgatory reading fails. With its parallel in Matthew 5:26, this clause has been cited for purgatory, since until seems to promise a way out at the end of the paying. But first, this is practical advice about a lawsuit, and doctrine cannot be quarried from the scenery of an illustration: pushed that way, the persistent widow would make God a judge who grants justice only to stop being pestered (18:1–8). Second, nobody earned wages in a debtors’ prison, so not getting out until the last penny is paid is the ordinary way of saying not getting out at all. Third, it would reverse the passage’s point: if there were a way to pay later, the advice to settle on the road would be optional.

An amnesty, not an instalment plan. Luke answered the question of the debt itself in a house where a woman wept over Jesus’ feet: when the debtors could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41–42). The record of debt that stood against us was not put on an instalment plan but set aside, nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). So settle now, while it is still called today, and know that the settlement is an amnesty purchased at the Judge’s own expense.

How do I settle with God? Not by offering to pay, because the debt is beyond you, and not by promising to do better, because that adds nothing to what is owed. You settle by agreeing with God about your sin, turning from it, and trusting Jesus Christ, who died to pay that debt in full and rose again. Tell him so, in your own words, today. Then you are no longer on the way to court as a debtor; you are walking home as a child. If you are already his, the parable also has a horizontal echo: where you have a quarrel with someone, settle it quickly (Matthew 5:23–25).

In everyday life. Where this applies: anyone who has put off the question of God for years, assuming there will be time later; and a believer with an open quarrel he keeps meaning to resolve. Where it would be wrong: frightening an assured believer into thinking he must keep paying for forgiven sin, or pressuring someone into a settlement that lets an abuser off.

For worship. The Lord who warns of the debtors’ prison stood up at Nazareth and read that he had been anointed to proclaim liberty to the captives and the year of the Lord’s favour (4:18–19). He has not shortened anyone’s sentence; he has opened the doors. There is not one penny left to pay for the forgiven. It is finished.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Luke 13 is about the call to repent and what happens when it is refused. It opens with two disasters, a massacre of Galilean pilgrims and the fall of a tower at Siloam, which the crowd assumes were punishments for exceptional sin. Jesus refuses the assumption and turns both into a summons to everyone: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. A barren fig tree is given one more year. On a Sabbath he frees a woman bent double for eighteen years, and exposes the synagogue ruler who objects.

The middle of the chapter moves from the mustard seed and the leaven, the kingdom’s small but unstoppable growth, to a question about how many will be saved. Jesus gives no number. He tells the questioner to strive to enter through the narrow door, because one day it will be shut, and nearness to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.

The chapter ends with the lament over Jerusalem. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, Jesus walks on to the city that kills the prophets, longing to gather its children as a hen gathers her brood. The willingness was all on his side, and the refusal all on theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The massacre of Galilean pilgrims by Pilate is recorded nowhere else, and it fits what is known of him. The crowd assumes the victims’ fate was a verdict on their sins. Jesus says no, flatly. That assumption was the working theology of the ancient world (John 9:2), and it is wrong.

He adds a second case, an accident this time, so that between them the two cover evil done by people and evil nobody did, and he gives the same answer to both. The parable of the fig tree follows. The tree has had every advantage and borne nothing, and the owner has waited years. The vinedresser accepts the verdict, asks for one more year, and offers to do the digging himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus does not say that God never punishes; he says these deaths are not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners, all will die, and all need to repent. The right response to someone else’s death is not analysis of their sins but examination of one’s own heart while there is time.

The fig tree and the vineyard were familiar pictures of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10). The one who stands between the tree and the axe is the one telling the story. But the reprieve has a term.
verseByVerse.examples:
This passage forbids both they must have done something and God had nothing to do with it. The honest answer to why them is that we are not told; what we are told is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs.

The vinedresser is also a model for patient labour with an apparently hopeless case, a child who will not turn or a church that has not grown. He neither writes the tree off nor pretends there is fruit. He asks for another year and gets the spade.

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 13 is a chapter about time running out and grace still running. Disasters in the news are a summons to the living; a barren tree gets one more year because someone pleads for it; a bent woman is straightened on the Sabbath; the kingdom grows from a seed, but its door is narrow and will be shut. Judgment is real, the patience is real, and the one who holds both is going to Jerusalem to die.

The setting. Jesus had just urged the crowds to read the signs of the times and be reconciled to God before judgment (12:54–59). Some in the crowd respond with a news item.

The Galileans and Pilate. The incident is recorded nowhere else: the kind of local atrocity that left no trace in the histories, though it fits the brutal Pilate whom Josephus describes. Some Galileans were killed in the temple courts while offering sacrifices, probably at Passover, when laymen slaughtered their own lambs: men killed at the altar, in the act of worship, by the governor of a pagan empire.

Why do they raise it? Luke does not say, and the silence is suggestive. They may be testing him. A Galilean teacher’s opinion on a massacre of Galileans would be useful to somebody: condemn Pilate and he is a rebel; say nothing and he has no sympathy for his own people. Perhaps they wanted him to say the victims deserved it. But the answer Jesus gives tells us what they were actually thinking.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? There it is, and he brings it out into the open before they can say it. The assumption behind the report is that the manner of a man’s death is a comment on his life. That was not a fringe view. It was the working theology of the ancient world. Job’s friends spent most of a book on it (Job 4:7). The disciples will ask it about a blind man: who sinned, this man or his parents (John 9:2)? It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong. And the reflex is attractive for a reason. If the dead deserved it, the living can feel safe, because a good enough life would keep the sword and the tower away. It is religion used as a way of staying in control, and Jesus takes it out of their hands.

Unless you repent. Then the turn nobody was ready for. He tells the living they are in the same position, and the only difference between them and the men on that temple pavement is timing. The real question is not why they died but whether you are ready to die. They brought a question about somebody else’s guilt, and he hands it back with their own name on it. And likewise may be meant literally: some forty years later many Jews died at Roman hands in the temple courts during the siege of Jerusalem.

The same governor, the same feast. Within months another Galilean would die at Pilate’s hands at Passover time, and he is the one answering the question. Three times Pilate found no guilt in him (23:4, 14, 22). He was not a worse sinner than all the Galileans; he was the one sinless Galilean. His blood was not mingled with the sacrifices. It was the sacrifice, shed so that those who repent will never perish.

What does perish mean here? More than dying, since the Galileans have already died and his hearers will die too whatever they do. To perish is to be lost before God: to die unreconciled and come under his judgment, for ever (John 3:16, where perishing is the opposite of eternal life). Jesus is not threatening that the unrepentant will all be killed by Pilate. He is saying that what happened to the bodies of those men is a picture of what will happen to every soul that meets God without repentance: sudden, unprepared and final. That is why the warning is urgent and not merely sad.

What is repentance? Repentance is turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as an offence against him, and grieving over it. It lays hold of God’s mercy in Christ, since sorrow with no hope in it only drives a sinner further from God. And it acts: by grace the sinner leaves the sin behind and sets out on a new obedience (Westminster Confession 15.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 15.3). It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life, and it is never too late to begin it while you are still breathing.

In everyday life. Watch for the reflex next time the news breaks: the faint relief that it was over there, the quick search for what they did differently. Let it send you instead to the one honest prayer the news can produce: Lord, I am no safer than they were; have mercy on me.
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tower in Siloam. He supplies a second case himself, and a different kind of disaster. The first was murder; the second an accident. Siloam was the area round the pool at the south end of Jerusalem (John 9:7); perhaps a tower in the wall gave way on eighteen people. Between them the two cases cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did.

Were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? The word for offenders (opheiletai) means debtors, the word Jesus taught them to use in prayer (11:4). Were they greater debtors to God? The question assumes there is a ledger, and that the falling masonry was the bailiff calling in one particular account. Jesus agrees there is a ledger. He denies that the tower was a reading from it.

Word for word, twice. Neither case is left open: whether by human evil or natural disaster, death comes to everyone, often unexpectedly, and the only safety is repentance.

Disasters and God. God is sovereign over all things, including disasters (Amos 3:6; Isaiah 45:7). But Scripture does not teach that every disaster punishes the particular sins of those who suffer. When Adam sinned, death entered God’s world and the ground itself was cursed (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 5:12). Towers fall and bodies fail because the whole creation now groans under that sentence (Romans 8:20–22), not because each victim earned his own particular blow.

Two sentences this passage forbids. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, two sentences will be offered. The first is the one he is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly. Never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either. Between those errors a Christian must stand: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it.

Esteemed stricken. One death would be read exactly as Jesus forbids these to be read. At the cross the rulers sneered, He saved others; let him save himself (23:35), and Isaiah had foreseen the misreading: we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted (Isaiah 53:4). He was not crushed for his own sins, because he had none, yet he was crushed by the will of God, for ours. His is the one death where God’s judgment truly can be read, and there it fell on the one man who had not deserved it.

So what may be said to the grieving? Very little about the dead, and a great deal to the living. The honest answer to why them is that we are not told. Do not offer explanations God has not given, and do not hurry anyone through their grief. Sit with them, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), pray with them, and speak of the God who is not distant from suffering because his Son entered it. The word Jesus gives here, that our own footing is no firmer than theirs, is not a change of subject but the only useful thing that can be said to people standing near a fresh grave and quietly assuming they are safe. It is usually a word for the preacher and for your own heart before it is a word for a widow.

And what about my own suffering? Is God punishing me? If you are in Christ, no. The punishment your sins deserved was laid on him, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, but discipline is a father’s training, not a judge’s sentence, and its aim is our holiness and good (Hebrews 12:5–11). You may not be able to say what a particular trouble is for. You can say what it is not: it is not God paying you back. It may be a call to search your heart, and it is always an invitation to draw near.
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fig tree in a vineyard. Only Luke records this parable, and it explains why the axe has not yet fallen, and why it will. A fig tree in a vineyard has been planted in prime cultivated ground: it has had every advantage. And the images were unmistakable to anyone who knew the prophets: Israel is the vineyard where God looked for grapes and found wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7), and the fig tree in which he came looking and found nothing (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1).

Found none. Fruit means righteousness, justice, repentance and faith, the fruits in keeping with repentance that John demanded (3:8): not leaves, not size, but the only thing a fig tree is for.

For three years now. Three years is not impatience. The law required that the fruit of the first three years be left untouched in any case (Leviticus 19:23), so the owner may have waited those years and then come three more. Some see a reference to the length of Jesus’ ministry, though that is uncertain. Certainly this man has given the tree every year it was owed and several it was not.

Cut it down. The charge is not that it has done harm, but that it is using up the ground. The verb (katargei) means to waste, to exhaust. A fruitless tree draws water out of good soil, takes the light, and occupies a space where something fruitful could stand. Barrenness here is not neutral: what the tree consumes belongs to somebody else.

He came seeking fruit. In a later vineyard story the owner sends servant after servant and at last says, I will send my beloved son (20:13). The owner who comes looking on this fig tree is God, and in the man telling the parable he had come in person, going through the towns of Israel looking for repentance and faith, until he wept over the city that would not have him (19:41). It is the Son standing in the vineyard, looking at the tree.

What fruit is God looking for in me? Not a religious performance, and not a quota of activity. Jesus means the life that grows from a heart turned to God: repentance, trust in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit that follows, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), along with honest dealings and mercy to the poor (3:10–14). Fruit is quiet and grows over time. You will often see it more clearly in others than in yourself, and a believer who fears he has none is often bearing more than he knows. The barren tree in the parable is not a struggling Christian; it is a life that has had every privilege and given nothing back to God at all.
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This year also. The vinedresser does not dispute the verdict. He accepts the whole case and asks for time: a picture of intercession, pleading with God on someone else’s behalf, and of God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9). And it is hard not to see the storyteller in him: the one who stands between the tree and the axe is standing in that crowd.

Dig around it. Let it alone is only half his sentence. He undertakes to dig round the roots, breaking up compacted ground so water can reach them, and to dung it: heavy, unglamorous labour on a tree that has given him nothing for three years, and he volunteers for it.

Well and good. The sentence in Greek is broken off: if it bears fruit next year, and then nothing. The translators supply well and good; Jesus leaves a silence.

But if not. Judgment is delayed, not cancelled. The intercession has a term: the vinedresser names the period, and concedes the outcome if nothing changes.

The point. The extra year is a gift: use it to repent (Romans 2:4). The parable ends without telling us what happened, because the hearers must decide. The disasters said the axe is real; this says the axe is being held, and by whom. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years’ time. Jesus puts them in the same paragraph.

Does this mean a Christian can be cut down and lost? The parable is spoken first to Israel, and then to everyone who has privilege without fruit: the person who has heard the gospel all his life and never truly turned. It does not teach that those who belong to Christ can be cut off. Jesus says his sheep will never perish and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). But it does warn that a fruitless profession is not safe, because fruit is the evidence of life (Matthew 7:16–20). If the warning troubles you, that is not a sign the axe is at your root. It is the vinedresser’s spade, and the right response is to turn to Christ now.

How do I pray for someone who seems hopeless? Like the vinedresser. His response to three barren years is not to write the tree off and not to pretend there is fruit. It is to ask for another year and go and get the spade. So pray specifically and persistently for the child who will not turn, the friend who shrugs, the church that has not grown. And add to your praying whatever digging is yours to do: the patient kindness, the honest conversation, the invitation, the Bible left open. The results belong to God. The asking and the labour belong to us.

In everyday life. This may be your extra year. If there is a sin you have been meaning to deal with, or a call to Christ you have been answering with later, the parable says: now, while the ground is being dug for you.

For worship. The Son of God came down into the vineyard and took up the spade himself. And when the axe did fall, it fell on him: the one truly fruitful tree was cut down, hanged on a tree and made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that barren trees might be spared and made fruitful. Every year of grace you have had was bought by his blood and asked for by his prayers (Hebrews 7:25).

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is teaching in a synagogue, the last time Luke records it. A woman who has been bent double for eighteen years is there, still coming to worship, asking for nothing. Jesus sees her, calls her over and lays his hands on her, and she stands straight and glorifies God.

The synagogue ruler is indignant. He does not address Jesus but lectures the people, telling them to come for healing on the six working days. His mistake is to count a healing as work, and to propose a schedule for a miracle to a woman who has waited eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke does not call the woman possessed, but Jesus says Satan had bound her: a physical condition with something darker underneath it, the strong man of 11:21–22 at work. Jesus calls her a daughter of Abraham, a phrase found nowhere else in the Gospels: she is inside the covenant with every right that carries (compare 19:9).

His argument comes from their own practice. Everyone untied an ox or a donkey on the Sabbath to water it, because mercy to an animal was not counted as work. So a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering, and the day that remembers a people brought out of slavery is the most fitting day of all to set a captive free.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler’s real failure was that he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building, and what registered was a problem with the timetable. There is a kind of religion that watches God act and thinks first about procedure, and from the inside it feels like carefulness.

And shame need not be the end. Luke does not say what the ruler did next, and the door was still open.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one of the synagogues. Only Luke records this healing, and it is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The doors are closing.

A disabling spirit. Literally a spirit of weakness. Her condition was caused by Satan (v. 16), though she is not described as possessed, and no demon is cast out: a physical condition with something darker underneath it, the fallen world’s disorder, exploited.

Bent over. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14) describes it precisely: perhaps a fusion of the spine. For eighteen years she could hardly have seen the sky or looked another adult in the face without twisting her whole body.

Still coming to worship. And she is in the synagogue. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still coming to worship. She asks for nothing when Jesus arrives; she may have stopped expecting anything. She had become the settled furniture of the place: the bent woman everybody knew and nobody expected to change.

The first synagogue and the last. Luke opened Jesus’ ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he read that he had been anointed to set at liberty those who are oppressed (4:18). Now, in the last synagogue scene, the promise is kept for one person nobody else had looked at. The synagogue had read the Scriptures over her for eighteen years. What it had not had, until this Sabbath, was the one the Scriptures were about, standing in the room.

Is sickness caused by Satan? Here Luke says this woman’s condition came from a spirit, and Jesus calls her one whom Satan bound (v. 16). But Scripture never teaches that every illness is demonic: the man born blind was not (John 9:3), and Paul’s thorn was a messenger of Satan that God used for his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). A believer cannot be owned by Satan, though God may permit him to be afflicted. The ordinary response to illness is prayer and medicine, not exorcism.

In everyday life. Look round your own church for the person who has become furniture: the one with the long illness, the one who comes alone, the one nobody expects to change. Jesus saw her. Ask him for eyes like his.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He saw her and called her. She did not ask. He saw her, a woman folded double and probably out of everyone’s sightline; the same verb is used of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), and there too the seeing led straight to action. He called her over, so she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her, and her healing became a public event. He took the initiative, as he always does with those he saves.

You are freed. The verb (apolelysai) is a perfect passive: you have been released, set loose, and the release stands. It is the vocabulary of untying, which Jesus will use three verses later of the ox. He does not say be healed. He says the knot has been undone.

He laid his hands on her. A healing touch, and a human one, which nobody may have given her for a long time. The Lord lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8).

She glorified God. The tense suggests she kept on doing it. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven, and the first use she made of standing upright was worship.

Why does Jesus heal some and not others, and should I expect healing? In the Gospels his healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that the one who will undo every curse is here. He did not heal every sick person in Israel, and he does not promise every believer healing in this life; Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God still heals today, in answer to prayer and through medicine, and we should ask him freely (James 5:14–15). But the miraculous gifts that marked the apostles were signs for the founding of the church, and we hold, charitably, that they are not given in the same way now, since the apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20). Many faithful Christians, in Pentecostal and charismatic churches, believe these gifts continue, and we gladly own them as brothers and sisters. What every believer is promised is the final straightening: a resurrection body with nothing bent in it (Philippians 3:21). Ask boldly, and rest in that.

For worship. He saw her before she saw him, called her before she asked, and undid in a moment a knot Satan had tied for eighteen years. One day the whole bent creation will stand up straight at his word.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruler of the synagogue. The man responsible for organising its services (8:41). A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God in his synagogue, and he is angry.

To the people. He does not speak to Jesus, who did it, but to the people, and effectively to her. Unwilling to rebuke Jesus directly, he lectures the congregation: public instruction aimed sideways, like the sermon everyone knows is about one person. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

Six days. He is quoting the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:9), and he is right that the Sabbath forbids work. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Come on those days. It collapses at once. He tells a woman who has not been healed on any working day for nearly two decades to come back on Monday, as though healing were a service with opening hours. Underneath is the real failure, and it is not exactly legalism. He did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building, and what registered was a diary problem.

Lord of the Sabbath. He talks as if a healer had opened a clinic on the wrong day. But the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath (6:5): the commandment the ruler quotes was given by the God whose Son was standing in his synagogue, doing the very work the day had always pointed to.

How do I know if I am like this man? Some religion can watch God act and think first about procedure. It is not rare, and it does not usually feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness. Ask yourself what your first reaction is when God moves in an unexpected way: in a person you had written off, in a church tradition not your own, in a service that ran late. Is it gladness, or a list of objections? Order matters, and Scripture asks for it (1 Corinthians 14:40). But when your love for the way things are done is stronger than your joy that a sinner is helped, the rule has taken the place of the Lord who gave it.

In everyday life. If you have a grievance with someone, take it to that person, not sideways to everyone else (Matthew 18:15).
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites! The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? The argument is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice, and everybody present did it. An animal tied in a stall cannot get to water, and animals could not go a day without it. Leaving a beast thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening was not an option any farmer would have entertained. The traditions later written down by the rabbis allowed livestock to be led out and watered on the Sabbath; untying and leading were permitted, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus is not asking them to adopt a new rule. He is asking them to apply the one they use every week of their lives.

Ought not this woman. Now the comparison, the sharpest thing in the chapter. Ought (edei) is the word of divine necessity that runs through Luke: it was not merely permitted to heal her; it was required. And this woman is set over against his ox or his donkey: the animal has an owner who will take trouble for it.

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham (compare Zacchaeus, 19:9); the title is handed to a bent, unnamed woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Of more value than an ox.

Whom Satan bound. He names who tied the knot: the strong man of chapter 11, whom a stronger one overpowers (11:21–22). This is not merely a medical misfortune but an occupation, and someone is being dispossessed. Eighteen years, against the ox’s overnight thirst.

Be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day? A play on words: you untie your animals; should I not untie this woman? They untie; he unties. And the final word is the one they thought was the problem. Not in spite of the Sabbath, but on it. The Sabbath was the most fitting day for it. The Sabbath was given as a sign of God’s rest and of his liberation of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). What better day to free a captive of Satan? Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of bondage is the day for a knot to be undone. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s liberation.

Does the Sabbath still bind Christians? Christians who love the Bible answer this differently. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment remains, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept holy for worship and works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the true rest, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Christians gladly gather on the Lord’s Day as the apostles did. This commentary’s view: the second view fits the New Testament best, and the Lord’s Day is a gift to be kept gladly, not a Sabbath law moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree on what this passage teaches: the day of rest is a day of mercy, deeds of kindness are never a breach of it, and its meaning is found in Christ, who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).

For worship. The first day of the week has been a day of untying ever since Christ rose on it, having broken the bonds of death itself. He counts a bent daughter of Abraham worth more than every ox in Israel, and he paid for his people’s release with his own life.
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put to shame. One verse, two reactions, side by side. The adversaries are opponents in a case; the synagogue ruler now belongs to a party. And they had no answer: not shouted down, but shown up, as all who set themselves against the Lord are put to shame (Isaiah 45:16).

All the people rejoiced. The ordinary people, with nothing invested in a ruling about Sabbath work, saw it rightly. The word for glorious things (endoxois) is used in the Greek of God’s mighty acts at the exodus (Exodus 34:10): something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it.

Two responses to one event. They all saw a woman folded double for eighteen years stand up. What divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, as at the gates of Jerusalem, where the disciples praise God and Pharisees tell him to rebuke them (19:37–39). He is appointed for the fall and rising of many (2:34).

Is there hope for the man who was put to shame? Yes. Being put to shame is not the end of a man. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and it is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed. If you have been shown up by Christ, in your pride or your hardness, the shame is not meant to drive you away from him. It is meant to bring you to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parables of the mustard seed and the leaven explain what the healing was. If this is the kingdom arriving, it does not look like much: one woman, one synagogue. Jesus answers that the kingdom starts as small as a seed and becomes a tree where the birds nest, the old prophetic picture of an empire sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12), and that it works like a pinch of leaven through a great mass of dough until all of it is changed. Here leaven, usually a picture of corruption (12:1), pictures how the kingdom spreads, quietly and from within.

Then someone asks whether those who are saved will be few. Jesus gives no number. He tells his hearers to strive to enter through the narrow door, which is wide enough for any sinner and too narrow for any sinner’s baggage, because one day the master of the house will shut it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question about the number of the saved is put in the third person, about other people, and Jesus turns it back on the crowd. The striving he commands is not a way of earning entry. It is the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going in. Nobody buys the door open, but many mean to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

The words I do not know where you come from are not a lapse of memory. To know, in Scripture, is to have a relationship (Amos 3:2): the people outside never belonged to his house. And the table they miss is full, with guests from east and west, the feast Isaiah foresaw for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6–8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Everything the people outside plead is true and beside the point. They ate in his company and heard him teach. Every claim is about nearness, and nobody says we trusted you. All of it describes where a person stood, not what he did about it.

In Luke the door is a Person, and those who enter, from the centurion (7:7) to the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38–39), each came to Jesus himself with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore, What is the kingdom of God like? The therefore ties this to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, and been attacked for it, and the crowd went home happy. Now he explains what that was. In the light of the healing and of the opposition, the kingdom is present, in small beginnings, and it will grow. If this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. One woman. One synagogue. One argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning.

A grain of mustard seed. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the standard picture of the negligible (17:6). The kingdom began with one man from Nazareth and a handful of followers. And it is sown in his garden, deliberately: somebody put a thing that small into the ground, as if it could possibly be worth the effort.

Became a tree. The mustard plant by the Sea of Galilee can grow ten feet (3 m) tall, large enough for birds to perch in. Calling it a tree is a stretch, and is meant to be.

The birds of the air. The image is Ezekiel’s and Daniel’s, and there it means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Daniel 4:12, 21; Ezekiel 31:6). So Jesus takes the picture of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. That is the joke, and it is also how God works. The empires start large and end in ruins. This starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The tender sprig. Ezekiel’s nesting birds are a promise about a king: the Lord takes a tender sprig from the broken royal house of David, plants it on a high mountain, and birds of every sort nest under it (Ezekiel 17:22–23). The kingdom grows from small to great because its King did, growing up like a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2): a carpenter’s son, a teacher with a few fishermen, a body in a borrowed tomb. The one telling this parable is the sprig the parable is about.

Does this mean my church should be large? No. The parable is about the kingdom across the whole sweep of history, not a promise that every congregation will grow big. Many faithful churches stay small for generations, and many large ones are not faithful. And if the church in your own country seems to be shrinking, remember that the parable takes in the whole world and the whole age: in the last century the gospel has spread across Africa, Asia and Latin America faster than at almost any time in history. What the parable forbids is despising the small and hidden as if God could not be at work there. The measure of a church is not its size but whether Christ is preached and his people are being changed. Small faithfulness is part of the great tree.

In everyday life. Do not despise small beginnings (Zechariah 4:10). The Sunday school class of six, the Bible study with three, the conversation over a fence: these are mustard seeds, and the Gardener knows what he has planted. Sow, and leave the growing to him.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like leaven. The second parable ought to bring a reader up short. One chapter ago, from this same speaker, leaven was the picture of everything that ruins: the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (12:1). Israel scoured it out of the house before Passover (Exodus 12:15), and Paul means malice and evil by it (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here, unusually, it is a positive picture: a small amount, working invisibly, spreading through the whole.

Why is leaven good here when it is bad elsewhere? Because the image is about the way leaven works, not about whether what it carries is good or evil. Some have concluded that Jesus must be warning of corruption spreading quietly through the church, but the sentence refuses it. He does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says the kingdom of God is like leaven, the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Turn the second into a warning and you break the pair in half. Everything that makes yeast a good image for hypocrisy, that it is small, hidden, works from the inside and does not stop until the whole batch is changed, is exactly what makes it a good image for the kingdom. Luke’s own two uses show the point: at 12:1 something false permeates a community; here something true permeates the world.

A man in the first parable, a woman in the second. Luke’s pairing again, as with Simeon and Anna. And the woman hid it: the kingdom works from within.

Three measures. About 50 pounds (22 kg) of flour, enough to feed a hundred people, about what Sarah baked for her heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:6). The comedy is deliberate: a pinch of yeast, invisible the moment it goes in, and a mountain of dough; and the pinch wins.

All leavened. The whole lump is transformed: the answer to anyone who has compared the size of the world and the size of the church and concluded that the arithmetic is hopeless.

The two parables together. The seed is seen from outside: something small becomes a thing the birds can find. The leaven is seen from inside: something small changes every part. One is the kingdom’s reach, the other its depth.

Christ in you. The New Testament names the hidden thing: not a rule laid on the outside but the King himself living within by his Spirit, Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). The risen Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) on about a hundred and twenty in one city (Acts 1:15), and by the last page of Acts the kingdom of God is being proclaimed in Rome (Acts 28:31). Nobody watching that upper room could have seen the dough rise. It rose.

What it does not mean. Not necessarily that the whole world will become Christian before Christ returns, the hope some godly Reformed teachers have held. The parables promise growth and transformation, not universal conversion, and other passages speak of persecution and falling away until the end (18:8; 21:12; 2 Timothy 3:1–5).

How does the kingdom work in me like leaven? Quietly and thoroughly. When Christ enters a life he does not stay in one compartment. He begins with the heart and works outward into habits, words, money, marriage, work, until nothing is left untouched. It is usually slower than we want and deeper than we notice. You may not see the change from one week to the next, any more than you can watch dough rise. But look back over years and you will often find that what once ruled you no longer does. That is the yeast at work, and the one who hid it will not stop until the whole is leavened (Philippians 1:6).

In everyday life. Christ is in you by his Spirit, so do the hidden work faithfully: the honest day’s labour, the kind word at home, the prayer no one hears. That is how leaven moves through a lump, and how the gospel moves through a street, an office and a family.
verseByVerse.note: Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Toward Jerusalem. Luke has been noting the direction of travel since 9:51. The question about how many will be saved is put to the one person on that road who knows, because he is going to Jerusalem to save them.

Lord, will those who are saved be few? The question was a live one in the schools. Jewish teachers debated how many of Israel would have a share in the age to come. Some said all Israel would be saved, with a few named exceptions; others were considerably tighter. And look at how the question is framed. It is a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking it has placed himself outside the calculation and is enquiring about the statistics. The questioner wants to discuss others, perhaps from curiosity.

No number given. He does not give the number. Wherever curiosity presses for information God has not given, the times and seasons, who is greatest, what will happen to that man, the answer is a redirection. And the reply is to them, plural: Jesus answers the crowd, and turns the question from theory to personal urgency.

So will few be saved, or many? Scripture gives two answers that sound opposite and are both true. Looked at from the road, the way is narrow, and in any generation those who find it are few compared with the crowd on the broad road (Matthew 7:13–14). Looked at from the end, John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9). God will save a vast people for his Son, and not one he has chosen will be lost (John 6:37–39). But you will not be in that number by being in a majority, a family or a church. Jesus’ answer is not a statistic. It is: make sure you are one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The door. The door leads into the kingdom feast (vv. 28–29), and the master who shuts it is Jesus himself (vv. 25–27). The way in is through him: I am the door (John 10:9).

The question that should have been asked. He answers not how many, but are you going in? Strive (agōnizesthe) is what an athlete does in the games (hence agony): to strain, to exert everything, as though something depended on it. Something does.

The door is narrow. Not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow: which says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it. Not your own righteousness, nor your pride, nor the sin you mean to keep. It is wide enough for any sinner and too narrow for any sinner’s baggage.

Will not be able. Not because they wanted Christ and were refused, but because they came too late (v. 25), or on their own terms. Plenty of people intend to go through later, and he is telling them that later is a door that shuts.

If I must strive, am I not earning my way in after all? No; look at what the striving is for. He does not say strive to become worthy, or strive until you have done enough. He says strive to enter. The effort is not payment offered at the door; it is the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going through it. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading. The tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13–14), and the dying criminal who has nothing whatever to offer is told he will be with Jesus in Paradise that very day (23:43). The striving is the striving of the drowning man for the rope, not of the labourer for his wages.

How do I know I am inside? The passage is about to be unsparing on false assurance, so it is worth saying plainly what genuine entering looks like. The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing us the entering all along in ordinary people. It is the centurion who asks Jesus only to say the word (7:7). It is the woman told that her faith has saved her and she may go in peace (7:50). It is the leper who came back (17:19), and the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38–39). Not one of them was admitted for being impressive. Each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside. If that is what you are doing, you are not outside knocking. And the one who comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

What if I have doubts about whether I have really come? Doubt is not the same as being outside. Many true believers struggle with assurance, and the Westminster Confession says plainly that a true believer may wait long and conflict with many difficulties before he has it (Westminster 18.3; the 1689 London Baptist Confession agrees, 18.3). Do not look first at the strength of your faith; look at the Christ it holds. Come to him again today, as a sinner, with nothing in your hands, and you are doing exactly what this verse commands. Assurance usually grows as you keep coming, as you see the Spirit’s fruit slowly appear, and as you rest on his promise rather than your feelings.

In everyday life. If you have been meaning to settle things with God, do not let another week pass with the matter only intended. And if you are inside, strive still, in the Spirit’s strength, because the door is the beginning of the road. Your welcome does not hang on your striving: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, his obedience is counted as yours, and for his sake the Father accepts your faltering steps.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The door shut. The scene moves to a house at night, and the decisive action has already happened: this is the day of judgment (Matthew 25:10). He shut the door once, at a time of his choosing, as any householder does at the end of the day.

Lord, open to us. They call him Lord, but too late (6:46). They are at the right house, asking the right person.

I do not know where you come from. Not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational: God knew Israel among all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Where you come from asks whose are you, what is your connection to this house? There is none (Matthew 7:23).

We ate and drank. Every word of the plea is true. They had eaten in his company and heard him teach in their streets. Their credentials are genuine, and beside the point: every claim is about proximity. Nobody says we trusted you. They had contact with Jesus, but not a relationship.

Workers of evil. The words are from Psalm 6:8, and they land hardest on the most religiously exposed people in any generation: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All true, and all a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it. They thought of themselves as guests; he calls them workers of evil, because a life never brought to him for cleansing is a life of unforgiven sin, however respectable it looked (Isaiah 64:6).

I have been in church all my life. Should this frighten me? It should make you honest, not hopeless. The question is not how long you have been near Jesus but whether you have come to him: whether you have owned your sin before him and trusted him alone to save you. If you have, being in church all your life is a great mercy, and you belong to him. If you are not sure, do not try to settle it by reviewing your attendance. Go to him now, in your own words, and ask him to receive you. The people in this parable are not those who came and were refused. They are those who never came, and assumed that being near was enough.

Does Jesus not know everyone? As God he knows everything about everyone, every thought and every deed (Psalm 139:1–4). But Scripture also uses know of the loving, saving knowledge he has of his own: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). That is the knowing these people lack. He is not saying he has no information about them. He is saying they were never his.

In everyday life. Take one familiar thing this week, the grace before a meal, the hymn you sing without thinking, and stop inside it long enough to speak to him rather than about him. And pray that children who have grown up near the gospel will come to belong.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weeping and gnashing of teeth. Grief, and anguish with perhaps rage still in it: the misery of those shut out of the kingdom (Matthew 8:12; 13:42).

Abraham and all the prophets. The forebears Jesus’ hearers were proud of. And the torment named is a sight: exclusion means knowing exactly what has been lost and who is at the table.

Cast out. The shock: Abraham’s children shut out, because they did not share Abraham’s faith. Not pagans, but men whose whole assurance rested on their descent, an assurance John had demolished when he warned them not to say that they had Abraham as their father (3:8).

Where Christians differ: is the punishment conscious and lasting? Some evangelicals, reading the Bible’s language of destruction (Matthew 10:28), hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist, and they hold it earnestly. Most Christians through history have held that the punishment of the lost is conscious and without end. This commentary’s view: the punishment is conscious and lasting. This picture is of people who are present and aware of what they have lost, and Jesus elsewhere speaks of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46), so that whatever one lasts, the other does. Hell is not annihilation but exclusion from the joy of God’s presence under his just judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:9). It is a terrible truth, and Jesus speaks it with tears, not relish.

From east and west. From all four points of the compass: the Gentiles, from every nation (Isaiah 49:12; Psalm 107:3). The table is full, and full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.

Recline at table. The messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6–8; Revelation 19:9), where Gentiles sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11). Christians differ on when it is spread: some place it in a thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns; this commentary holds that it is the feast of the new creation after his one visible return, because the New Testament joins that return directly to the resurrection, the judgment and the new heavens and earth (John 5:28–29; 2 Peter 3:10–13). Both wait for the same feast and the same Host.

At my table in my kingdom. Luke tells us whose table it is. Every meal in this Gospel has Jesus at its centre, and at the last supper he promises the Twelve that they will eat and drink at my table in my kingdom (22:30). The feast with Abraham is his feast, and to recline is not a snack at the door but a seat at the King’s own table, with nothing more to do but enjoy him.

Last who will be first. The great reversal: Gentiles, last in privilege, first in the kingdom; many in Israel, first in privilege, last. It is Luke’s signature since the Magnificat (1:52). But it is not a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is grace, which can only be received with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

Who are the first who will be last today? Anyone whose confidence rests on what he has rather than on Christ: a Christian upbringing, a good church, a long record of service, sound doctrine held at arm’s length. These are gifts, and the first in privilege can be first in the kingdom too, if they come as beggars. But privilege trusted becomes a wall. And the last who will be first are those who knew they had no claim at all: the convert from a wrecked life, the believer in a land that never heard the gospel until yesterday, the child with simple faith. The warning falls where it does because it is aimed at people who were sure they were near him.

In everyday life. Thank God for every advantage you have had, then come to him as though you had none. Be glad, not jealous, when someone from far off is welcomed to the table, and look round your church for the newcomer, a guest of the same King.

For worship. Blessed be the Host who was himself shut out for us, crucified outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that strangers from east and west might sit down with Abraham and never be sent away. Not one seat will stand empty, and at that feast death itself is swallowed up for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him; Luke leaves their motive open. Jesus calls Herod a fox, a small predator and a nuisance rather than a power, and sends back a timetable that Herod does not set: he will go on with his work until it is finished, and he will die in Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets.

Then he speaks to the city. How often would he have gathered its children, he says, as one who has been calling it through every prophet it killed. A fox is on the prowl, and a hen, with no talons and no means of fighting, can only spread her wings over her chicks and take what is coming for them. That is the picture he chose for himself on the road to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.theology:
Your house is forsaken: the temple God called my house is handed back to them, because its owner is leaving. Ezekiel had seen the glory depart before the first temple fell (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23), and in AD 70 the second was destroyed.

But the sentence ends with until. The words of Psalm 118:26 were sung over Jesus as he entered Jerusalem (19:38), yet within the week the city handed him over, so many look further on, to a day when he is gladly welcomed; Christians differ on whether Paul’s all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26) means a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ. Either way the last line is a welcome, not a cry of terror.
