verseByVerse.examples: The lament is the model of grief for those who hear the gospel and turn away. It is not anger but refused love, and every parent praying for a child who will not turn, and every pastor who has watched someone come close and walk away, has tasted something of it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get away from here. It is the only time in the Gospels that Pharisees warn Jesus of danger, and their motive is uncertain. Not all Pharisees were hostile: Luke records three who invite him to dinner. Or the warning may be a manoeuvre to drive him out of Herod’s territory towards Judea, where his real opponents were waiting. Luke does not tell us, and it is better not to decide.

Herod Antipas. The threat is credible: this is the ruler of Galilee and Perea who had beheaded John (9:9).

Go and tell that fox. In Jewish usage a fox was the small, destructive predator, set against the lion: Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power. Which is what he was. Rome never let him be king, and he would end his days exiled to Gaul.

The third day. The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Today and tomorrow and the third day is an idiom for a short time set by God, not by Herod. And the verb (teleioumai) means I am brought to completion, perfected, the end his work would reach at his death and resurrection in Jerusalem (Hebrews 2:10), the same family of words as it is finished (John 19:30).

I must go on my way. There is the must again (dei), the divine necessity that has driven this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Herod’s threats cannot change God’s plan.

Away from Jerusalem. Bitter irony. Jerusalem had a long history of killing the prophets (Jeremiah 26:20–23). Jesus is not saying merely that it is dangerous but that it is the appointed place: the city that exists to bring men to God has a settled record of killing the men God sends, and a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Did Jesus insult a ruler? He spoke as a prophet with authority over Herod, giving God’s verdict on a cunning and destructive man. It is not a pattern for Christians to speak of rulers with contempt. Paul apologised for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5), and Peter tells believers to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). We may and sometimes must speak plainly about injustice, and we must never be ruled by fear of the powerful. But our ordinary duty is to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and to speak of them with respect, even when we oppose what they do.

What if someone is threatening me? Jesus did not ignore the danger, and he did not run from his calling either. He went on doing the work God had given him, in the place God had given it, until the time God had set. Take sensible precautions, seek help, and where there is abuse or real danger, go to those who can protect you; Scripture never asks you to stay under violence. But do not let fear decide your obedience. Your days are written in God’s book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:16), and no Herod can add a minute to them or take one away.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double address shows deep emotion, grief and love, the same register as Martha, Martha and Simon, Simon (10:41; 22:31). It is what he says when he sees the whole of someone and grieves.

The city that kills the prophets. This is what the city does, as a settled practice, and the charge is historical. Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:21); Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern to die (Jeremiah 38:6). And it is about to kill the greatest of the prophets.

How often. This is the phrase that matters. Jesus had visited Jerusalem several times (John 2:13; 5:1; 7:10), but how often is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time, with every prophet who was sent and killed behind it. The one speaking is the one who sent them: Jesus speaks as God, who longed to gather his people.

As a hen. Luke sets this lament straight after the message to that fox: a fox is on the prowl, and a hen stands between it and her chicks. In the Old Testament God shelters his people under his wings (Ruth 2:12; Psalm 91:4), often as an eagle (Deuteronomy 32:11). But a hen has no talons and cannot fight. The way she saves her chicks is by spreading her wings and staying where she is, taking on herself what was coming for them. That is the image he chose for himself, on the road to a city that was going to kill him.

You were not willing. Every verb before these words is his: would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal on the other. Not unable: not willing, and that is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

Where Christians differ: God’s will and human refusal. Arminians, Christians who follow the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), many of them deeply devoted to Christ, take this verse to show that God wills all to be saved but that human free will can finally resist his saving purpose. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches both that God is sovereign in salvation (John 6:37, 44; Ephesians 1:11) and that he sincerely calls sinners and grieves over their refusal (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11). Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will, what he commands and desires (that people repent and come), from his secret decree, what he has determined will happen. Jesus’ lament is genuine: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The responsibility for refusal lies entirely with those who refuse. Both truths stand; we should not cancel one by the other.

If God is sovereign, how can his tears be real? Because he means what he says. The Son who wept over Jerusalem is not acting a part. God truly delights in mercy, truly calls, and truly grieves when his call is refused, and none of that is pretence because he has also purposed what will come to pass. We cannot fit both truths into one neat sentence, and Scripture does not ask us to. It asks us to believe both: that no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and that whoever refuses Christ does so freely and is answerable for it. The tears of Jesus are the clearest window we have into the heart of God towards sinners.

Can I still come? Yes. The wings that were spread over Jerusalem are spread still, and the invitation has never been withdrawn from anyone who will come. If you are afraid you have refused him too long, know that the very fear is a sign he is still gathering you. Those who are finally lost are not those who wanted to come and were turned away. They are those who would not. Come to him today, and you will find there is room under his wings.

In everyday life. Let the tears of Jesus shape the way you speak about those who reject him. Not with contempt, and not with indifference, but with longing. Pray for the people you know who have refused him, by name, with something of his grief. And if there is any part of your own life you have been unwilling to bring under his wings, bring it today.

For worship. Glory to the Lord God of Israel, who sent prophet after prophet into a city that killed them, and then came himself, grieving on the road. How often is the voice of a love that kept count of every rejection and kept on calling. His wings are spread still, and no chick that ran under them has ever been turned away.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your house is forsaken. Your house: it had never been theirs. The prophets called it my house, a house of prayer (Isaiah 56:7), as Jesus will say in that very building (19:46). To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say that the owner has moved out (Jeremiah 12:7; 22:5). The sentence was carried out in AD 70, when Roman armies burned the temple (19:43–44; 21:6).

Israel had seen this before. Ezekiel watched the glory of God leave the temple for the mountain on the east (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23), and the building was flattened a few years later. And the glory that left in Ezekiel’s day had come back in person, a baby carried into the temple in Simeon’s arms (2:27–32), and was now being refused.

Until you say. The quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving for the feasts, and the crowds will sing it over him as he comes down the Mount of Olives (19:38). But within the week the city handed him over, so many see the deeper fulfilment at his return. And blessed is he who comes is a welcome, not a cry of terror.

Does this mean a future turning of Israel to Christ? Paul teaches that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–27), which many understand as a future conversion of large numbers of the Jewish people before Christ returns. Others take it of the full number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. Either way, the verse holds out hope as well as judgment.

The shape of the sentence. What is certain is that it ends with until. He pronounced a terrible sentence over the city he was born to save, and he put a door in the last line. The words on the far side of it are not a list of terms but a welcome, the one thing that city never gave him.

In the flow. The chapter opened with blood in the temple courts and a barren tree granted one more year; now the year is running out for the city itself. Yet Luke ends not on the axe but on until.

How should Christians think about the Jewish people today? With love, gratitude and longing. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22): the patriarchs, the covenants, the Scriptures and the Messiah himself came through them (Romans 9:4–5). Paul had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen and prayed for their salvation (Romans 9:2–3; 10:1). Any contempt for Jewish people is a denial of the gospel, not a defence of it. At the same time the way of salvation is the same for Jew and Gentile: faith in Jesus the Messiah, the only name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). So we pray, we love, and we tell the good news, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
this house shall become a desolation

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Luke 14 is built around a dinner table. Jesus is at a meal in the house of a leading Pharisee, being watched. He heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and silences the lawyers. He sees the guests scrambling for the best seats and tells a parable about the kingdom’s reversal of honour. He tells the host to invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who cannot repay. And when a guest speaks piously of eating bread in the kingdom of God, Jesus answers with the parable of the great banquet: the feast is ready, the invited make excuses, and the house is filled from the streets and the hedgerows.

The second half moves from the table to the road. To the crowds following him Jesus names the cost of discipleship: first place above every love, a cross carried behind him, everything let go. Two parables, a tower and a war, tell them to count that cost. The banquet of grace and the cross of discipleship belong to the same gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On a Sabbath Jesus goes to dinner at a leading Pharisee’s house, the third such meal Luke records, and he is watched closely: not curiosity but surveillance. A man with dropsy is placed before him, perhaps to see what he will do. Ancient moralists used dropsy, a swelling that made its sufferer ever more thirsty, as a picture of greed, which is worth remembering in a chapter about guests who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Jesus does not wait for the trap. He asks the lawyers whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and they say nothing. He heals the man and sends him away, sparing him the argument, and then asks who would not pull a son or an ox out of a well on the Sabbath. They cannot reply.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument has the same shape as the one in the previous chapter (13:15), but it is sharper: there an animal was thirsty; here something is drowning, and the rescue is immediate. If you would break the Sabbath for your child and for your livestock, a man with dropsy cannot be worth less than both.

They are beaten by their own practice. Jesus has quoted no obscure text; he has described what every man in the room does when something valuable falls into a well.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals before he argues. The mercy is shown first and defended afterwards, and the man is sent home before the debate, not kept as an exhibit.

The double standard being exposed is a common one: rules applied strictly to other people and generously to oneself and one’s own. It is rarely noticed by the person doing it, because the exceptions feel like common sense.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 14 happens around a table. At a Pharisee’s Sabbath dinner Jesus heals a swollen man, tells grasping guests to take the lowest couch, and tells the host to fill his table with people who cannot repay. Then a parable: the feast is ready now, the invited make excuses, and the house is filled from the back streets and hedgerows. Then, to the crowds, the cost of following him. The God of this chapter feasts those who cannot repay, and its Christ asks for everything because he is about to give everything.

The setting. The whole chapter is about banquets: who is invited, where they sit, who comes, and the great banquet of the kingdom.

At a Pharisee’s table. This is the third such invitation Luke records (7:36; 11:37), and every one ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway. A ruler of the Pharisees is a leading Pharisee, and Sabbath meals, prepared the day before, were the week’s occasion for entertaining.

They were watching him carefully. The verb is used of watching for a purpose, as of the plot to kill Paul, watching the gates day and night (Acts 9:24). It is surveillance (6:7): the guests’ real business is to collect evidence.

Dropsy. Dropsy (oedema) is swelling from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness of the heart, liver or kidneys, and the term (hydrōpikos) is a physician’s word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible. Only Luke records this healing. A man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty, and Greek moralists used the illness as an image for insatiable greed: consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Hold that detail, because the rest of this chapter is about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Was he planted there? He was before him, prominently placed, in a private house, at a formal dinner, on the Sabbath. Luke does not say how he came to be there, and a sick man would not normally be at such a table. He may well have been put there to test Jesus, a pawn in their game. If so, the only person in the room who was treated as a person that evening was the one the others were using.

Why did Jesus keep accepting invitations from people who opposed him? Because he came to seek and to save the lost, and the self-righteous are lost too (19:10). He ate with tax collectors and with Pharisees alike; he never refused a table because of the company. That does not mean we must put ourselves under abuse or keep going where we are only mocked. But it does mean that hostility is not, on its own, a reason to withdraw. Some of the people who watch you most critically are the ones who most need to see Christ in you up close.
verseByVerse.note: Dropsy is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not? Luke says he responded, though nobody has said anything. He is answering their unspoken thoughts, what is in the room. And look who moves first. They have set the trap and are waiting for him to walk into it; he asks the question himself, out loud, before touching anybody. There is nothing to catch him at, because he has put the whole matter on the table in advance. And the question is framed exactly as they would have framed it: is it lawful, the technical language of their own debates, addressed to the experts, inviting a ruling. If they say yes, they cannot object. If they say no, they show themselves heartless.

They remained silent. They cannot say yes, because their whole position depends on saying no. They cannot say no, because a swollen man is standing in the room. So they say nothing, which is not neutrality: a decision taken in front of a suffering man.

Took, healed, sent away. He took him, contact with a diseased body in front of men obsessed with purity. He healed him. And he sent him away, a mercy of its own: the man does not have to stand there for the argument that is coming. Whatever he was brought for, he is not going to be used for it.

When should I speak up rather than stay silent? When someone is being wronged or a plain truth of God is being denied, and you are in a position to say something, silence is not safe ground. You do not need to speak about everything, and wisdom chooses its moment (Proverbs 26:4–5). But ask yourself honestly why you are quiet. If the answer is that speaking would cost you, the approval of the room, your standing at work, an awkward evening, that is exactly the silence Jesus exposed here. Say the true and kind thing, briefly and without heat, and leave the outcome to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out? The argument runs, as in the previous chapter, from what they already do to what they will not allow, but it is sharper. There the animal was merely thirsty (13:15). Here something is drowning, and the word is immediately: nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling. Many Jews of the day would rescue a son, or an animal, from a well on the Sabbath; only the strictest, such as the community at Qumran, forbade lifting a beast out of a pit on that day.

A son or an ox. The pairing is deliberately shocking. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read a donkey for a son, the more expected pair; son or ox is the harder reading and very probably what Luke wrote. If you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both? And there is a quiet irony: a man with dropsy was full of water; a man in a well is surrounded by it.

They could not reply. The second silence of the evening (v. 4), and this time it is inability rather than choice. He has simply described what every man in that room does when something valuable falls down a hole on a Sabbath afternoon.

The day made for release. Israel kept the day remembering that the LORD had brought them out of slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jesus opened his ministry announcing liberty to the captives (4:18), and a chapter earlier loosed a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound (13:16). The Lord of the Sabbath (6:5) is doing on the day of rest what the day was meant to celebrate: pulling the drowning out of the well.

Where is my real theology? Most people’s real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself. Try it on yourself. Where are you strict with others and generous with yourself: about lateness, about money, about speech, about forgiveness? The place where your rules bend for you is the place where you will find what you actually believe.

And the Sabbath today? Christians who love the Bible answer differently. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept for worship and for works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17), while gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28), and the Lord’s Day is a gift, set apart gladly for worship, fellowship and rest, not a law about work; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5), and the Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. On what this passage teaches, both agree: works of mercy are always right on the day of rest, and human need is never an interruption to be ignored, on any day of the week.

For worship. The Son of God did not merely reach down into the well; he went down into it, into the pit of our sin and death, and drew us out, and set our feet upon a rock (Psalm 40:2). He did it immediately, without waiting for us to deserve it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Guests reclined on couches ranked by nearness to the host, so choosing a couch was choosing a public estimate of oneself. Jesus tells them not to take the place of honour, lest a more distinguished guest arrive and they be sent, in shame, to the lowest place. Then comes the principle that turns the advice into a statement about God: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Taking the low seat in order to be moved up is only pride in disguise.

Jesus then turns to the host. Hospitality in that world ran on exchange: an invitation created a debt, repaid by a return invitation. He tells the host to invite those who cannot repay, and the inability to repay is exactly the qualification.
verseByVerse.theology: The reversal of honour runs through Luke (1:52; 14:11; 18:14), and the accounts are settled at the resurrection of the just, not in this life. The parable cannot be obeyed as a technique, only by someone who knows he is at the table by invitation, not merit. And the one who said this was on his way to the lowest place of all, the cross, from which God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9).
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction to the host is not a ban on family meals but a refusal to let the table be only that. The host who invites only those who will invite him back has traded, not given. The host who invites those who cannot repay imitates the God who invites sinners with nothing to offer, and the debt is not cancelled but moved: God himself will repay it at the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The places of honour. The Pharisees watched Jesus; Jesus watched them, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The seating. Guests reclined on couches ranked by closeness to the host. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself, in a culture where honour was gained and lost in front of witnesses.

A parable. It opens as etiquette, the sort of thing a wise uncle might say, and ends with a statement about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Demoted. Important guests might well arrive late, so the scenario is realistic and would have made everyone wince. The man has to get up, in front of everybody, and walk the length of the room.

Begin with shame. By then the middle places are taken, and every guest watches you go to the very bottom, and the shame goes on for the evening. Proverbs had said it: it is better to be told, come up here, than to be put lower in the presence of a noble (Proverbs 25:6–7).

Someone more distinguished than you. There was such a guest at that table, and nobody was jostling to give him their couch: the one whom David called Lord (20:41–44). And he did not scramble at all; Luke does not even tell us where he reclined. The one who had every right to the top couch was the only man in the room who did not need it, because his honour came from his Father and could not be added to or taken away by the seating plan (John 5:41–44).

Is it wrong to want to be recognised? The desire to be honoured is not itself evil: God made us for glory, and he promises honour to those who seek it by patient well-doing (Romans 2:7). What Jesus condemns is seizing it, ranking yourself above others and pushing for the place. The question is who you want the honour from. If you live for the room’s estimate, you will always be anxious about the next guest through the door. If you live for God’s, you can sit anywhere, and let him do the honouring in his own time.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lowest place. The advice is exactly reversed. If it stopped here it would be shrewd manoeuvring: take the bottom seat as a tactic and enjoy being moved up. The next verse closes that trap.

Humbled and exalted. The passive means humbled by God, exalted by God: God’s own way with the world, repeated in 18:14 and sung by Mary (1:52), and lived by Jesus, who humbled himself to the cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:5–11).

What it does not mean. Not false humility: taking the lowest place in order to be promoted is pride in disguise. True humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less, and leaving your honour to God (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Why humility is accuracy. Here the parable turns into gospel. It cannot be obeyed as a technique, only by somebody who has stopped competing, and what produces that is knowing your actual standing. The man who takes the low seat is not being humble so much as accurate: he is at the table by invitation and not by merit. Which is why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it.

Does humility mean I should never accept a responsibility or say I can do something well? No. Humility is not pretending to be less gifted than you are, and refusing a task God plainly calls you to is not modesty but disobedience. Paul could say he worked harder than all the apostles, and add at once that it was the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Humility is honest about gifts, because it knows they are gifts (1 Corinthians 4:7). It serves without needing the credit, rejoices when others are honoured, and does not grasp. You may sit at the head of the table if the host puts you there. Just do not put yourself there.

In everyday life. Let someone else have the parking space, the last word, the credit for the idea. Do one piece of good this week that nobody will ever know was yours.

For worship. The one who said this was on his way to the lowest place there is: a cross between two criminals. And from there he answered as only the Host can: today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). He went to the bottom of the table so that every sinner could hear, Friend, move up higher.

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the host. Then he turns to the host, at his own table, having eaten his food: one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

The ordinary guest list. Friends, brothers, relatives, rich neighbours: the four categories are the entire ordinary guest list of any household.

Repaid in return. In that culture an invitation created a debt, discharged by a return invitation of matching quality: a transaction with a settlement date. That is not grace; it is business (6:32–34).

The poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. People often excluded from religious gatherings (Qumran barred the lame and blind from its meals), and the exact opposite of the first four: they create no obligation because they can discharge none. They are the people God will bring to his banquet (v. 21).

They cannot repay you. Not that the poor are more deserving: their inability to repay is the qualification.

The guest list of his own ministry. Luke’s reader has heard this list before: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, and the poor have good news preached to them (7:22). The host is told to set his table the way Jesus has set his ministry. These are not a charity project tacked onto the kingdom but the people the Messiah was anointed to reach (4:18), and every table that welcomes them is a small copy of his.

The resurrection of the just. The resurrection to life of the righteous at the last day (Acts 24:15; John 5:29). The account is not cancelled but moved: a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

So am I forbidden to have my family round for Christmas dinner? No, and the same chapter tells you why. A dozen verses on, Jesus will say that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends; it is do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends, at Levi’s feast, in Martha’s house, and at this very Pharisee’s dinner while he said it. So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does.

Does giving in hope of a heavenly reward spoil it? No. Jesus himself sets the reward before us, so it cannot be wrong to want it (Hebrews 11:6). What spoils giving is wanting the return from people: thanks, status, an invitation back. To give looking to God for your reward is to give freely to people, since you need nothing from them. And the reward itself is a gift of grace, not wages earned. God crowns in his children what his Spirit has worked in them, and the greatest part of the reward is the Giver himself.

In everyday life. God fed you when you could not repay. Who could you invite who could never invite you back? Start with one name: the widower from church, the international student, the struggling family, the man nobody sits with.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something true: blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God. But it is said in the third person and the future tense, and after Jesus has spoken about this table tonight, it moves the talk somewhere safe. Jesus answers with a parable about a feast that is ready now.

The guests had accepted the first invitation; the servant comes with the second, on the day, to say that everything is now ready. The work is done and the only thing missing is the guests. Then the excuses: a field, five yoke of oxen, a marriage, all good things and none of them wicked. Nobody refuses outright. They express regret and stay at home, which is the form the refusal of the gospel very often takes.
verseByVerse.theology: The master’s anger is the response of generosity treated as an inconvenience: the food was ready and the gift already paid for. But the anger does not cancel the feast; it redirects it. The servant brings in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, the very guests Jesus had told the host to invite (v. 13), and then goes beyond the town to the highways and hedges, which suggests the Gentiles and the mission of Acts. The original guests are shut out by their own choice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Still there is room: the servant has swept the city and the hall is not full. The house was built larger than anyone expected.

The words compel people to come in were later used to justify forcing people into the church, the opposite of their meaning: those compelled are people who thought themselves too far outside to be wanted. The verse presses on the church an urgency of love, not force.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bread in the kingdom. Somebody breaks the silence, and what he says is entirely correct. The messianic banquet was the settled hope of Israel, the feast of rich food for all peoples when death is swallowed up for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8; 13:29). He assumes he will be there. The parable that follows asks: will you?

Why does Jesus answer a true remark with a warning? Listen to the sentence again and the reason surfaces. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense: blessed is everyone who will eat. Nobody in the room is implicated by it. It is the kind of thing a man says at a dinner table when the conversation has become uncomfortable and he wants to return it to safe and elevating ground. And the timing gives it away. Jesus has just told this room to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them. Both remarks were about this table, tonight. What comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The bread was already at the table. The guest spoke of eating bread in the kingdom as something far off, across the table from the one who would give that bread. On the night he was betrayed Jesus would take bread and say, this is my body, which is given for you, and promise that his disciples would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (22:19, 30). The blessing the man admired from a distance was sitting opposite him.

The tense changes. The man wanted to talk about the guest list of the kingdom. He is about to be told that the invitations have gone out and the replies are coming in.

In everyday life. Watch for the moments when you change the subject to something true and general because the specific was getting close: a sermon applied to someone else, a talk about the church’s needs that never reaches your diary.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great banquet. The host is God, preparing the feast of the kingdom. A formal banquet, it seems, involved two invitations: the first well in advance, so that the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals; the second on the day, when everything was ready. So these people are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They said yes weeks ago, and the host has bought and slaughtered on the strength of it. Israel had been invited long ago, through the prophets, and had said yes.

He sent his servant. A servant, sent on foot to the houses of men who outrank him, with words that are not his own. Many see in him Jesus himself, and after him those who preach the kingdom. The servant does not prepare the feast and cannot add to it; the message that it is ready is the whole of his commission.

Everything is now ready. Not would you consider coming. The work is done, the cost met, the table laid, and only the guests are missing. That is the gospel in a sentence: the invitation is never to do something but the announcement that something has been done, and the only question is whether a man will come and sit down.

What made everything ready. When Jesus told this parable the most expensive part of the preparation was still ahead of him, at Jerusalem: not animals killed for a dinner, but the Son himself given up. The servant carrying the summons is also the one whose body and blood would lay the table. By Pentecost nothing at all remained to be done (Acts 2:38–39).

What does it mean for me to come? To come is to trust Christ: to stop relying on anything you bring and to rely on what he has done. It is not first a matter of feelings or of cleaning yourself up; the guests at this feast are fed, not inspected. You come by turning from your sin and resting on Christ, telling God in your own words that you have nothing and asking him to receive you for his Son’s sake. And having come, you keep coming: to his word, his table and his people. The banquet is ready today, and the invitation is addressed to you.

In everyday life. If you speak to anyone about Christ this week, remember what you are carrying: not a programme of self-improvement, but news. You are a servant with a message, not a salesman with a pitch.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Excuses. All alike: with one accord, as though it had been arranged. These are men who had already accepted, and to refuse after accepting was a grave insult. Three excuses are given as samples, and not one is disreputable.

A field. Possessions. Nobody bought land unexamined, and the field would still be there tomorrow.

Five yoke of oxen. Business. Ten oxen mean a wealthy man, and you would test them before buying, not on the evening of a feast.

A wife. Family, and different in tone. The first two say please have me excused; this one simply states it. He may be leaning on the law that excused a newly married man from war for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5). But a banquet is not a war, and that law was given to protect a marriage, not to excuse a man from a feast.

The point. Possessions, work and family are all good things, and here they become excuses for refusing God’s invitation (8:14; 9:57–62). Nobody says I do not want to come. They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home. That is the form the rejection of the gospel very often takes: not I refuse Christ, but not now, there is something I have to deal with first, said politely for forty years. It is not a postponement. It is the refusal. And behind each excuse sits a heart that has made a good thing into the thing it cannot do without: a gift allowed to take the Giver’s place.

The one who let nothing keep him away. Against these excuses stands the man telling the story, his face set for Jerusalem (9:51), answering would-be followers who wanted first to bury a father or say farewell at home (9:59–62). Jesus had a mother, brothers, a trade and a home town, and none of them became his apology. He came to the feast his Father appointed, and it was the cross. Every guest who will finally sit at the table is there because one man never sent an excuse.

But surely my family and work are things God gave me? They are, and that is exactly what makes them dangerous as excuses. God gives fields, oxen and wives so that we might enjoy them with thanksgiving under him (1 Timothy 4:4). Coming to Christ does not take them away; it puts them in their place, and they are better there. The trouble begins when a gift is used to keep the Giver at arm’s length. If your reason for not coming to Christ, or not following him fully, is something good, you are in precisely the position of these men. Bring the field and the oxen and the marriage with you to the feast. Do not send them as your apology.

For worship. The Son who told this story was turned away by the guests his Father had invited, and went on to the cross to make a place for people who had refused him. Every one of us once sent our apology to that table, and the Host sent the invitation again.
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year — but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master became angry. Rightly: it is the only emotion attributed to the host, and not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He had his guests’ word and spent accordingly. What has been refused is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were unanimous and casual.

Is God really angry with people who decline his invitation? Yes, and it would be a lesser God who were not. His anger is no outburst; it is the settled response of holy love to generosity treated as an inconvenience. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved. That is sobering for anyone who has been treating the gospel as an offer with no deadline. But see what the anger does next. It does not cancel the feast. It sends the servant out again, to people nobody else wanted. God’s anger at refusal and his eagerness to fill his house stand together.

Streets and lanes. Then the anger redirects the banquet, quickly, because the food is ready. The streets and lanes are the thoroughfares and back alleys where the outcasts lived: within Israel, the tax collectors, sinners and poor whom the religious elite kept out.

Bring in the poor. Exactly the list of verse 13: God does what he told the host to do, the parable’s quiet accusation to a room that had just let the instruction pass. The people who cannot repay him end up at the table not as a second-best arrangement, but because that was always the guest list he wanted.

Where Jesus had been eating. The men at that dinner knew where Jesus went when he was not at their tables: Levi’s great feast with a large company of tax collectors (5:29), and soon the grumble again, this man receives sinners and eats with them (15:2). The servant in the back streets is a picture of what they had watched Jesus do all along, who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (5:32).

What if I feel too broken to belong at God’s table? Then you are exactly the kind of guest this verse describes. The poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame were not brought in because they had recovered; they were brought in as they were. Your sense of unworthiness is not a barrier to coming. It is, in this parable, the very mark of those who are carried in. Come as you are, and he will make you what he wants you to be.

In everyday life. Who in your town is in the streets and lanes, sure that church is not for them, or on the edges of your own congregation? You were brought in from the lanes yourself. Make your church a place where the poor and broken are not tolerated but wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still there is room. The most hopeful sentence in the parable, spoken by the servant. Every street has been swept, and the hall is not full: God’s house was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

Highways and hedges. Now he is sent outside the town, to the roads between towns and the hedgerows where vagrants sheltered: people with no address, suggesting the Gentiles. This is the mission of Acts, to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8; 13:46).

A light for the hedgerows. That outward sweep began with Christ himself. Simeon called the baby a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:30–32), and the risen Lord said that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:47). Every stranger who comes in from the hedges comes in by his name.

Compel them. Compel means urge strongly. A man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman’s banquet would assume a mistake had been made, and would need pressing before he believed the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is a servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying: no, truly, he means you.

Where Christians differ: compel them to come in. Augustine used this verse to justify using the power of the state to force heretics (the Donatists) back into the church, and it was later used to justify forced conversions and persecution. This commentary’s view: this is a grievous misreading. The compulsion is the urgency of love and persuasion, not force. Faith cannot be coerced. The gospel is to be pressed on people earnestly, but never by violence (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20). Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will.

How do I urge someone without being pushy? Urgency and respect belong together. Speak plainly about Christ, and do not be embarrassed to ask someone to come, more than once if need be: to church, to a Bible study, to Christ himself. Tell them the invitation is truly for them, especially if they think they are too far gone. But never manipulate, never bully, and never use pressure that bypasses the conscience; God opens hearts, and we only persuade (Acts 16:14). Pray before you speak, listen as much as you talk, and let your life make the invitation believable. Love presses; it does not coerce.

That my house may be filled. God’s banquet will be full, and refusal will not thwart his purpose (John 6:37–39).

None of those men. Those who refused will be shut out (13:28), by their own choice. The last line is plural, addressed to someone other than the servant: Jesus stepping out of the parable to address the dinner party he is sitting at.

In everyday life. Name to yourself the person you have assumed would never be interested, beyond the hedges of your usual circle, and tell them, kindly and plainly, that the invitation is for them.

For worship. Still there is room: no words are more welcome to a sinner. The Father’s house has many rooms, and the Son has gone to prepare them (John 14:2). His grace has run out to the hedgerows and found us there, and it will not stop until the house is full.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come — the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds travel with Jesus, and he turns and tells them what following him costs, which is not what a man does who wants to keep a crowd. Hate is a Semitic way of saying love less (Genesis 29:30–31; compare Matthew 10:37), and the rest of Scripture rules out a literal reading (Mark 7:9–13; John 19:26–27). The last item on the list, his own life, governs the rest.

To that crowd a cross-bearer was a condemned man carrying the beam of his execution through jeering streets. Two parables follow, each beginning with someone who sits down first: a builder who must count the cost before he starts, and a king who must weigh his army and, if he is outmatched, ask for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
These words are spoken to people already following and already enthusiastic. Jesus is not recruiting; he is telling a large crowd to stop and calculate, because a following that has not counted the cost becomes a field of abandoned foundations.

The king’s parable adds what the builder lacks: a way out. A man facing twenty thousand with ten thousand cannot win by effort; sending a delegation while there is still distance is not defeat but the only wise move. That is what the counting is for: to bring a person to seek peace with God on his terms. And renounce means to let go, like a man taking leave at a door.
verseByVerse.examples:
Most of the time loving Christ makes a person a better son, husband and father, and there is no conflict. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims cannot both be honoured. Then the cost is real, and the grief is no sign of having done wrong; but the command never licenses coldness. You go on loving your family, usually better than before, and simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

The salt saying closes the chapter: impure salt with the salt leached out, still in the jar and still called salt, and no longer working.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great crowds. He has an enormous following, and he stops the procession, deliberately, to say one of the hardest things in the Gospel: not what a man does who is trying to keep a crowd. He wants disciples.

In the flow. The parable has just shown that the feast is free and the house filled with people who bring nothing; these verses show what it means to come in. The invitation costs the guest nothing, and coming to the Host costs him everything else, because the one who gives the feast asks to be loved above every gift he gives.

Hate as loving less. Hate here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and the Hebrew says Leah was hated, which the ESV renders unloved (Genesis 29:30–31). Matthew gives the plainer form: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37).

Even his own life. The closest relationships are named one by one, so that no one can think his case the exception, and the last name governs the rest. The self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation.

Cannot be. Not may not be a very good disciple, but cannot be. No prophet ever said, love me more than your mother. Moses said, love the LORD your God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5). Jesus puts himself where Moses put God: either he is God, or this is outrageous.

Is this not a convenient softening? The idiom explains the word, but a reader may still suspect the explanation of being a rescue operation, a hard saying softened because we do not like it. It is not; it is the only reading the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity. When the scribes devised Corban, a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not support aged parents, Jesus said they were making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). That is precisely what a literal reading of this verse would license, and he condemned it. He kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment, giving his mother into John’s care from the cross (John 19:26–27). And Paul says that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

When does the conflict actually come? Most of the time there is no conflict at all: loving Christ makes a man a better son, a better husband, a better father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured. A convert from another faith whose family cuts him off. A believer whose spouse demands that she stop going to church. A son whose father insists he join a dishonest business. A parent who must choose between a child’s approval and the truth. In those moments Jesus must win, gently and without contempt, and with the door kept open. And where a family relationship involves abuse, putting Christ first never means submitting to it; it may mean seeking safety and help.

For worship. Only one who is God can ask for this, and only one who loves like God would deserve it. Christ asks for first place because he gave up his first place, and every one of our loves came from him. To put him first is not to lose them. It is to love them at their source.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His own cross. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:23), where it was daily. Here the verb is bear, the sustained business of walking under a load, and it is his own cross: each man carries the one with his name on it.

What the image meant. To that crowd it was no worn metaphor: a man already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through jeering streets. It carries finality, since nobody carrying a crossbeam is coming back; shame, since crucifixion was designed to degrade; and submission, since he has stopped fighting. To bear your cross is to accept rejection, shame and death for Jesus’ sake, as a way of life.

After me. The cross is carried behind someone. And the second cannot: there is no discipleship without a cross.

Behind Jesus. Luke shows the verse acted out at the end of his Gospel: Simon of Cyrene, with the cross laid on him, to carry it behind Jesus (23:26). But that day Jesus went in front to his own death, and the beam Simon carried was the one on which the Lord would hang. Every disciple’s cross is carried behind the one cross that saves. Ours is borne in his company; his was borne for us.

Is my cross the illness or difficulty I have? Not exactly. Every Christian suffers the ordinary troubles of a fallen world, and God uses them; but the cross Jesus means is what comes to you because you follow him. It is the cost of saying no to yourself and yes to Christ: the career move declined because it meant dishonesty, the friendships lost because you would not join in, the mockery at work, the sin you go on refusing year after year, the persecution that in many lands means prison or death. A cross is chosen in the sense that you could put it down by abandoning Christ. Bearing it means you will not.

In everyday life. Name the place where following Jesus costs you something this week, and, in the strength he gives, do not quietly lay that cross down.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost? Having said what discipleship costs, he insists that people work out whether they can pay. A tower might guard a vineyard (Isaiah 5:2) or be a farm building: an ordinary landowner’s project, not a civic monument. And the verb is sit down: stop, sit, and do the arithmetic before the first stone is laid.

Not able to finish. The failure is public and permanent: an abandoned foundation in the field, visible from the road, and Jesus supplies the neighbours’ sentence.

The point. Before you follow Jesus, think about what it will cost, and do not start enthusiastically and give up halfway (8:13).

He is not recruiting. With a great crowd attached, he tells them to stop and calculate whether they can afford it, the opposite of every technique for gathering a following, and uncomfortable for any appeal that keeps the cost out of sight until the decision is made.

The builder who finished. The one telling this parable had counted his own cost: the third day I finish my course (13:32), his face set to Jerusalem knowing what was there (18:31–33). No disciple’s tower is safe because the disciple is a good builder. It is safe because the Lord who lays the foundation of his people never began anything he could not finish.

If I must count the cost, how can anyone afford it? No one can pay it in his own strength, and that is part of what the counting reveals; the next parable will say so. The cost is real: Christ asks for everything. But the one who calls also supplies. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), and those who build on him are kept by his power, not their own (1 Peter 1:5). The counting is not meant to deter anybody. It is meant to make the commitment real, so that what begins actually gets finished, and so that the tower, when it is up, is a witness rather than a joke.

In everyday life. When you speak of Christ, tell the cost honestly as well as the joy. And if you have stalled halfway, with a foundation laid years ago and little built since, come back to him today. He finishes what he starts.

For worship. At the cross the mockers thought they were looking at an abandoned foundation: he saved others, let him save himself (23:35). They were watching the last stone go in. Three days later the work stood complete, our redemption, finished by the one who knew the cost before he began.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate? A second parable, and a greater matter: a war, not a building. The change of scale is deliberate, from a farmer with a half-built shed to a king with an army, from money to survival. Sit down first again: the same instruction as the builder’s. Do the sum before you move.

Whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Outnumbered two to one. Not hopeless, but the kind of arithmetic that requires an honest man to face a difficult conclusion.

A delegation. Here the two parables part. The builder can only finish or be mocked. The king has a third option: while the other is yet a great way off, he sends envoys and asks for terms.

The point. Two readings, both true. As with the tower, count the cost. And God is the king coming against you with superior force: make peace with him now, while he is still far off, by surrendering everything to him (12:58).

Who is the greater king? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size, in a chapter about what it costs to follow Jesus, is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. He cannot. Nobody can. What is left is the delegation: going out, while there is still distance between you, and asking for terms. And that is not defeat in this parable. It is the only wise move on the board, and it is the one the king is commended for making. The disaster is not surrender; the disaster is a man who marches out with ten thousand against twenty thousand because he never sat down and did the sum. Which is what the counting of the cost is actually for. It is not to establish that you can afford discipleship. It is to bring you to the point of sending the delegation.

What are the terms of peace? Astonishingly generous. The King who comes against us does not demand that we make up our losses or pay reparations. He has already provided the peace himself. In Christ, God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and he has sent ambassadors to plead: be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). The terms are unconditional surrender to his Son and trust in what his Son has done. We give up our arms; he gives us his friendship. To a proud heart that sounds like humiliation, but it is no more humiliating than a drowning man letting go of the wreckage to take hold of the rope. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). To be justified means to be declared righteous by God the Judge: not made sinless overnight, but counted right with him because Christ’s obedience and death are credited to us (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

In everyday life. Is there a part of your life where you are still at war with God: a command you resent, a providence you will not accept? Send the delegation today. Tell him you give it up, and ask for his peace.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Renounce. The so therefore ties this to both parables. The verb (apotassetai) meant to say goodbye, as of the man who wanted to say farewell at home (9:61): a man releasing his hold on what he is leaving. It does not necessarily mean literally selling everything; it means giving up ownership of everything to Christ. Then the third cannot (vv. 26, 27, 33): Christ above family, above self, and above possessions.

Must I sell everything I own? No, and Luke himself will not allow that reading. Zacchaeus gives half and is told salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 funded the ministry out of means they must still have had. Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on the fact that the property was his to keep (Acts 5:4). What is required is that a man stop holding. Some are called to give up a great deal literally; all are called to hold everything open-handed, as stewards and not owners, ready to give whatever he asks. The test is not what percentage you give but whether anything you have is off limits to him.

All that he has. The phrase goes past property to reputation, plans, rights and the future a man has drawn up. The thing you are most certain God would never ask you for is the thing this verse is about.

The one who let go first. Jesus asks for nothing he did not give up himself: no place to lay his head (9:58), and at the end stripped even of his clothes, which the soldiers divided by lot (23:34). He renounced all that he had, not to buy a disciple’s freedom from possessions but to buy the disciple.

The freedom of letting go. There is mercy in the severity. A man who has let go of everything cannot be robbed or blackmailed, and cannot be moved from the low seat because he has nothing to defend.

In everyday life. Name in prayer what you have not yet surrendered: savings, retirement plans, your children’s futures, your reputation, your time. Then live this week as a steward of it. You will not let go perfectly, but the one who renounced all for you did, and for his sake your faltering surrender is accepted.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt is good. Salt kept meat, seasoned food, and in small amounts fertilised fields. The saying closes the chapter: this is what happens to a disciple who will not pay the cost.

But if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? Pure salt cannot lose its taste. But much of the salt used in Palestine, it is usually explained, was not pure. Impure salt, collected from the Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum and other minerals, could have its salt leached out by moisture and lose its taste, leaving a useless white powder. Which is the whole force of the image. This is not salt that has disappeared. It is salt that is still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt, and it has stopped working.

Not even for the manure pile. Luke’s detail is the sharpest of the three Gospels: even the dunghill will not take it.

It is thrown away. A fair description of what a half-committed disciple is for. Not wicked, not anybody’s enemy, simply useless for the one thing that was the point of him: he has kept the appearance and lost the function.

The point. Discipleship that is not costly is not discipleship, and a church that has lost its distinctiveness is useless to the world.

Where Christians differ: can a true Christian lose his saltiness and be thrown away? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read the verse that way, and they press its warning with real seriousness: a real disciple may fall away and be finally lost. This commentary’s view: Jesus is warning those who follow at a distance without counting the cost. A disciple in name who will not carry his cross shows that he never truly had the salt (1 John 2:19; John 15:6). Those whom Christ has truly made his own he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and it is one of the very means by which Christ keeps his true disciples faithful: they hear it, and they hold on to him.

Ears to hear. The same words followed the parable of the soils (8:8): the hearing that lets the thing in. The sentence hands the chapter back to the reader. A cost has been counted or not; a table serves people who can repay or people who cannot; a seat has been grasped or given up. What is left is the hearing.

I feel I have lost my saltiness. Is there hope? Yes. The very fact that you feel it and care about it is a sign that the Spirit is still at work in you. Salt that has truly lost its savour does not grieve over it. Return to Christ, confess where you have grown cold or compromised, and ask him to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). Saltiness is not something you manufacture by trying harder to be different. It comes from closeness to Christ, and it returns as you return to him: to his word, to prayer, to his people, and to the cost you had begun to avoid.

For worship. The Lord who warned about salt thrown away said to Peter on the night of his denial, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (22:32). Peter wept bitterly, and he was not thrown out; he was turned again and sent to strengthen his brothers. Christ keeps his own by his intercession, and the savour he gives he does not let go.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Luke 15 answers one complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” Jesus does not deny it. He tells three stories that give one answer to why he eats with sinners: because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who goes after one lost sheep, the woman who sweeps the house for one lost coin, and the father who runs to meet his son while he is still a long way off.

The stories build. A sheep wanders, a coin simply lies where it fell, and a son leaves on purpose. The son comes home with a speech about his unworthiness, and the father answers it with a robe, a ring, sandals and a feast.

The chapter ends with the elder son, who never left and is angry at the welcome. He stands for the grumblers who prompted the parables. His father goes out and pleads with him, and Luke does not say whether he went in. The invitation is left open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this chapter depends on the first two verses. Sinners keep coming to hear Jesus, and the religious leaders grumble, as Israel grumbled in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2, 7–8). Their complaint is not that he preaches to sinners but that he eats with them, and in that world a shared meal said plainly who your people were.

His answer is three stories that Luke calls one parable (v. 3): one argument in three movements, each about something lost and each ending in a party. The first puts his critics inside the story, with a shepherd who will not come home until he has found the one sheep, carries it home rejoicing, and calls in the neighbours.
verseByVerse.theology:
