The shepherd seeks the sheep; the sheep does not seek the shepherd. That is the pattern of grace: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19), and “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be read two ways, and serious readers hold both. It may simply mean those already safe in the fold. But the men grumbling at verse 2 would have described themselves in exactly those words, and by the end of the chapter Jesus paints one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father’s house. Read against that ending, the phrase has a dry edge.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ninety-nine are safe in the shepherd’s care while he searches. A church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has misunderstood its own situation: it was once the one, and is now among the ninety-nine.

The men it was told to were sure they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was built so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment it closed on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 15 is Jesus’ answer to a complaint: this man receives sinners and eats with them. He does not deny it. He tells three stories of lost things found, a sheep, a coin and a son. In each the one who has lost goes looking or watching until the lost is home, and the finding produces a joy that must be shared. The last story turns to the son who never left, angry outside the feast, while his father comes out and pleads with him too. It shows the heart of God towards sinners of both kinds.

In the flow. The previous chapter left us with a banquet thrown open to the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame (14:21). Chapter 15 opens with exactly such people coming to hear, while the religious men who should have been first at the feast stand back and complain. The whole stretch is moving towards the sentence that sums it up: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

All drawing near. The form of the verb suggests they kept coming: not one occasion but a settled pattern. Tax collectors were Jews who collected Rome’s revenue, regarded as traitors as well as extortioners. Sinners is broader: the openly immoral, but also, to the scrupulous, anybody who did not keep the purity code. And they came to hear him: not for bread or healing, but to listen to a preacher, the last thing anyone would have predicted of that crowd. Something in him made sinners feel welcome.

Grumbled. The verb (diegongyzon) means muttered among themselves, the word the Greek Old Testament uses of Israel grumbling in the wilderness about the water and the bread (Exodus 15:24; 16:7–8). Not argument, but a noise made by people who have decided not to engage.

Receives sinners and eats with them. It is meant as an accusation, and it is completely accurate. Receives (prosdechetai) means welcomes. And eats with them was the part that mattered most: to eat with a man was to accept him, his reputation attached to yours. The offence was not that he preached to sinners but that he sat down with them. Their complaint is the gospel.

The holy one at the sinners’ table. The scandal only makes sense if Jesus is who Luke says he is. A lax teacher eating with sinners would have surprised nobody. This is the one whom even the demons named the Holy One of God (4:34), whose touch made a leper clean instead of making himself unclean (5:13). The Pharisees thought a holy man must be protected from sinners. Jesus is the holiness from which sinners need no protection, because it heals what it touches.

Does receiving sinners mean Jesus approves of sin? No. He receives sinners in order to save them, and the word that runs through the chapter is repentance (vv. 7, 10). The doctor sits with the sick because he means to heal them (5:31–32). Jesus never said to a sinner that what he had done did not matter; he said that their sins were forgiven, and called them to follow him, as he did Levi (5:27–28). His welcome is not an endorsement of the far country. It is the open door out of it. That is the pattern for his church: a table open to any sinner, and a gospel that calls every sinner home.

So should Christians spend time with people whose lives are a mess? Yes, gladly, as Jesus did, with the aim of drawing them to him. That means real friendship, meals, hospitality and patience, not a project kept at arm’s length. It also means wisdom: you go as one who belongs to Christ, not to join in the sin, and if a friendship is pulling you away from him rather than drawing them towards him, something needs to change (1 Corinthians 15:33). But the danger in most churches is not that we are too close to sinners. It is that we are as far from them as the Pharisees were.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What man of you. The question puts his critics inside the story and is framed to compel agreement: any shepherd would do this. That is the trap. He is describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to. Shepherding was humble, dirty work, and later rabbinic writings list shepherds among the suspect trades, yet Jesus asks these respectable men to imagine being one, and God himself is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34).

If he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country? One percent, hardly worth worrying about, you might think. But a lost sheep is genuinely lost: a sheep that has strayed rarely finds its own way back. The ninety-nine are in pasture, presumably with other shepherds, so this is not the recklessness it sounds.

And go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? The shepherd takes the initiative. The sheep does not find its way back; the shepherd seeks it. Until he finds it: four words that govern the whole search. Not until dark. Not until it seems hopeless. There is no clause in this sentence that allows the shepherd to come home empty. This is God’s seeking love, the love he promised through Ezekiel when he said he himself would search for his sheep (Ezekiel 34:11, 16), and the mission Jesus will name at Zacchaeus’ door: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. A frightened, exhausted sheep, it is often said, will lie down and refuse to move, and it cannot be herded, so the shepherd hoists it across his neck, front legs in one hand and back legs in the other, and carries it home over the same country he searched. No scolding, no punishment: the whole weight of the animal that caused the trouble is on his shoulders, and he is glad about it all the way home. Isaiah had seen it: he will gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11).

If the shepherd does all the work, what do I do? You are found. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried, and that is a true picture of salvation: God seeks us before we seek him, and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Our coming to him, our repentance and faith, is real, and we must do it; but it is the sheep’s response to the shepherd’s arms, not its own way home. If you have come to Christ, you can trace it back to his seeking. If you are still lost, know that he is the one who goes looking. Cry out to him, and you will find you have been sought.

What about the ninety-nine? Does God care less about faithful believers? No. The ninety-nine are not abandoned; they are left safe in the pasture. The parable is not ranking the sheep. It shows how much one lost sheep matters to a shepherd who already loves all of them. If you have been in the fold for years and feel overlooked, remember that you, too, were once the one he went after, and the joy over your finding was no less. The shepherd who carried you home has not put you down.

In everyday life. Somewhere near you is a sheep who has wandered: a friend who has stopped coming to church, a child who has turned away. Go after them, in prayer first and then in person, gently, without scolding. A phone call, a meal, a note: the shepherd’s work is often as plain as that.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calls together his friends. Joy must be shared. He throws a party over one sheep out of a hundred, perhaps at a cost greater than the sheep was worth. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.

The party at Jesus’ table. So the meals the Pharisees complained about are this party: the Pharisees object to a man who eats with sinners, and Jesus describes a man who calls in the neighbours for a meal over what was lost. When he sat down with tax collectors he was doing on earth what heaven was doing over the same people, and the grumblers were standing at the edge of heaven’s celebration calling it a scandal.

Over one sinner who repents. The word repents appears here for the first time in the chapter, in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep is found; in reality the sinner repents. They are the same event seen from two sides.

Ninety-nine righteous persons. This is irony: there are no righteous people who need no repentance (Romans 3:10, 23). But it is exactly how the grumblers saw themselves (18:9), and by the end of the chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an older brother refusing to come in. Nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.

Does God really feel joy? Yes. Scripture does not picture God as cold or unmoved. The LORD your God will rejoice over you with gladness and exult over you with loud singing (Zephaniah 3:17). His joy is not like ours, needy or fluctuating; he is eternally blessed in himself. But he truly delights in mercy (Micah 7:18), and the repentance of a sinner is the occasion of real gladness in heaven. If you have come to Christ, you were the cause of God’s rejoicing. That is not sentiment but what Jesus said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second parable moves indoors: God, just pictured as a shepherd, is now a woman with a lamp and a broom in a dark house. The coin can do nothing at all to be found, which deepens the point of the first story. In the application the joy moves into the present tense, and it is joy “before the angels of God”: they watch while God is glad.
verseByVerse.theology: The angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). They are not detached from the gospel. The finding of one lost sinner is gladness in the presence where they stand, and they know what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman’s method is a pattern for prayer and pastoral work that will not give up. She lights the lamp, she sweeps away what covers the coin, and she keeps at it. The sweeping is the least glamorous part, and it is the part that finds the coin.

The coin’s helplessness is a comfort. Anyone who has watched someone they love become unable to help themselves, through addiction, illness of the mind or a hardness they cannot break, is looking at the coin. It cannot call out or move towards the light, and that changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
What woman. The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman. Luke’s pairing again: a man and a woman (13:18–21). God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a woman searching her house, on her hands and knees.

The coins. Each coin was a drachma, roughly a day’s wage. Ten coins may have been her savings, or coins worn as her security and the sign of her marriage. Either way, losing one was a real loss for a poor woman.

A lamp and a broom. A poor house had few or no windows, and a beaten earth floor, perhaps covered with straw, so even at midday the corners were dark: hence the lamp. Finding a small coin meant lighting a lamp and sweeping carefully, listening for the clink, because in that gloom you might well hear it before you saw it.

Until she finds it. The same until as the shepherd’s, the same refusal to stop, and the same party.

The difference. A sheep wanders away by its own folly; a coin is lost through no will of its own; a son will walk away deliberately. All lost; all longed for; all found. And the coin deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin cannot do anything at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, and no amount of time will improve its position. It is simply lost, and then it is simply found, and everything in between was done by somebody with a lamp.

Salvation has come to this house. The grumblers did not have to imagine a searcher going through a house. A few chapters on, Jesus will stop under a tree in Jericho, call a chief tax collector by name and say, today I must stay at your house (19:5). The crowd will grumble with the very verb of this chapter (19:7). The seeking in these parables is what Jesus was doing, house by house, in the towns where they lived.

Is it right to picture God as a woman? The parable pictures God’s searching love through a woman’s action, as Scripture elsewhere compares his care to a mother’s (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus has just compared himself to a hen (13:34). These are images of what God does, and they are precious. But Scripture never addresses God as mother or calls him she. He reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we name him as he has named himself. We can rejoice in every likeness Scripture gives, and still pray, as Jesus taught us, Our Father.

In everyday life. If you feel as helpless as a coin under the furniture, unable to do anything to get yourself found, take heart: that is precisely the kind of lost thing this woman went looking for.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius — about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joy before the angels. The same application as the sheep, with two changes. The tense: over the sheep there will be joy; here there is joy, now, every time. And the location: before the angels of God, the joy of God himself, with the angels as onlookers.

Whose joy are they watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already told us. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. And in the parable still to come, a father will run down a road and kill the best animal on the farm. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted. So the picture is this. Somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round, and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

Over one sinner who repents. The arithmetic never changes: one sheep out of a hundred, one coin out of ten, one sinner of no particular importance to anybody, whose repentance stops heaven in its tracks. That is a long way from the God the grumblers were defending, and from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable and disappointed. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

Do the angels know when someone is saved? The verse says there is joy in their presence, and Scripture elsewhere shows angels longing to look into the gospel (1 Peter 1:12) and serving those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). It is natural to think they share heaven’s gladness. But we should not speculate beyond what is written, and the point is not the angels but the God before whom they stand. The joy that fills heaven at a sinner’s repentance is first and most of all his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third story is announced as being about two sons, though it is usually preached as if it were about one. The younger demands his share early, wastes it in a far country and ends among the pigs, until he comes to himself and heads home with a speech prepared. The father sees him a long way off and runs. The second half belongs to the elder son, who never left, and who stands outside the feast while his father pleads with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father’s running and the feast both protect the son. The father reaches him on the road before the village can, and everyone who eats the fattened calf has, by coming, accepted the father’s verdict on his son.

Some have argued that because the parable has no sacrifice, no blood and no mediator, the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel. But the parable is not costless; we have been reading it from the son’s side. The squandered portion was real property and is not coming back, and the robe, the ring, the sandals and the calf all come out of what remains. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the cost himself, in silence, and never mentions it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy came home because he was hungry, and the father does not interrogate the motive. He sees him a long way off and runs. Luke shows the same thing elsewhere: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes went home justified (18:13–14), and the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else to try (23:42–43).

The elder brother is the parable’s real target. He calls his life in his father’s house service, wants a goat to celebrate with his friends, and will not call the boy his brother. Jesus told this to the men who grumbled at verse 2, and left the ending for them to write.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man who had two sons. Only Luke records this parable, and it is announced as being about a man and two sons, though it is usually preached as though it were about one. The younger son stands for the tax collectors and sinners (v. 1), the older for the Pharisees and scribes (v. 2), and the father for God. The story is left open at the end, because the older son, the Pharisees, must decide.

In the flow. The three stories narrow as they go: one sheep in a hundred, one coin in ten, one son in two. This story adds a second son who never left and is still lost, and through him the parable speaks to the grumblers of verse 2, not only about them.

The Son who tells of the Father. It matters who is telling this story. Jesus had said that no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). Here the Son draws the portrait. And he draws it to explain his own behaviour: he receives sinners because this is what the Father is like. Watch Jesus at a table with tax collectors and you are watching the father of the parable at the gate.

Give me the share. The shock of that sentence is the doorway into the whole parable. A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive one-third (the elder received a double portion, Deuteronomy 21:17). A father could distribute property early, but the son had no standing to ask. To ask for it now was, as many have put it, like saying: I wish you were dead; I want your things, not you. And the words are careful: the share that is coming to me, his by right. He has not asked for a gift but for what he considers already owed.

He divided his property. Astonishingly, the father agrees, without a recorded word, argument or condition. He does not force his son to stay. And note the plural: between them. The elder son receives his share too, which will matter when he complains that he has never been given anything. This is what every sinner does to God: takes his gifts, life, health and abilities, and wants to live without him. Sin does break God’s rules (1 John 3:4), but underneath the broken rule lies a broken relationship. So the deepest wrong in sin is not a line crossed but a Father turned away from, his gifts kept and his company refused.

Why does God let people walk away from him? The father does not hold his son by force, and God does not drag sinners into his house against their will. He lets people have what they insist on, and sometimes that is the most terrible judgment there is (Romans 1:24). But the letting go is not indifference. The father’s eyes are on the road from the day the boy leaves. God’s patience gives a sinner room to discover what the far country is really like, and his providence, as the next verses show, is at work even there. If someone you love has walked away, the parable does not tell you to stop loving or praying. It tells you to keep watching the road.

In everyday life. Are you enjoying God’s gifts while keeping him at a distance? That is the heart of sin. Look at the good things in your hands today, your health, your money, your time, your mind, and ask whether you are using them with him or without him. The request of verse 12 is rarely made out loud. It is made in the way we spend a Saturday.
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third — the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gathered all he had. He did not even wait. He turned his share of the estate into cash, which probably meant selling family land, itself a shameful thing: land in Israel was the family’s portion in the inheritance of God’s people, held in trust across generations (Leviticus 25:23–28). To sell up was a public act, and the whole district would soon have known what the boy thought of his father.

A far country. Probably Gentile land, as the pigs suggest, far from his father, his family, his people, and his God. Distance was the point: a far country, where nobody had heard of his father and nobody would report on him.

Squandered in reckless living. The verb (dieskorpisen) means scattered, like seed thrown to the wind. Reckless (asōtōs) describes a wasteful, dissolute life, spending without restraint, the absence of any brake rather than a particular vice. His brother will say: with prostitutes (v. 30), and the story never confirms it. Freedom from his father became slavery to his appetites.

Two sons, two prayers. Luke sets another Son beside this one. The younger son’s first words in the story are give me (v. 12): the Father’s goods, without the Father. The Son who tells the story will kneel on the Mount of Olives and pray, Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42), and his last words on the cross will be, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). One son took his share and spent it on himself. The other gave up everything that was his and spent himself on his Father’s will, so that sons like the first could come home.

What is my far country? It may not involve travel at all. It is anywhere you go to be out of your Father’s sight, or so you think: the screen at midnight, the second life at a conference, the hidden spending, the resentment nursed in private, the corner of your heart where God is not consulted. It always begins with wanting the gifts without the Giver, and it always promises freedom. Name it honestly before God. The first step home is admitting where you are.
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A severe famine. First the money runs out, then the famine arrives on top of the spending, and the two together remove any possibility of recovery. He chose the far country and the spending; he did not choose the famine. Sin puts a man in a place where circumstance can destroy him, and circumstance does not ask his permission.

He hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country. The verb means he attached himself, clung to him. This is not applying for a post. It is a starving man fastening himself to a Gentile who does not want him, and the employer’s response reads as a way of getting rid of him.

To feed pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and a rabbinic saying pronounces a curse on the man who raises them. A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as a person could go: cut off from his people, his worship and his God.

Longing to be fed. Probably carob pods, the long dark seed pods of the carob tree, fed to animals and eaten by the very poorest in hard times. Coarse and barely nourishing, and he cannot get them: he is not eating them; he is longing to. He left home with a third of an estate, and he now ranks below the livestock.

No one gave him anything. There were plenty of people around him while the money lasted. The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

He has filled the hungry. Luke’s Gospel has been listening for this hunger since its first chapter. Mary sang of a God who has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53). In a desolate place he fed five thousand until everyone was full (9:17). The far country gives the hungry nothing; the Son who tells this story is the one in whom God fills them. The pigsty is exactly where his kind of mercy is aimed.

Is God behind the famine? God rules over famines as over everything (Psalm 105:16), and in this story the hardship is the very thing that turns the son homeward. That does not mean every hardship is a punishment for a specific sin, as Jesus has just insisted (13:1–5). But it does mean that the bottom of the pit is never outside God’s reach, and that he often uses empty hands to make a sinner look up. If you are at the bottom now, your misery may be the severe mercy that brings you home. Do not waste it.

In everyday life. If someone you love is in the pigsty, do not be in a hurry to rescue them from every consequence; pray that the famine will do its work, and be ready for the day they come to themselves.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he came to himself. An exact phrase: came to his senses, woke up. He does not become someone else. He comes to himself: everything from the request in verse 12 onwards was the aberration. Sin is a kind of madness; repentance is coming back to sanity. Sin believes lies: that God is holding out on us, that the far country gives life, that we would be freer without him. The Lord calls sin leaving the fountain of living waters to dig cracked cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). Repentance begins with seeing things as they really are: where I am, and where I could be.

More than enough bread. He remembers his father’s goodness, and he is honest about his own condition. The detail he remembers is that even the lowest grade of worker on the estate has more than enough. He is remembering the one thing he had never valued. Remembering God’s goodness draws sinners back (Romans 2:4).

I will arise and go to my father. Repentance is a decision, followed by action: turning around, going back. There is no agonising. He has been in the pigsty long enough.

Against heaven and before you. Against heaven: against God. All sin is first against God (Psalm 51:4). He does not blame the famine, or his friends, or his father. He names it as sin, not misfortune, against God first and his father second.

Sin against heaven, pardon on earth. If sin is first against heaven, then only heaven can forgive it, and the scribes in Luke knew it: who can forgive sins but God alone? (5:21). Jesus answered them by healing a paralysed man, so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (5:24). The confession the boy rehearses in the pigsty is the confession sinners were bringing to Jesus, and they were receiving from him what only heaven could give.

No longer worthy. True: he has forfeited every right. Hired servants were day labourers with no place in the family, paid at the end of each day. He plans to work off his debt. His repentance is real, but he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

Was his repentance real if he only came home because he was hungry? This troubles more honest Christians than almost any other question. The boy did not come home because he missed his father; the text is candid that he came because he was starving. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: I turned to God when my marriage collapsed; I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real? The truth is that nobody’s repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace, the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards. And motives are purified on the way, as the father’s embrace is about to show.

In everyday life. Make your confession to God specific: not I have not been very good, but the thing itself, by name. And if you are rehearsing a hired servant’s speech, planning how you will make it up to God: he is not looking for a labourer. He is looking for his son.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He arose and came. He did what he said. Luke gives the journey half a sentence. What it cost him to walk back into that village with the smell of pigs on him is not described.

A long way off. Which tells you what the father had been doing. You do not identify a figure at that distance unless you are looking, and you do not look unless you have been looking for a long time. The old man had been watching a road for a boy who had every reason never to appear on it, and he saw his son before his son saw him.

And felt compassion. The word (esplanchnisthē) means moved in his innermost being, the compassion that turns over inside a person. It is the word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the good Samaritan (10:33).

And ran. It is the most shocking thing in the parable. In that culture, it is widely thought, it was undignified for an older man to run: he would have to hike up his robe and show his legs. So the father makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village. Some have also suggested that a son who lost his inheritance among Gentiles could be cut off by the village; the father reaches him first, taking the shame on himself and protecting his son.

Embraced him and kissed him. Literally fell on his neck, as Esau embraced Jacob (Genesis 33:4). He is filthy, he stinks of a pig field, and he is ceremonially unclean. The father has him by the neck and kisses him again and again (the verb is intensive), the sign of reconciliation (2 Samuel 14:33), before the son can say a word of his confession.

The heart of God. This is the centre of the parable, and the answer to the Pharisees’ complaint: God is not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to forgive but a father who runs to meet repentant sinners while they are still far off. And it is not because he takes sin lightly. He is the holy God before whom Isaiah cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5), and that is what makes the running so astonishing: the one who has every right to keep his distance is the one who closes it.

If God runs to forgive, does it matter how I live? It matters more, not less. The son who has been met on the road like this does not go back to the pigs; he has found his father’s heart, and the far country has lost its charm. Grace that is truly received produces a new life, because it changes what we love (Titus 2:11–12). Paul faced this objection directly: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The father’s running is not permission to leave again. It is the most powerful reason never to want to.

In everyday life. If you have been putting off coming back to God until you have cleaned yourself up, look at this verse: the Father is already running. And when someone who has hurt you comes back, go out quickly to meet them, as you were met.

For worship. The God of all majesty set aside his dignity and ran. And behind the running lies a greater shame borne for us: the Son of God, stripped and lifted up outside the city, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), so that the Father could embrace sinners without compromising his holiness.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The confession after the embrace. The embrace does not make the confession unnecessary. He still says it, and both statements are entirely true.

What he does not say. He leaves out the last line of his prepared speech: Treat me as one of your hired servants (v. 19). A few early manuscripts add that line here, but most scholars think a copyist brought it in from verse 19. Grace does not negotiate. You cannot earn your way back to a father who has already forgiven you. He comes as a son, or not at all.

Who makes the unworthy worthy? The boy is right: he is not worthy. The parable does not explain how a holy Father can call such a son his son without pretending that nothing happened, and it does not need to, because the one telling it was on his way to Jerusalem. There he would be numbered with the transgressors (22:37) and die between two criminals, the only Son who was ever worthy. The welcome at the gate costs the son nothing because it cost the Son everything. Sinners who say not worthy are received as sons in him.

Why confess, if I am already forgiven? Because confession is not payment; it is honesty. Grace is sometimes preached in a way that makes confession unnecessary, and the son shows otherwise: he says the words. What he does not get to do is set the terms on which he will be taken back. For the believer, daily confession is not a way of earning back a lost sonship. It is a child being truthful with his Father, and receiving again the assurance of a pardon already given (1 John 1:9). There is only one thing a returning sinner has to bring, and he brought it: an honest account of himself. Everything else in this scene is supplied by somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bring quickly. He does not even reply to the confession. He acts, giving orders about clothing in which every item restores something specific. Quickly comes first and governs the rest: no delay, no probation, and nobody is sent to wash first.

The best robe. Literally “the first robe”: the finest in the house, perhaps the father’s own. It covered his rags and showed everyone in the village that he was restored to honour. The parable is about the Father’s joy over a returning sinner (vv. 7, 10), not about how forgiveness is achieved. But the Old Testament often pictures God clothing his people with salvation (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5), and the rest of the New Testament shows that God clothes sinners with Christ himself (Galatians 3:27). So Christians have rightly heard in the robe an echo of the righteousness God gives in Christ, from the rest of Scripture rather than the parable alone. When God justifies a sinner, he declares him righteous, not because the sinner has become good, but because Christ’s perfect obedience is counted as his, like a robe put over rags (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9).

A ring. Probably a signet ring, used to seal documents, which gave him authority to act on his father’s behalf (Genesis 41:42). It is not jewellery but authority, handed to the one member of the family who has demonstrated beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money.

Shoes on his feet. Sandals were a mark of the free; slaves often went barefoot. It settles the question the boy had been rehearsing all the way home. He had come to ask for a place among the hired men. Before he can propose it, his father has put shoes on him.

Three gifts at the gate. Between them they restore his standing, his authority and his freedom, without a single condition attached. The father does not restore him gradually as he proves himself. He restores him completely at the gate, before the boy has done one honest day’s work, and then lets him live the rest of his life as what he has been declared to be. If you are in Christ, that is you: not a hired servant on probation, anxiously working to stay in favour, but a son in the robe, the ring and the sandals.

Is the prodigal a believer who fell away? The parable is aimed at the Pharisees’ complaint about tax collectors and sinners (vv. 1–2), and the younger son stands for sinners coming home to God. He is a son throughout; the father calls him my son (v. 24). It may also comfort a believer who has wandered for a season, but it does not teach that sonship can be lost and regained. If you are a Christian who has drifted, the way back is the same road: come to yourself, confess, and go home. You will find your Father has not changed.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fattened calf. A peasant household rarely ate meat, and a fattened calf was grain-fed and kept back for a single great occasion, with enough meat to feed a large gathering, perhaps the whole village. The father throws a feast for the community, to restore his son publicly, calling in the same village that had watched the boy leave. That is a further piece of protection. Everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father’s verdict on his son. It becomes very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Let us eat and celebrate. Eating together is the very thing the Pharisees complained about (v. 2). Jesus eats with sinners because God celebrates their return.

Dead, and is alive again. My son: not a hired servant. The boy had just said he was no longer worthy to be called it; the father does not argue the point but simply uses the word. Dead and alive: the language of resurrection. In that culture a son who had done what this one did may well have been reckoned dead to the family, and the father takes the household’s own language and reverses it. Coming home to God is passing from death to life, God’s own work of making the dead alive (Ephesians 2:1–5), and repentance is the first sign of that new life.

They began to celebrate. Luke says they began: the celebration is not finished when the chapter ends. It is still going on in the last verse, with music audible from the field, and one son standing outside it.

Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross? Some have argued that this parable shows God forgives freely, without any need for atonement: the father simply forgives, with no sacrifice. This commentary’s view: a parable teaches one main point, not every doctrine. This one shows God’s welcome to repentant sinners, in answer to the Pharisees. It does not explain how forgiveness is possible for a holy God. The rest of Scripture does: Jesus came to give his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (22:20; Matthew 26:28), and Luke ends with the Christ who must suffer so that forgiveness may be proclaimed (24:46–47). The father’s running, at cost to his own honour, is a hint of the cost God himself bore. And the one telling the story was on his way to Jerusalem to die.

Who paid for the calf? Somebody paid for it, and it was not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Every single thing he receives in this scene is drawn from his father’s own resources, and the father never once mentions the cost. That is the gospel’s logic, and the cross is where the bill was met: God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). Propitiation is the sacrifice that takes the full weight of God’s holy anger against sin and so turns it away. The boy came home to a feast because the Son would go to a cross.

In everyday life. Make your church and your home a place where returning sinners are celebrated, not merely tolerated. When someone is baptised, or comes back after years away, show up, rejoice, and eat with them. And if you have never quite believed that God is glad you are his, read verse 24 again, with your own name in it.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the field. Jesus is telling the story to the Pharisees (v. 2), and now comes their part. The older son is working, dutiful, as always. Whatever else is true of him, he is not a bad son by any ordinary measure. He is out working while his brother is being kissed at the gate.

He heard music and dancing. Nobody sent for him. A party is under way at his father’s expense, involving the whole village, and the elder son of the household learns about it by getting close enough to hear the band.

He called one of the servants. He does not go in and ask his father; he stops outside, gets hold of a servant and interrogates him. That is the first sign of the distance. He is standing in his own yard, treating his own home as somewhere he needs to be briefed about before entering.

Your brother has come. The servant says your brother, without hesitation; the elder son will refuse the word. The servant’s answer is artless and accurate, and it contains every fact the elder brother will later distort.

The brother who went looking. The elder son will not use the word brother, and he never went out to look for the boy. The parable leaves that gap, and the one telling it fills it. He is the Son who left his Father’s side to come and find his lost brothers, and who is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Where the elder son counted the cost of the calf, this Son paid the cost of the feast. That is not a hidden meaning in the story, but the contrast it invites.

Safe and sound. The word (hygiainonta) means healthy, whole. Not because your brother has proved himself: the stated cause of the celebration is simply that he is home and he is well. A servant who has been in that house all his life has understood the father exactly. The son standing in the yard is about to demonstrate that he never has.

Can someone be in the church and still outside the feast? Yes, and this is the most searching part of the chapter. The older son lives on the estate, works the fields and keeps the rules, and he does not know his father’s heart. It is possible to grow up in a Christian home, serve faithfully for decades, hold sound doctrine, and still relate to God as an employer rather than a Father, and to grace as something for other people. The test is not how long you have been in the field. It is whether the music of grace makes you glad. And if you fear you are the older brother, the fear itself is a good sign: the son in the story felt none, and the Father has come out to plead with you to come in.

For worship. The Father’s house is full of music because the Father is full of joy, and he needs no reason beyond this: the lost is home, safe and sound. Safe and sound is the Son’s report on all his people. He will bring every one the Father gave him through the far country and the dark, and on the last day present them whole before the Father’s face, without a single one missing.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Angry and refused to go in. He grew angry, like the grumbling Pharisees (v. 2), and the tense of the second verb suggests he kept refusing. It was a public insult as great as the younger son’s demand, since the guests would soon know he was outside. The younger son had shamed his father by leaving; the elder is now shaming him by standing in the yard.

His father came out. For the second time in one evening the old man goes out to a son who has humiliated him. It is the same movement as the running in verse 20: he does not summon the boy or send a servant. He walks out of his own celebration and goes to find him. Entreated (parekalei) means urged, begged, pleaded. The father, who has every right to order his son indoors, stands in the dark asking. Jesus is pleading with the Pharisees, through this very parable.

Is God kind to sinners and severe to the religious? Not in this parable. The father goes out twice, and the second time is harder, because the second son does not want to be found. Whatever else the elder brother is about to say, he says it to a father who came out and asked. And there is a warning in the staging for anyone who has ever been the one outside. Standing in the yard feels like taking a position. It usually is just standing in a yard, in the dark, near a house where people are happy, waiting to be persuaded to enjoy something you have already decided not to enjoy. The father will not force him in. The door is open, the music is audible, the invitation has been delivered in person, and after that the yard is a choice.

In everyday life. If you are standing in the yard about something, resentful of how God has blessed someone else, angry that grace has gone where you think it should not, recognise the father’s voice pleading with you. Go in. And if you lead or love someone who is standing outside, go out to them as the father did, gently and more than once.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look. He does not even say Father. The younger son began his confession with that word; the older son begins with Look. The word (douleuō) means I have slaved for you. It is the whole tragedy in one verb: he has been a son for the entire story and has experienced it as employment. The younger son wanted to come back as a hired servant; the older son had been living like one all along.

I never disobeyed. Outward obedience, like the rich ruler (18:21) and Paul before conversion (Philippians 3:6). But his heart was far from his father. He was as lost as his brother, though he never left home.

A young goat. He wanted to celebrate, but with his friends, not his father. A young goat is a modest animal, a small grievance carefully preserved, and the complaint does not stand. His share of the estate had been made over to him in verse 12. He had been living on his own property, asking permission he did not need, and resenting a father who had already given him everything. Self-righteousness is always resentful of grace.

This son of yours. Not my brother, but this son of yours: the servant managed the word without effort; the elder son cuts the boy out of his own family. And he announces the worst interpretation, because he wants his brother’s sin remembered: verse 13 says reckless living and nothing more. Resentment fills in the blanks in the worst available way and calls it honesty.

You killed the fattened calf for him! He cannot bear grace being given to someone who does not deserve it. This is the Pharisees’ complaint, this man receives sinners: not a complaint about justice, but about somebody else’s welcome.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners. The elder son will not call the sinner brother. His enemies had already given Jesus the opposite name. Look at him, they said, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). He wore the insult. Where the elder son kept the record of his brother’s sins and refused the relationship, Jesus took the relationship and carried the record away. The name the grumblers threw at him is the best news the far country has ever heard.

How do I know if I am an older brother? Watch for the signs this verse gives. You keep score of your service and feel God owes you. You find obedience a grind, done for reward rather than love. You resent it when God is generous to people with worse records. You find it easy to remember other people’s sins in detail and hard to call them brother. You enjoy your friends more than your Father. Most of us find some of this in ourselves. The cure is not to try harder at being a good son. It is to see that you, too, have needed grace every day, and that everything the Father has was always yours as a gift.

Is it not unfair that the son who wasted everything gets the party? Only if the party were wages. But nothing was taken from the older son: every goat on the farm was already his (v. 31). Grace is unfair to no one, because no one receives less than he was promised; it only gives more than anyone deserves. Strict fairness would leave both sons outside, one for his rebellion and the other for his contempt, for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Nor is justice ignored. At the cross God bore the cost of the welcome himself, so that he is both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26).

In everyday life. If there is someone whose sins you rehearse, aloud or in your head, call them brother or sister in your prayers this week, and ask God to bless them.

For worship. The Father bears with the insults of both his sons, the one who wished him dead and the one who served him as a slave. He is not a hard master but the giver of every goat and every calf, and he gives himself to his children. And the true Son, who alone could have said I never disobeyed your command, and said it truly, did not resent the Father’s welcome of sinners. He died to make it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son. The word (teknon) means child, the tender word, the one a parent uses. After everything that has just been said in the yard, the father’s first word is an endearment.

Always with me. Everything he wanted, he already had: his father’s presence, and the whole estate. He has had every day for years the one thing his brother threw away, nearness to his father, and he has been counting goats. The Pharisees had the covenants and the temple (Romans 9:4–5), but they lived as servants, not sons. And the sharpest thing in the parable is not aimed at the disreputable. A man can live in his Father’s house for decades, keep every rule, resent the whole arrangement, and never once take anything out of a storehouse he has always owned.

It was fitting. The word (edei) means it was necessary, it was right: the word Luke uses all through his Gospel for what God’s purpose requires. Given what has happened, a party was the only proper response, and any other response would have been wrong.

The same must. Luke’s readers know this necessity from the lips of Jesus. The Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22), and after the resurrection he will ask, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26). The party over a returning sinner is necessary in the same way the cross is necessary: both are what God’s purpose of mercy requires. The feast had to be held because the Son had to die.

Your brother. Not this son of yours, but your brother: the father hands the word back, corrected. There is only one relationship in dispute here, and it is not the one between the father and the younger boy.

The open ending. Jesus does not tell us whether the older son went in, because the Pharisees and scribes, listening, had to decide: would they come in to the feast, and rejoice that sinners were coming home? Or would they stay outside? Both sons had wanted the father’s goods more than the father, one by breaking the rules and the other by keeping them. Jesus has put the grumblers of verse 2 on the doorstep of a lit house, with the music still playing, and left them there. The ending was theirs to write. It still is.

What does all that is mine is yours mean for me as a Christian? It means that in Christ you are an heir, not a hired hand. All things are yours, Paul says, whether the world or life or death or the present or the future, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The Father’s presence, his promises, his Spirit, the riches of his grace, and an inheritance kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) are already yours, not as wages but as a son’s portion. So pray as a child who has access, give as one who cannot be impoverished, and serve as one who is already loved.

For worship. All that is mine is yours: the Father said it to a resentful son standing in the dark, and he says it to every child he has brought in. The Father who ran to the younger son and walked out to the elder is the God who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). His house is full of children, every one an heir.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is about money, and through money about the heart. Two stories, the dishonest manager and the rich man and Lazarus, bracket a group of sayings about the Law, divorce and what God values. How a person handles wealth shows the condition of his heart before God.

In the first story Jesus seems to commend a fraudster, but the praise is for his shrewdness, not his dishonesty: he thought clearly about his future and used what he still controlled to secure it. Jesus turns it into a rebuke of disciples who think less clearly about eternity than worldly people do about money.

The second story is the only parable in which a character is named, and it closes the chapter with a sobering line: those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead. It is a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy of how many would respond to Jesus’ own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells this parable to his disciples while the Pharisees listen (v. 14). The manager has been doing with his master’s goods what the prodigal did with his inheritance (15:13). He is dismissed first and audited second, and the whole parable turns on the gap between: he is no longer trusted, but the seal is still in his hand. He uses that interval to turn his master’s debtors into friends who will open their doors to him. What is commended is the structure of the act: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent it, at once, on the only thing that would outlast the deadline.
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful. He is still called the dishonest manager, and what is praised is his shrewdness: the ability to see a situation clearly and act.

The three descriptions of money in verses 10 to 12 are each deflating: it is unrighteous, the currency of a fallen order; it is a very little; and it belongs to another. But the promise on the other side is easily missed: the true riches, and that which is your own. Something is coming that will actually belong to you.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 has been read as though a man could purchase his welcome into heaven, in defence of almsgiving as accumulated merit. The verse answers that in three words: “when it fails.” Money is the thing that runs out, and a currency bound to become worthless is not the price of eternity. Generosity is evidence of faith, not currency.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 16 is about money, and through money about the heart, eternity and the word of God. It has three movements: a dishonest manager who acts shrewdly before his dismissal takes effect (vv. 1–13); the money-loving Pharisees who sneer, and the permanence of God’s law (vv. 14–18); and a rich man and a poor man whose places are reversed at death (vv. 19–31). The puzzling first parable has a clear point: everything we hold belongs to Someone else, the arrangement is ending, and the wise use what they still control for what will last.

The setting. Chapter 15 answered the grumbling Pharisees with three stories of the lost being found. This chapter is spoken to the disciples, though the Pharisees are still listening (v. 14). The manager is wasting, diaskorpizōn, his master’s possessions, the verb Luke used of the younger son squandering his inheritance (15:13). The prodigal was welcomed home by a father; the manager will have to find a welcome by his wits.

A manager. The manager is an oikonomos, the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or a freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts, collected rents and ran the property in his master’s name. With absentee landlords common in that region he could do a great deal of damage before anybody opened the books.

Wasting his possessions. Whether by incompetence or dishonesty, the property was leaking away. When he is confronted, he does not dispute the charges. Luke never says whether they were true, but the manager’s silence, and his immediate move to plan for unemployment, answer the question well enough.

Turn in the account. The dismissal is announced first and the audit demanded second: he is finished, and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap. He is no longer trusted and not yet stripped of authority; the debtors have not been told; the seal is still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

The Steward who lost nothing. Set beside this manager the one who is telling the story. Jesus too had been entrusted with his Father’s house. John records him saying that this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me (John 6:39). Stewards in Scripture are so often found wanting; this one never was, and when charges were brought against him at the end, they were false (23:2, 14).

Who is the manager meant to be? Not a cipher for any one person, and the parable does not need us to decide whether he stands for the Pharisees, for Israel’s leaders or for the disciples. He is a picture of every human being before God. Everything you have, your money, your body, your time, your gifts, your years, belongs to God, and you are its steward (1 Corinthians 4:2, 7). The notice of dismissal has already been served: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The only open question is what you will do with the time in between.

For worship. The faithful Steward rendered his account in full at the cross, and it was found perfect, and it is the account God now reads over the wasteful stewards who trust him. We scattered our Master’s goods; he gathered us, and the audit we dreaded has become the place where his perfect record is read out in our name.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the manager said to himself, What shall I do? The parable now goes inside his head, which is where Luke has taken us twice already: the rich fool talking to his own soul (12:17), and the prodigal coming to himself in the pigsty (15:17). It is a similar move each time, and it is always a man at the end of his options. But this man, unlike the rich fool, thinks ahead.

Not strong enough to dig. Two doors, and both shut. He is not able to dig, and he is ashamed to beg: the first is a limitation and the second a decision. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

I have decided. The tense suggests a flash of clarity. Notice what he is buying. Not money: he does not embezzle for himself. What he wants is houses, an open door and a place at a table when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth, while he still controls it, can be converted into them. It took a dismissal notice to make him see it.

Who will receive me? The manager’s question has already been answered, one chapter earlier, in the complaint of the Pharisees: this man receives sinners (15:2). The man who has nothing left to trade, who can neither dig nor bring himself to beg, does not have to buy his way into a house. There is one who receives people precisely when they come with nothing. The manager schemes for a welcome because he does not know the Host. The sinners at Jesus’ table had found one without scheming at all.

Is it wrong to plan for my future, or to save for retirement? No. The manager is not blamed for planning; he is held up as an example of it. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and calls a man who will not provide for his household worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool of chapter 12 was not condemned for having barns but for being rich toward himself and not toward God (12:21). The question this verse presses is not whether you plan but how far ahead. Most people plan carefully for thirty years and not at all for eternity. Prudent saving is stewardship; a pension that has become your security in place of God is idolatry, and only you and he know which yours is.

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
One by one. One by one, and quickly, before the news gets out. These are not petty debtors but probably tenant farmers who paid rent in produce, or merchants who had bought on credit, and they have serious contracts.

A hundred measures of oil. A hundred measures of oil was a very large amount, perhaps 3,000 litres, the yield of some 150 olive trees; a hundred measures of wheat was the crop of something like a hundred acres. Each debt represents years of a labourer’s wages.

Write fifty. The debtor writes it himself, on his own bond, so the document looks entirely legitimate and carries no trace of the manager. On one common estimate the reduction on the oil, fifty measures, was worth about 500 denarii, more than a year and a half’s wages; the reduction on the wheat, write eighty, is twenty measures, worth about the same. Each debtor now owes the manager a very large favour.

Was it dishonest? The reductions are curiously uneven: fifty per cent on the oil, twenty per cent on the wheat. That unevenness has led some scholars to suggest that the manager was removing something that varied by commodity: his own commission, the surcharge a steward customarily added to a contract, or the interest that the law forbade charging to fellow Jews (Deuteronomy 23:19). On that reading he is waiving his own fee to buy goodwill. But Jesus calls him dishonest (v. 8), and the simplest reading is that he cheated his master to make friends of the debtors, who would now be grateful and in his debt. It cannot be settled with certainty, and the parable does not require it to be. Jesus commends neither the honesty nor the dishonesty. What is commended is the structure of the act.

The structure of the act. He took a resource that was about to stop being his, and spent it, immediately, on the only thing that would still exist after the deadline. Sit down quickly: part of his prudence is speed.

Five hundred, fifty, and nothing. Luke’s reader has met two debtors before. At a Pharisee’s table Jesus told of a moneylender with two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and when they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41–42). The manager trims a bill by roughly that larger sum to buy a welcome for himself. Jesus is the creditor in person, and he does not trim. He cancels, and he does it for people who could never return the favour.

In everyday life. A man who learns that his firm is closing updates his CV that night. What do you know about eternity that you have been treating as if there were all the time in the world: a reconciliation postponed, a sin you meant to deal with, a conversation about Christ you meant to have? The manager had hours; you do not know how long you have, and that is a kindness as well as a warning.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master commended. The surprise of the parable, and the sentence is careful. He is still called the dishonest manager, literally the steward of unrighteousness, a man characterised by it. The commendation does not rehabilitate him. What is praised is that he acted phronimōs: with prudence, practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act on it. A commander can admire an enemy’s manoeuvre without approving of the war.

Who is the master who commends him? Most likely the rich man in the story, since Jesus speaks in his own voice in the next sentence and again in verse 9 (and I tell you). Some take it as the Lord himself. Either way, what is praised is the manager’s foresight, not his dishonesty.

The sons of this world. Here is the sting, and it is an uncomfortable sentence for his own people. The sons of this world are worldly people, who live for this age. The sons of light are God’s people (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). It was a title some devout groups used of themselves. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at dealing with their own generation: at reading a situation, seeing where it is going, and acting in time.

Sons of the light. The title is not a native quality. Zechariah sang of the sunrise from on high, to give light to those who sit in darkness (1:78–79), and Simeon held that light in his arms (2:32). A son of light is someone on whom Christ has risen. And the shrewdness Jesus asks of them is the shrewdness of people who know that the light is shining now and will not wait.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not commending dishonesty, or teaching that the end justifies the means. A parable can use a bad man to make a good point, as Luke does again with the unjust judge (18:1–8). The argument in both runs from the lesser to the greater: if even a scoundrel acts decisively to secure a few years of comfort, how much more should the sons of light act for eternity.

How would I actually be shrewd about eternity? The same way a sensible person is shrewd about anything: by looking at where things are going and acting now. Shrewdness for the kingdom looks like setting your giving before you see what is left, not after. It looks like choosing a church, a house and a job with an eye on what they will do to your soul and your children’s, not only on salary and schools. It looks like investing in people, in friendships with believers, in hospitality, in the young, because people are the only part of this world that goes on into the next. And it looks like dealing with sin today rather than meaning to, because the window is not as wide as it seems.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make friends by means of unrighteous wealth. The hardest sentence in the chapter. Unrighteous wealth renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions; literally, the mammon of unrighteousness. It does not necessarily mean wealth gained dishonestly. It means wealth that belongs to this unrighteous world, the currency of a fallen order. Nobody’s money is clean all the way back. And Jesus says: use it. Use it wisely, to make friends, by giving to the poor and supporting the work of God.

So that when it fails. When money runs out, or when you die and it is useless to you. The money is explicitly described as the thing that fails, and a currency guaranteed to become worthless is not the purchase price of eternity.

The eternal dwellings. The manager made friends who would receive him into their houses; you can make friends who will welcome you into eternal homes. Who are they? Some take it of the friends themselves: those you have helped with your money, the poor and those who came to faith through the gospel you supported, standing at the door of the next life, glad to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who will carry Lazarus a few verses later. And many take it as the Semitic way of saying you will be received by God without naming him, as at 12:20, where the Greek literally reads they require your soul. Either way the point is the same: use money now with an eye on eternity. Lay up treasure in heaven (12:33).

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Luke’s second volume shows who stands at that door. As the stones fell on Stephen, he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God, and he prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:56, 59). The friends made by generosity may be glad to see us, but the welcome itself belongs to the risen Christ, and he receives his people as a host, not as a creditor collecting on the investment.

What it does not mean. Not that you can buy your way into heaven. Read flatly, the verse has been taken to mean that almsgiving buys a welcome. Luke will not let that stand. The tax collector who could offer nothing but his beaten breast went home justified (18:13–14); the criminal a few hours from death bought nothing whatever and was told he would be with Christ in Paradise that day (23:43); and in this very chapter a rich man’s fortune procures him not one drop of water. Salvation is by grace, but true faith is generous: generosity is evidence, not currency, and how a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him (v. 13).

So how much should I give, and to whom? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for the Christian, but it sets a direction and a spirit. Give regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2); give cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7); give first to the ministry of the word in your own church (Galatians 6:6) and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find a tenth a sensible starting place, not a ceiling. The test of this verse is simple: ten years from now, will there be people, in heaven or on the way there, who are there partly because of what you did with your money? If you cannot say yes, start this month with something that costs you.
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches?
