And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful in a very little. The parable is finished and the application widens, and this is the principle underneath it. Character does not change with scale. The way a man handles a small thing is not a warm-up for how he would handle a large one; it is a sample of it.

Subject to them in Nazareth. Of Jesus between twelve and about thirty Luke gives us only this: he went down with his parents to Nazareth and was submissive to them, (2:51–52). Those were the very little years. And when they were over, before a single miracle, the Father spoke from heaven: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). The one who says faithful in a very little had been faithful in a very little for most of his life.

Dishonest in a very little. Small dishonesty reveals a dishonest heart. We easily believe we would be generous if we had more, honest if the stakes were higher; Jesus says the evidence is already in, in the small things. The expense claim rounded up, the hours padded, the change not returned, the excuse that was not quite true: none of these is small in what it reveals.

If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? Three descriptions of money follow, and each is deflating. It is unrighteous wealth: the currency of a fallen world. It is a very little. That is an extraordinary thing to say to people for whom money was the difference between eating and not eating, and Jesus says it anyway. Whatever the sums involved, compared with eternal things they are small. And the true riches are the spiritual riches of the kingdom: God’s word, his grace, responsibility in his kingdom, eternal reward. How we handle money is a test of whether we can be trusted with greater things.

If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own? And money is another’s. Not yours. It belongs to God, and you are the steward of the parable, running an estate you did not buy, and the audit is coming. Then the promise on the other side, which is easily missed under the warnings: that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you, an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Everything held now is on loan and will be handed back; what is being trained for is an inheritance that cannot be taken away, and the training ground is a bank account.

Why would God care so much about money? It seems beneath him, and in one sense it is: he owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) and does not need a penny of yours. He is not interested in the money. He is watching what a man does with a small sum of somebody else’s cash, because that is the most reliable evidence available of what he would do with anything. Money is concentrated life: hours of work, choices, security, pleasure, power, all in a form you can count. What you do with it shows what you love, and God cares very much about what you love.

Does this mean I earn my place in heaven by being faithful? No. That which is your own is a gift, an inheritance, and an inheritance is never earned by the heir. But God is pleased to reward the faithfulness that his grace produces, and Scripture speaks plainly of rewards differing (19:17; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The believer is not saved by his faithfulness; he is saved for it, and then, in a kindness that is almost embarrassing, rewarded for what God himself worked in him. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts.

In everyday life. The Son who was faithful in the hidden years at Nazareth was faithful for you, and his Spirit now makes you faithful in small things. This week, put right one small dishonesty you have let stand: the overcharge, the borrowed thing not returned, the claim that was not quite accurate. Nobody else may notice; that is exactly why it matters.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No servant can serve two masters. Servant here is oiketēs, a household slave: a man may hold two jobs, but a slave’s whole time, body and will belonged to his owner. So the sentence is not advice about priorities. It is a statement about what is possible.

Hate the one and love the other. Whichever way round it falls, one master ends up with the loyalty and the other with the contempt. Hate and love is the Hebrew idiom for preference (14:26): one will always come first. But the strength of the language is deliberate: the divided man does not end up mildly disappointing one of his masters; he ends up with something like contempt for him.

The conflict that rarely surfaces. Most people who are serving money would sincerely say they love God. What Jesus describes becomes visible only when the two masters give conflicting orders. The promotion that would mean leaving a faithful church; the giving that would mean a smaller car. Then a man often discovers which master he had been serving all along. The division most people actually attempt, God at the centre and money in a firm second place, is not a compromise between two positions. It is one of them, held by a man who has not noticed which.

You cannot serve God and money. Money is again mammon, and Jesus treats it here as a name: not a thing you own but somebody who owns you. It is a rival lord, and it makes demands, and it has slaves. It promises security, power and happiness, the things only God can give. Then the flat impossibility: you cannot. Not should not, and not will find it difficult.

Him only shall you serve. One man has made this choice without wavering. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offered him their authority and glory if he would worship him, and Jesus answered from Scripture: you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (4:5–8). Every promise mammon makes was laid in front of him at once, and he refused it, hungry and alone. The one who says you cannot serve two masters is the one Servant who never tried.

How do I know which master I serve? Ask what you worry about, because worry is the prayer we pray to the god we fear will fail us. Ask what you would find hardest to give up if God asked. Ask whether your giving is the first line of the budget or the last. Ask whether money decides where you live, what church you attend and how much time you have for your family, or whether God does. And ask how you feel when the markets fall. A Christian may feel the loss; but if a bad month on the statement shakes your peace more than a month without prayer, mammon has a stronger claim on you than you thought.

Is it wrong to be rich? No. Abraham was very rich, and he is the host at the banquet a few verses later. Joseph of Arimathea was rich and a disciple (Matthew 27:57). Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). It is not wrong to have money; it is fatal to serve it. But Jesus speaks of the danger of wealth far more than of its blessing, because wealth makes the service so easy to slide into and so hard to notice.

For worship. There is a Master worth serving with everything, and he is not a hard one. Mammon takes everything and gives back anxiety; this Lord gave everything and gives back rest. He was sold by a disciple who chose the other master (22:5). He let himself be bought so that we might be bought back, and the slaves of mammon he redeems he does not take as slaves but calls his friends.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
These verses answer the Pharisees, who loved money and sneered. In that day prosperity was widely taken as a sign of God’s approval, so their love of money did not feel like a vice. Jesus goes past the ridicule to what lies under it: they justify themselves before men, but God knows their hearts, and what men exalt in pride is to him in the same category as an idol.

Then two verses that must be held together. The era of the Law and the Prophets ran until John, yet not one dot of the Law will become void. The word that joins them is fulfilment: the Law has been kept by the one saying this, and its moral claim stands. The divorce saying follows as an example, not a change of subject. Their own tradition had loosened the Law on marriage, and Jesus shows who was really relaxing it.
verseByVerse.theology: Since John announced the King, the kingdom is entered the way a man presses through a closing door (compare Matthew 11:12), and the most unlikely people are pressing in. Because the Law still stands, Jesus reaffirms the design of marriage in Genesis 2:24 as its continuing moral claim, not something the kingdom relaxes. Jesus does not allow divorce for almost any reason.
verseByVerse.examples:
Read alone, Luke’s flat saying would make every divorce and remarriage adultery. Matthew adds the exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; 19:9) and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15), and these two grounds are what the Westminster Confession recognises (24.5–6). Luke states the rule; the exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall.

For those already divorced and remarried on no ground the New Testament allows, the way forward is not to unpick the second marriage but to confess the sin, receive forgiveness, and be faithful now (1 Corinthians 6:11).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lovers of money. Lovers of money is philargyroi, literally silver-lovers, a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. Not all Pharisees were wealthy, but the love of money did not feel like a vice, because much popular theology connected prosperity with divine approval. The covenant blessings promised full barns to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and it was a short step to reading the balance sheet as a certificate of righteousness.

They ridiculed him. The verb means they sneered, turned up their noses. A poor teacher from Galilee, telling them about money! And that is the tell. They do not argue or appeal to Scripture. They sneer, which is often what people do when something has landed and cannot be answered: ridicule lets a whole room off the hook by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Justify yourselves before men. He goes straight past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. They made themselves look righteous in people’s eyes; their wealth and religious reputation impressed others. To justify yourself before men is the exhausting effort of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience. It is the opposite of the tax collector who will stand at the back of the temple two chapters later, with no audience and no defence, and go home justified by God (18:14). These men were their own defence counsel before a human jury; God is the Judge, and the verdict he gives the tax collector rests on mercy, not on a record (18:13).

But God knows your hearts. He sees through appearances: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The verdict of the audience and the verdict of God are two different courts, and only one of them is final.

The one who reads hearts. The men who sneered had already watched this sentence at work. Again and again Luke says that Jesus knew their thoughts (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). The one who says God knows your hearts is himself reading theirs as he says it. They were not being judged by a Galilean teacher’s opinion, but by the searching gaze of God in the face of a man.

An abomination. Abomination, bdelygma, is a heavy word: in the Greek Old Testament it is the standard term for idols, and Proverbs calls everyone who is arrogant in heart an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 16:5). So the thing this society most admires, visible success, honour, religious reputation, when it flows from pride and self-love, is in the same category as an idol.

Does God hate success, then? No. God gives wealth, skill and honour, and Scripture praises the man skilful in his work (Proverbs 22:29). What is an abomination is the exaltation: success turned into a throne, reputation turned into a righteousness, the applause of men treated as the verdict of heaven. The same promotion can be received with gratitude by one man and worshipped by another. The question is not what you have achieved but what you are leaning on, and whose praise you are living for (John 5:44).

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely. A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Proverbs 22:1), and an elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). But reputation is a by-product of faithfulness, not its goal. The danger begins when the audience becomes the judge: when you would rather be thought generous than be generous, thought godly than be godly. A simple test: what do you do when no one will ever know? Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret, and promised that the Father who sees in secret will reward (Matthew 6:4).

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets were until John. A hinge verse. The Law and the Prophets names the whole Old Testament, and Jesus dates its era: until John. Not abolished at John, as the following sentence makes emphatic, but the time of promise has closed, because what it pointed to has come. John stands on the seam, which is what Jesus meant when he said no one born of women is greater than John, and yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he (7:28).

In the flow. Verses 16 to 18 can look like three stray sayings, but they answer the men who justify themselves (v. 15). Those men claimed the Law as their ground. Jesus replies that the Law and the Prophets were pointing to the kingdom now being preached (v. 16), that the Law still stands and judges (v. 17), and that their own divorce rulings show how they bent it (v. 18). The rich man’s story then ends on the same words, they have Moses and the Prophets (v. 29): the Scriptures these men claimed will testify against them if they will not hear.

The good news of the kingdom. A new era has begun: the time of fulfilment. The kingdom of God is God’s rule as King, breaking into the world in Jesus to forgive sinners, to heal what sin has spoiled, and to gather a people who live gladly under him (17:20–21; Colossians 1:13). The verb is euangelizetai, the gospel is preached: the kingdom is not a programme for people to implement but a report of what God has done, and its centre is a person. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah’s words about the one anointed to preach good news to the poor, rolled up the scroll and said, today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:18–21). The era of promise ended because the Promised One was standing in the room.

Everyone forces his way into it. A difficult phrase, because the Greek verb can be read more than one way. It may be middle voice: everyone is pressing urgently to enter, with the earnest striving of 13:24 (strive to enter through the narrow door), as the tax collectors and sinners are doing. Or passive: everyone is being urged in, pressed to come, like the guests compelled in from the highways (14:23); the ESV notes this in its margin. Or, as in Matthew 11:12, it may speak of the kingdom suffering violence from its opponents. In Luke’s context the first seems most likely.

Entered like a closing door. Since John announced the King, the kingdom is entered the way a man presses through a closing door, with decision and urgency. And there is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone: tax collectors and sinners are pushing their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

Does this mean I get into the kingdom by my own effort? No. The kingdom is preached as good news, and good news is received, not earned. The striving here is not the effort that earns entry but the urgency of a man who will not let anything keep him from the gift: not pride, not fear of what people think, not the pleasures he must leave behind. Those who press in are precisely those who have stopped trusting their own righteousness. And behind every human pressing in is the God who draws: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). The urgency is ours; the power is his.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One dot of the Law. Immediately after saying that an era has ended, he says the Law is untouchable. Heaven and earth are the most permanent things imaginable, and Jesus says they are less secure than what God has written. The dot is the keraia, literally a little horn: the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

How the law continues. The two verses are held together by one word: fulfilment. Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17–18). The Law’s era has closed, but the Law itself has not been cancelled; it has been kept, by the man saying this. Its moral demands remain, its ceremonies find their reality in him (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1), and its promises are kept in him.

Must Christians, then, keep the Old Testament law? Reformed Christians distinguish three kinds of law in the Old Testament. Its ceremonial laws, the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind us (Hebrews 9–10). Its civil laws were given to Israel as a nation and expired with that nation, though their general equity still teaches wisdom (the Westminster Confession 19.4; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.4). Its moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still guides believers, not as a way to earn God’s favour but as the shape of the life he has given us (Westminster 19.5–6; 1689 19.5–6). Not a dot of the law fails, because Christ fulfils all of it, some by completing it and some by writing it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Two opposite errors. One man reads the Law and the Prophets were until John and concludes that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity; verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes that nothing has changed, that he must still produce a righteousness of his own; verse 16 exists to stop him. The good news of the kingdom is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

Why does Jesus turn straight from the law to divorce? The subject has not changed. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things; and among the Pharisees who sneered at his teaching on money, the school of Hillel read the divorce law very permissively. So he takes the point at which their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law, and shows who is actually relaxing it. Verse 18 is an example of verse 17.

In everyday life. When a commandment is inconvenient this week, and one will be, notice the instinct to treat it as a dot that surely does not matter: a small lie, a small lust, a small theft of time. Then remember the One who kept every dot for you, and keep it for love of him.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why here? An example of the permanence of God’s law (v. 17), aimed at the Pharisees, who used the law to allow easy divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1 permitted a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce if he found some indecency in her, and the school of Hillel read that so broadly that a burnt dinner could count, and Rabbi Akiva later added finding a prettier woman. They justified themselves (v. 15) by quoting Moses, while breaking the deeper intent of God’s law for marriage. And perhaps there is a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, his brother’s wife, and had imprisoned John for saying so (3:19–20).

Divorces his wife and marries another. In God’s eyes the marriage bond still holds, so remarriage is adultery (Mark 10:11–12). Divorce in that world was a man’s prerogative: he wrote the certificate, and she was put out. The man who discards his wife for another woman has not left a contract; he has broken a covenant, a solemn promise made before God: Malachi calls a man’s wife his wife by covenant, and says the LORD was witness between them (Malachi 2:14).

Marries a woman divorced. The second husband too. The sin is not confined to the man who started it; it reaches everyone who treats the first marriage as though it had never been.

The exceptions. Luke, like Mark, gives the saying flat, with no exception attached. Matthew records the same teaching twice and both times includes an exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Corinthians 7:15). Luke is giving the rule, not the case law: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are exceptions, narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced person ever remarry? Some Christians hold that there is no ground for remarriage while a former spouse lives, reading this verse without exceptions. Others allow divorce and remarriage on wider grounds, such as incompatibility or the breakdown of love. This commentary’s view: the position of the Westminster Confession (24.5–6) is best: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied by the church or the civil authority, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and, after the divorce, remarry as if the offending party were dead. Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and Paul for desertion by an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:15); Luke gives the principle, and Matthew and Paul give its exceptions. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to such desertion, and the elders help judge each case; the abused should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated. Those who have sinned in divorce and remarriage can find full forgiveness in Christ.

What about the person already divorced and remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? This is the question that keeps people out of church. Is every day of the new marriage a fresh sin? Is the only repentance available to break the second home apart? No. Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18); he calls them husbands, he names the truth exactly, and he does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage. It is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that now exists and carries real obligations to a real spouse and real children. Where there was sin, it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. If that is your history, the word to you is not go back. It is be washed, and be faithful now.

Such were some of you. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then writes a sentence that has rescued many consciences: and such were some of you (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The one who drew the line on marriage in this verse is the same Lord in whose name the adulterer is washed. The fence stands exactly where Jesus put it, chiefly to protect the wife who could be dismissed and left with nothing; but the gospel does not leave a man locked outside his own forgiveness.

What if my spouse is abusing me? Then this verse is not a chain to keep you in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, in the church or in the home, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires a husband or wife to remain under the same roof as someone who threatens, beats or terrorises them. Get yourself and your children to safety; tell your elders and, where a crime has been committed, the police (Romans 13:4). Separation for protection is not the sin this verse condemns. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse has broken the marriage in the way Scripture recognises, by the abuser’s wilful abandonment of the covenant’s every duty, is a question to be weighed carefully with faithful elders, and many Reformed churches have judged that it can. What is never right is to tell a victim that God wants her to stay and suffer. Jesus’ words protect the vulnerable; they were never meant to be turned against them.

Is there a way back if I was the one who sinned in my divorce? Yes, and the way is the same as for every other sin: confess it to God without excuse, put right what can still be put right, and receive his forgiveness fully. That may mean seeking reconciliation with a former spouse if both are unmarried and it is possible; it will certainly mean honesty, humility, and faithfulness to the obligations you still have, especially to your children. It does not mean living for ever under a cloud. David, who took another man’s wife and killed him to cover it, wrote the psalm the church still prays: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Psalm 51:7).

For worship. Behind this hard saying stands a Bridegroom who has never once divorced his bride. Israel went after other lovers, and the LORD said through Hosea that he would betroth her to himself for ever (Hosea 2:19). The church is no better, and he gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). When our marriages are broken, his is not. He hates the breaking of covenant because he is faithful, and he is faithful to us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the fullest picture of life after death in the first three Gospels, told as the sequel to the teaching on money. A rich man dressed and fed like a king passes a sick beggar at his gate every day. At death the places are reversed: Lazarus is carried to Abraham’s side, the place of honour at the feast, and the rich man is in torment, seeing Lazarus far off. Nothing he then says shows he has learned anything.
verseByVerse.theology: The story teaches that there is conscious existence after death, before the resurrection: the rich man sees, recognises, feels pain and argues (compare 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). The punishment of the wicked is real torment, and the separation is fixed in both directions. Jesus uses imagery his hearers knew, and it is not a map of the afterlife, but the warning must not be softened by that caution.
verseByVerse.examples:
The story does not teach that poverty saves and wealth damns; Abraham, who was wealthy, is at the feast. What condemns the rich man is the gate he walked past daily, and what saves Lazarus is the God who knew his name.

The rich man had heard the Law and the Prophets read every Sabbath of his life, and walked home past Lazarus. The problem was never a shortage of evidence. When another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests planned to kill him too (John 12:10). The test was run, and it went exactly as Jesus said.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich man and Lazarus. Only Luke records this story. It illustrates the danger of wealth (v. 13), the reversal promised in the beatitudes and woes (6:20–26), and the sufficiency of Scripture (vv. 29–31), and it answers the Pharisees who had just sneered: they loved money and thought it a sign of God’s favour, and here is a man who had all of it.

Purple and fine linen. Every detail is a price tag. Purple dye came from the murex shellfish, thousands to a garment, and was so costly that some societies restricted it to royalty; the fine linen was a luxury cloth. And he is unnamed (tradition calls him Dives, Latin for rich). The man who had every name worth having in this life has no name before God.

Feasted sumptuously every day. Not on feast days, when ordinary people ate meat, but every day, and the word suggests not just plenty but display: he made merry, splendidly.

At his gate was laid. The verb may suggest that somebody put him there because he could not move himself. And the gate is the gateway of a great house: the rich man could hardly enter or leave his own property without passing him.

Named Lazarus. The only character in any of Jesus’ parables to be given a name. Lazarus, from Eleazar, means God helps, or God has helped. No one else did. God knows the poor by name, and the name is the single hint the parable gives about where this man’s hope actually lay.

God has visited his people. The name says God helps, and the one telling the story is that help in person. When Jesus raised a widow’s only son at the gate of Nain, the crowd said, God has visited his people (7:16). No one at the rich man’s gate helps Lazarus, but the man speaking had been stopping at gates all over Galilee, touching lepers and feeding the hungry. The hope hidden in the beggar’s name was walking the roads of Israel.

What fell from the table. Ulcerated, perhaps from malnutrition. He wants what falls: not a place at the table, the scraps that go on the floor, like the prodigal longing for the pigs’ pods (15:16). Even those were not given to him.

Even the dogs. The dogs are most likely not a comfort but scavenging street dogs, unclean animals, reaching him when no human being will. He was too weak to keep them off: the final degradation.

The rich man’s sin. Not that he was rich, nor that he had done anything to Lazarus. He did nothing. He walked past the poor man at his gate every day and ignored him. His sin was neglect, indifference, the failure to love his neighbour, and behind it the failure to love God, because a man who loves God cannot step over his image every morning.

What it does not mean. The story’s shape invites a wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything; the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns. Luke has already guarded against that: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was a wealthy man. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily. What saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

Who is the Lazarus at my gate? Usually someone you pass so often you have stopped seeing him. It may be the homeless man outside the station, but it is just as often the widow two doors down who has not had a visitor in a month, the colleague whose marriage is collapsing, the asylum-seeking family at the back of church, the believer in your congregation who cannot pay the gas bill. Your gate is wherever your daily path brings you within reach of real need. You cannot meet every need in the world, and God does not ask you to. He asks you not to step over the one he has laid where you will see him.

Should I give to every beggar who asks? Not necessarily, and wisdom is not the opposite of love. Giving cash to someone feeding an addiction may not help him, and Scripture expects the able to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But the rich man’s problem was not careless giving; it was no giving and no seeing. A good rule is never to walk past without at least seeing the person: a word, a name asked, a meal bought, a referral to a church or charity that can do more than you can. And support, regularly, those in your church and town who do this work well. Love may be wise; it may not be blind.
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury — the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man died. The story does not say he was buried. A man in his condition would most likely have gone into a pauper’s grave, and the parable passes over it, because something else was happening that nobody could see.

Carried by the angels. The same passivity as verse 20: he was laid at a gate by men, and he is carried through death by angels, and he does nothing in either case. Abraham’s side is literally Abraham’s bosom, the language of a banquet, where the guest in the place of honour reclined beside the host (John 13:23): a picture of paradise, at the messianic banquet where many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (13:28–29). So the beggar who longed for what fell from a table is now in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

In Hades. Hades is the Greek term for the realm of the dead (the Hebrew Sheol); here it is the place of punishment for the wicked. Torment, basanois, is agony. What the parable describes is conscious existence: he sees, he recognises, he is in pain, he will shortly argue. The reversal is complete: the rich man has nothing, Lazarus has everything. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53).

He lifted up his eyes. He can see what he has lost, and the first person he picks out is Lazarus: the one face he had trained himself not to register, every day, for years. And he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Where Christians differ: parable or history? And what happens after death? Some argue this is a literal description of the afterlife; others that it is a parable using popular imagery, and should not be pressed for details. It begins like other parables, there was a rich man, but names Lazarus, which no other parable does. Some, holding soul sleep (the view that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection) or annihilationism (that the lost finally cease to exist), deny that the dead have conscious existence, or that the lost suffer for ever; among them are Christians who love Scripture and hold it sincerely. This commentary’s view: it is a parable, and its details (seeing across the chasm, speaking, a drop of water) are pictures, not a map of the afterlife. But Jesus would not use a picture that taught falsehood. The story teaches clearly that at death there is conscious existence, that the righteous are comforted and the wicked suffer, immediately after death, that there is a fixed separation, and that destiny is settled at death. The fuller picture comes at the resurrection and final judgment, when Hades itself gives up its dead (Revelation 20:13–15) and the lost go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The punishment is conscious and it is without end.

Hades and Abraham’s side. Hades here is the place of the dead before the final judgment, not yet the lake of fire, and Abraham’s side is the blessedness of believers with God, the same Paradise Jesus promised the dying thief that very day (23:43). The souls of the righteous, says the Westminster Confession, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, reserved to the judgment of the great day (Westminster 32.1). Then the bodies are raised, and soul and body together enter their final state.

When a Christian dies, does he sleep until the resurrection? No. The body sleeps in the grave, which is why the New Testament can call death falling asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the soul does not. Lazarus is carried at once to Abraham’s side; the thief is with Christ today; Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Your believing mother, your child who trusted Jesus, the friend you buried last year: they are not unconscious and they are not waiting in some grey place. They are with Christ, awake, at rest and rejoicing, and they await only the resurrection of their bodies.

Is there a purgatory, a place where souls are cleansed before heaven? No. Lazarus goes straight from the gate to the banquet, and there is no third place in the story, only comfort and torment. Christ’s blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid off. Believers are made perfect in holiness at death and pass immediately into glory (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1). Purgatory would add our sufferings to Christ’s sacrifice, as though his were not enough. It was enough.

In everyday life. Think of the two funerals: one with no mourners and angels in attendance, one with every honour and none of the things that mattered. Then ask which of the two your life is preparing. And if you are grieving a believer this week, read this verse again. They were carried.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom” — the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father Abraham, have mercy on me. Two things in that request show the man has not changed. The first is Father Abraham: he is pleading descent, which is exactly what John the Baptist had warned against at the start of this Gospel: do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father (3:8). His claim is ancestry, and it is the only one he makes. And have mercy on me: he never showed mercy to Lazarus. Now he begs for it.

Send Lazarus. The second is worse. He knows the name, he can see the man in the place of honour beside Abraham, and his instinct is to have him fetched, like a servant, to bring water. Even now, he thinks of Lazarus as somebody who ought to be running errands for him. Nothing has been learned. Hell does not reform; it reveals.

Cool my tongue. Not release, not reversal, but a single drop: he who feasted every day begs for one drop of water, the exact reversal of the scraps from his table, and even that is refused.

In this flame. Fire is a picture of the suffering of the lost, used by John the Baptist and by Jesus himself (3:17; Mark 9:43–48). Whether or not the flame is physical, what it pictures is real, and Jesus chose the most terrible image available because nothing less would be true.

Child, remember. Abraham’s answer opens with Child. There is no cruelty in this scene, and no gloating; the word is tender. But the answer is no, and it is an accounting, turning on one word: remember. Abraham does not produce a list of sins; he asks the man to recall his own life.

Your good things. The possessive is exact. He had his comfort in this life, and chose it as his portion: woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation (6:24). He lived for himself and got what he lived for, and it lasted exactly as long as he did.

Bad things. Not that Lazarus was saved because he was poor; his name suggests he trusted God. But in this life he received bad things, and his share of good things never came in this life.

Comforted here. This great reversal is the whole indictment, without a single charge laid. The tragedy is not that he was punished for enjoying it. It is that he wanted so little. He could have had God himself as his portion, as the psalmist did (Psalm 16:5; 73:26), and he settled for linen and dinners, a portion that ended with his last breath.

A son of Abraham. The rich man rests his claim on Abraham. Jesus in Luke makes children of Abraham another way. He laid his hands on a woman bent double for eighteen years and called her a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound (13:16). He went into the house of a chief tax collector and said, today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham (19:9). The children Abraham actually welcomes are the ones Christ has found, freed and brought to his side.

How can heaven be happy if people we love are in hell? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian carries, and Scripture does not answer it with a formula. But it gives us this: in the parable, Abraham is neither cruel nor tormented. He speaks with tenderness and with perfect agreement with God’s justice. In glory we will see as God sees, and we will love what he loves; no one will be in hell whom God has wronged, and no one in heaven will doubt that the Judge of all the earth has done right (Genesis 18:25). Until then, the question should drive us to pray and to speak to those we love while the door is open, and to trust that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

For worship. There was One who did cry out in anguish and thirst, and whose cry was answered with mockery and sour wine (23:36). He drank the cup of wrath to its last drop, so that no one who trusts in him will ever beg for a drop of water in the flame. The rich man received his good things in his lifetime; Christ received our bad things in his, so that we might be comforted for ever. He is the portion that cannot be used up.

parallels.desc: men whose portion is in this life

verseByVerse.quote: And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great chasm has been fixed. A second reason, not about what the man deserves but about what is possible. Has been fixed is perfect tense: it was established, and it stands, and it was God who fixed it.

None may cross. The barrier is described as working in both directions: nobody crosses from there, and nobody crosses from here, not even out of compassion. That second clause rules out a sentimental reading: it is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him. It is that the door is now shut, by God, and neither pity on one side nor pleading on the other can open it.

No second chance. After death, destiny is fixed: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The same sentence in Hebrews goes straight on to Christ: so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him (Hebrews 9:28). Men die once; Christ was offered once; and that single offering is why the time before the chasm is fixed is a time of open mercy. The time to repent is now: behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

The same chasm. And this is the reason the parable sits in a chapter about money. The gulf in verse 26 is not a new thing. In verses 19 to 21 there was a gulf too, and it was a gate: the space between the rich man and Lazarus, which he could have crossed any day of his life. He never did. Now he is on the far side of a chasm he cannot cross, and it is the same chasm.

What about people who never heard the gospel, or who died as infants? The parable is spoken to people who had Moses and the Prophets, and its warning is aimed at those who hear and will not listen. Scripture is clear that salvation is only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church must send preachers, not wait for the dead to be given a second hearing. Those who never heard are judged by the light they had, and all have sinned against that light (Romans 1:20; 2:12). Infants who die in infancy are a different case: Scripture gives grounds for hope, and the confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). If you have lost a little one, you may rest your grief on the Lord who called the infants to himself (18:15–16). Neither case offers a second chance after death.

Is never-ending punishment not out of all proportion to one lifetime of sin? Only if sin is measured by how long it lasted. But a wrong is weighed by the one it is against. Striking a stranger is serious; striking a king was treason. Sin is rebellion against the infinitely holy God, and its guilt is measured by his majesty (Psalm 51:4). Nor do the lost become penitent. The rich man in the flame is still giving orders about Lazarus; he asks for relief, never for God. Hell is God’s righteous judgment, giving the lost, justly and for ever, the life without him that they chose (Romans 2:5–8). And the one who spoke of it most plainly went to the cross to save sinners from it. The door is open today.

parallels.desc: to die once, and after that comes judgment

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
My father’s house. The second request is usually read as the one decent thing the man does, and the concern for his family is real. But it is still send him: twice now Lazarus is treated as an errand boy. And look at which house he wants him sent to: his father’s house, where his brothers are presumably still feasting sumptuously and stepping over somebody at the gate.

Five brothers. They are living as he had lived. Warn, diamartyrētai, is to testify earnestly, solemnly. And the request reads, faintly, like self-justification: if only I had been warned properly. Abraham’s answer meets it exactly.

They have Moses and the Prophets. Moses and the Prophets means the Old Testament Scriptures. The brothers have not been left without warning. The Law commands that the poor at your gate be provided for and that the corners of your field be left for the poor and the sojourner (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). The Prophets return to it again and again (Amos 6:4–7; Isaiah 58:6–7). And the Scriptures point beyond care for the poor to repentance and faith in the Messiah they promise.

Let them hear them. Listen and obey. The rich man would have heard it read in synagogue Sabbath after Sabbath, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner. Nobody in that house lacks information. What is being asked for is something more compelling than the word of God, and Abraham’s reply is that they already have the word of God, and it is enough, and the problem was never the evidence.

Listen to him. Moses and the Prophets have already been heard in Luke speaking of one person. On the mountain of the transfiguration Moses and Elijah stood with Jesus and spoke of his departure at Jerusalem, and a voice from the cloud said, this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him! (9:30–35). After the resurrection he interpreted to his disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:27). To hear Moses and the Prophets rightly is to hear them pointing to Christ. The brothers had a Bible whose whole message was the one telling this story.

The sufficiency of Scripture. God’s word is enough to bring people to repentance and salvation. The sacred writings are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). They do not need a special messenger from the dead. The whole counsel of God is either set down in Scripture or deduced from it, and nothing is ever to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men (Westminster Confession 1.6).

Should I look for visions, dreams or messages from the dead to guide me? No. The story gives no warrant for contact between the living and the dead, and Scripture forbids seeking it (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 8:19). The rich man’s request is refused, and the point is that the living have the Scriptures. God has spoken, finally and fully, in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the canon of his word is closed. Christians differ over whether God still gives prophecy or dreams today, but even those who believe he does agree that nothing may be added to Scripture or set above it. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible: he will never say anything elsewhere that contradicts it, and he will not say anything outside it that you need more.

In everyday life. You have more than the five brothers had: the Gospels and the letters as well. Ask honestly whether you are waiting for something more before you obey: a sign, a feeling, a clearer word. Then take the next plain command you find in the page this week and do it, trusting the Spirit who speaks there to give what he asks.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures.

parallels.desc: if you believed Moses, you would believe me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, father Abraham. He contradicts Abraham flatly, which is a remarkable thing to do from where he is standing, and entirely in character. He has been managing people all his life and is still doing it.

If someone goes to them from the dead. A spectacular sign would convince them. Many hold this theory: if only there were more evidence, people would believe. It is worth admitting how reasonable that sounds. Most Christians have thought it about somebody they love: if he could only see something, he would believe.

If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets. The rich man’s brothers lacked not evidence but a willing heart. Where a heart is set against God’s word, more evidence rarely moves it, because the resistance is not only in the mind. Miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it; they only raise the stakes.

Neither will they be convinced. A haunting prophecy. Somebody did rise from the dead, not long after this was spoken, and the leaders who had heard this kind of teaching were not convinced. Matthew tells us they paid the soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). And in John’s Gospel, when another Lazarus was raised from the dead at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him and Jesus too (John 11:43–53; 12:10–11). The test was run. It went exactly as he said.

How faith actually comes. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), by the work of the Spirit. When the dead do come to life, it is not because a ghost has visited them but because God has spoken through his word and opened their hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). That is why the church preaches rather than performs: the power is in the message, because the Spirit works with the word.

Should I pray for a sign for a relative who will not believe? Pray for him, constantly and by name; but pray above all that God would open his heart to the word, because that is how God saves. A sign without a new heart would only harden him further, as this verse warns. So put the word in front of him: your life, which he reads first, then your words about Christ, a Gospel to read, an invitation to hear the Bible preached. And do not despair if nothing seems to happen. The Spirit is not in a hurry, and many who resisted for decades were finally won by a verse they had heard a hundred times.

For worship. Someone has risen from the dead. Not a beggar sent back on an errand, but the Lord of glory, who now holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The rich man asked for a messenger; God sent his Son, and raised him on the third day, just as the Scriptures had said (24:46). He stands at the gate of every hearer of this story, not as a beggar, but as a King with his hands full of mercy.

parallels.desc: after Lazarus of Bethany is raised, they plot to kill Jesus

16.text: <sup>1</sup> He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. <sup>2</sup> And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ <sup>3</sup> And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. <sup>4</sup> I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’ <sup>5</sup> So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ <sup>6</sup> He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ <sup>7</sup> Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ <sup>8</sup> The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. <sup>10</sup> “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. <sup>11</sup> If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? <sup>12</sup> And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own? <sup>13</sup> No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.” <sup>14</sup> The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 moves from the life of the church to the end of the world. Disciples are warned not to cause others to stumble, told to forgive without limit, taught that small faith in a great God is enough, and reminded that obedience earns no credit. Ten lepers are cleansed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks; Jesus tells him his faith has made him well, or, as the ESV margin gives it, has saved him.

The closing teaching (vv. 20–37) holds two things together. The kingdom does not come with signs that can be observed, because it is already present in Jesus (vv. 20–21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come as suddenly and visibly as lightning (v. 24). The kingdom is present in the King, and its final unveiling is still to come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four short teachings press the disciples on different parts of their calling: do not trip the weak, rebuke and forgive the brother who falls, trust God for the faith to do it, and claim no credit when you have. Each makes the disciple lean harder on his Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching echoes the Lord’s Prayer: “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes what justification does to a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The servant parable checks the pride that obedience produces, and it speaks of the best possible day, when everything commanded has been done. Even then there is no credit. Yet the same Lord says he will serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage; there is a Master who pays anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act: forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart; reconciliation takes two, and Jesus ties it to the brother’s repentance.

The servant parable can sting anyone who has served for years without thanks. It is not the whole picture. Both households in Luke are Christ’s, and in the second he serves his servants at his own table (12:37).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 17 moves from the life of the church to the end of the world, and the same Lord rules both. Four short teachings open it: do not trip others, rebuke and forgive without limit, use the faith you have, and serve without seeking credit (vv. 1–10). Ten lepers are cleansed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to give thanks and hears that his faith has saved him (vv. 11–19). Asked when the kingdom will come, Jesus says it is already among them in his own person, and then describes his sudden return (vv. 20–37). The thread is direction: who turns back to Christ, and who looks back to the world.

The setting. After chapter 16, Jesus turns to his disciples on the road to Jerusalem (9:51), and Luke gathers sayings that teach a community how to live while its Lord walks towards the cross.

Temptations to sin. The word is skandala: snares, stumbling blocks. Its oldest sense was the trigger of a trap: anything that trips a person into sin or out of faith. In a fallen world such snares are inevitable, and Jesus does not promise a church in which nobody is ever tripped up.

Woe to the one. But inevitability does not excuse responsibility. Each person who causes another to fall is accountable. And Luke’s woe is the prophets’ word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict. Judas was the stumbling block God had foretold, and still the Son of Man said woe to that man by whom he is betrayed (22:22). God’s sovereignty over sin never turns the sinner into a victim. Peter holds both truths in one sentence: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23).

A millstone. The image is deliberately extreme. A millstone was the heavy upper stone of a mill, far too heavy to struggle free of, and for a Jew drowning with it carried a particular horror: a body that could never be buried. And this is described as the better outcome, better than the judgment awaiting whoever destroys the faith of another.

These little ones. The phrase includes children, but here it reaches wider: humble, ordinary believers, the young in faith, the recently converted, the tax collectors and sinners who have just come to Jesus (15:1), anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The weight falls on the influential. Nobody trips a person who is not following them. So this is a word for parents, and for anyone who teaches, leads, or is simply admired by a younger believer. To ruin your own soul is a catastrophe. To be the stumbling block under somebody else’s is worse, and he measures it with a millstone.

The Shepherd’s anger. Behind this woe stands a long quarrel in the prophets. Through Ezekiel the LORD charged the shepherds of Israel that they had not strengthened the weak or brought back the strayed, and so the sheep were scattered (Ezekiel 34:4–5). Then he promised to come himself (34:16), and Luke has just shown him carrying one sheep home on his shoulders (15:4–6). So the millstone is not the temper of a harsh teacher. It is the anger of the Shepherd himself, who has come at great cost for the weak, against anyone who would drive them off again.

How might I cause someone to stumble without meaning to? Most stumbling blocks are not set deliberately. A church leader whose private life contradicts his preaching. A parent who teaches prayer and never prays, or who mocks other Christians at the dinner table. A mature believer who flaunts a freedom, in drink or entertainment or speech, in front of someone fresh out of the very thing (Romans 14:13–21). Harsh legalism also trips people, by teaching them that God is impossible to please. And in its gravest form, it is the abuse of a child or a vulnerable person by someone they trusted, which has driven many out of the faith and is exactly what this millstone is for. Such abuse must be reported, never hidden to protect a church’s name.

What if I have caused someone to stumble? Then repent, and do not let the millstone become despair. The warning is spoken to disciples, to bring them to their senses, not to push them past forgiveness. Confess it to God, and where possible go to the person, own it without excuse, and ask how you can help put it right. Then live differently in front of them. Peter denied his Lord three times in front of servants who were watching, and was restored to feed the very lambs (John 21:15–17). The blood of Christ covers the sins of influence too.

In everyday life. Think of three people younger in faith or in years who watch you: a child, a new Christian, a colleague who knows you go to church. Ask what they have learned about Christ from you this month. If one of those lessons is false, correct it in front of them.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to yourselves! Watch yourselves: your own example, and your own heart. Before a word is said about rebuking anybody, the man doing the rebuking is told to look at himself.

In the flow. Pay attention to yourselves looks both ways: back to the millstone (the surest way not to trip a weaker believer is to watch your own feet), and on to the rebuke and the forgiveness that follow. Verses 1–10 are one short course for a church on the road: do not cause a fall, rebuke and forgive, trust God for the strength, and claim no credit.

If your brother sins, rebuke him. Love does not ignore sin. A fellow believer who sins should be lovingly confronted, privately first (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). The rebuke is not optional and it is not unkind. What makes it bearable is the order. A man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not.

If he repents, forgive him. The goal of rebuke is restoration, not humiliation. A rebuke that does not hope for repentance is only an attack.

Seven times in the day. Seven is the number of completeness: not a limit, but limitless forgiveness, like the seventy-seven times Jesus gives Peter (Matthew 18:21–22; older versions read seventy times seven). And seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, meant to kill the arithmetic: anyone who apologises seven times before evening is, by ordinary judgment, not sincere, and Jesus names the number himself. The test is not whether the repentance convinces. It is whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

Forgiveness from a forgiving Lord. The command does not come from a teacher of ethics. It comes from the one who said of a weeping woman, her sins, which are many, are forgiven (7:47), and who receives sinners and eats with them (15:2). So seven times a day is not a quota laid on a reluctant heart. It is the overflow of a Lord whose own forgiving has never run dry, passed on by people who know they are the larger debtor.

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong, or always restoring full trust at once, or removing all consequences. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not be given the chequebook again. But forgiveness means letting go of the debt and of revenge, and being ready to restore the relationship.

What if he never says he repents? Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents, and leaves the other case open, and that silence is worth pressing, because that is where most real wounds live. The answer begins with a distinction Luke’s own wording invites: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart: releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus prays for this from the cross for men who had not repented (23:34; the prayer is missing from some early manuscripts, but many scholars judge it genuine). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two; Jesus attaches it to if he repents. You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally. You cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends. And that protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from the cruelty of having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for.

And if the sin is serious and goes on? This private rebuke is the first step Jesus describes more fully in Matthew 18:15–17, where unrepentant sin is taken to one or two others and then to the church. Forgiveness in your heart does not mean the church must look away. And where the sin is a crime, abuse of a spouse or a child, or anything that endangers others, forgiving does not mean staying silent or staying in danger. Report it, protect the vulnerable, and let the elders and the civil authorities do their work. You can release your own claim to revenge and still insist that justice be done.

In everyday life. You will not find seven pardons a day in yourself; the Spirit of the Lord who forgave you is the one who gives them. Name in prayer the brother or sister you need to confront lovingly, or forgive again, and ask God to show you your own part. Then either go and speak, gently and privately, or tell him plainly: I forgive you, and I will not bring it up again. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Increase our faith! Note when they say it. They have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in a day, and their response is that they have not got enough of whatever it takes. It is an honest request and a good prayer.

Asked of the right Lord. Luke’s wording is careful: the apostles said to the Lord, the title the Greek Old Testament gives to God. They bring a request that only God can grant. Faith is not a quantity a man can raise in himself; it is given, and in Luke it is Jesus who guards it. On the night of his arrest he will tell Peter that Satan has demanded to sift him like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (22:31–32). Peter’s faith faltered that night, and it did not fail, because it hung on the prayer of his Lord.

A grain of mustard seed. They wanted more; he tells them the quantity was never the issue. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny (Mark 4:31). Jesus does not say they need more faith, but real faith. The size of faith matters less than its object. Tiny faith in a great God can do great things.

This mulberry tree. The mulberry, or sycamine, tree, the black mulberry of Palestine, has a deep, spreading root system and was very hard to uproot.

Planted in the sea. Doubly absurd: a tree that cannot be moved, put where nothing grows. Faith does the impossible, because God does. Forgiving seven times a day may feel like uprooting a mulberry tree; faith in God makes it possible.

What it does not mean. The verse has been lifted out of this paragraph and turned into a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough, and so, it follows, did the tumour and the sick child. That has been preached to many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it cannot be got out of this text. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have asked for help to forgive, and the mulberry tree is his answer about that.

The prayer that was not granted. In the whole of Acts, men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). The cup was not removed, and nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small. What is promised is not that faith is a force whose output rises with its volume, but that its power lies in what it is attached to.

My prayer was not answered. Was my faith too small? No. If your faith was the size of a mustard seed, it was enough, because the power never lay in your faith but in God. When he does not do what we asked, it is not because we failed a test of believing hard enough; it is because our Father, who loves us and knows what we do not, has a better purpose, as he had for Paul, whose thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith is not the confidence that God will do what I want. It is trust that he is good, and wise, and will do what is right, and the willingness to keep obeying while I wait.

So how does my faith grow? Not mainly by trying to feel more certain, but by looking at the One you trust. Faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), so read and hear it. It grows by use, like a muscle: the next time you forgive when it is hard, or give when it is costly, you will find that God was there. It grows in the fellowship of believers and at the Lord’s Table, where Christ is set before us. And it grows by asking: the apostles’ prayer, increase our faith, is one God loves to answer.
verseByVerse.note: The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant plowing. The question expects the answer no, and every man listening would have given it. Picture a small farm: a farmer with one slave, who ploughs by day and works in the house in the evening. When he comes in, the supper has not been made, because he is the one who makes it.

Say to him when he has come in from the field, Come at once and recline at table? Recline at table is the posture of a guest at a formal meal. The suggestion is not that the master might let him sit down; it is that he might treat him as an honoured visitor in his own master’s house. No master would serve his slave first. That was not how things worked.

Prepare supper for me. The slave’s duty continued; it is simply how a household ran, and everybody knew it. Dress properly is, in the ESV margin, gird yourself: tuck up the robe for work, as the servants waiting for their master did in chapter 12.

Afterward you will eat. Note the last clause, easy to miss under the severity. The servant is not going hungry; he eats second. This parable is about to say something hard about deserving, and it says it inside a picture where the servant is fed.

Does Jesus approve of slavery here? No. He uses the household as his listeners knew it to make a point about God, just as he uses a dishonest manager and an unjust judge without approving of them. Slavery in that world was a fact of life. The Old Testament regulated a form of servitude rather than abolishing it, and that is a real difficulty for modern readers; but its laws protected the servant, and the gospel set to work on the institution from inside: Paul tells a master to receive his runaway slave no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and the Bible condemns man-stealing outright (1 Timothy 1:10; Exodus 21:16). The parable’s subject is not human employment but the relation of a creature to his Creator, who owns us by right and whom we can never put in our debt.

For the one who serves unseen. For some readers the scene will sting. Anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement will recognise this household exactly: the work that is simply expected, the meal made after everybody else has eaten. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. This same Gospel has already given a second picture of the household, and it is the ending: a master who comes home and serves his watching servants at his own table (12:37).

The Master who took the servant’s place. Luke makes sure the reader meets this household again. At the last supper the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest, and Jesus answers in the very terms of this parable: who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). The Lord of the household, who had every right to sit, took the servant’s place, and the next day his service went to the uttermost, his body given for the very servants who had argued over seats (22:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? Again the answer is obvious and again it is no, not because thanks would be wrong, but because thanks are for something over and above. A slave doing his job puts no one in his debt. Nobody is owed gratitude for meeting the terms.

When you have done all. Note the condition. This is the sentence for the day a man has done everything, with nothing outstanding, and no ordinary sinner has ever had that day (Romans 3:23). Even then there would be no credit.

Unworthy servants. Unworthy, achreioi, means unprofitable, owed nothing. It does not mean worthless in God’s sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. It means having no claim on the Master: at the end of the accounting there is nothing on the credit side that God did not first supply.

Only our duty. Obedience to God is our duty, not a favour to him. We cannot put God in our debt: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? (Romans 11:35). This destroys the idea of earning salvation or merit by good works. Any reward he gives is pure grace, undeserved favour. A wage is owed; a gift is not, and Paul draws exactly that line: to the one who works, his wages are counted not as a gift but as his due (Romans 4:4).

The one Servant who did all. The sentence imagines a man who has done all that he was commanded, and Scripture knows only one. The Son of whom the Father said, with you I am well pleased (3:22), prayed in the garden, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). He alone could have come in from the field with nothing outstanding and claimed the wage. He did not claim it for himself. He was numbered with the transgressors (22:37), so that his obedience might be reckoned to servants who had no credit at all.

Why this parable sits here. Chapter 17 has just demanded three enormous things: do not trip the weak, forgive seven times a day, exercise the faith you have.
