A disciple who manages any of that will feel the thought rise that God now owes him a little. That thought is the target: the oldest religion in the world, the hope of putting God in our debt, and it lives most comfortably in the busiest servants of the church. The irreligious man thinks he owes God nothing; the religious man is tempted to think God owes him something; and the gospel undoes both.

Where Christians differ: merit. Medieval theology developed a doctrine of merit, including works of supererogation, good works beyond what is required, which built up a treasury of merit in the church that could be applied to others. This commentary’s view: this verse refutes it. No one can do more than duty requires. Even after doing everything, we are unworthy servants. Reward is grace. The Reformers saw it clearly: we cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin or eternal life, and when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty and are unprofitable servants (the Westminster Confession 16.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.5, which echoes this very verse).

What it does not mean. This saying needs guarding from the opposite error, because it has been used to flatten people who were already flat. It does not mean God is indifferent to what his servants do. The same Lord says he will serve his watching servants (12:37), and that the faithful man will be set over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage. There is a Master who pays anyway, and the whole point of the parable is that the second sentence is a gift and not an invoice.

Then why bother working hard for God? Because love does not work for wages. A son does not help his father in order to be paid; he helps because he is a son, and because he loves him. Freed from the need to earn, the Christian can serve with joy instead of anxiety, and God, who owes us nothing, has promised to reward even a cup of cold water given in Christ’s name (Matthew 10:42). As Augustine put it, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts. We work hard because we are already accepted, not in order to be.

In everyday life. Catch the quiet bookkeeping in your heart this week: I have served on the rota for three years, I tithe, I gave up that job for the church, surely God will see me right. Name it, and hand the ledger back to him. Then do your duty gladly, as one already accepted for Christ’s sake, and when a blessing comes, receive it as a gift, not a payment.

parallels.desc: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the border of Galilee and Samaria, ten lepers stand at a distance, as the law required (Leviticus 13:45–46), and cry for mercy. Jesus does not touch them; he sends them to the priests for the inspection given to those already healed (Leviticus 14), and as they go they are cleansed. The nine go on, doing exactly what they were told. One, the Samaritan, turns back.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story shows the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one came back to the Giver. The failure of the nine was not defiance but distraction: they moved from the gift to the system without returning.

Luke shows Samaritans in a good light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5). The man the temple fenced out is the one who came back to God at the feet of Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples: The nine were ordinary, not villains. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers, and within weeks thankfulness has given way to relief and normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem. The journey continues (9:51), and only Luke records this healing. Every step of it is taken by a Man walking towards a cross.

Between Samaria and Galilee. The border country, where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory: a detail that will matter in five verses.

Ten lepers. They are outside the village, which is where the law required them to be. Leviticus put a man with the disease outside the camp, in torn clothes, with his hair loose, calling out unclean, unclean as anyone approached (Leviticus 13:45–46). Leprosy in that world covered a range of skin conditions, but the consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis: total exclusion from worship, from family, from work, from touch.

A colony of the excluded. Ten of them are together. Luke saves a detail for verse 16: one of these ten is a Samaritan. Jews and Samaritans did not eat together, worship together or share a cup, but here they live together outside a village, because shared misery has done to their divisions what no argument would ever have done.

At a distance. Lepers were required to keep their distance, and it is where each of them had perhaps been standing for years.

Is leprosy a picture of sin? In a sense, yes, and the church has long read it that way, though carefully. The leper was not more sinful than his neighbours; his disease was not necessarily a punishment for a particular sin (compare John 9:3, about a man born blind), though Scripture records cases where it was (Numbers 12:10; 2 Kings 5:27). But the law made leprosy a living parable of uncleanness: it spread, it disfigured, it cut a man off from God’s house and God’s people, and no one could cure it but God (2 Kings 5:7). That is what sin does to every one of us. And Jesus, who could not be made unclean by touching lepers, made them clean, which is exactly what he does with sinners.

In everyday life. Ask who in your town stands at a distance: the long-term ill, the person with a disfiguring condition, the prisoner’s family, the one everyone avoids at the school gate. Then go nearer than is comfortable, because your Lord did.
verseByVerse.note: Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have mercy on us. They shout, because the law kept them at a distance. Master is epistata, a word only Luke uses, and everywhere else in this Gospel it is on the lips of disciples (5:5; 8:24; 9:33). These men are not disciples, but they use it correctly. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, the cry that echoes through Luke (18:13, 38), and leave the content of it to him.

Show yourselves to the priests. He does not touch them, as he had touched the leper in chapter 5, or pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand. A priest had to declare a healed leper clean before he could rejoin society (Leviticus 14:2–32): it is the inspection you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence, before they are healed. Will they go, still leprous, trusting his word?

As they went. The timing is the whole point: not before they went, but as they went, as they obeyed. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed. Faith acts on Christ’s word before seeing the result, like Naaman, who was healed when he obeyed and washed (2 Kings 5:14).

Does this mean I must obey before I am saved? No. The order in salvation is grace first: God gives life, and faith and obedience flow from it. These men did not earn their cleansing by walking; their walking was their faith, trusting a word that had already been spoken by the one with power to fulfil it. That is what faith always does. It hears Christ’s word and acts as if it were true, because it is. You do not need to feel forgiven before you believe you are forgiven; you take him at his word, and the feelings come on the road.

In everyday life. Is there a plain command you are waiting to feel ready for: to forgive, to confess, to be baptised, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ? Start walking this week, on his word alone, and watch what he does on the road.
verseByVerse.note: A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin the community.

parallels.desc: he shall be brought to the priest

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turned back. He is the only one who stops. The other nine are usually called ungrateful, and it is not quite that simple. They were obeying: until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards what they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them turns round.

With a loud voice. As loudly as he had cried for mercy from a distance (v. 13): the same volume, redirected.

At Jesus’ feet. Not only the posture of gratitude but of worship. He has not merely worked out that a benefit came from somewhere. He has worked out where.

Giving him thanks. The word is eucharistōn, from which comes Eucharist, the church’s ancient name for the Lord’s Supper, the meal of thanksgiving. In a picture, this man is a eucharist on the Samaritan border: a cleansed sinner on his face before the One who cleansed him.

A Samaritan. The punchline, delayed for effect. To many Jews a Samaritan was a heretic and a half-breed. The nine were going to the priests and the temple, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place that was open. And it turned out to be the right one.

Why do outsiders so often respond better than insiders? Because they have nothing to lean on. The insider has his upbringing, his church, his knowledge, his standing, and it is very easy to receive a blessing and file it with the rest. The outsider knows he deserves nothing, so a gift astonishes him. That is why Jesus could say that tax collectors and prostitutes were going into the kingdom ahead of the religious (Matthew 21:31). The cure for a church full of insiders is not to become less churchly but to remember what we were, and where we would be if he had not turned to us first.

In everyday life. Take one specific mercy from the last year and turn back with it: not a general thank you, but this one, named, out loud, to Christ. Then tell one other person what he did.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other; shared misery had joined these ten.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus answered, Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Three questions, and they are not rhetorical flourishes. Something is being registered. Jesus notices. He notices our gratitude, and our ingratitude. And it is a rare moment in Luke: a note of something like disappointment about how he has been treated. He seldom voices it on his own behalf: when a Samaritan village would not receive him, he simply went on to another (9:53–56). Here he asks where the other nine are.

Every one of them got what he asked for. The healing was not withheld from the ungrateful. All ten were cleansed before any of them had shown what he would do about it. God is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (6:35).

Where are the nine? Down the road, doing what they were told, about to be certified, perhaps rushing home to their families. Not villains. Ordinary. Which is what makes the question searching rather than merely sad. Nobody in that group made a decision to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight on to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. But they did not return.

Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner? Foreigner, allogenēs, is a startling word to find here, because it names exactly what the stone barrier in the temple court was built to keep out: it is the word on the temple inscription that warned foreigners not to pass into the inner courts on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him. The only man in the story who was fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God, to Jesus, the true temple, to worship.

Praise to God at the feet of Jesus. Listen to how Jesus describes what the Samaritan did. The man came back to Jesus, fell at his feet and thanked him, and Jesus calls it returning to give praise to God. He does not redirect the worship, as Peter did when Cornelius fell at his feet (Acts 10:25–26). The LORD gives his glory to no other (Isaiah 42:8), and here a man gives God glory at the feet of Jesus, and Jesus calls it exactly that.

A matter of direction. Jesus does not say the nine failed to feel grateful. He says nobody was found to return. Gratitude is usually discussed as a feeling, and this passage will not let it be one. All ten were presumably delighted. Only one changed course.

The root of idolatry. Paul traces the whole downward slide of humanity to exactly this: although they knew God, they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him (Romans 1:21). Ingratitude is not a small fault of manners. It is the root of idolatry, the refusal to let the Giver be seen behind the gift.

Does God really mind if I forget to say thank you? Yes, because he loves you, not because he is touchy. A father minds when his child takes his gifts and never looks up at him, not because he needs the thanks but because the child is missing the father. Thanksgiving is how a gift becomes a meeting. And the habit protects us: the heart that gives thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18) is guarded against both pride, which thinks it earned its blessings, and despair, which forgets it ever had any.

For worship. He counted to ten on that road, and he knows exactly who came back. No mercy he gives is lost in a crowd. And when one turns round, there is joy before the angels of God (15:10). The Lord who asks where the nine are rejoices over the one, and his joy, not his disappointment, is the last word on that road.

parallels.desc: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rise and go your way. He is sent home like the others, with a certificate no priest issued and a body no priest examined.

In the flow. A few verses earlier the apostles asked for more faith (v. 5) and were told that faith the size of a mustard seed is enough. Here is the proof: a Samaritan with almost nothing but a cry and an errand obeyed, and Jesus says that faith has saved him. Next, the Pharisees will ask when the kingdom of God is coming (v. 20), while the one man who has found it is a foreigner at the King’s feet.

Your faith has made you well. All ten were cleansed (vv. 14, 17), so what is left for this man to get? The answer is in the verb. For made you well the ESV margin gives has saved you: sesōken. Luke has used the phrase twice before, and both times about something more than a body: to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48). The word can mean healing or salvation, and Luke’s usage seems deliberate. Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved.

What his faith consisted of. It was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men. He obeyed an instruction that made no sense. And when he saw what had happened, he stopped, turned round, and went back to the one who did it. That is all of it. Saving faith is not a great achievement of the soul. It is an empty hand that comes back to Christ.

Can a person enjoy God’s blessings and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and this is one of the most searching truths in the Gospels. Answered prayers, a healed body, a happy family, even religious experiences: all of these can be received from God by people who never bow to his Son (Matthew 7:22–23). The test is not what you have received but whether you have come back to the Giver. If you are uncertain, do what the Samaritan did. Do not wait to feel worthy. Turn round, go to Jesus, fall at his feet and thank him, and hear him say what he said to that man.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, as though it were a datable event to be watched for. Jesus answers that it cannot be tracked by signs, because it is already in their midst in him. Then he turns to the disciples: they will long for his presence and must not chase rumours of his return, which will be as public as lightning. First, though, he must suffer. The examples of Noah and Lot show a world caught in the middle of ordinary life, and the section ends with a warning to let nothing turn the heart back.
verseByVerse.theology:
The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus, and it has not yet come in fullness. Believers live between the two comings.

Some Bibles print a verse 36 about two men in the field. It is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Luke and was probably copied in from Matthew 24:40, so modern versions put it in a footnote and keep the old numbering. Nothing has been removed.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian can genuinely leave something behind and spend the rest of his life half-turned towards it, like Lot’s wife, who got out and did not get away.

The disciples’ “Where, Lord?” is our instinct too: told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, they want the geography. The proverb about vultures tells them nothing about location, and that is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the kingdom would come. The question assumes the kingdom is a future event with a date that can be worked out, and that the people asking are in no relation to it except waiting. Many in Israel expected a visible, political kingdom, with signs announcing it: the defeat of Rome and the restoration of Israel.

In the flow. The chapter turns on verses 20–21. Up to here Jesus has taught his disciples how to live; from here to verse 37 he speaks about the end. He answers the question about when by pointing to who: the kingdom is present because the King is, and the future kingdom belongs to the King who is already here.

Not in ways that can be observed. The word is paratērēsis, used of a physician watching for symptoms or an astronomer observing the heavens: surveillance for signs. He is not saying the kingdom is invisible. He is saying it is not the kind of thing you detect by scanning for indicators, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

Here it is, or there. It is not a place you can point to on a map. Anything requiring a guide is not it.

In the midst of you. The King James renders it the kingdom of God is within you, and that has been carried off to mean something Jesus never said: that the kingdom is an inner spiritual glow native to every human heart, needing no king outside us. The Greek entos can mean within, and the ESV notes that alternative. What settles it is who Jesus is talking to: the Pharisees, men who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53–54), in whose hearts the kingdom certainly was not. So most scholars prefer in the midst of you, or among you: it is standing in the room.

The King in front of them. The kingdom is present in the person of Jesus, the King, standing among them, and in his works: if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (11:20). It is a Person they have so far managed to look straight past, and they are asking him when he is going to arrive. And the kingdom is also present wherever God reigns in human hearts, because the King has taken his throne there by his Spirit.

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Luke holds both within a few verses. It is in the midst of them, because the King is in the room; and at once Jesus turns to his disciples and speaks of the day of the Son of Man still to come (vv. 22–37). The kingdom has begun in Christ and his people, and it will be revealed in its fullness at his return. Theologians call this the already and the not yet. We live between the two comings: the King has come, won his decisive victory at the cross and the empty tomb, and reigns now from heaven; and he will come again to finish what he began, raising the dead, judging the world and making all things new.

So is the kingdom of God a political programme? No. Christians should be good citizens, work for justice and love their neighbours in public life, and the gospel has transformed whole societies. But the kingdom is not built by votes, revolutions or legislation, and it is never identical with any nation, party or movement. My kingdom is not of this world, Jesus told Pilate (John 18:36). It comes where Christ is preached and believed, and it will come in fullness only when he returns. A church that confuses the kingdom with its politics will be disappointed by every election and will lose its message in the process.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the kingdom of God is within you”; “in the midst of you” fits the setting — the King stood among them.

parallels.desc: the kingdom has come upon you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to the disciples. The audience changes. What follows is not for the Pharisees but for the men who will still be here when he is not.

One of the days of the Son of Man. A tender sentence and a bleak one. After Jesus’ departure, in times of persecution and waiting, his disciples will long for one of the days, an ordinary day of walking about with him, and they will not get it. He says so plainly.

For the believer who feels far from God. For anyone who has known a season of unusual nearness to God and now does not: the longing is not a fault, and it is not answered here with a technique for recovering the feeling. It is named, and allowed. The Lord is not absent because you cannot feel him. He has promised to be with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20), and the longing itself is a sign of his Spirit in you. Keep to the means he has given, his word, prayer, the Supper, the fellowship of his people, and wait for him. He will come.

Do not go out. That is what longing makes a person vulnerable to: a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will drive to where somebody says he has (21:8). The instruction is blunt and doubled: do not go out, and do not follow.

As the lightning flashes. And there is the test. Nobody has ever been told where the lightning was, or had to travel to see it. It fills the sky from one horizon to the other, and everybody sees it at once. His return will be sudden, visible to all, unmistakable. Every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

Anything that has to be pointed out is not it. Every claim that Christ has returned quietly, or secretly, or to a particular place or group, is refuted by one sentence about weather, issued in advance so that his people would not spend the centuries chasing rumours.

What about people who predict the date of his return? Do not follow them. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know times or seasons (Acts 1:7). Every date ever set has passed, and many who trusted them were shipwrecked in faith. The right posture is not calculation but readiness: live every day so that you would be glad to see him come that evening. Watchfulness is a way of life, not a reading of the news.

For worship. He will not come quietly. The One who was laid unnoticed in a manger and led out of the city to die between criminals will come the second time in a glory that fills the sky. The longing of every lonely disciple will be answered in a single flash, and the face they waited for will be the one thing everyone sees.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But first. Before the glory, the cross: one sentence dropped into the middle of a discourse about the end, and it changes the shape of everything around it.

He must suffer many things. Must is dei, the divine necessity that has run through this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). The suffering is not a setback on the way to the glory: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26).

Rejected by this generation. Note who does the rejecting. Not Rome, though Rome will drive the nails, but this generation: his own people, including the Pharisees he was answering a few verses ago. Luke has recorded the prediction twice already (9:22, 44).

Why put it here at all? Because the disciples have just been told about a day of unmistakable, sky-filling glory, and a man can build a very attractive religion out of that alone. Jesus will not let the second coming be detached from the first. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man who is going to be spat at, flogged, and hung up outside a city wall, and he is going to be that first. Any expectation of his return that skips the cross has the wrong person coming back.

Why must he suffer? Why could God not simply forgive? Because God is just as well as merciful, and sin is a real debt against a holy God. He cannot pretend it does not matter without ceasing to be good. At the cross the Son bore the penalty our sins deserved, so that God could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). To justify means to declare righteous, as a judge acquits: God counts the believer right with him because the penalty for his sin has been paid in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:21). He was pierced for our transgressions, and the punishment that brought us peace was laid on him (Isaiah 53:5). The must is not a cruel necessity imposed on an unwilling Son; it is the plan of the Father and the Son together, freely embraced in love for us.

In everyday life. It is possible to be thrilled by prophecy and unmoved by Calvary. If you think more often about the end of the world than about the cross, turn it round this week. Read one of the passion narratives in a single sitting, Luke 22 and 23, and ask the Spirit to move you by the suffering as much as by the glory. And if you are suffering for Christ, remember the order: first the cross, then the crown, for him and for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The days of Noah. The first of two examples, from Genesis 6–7, and Jesus treats the flood as real history. Notice what he does not say about Noah’s generation. Genesis is not gentle about them: the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually (Genesis 6:5, 11). Jesus could have made that the point. He does not.

Eating and drinking and marrying. Four activities, and not one of them is a sin: ordinary life in a village. The problem was that they were absorbed in it and ignored God’s warnings through Noah, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), living as if judgment would never come.

Until the day. The ark was probably years in the building, in public. Then one day Noah went inside, and the LORD shut him in (Genesis 7:16), and the day he went in was the day it came. Luke does not soften destroyed them all, and he uses the identical phrase about Sodom two verses later.

They were not short of warning. Noah’s generation had a preacher and a boat going up in their own neighbourhood, and they went on eating and drinking, not because they had weighed the evidence and rejected it, but because life was going on as it always had. Nobody in Noah’s village decided to drown. They simply had a normal week, and then another, until the last one.

The Son of Man in the place of the LORD. Look at whose days Jesus sets beside the flood. In Genesis it is the LORD who sees the earth’s corruption, who sends the waters, and who shuts the door of the ark (Genesis 7:16). Jesus calls the coming judgment the days of the Son of Man, his own days. He is claiming the part God played in Noah’s generation. And that is why the warning is mercy: the Judge has come first to give it himself.

Is it wrong, then, to enjoy ordinary life? No. Eating, drinking and marriage are good gifts of God, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), and Jesus himself came eating and drinking (7:34). The Christian does not escape ordinary life; he lives it before God, with an eye on the door. The difference between Noah and his neighbours was not that Noah stopped eating. It was that he believed God’s word and built accordingly. Enjoy your meals, your marriage, your work; just do not let them become a reason to ignore the one who gave them, or the day he has appointed.

In everyday life. Look at your week: is there one hour in it given to getting ready for that day? And if you know someone who is not in the ark, do what Noah did: keep building and keep preaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The days of Lot. The second example, from Genesis 19, and Jesus adds it because the first could be dismissed. Noah’s flood was at the dawn of history; Sodom was a real town, in country Jesus’ hearers could have walked to.

Buying and selling, planting and building. Six activities, and again not one is wicked: the busyness of a prosperous city with no thought of God. Two of them, planting and building, are the most hopeful things a person can do, because both invest in a future. That is what makes the list so bleak. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards and laying foundations.

What Jesus selects. Sodom was notorious for its wickedness, and Genesis records it: the city is a byword for a particular sin, and elsewhere Scripture names its pride, excess of food, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus mentions none of it. What he selects is the property market and the planting season.

The day when Lot went out. The same hinge as Noah: the rescue of the righteous and the arrival of the judgment are the same day. Genesis is explicit that the angels could do nothing until Lot was out: escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there (Genesis 19:22).

Fire and sulfur. Sudden and complete. The phrase is the same as for the flood, and the point is the same: no one in the city expected it that morning, and no one escaped who had not left.

When the Son of Man is revealed. Revealed, apokalyptetai: unveiled. He will not arrive from somewhere else, like a visitor; he is not absent now, merely unseen, reigning at the Father’s right hand. The day does not change where he is. It changes what can be seen, and the judgment will be as sudden and complete as Sodom’s.

How can a loving God destroy whole cities? Because his love is holy love, not indifference. A judge who shrugged at violence and cruelty would not be kind; he would be complicit, and the outcry against Sodom had reached heaven (Genesis 18:20–21). Even so, God did not rush. He listened to Abraham plead, and agreed to spare the whole city for the sake of ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32), and in the end he led Lot out by the hand. He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). And the Jesus who warns of the fire went to the cross so that people from the worst of cities could be spared it.

Will Christians be taken out of the world before the judgment, like Lot? Lot was rescued on the very day the fire fell, not years before it; Noah entered the ark on the day the flood came. Many faithful Christians expect a rapture before a time of tribulation, and they love the Lord’s appearing as much as anyone. But the pattern in these verses points to one public day on which his people are gathered to him and the world is judged (2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Believers are not promised escape from all suffering before that day; Jesus told them to expect tribulation (John 16:33), and they have always had it. But they are promised that not one of them will be lost when the day comes. The same Lord who took Lot by the hand will not forget a single one of his own.

In everyday life. When you sign a contract, plant a garden or plan an extension this year, add a sentence to the plan: if the Lord wills (James 4:15). It changes nothing in the paperwork and everything in the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the housetop. Roofs were flat and often reached by an outside stair, so a man on the roof can get to the street without entering the house at all. He must leave with what he is wearing.

Not this, but the end. Similar words in 21:21 and Mark 13:15–16 concern the flight from Jerusalem before its fall in AD 70. Here the point is different: on the day of Christ’s coming, there will be no time to save possessions, and no point. The pattern is the same; the event is the last. Attachment to things will be fatal.

In the field. On the day of the Son of Man nothing behind a disciple is worth a single step backwards: not even the field-worker’s instinct to go back and fetch one thing first. Jesus has already said in this Gospel that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (9:62), and this field is that plough’s furrow on its final day.

Remember Lot’s wife. One of the shortest verses in Luke. He does not tell the story; he does not need to. She had been brought out by the hand: the angels seized Lot and his wife and daughters and set them outside the city, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back to Sodom as she fled, and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26).

What her looking back was. It sounds like a small thing punished enormously, but it was probably not mere curiosity: everything she had was in that town, and to turn round was to have her heart still in it. She was out of Sodom, and Sodom was not out of her.

Half-turned. This is the warning to a disciple. You can meet a Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the relationship broken off and still visited in the imagination, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward. He is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say remember Sodom. He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

The face that was set. Luke has already shown us the opposite of Lot’s wife, and it is Jesus himself. When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and nothing on the road turned it. Lot’s wife turned back towards the place of judgment because her heart was there. Jesus walked forward into the place of judgment because his heart was with the people he came to save. She looked back and was lost; he did not look back, and the lost are saved by it.

Can a true believer be lost like Lot’s wife? No one whom Christ has truly saved will finally perish (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6); God keeps his own to the end. But that promise does not make warnings like this unnecessary. They are among the very means by which God keeps us, waking us up when our hearts drift back. Lot’s wife shows what an outward rescue without an inward change looks like: someone who left Sodom with her feet but not with her heart. If this verse troubles you, that is a mercy. Turn your face to Christ, and keep it there.

In everyday life. Name what you are tempted to look back to. Then tell God what it is, ask his Spirit to break its pull, and do one thing this week that puts it further behind you.
verseByVerse.note: Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever seeks to preserve his life. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:24). Here it follows a man on a roof told to leave his possessions and a woman remembered for looking back: the principle is the same, but the application has moved from a lifetime to a moment.

Seeks to preserve. To secure as one’s own possession. What the man on the roof and Lot’s wife are trying to keep is the shape of a life that is being taken away, and the grip is what loses the thing.

How reality is built. This is a statement about how things are, not only moral advice. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the person who cannot bear to be disliked ends up with no friendships of any weight; the man who protects his reputation above everything is eventually left with nothing but a reputation.

Whoever loses his life. Keep is zōogonēsei: preserve alive, keep living. Those who give up their lives to Christ gain eternal life: not a heroic sacrifice with nothing on the other side but the only route by which anything survives at all. The man who lets go is not choosing loss over gain; he is choosing the one grip that does not crush what it holds.

He saved others. Luke will show this sentence carried out to the letter. At the cross the rulers sneered, he saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One (23:35). Every voice at Golgotha urged him to preserve his life, and he would not; he committed even his spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). The man who refused to save himself is the reason anyone else is saved, and the one life that was wholly given up is the life that was given back on the third day.

What does losing my life look like for an ordinary Christian? Rarely martyrdom, though for some it is, and has been for millions. More often it is the daily surrender of what you would hold on to for yourself. It is choosing obedience when it costs you a promotion; telling the truth when it costs you a friend; giving away money you could have kept; opening your home when you would rather close the door; being known as a Christian at work. And at the end, it is dying in faith, letting go of everything into the hands of Christ. None of it is wasted. All of it is kept alive in him.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two in one bed. The coming of the Son of Man will divide people who were closest, outwardly the same and inwardly different.

Two women grinding. Two women at a small hand mill, sitting opposite each other, a task often done at dawn. Night and day: whenever he comes, and one of each pair is taken.

The child set for the fall and rising. What divides the two in one bed is nothing the eye can see. It is how each stands with the Son of Man. Luke announced this at the beginning, when old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said, Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel (2:34), and Jesus has said it himself: he came to bring not peace but division, even within one house (12:51–53). The separation of that night is the last unveiling of a line that already runs through households now, and he is the line.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36: Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left. The KJV includes it, but the line is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Luke and was probably copied in from the parallel in Matthew 24:40. Modern versions put it in a footnote and keep the old numbering, which is why the gap is visible in some Bibles. Nothing has been hidden, and no teaching of Scripture depends on it.

Taken and left. The verb for taken can also mean received (John 14:3), so the word alone does not settle it; the context must, and in the examples of Noah and Lot it was the judgment that did the taking (vv. 27, 29).

And they said to him, Where, Lord? Where will they be taken? And there it is: the disciples’ instinct, and ours. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want to know is the geography.

The vultures. A proverb, and it tells them nothing useful about location; the uselessness is the sermon. As certainly as vultures gather round a dead body, judgment will fall wherever there is spiritual death, as visibly as vultures circling, and nobody will have to be told where. Those taken are taken to judgment.

Where Christians differ: one taken, one left. Dispensationalists (who divide God’s dealings into distinct eras and keep Israel and the church apart) teach that one will be taken describes the secret rapture of believers before a tribulation, as in the novels and films about being left behind, reading it alongside the catching up of believers to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) and his promise to take them to himself (John 14:3). This commentary’s view: those who hold that view are brothers whose hope in Christ’s coming is real; but in context, the comparisons with Noah and Lot (vv. 26–30) show that those taken are taken in judgment, like those swept away by the flood, while those left are like Noah and Lot, spared. And the vultures (v. 37) show that being taken means death. There is no secret rapture here. Christ’s coming will be visible like lightning (v. 24), and will bring both the gathering of his people and judgment, at one public return. The point is the same on any reading: be ready. Scripture names things that will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but no date is given, and the day will come suddenly on all who are not watching.

Then what do I make of the catching up in 1 Thessalonians 4? It is real and glorious, but it is not secret. Paul describes it with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16), about as loud an event as can be imagined. At Christ’s one return the dead in Christ rise, the living believers are caught up to meet him in the air, and they come with him as he arrives in judgment, as citizens go out to meet a king and escort him into the city. Believers are not left behind, and they are not taken away years early. They are gathered to their Lord on the day the whole world sees him.

Will my believing spouse or parent save me on that day? No. Two in one bed, two at one mill: the nearest relationships on earth, and one is taken and the other left. You can sleep beside a believer, work beside one, be raised by one, and still be lost. Faith is personal: each must come to Christ himself. That is not a cold truth but an urgent invitation. If you have been sheltering under someone else’s faith, come to Christ for yourself today. And if you love someone who is not yet his, pray, and speak, while it is still today.

For worship. The same night that brings the vultures brings the Bridegroom. For those who are his there is no terror in that separation; not one of his own will be overlooked in the dark, because the Shepherd knows every one of his sheep by name. And the Judge at whose coming the earth will tremble is the Saviour who was judged in their place, so that the day which divides the world will unite his people with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36, “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” and that “vultures” may also be rendered “eagles.”

If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. 18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is built on contrasts: a persistent widow and an unjust judge; a Pharisee and a tax collector; disciples who would keep the infants away and a Jesus who receives them; a rich ruler who goes away very sad and disciples who have left everything; a blind beggar who cries out and a crowd that tells him to be quiet. In each pair the unexpected person receives, and the rule is the same: those who come to God with empty hands are filled, and those who come sure they already have what is required leave with nothing.

Luke tells us why Jesus told the opening parables: so that his disciples would always pray and not lose heart (v. 1), and as a word to those who trusted in themselves and despised others (v. 9). The chapter closes with the third passion prediction, which the Twelve cannot understand, and with a blind man who sees exactly who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke gives the point before the story starts: pray and do not lose heart, because the only alternative to persistent prayer is quitting. The parable follows a discourse about a day that comes without warning after a long wait (17:22–37); this is what to do in the meantime.

The judge neither fears God nor respects man; the widow has no husband, no money and no standing, and is exactly the person the law told him to protect. He gives her a verdict only to stop her wearing him down. The argument then runs by contrast: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a way of overcoming God’s reluctance. The judge is the contrast, not the model, and every term in verse 7 is set against him: this is God, these are his elect, and they cry to him day and night. Jesus does not hide the delay; what he denies is that it means God does not care.

Speedily does not promise a quick answer by our clocks. It means nothing is held up by reluctance at God’s end. And the elect are crying for justice, the setting right of all things, which comes in full when the Son of Man comes.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends by turning the question round. We ask whether God will keep faith with us; Jesus asks whether he will find faith in us. Justice is certain; the danger is a widow who stops coming.

There is a word here for the believer whose daily prayer has quietly collapsed, who prays in a crisis but thinks regular prayer pointless since God knows what he needs. Persistent prayer is not meant to inform God. It keeps the heart turned towards the only Source of help.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 18 is about how people come to God, and the answer is always the same: with nothing in their hands. A powerless widow, a tax collector begging for mercy, babies, and a blind beggar all receive; a self-satisfied Pharisee and a rich ruler go away with what they brought.

The link. Jesus has just spoken of days when his disciples will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man and will not see it (17:22), and of a day that will come without warning after a long wait. How should they live in the meantime? This parable answers: by prayer.

Always to pray and not lose heart. Luke gives the point before the story starts. Losing heart, enkakein, means to grow weary, to give out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting. Nobody stops praying because he has found something better to do with the time.

Neither feared God nor respected man. The Old Testament asks two things of a judge: that he fear God and that he regard the people in front of him (2 Chronicles 19:6–7). This man has neither, and Luke says so twice, once here and once in the man’s own mouth (v. 4). He is in the story to be the opposite of somebody.

The teacher who never stopped praying. The one who tells this parable is the most persistent man of prayer in Luke’s Gospel. Luke, more than any other Gospel, shows him at prayer (3:21; 5:16; 6:12; 9:29), and he will die praying (23:46). When he tells his disciples always to pray and not lose heart, he is asking them to walk a road he walked every day, and on which he never once gave up.

What does always to pray actually mean? It cannot mean doing nothing but pray, since Jesus also worked, ate, slept and taught. It means never giving up, and living in a settled habit of turning to God. Paul says the same: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). In practice that means fixed times, morning and evening, when you deliberately bring your needs and other people’s to God; short prayers through the day as things happen; and refusing to drop a request just because the answer is slow. It is not a feeling of constant devotion. It is a direction of the heart that keeps coming back.

In everyday life. Most of us do not stop praying by a decision. We drift, and one day the old request is simply no longer on our lips: the prodigal, the illness, the marriage, the salvation of a parent. This parable is Jesus coming after that drift. The request you quietly let go of is allowed back, and he is the one inviting it.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A widow. The other end of the scale. A widow in that world was the Bible’s shorthand for defencelessness: no husband to represent her, no money for a bribe, little standing in court. And the law singled her out for protection: God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18). So the one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

Kept coming. The tense means repeated, continual coming; her only weapon was persistence. The case may have been a debt, or her inheritance being stolen. She asks not for charity, leniency or revenge, but for justice: vindicate me, settle my case. She believes she is in the right, and she is asking for a verdict rather than a favour.

He said to himself. Inside his own head the judge repeats the narrator’s assessment of himself almost word for word. He knows exactly what he is and it does not trouble him, and when he gives in it is not from love of justice or compassion, but from annoyance.

Beat me down. The verb comes from the boxing ring: to give somebody a black eye. Perhaps the judge means she will wear him out, or shame him publicly. Either way he is not moved by sympathy or conscience; he gives her the verdict to make it stop. Justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, because one powerless woman would not go away.

The widows’ Lord. Luke keeps putting widows in front of Jesus, and every time he is the opposite of this judge. At Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s bier, had compassion on her, and gave the boy back to his mother (7:12–15). He will single out a poor widow’s two small coins (21:1–4) and warn against the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47). The God who executes justice for the widow has come into Israel’s towns in person, and he needs no beating down. At Nain he saw the widow before she had said a word.

Does God answer only if I nag him? No, and the next verses say so. God is not the judge. The widow had to wear down a man who did not care; you come to a Father who does. Persistence in prayer is not a technique for overcoming God’s reluctance, because he has none, and the Son who prayed through the nights on earth lives for ever to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). It is what faith looks like while it waits: it keeps coming because it believes there is Someone worth coming to. Jesus warned against heaping up empty phrases as if many words would earn a hearing (Matthew 6:7). Pray often, not because God is hard of hearing, but because you are dependent, and he loves to be asked.

In everyday life. If you are fighting a long battle for justice in this world, against an employer, a landlord, an ex-spouse, a system that will not listen, take the widow as your companion. Pursue what is right by every honest means, and bring the case to the higher court every day.
verseByVerse.note: Widows had no one to plead their case; the law singled them out for protection.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear what the unrighteous judge says. Jesus tells them to listen to the villain. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater, like the father who gives good gifts (11:13), and such arguments work by contrast, not comparison. God is not the unjust judge; he is his opposite in every particular. The parable does not say God is reluctant, so keep pestering him. It says: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.

Will not God give justice. Every term is set against the judge. He had no fear of God; this is God. He is just, and he cares. The widow was a stranger to him; these are his elect, eklektōn, his chosen ones, the people he has bound himself to, against whom no charge can stand because God himself justifies them (Romans 8:33).

Chosen in the Chosen One. Luke uses the word elect sparingly, and its centre is not us. On the mountain the Father’s voice said of Jesus, This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (9:35). The elect are chosen in that Chosen One, loved with the love the Father has for his Son. Their cry is heard because it comes through him, and their vindication is sure because his was: the one the rulers mocked as a Chosen One who could not save himself (23:35) was raised and seated at the Father’s right hand.

Who cry to him day and night? She was a nuisance at his door; they cry to him day and night, which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile. And the verb for their crying is a strong one. This is not the recitation of a list. It is the sound people make when something is badly wrong and they know who to shout at. It is the persistent prayer of God’s people, suffering in a hostile world, longing for justice and for Christ’s return, the cry of the martyrs under the altar: how long, O Lord (Revelation 6:10).

Will he delay long over them? Or: will he be patient with them, or keep them waiting? The question is put to be answered, and Jesus raises the delay himself. He does not pretend it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming for a long time and elect who are crying day and night, which is to say, the waiting is written into the story. What is being denied is not the delay but its meaning. The widow’s problem was that her judge did not care. That was the reason for her wait, and it was the only reason. Jesus is telling people whose prayers have gone unanswered for years that whatever the reason for their wait, it is not that one, because the one they are asking chose them. God is patient (2 Peter 3:9), but he will not abandon his people.

What does elect mean, and why mention it here? The elect are those God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them but out of sheer love (Ephesians 1:4–5). Many Christians, often called Arminian, understand election as God choosing those he foresaw would believe; Reformed churches, with this commentary, read Ephesians 1 as resting it on his free love alone, and both find in it a reason to pray with confidence. Jesus mentions it here as the strongest possible ground for confident prayer. You do not have to wonder whether God is interested in you. He set his love on you before you existed, and the One who chose you will not ignore you now. Election is not a puzzle to make you anxious; it is a pillow for a weary pray-er. If you are crying to him day and night for his justice and his kingdom, that cry is itself the mark of his chosen.
verseByVerse.note: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge acts, how much more God.

parallels.desc: I cry out day and night before you

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Speedily. Here is the word that snags on real life: en tachei, quickly, or suddenly. Many have prayed for the same thing for a decade or more. The promise does not promise a quick answer by our clocks; with the Lord one day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8). It means that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And when justice comes, at Christ’s return, it will come suddenly.

What the elect are crying for. The elect are asking not for relief but for justice, which is precisely what arrives at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line, when the one who was denied justice in Pilate’s court returns as Judge. Some prayers are answered in this life. Every prayer of God’s people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.

Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come to a passage like this asking whether God will keep faith with us. He settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us. In Greek the word has the article, the faith, which points to the particular faith the parable has just shown: persistent, praying faith like the widow’s. Will his people still be praying, still trusting, when he returns, or will they have given up? The question is not answered. It is put to each reader, and that is more unsettling than any answer would have been. The nevertheless is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is set before them as a question. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address. The risk here is not an unanswering God. It is a widow who stops coming.

Does this mean true believers might lose their faith? No. Scripture is clear that those whom God has truly called he keeps to the end (John 6:39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). But he keeps them through means, and one of those means is exactly a searching question like this. The warning is not meant to make the elect doubt their election. It is meant to keep them praying. A believer who hears it and says, Lord, keep me faithful, is doing what the question was asked to produce. The ones who finally fall away show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The ones who keep crying day and night are the faith he will find.

For the one who has prayed for years. If you are still praying after many years, and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

For worship. The Son of Man is coming, and when he comes he is looking for something. He is looking for faith: the widow still knocking, the old saint still praying for her grandchildren, the persecuted church still crying how long. And the faith he looks for is the faith he gives, kept alive by the Spirit he sends and the intercession he makes. He is the Author of our faith and he will be its Finisher (Hebrews 12:2). When he comes, he will find what he planted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke names the target first: some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and treated others with contempt. The two belong together: a righteousness that must be kept up needs other people beneath you.

The pairing is as wide as the day allowed: a serious, respected keeper of the law and a man who collected taxes for the occupying power from his own people. The Pharisee’s claims are probably true and go beyond what the law required. His problem is not insincerity but trust in himself and contempt for the man behind him.
verseByVerse.theology: Here, in a parable, is justification by faith alone. The tax collector brings nothing but his need: no promise of reform, no record, no favourable comparison. He asks God to be merciful on the only terms the temple knew, sin dealt with by sacrifice, the propitiation Paul will name in Christ (Romans 3:25). And he goes home justified, declared right with God by a verdict entered in his favour by somebody else.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Pharisee’s religion needed somebody underneath him: he looked round the courtyard, found the tax collector, and put him in the prayer. The same thing can happen in any church.

In a small group one man shares requests that are articulate, theologically careful and mostly about what he is doing for God. A woman prays, Lord, I do not know what to say; I am a mess; have mercy. Prayer is not measured by eloquence but by honesty about need, and one of those two is much closer to going home justified.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: 'Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second prayer parable. The first parable was about persistence in prayer; this one is about humility, and it is one of the clearest pictures of justification in the Gospels.

Trusted in themselves. Again Luke names the target first: trusting in one’s own goodness to be right with God. A righteousness that has to be maintained needs a scale, and a scale needs other people on it.

Treated others with contempt. The verb means despised, counted as nothing, and it follows from the first clause as effect from cause. The contempt is not a personality trait; the position generates it. A man who is sure of himself by comparison needs somebody to be worse. And Luke does not say to the Pharisees but to some who: a description rather than a party.

The friend of sinners. The posture Jesus is exposing is the one he met wherever he went (15:2; 7:34). The contempt that looked down on the tax collector fell, sooner or later, on the one who sat beside him. Luke uses the same verb for Herod and his soldiers, who treated Jesus with contempt and mocked him (23:11). The Son of God took his place among the despised, and was despised with them, so that the despised could be received by God.

Two men went up. Probably at the hours of prayer, the morning or afternoon sacrifice, when people gathered to pray (Acts 3:1), with the sacrifice being offered and a crowd in the court. It puts them in the same place at the same time.

A Pharisee and a tax collector. The pairing is as wide as first-century Judaism could make it. A Pharisee was not a hypocrite in the popular sense but a serious man who organised his life around the whole law, by any ordinary measure the best sort of person available. A tax collector extracted money from his own people for the occupying power and lived on what he could collect above the assessment (3:12). Everybody listening knows which of them is going home right with God, which is why the last verse detonates.

Who are the Pharisees today? Not a group you can point to across the street. The Pharisee is the person in any church who trusts in his own record and measures himself against others, and he is very often the person reading this. The trap is that reading this parable can produce a new kind of Pharisee: God, I thank you that I am not like that Pharisee. The parable is aimed not at a party but at a posture of the heart, and the only safe place to stand while reading it is where the tax collector stood.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were respected for their devotion to the law; tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats. Public prayers were offered at the temple morning and afternoon.

parallels.desc: the hour of prayer, the ninth hour

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing by himself. The Greek can mean that he stood apart, so as not to be defiled by others, or that he prayed to himself. What is certain is the content, and the content settles the question without any help from the grammar.

God, I thank you. The opening is correct; it begins exactly as a good prayer should. But he thanks God for himself, not for God’s mercy. He asks for nothing; he does not think he needs anything. He says I five times in two verses.

Another thanksgiving. Luke has already recorded a very different prayer that began the same way. When the seventy-two came back, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (10:21). The two prayers open with the same words and face opposite ways: one looks up in delight at what God gives the small, the other looks down in satisfaction at what he has made of himself.

Not like other men. Then it turns into a list of other people: he compares himself with notorious sinners, and of course comes off well.

This tax collector. Four categories, and the fourth is standing in the same courtyard. He has looked, identified him, and put him in the prayer with contempt.

I fast twice a week. The law required only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Strict Pharisees fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. He did more than required.

Tithes of all. The tithe was on agricultural produce; he tithes everything that passes through his hands, probably including produce he had bought, which the grower should already have tithed (compare 11:42). This is not fraud; he is doing more than God asked.

The problem. He was probably telling the truth about his outward life, and that is what makes the parable so uncomfortable. His problem was not insincerity, and not his deeds, but his heart: he trusted in them, compared himself with others rather than with God, and despised sinners. He came to the temple with a credit balance, and he left with it, which is the one thing you cannot do anything with at that address.

Is it wrong to thank God that I am not living in some sin? Not in itself. If God has kept you from drunkenness or adultery, that is his grace, and you should thank him for it. The difference is where the thanks points. Grateful humility says: but for the grace of God, there go I, and it makes you gentler with the fallen. The Pharisee’s thanks said: look at me, and it made him harder. If your thanksgiving ends with you feeling superior to someone, it has turned into the Pharisee’s prayer. Paul, who could list more virtues than this man (Philippians 3:4–6), counted them all as loss, and called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

For worship. There is only one Man who could have prayed the Pharisee’s prayer honestly: I am not like other men. Jesus was holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). And he never once prayed it. Instead he was baptised in the line of sinners and numbered with the transgressors. The only one with a true credit balance gave it away to men with nothing, and went to the cross with our debts on his account.
verseByVerse.note: The law required only one yearly fast (the Day of Atonement); the Pharisee fasted twice a week and tithed even what the law did not require.

verseByVerse.quote: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing far off. Everything about him is measured in distance: as far into the court as he judged himself entitled to come. The two men are alone in the same building for opposite reasons.

Would not even lift up his eyes. The normal posture for prayer was standing, looking up, with hands raised. He cannot do the ordinary thing: O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you (Ezra 9:6).

Beat his breast. Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse, and it seems to have been unusual for a man in that culture: it belonged chiefly to mourning, to funerals. Luke will record it once more, from the crowd walking home from Golgotha (23:48). He beats his heart, the source of his sin.

Be merciful to me. Six words in Greek, and the whole gospel in a prayer. Be merciful, hilasthēti, is not the ordinary word for mercy. It means be propitiated, and belongs with the word for the mercy seat, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled (Hebrews 9:5; Romans 3:25). Propitiation means the turning away of God’s just anger against sin by a sacrifice that meets it. The wonder of the gospel is that the offended God provides the sacrifice himself: he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). He is not asking God to overlook anything. He is asking God to accept the atoning sacrifice on his behalf and turn away his wrath, and he asks it standing in the temple, very possibly at the hour when a lamb was being offered.

The sinner. He does not say a sinner but the sinner, as if he were the only one, which is what a man says when he has stopped comparing. The Pharisee could see four categories of people and himself above them. This man cannot see anybody else in the building. He brings nothing but his need.

What he does not say. He offers no undertaking. No promise to leave the profession, no schedule of restitution, all of which he might have thought were the price of being heard. He asks for mercy and stops talking.

So does repentance not involve change? It does, and the change will come; Zacchaeus, another tax collector, will give back fourfold in the next chapter (19:8). But the change is the fruit of mercy, not its price. A man does not clean himself up in order to come to God; he comes to God to be cleaned. If you are waiting until you have sorted yourself out before you pray this prayer, you have reversed the gospel. Come as you are, with the prayer of the sinner, and let the God who justifies you begin to make you new.

For worship. The tax collector asked God to be propitiated, and God answered him, though not with anything on that day’s altar. The true Mercy Seat was walking towards Jerusalem while the parable was told. Every sinner who beats his breast and asks for mercy is asking for the cross, and the cross has already been given. No prayer has ever been surer of an answer than a sinner’s plea for what God has already provided.
verseByVerse.note: Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Went down to his house justified. A verdict on Jesus’ own authority. Justified is a courtroom word: declared right with God, acquitted. Not made morally perfect, but declared righteous by God the Judge, and the perfect tense means it is done and it stands. A man who had defrauded his neighbours for a living walked out of that temple with a standing before God that the most religious man in the country did not have, having offered nothing except an accurate description of himself and a request for mercy.

Rather than the other. Not more than. The Pharisee was not justified. All his good works did not make him right with God, because he trusted in them. He went home exactly as he arrived, which is the quiet tragedy of the parable: nothing happened to him at all.

The doctrine of justification. Here, some twenty years before Paul wrote a word about it, is the doctrine he would set out: a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28), and God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). The tax collector contributes nothing, and receives a verdict.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification is a process in which God makes us inwardly righteous by infusing grace, received through baptism and increased by good works and the sacraments; it can be lost through mortal sin and restored through penance. This commentary’s view: the Reformers rightly taught that justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed (credited) to him, received by faith alone (Romans 4:3–8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). The tax collector went home justified that day, at once, not after a long process of becoming righteous. Good works follow as the fruit of justification, never as its ground.

Is it fair that the fraud goes home justified and the decent man does not? It would be unfair if justification were a prize for the best life, but it was never that. It is a pardon, and a pardon can only be received by someone who admits he needs one. The Pharisee was not turned away for being too good; he received nothing because he asked for nothing. And the tax collector was not let off lightly. His sin would be paid for in full, by the Son of God on the cross (Romans 3:25–26). Grace never pretends the standard is lower than it is. At the cross God meets it in full himself, for anyone, decent or not, who stops pretending.

Can I be sure I am justified? Yes. Justification is not a feeling that comes and goes or a grade that rises and falls with your performance; it is God’s verdict, and God does not revise his verdicts. If you have come to him as the tax collector did, with nothing but your sin and his mercy in Christ, you went home justified too, and nothing can bring a charge against you (Romans 8:33–34). Your sense of it may waver, especially when you sin; then go back and pray the same prayer, and remember that the verdict rests on Christ’s righteousness, not yours, and his does not waver.

Everyone who exalts himself. The principle of 14:11, and the passive verbs leave God unnamed as the one who does the humbling and the lifting.

Humility that is not a technique. The saying needs one guard, because it can be turned into a technique.
