A man who humbles himself in order to be exalted has exalted himself, and the sentence has already seen him. The tax collector was not performing humility. He was telling the truth, and it happened to be devastating, which is the only humility that has ever done anybody any good.

The one who went lowest. The saying has one perfect fulfilment, and it is Christ, who did not humble himself as a technique either. Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6–9). The tax collector goes down to his house lifted up because the Son went further down than any sinner, and was raised higher than every name.
verseByVerse.note: “Justified” means declared right with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke’s word is infants: babies in arms, whose parents want only that Jesus should touch them. The disciples are protecting his diary, and Jesus will not have it.

The verb for hinder, kōluein, is used again in Luke’s second volume when the Ethiopian asks what prevents him from being baptised (Acts 8:36): it is the word for keeping out someone who should be let in. The kingdom belongs to such, not because children are innocent, but because an infant has nothing to bring and can only be carried and received.
verseByVerse.theology:
Does this passage support the baptism of infants? Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus blesses children who can offer nothing and declares the kingdom theirs, and that God has dealt with families since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Those who baptise only believers answer that Jesus blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism in Acts follows a profession of faith. That second point is the weightier, and the believer’s-baptism view is the better reading (see on Acts 2:39), held charitably towards brothers who differ. This verse alone will not settle the question.

What it does say, with force, is what both sides agree on: no one enters the kingdom by contributing, and every adult comes in on the same terms as the baby in his mother’s arms.
verseByVerse.examples:
The crowd will use the same verb of rebuke against a blind beggar later in this chapter (v. 39). Twice in one chapter the people nearest Jesus try to clear his road of those with nothing to offer, and twice he overrules them.

When a family brings a newborn into church and asks for prayer, this passage gives the content: the child is being brought to Jesus, as these infants were, and his posture is welcome, not reluctance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The placing. Here Luke rejoins the order Mark follows (Mark 10:13), and the story fits after the tax collector: the kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing, like children.

Even infants. Luke’s word is brephē: not children generally but babies, infants in arms (compare 1:41). Matthew and Mark use the broader term.

That he might touch them. To bless them, as Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing. Luke tells us nothing about the parents except what they wanted, and what they wanted was contact: a conviction that whatever was in this man was worth getting their children within arm’s length of.

They rebuked them. It is easy to be hard on the disciples, but it was not cruelty. The pressure on him is enormous and the time visibly short (17:25), and a queue of mothers has formed with babies who cannot understand a word. The disciples are protecting his diary. But the verb for their rebuke is a strong one, used of Jesus silencing a demon (4:35), and they are about to be corrected in front of the parents.

The judgment that never feels like a fault. The people with no standing and nothing to contribute are still the ones edged out of the schedule, not by hard men but by conscientious ones with a great deal to get through. Children in a church service, the elderly, the disabled: it is easy to treat them as interruptions to the real ministry. Jesus treats them as the ministry.

The baby who became the one they came to. Luke’s word carries its own wonder. He used it of the baby Jesus wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (2:12, 16), and weeks later that baby was carried into the temple and lifted into old Simeon’s arms (2:28). Now the one who was carried in as a baby is the one to whom babies are carried. The Son of God passed through infancy on purpose, and so infancy is not a waiting-room outside his concern; it is ground he has walked.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus called them to him, saying, 'Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus called them to him. He calls them, the children, or possibly the parents; the wording allows either, and it hardly matters, since one comes with the other.

Do not hinder them. This is the language used when somebody is being kept out who should be let in. Nothing must stand between a child and Jesus.

To such belongs the kingdom. Not the kingdom is like them, and not they may come in later. It belongs to them, and to such widens it past these particular babies to everyone of that kind: dependent, helpless, receiving as a gift.

Come to me. Look where Jesus places the door of the kingdom. He does not say to God, or to the temple, or to the teachers of the law, but to me, and in the same breath he gives them the kingdom. Coming to Jesus and receiving God’s kingdom are, on his own lips, one movement. Moses and John the Baptist pointed beyond themselves; Jesus points to himself, and calls the smallest people in the land to the place where the kingdom is given.

Like a child. The reason is not what sentiment expects. Children are not held up as innocent; anyone who has raised one knows better, and Scripture nowhere claims it (Psalm 51:5). What an infant in that world had was nothing: no legal standing, no achievements, no capacity to give anything back. It can only be carried and received. To receive the kingdom like a child is to receive it with no credentials, no negotiating position, and nothing whatever to bring.

Between the tax collector and the ruler. The kingdom is received, not achieved, and this paragraph sits exactly between a tax collector who had nothing and a ruler who had a great deal, and the ruler is about to ask what must I do, one verse after Jesus has said that the kingdom belongs to people who cannot do anything.

Where Christians differ: does this passage support infant baptism? This is one of the texts most often brought to the question, and honestly it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it. Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them, and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that he blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith. This commentary’s view: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, but does not mention baptism and cannot settle that question. The New Testament pattern of baptism following repentance and faith fits the credobaptist position, baptism for those who profess faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12), held charitably. The text will not carry the whole argument alone. What it does say, with force, is the thing both sides agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing, and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother’s arms. Brothers who baptise their infants do so out of a sincere desire to bring their children to Christ, and they are honoured here.

What of little children who die? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no explicit promise. But Luke’s own scene gives good ground for hope: these are infants who could profess nothing, and Jesus says the kingdom belongs to such. David, burying a baby son, said he would go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and Abraham’s question still stands: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25). The Westminster Confession (10.3) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3) both state that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases. Salvation is still by grace through Christ alone; but grieving parents may entrust their child to the one who called little ones to himself, and many believers have found in this very verse the strength to bury a baby with hope. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35); grief like this is not a failure of faith, and he does not hurry it.

How do we bring our children to Jesus today? Pray for them and with them, every day, from before they can understand. Read the Bible to them and tell them the stories of Jesus. Bring them to church, and let them see you love it. Live the gospel in front of them, including saying sorry when you sin against them. Talk naturally about God at the table and in the car (Deuteronomy 6:7). And when they come to trust Christ, as you pray they will, do not tell them they are too young to mean it. Their faith may be small and simple; so is everybody’s, at first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A rich and respected ruler asks a sincere question, but its shape is the problem: what must I do to inherit? It comes one verse after Jesus has said the kingdom belongs to infants. Jesus points him to commandments that are all from the second table and outwardly checkable, and the ruler has kept them. But the first commandment and the tenth have been left out, and verse 22 applies them: his wealth has his heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus is not prescribing poverty for every disciple; he does not say this to Zacchaeus (19:8–9) or to the women who supported him from their means (8:3). He is testing this man at the one point where the first commandment would cost him.

The crowd’s dismay (then who can be saved?) shows they assumed wealth was a sign of God’s favour. Jesus grants that salvation is impossible for anyone, rich or poor, and then names a different actor: what is impossible with man is possible with God. That sentence is the pivot of the chapter.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter’s we have left our homes is better heard as a question than a boast. The answer is generous, but it is qualified: for the sake of the kingdom of God, which is no licence for abandoning a family (1 Timothy 5:8). What is returned in this life usually comes in a different currency, the homes and brothers and sisters of the church, and Mark adds, with persecutions (Mark 10:30).

A church member may serve faithfully on every committee and give generously, and still have one area he has never let Christ touch. The ruler was exemplary by most measures. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler. After the infants who receive comes a man who wants to achieve. A ruler is a man of official standing, perhaps a synagogue leader; Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), and he was rich (v. 23). Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap. Whatever is wrong here, insincerity is not it.

Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? But listen to the shape of the sentence, because the whole problem is in it. It is the lawyer’s question (10:25), a doing-word and a receiving-word in one breath. He thinks of eternal life as something to be earned. And an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. Jesus does not deny that he is good or that he is God; he makes the ruler weigh his own word. Either it was flattery, or he has said far more than he intended. And if only God is good, then the ruler is not good either. (See Mark 10:18 for the fuller answer.)

Is Jesus denying that he is good, or that he is God? Neither. The title is true: Jesus is good because he is God, without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His question presses the man to think about what he is saying: if only God is good, and you call me good, what do you think I am? Jesus is not denying his own goodness or deity, but challenging the ruler’s shallow understanding of goodness. And there is a reason he starts here rather than answering the question. A man who hands out the word good that easily has a scale on which the word can be applied to people, and he is standing somewhere on it. Everything that follows is going to be about where.
verseByVerse.note: Luke calls him a ruler; Matthew adds that he was young.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments. Jesus teaches him nothing new; he points him to the law the man already knows.

The list. Five commandments, all from the second table, governing how a man treats his neighbour, and all observable. What is missing is the first table: nothing about other gods, idols, the name or the Sabbath. And nothing about the tenth, you shall not covet, the one commandment that is entirely interior and cannot be verified by anybody. That is where the ruler’s problem lies: his wealth is his god (Exodus 20:3), and he covets. The omission will be filled in at verse 22.

All these I have kept. Sincere, and outwardly perhaps true, and Jesus takes the claim seriously; nothing in the passage suggests the man is lying. By any measure a community could apply, this is an exemplary man, and that is why the passage is uncomfortable. The ruler is not a warning about scandalous living. He is a warning about a life that passes every test a person can be set, and a man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

Another boy who kept the law. Luke has shown us one youth of whom the claim was simply true. At twelve the boy Jesus went down to Nazareth and was submissive to his parents (2:51). He honoured his father and mother as no son ever has, and loved his Father in heaven with his whole heart. The ruler’s record was real by every outward test; Christ’s was real by every test, the heart’s included. The one man who could truly say all these I have kept was standing in front of the man who said it.

Was the ruler really blameless? Only by outward measure. He has not understood how deep the law goes: to the heart. No one keeps the law as God requires (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–11), and Jesus had taught that anger and lust break the commandments (Matthew 5:21–28). He has never seen himself as a sinner, unlike the tax collector. Jesus is not offering law-keeping as the road to eternal life; he is using the law to show the man his need. His next words expose that his wealth was his god (v. 22), and the answer comes at verses 26 and 27: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

Why does Jesus point him to the law, if no one is saved by keeping it? Because the law is the mirror that shows us our need of a Saviour. Through the law comes knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20), and the law was our guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he is healthy will not go to a doctor, so the Physician first shows him his disease. That is still how God brings people to Christ: the commandments, rightly understood, strip away every claim of our own and leave us looking for mercy. The ruler had measured himself by what he could see and had not yet found his limit. It is about to be located for him with a single sentence.

In everyday life. Take the tenth commandment this week, you shall not covet, and watch your heart for seven days. You will find out quickly that you have not kept all these from your youth, and you will find yourself where the tax collector stood, which is the best place to be: he went home justified.

For worship. Christ’s perfect obedience was not kept for himself. Every commandment he honoured, first table and second, outward and inward, from the manger to the cross, is counted to everyone who trusts him. His record becomes ours. The ruler offered his own righteousness and was found wanting; the believer offers nothing but Christ, and is found complete in him (Colossians 2:10). The law that sent one rich man away sad has been satisfied on our behalf by the only man who ever kept it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One thing you still lack. It sounds like a small balance on an otherwise settled account. It is not: the one thing is the whole thing. His wealth had his heart, and he had broken the first commandment.

Sell all that you have. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing this man loved more than God. It is not a universal rule for disciples. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8–9), nor to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3), nor to Martha, whose house he was glad of. What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses ago, has just been applied. You shall have no other gods before me, and the man is being asked to show that he has none, in the one area where it would cost him. It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

Treasure in heaven. Not a loss, but an exchange (12:33). Everything he gives up is banked where moth and rust do not destroy.

Come, follow me. The real goal. This is not mainly a command about money; it is a call to discipleship with an obstacle removed first. In the place of the idol Jesus does not add a further rule; he names himself. The whole heart that the first commandment claims for God, Jesus claims as the one to be followed, because to follow him is to have God as God. Eternal life is not found in the selling. It is found in the Person the selling would free him to follow.

Very sad. Perilypos is strong: deeply grieved. He does not argue; he understood exactly what was offered and what it cost. He wanted eternal life, but not more than his money. Luke leaves him standing there, sad, in front of Jesus. The contrast is with the tax collector, with the disciples who left everything (5:11, 28), and with Zacchaeus, who will give half his goods away (19:8).

Must I sell everything to follow Jesus? Not necessarily, as Zacchaeus and Mary and Martha show. But you must be willing to, and you must give up whatever Jesus puts his finger on. For one person it is money; for another a relationship, a career, a reputation, a grudge, a habit. The question is not whether you have possessions but whether they have you. Ask: if Jesus asked for it today, would you be sad, like the ruler, or glad, like the man who sold all he had to buy the field with the treasure (Matthew 13:44)? Whatever you cannot give up has become your god, and Jesus loves you too much to leave it there.

For worship. Mark records that Jesus looked at this man and loved him (Mark 10:21), and he asked for everything because he was offering everything. The one who said sell all that you have had already done it. He became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and at the end was stripped even of his clothes (23:34). He gave up all he had to purchase a people, and they are his treasure. Whatever he asks of us, he has already outgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, seeing that he had become sad. The words that follow are spoken over a grieving man still standing in front of him, by the one who would weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the things that make for peace (19:41–42). The Lord who will not lower the price takes no pleasure in the man’s refusal. He tells the truth about riches with sorrow in his face, which is the only way the truth about riches has ever been told well.

How difficult it is. It is not that wealth is wicked, or that God objects to comfort. It is that this kingdom is entered with empty hands, and wealth is the most effective device ever invented for keeping them full. A rich man’s difficulty is not that he loves money more than a poor man does; that is often untrue. It is that his life is arranged so that he never has to depend on anybody, and the kingdom is entered only by people who have run out of alternatives.

A camel through a needle. The image is deliberately absurd: the largest animal in the land, the smallest opening in common life. It is comic exaggeration, and the sentence means what it appears to mean: impossible.

Two softenings to set aside. One softening says the eye of the needle was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall; there is no evidence that any such gate existed, and the story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. Another reads rope for camel, as a few late manuscripts do, but a rope will not go through a needle either. The needle’s eye is not too small for a camel because God is stingy about the entrance. It is exactly the right size for a person carrying nothing.

Is the camel me? By any global standard, almost everybody reading this is the camel. If you have a roof, more than one set of clothes, food for tomorrow, a phone in your pocket and some money put by, you are among the wealthiest people who have ever lived. So the danger in this verse is not for someone else. It is for you. The safeguard is not guilt but generosity and dependence: holding everything with an open hand, giving freely, and praying for daily bread as if you had none in the cupboard.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who heard it said, Then who can be saved? The reaction is not what a modern reader expects. We hear hard for a rich man and think: yes, wealth is a spiritual danger. They concluded that nobody could be saved at all, because they shared an assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16: that prosperity was evidence of God’s approval. The rich had the means to give alms, to keep the law without economic pressure, to be visibly blessed. If they cannot be saved, who can?

The right question. The question is despairing and logical, and it is at last the right one, because it no longer begins with what I must do. The ruler asked what must I do? The crowd asks who can be saved? Passive, and with no candidate in mind.

Possible with God. One sentence, and it is the gospel. He grants the whole objection: salvation is humanly impossible, for anyone, rich or poor. The camel does not get smaller and the needle does not get wider. What he adds is a different actor. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish: by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through.

The pivot of the chapter. Everything before this has been preparing for it. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did it. The infants could not come; they were carried. And a rich man cannot enter the kingdom, and God can put him there. Salvation, on this account, is not a difficult thing made possible by effort. It is an impossible thing done by somebody else.

How God does the impossible. Luke shows the answer in two steps, and both are Christ. A few verses on, Jesus tells the Twelve that he will be handed over, mocked, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day (vv. 31–33): that is the price of the impossible. And a chapter later a rich chief tax collector hears that today salvation has come to his house (19:9–10). What is possible with God arrives as the Son of Man, walking in through a rich man’s front door on his way to die.

If salvation is God’s work, what part do I play? You repent and believe; but even that is his gift working in you. Faith is not your contribution that God rewards; it is the empty hand with which you receive what he gives. God does not drag people into the kingdom against their will; he changes the will, so that they come freely and gladly (John 6:44; Philippians 2:13). The Bible calls this the new birth, or regeneration: God gives a new heart that wants what the old one refused (Ezekiel 36:26; John 3:3–8). That is why no one in heaven will boast, and why you can pray with real hope for the hardest person you know. If God can bring a camel through a needle, he can save your brother.

In everyday life. Think of the person you have privately given up on. Possible with God is written over him too, and over every prayer you still pray for him. And when you look at your own heart and despair of ever changing, read the same sentence over yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have left our homes. It is easy to hear this as boasting, but Peter has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions, and his sentence is less a claim to merit than a question with the question mark missing: we did it; is it all right? And our homes is understated. Luke has recorded what they left: boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

House or wife. Only Luke includes wife (also 14:26). Peter was married (4:38), and his wife later travelled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Leaving here means putting the kingdom first, sometimes literally leaving family behind for mission.

The Son who made a new family. Jesus asks nothing here he has not lived. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58). When his mother and brothers came and could not reach him for the crowd, he said, my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21). He left his home to make a household. The many times more that he promises is the family he himself gathered, brothers and sisters drawn round him to hear the word, and every convert who loses a home finds a place at his table.

For the sake of the kingdom of God. The qualifying phrase matters: this is not a licence for abandoning a family, and Scripture elsewhere rules out the reading that would make this an excuse for neglect: a man who will not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

Many times more in this time. Something is returned now, though not usually in the same currency. Mark names houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30): a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. But Mark adds two words Luke omits: with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable.

In the age to come. The answer to the ruler’s question (v. 18), and what he was left without. Those who give up everything for Christ gain eternal life, not as a wage for leaving but as the inheritance of those who have found the treasure worth more than everything else.

What if following Christ has cost me my family? Then this promise is for you in particular, and Jesus knew exactly what he was saying. Many converts from other religions, and some from secular families, are cut off by parents or spouses for their faith. The church is meant to be the answer: real homes opened, real meals shared, real brothers and sisters who stand with you at weddings and funerals. If you are such a believer, tell your church what you have lost; and if you are a member of a church, look for such believers and become their family. Keep praying for those who rejected you. Many have later come to faith themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third and fullest passion prediction is the only one that grounds the events in what the prophets wrote; the cross is not a disaster overtaking a good plan but Scripture being fulfilled. It is new, too, in naming the Gentiles, and much of what it lists is humiliation rather than pain.

The Twelve understand none of it, and Luke says so three times. Then, outside Jericho, a blind beggar who has heard one sentence from a stranger calls Jesus Son of David, the first person in this Gospel to say it aloud. Those in front tell him to be quiet; he cries out all the more, as the widow at the start of the chapter would have done.
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus left Jericho, Luke as he drew near, and Matthew has two blind men where the others have one. There were two Jerichos in the first century, about a mile apart, and a traveller between them was leaving one and approaching the other: a likely explanation rather than a proven one. Differences left unsmoothed are what honest reports look like.
verseByVerse.examples:
The slowness of the Twelve is a comfort to anyone who has read a passage many times and seen nothing: understanding came only when the risen Christ opened the Scriptures and their minds (24:27, 45).

Then Jesus stopped. On the last stretch to Jerusalem, having just described what waits for him there, he halts for a beggar the crowd wanted silenced, asks him to name his need, and gives him his sight. The first road the man walks with working eyes is the road to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third passion prediction. The last and fullest of his formal announcements (9:22, 44; compare 17:25), and he takes the Twelve aside to give it. What follows is not for the crowd.

Going up to Jerusalem. Jerusalem sits high, and pilgrims always went up to it; but the word carries more here, because Luke has had his face set that way since 9:51. This is the last stretch.

In the flow. The prediction comes straight after the promise of many times more and eternal life (v. 30): now he shows what those gifts will cost, and who will pay. Chapters 22 to 24 will carry out every word.

Everything that is written. Only Luke adds this: not this will happen, but everything written will be brought to completion. What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan but a text being fulfilled, Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and much more, and Jesus will explain it after his resurrection, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (24:25–27, 44–46).

Delivered over to the Gentiles. To Pilate and the Roman soldiers. Handed to Rome, which is new information; the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

Shamefully treated. Insulted, outraged, abused. Isaiah’s Servant did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6), and the psalmist is mocked (Psalm 22:7–8). Much of the list is about humiliation rather than pain, and every item happened (22:63; 23:11, 36; Mark 14:65).

Flogging. Roman scourging, with whips weighted with bone and metal, then crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels.

On the third day. The promise of resurrection, as in the first prediction (9:22). Whenever he lays out the whole road, he does not stop at the grave.

The turn in the verbs. Every verb in this list is passive or has somebody else as its subject: things done to a man who is not doing anything. And then the last clause turns: he will rise. Active, and his own. Everything up to the grave happens to him; the thing after it is something he does.

If he knew all this, why did he go? Because he chose to. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). Luke shows it from start to finish: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), prayed in the garden, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42), and on the cross committed his own spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). He went up to Jerusalem not as a victim caught by events but as the Lamb walking to the altar, because the Father’s will and his own love were one. He knew every blow in advance and went anyway, for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2): the joy of bringing many sons to glory (2:10). The prophecy is not a fate he was trapped in; it is a promise he came to keep.

In everyday life. Read Isaiah 53 this week, and then Luke 23, and mark every place where the one fulfils the other. Let the precision of it steady your faith: the God who kept these promises to the letter will keep every promise he has made to you.

verseByVerse.quote: But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They understood none. Three statements of the same fact in one verse: they did not understand, it was hidden, they did not grasp. Jesus has just given six specific things, in plain language, and twelve men who had been with him through his whole ministry took in nothing.

Hidden from them. A passive verb that leaves the one acting unnamed, as at 9:45: it points to God, and the hiding was for a time. The same Gospel ends with the risen Christ himself lifting it, when he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). The cross is not explained by those who stand near it. It is explained by the one who hung on it, from the far side of the grave.

They did not grasp it. What was blocking them was not stupidity. They had a settled picture of what Messiah meant, with no room in it for a crucifixion, and the words found nowhere to lodge. That is how most misunderstanding of Scripture works: a frame that will not accommodate the sentence, invisible to the person holding it.

A mercy to the reader. These men would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony: the early church would hardly invent a story in which its founders were told in advance and understood not a word.

Why do I read the Bible and sometimes get nothing from it? The disciples heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity. It arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45). So keep reading, and pray before you read: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Ask what frame you might be bringing that the text does not fit. Read with others, and sit under preaching. The Spirit who wrote the word is the one who gives light to it, and he delights to answer that prayer, often in a quiet moment long after the reading.

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he drew near to Jericho. Jericho lay some 15 miles (about 25 km) from Jerusalem, down in the Jordan valley. A reader with three Gospels open will stop at this first line. Luke says the healing happened as he drew near to Jericho, and then opens the next chapter with Jesus entering the town (19:1). Matthew and Mark both say it happened as he was going out of Jericho (Matthew 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew also reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark supplies a name, Bartimaeus.

One man or two, entering or leaving? The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives not just a name but a father’s name, Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had probably become known in the church, and both Mark and Luke follow the man who mattered to the tradition, while Matthew notes there were two. The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes, and Jesus may have been between them. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. If so, both are true of one man on one road on one afternoon. It is a likely explanation rather than a proven one, and others have been offered; believers who hold Scripture true can say so honestly and leave the detail open.

By the roadside begging. Pilgrims for Passover passed by in crowds, and were generous at festival time. For a blind beggar this road in this week was the best pitch of the year.

He inquired what this meant. He cannot see, so he has to work out from sound alone that something is happening, and he does not let it pass.

Jesus of Nazareth. The crowd’s name for him is accurate and small. And passing by: this was his one chance, for as far as the Gospels tell us, Jesus never came that way again.

The man from Nazareth and the blind. The crowd’s label holds more than they knew. In the synagogue at Nazareth, at the start of his ministry, Jesus had read from Isaiah that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim recovering of sight to the blind, and had said, today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:18–21). Now the man from Nazareth is passing a blind beggar on the Jericho road, and the promise he read aloud is about to be kept.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 17 miles by road east-north-east of Jerusalem. Mark names the man Bartimaeus; Matthew mentions two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son of David. He was told Jesus of Nazareth. What comes back is Son of David. That is a messianic title, the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and it is the first time in Luke’s Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud, a blind beggar sitting in the dust outside a town. He knows what the Messiah was to do: give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1).

The blind who see. Twelve men who could see understood none of it; a man who cannot see, working from a sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right. Luke has put the two side by side on purpose.

Have mercy on me! The tax collector’s prayer again (v. 13), in substance if not in the same Greek word. A beggar, with no claim, only need. He asks for mercy and leaves the content of it to Jesus.

Those in front rebuked him. The same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the infants (v. 15). The crowd is doing again what the disciples had just been corrected for doing, and the people nearest to Jesus are the ones telling this man to be quiet.

All the more. He does not lower his voice; he raises it, because this is the only chance he is going to get. He has the widow’s persistence (vv. 1–8).

What if the people around me discourage me from coming to Jesus? Do what the blind man did: cry out all the more. Sometimes it is friends who mock, family who think you have gone too far, a culture that tells you faith is foolish. Sometimes, sadly, it is people in the church who make the needy feel unwelcome. Jesus is not like the people at the front. He hears the voice they tried to silence. And if you are one of those at the front, near Jesus, make sure you are not the one standing between him and someone crying for mercy.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stopped. He is on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery, the flogging and the death ahead of him, and he stops, because somebody is shouting. The entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for one blind beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

Commanded him to be brought. Those who tried to silence him now bring him (Mark 10:49).

And when he came near, he asked him, What do you want me to do for you? Which is, on the face of it, an unnecessary question. The man is blind and has been begging by a roadside; anybody could name the need. So why ask? Partly because being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. It may have been a long time since anyone in that town had put a question to him. But mostly because a request has to be made. Jesus asks him to say it. He will not heal him over his head either. The mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

Let me recover my sight. He asks plainly, without preamble, without hedging or asking whether it is too much. Set that beside the ruler at verse 18: the ruler wanted to do something; the blind man asks Jesus to do something for him.

If God knows what I need, why should I ask? Because he wants us to. You do not have, because you do not ask (James 4:2). Asking is not informing God; it is trusting him, and it brings our needs out of the vague background of worry into the light of his face. Jesus knew exactly what the blind man wanted and still made him say it, because the asking was part of the healing: a beggar who had always been spoken about was spoken to, and answered. So be specific in prayer. Name the thing. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matthew 6:8), and he still loves to hear you say it.

For worship. The question asked on the Jericho road is still asked from the throne. The same Jesus who asked a blind beggar what he wanted sits at the right hand of God, a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, and the throne he sits on is a throne of grace, where the needy receive mercy and find help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). The King of kings hears the specific request of the smallest of his people, the eyes, the rent, the son, the fear, and none is beneath his attention.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Recover your sight. A word of command, no touch, no procedure, and it is done.

Your faith has made you well. And the second half is the phrase Luke keeps for the moments that go past the body: has saved you, sesōken, the same words spoken to the sinful woman (7:50), the woman with the bleeding (8:48), and the Samaritan leper (17:19). The verb means both healed and saved: something has happened here that is more than a pair of eyes.

What his faith was. There was not much of it: he had heard a name, shouted a title, refused to be silenced, and asked for the obvious thing, and Jesus calls it faith and says it has saved him.

And followed him. At once, though he was not told to; Jesus had sent others home (8:39). The first thing he does with a pair of working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one up to Jerusalem. The rich ruler would not follow (v. 22); the beggar does at once.

Glorifying God. As the Samaritan did (17:15). The gift turns into worship, and the worship is directed to God through the One who gave it.

All the people. His healing leads others to praise. The chapter that began with a widow being ignored ends with a whole crowd praising God, including the people who had told the man to be quiet.

The chapter’s pattern. Throughout chapter 18, those who come with nothing receive everything: the persistent widow, the tax collector, the infants, the blind beggar. The one who came with much was left standing, sad, with everything he owned and nothing he needed.

Does Jesus still heal the blind today? He can, and God still answers prayer for the sick, sometimes wonderfully. But this healing was a sign of who Jesus is, the Messiah who opens blind eyes as Isaiah promised, and Scripture does not promise that every prayer for healing will be granted now. The gifts of miraculous healing given to the apostles confirmed their message (Hebrews 2:3–4) and are not, in our judgment, the normal pattern for the church today (a cessationist view, held charitably towards brothers who see it differently), though God remains free to heal as he pleases, and we should pray for the sick in faith (James 5:14–15). Many faithful Pentecostal and charismatic believers expect such gifts today and pray accordingly; the difference is over the normal pattern, not over God’s power. The greater miracle, which he does every day, is the opening of blind hearts to see his glory. And the full healing of every believer’s body is certain, at the resurrection.

In everyday life. Tell someone this week what Christ has done for you, simply, like a man describing the day he first saw. And follow him where he is going, even when the road leads up to Jerusalem.

For worship. The Son of Man had set out for a city where he would be handed over and killed, and his friends had not understood a word of it. On the way he gave a beggar his eyes and gained a follower. That is the grace of God in Christ: unhurried towards the cross, and never too hurried for a sinner on the way to it.

18.text: <sup>1</sup> And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. <sup>2</sup> He said, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. <sup>3</sup> And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ <sup>4</sup> For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, <sup>5</sup> yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says. <sup>7</sup> And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” <sup>9</sup> He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’ <sup>13</sup> But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>15</sup> Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. <sup>16</sup> But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>17</sup> Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>18</sup> And a ruler asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>19</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>20</sup> You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>21</sup> And he said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>23</sup> But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. <sup>24</sup> Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, “How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup> For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup> Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup> But he said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” <sup>28</sup> And Peter said, “See, we have left our homes and followed you.” <sup>29</sup> And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, <sup>30</sup> who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.” <sup>31</sup> And taking the twelve, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. <sup>32</sup> For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. <sup>33</sup> And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” <sup>34</sup> But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said. <sup>35</sup> As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. <sup>36</sup> And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. <sup>37</sup> They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.” <sup>38</sup> And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>39</sup> And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, <sup>41</sup> “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me recover my sight.” <sup>42</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.” <sup>43</sup> And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview: Luke 19 is a chapter of arrivals. In Jericho Jesus finds Zacchaeus, a rich and despised chief tax collector who has climbed a tree to see him, and salvation comes to his house. On the road Jesus tells the parable of the minas, about a king who goes away to receive a kingdom and returns to call his servants to account; it gives the frame for everything that follows. Then he rides into Jerusalem on a colt, hailed as King by his disciples, weeps over the city that does not know the things that make for peace, and clears the temple.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus was passing through Jericho, not stopping, and a man got in the way. Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector and rich, which by this point in Luke carries weight: a rich man in torment (16:19–31), a rich ruler who went away sad (18:23–25), and the disciples asking who can be saved. The next rich man in the Gospel is up a tree.

He climbs a sycamore-fig in full view of the street. Jesus stops, calls him by name, and announces that he must stay at his house today. The crowd grumbles; Zacchaeus gives away half his goods and repays fourfold; and Jesus says salvation has come to the house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The episode is a picture of sovereign grace. Jesus claims the house before any repentance has been spoken, and the restitution follows as the fruit of salvation, not its ground, as in chapter 15 the shepherd finds the sheep.

Fourfold is the law’s heaviest common penalty for theft (Exodus 22:1), far above the fifth added for fraud (Leviticus 6:5): he sentences himself at that rate, unasked.
verseByVerse.examples: The story is also addressed to the crowd. When a church receives a man with a known past, the financial wrongdoing, the trail of damage, it can welcome him into membership and still treat his place as provisional. That is the theology of the street in Jericho, not of the Lord who went in to eat with Zacchaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 19 ends the long road to Jerusalem that began in 9:51, and it gathers the whole Gospel into one chapter: a lost man found in Jericho (vv. 1–10), a King who goes away and comes back (vv. 11–27), a humble King riding into the city (vv. 28–40), tears over Jerusalem (vv. 41–44) and the temple claimed (vv. 45–48). The thread is the King himself, seeking the lost, going away and coming back, welcomed by some and refused by others.

The setting. This is the last stop before the city. Jericho lies about fifteen miles (some 25 km) from Jerusalem, and from here the road climbs through the desert to the Mount of Olives. A blind beggar has just received his sight outside the town (18:35–43), so the crowd moving through it is large, loud and celebrating, and Passover is near. Only Luke records the story of Zacchaeus.

Passing through. The story turns on the second clause. He was not stopping; he was walking through Jericho on his way to a cross. Before he left, he would change a household by stopping where nobody expected.

Jericho. It was not a backwater. It was the city of palms, a winter resort for the wealthy on the trade route from the east. Herod the Great had built palaces there, and his son Archelaus rebuilt them, a fact that will matter for the parable in v. 12. The customs post was probably one of the most lucrative in the country. It was also the city whose walls fell to Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus. The first Joshua came to Jericho to destroy it; the second comes to Jericho to save a man in it.

A man named Zacchaeus. The behold is Luke pointing at somebody who would not otherwise have been noticed. The name is Hebrew, Zakkai, which means pure or innocent. The town had long since drawn its own conclusions. He is about to become what his name said, but not by any effort of his own.

A chief tax collector. The title, architelōnēs, appears, so far as we know, nowhere else in surviving Greek literature. He held the contract for the district and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of everything each of them took. To his neighbours that made him a traitor who worked for the occupying power, and a thief who grew fat on his own people.

Rich. Luke states it flatly, and by this point in his Gospel the word has weight. Three chapters back a rich man was in torment and a beggar in Abraham’s side (16:19–31). One chapter back a rich ruler went away very sad, and Jesus said that what is impossible with man is possible with God (18:23–27). Luke places the next rich man straight after that saying, and the next rich man is up a tree. Zacchaeus is the camel going through the needle, and this chapter shows how God does the impossible.

Why does Luke tell us he was rich? Because his money was the very thing that should have shut him out. The rich ruler had kept the commandments from his youth and still went away sad, because his wealth held him. Zacchaeus had broken the commandments for years and his wealth was dirty as well as heavy. If anyone was beyond the kingdom, it was this man. Luke wants us to see that the difference between them is not that one was better. The difference is that Jesus stopped at one man’s tree. Salvation is not the reward of the less sinful. It is the work of a God who does what is impossible with man.

The impossible walks into Jericho. Luke does not answer the question asked in 18:26 with a statement about divine power in general. He answers it with Jesus himself, entering Jericho on foot. The God for whom all things are possible is here in person, with a face and a road and a name, on his way to the cross that will pay for everything Zacchaeus ever took. That is how the impossible is done. The rich man does not shrink his fortune or his guilt until he fits. The Saviour comes to where he is, and the door that wealth had shut is opened from the other side.

In everyday life. Who is the person you would least expect to become a Christian? Pray for that person by name this week, and refuse the quiet conclusion that he or she is beyond it. And if you are the one who feels beyond reach, because of what you have done or what you have, this story was written with you in view.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route. A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.

parallels.desc: how difficult for those who have wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking to see who Jesus was. The verb is continuous: he kept seeking. And it is Luke’s own word for what will be said about Jesus seven verses later: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Two searches are running in this story and they meet under a tree. Perhaps he had heard that this teacher was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). Luke does not say whether it began as curiosity or something deeper.

Small in stature. A short man can usually work his way to the front of a gathering. A short and thoroughly hated man, in the town where he holds the tax contract, will find that the people in front of him do not move. The crowd that surrounds Jesus can be the very thing that keeps people from him.

He ran on ahead. It is often pointed out that grown men of position did not run in that culture: it meant hitching up the long robe and showing the legs, which is part of what makes the father’s run in chapter 15 so striking (15:20). A rich and powerful man, very likely dressed better than anyone around him, sprints down the road ahead of a procession.

A sycamore tree. Not the plane tree of northern Europe but the sycamore-fig, a broad tree with short trunk and low branches, easy to climb. And climbing a tree is worse than running. It is a boy’s activity, and it puts him where the whole street can see him. He was willing to look ridiculous in front of the people who despised him, because there was somebody he had to see.

Does a person have to seek Jesus before Jesus will find him? No. Zacchaeus’s seeking is real and Luke honours it, but the story is built so that his search turns out to be the smaller one inside a larger one. He thought he had found a way to see Jesus; in fact Jesus had come to Jericho to find him (v. 10). Scripture says that no one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11), and that when anyone does begin to seek, it is because the Father is already drawing him (John 6:44). So the desire you feel to know Christ is not your achievement. It is the first sign that he is calling you. Follow it, and do not wait to be sure of your motives first.
verseByVerse.note: The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He looked up. Zacchaeus climbed up to see. He had not expected to be seen. The Lord of glory, who came down from heaven, looks up into the branches at a sinner.

Zacchaeus. He knew the name, and nothing in the story explains how. The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). Jericho had called him many names, none of them kind. Jesus uses the one his parents gave him, the one that means pure.

Hurry and come down. The urgency is on Jesus’ side. All through Luke the one who searches is the one who hurries: the shepherd, the woman sweeping for her coin, the father running down the road.

I must stay at your house today. Each word is startling. Must is dei, the word of divine necessity that Luke uses at every hinge of this Gospel, ever since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). It has governed a preaching circuit (4:43), the prediction of the cross (9:22) and the journey to Jerusalem (13:33). Here it governs an evening in a tax collector’s dining room. This meeting was part of God’s plan. Today is Luke’s sēmeron, the word for the present moment of salvation (2:11; 4:21; 23:43), and it will come back four verses later. And Jesus does not ask. He announces. To stay in a man’s house was a public sign of friendship and acceptance, and of all the houses in Jericho he chooses the house of a notorious sinner.

Why does Jesus invite himself? It is a mercy, and anyone who has ever been the disreputable one in a room will see why. A man in Zacchaeus’s position does not issue invitations. He has learned not to put himself where he can be refused. If Jesus had waited to be asked, he would have waited under that tree until dark. So grace does not wait for us to work up the courage to invite it. It comes and says, I must stay at your house today. That is how every conversion begins: not with our invitation to Christ but with his claim on us.

Received him joyfully. Welcomed as a guest, and with the joy of the found, the joy of chapter 15 (15:5–7, 9, 32). The rich ruler went away sad; Zacchaeus receives Jesus with joy. Nothing has yet been said about sin or restitution. That is coming, and it comes from Zacchaeus.

For worship. He knows your name. He knew it before the tree, before the road, before the world (Ephesians 1:4). He stopped at the place where you were hiding and looked up, and said that he must come in, today. There is no greater honour on earth than to have the Son of God insist on being your guest.

parallels.desc: I will come in to him and eat with him

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They all grumbled. All of them: not only the scribes and Pharisees of 15:2 but the whole crowd, probably including people who had been praising God about a blind man shortly before. The verb is the one used of Israel murmuring in the wilderness. A crowd can rejoice at a miracle of power and resent a miracle of grace in the same hour.

The guest of a sinner. Accurate on every point, and meant as an indictment. To eat in such a house was, in their eyes, to share its uncleanness and to approve its owner. They were right that Jesus had joined himself to a sinner. They were wrong about which way the defilement would run. He is not made unclean by Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus is made clean by him.

Zacchaeus stood. Probably rising at the meal, the posture of a formal, public declaration. Luke calls Jesus the Lord, and Zacchaeus calls him Lord: the narrator and the new disciple say the same thing. The grumbling outside has been heard inside, and Zacchaeus answers it not with argument but with a changed life.

The half of my goods. Half is far beyond anything the law required, and nobody asked for it. Jesus told the rich ruler to sell everything (18:22) and he could not; Zacchaeus gives half, unasked. The man who had spent his life taking now cannot wait to give.

Fourfold. If is probably not doubt; it is the form a man uses when he knows exactly what is coming. Defrauded is the word John the Baptist used to the soldiers: do not extort by false accusation (3:14). Fourfold is the law’s penalty for the aggravated case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1); for fraud the law required only the sum plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5). He sentences himself at one of the heaviest rates in the law. With half his goods given away and fourfold restitution paid from the rest, he would be left with little. He does not care.

Is Zacchaeus promising, or defending himself? Both verbs are in the present tense: I give, I restore. Some modern commentators read them as habitual, so that Zacchaeus is protesting that he already gives half and already repays, and that the grumbling is unjust. It is a possible reading of the grammar, but the passage itself points the other way. Luke has told us the man was rich (v. 2), and a chief tax collector who already gave away half and repaid fourfold would not have stayed rich for long. Jesus replies that today salvation has come to this house, a strange thing to say to a man who had been fine all along. And the present tense is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot, as a man at the altar says, I take you. So the best reading is that Zacchaeus is vowing a new life from this moment: from now on, I give; from now on, I restore.

What it does not mean. Not that his giving earned his salvation. Salvation came to his house when Jesus came (v. 9); the vow is the fruit of a heart already changed by Jesus’ welcome, not the price of it (Ephesians 2:8–10). He could give so freely because a greater restitution was about to be made for him, on a cross. Nor does it mean that every Christian must give away half his goods. Zacchaeus chose it freely, and he was undoing a fortune built on theft. The test for every believer is a loosened grip on money and an open hand.

Must a new Christian make restitution for past wrongs? Where it is possible, yes. Repentance includes putting right what we have wrongly taken or damaged (Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:1–5). It is not the ground of forgiveness, which is Christ’s blood alone, but it is how forgiven people behave. In practice: repay the money you took, return what you borrowed and kept, correct the false report you made, confess the lie to the person who was harmed by it. Where the person cannot be found, or repayment is beyond you, give what you can to the poor, as Zacchaeus did, and leave the rest with God. Take wise counsel where restitution might harm others, such as in a confession that would wound an innocent party.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold; for ordinary wrongs, the amount plus a fifth.

parallels.desc: restore it in full and add a fifth

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Today salvation has come to this house. Today is one of Luke’s great todays, and together they form a spine through the Gospel: unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21); this one; and, from a cross, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). And notice what is said to have arrived. Not you have been forgiven, though he has been. Salvation has come, and it came up the road that afternoon and is sitting at the table. Salvation is not first a thing but a person. Simeon held a baby and said, my eyes have seen your salvation (2:30). So to be saved is not to be handed a pardon at the door while Jesus walks on down the road. It is to have him. Jesus came in and stayed, and whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12).

To this house. Not merely to Zacchaeus. The wife, the children, the servants, all of whom had lived on the proceeds, now live in a house where half of it has just been given away. Where Christ is welcomed, everyone under that roof is brought near to grace.

Does this mean his family and servants were saved with him? Salvation arrived in his home when Jesus came, and blessing spreads through a believing household. But each person must still believe for himself. At Philippi the jailer was told to believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household, and then Paul spoke the word to all who were in his house, and the household believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:31–34). Faith is never inherited. Children of believing parents have enormous privileges, and parents should pray and expect great things, but each child must come to Christ personally. For this reason this commentary holds to believer’s baptism, while honouring brothers who baptise the children of believers. In the New Testament baptism follows a person’s own repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41); paedobaptist churches, which baptise infants, see believers’ children as included in God’s covenant promise as Abraham’s were (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39), and faithful Christians have long differed here.

A son of Abraham. A deliberate provocation, because it is what the grumblers would have denied. In the popular reckoning a tax collector had forfeited his place in Israel. Jesus hands him the title back, as he did for a woman bent double for eighteen years: a daughter of Abraham (13:16). And it is more than birth. Zacchaeus is a son of Abraham now by faith as well as by blood (Galatians 3:7; Romans 4:11–12).

To seek and to save the lost. The sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel answers the grumbling of v. 7 completely. Going to a sinner’s house is not an exception for a promising case: it is the stated purpose of his coming. The verbs are the shepherd’s from chapter 15, and the Lord’s own words through Ezekiel, when he condemned Israel’s faithless shepherds and promised to shepherd his flock himself: I will seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:11–16). The Son of Man claims to do what the LORD promised to do: to be the divine Shepherd in person.

Seek, save, lost. He takes the initiative; he does the saving, by giving his life on the cross ahead; and he comes for sinners, not the righteous (5:32). Lost means gone astray, missing from where one belongs, as a coin is lost from a purse. To be lost is to be missed. Heaven noticed Zacchaeus was gone.

Who are the lost? Everyone, until Christ finds them. The word does not describe a special class of very bad people; it describes all of us apart from him (Isaiah 53:6). The difference in this story is not between the lost and the found, as though the crowd were safe. It is between those who know they are lost and those who think they are not. The grumblers were as lost as Zacchaeus, and further from being found, because they did not know it. If you know you are lost, you are exactly the kind of person he came for.

In everyday life. If the Son of Man came to seek the lost, his people cannot be content to wait in the building for them to arrive. Who is the Zacchaeus in your street or office, the one others avoid? Go to their house, or invite them to yours, and let them see what grace looks like at a table.

For worship. Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him. That is the gospel in one afternoon. Blessed be the Son of Man, who came to seek and to save, and who never once came back from a search empty-handed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke gives two reasons for the parable: they were near Jerusalem, and they supposed the kingdom would appear immediately. So the story puts a delay where they expected a coronation: a nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom, leaves his servants to trade, and comes back to call them to account. The King receives his kingdom by going away and coming back, as Luke’s second volume describes (Acts 1:9–11).

Each of ten servants gets the same modest sum, so the only thing measured is what each man did. The rebel citizens recall Archelaus. Two servants are rewarded, the third returns his mina wrapped in a cloth and is condemned by his own words, and the parable ends with the judgment of the King’s enemies.
verseByVerse.theology:
The kingdom has a not yet: the King goes away and returns, and his servants work in between. The reward for faithfulness in a very little is out of all proportion, ten cities for a mina, and it is more responsibility, not retirement: his servants will reign for ever and ever (Revelation 22:5).

To everyone who has, more will be given describes how entrusted things behave. Gifts grow by use and wither without it. Luke’s parable, unlike Matthew’s talents, adds one more question: whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant’s fear was not reverence: it produced nothing, and his picture of a harsh master was false. He is called wicked not for stealing or wasting but for doing nothing. A life that has carefully avoided wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 is spoken by a king inside a story borrowed from a tyrant’s homecoming, and no command in the parable tells the servants to act against the citizens; their task is to trade. Its horror is meant: it shows what it is to refuse a King who is coming back anyway, and the one who tells it weeps over the city fourteen verses later.

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He proceeded to tell a parable. Luke, unusually, gives two reasons. The first is that he was near to Jerusalem. It was Passover season, with a man who had raised the dead at the head of the procession, and every expectation they had seemed about to be fulfilled.

To appear immediately. They expected him to set up the kingdom at once, throwing off Rome and taking David’s throne, and they were wrong about the timing in a way that would nearly destroy their hope within the week. So everything in the parable inserts a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, work to do, and an accounting on the return.

A nobleman went into a far country. There is the shape of it. Before there is a kingdom there is a journey, and the throne is granted somewhere else. Jesus’ hearers would have known exactly where he got the picture. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship over Judea confirmed by Caesar, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17). Archelaus came back with a lesser title, ethnarch rather than king, and ruled so brutally that Rome deposed him ten years later. And he had rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, the very town Jesus is leaving. Many on that road would have remembered it.

The meaning. Jesus is the nobleman. The King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem. He receives it in a far country, and comes back. Through his death, resurrection and ascension he went to the Father, and like the Son of Man in Daniel’s vision he came to the Ancient of Days and was given dominion and glory and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). He reigns now from heaven, and he will return (Acts 1:9–11).

An error of timing, not of hope. Jesus corrects one thing only: the kingdom will come in its fullness later than they think, and there is work to do meanwhile. Both halves have been lost in turn by the church. A Christianity that expects nothing has stopped believing there is a return. A Christianity that sets dates has generally stopped trading.

Where Christians differ: what kind of kingdom is the nobleman receiving? Some read the parable within a premillennial scheme (Christ returning before a thousand-year reign on earth): the nobleman receives the kingdom in heaven, but the kingdom itself is only set up on earth after his return, in a thousand-year reign in which the faithful servants govern actual cities. Others, the amillennial view (which takes the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of Christ’s present reign), read it this way: the kingdom is received at the ascension and Christ reigns now, over his church and over all things for her sake (Ephesians 1:20–23); his return will bring not a further earthly stage but the final judgment and the new creation, in which his people share his reign for ever. This commentary’s view: the second reading fits the parable and the New Testament best. Jesus says the kingdom was given to him in the far country, not that it would begin later, and Peter declares at Pentecost that Jesus has already been exalted to David’s throne (Acts 2:30–36). The return is one public event that brings reward and judgment together, as the parable itself shows (vv. 15–27), not a secret coming before the end. Brothers who hold other views of the millennium, including many who expect the church to be caught up before a time of tribulation, read these texts with equal love for Scripture and confess the same returning King.

In everyday life. You live in the interval this parable describes. If you have been unsettled by prophecy charts and predictions, set them down: Jesus told this parable precisely to cool date-setting. Your task is not to calculate the day but to be found faithful on it.
verseByVerse.note: Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. Herod’s son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it.

parallels.desc: will you at this time restore the kingdom?

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten minas. They are his slaves, trusted to manage his affairs while he is away, and each receives one mina. That detail matters. In Matthew’s cousin-parable of the talents, the master distributes different amounts to different men, each according to his ability (Matthew 25:15). Here everybody gets exactly the same.
