That changes what the parable is measuring. Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity. Where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did.

A mina. A hundred denarii, about a hundred days’ wages for a labourer. For a nobleman about to receive a kingdom it is a trifle: a test of faithfulness in small things (16:10).

What is the mina? The parable does not say, and that has allowed many answers. Because each servant receives the same, it most likely pictures what all disciples equally receive: the word of the gospel, the knowledge of the King, and the calling to serve him while he is away. Particular gifts, money, time and opportunities differ from person to person and are better pictured by the talents in Matthew. Here the point is that no servant can say he was given nothing. Every believer has the gospel, and every believer is sent to trade with it.

Engage in business. The verb is commercial: trade with it, put it to work. It is not look after this. Until I come is both a promise that he will and a statement that the trading has an end date. A sum of money, an instruction to risk it, and a return that is certain but unscheduled: that is the situation of the church, stated in a sentence.

The freedom of the instruction. He does not tell them what business to engage in or how he will assess them. He gives them the money and goes. So the timid servant’s failure is not a failure to follow a rule. It is a failure to believe the freedom was genuinely given, and that the master would be pleased with the attempt.

The commission of the departing King. The parable’s picture is not left to guesswork, because Luke records what the real King said before he went to the far country. The risen Jesus opened the Scriptures to his disciples, showed them that the Christ must suffer and rise, and told them that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:46–47). Then he was carried up into heaven (24:51). That is what the trading looks like: a crucified and risen Lord’s gospel, put into ordinary hands, with orders to spend it everywhere until he comes back.

In everyday life. Think over what Christ has entrusted to you: the gospel, the people near you, the hours of this week, your money, a skill you take for granted. Pick one and ask what trading with it would look like before Sunday, asking the Spirit who gave it for the courage to risk it. Do not wait for a perfect plan. The master did not give one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his citizens hated him. A second plot enters the parable, and it has nothing to do with the servants and their money. These are the nobleman’s own people, as the Jews sent a delegation after Archelaus.

We do not want this man. He is walking toward the city that is about to say exactly this; within days its chief priests will say, we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). The wording is not this man is unfit, or we prefer another. The issue is not his credentials but his rule, and it is the cry of every human heart since Eden that will not have God for its King. Today the cry is usually quieter: I am glad for Jesus to help me, but not to be in charge of me. Yet no heart goes unruled. Career, approval, comfort or a person will take the throne he is refused, and none of those kings has ever died for its subjects.

Having received the kingdom. The objection was lodged, considered and overruled somewhere far away, and the kingdom was granted anyway. The nations rage, and the One who sits in the heavens laughs; he has set his King on Zion (Psalm 2:1–6).

These servants to be called. The first thing he does on arriving with a kingdom is not to deal with the rebels but to send for his own servants. Judgment begins with the household of God (1 Peter 4:17), and all of us must stand before Christ’s judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10).

What it does not mean. The accounting is not a trial to decide whether the faithful servants belong to the master. They were his servants before he left, and no condemnation awaits those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). What is examined is what they did with what he gave them, and what is given is reward. That should make us serious, and not afraid.

Is it wrong to want rewards? No. Jesus offers them, and he offers them to motivate us (6:23, 35; 12:33). The desire to hear him say well done is not selfish ambition; it is love wanting to please the one it loves. What would be wrong is to think we earn heaven, or to serve for the reward rather than for the Master. But the two do not compete. The reward is mostly the Master himself: his pleasure, his presence and a share in his work.

In everyday life. Where in your life are you saying, I do not want this man to reign over me? Rarely in words. Usually in a single room of the house kept locked: money, sexuality, a grudge, your ambitions, your time. Open the room to him today, while he is still asking.

parallels.desc: we have no king but Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your mina has made ten minas. It is his master’s mina. Not I have made ten; your mina has made ten. The servant reports a result without claiming it. Paul said the same: it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Well done, good servant! It is the first thing the returning king says to anybody in the parable. Before the rebels are dealt with, the man who traded faithfully hears his master say good, and he is praised not for being gifted but for being faithful in what the master calls a very little.

The one Servant who earned the word. Only one servant has ever heard the Father’s approval on his own merit: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). Every other well done is spoken over servants who have been joined to him. That is why the first servant says your mina and not my work: his trading was itself a gift, and his welcome rests on Another’s faithfulness.

Ten cities. Now the disproportion, which is the whole point. Not ten minas, not a hundred, but cities, with people in them. The exchange rate is absurd, and it is meant to be: the parable calls the mina small precisely to make the reward look impossible.

The reward is more responsibility. Not rest, and not payment, but a larger share in the King’s rule. The popular picture of heaven is largely of idleness; Scripture’s images run the other way: his servants will worship him, and they will reign for ever and ever (Revelation 22:3–5; 2 Timothy 2:12). The life to come is not retirement, and the training for it is going on now.

Will we really rule cities? The parable uses the language of its story: a king’s servants rewarded with towns. The reality behind it is that the redeemed will share in Christ’s reign over the new creation, with real responsibility, real work and real joy, when he makes all things new (Revelation 21:1–5; 22:5). We are not told what that will look like in detail, and it is wise not to build a map from a parable. What we are told is enough: the faithfulness you show now is not wasted, and it is preparing you for something far greater than you can imagine.

In everyday life. You will probably not see great results this week. You will see a lunch box packed, an email answered honestly, a child put to bed with a prayer, a lesson taught to six children. The King calls that very little, and he is watching it. And when something goes well, say aloud, your mina did this, and give him the credit.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five minas. The second man has produced exactly half what the first produced: same sum, same absence, same instruction, half the result. Less than the first, but still faithful.

Over five cities. There is no rebuke of any kind and no comparison with his colleague. What he gets is five cities: a reward proportioned to the return, and every bit as real. There are degrees of reward in the kingdom (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but there is no disgrace in having fewer cities than the man next to you.

No well done? The master’s reply to the second man is noticeably shorter. He gets the reward, and no well done is recorded. It is better not to press that. Luke is compressing, as he does everywhere, and the parable’s contrast is not between the ten and the five. It is between both of them and the man with the handkerchief. What the two together establish is the principle: the King rewards what was actually done, at the rate it was done, without grading on a curve.

He came. The second servant had a smaller result than the man in front of him and he came anyway, and said out loud in front of the whole court exactly what he had produced. The third servant will arrive with an explanation.

The Judge who counts small coins. The King who sets the five-mina servant over five cities without reproach is the same Lord who, in a few days, will watch a poor widow put in two small copper coins and say that she put in more than all of them (21:1–4). He measures what was given against what was held back, and he never confuses a small return with an unfaithful one.

What if I have done much less than other Christians I know? Then this verse is for you. You are not being measured against them. Faithfulness is judged by what you did with what you were given in the life God appointed you: your health, your circumstances, your years. A mother with three small children, a man caring for a dying parent, a believer with a long illness may trade quietly, and be over cities. Comparison is not the King’s method; do not make it yours. Bring him what you have, honestly, and expect his kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is your mina. Literally the other, the third of the ten Jesus describes. He has it, and that is what he thinks will save him. Nothing has been lost, spent or risked. The others reported what the mina had made. He reports where he put it.

Laid away in a handkerchief. A soudarion, a cloth for wiping the face, the word used of the cloth over Lazarus’s face (John 11:44). Burying money was the recognised secure method, and according to later rabbinic law a man who did so was not liable if it was stolen. He did not even take proper care of it.

A severe man. He offers it as an explanation; it is in fact an accusation. Severe is austēros, used of unripe, sour fruit and of a man with no give in him.

You take what you did not deposit. The two charges describe a profiteer: someone who collects where he has not invested and harvests fields he never planted. So the servant’s defence is that his master is grasping and unfair, and that his own inactivity was a rational response.

His fear was not reverence. It is not the fear of the Lord, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey. He was too frightened to act, and he has been calling it caution for the whole of the master’s absence. His fear was really unbelief. This is what religion looks like when it is run on self-protection: the aim is not to please the master but to stay out of trouble with him, and a person who lives that way will always do as little as he safely can.

His picture of the master was a slander. This is a master who handed out money to ten men with no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant has constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about. A false view of God is never harmless, and very often it leads to a life of doing nothing for him.

The Master’s face. The servant called his master a man who takes what he did not deposit. The Son who told the story was on his way to Jerusalem to give, not to take: to pour out his blood for his people (22:20). Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9), and nothing in that face is austere. He wept over the city that rejected him and prayed for the men who crucified him.

What if I find myself afraid of God? There is a right fear and a wrong fear. The right fear is reverent awe of his holiness, combined with trust in his mercy, and it draws you toward him and makes you eager to please him (Psalm 130:4). The wrong fear sees him as a harsh taskmaster waiting to catch you out, and it drives you to hide. If that is your fear, the cure is not to try harder but to look again at who he is. Look at the cross: a God who gives his Son for his enemies is not severe. As you see his love, fear of punishment gives way to the reverent, glad fear of a child (1 John 4:18).
verseByVerse.note: A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was safer.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
With your own words. The master does not argue the description. He takes the servant’s own account and turns it round. And the servant has not stolen the money, wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth: doing nothing with what God gives is sin.

You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? The logic is plain: very well, suppose I am exactly what you say. The master does not accept the description, but argues on its own terms.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank? There is the trap closing. Bank is trapeza, a table: the money-changer’s table. Banking existed and paid interest; the money-changers took deposits, and there was nothing exotic about it. It required no skill, no judgment and no courage. A man could walk in, hand the mina over, and walk out.

With interest. So the servant’s own premise convicts him. If the master really were a hard man, the sensible response would have been to make certain he got something. The one course his stated fear cannot justify is doing nothing. The fear was a cover story: he did nothing because he did not care about his master’s interests.

Is the third servant a believer who loses reward, or an unbeliever who is lost? He belongs to the household outwardly. He was given a mina and called a servant. But his picture of the master as harsh shows that he never knew him, and in Matthew’s cousin-parable the worthless servant is cast into the outer darkness (Matthew 25:24–30). He represents those who receive God’s gifts and do nothing with them: outwardly religious, perhaps in church for years, but never truly serving Christ because they never truly trusted him. Faithfulness is not the ground of salvation; it is the fruit of knowing a gracious master. The servant who buries his gift shows that he does not know him.

Then can a true Christian lose his salvation? No. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). This parable does not describe a believer falling away. It describes someone who was near the master and never knew him, and it is a warning to search ourselves, not a threat hanging over those who trust Christ. A true believer may be weak, fearful and slow, and will still bring something, however small, because the Spirit is at work in him (Philippians 1:6). What the parable exposes is the settled heart that has never loved the master at all.

The Servant who left nothing undone. Nothing bad was done: that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. Set beside him the one Servant who did everything his Master asked. Jesus did not merely avoid sin. From the boy who must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the man who committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46), he did his Father’s will, and that whole-hearted obedience is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 5:19). Counted means credited to our account, as a debt is cleared when someone else pays into your name: the guilty pronounced righteous, not because they have become good but because Christ’s righteousness is reckoned to them (Romans 4:5). It is the only righteousness that will stand when the King asks what was done with what he gave.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the mina from him. The idle man loses even what he had, and the man who traded best is trusted with what the idle man buried. The bystanders’ objection is the one most readers share.

To everyone who has. Not a rule for distributing prizes, but a description of how entrusted things behave. The saying has appeared before, attached to hearing: take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given (8:18). Capacity grows by use. This is true of spiritual gifts, opportunities, and understanding of God’s word: the one who obeys what he knows is given to know more.

From the one who has not. The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master’s reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for the whole of an absence is not a possession at all. And a man who hides what he was given loses even the ability to use it. Nothing is more perishable than an unexercised gift.

The enthroned King still gives. Exalted at the right hand of God, Jesus poured out the promised Holy Spirit on his waiting people at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The nobleman who received a kingdom does not sit on it like a miser. Every increase of faith, understanding and fruitfulness in his servants is the overflow of his throne.

Is this the rich getting richer? No. The parable is not about money or social advantage; Luke has spent chapters warning the rich and lifting the poor (1:53; 6:20–24; 16:19–31). It is about the gifts of the King. In his kingdom those who use what he gives receive more of the same, and those who despise his gifts lose them. A poor widow who prays faithfully is the one who has, and a wealthy churchgoer who buries the gospel is the one who has not.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
These enemies of mine. The citizens of v. 14 return. The servant was idle; they are open rebels.

Slaughter them before me. It is one of the hardest sentences in Luke, and some have quoted it as though Jesus were commanding violence against opponents. Two things keep it in its place.

Words inside a parable. First, these are words spoken by a character in a story, not an instruction to disciples. The picture is borrowed from Archelaus, whose reprisals were remembered with horror. Not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. Christians are never to take up the sword against those who reject Christ (22:49–51).

The horror is the point. Second, the horror of the image is not an embarrassment to be explained away. Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway. The picture points first to the destruction of Jerusalem, which he will foretell with tears in a few minutes (vv. 41–44), and ultimately to the last judgment, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven and those who do not obey the gospel suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). The parable and the tears over the city belong to the same person, fourteen verses apart, and a judgment described in terms this stark by a man about to weep over it is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

Three groups. The faithful servants are rewarded, the unfaithful servant loses everything, the enemies are destroyed: reward and judgment together, in one event. There is no neutral fourth group. Everyone who hears of the King is either trading for him, burying what he gave, or refusing his reign.

This is not the parable of the talents. The two are cousins, but in Matthew the sums are enormous and unequal and there are no rebel citizens (Matthew 25:14–30). Jesus taught constantly and very likely reworked his material for the moment he was in.

How can a loving Jesus speak of slaughter? Because love is not indifference. A King who did nothing about those who destroy his people and despise his rule would not be good. Final judgment is real and it is eternal; Jesus speaks of it more than anyone in the Bible. But notice who says this, and where he is going. He is on his way to Jerusalem to bear judgment himself, so that rebels who come to him will never face it. The same Jesus prayed for the men who crucified him, Father, forgive them (23:34). Some early manuscripts lack that prayer, but many scholars judge it a true saying of Jesus, and most Bibles print it. The door is open now. The parable is spoken so that no one need be found among the enemies when he comes.

For worship. Before grace found them, every one of his people was among those who said, We do not want this man to reign over us. The King who will summon rebels to judgment went first to a chief tax collector’s house, and was welcomed there with joy.

parallels.desc: kiss the Son, lest he be angry

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus leads the climb from Jericho, far below sea level, up through the desert to the Mount of Olives, the hill where Zechariah said the LORD’s feet would stand (Zechariah 14:4). In riding the colt he claims Zechariah’s picture of the King who comes humble and mounted on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), not on a horse of war.

His disciples lay their cloaks on the road, a coronation gesture (2 Kings 9:13) made with what was often a poor man’s most valuable possession, and they praise God for the mighty works they have seen. Then, where the road brings the whole city into view, he weeps aloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples add one word to Psalm 118:26: blessed is the King who comes. That turns a pilgrim greeting into a public claim, and it is why the Pharisees object. Their peace in heaven answers the angels’ song at his birth (2:14): there will be no peace on earth this week, but peace with God is being made by the very week that will look like defeat.

If they were silent, the stones would cry out, as the stone cries from the wall in Habakkuk 2:11; and within a generation the stones of this city would lie in heaps. In AD 70 the temple was burned and pulled down.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke’s word for the weeping is the loud one, used of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62). The singing goes on around a man who is sobbing.

A preacher on Palm Sunday may be tempted to stop at the shouting. The passage will not let him: the day is triumphant and heartbroken at once. God visited his people (1:68), and a visitation that saves those who receive it leaves nothing but judgment for those who refuse it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on ahead. In front of them, leading, resolute, as he set his face to go to Jerusalem in 9:51. Nobody is dragging him up that road. Jericho lies about 850 feet (260 m) below sea level and Jerusalem about 2,500 feet (760 m) above it, so the fifteen miles are a climb of some 3,400 feet (1,000 m) through the desert. He has just told a parable about a king who goes away to receive a kingdom, and he now walks toward the place where that departure will begin.

Bethphage and Bethany. Villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem; Bethany was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1). Zechariah had prophesied that on the day of the LORD his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4).

A colt tied. The instructions are startlingly specific. Luke does not tell us whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge, but nothing about the next hour is improvised. Jesus is in control of his own entry into the city where he will die.

On which no one has ever yet sat. In Israel an animal never put to ordinary use was fit for sacred purposes, like the cows on which there had never come a yoke that drew the ark (1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for a holy use. It will carry the King.

If anyone asks you, Why are you untying it? you shall say this: The Lord has need of it. Which is either a password arranged in advance or a claim of extraordinary boldness, and either way it is the only explanation offered. The Lord is ho kyrios. To the owners it could sound like simply the master; on Jesus’ lips it means the Lord of all.

The animal is the prophecy. A conquering king rode a horse, the animal of war. Zechariah had described the alternative: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), and he shall speak peace to the nations (9:10). As far as the Gospels tell us, he has walked everywhere. On the one recorded occasion he rides, the animal is the prophecy.

In everyday life. If the Lord has need of something you have, he owes you no other explanation, and he asks for ordinary things at short notice: your car on Sunday morning, your spare room, your evening for a grieving friend, your savings. Which of your possessions would you struggle to untie if two strangers came and said these words? That is the one to offer first.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as he had told them. Luke records the match on purpose, as he will when the disciples find the upper room (22:13). For chapters the disciples have heard things they could neither understand nor test (18:31–34). Here is a prediction they can verify within the hour, and it holds to the last detail. The Lord who is right about a tethered colt can be trusted about a cross and an empty tomb.

And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, Why are you untying the colt? So the challenge came, precisely as he said it would. The word owners is plural. Only Luke has it, and the Greek is kyrioi, literally lords. This is somebody’s animal, and they are standing right there, watching two strangers untie it.

The Lord has need of it. The owners let it go. Owners is kyrioi, literally lords: the lords of the colt ask, and the answer is that the Lord needs it. The most likely explanation of how it worked is the simplest: Jesus had friends in Bethany, and an arrangement had been made or the phrase was recognised.

The Lord who borrows. The one who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) sends two men to ask for the loan of a donkey. He was born in borrowed lodging, rode on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room and was buried in a borrowed grave. He who was rich became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Why would the Lord of all need anything? He does not need anything in the sense of lacking it; he is served by human hands as though he needed anything only because he chooses to be (Acts 17:25). His need here is the need of a King who has decided to use ordinary things and ordinary people in his work. That is the dignity he gives us. He could have summoned angels. He asked for a donkey from a family in that village, and their name is not recorded, and their colt is in the Gospels for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They set Jesus on it. The cloaks go on first, because there is no saddle. And there is a royal echo: when David’s son Solomon was made king, he rode on David’s own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33–40). The Son of David rides to his capital the same way.

Cloaks on the road. This gesture has a precedent every Jew would recognise. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the officers every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and proclaimed, Jehu is king (2 Kings 9:13). Cloaks under the feet of a man are a coronation. Luke does not mention palm branches, and he does not need them.

What a cloak cost. To a poor Galilean his cloak was his blanket at night and often the most valuable thing he owned, so valuable that the law forbade a creditor to keep one overnight (Exodus 22:26–27). They lay it in the dust so that a donkey can walk over it.

What makes it worship rather than waste. Nothing is achieved by putting a coat under a colt. The gesture is pure declaration: this man is the King, and nothing I own is too good to be walked on by him. Nobody got anything back except a dirty cloak. That is worship: not a transaction, but honour given because it is owed, like Mary of Bethany’s ointment (John 12:1–8).

On the road out. Within the week, other men will take his clothes from him and cast lots for them at the foot of a cross (23:34). On the road in, his people threw down everything they had so that he could pass over it. On the road out, the last garment he owned was divided by strangers. Of everyone in that procession, the only one who understood where it was going was the man on the donkey.

Why a donkey and not a warhorse? Because of the kind of King he is and the kind of victory he came to win. A horse would have announced a war against Rome, which is what many in the crowd wanted. The donkey announces a King who is humble, who comes in peace, and whose victory will be won not by killing his enemies but by dying for them. His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). That is still how he comes: not by force, but by the gentle power of the gospel, winning hearts rather than seizing territory. He will come once more in visible glory, but even then his first coming will have told us his heart.

In everyday life. What is your cloak: the thing you value most that you could lay at his feet? Your reputation at work, your plans for retirement, your hold on a child who wants to go to the mission field. Worship is laying down something costly because he is King.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way down the Mount of Olives. At a particular point on the descent the whole city comes into view at once: the Kidron valley below, the wall opposite, and the temple platform filling the eye, its white stone and gold catching the light. That is where the shouting starts.

The whole multitude of his disciples. Only Luke specifies it. Matthew and Mark have the crowds; Luke says it was his own followers: the many who had come with him from Galilee, the women who had provided for him, the healed and the forgiven.

With a loud voice. Joy and loud praise, as at his birth, when the shepherds returned glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen (2:20).

The same hillside. Luke will bring his readers back to this slope. After his resurrection Jesus leads his disciples out as far as Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven from the mount called Olivet (24:50–51; Acts 1:9–12). Today the King comes down that hill to be rejected and crucified; then he will go up from it to the right hand of God. The road runs down to a cross and back up to a throne, over the same ground.

All the mighty works. They are praising God for what they have already watched him do: a widow’s son sitting up on his bier, a legion evicted, five loaves and twelve baskets, a blind man at the gate of Jericho, very likely still with them and shouting louder than anybody. They were wrong about the week ahead. They were not wrong about him, and the reasons they gave were sound.

What if I do not feel like praising? Then do what they did: remember. Praise in Scripture is rarely a feeling first. It is a telling of what God has done, and feeling usually follows the telling (Psalm 103:1–5). Begin with the mighty works you know for certain: the cross and the empty tomb, your own conversion, the prayers answered, the troubles survived. Say them aloud, or sing them with the church when you would rather stay silent. You are not being dishonest when you praise without strong emotion. You are telling the truth about God, which is always the right thing to do.
verseByVerse.note: The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with the city and temple in full view.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the King. The line is Psalm 118:26, from the Hallel sung at the great festivals, and pilgrims arriving at Jerusalem were probably greeted with it. But the psalm reads, blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Luke’s disciples insert one word: blessed is the King who comes. That is a claim about the man on the donkey, made in public, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem, and it is why the Pharisees object in the next verse.

The words he said they would say. Jesus had told Jerusalem, you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (13:35). Now his own disciples say almost exactly that. Jerusalem as a whole will not say it this week. One day every tongue will.

Peace in heaven. Here Luke closes a circle he opened in his second chapter. Over a field outside Bethlehem the angels had sung, glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). Now human voices sing it back, with the terms reversed. The angels said peace on earth; the disciples say peace in heaven. Luke omits the word Hosanna, which his Gentile readers might not have understood, and gives us this instead.

Why peace in heaven and not on earth? Because that is exactly where things stand. There will be no peace on earth this week. There will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution, and the man they are singing about will be dead within days. Peace on earth is about to be rejected by the city of peace (v. 42). What is settled in heaven is another matter. The reconciliation between God and sinners is being accomplished, and it is being accomplished by the very week that will look like total defeat. Through the blood of his cross God made peace (Colossians 1:20). Peace in heaven means that God’s just anger against our sin has been dealt with, so that God himself is no longer against the sinner who trusts Christ. That is propitiation: Christ’s death turning God’s wrath away by taking it on himself (Romans 3:25). It is not first a calm feeling in us but a changed standing with God (Romans 5:1, 10). Peace on earth will follow from peace in heaven: first in every heart that believes, and finally in a new creation where there is no more war.

In the flow. Only a day’s walk back Jesus told a parable to cool the hope that the kingdom would appear at once (v. 11), and now his disciples hail him as King. Each explains the other. The shouting is true, and the parable never denied it. But the parable tells how his kingdom comes: by a journey to a far country, which for Jesus means the cross, the grave and the ascension, and then a return. The procession is not the end of the story. It is the King setting out on that journey.

The singers do not know how right they are. They think they are welcoming a king to a coronation. They are walking beside him to an altar, singing the anthem of a peace that will be made in blood on Friday afternoon, and it will hold for ever.

For worship. He came once on a donkey, to be refused by his city and to make peace in heaven by his blood, and he will come once more in a cloud with power and great glory (21:27). Between the two comings the hillside choir has never fallen silent, and every generation that takes up the line is right about him.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
glory in the highest, peace on earth

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, rebuke your disciples. It is the last time the Pharisees appear in Luke’s Gospel, and their final recorded words are a request to stop the worship. Their concern may have been partly genuine. A messianic acclamation at Passover, with Roman troops reinforced in the fortress overlooking the temple and the governor in town precisely because festivals produced riots, was a dangerous thing to be shouting. Men had died for less. But listen to the address: Teacher. They will not use the word the disciples have just used. The disciples said King; the Pharisees say Teacher, and the whole dispute is contained in the gap between those two nouns. And they ask not that he deny the claim, only that he silence them. It is enough for their purposes if nobody says it out loud.

The very stones would cry out. If these voices stop, the created order will take over. The praise is not generated by enthusiasm; it is owed. Creation was made by him and for him (Colossians 1:16), and it knows its Maker even when men do not.

The stones as witnesses. Habakkuk, denouncing the man who builds by injustice, says the stone will cry out from the wall (Habakkuk 2:11). And he is looking at a city of magnificent stonework of which, within four verses, he will say that not one stone will be left on another (v. 44). Within a generation they will be lying in a heap in the valley, saying something after all.

Is it wrong to worship loudly or emotionally? No. Jesus refused to silence it, and Scripture is full of shouting, clapping and singing with a loud voice (Psalm 47:1; 98:4). Nor is quiet worship less real. What matters is that praise is true, directed to Christ, and done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40). The danger this passage exposes is not the noisy church or the quiet one. It is the person who is embarrassed that Jesus should be praised at all, or who would rather the claim that he is King were not made in public.

In everyday life. Where do you go quiet about Jesus because someone would rather you did not speak of him: at a family meal, in an office, with a friend who has asked a direct question? Do not mistake the pressure for wisdom. You do not have to shout, and you are not left to your own nerve: the Holy Spirit teaches his people in that very hour what to say (12:12).

parallels.desc: the stone will cry out from the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He wept over it. The shouting is still going on. He is on a donkey, surrounded by people singing that he is the King, at the summit of the greatest public acclaim he ever received, and he is crying. Only Luke records it. Wept is eklausen: not quiet tears but loud weeping, sobbing, the word used of mourners at a funeral. He has lamented over this city before, in the saying about the hen and her chicks (13:34). Now the lament becomes tears. He has been carrying this the whole way. Not for himself, though he knew he was riding to his death, but for the city that would reject him.

Would that you had known. In Greek the sentence is unfinished, exactly as a sentence breaks off when the speaker cannot complete it. Even you: of all the cities on earth, this one, the city of David, the place of the temple. And there is a play on the city’s name, popularly understood as city of peace. Jerusalem, of all places, did not know the things that make for peace.

The things that make for peace. They are Jesus himself, the King of peace riding on Zechariah’s donkey, and the peace with God he came to bring. On this day, the day of God’s visitation, the King has come, and the city does not know him.

Hidden from your eyes. Not they were never offered. Hidden: now, after everything. Because they had rejected the light, it was now withdrawn from them: the judgment that gives people over to what they have chosen (8:10; John 12:37–40).

Who hid these things from their eyes? Luke’s phrase points to God, who hides in judgment what people have refused to see (10:21; Isaiah 6:9–10; Romans 11:7–10). Yet Jerusalem’s refusal was its own, and Jesus weeps over it. Divine hardening and human responsibility stand together, and so do God’s judgment and Christ’s tears. We are not asked to reconcile them in a formula. We are shown both in the face of one man on a donkey, and that is enough to keep us from two errors: thinking God is helpless before human refusal, and thinking he is cold toward it.

Does this mean God is finished with the Jewish people? No. Jesus is weeping over the city that rejected him and foretelling its judgment in that generation, not announcing that no Jew can be saved. Within weeks thousands of Jews in this same city were converted at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and Paul insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians differ on Romans 11:25–26: some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, others read all Israel as the full number of the elect from Israel and the nations. Both agree that Jews, like Gentiles, are saved only by faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians should long and pray for it, as Jesus wept for it.

Can a person today reach a point where it is too late? Scripture warns that it is possible to harden yourself until God gives you over (Romans 1:24; Hebrews 3:12–15), and that is why today matters. But anyone who is troubled by the fear that it is too late shows by that very concern that God is still at work in him. The hardened do not weep over their hardness. If you want Christ, come to him; he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

In everyday life. Who do you know who is turning away from Christ: a child, a friend, a former churchgoer? Do you weep for them, or only worry, or have you quietly stopped thinking about them? Plead for them with God this week. And let Christ’s tears shape how you speak to them: not judgment with a hard face, but the warning and the invitation of a Saviour who wept.

parallels.desc: that I might weep day and night

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A barricade around you. Within one generation every clause of this prophecy happened. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem and built exactly what this verse describes: a wall right round the city, nearly five miles (7 km) of it, thrown up in three days, so that no one could get out and no supplies could get in. Josephus, who was there, describes it. Some scholars think Luke shaped the wording by the event; but Jesus’ warnings against the temple appear in every Gospel, and the language is the prophets’ own language of siege (Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:2).

Hem you in. The siege lasted about five months. Josephus records people eating leather, and the dead thrown over the walls because they could not be buried.

Tear you down to the ground. The verb, to dash to the ground, is used in the Greek Old Testament of infants killed in a captured city (Psalm 137:9). Huge numbers were killed, and many thousands of survivors were sold into slavery.

Not one stone upon another. As Jesus will say of the temple (21:6). The temple was burned and dismantled, and some of the great stones thrown into the street below still lie at the foot of the temple mount, the paving cracked under them.

The time of your visitation. Here is the only cause given. Visitation is episkopē, God coming to see about his people, the word of Zechariah’s song: he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68). God came to Jerusalem, on a donkey, weeping, and the city did not recognise the day.

A visitation cuts both ways. In Scripture a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue. The coming that saves those who know it condemns those who do not, not by a change in God, but because there is no other Saviour to send.

Was AD 70 the final judgment? No, but it was a preview of it. The fall of Jerusalem was a real judgment in history on the generation that rejected the Messiah, and Jesus tells it in the language of the prophets who foretold the fall of the first temple. It also stands as a picture of the last day, when Christ will return to judge the whole world (21:25–28; Acts 17:31). Both are real. The first came on one city in one generation; the second will come on all. Nor does this give any Christian licence to despise the Jewish people. Jesus wept as he said it, and so should we.

For worship. Not one of his warnings has failed, and not one of his promises will. The same Jesus who foretold the stones thrown down gave himself to be torn down in our place, so that all who know the day of his visitation will be built into a temple that can never fall, made of living stones (1 Peter 2:4–5).
verseByVerse.note: The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall round it, and destroyed the city and temple. A “visitation” is God coming in mercy or judgment.

parallels.desc: I will encircle you with towers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke tells the clearing of the temple in one clause and gives most of his space to the words. The trade in the Court of the Gentiles served real needs, animals for sacrifice and the right coin for the temple tax, but it had taken over the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, the house of prayer for all peoples, and Jeremiah 7:11, the den of robbers from the sermon that foretold the first temple’s fall. Then he stays, teaching daily in the court as its owner.
verseByVerse.theology:
The clearing is a prophetic act, not a reform. Set side by side, the two texts say: you were called to be the one; you have become the other. A den of robbers is where robbers go to feel safe, and it names religion used as cover for lives that will not change.

The last verses describe a strange week. The leaders want him dead and cannot touch him, because he stands in the most public place in the city surrounded by people hanging on his words. The authorities did not overpower him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The trade Jesus drove out was not frivolous: this was religion crowding out prayer, which is much harder to see from inside, and it blocked the door for those furthest from God.

A church known mainly for its events, café and programmes, good in themselves, may find that sustained prayer together has been crowded out. The question this passage puts to any congregation is not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the temple. The prophet had said it: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; but who can endure the day of his coming? (Malachi 3:1–2). He comes as its owner, not its visitor, and the first thing he does is clean house.

Drive out those who sold. Luke’s account is the briefest of the four, one clause for the action (Mark 11:15–17; John 2:15). He gives the words. The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles and was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims needed sacrificial animals and the right coin for the temple tax, and the trade was probably under the control of the high-priestly families. But the provision had taken over the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

A house of prayer. The first quotation is Isaiah 56:7, which in full says my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it. And my house: Jesus claims it as his own.

A den of robbers. The second quotation is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah’s temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety, chanting, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, while cheating and oppressing outside it. And it went on to announce that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:14), which was to destroy it. So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

The exact charge. A den of robbers is not where robbery happens. It is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards. The temple had become a hiding place: a religious system people used to feel secure while their lives were indefensible. It is a use religion has never stopped being put to.

Was this the clearing John describes? Probably not. John places a clearing of the temple near the beginning of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–17), while Luke places this one in the final week. Two separate events is the likelier explanation: the Passovers differ, the words differ, and a trade driven out once would soon have crept back. Some scholars think John placed the one event early for his own purposes; believers have held either view without doubting either Gospel. Nor does this passage forbid every sale in a church building. The offence was that commerce had crowded out prayer in the one court open to the nations. And it was the Messiah acting with authority over his Father’s house, not a pattern for Christians to use force.

What does this mean for the church? The temple has given way to Christ and his people: the church is now God’s house, built of living stones (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22). So the same two tests apply. Is it a house of prayer for all peoples, where the outsider and the stranger are welcomed to seek God? And is it a den, a place where people come to feel safe while refusing to repent? A church can fail either test without selling anything: by being closed to outsiders, or by offering comfort without holiness.

Did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice? Most likely twice: John’s cleansing comes at the first Passover of the ministry, with different words and setting (John 2:13–17), and Luke’s stands at the head of the last week. (See Matthew 21:12 for the fuller answer.)

Was Jesus losing his temper? No. Luke tells it in one brief clause and gives most of his space to Scripture, not to the action. This was the King’s judgment, not a fit of rage. And anger at what destroys people is part of love, not its opposite. A God who felt nothing about religion being used to fleece pilgrims and to crowd the nations out of prayer would not be good. The same Jesus who drove out the traders had wept over the city only a little earlier (v. 41).

In the flow. Luke moves straight from the tears to the temple, without the fig tree that Mark includes (Mark 11:11–14), so that the King’s first act in Jerusalem is to claim his Father’s house.

For worship. Some twenty years earlier a boy in this temple had said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Now the Son returns as its Lord, clears its outer court for the nations, and within days gives his body to be broken for the very sins that had made it a den. The Son has made a house of prayer for all peoples, and he built it with his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teaching daily in the temple. Having driven out the sellers, he stays, teaching every day for the rest of the week (21:37–38), as an owner, not a protester.

The principal men. The temple establishment, the experts in the law, and the leading laymen: between them the entire leadership of the nation, the Sanhedrin.

Were seeking to destroy him. The plot that began in Galilee (6:11; 11:53–54) now becomes determined. The decision has been taken; only the method is outstanding.

Nothing they could do. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him: not because he is hiding, but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds.

Hanging on his words. The verb is exekremato: literally hanging from him, the picture of a crowd leaning in, spellbound. The people protected him, for now. What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly (22:3–6).

He let them have him. The authorities did not overpower him. He walked into that city on a colt he had sent for, cleared the temple and taught in it daily under the eyes of men who could do nothing about it, until the hour came that he had been walking toward since chapter nine, and he let them have him. His death was not a defeat. It was an offering.

In the flow. Luke’s long journey to Jerusalem, begun in 9:51, ends here. In chapter 20 the leaders send question after question, each one a trap, and each answer leaves them silent (20:26, 40).

Why did the same crowd turn against him? Crowds are fickle, and Luke shows it. Many hung on his words for the excitement of a prophet who confounded the leaders, without bowing to him as King. When he did not overthrow Rome, and the leaders worked on them, they turned (23:13–23). It may not have been exactly the same people: the crowd before Pilate gathered early and was stirred up by the leaders (Mark 15:11); but Luke shows the people as a whole drawn into the cry (23:13). It is a warning that enthusiasm for Jesus is not the same as faith in him. Hanging on someone’s words for a week is not the same as building your life on them (6:46–49). The test is what you do when following him becomes costly.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview: Luke 20 is a day of confrontation in the temple during the last week before the cross. The leaders challenge Jesus’ authority, and he answers with a question about John and then with the parable of the tenants, his own account of Israel’s history, his coming death and the judgment on those who reject the cornerstone. Then come the trap questions: tribute to Caesar, and the Sadducees’ riddle about the resurrection. Each is turned back on those who ask it, until no one dares ask more. Jesus then asks his own question, how David can call his son Lord, and ends by warning against scribes who love honour and devour widows’ houses, just before a poor widow gives everything she has (21:1–4).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sanhedrin’s delegation asks by what authority Jesus does these things. The question is fair on its face, but it is a trap with both jaws shut, and entirely about credentials.

Jesus answers with a question about John’s baptism. That is not evasion: the two questions are one, because John had pointed to Jesus, and it offers them a way to the truth without public surrender. Their huddle weighs only consequences, never truth, and they answer that they do not know.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority of Jesus is the central question of the Gospels, and the answer they avoid is that he acts as the Son sent by the Father. Their refusal to judge John is moral, not intellectual. And God does not give further light to those who refuse what they already have (8:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
The manoeuvre survives in every institution, the church included, and it rarely feels like dishonesty from inside. It feels like responsibility: there is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now. The test is what moves first in you when a hard question comes: what is true, or what it will cost.

Jesus is endlessly patient with people who honestly do not know. What he will not join is a conversation designed never to end, where each answer is simply replaced by the next question.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 20 is a day of questions in the temple in the last week before the cross. Israel’s leaders come at Jesus one after another, each with a trap, and each answer reveals more of who he is. Between the traps he tells of tenants who kill the owner’s beloved son, his plainest public claim to be the Son they are about to kill (vv. 9–19), and he ends with the question nobody can answer, how David’s son can be David’s Lord (vv. 41–44). Here is the King in his Father’s house, wiser than all his enemies, walking with open eyes toward the death he has just described.

The setting. These are Jesus’ last days of public teaching. He has entered Jerusalem, wept over the city, cleared the temple and taken up residence in it, while the leaders look for a way to destroy him and cannot (19:45–48).

Preaching the gospel. That is where he is when they come for him: in the temple court, in the middle of a sentence, teaching. The phrase preaching the gospel is Luke’s own addition, his favourite word for announcing good news. Even in the last week, to the very people whose leaders would hand him over, it is gospel.

The chief priests and the scribes. With the elders, they are the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council. This is an official delegation.

By what authority. These things is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means: a king’s entry, the traders thrown out of the building they administered, and the teaching since. The question is not unreasonable on its face. The temple was under the high priest’s authority.

The shape of the trap. Both jaws are shut. If he claims human authority, they can show he has none. If he claims divine authority, they have a charge of blasphemy. And nobody asks whether what he did was right, or whether the trade had crowded out the prayer the court existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials, the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.

Who gave Jesus his authority? The Father did, and the whole Gospel has been answering this question. The voice at his baptism called him the beloved Son (3:22). He forgave sins, and proved his authority to do it by healing a paralysed man (5:24). He commanded demons, winds and death, and they obeyed. He has already said that all things have been handed over to him by his Father (10:22). After his resurrection he will say that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So the question the leaders ask in hostility is the question every reader must ask in earnest, and the answer changes everything. If his authority is from God, then his words are not advice to be weighed but commands to be obeyed, and his promises are as sure as God.

In everyday life. Every life has to settle what the Sanhedrin asked. Most of us accept his authority in general and quietly question it in particular: money, sexuality, time, speech, plans. Find the one area where you most often argue about his credentials when the real issue is that you do not want to change, and settle it with him today.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I also will ask you a question. A normal move in rabbinic debate, and not evasion but precision, because the answer to his question answers theirs.

Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? From heaven means from God. And the two questions are the same question. John’s whole ministry had raised the identical issue: a man with no priestly appointment and no institutional backing, baptising in the Jordan, calling the nation to repent. By what authority? They had faced it once already and had never given an answer. The alternatives are exhaustive. A prophetic ministry is either God’s or it is not, and every person in Israel had already made a private judgment about John.

The connection runs deeper. John had said who Jesus was: he who is mightier than I is coming (3:16), and the voice from heaven had answered their question at the Jordan (3:21–22). If John’s baptism was from heaven, the man John pointed to needs no further credentials.

A generous question. So this is not a clever deflection. It is Jesus offering them the answer, in the one form they could have accepted without losing face: by working it out themselves. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to surrender in public. And notice what the question exposes. He does not ask them about himself. He asks about a matter they had had years to settle, on which the evidence had been public. Their difficulty was never a shortage of information about Jesus of Nazareth. It was what they had already done with the last man God sent.

Is it right for a Christian to answer a question with a question? Sometimes, yes, when it is done as Jesus did it: not to dodge, but to bring the real issue into the light. Many hostile questions rest on a hidden assumption, and a good question can show it gently. If someone asks how you can believe in a God who allows suffering, you might ask what makes them so sure suffering is wrong. But Jesus also answered sincere questions directly and patiently. The skill is to tell the difference, and the aim is always to help the person to the truth, not to win.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it. Luke lets us hear the huddle, and its question is not what is true? but what is safe?

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why did you not believe him? They see the trap instantly, and note what it consists of. Not a logical difficulty, but a personal exposure. They had rejected John (7:30). If John was from God, their failure to receive him is a public fact requiring explanation.

Stone us to death. Only Luke says the fear was of stoning, the penalty for blasphemy and false prophecy. John had been killed by Herod, and the popular verdict on him had hardened into reverence for a martyr. To deny him in a temple court full of Passover pilgrims would have been physically dangerous. The people were convinced, and the leaders were calculating.

Truth is missing. Not one clause in the deliberation considers what John’s baptism actually was. The whole discussion is about consequences. These are the religious leaders of the people of God, in the temple, weighing a question about a prophet, and truth is not a factor.

The listener in the huddle. They spoke among themselves, but not out of his hearing in any sense that mattered. Luke has shown again and again that Jesus knew the reasonings of scribes and Pharisees before they said a word (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). The men calculating what was safe were doing it in the presence of the Mightier One whom John had announced (3:16), the Son on whom the Spirit came down at John’s baptism. Their question was never really about a dead prophet. It was about him, and the one thing they would not weigh was that the truth they were avoiding stood a few feet away and could read them.

How do I know if I am deciding by what is safe rather than what is true? Watch what moves first in you when a hard question arrives. If your first thought is what will people think? or what will this cost me?, you are in the huddle. Other signs: you find yourself changing your answer depending on who is asking; you avoid reading the parts of Scripture that would settle a matter you would rather leave open; you say I am still thinking about it for years. The remedy is to ask God, before anyone else, what is true, and then to trust him with the cost (Proverbs 29:25).

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They did not know. It is almost certainly untrue, and everybody present knows it. They take refuge in an agnosticism they do not hold, the safest position available, because it commits to nothing and cannot be attacked.

The price of the answer. These are the official teachers of Israel, whose duty was to judge true and false prophets, and they have just declared publicly that they cannot tell whether the greatest prophetic movement of their age was from God. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.

Neither will I tell you. The refusal is not petulance. He had made them a real offer, and they declined, not for want of information. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have (8:18).

And yet he does answer. Not in a proposition they can take to court, but in a story, in the very next breath, in which the owner sends his beloved son (v. 13): an answer only an honest heart can receive.

What about people who genuinely do not know? Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience: the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross, the disciples themselves, who ask badly and are answered anyway. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and there are people whose questions are a way of never arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or whether it is simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end. If you are honestly unsure, tell him so, and keep reading what he said. He has never turned away an honest seeker.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus turns to the people and tells a story about their leaders in their hearing. It opens with Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, which ends by naming the vineyard as the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7), so the meaning comes attached. The tenants did not plant or build anything; all of it was handed to them on terms.

The owner sends servant after servant, the prophets, and keeps sending when any landlord would have gone to law. Last he sends his beloved son, the phrase from the voice at the Jordan (3:22), and the tenants throw him out and kill him to keep the inheritance, as Jesus would be crucified outside the city wall (Hebrews 13:12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of Luke’s plainest statements of Jesus’ divine sonship: the son is not one more servant but the heir. Perhaps they will respect him does not mean God did not know; the Son was delivered up according to his definite plan (Acts 2:23). It is the language of a real appeal, leaving the tenants without excuse.

The vineyard given to others is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people, a question Paul answers with by no means (Romans 11:1). The judgment falls on the tenants, the leaders Luke names in verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus answers the crowd’s horror with Psalm 118:22: the experts in stone threw this one out, and God set it at the corner. Verse 18 adds Isaiah’s stone of stumbling and Daniel’s stone that grinds the kingdoms to dust. A man who stumbles on the stone can be mended; one on whom it falls cannot. No one walks past it.

The leaders understood the parable at once and tried to arrest him that hour. Telling people plainly what they are doing does not by itself change their hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the people. The council has just refused to answer him, so he tells the crowd a story about them, in their hearing, and the leaders will understand every word (v. 19).

A man planted a vineyard. Every literate Jew in that court would have heard the quotation. Isaiah’s song of the vineyard tells of a beloved friend who planted choice vines on a very fertile hill, and ends: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7). The parable comes with its identifications attached. God planted his people and did everything to make them fruitful.

Let it out to tenants. The tenants are Israel’s leaders, and the arrangement is ordinary: absentee landlords letting estates for a share of the crop were common in Galilee. But the tenants did not plant the vineyard. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

For a long while. Only Luke adds for a long while: the long centuries of God’s patience with his people.

Some of the fruit. The owner’s share, which was the agreement. The servant is a prophet, sent to call Israel back to fruitfulness.

Sent him away empty-handed. Not a rent dispute: nobody pleads a bad season. It is a declaration, we are not paying, and Israel’s long history of rejecting the prophets (Nehemiah 9:26).

What is the fruit God looks for? The fruit Isaiah’s vineyard should have borne was justice and righteousness (Isaiah 5:7): faith toward God, and lives of love, truth and mercy toward others. It is the fruit John the Baptist demanded (3:8), and the fruit of the Spirit Paul describes (Galatians 5:22–23). It is not a percentage of income or a level of church activity, though both may be part of it. God wants himself acknowledged as owner, and wants the life he has given returned to him in love and obedience. And he is looking for it in every life to which he has given anything.

The storyteller in the story. As the parable opens, nobody in the court yet knows where it is going, but the man telling it does. He is the beloved son who will be sent last, and he is standing in the vineyard as he speaks, in the temple, days before the tenants throw him out. Every servant in the story was sent to collect fruit and was refused. Jesus is about to describe his own coming as the owner’s final appeal and his own death as the tenants’ final answer, and he tells it with the men who will carry it out listening. No prophet ever told his own story like that. Only the Son could.

In everyday life. God looks for fruit from what he has given you, and fruit is not squeezed out by effort: it grows from the Spirit he gives to those joined to his Son (Galatians 5:22). Pick one gift, time, money, an ability, a relationship, and offer its fruit to him deliberately this week, as a thank-offering to the owner who gave it.
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
