Another servant. Beaten; then beaten and treated shamefully, publicly humiliated, which in that culture was the worse injury. Each envoy is treated worse than the last, and the tenants grow bolder because nothing has happened to them.

Yet a third. In Luke’s telling no servant is killed until the son, which makes the son’s death the climax.

The sending. A landlord with any sense would have gone to law after the first assault. This one sends a second servant, then a third. It is the patience of God set out as a plot: he keeps sending because what he wants is not damages but his tenants back.

The history in three sentences. The whole tragic history of Israel and the men God sent to it is put into three sentences: the LORD kept sending his messengers out of compassion for his people, and they kept mocking them and scoffing at his prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD, on this same site (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). The men listening were hearing their own history read back to them.

The ownership is the problem. The tenants do not argue with the owner or try to renegotiate. They simply will not have anyone come from him. The messenger is attacked before the message is heard, because the message is not the problem. The ownership is.

How often would I. The patience in this parable has a face. Only a little earlier on the road Jesus had cried, O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (13:34). How often would I: he speaks of the city’s whole history as one who had been reaching for it all along. Father and Son share one heart toward the rebellious vineyard, and the patience that kept sending prophets now stands in the temple court in person, telling the tenants their own story one last time.

Why is God so patient? Because patience belongs to his very name: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). He is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). His long sending is not weakness, and it is not that he does not care. Every servant sent was another invitation, and it left the tenants more and more without excuse. If God has been patient with you, through years of half-hearted faith or outright rebellion, it is not because he does not care. It is because he has been sending, again and again, to bring you home.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the owner of the vineyard said, What shall I do? Only Luke records this deliberation. The question is not helplessness; it is deliberation made audible. The owner has exhausted the ordinary options and is deciding. Here is the heart of God, pondering how to reach his rebellious people.

I will send my beloved son. Every word has been chosen. My beloved son is ton huion mou ton agapēton, the very words spoken from heaven at the Jordan: you are my beloved Son (3:22), close kin to the voice from the cloud on the mountain, this is my Son, my Chosen One (9:35). There is no possibility that Luke’s readers, or the men in the courtyard, are meant to miss it. And so Jesus answers the question of his authority after all. He is not another servant. He is the beloved Son. And the logic is a father’s rather than a landlord’s. He has run out of servants, and he will send the one person he cannot replace.

Perhaps they will respect him. Was heaven hoping for an outcome it could not foresee? But the same Luke records that the Son was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has told his disciples three times how this would end.

Did God not know what would happen? He knew. The perhaps is spoken from the owner’s side of the story, the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last was the owner’s own beloved son, and that their rejection was therefore without excuse. God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway. That is not a father caught out. It is a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was not knocked upon. It is the extraordinary hope of love.

Let us kill him. They recognise him, and they kill him for that reason. Remove the owner’s representative and the property is ours. It is what the serpent offered in a garden: you will be like God. And Jesus foretells his own death to their faces, days before it happens.

Did the leaders know Jesus was the Son of God? Not in the full sense, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8; Acts 3:17). But they knew enough. They saw his works, heard his claims and understood this parable (v. 19), and their opposition was not ignorance but refusal. In the parable they recognise the heir and kill him because he is the heir. That is the heart of all unbelief: not a lack of evidence, but an unwillingness to let God be God. People do not reject Christ because they cannot see who he is, but because they see enough to know he would claim them. That is the root Scripture names; it does not make every honest doubter a liar, and Jesus was patient with real doubt, as he was with Thomas (John 20:27).

In everyday life. Where are you saying, in small ways, let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours? It is the impulse to enjoy God’s gifts, family, career, health, comfort, while keeping the Giver at the edge. Name one gift you treat as your own, and give thanks to the owner for it today.

For worship. The Father asked, What shall I do? and the answer emptied heaven of its dearest treasure. He sent the Son he loved into the hands of those who would kill him, so that the death they meant as a theft of the inheritance became the way the inheritance was given away. The heir they killed has made heirs of rebels (Romans 8:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Threw him out and killed him. Cast out first, then killed: Mark puts the killing first; Luke keeps the sequence of what was about to happen, for Jesus was crucified beyond the city wall. Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12–13).

What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He asks the crowd for the verdict. In Matthew’s telling the hearers supply the answer and condemn themselves out of their own mouths; here Jesus gives it, and the effect is the same.

Destroy those tenants. Judgment on the leaders, and it landed within a generation, in AD 70 (19:41–44).

To others. The tenancy is transferred: to the apostles whom Christ appoints over his people, and through them to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). The vineyard is not destroyed. It is now gathered from every nation, Jew and Gentile together in Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22), and that would have been the most offensive part of the story.

Surely not! Only Luke records it: literally may it not be!, the phrase Paul uses again and again in Romans. The crowd has understood, and the thought is unbearable. Within days a crowd in this city will call for the death of the son and get it.

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No, and this parable has been misused to say so. Paul, writing after the resurrection, asks exactly this question: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Romans 11:1). The tenants in the parable are the leaders, and the men Jesus is looking at are named in v. 19. Many Jews believed: the apostles, the first church of thousands in Jerusalem, Paul himself. Christians differ on what Romans 11 expects for the Jewish people in the future. Some look for a great turning of Israel to Christ before his return; others understand all Israel as the whole number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles. All agree that there is one vineyard and one way into it, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians should long and pray for Jewish people to come to him.

In the flow. These verses answer the question that opened the chapter (v. 2): he is the owner’s beloved son. And the vineyard given to others is the story Luke goes on to tell in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he looked directly at them. The verb means to fix the eyes on someone, the word used of Jesus looking at Peter after the rooster crowed (22:61). The parable was told to the people; the look is for the men who came with the question, and it could have broken a heart open.

The stone that the builders rejected. If judgment on Israel cannot happen, as the crowd has just cried, what then is this that is written? He answers from Psalm 118:22. His disciples had sung from the same psalm on the descent of Olivet, hailing the King (Psalm 118:26; 19:38). Now he hands the same hymn, four verses earlier, to the authorities.

The builders and the stone. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so that everything built after it is squared by it: the most important stone in the building. The picture is of professionals doing their job. Men whose whole competence is judging stone look at this one, assess it, and throw it on the discard pile as unfit. That is exactly what was happening in that courtyard. The chief priests and scribes were the builders, trained and appointed to recognise what God was doing. They examined the stone, and their professional judgment was that it would not do.

Has become the cornerstone. Then the turn. Not somebody else used it. It was taken up and set at the corner by an authority above the builders, and their verdict was simply overruled. This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes, the psalm goes on (Psalm 118:23). It was fulfilled in the resurrection. The early church seized on this verse and could not let it go. Peter quotes it to the Sanhedrin itself (Acts 4:10–12) and again in his letter (1 Peter 2:4–8). It became the standard text for what the resurrection did to Friday’s verdict.

Why does it matter that the experts rejected him? Because it means the verdict of the experts is not the last word. In every generation scholars, institutions and cultured voices have looked at Jesus and set him aside, and some Christians are shaken by it. This verse expected it. The rejection of the stone by the builders is part of the prophecy, not a refutation of it. God has always overruled the builders. The question is not what the professionals think of Christ, but what God has done with him: he raised him and set him at the corner, and everything is now squared by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Broken to pieces. The image turns twice, and both halves come from the prophets. Isaiah had said the LORD would be a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and many shall stumble on it, they shall fall and be broken (Isaiah 8:14–15).

It will crush him. Daniel had seen a stone cut out by no human hand grinding the statue of the world’s kingdoms to dust and becoming a mountain that filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45). The verb means to winnow, to reduce to dust and blow away.

Broken or crushed. To fall on the stone is to trip over it. That is survivable: broken things can be mended, and Saul of Tarsus fell on this stone on the Damascus road and rose an apostle. When the stone falls, it is the last day, and there is nothing left to mend.

The point. No one can be neutral toward Jesus. This stone can be built on, tripped over or fallen under, and there is no fourth option. Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 21:44), though some manuscripts lack it there.

If I have stumbled over Jesus, is it too late? No. The men listening had already stumbled, and what the sentence holds out, terribly and graciously, is that a stumble is not yet the end. Many who once mocked Christ, or walked away, have been broken by him and then healed by him. Peter preached to the very builders who rejected the stone, and thousands of them believed (Acts 2:36–41). But there is a day coming when the stone is no longer lying in the road. The time to fall on him in repentance is now, before he falls in judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very hour. They have just heard a story in which tenants kill the owner’s son, been told it is about them, and their response is to try to arrest the son on the spot. The parable is being fulfilled in the hearing of the parable.

Against them. They understood it, and it settles something about the parables: they are not a code only insiders can break. Their problem was not understanding. It was the will.

Why does God not simply tell people plainly what they are doing? He did. There is no gentler or clearer way to say you are about to kill me and you will be judged for it than the story he had just told, and it produced a decision to do it sooner. Clarity alone does not change a heart. Only the Spirit of God, opening blind eyes and giving a new heart, can do that (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why we pray as well as speak when we share the gospel.

They feared the people. Luke has now said this three times in two chapters (19:48; 20:6). The fear running the council is not the fear of God, which would have stopped them entirely, but the fear of a riot and of losing position. It will govern the decision they finally take, to arrange the arrest away from the crowd (22:6).

In the flow. The first round of the day’s contest ends here. The parable’s warning is answered not with repentance but with a new plan: spies (v. 20).

In everyday life. Notice your reaction the next time a sermon or a passage of Scripture lands too close: is it humility, or anger at the preacher? Ask God for a soft heart, and when the word cuts, say yes to it before you say anything else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — The Question about Tribute to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The direct approach has failed, so the leaders send spies posing as sincere enquirers, aiming for a political charge the governor would act on. Their flattery is a fence: having praised him for showing no partiality, they ask whether it is lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, the hated poll tax. Yes would lose the crowd; no would hand them a charge for Pilate, the very charge they later bring falsely (23:2).

Jesus asks for a denarius, and they produce one in the temple, bearing Tiberius’s portrait and a claim to divinity. The trap is sprung without a word of doctrine.
verseByVerse.theology: Render means pay what is owed. Civil authority is real, and taxes are its due (Romans 13:1–7). But the weight falls on the second half. If the coin bears Caesar’s image and belongs to Caesar, what bears God’s image? Every listener knew: man (Genesis 1:27). Caesar may have the coin, and nothing that belongs to God: not worship, not conscience, not a life’s final allegiance. God claims the whole person, because his image is not stamped on part of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian facing a law he thinks unjust can reason from this: the state has a real but limited sphere, and the question is whether a particular demand crosses into what belongs to God alone.

They marvelled at his answer and fell silent, and that week they had him killed. It is possible to admire the truth and stay unmoved by it, and a good answer, though Christians should give one (1 Peter 3:15), does not on its own change a heart.

verseByVerse.quote: So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him, 'Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spies. The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. Spies is enkathetous, men hired and planted, and they pretended to be sincere: actors playing devout enquirers, hypocrites in the old sense of the word.

To the governor. Only Luke states their aim so plainly. They want a political charge that Rome will act on, and Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

We know that you speak rightly. The flattery is thick, and it is a trap in itself. They are not merely being pleasant; they are building a fence. If he is a man who shows no partiality, he cannot now give a diplomatic answer. They have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question. And the terrible thing about the compliment is that every word of it is true. He does speak rightly, he does show no partiality, he does teach the way of God. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is possible only for people who know well enough who he is and have decided against him anyway.

Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not? The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, paid directly to Rome by every adult in Judea since it became a Roman province in AD 6, and bitterly resented. It had provoked the armed revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). So the question is live and dangerous. Say yes, and he endorses the occupation in front of a Passover crowd of patriots and loses them. Say no, and there are witnesses standing ready to report a man inciting tax refusal to Pilate. And the irony is that they will bring exactly that charge anyway, falsely: we found this man forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar (23:2).

How should a Christian respond to flattery? With gratitude for kindness, and with a guarded heart. Flattery is praise with a purpose: it wants something from you, and it is often the prelude to a request you would otherwise refuse (Proverbs 29:5). Jesus was not moved by it at all, because he did not live for human approval (John 5:41). The more you need to be thought well of, the easier you are to manipulate. So when someone praises you before asking something hard, pause, pray, and answer the request on its merits, not on the warmth of the introduction.
verseByVerse.note: The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason before the governor.

parallels.desc: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, 'Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?' They said, 'Caesar's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their craftiness. The word is the quality Paul ties to the serpent in Eden (2 Corinthians 11:3). The one who knows what is in man (John 2:25) sees through the actors at once.

Show me a denarius. He does not answer. He asks them for a coin, and somebody produces one immediately, in the temple. The man they are trying to trap on taxation has the currency produced by his accusers.

Whose likeness and inscription does it have? That matters more than it looks. The denarius was a silver coin bearing the head of the emperor Tiberius, and around the head an inscription calling him Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, with the title high priest on the reverse. It was a portrait, which strict Jews regarded as a graven image forbidden by the second commandment, and it carried a claim to divinity in writing. The men who had come to catch him on a point of faithfulness to God were carrying it in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds.

Caesar’s. The only possible answer, and it concedes the whole question. They are in Caesar’s economy and using his money, and a man who uses a currency, and benefits from the roads, order and trade it pays for, has accepted the authority that mints it.

The method. The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, and they have been made to say the awkward thing themselves. Christians in hostile conversations reach for the wrong tool almost every time. He does not find a form of words careful enough to survive being quoted. He asks for an object and asks what is written on it. Nothing has been conceded and nobody has been insulted.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and his titles.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Render to Caesar. The verb is apodote: pay back, hand over what is due, the language of a debt settled rather than a gift made. If the coin carries Caesar’s face, giving it to him is not a betrayal of God; it is returning what is his. Civil authority is legitimate. Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul will develop it at length: let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and pay to all what is owed to them, taxes to whom taxes are owed (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17).

To God the things that are God’s. The weight falls on this second half. Jesus has just made ownership a matter of image: whose likeness and inscription does it bear? The clause leaves a second question hanging in the air: what bears the image of God? Every listener knew the answer from the first page of the Scriptures. God created man in his own image (Genesis 1:26–27). The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

A far larger answer. That makes this a far larger answer than the tax question deserved. Caesar may have the metal; he has a genuine claim, and it is limited to things with his face on them. God’s claim is on the person, and not on a portion of the person, because the image is not stamped on part of a man. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, wholly. What does that mean in practice? It means that no part of you is private property kept back from him: not your body, your money, your ambitions or your thoughts, for you are not your own; you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). And Caesar’s claims are bounded by God’s. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. The moment he asks for what belongs to God, worship, conscience, the ultimate allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his, and the answer is the apostles’: we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The verse also exposes two idols of the heart. Some make Caesar their saviour, hoping that the right ruler or party will finally put the world right; others make Caesar’s coin their security. Jesus gives each its proper place, and neither is God.

The Image who rendered everything. Only one man has ever given God all that is God’s. He is himself the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and within days he would hand over the last thing a man has: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). The coin went to Caesar; the Son gave himself to God, entire, and by that offering he redeems those who have kept back from God what was always his.

Where Christians differ: how do the two claims relate? Some have read this verse as dividing life into two equal and separate realms, a sacred one where God rules and a secular one where the state rules, each sovereign in its own sphere and neither answerable to the other. Others read it as placing Caesar’s realm inside God’s: the state has real authority, but only as a servant of God, accountable to him and limited by his law. This commentary’s view: Jesus does not make God and Caesar equal partners. All authority is under God; the governing authorities exist because God has instituted them (Romans 13:1), and even Pilate had no authority except what was given from above (John 19:11). Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers, praying for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), but their final loyalty is to God alone.

What if my government uses my taxes for things I believe are wrong? Pay them anyway, as a rule. The tax Jesus told them to pay funded a pagan empire that crucified people, kept armies of occupation and supported idol temples, and Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. The responsibility for misuse lies with those who spend the money, not with the citizen who obeys God by paying what is owed. Use every lawful means to work for justice: vote, write, speak, protest peacefully. The line is crossed only when the state commands you yourself to do what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. Then obey God, and accept the consequences without violence.

In everyday life. Pay your taxes honestly: no cash-in-hand work kept off the books, no invented expenses. That is rendering to Caesar. Then begin the morning by offering yourself to God, by the mercies of God (Romans 12:1), and end it by asking where you kept something back. You will always find something; but the Son rendered himself to God entire in your place, his obedience is counted as yours, and your halting offering is accepted for his sake.

For worship. When sin defaced God’s image in us, the Maker did not throw the coin away. He came to recover it himself, and he is renewing his people after the image of their Creator (Colossians 3:10). Caesar’s coins wore thin within a generation; every one of his people is his twice over, by making and by purchase.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of the people. They needed witnesses to a seditious answer, and instead they have witnesses to a devastating one. It is the second failed attempt in this chapter, and a third is coming.

They became silent. Marvelling is the surprising word. These men had rehearsed the flattery and framed a question with no safe answer, and when the answer came, something in them responded to it.

Marvelling in the temple again. When Jesus was twelve he sat in this same temple among the teachers, and all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers (2:46–47). Now the teachers of Israel are amazed again, against their will. The wisdom has not changed; only their hearts have.

Admiration is not faith. It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it. Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8–9). Agrippa asked Paul whether in so short a time he would persuade him to be a Christian (Acts 26:28). There is a way of appreciating an answer that works as a substitute for obeying it. They became silent. Not persuaded: silenced. And the silence is not repentance. It is the end of a line of attack, and they will send the Sadducees in next.

Why did the best answer not convert them? Because the problem was never the quality of the answers. Set this beside v. 7, where the same men said we do not know. Twice now this delegation has been reduced to saying nothing, once by choosing not to answer and once by having nothing left to say. There is a hard lesson in that for anyone who assumes that a good enough answer will settle the matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed that week. Answers matter, and Christians should give them well (1 Peter 3:15). But only God can change a heart that does not want to be changed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–47 — Sadducees on Resurrection, the Son of David, and Scribal Warning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who denied the resurrection (Acts 23:8), turn the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), a good law meant to protect a widow, into a joke about seven brothers in which the woman is nameless property. Their argument assumes that the age to come is this age made permanent, and Jesus answers by dismantling that premise, then proves the resurrection from Moses himself.

The scribes commend him and no one dares ask more. Jesus asks his own question about Psalm 110 and ends with a warning about the scribes.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage does not continue because death does not continue: where no one dies, no one needs to be born to replace them. Equal to angels means deathless, not bodiless.

At the bush God says I am the God of Abraham, centuries after Abraham’s burial, and to be someone’s God is to be bound to him by covenant and promise. Either the covenant is with dust, or Abraham lives. The argument rests not on anything in us but on God’s faithfulness: all live to him.

In Psalm 110 David calls his descendant my Lord, which in a world where honour ran upward is impossible unless the son is more than a son. Luke has answered the riddle since his first chapter: David’s son by birth, and the Son of God (1:32–35).
verseByVerse.examples:
The widow who has buried a husband of forty years may read neither marry nor are given in marriage and fear she will lose him. Jesus says the institution ends, not the people or the love. Marriage was a signpost to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32), and what waits at the end is a wedding (Revelation 19:6–9).

The chapter ends with predation. The scribes’ long prayers are the instrument of their theft from widows. Scripture keeps its severest language for those who use the things of God to get things from people, and Luke turns at once to a widow giving all she had (21:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, 'Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some Sadducees. The third delegation of the day. The Sadducees were the priestly, aristocratic party, the men who controlled the temple and managed the relationship with Rome: fewer than the Pharisees and far more powerful. They seem to have accepted the five books of Moses as fully authoritative and treated the rest of the Scriptures as secondary.

Deny that there is a resurrection. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8), on the ground that these are not in the Pentateuch. So rather than answer from Daniel 12, which teaches the resurrection plainly, Jesus meets them in Moses.

Moses wrote for us. The law is real. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 provides that if a married man dies childless, his brother should marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man’s name and inherit his portion, so that no family line was blotted out and the land stayed with the family. A related custom lies behind the book of Ruth, and through it comes the line of David and of Christ. It is a good and compassionate law.

A true text used falsely. Every word of their citation is accurate. They are using a true text, pushed to an extreme its author never envisaged, to make a doctrine they dislike look ridiculous, a technique available to anybody with a Bible and a grievance.

Is belief in the resurrection not just wishful thinking? The Sadducees thought so, and they were the educated sceptics of their day. But the first Christians were not people inclined to believe it. When the women reported the empty tomb, the apostles thought their words an idle tale and did not believe them (24:11). What changed their minds was not a hope but an event: a tomb that was empty, and a Lord who was seen, heard and touched, by Peter, by the Twelve and by more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Paul passes that list on as something he had himself received, a summary most scholars date to within a few years of the events, not a legend grown up long afterwards. Christian hope does not rest on what we would like to be true. It rests on what happened outside Jerusalem on the third day.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven brothers. The case is constructed, not reported: probably a standard argument used to ridicule the Pharisees’ belief in the resurrection, with seven chosen to make the situation as absurd as possible.

What the story does to the woman. Nobody in the story has a name, but the brothers are at least counted, first, second, third; she is not even that, and she is given no words. She exists in the riddle purely as a piece of contested property, the thing seven men had a claim on. And the question at the end is not what became of her? but whose wife will the woman be? That tells you something about the men asking. They have taken a law given to protect a widow and used it to build a puzzle in which the widow is an object.

In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife. There is the question, with its last clause driving the point home. The argument underneath is a reductio: if the resurrection were true, and Moses’ law were true, you would end up with an insoluble situation in the age to come; therefore the resurrection cannot be true. Moses could not have believed in it.

The hidden assumption. The argument rests on one assumption the Sadducees have never noticed they are making: that the age to come is this age carried on, the same arrangements, only permanent. Jesus is not going to tell them which brother gets her. He is going to dismantle the premise, and the puzzle will go with it.

Seven graves and an empty tomb. The riddle is made of seven funerals and then an eighth, offered as the last word on human life. But they put it to the one man in history who would not stay in a grave. Within the week Jesus would die and rise, so that by dying he might break the power of the one who held the power of death (Hebrews 2:14–15). The chain of graves in their story was about to be broken from the inside.

In everyday life. When an argument against the faith seems unanswerable, look for what it takes for granted: that God is like us, that the future must be like the present, that what we cannot imagine cannot be. And never let a debate about doctrine make you careless of the people it concerns. The woman was a person, not a puzzle.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of this age. He names a category the Sadducees did not have: this age and that age. Marriage is good, given by God in Eden, and it belongs to the first.

Considered worthy. Only Luke has this fuller form. Considered worthy is a verdict God gives, through grace, not a merit earned (2 Thessalonians 1:5). Resurrection life is not this life continued.

They cannot die anymore. Only Luke gives the reason. Where people die, people must be born, and the institution that provides for that is marriage. Remove death and that purpose is no longer needed, the way scaffolding is no longer needed once the building stands. The Sadducees’ whole puzzle falls apart.

Equal to angels. Like angels, immortal, not disembodied. The resurrection is of the body, and Luke’s last chapter has the risen Christ eating broiled fish to prove it (24:39–43).

Sons of the resurrection. Children of God by resurrection, sharing his life. We wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23), and when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). Believers are God’s children already, by adoption, welcomed into his family through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:26; 4:4–7). The resurrection will make it visible: the family likeness, now hidden and half-formed, will be complete in body and soul, and no one will be able to mistake whose children they are.

Who are those who are considered worthy? Jesus is speaking of the resurrection to life of God’s people, those whom God counts worthy through faith in Christ. Elsewhere he says that all the dead will rise, those who have done good to the resurrection of life and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). No one is worthy in himself. The worthiness is Christ’s, credited to those who trust him.

What it does not mean. All of this is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, and she reads neither marry nor are given in marriage and hears the one thing she was most afraid of: that she will not have him again. So let the verse be read to her properly, because it does not say that. Jesus says the institution ends: the marrying, the giving in marriage, the arrangement by which this age replaces its dead. He does not say the people end, and he does not say the love ends. Married love is not lost or forgotten; it is taken up into something greater. You will not know your husband less there. You will know him better than you ever managed here, without the tiredness and the half-attention that got between you every day of the forty years.

Marriage was a signpost. Marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: the one-flesh union of husband and wife is a profound mystery, and it speaks of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. And what waits at the end of this age is a wedding: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:6–9). Marriage does not carry over into that day, not because it was too much but because it was the picture, and that is the reality.

What about those who never married, or whose marriages were unhappy? This verse is good news for them too. The single believer is not missing out on the final reality; he or she is heading for the same wedding as everyone else, the marriage of Christ and his church, and will lack nothing there. Jesus himself never married. And for those whose marriages were marked by pain, or by a spouse who did not believe, the age to come will not prolong what was broken. Every relationship will be healed in its proper place, and every believer will be satisfied in Christ.

In everyday life. If you are married, love your spouse today as a signpost to Christ: serve, forgive and speak kindly, because your marriage is preaching a sermon about him and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Moses showed. Having dismantled the riddle, he proves the doctrine on their ground: Moses, at the burning bush (Exodus 3). Before chapter and verse numbers existed, passages were located by their subject like this.

The God of the patriarchs. In Exodus 3:6, spoken centuries after the patriarchs died, God introduces himself by naming his relationship to three men long dead.

Not God of the dead. The argument turns on the relationship. God does not say, I was the God of Abraham. He says, I am the God of your father, centuries after Abraham was buried at Machpelah. Now, what does it mean to be somebody’s God? It is covenant language. It means to have bound yourself to a person: to be his shield and his very great reward, to have promised him a future (Genesis 15:1; 17:7). So if God is still Abraham’s God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive. A covenant relationship with God cannot be broken by death. If God is their God, they live to him, and he will keep his promises to them, body and soul.

The ground of hope is in God. The argument rests not on the immortality of the soul, which Scripture teaches elsewhere (Matthew 10:28), nor on the resilience of the human spirit, but on the character of God. He does not bind himself to a man and then let death end it. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us. It is something in him.

All live to him. Only Luke adds this, and it carries great comfort: those who have died in the Lord are alive to God now (23:43; Philippians 1:23). Nobody who belonged to him has ever been lost track of, and the graves of the patriarchs did not interrupt a single conversation.

The God of Abraham raised his servant Jesus. Within weeks Peter stood in this same temple, in Solomon’s Portico, and used the very words of the bush. The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, he said, had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they had killed and God had raised from the dead (Acts 3:13–15). The argument Jesus made to the Sadducees from Moses was answered in his own body. The covenant God who will not be the God of dead men did not leave his Son among the dead. On Easter morning the angels asked the women why they were seeking the living among the dead (24:5), and the first fruits of the resurrection Jesus defended in the temple was Jesus himself.

Are the dead asleep until the resurrection? Not in the sense of being unconscious. Scripture uses sleep as a gentle picture of the believer’s death, because the body rests and will wake (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the person is not extinguished or unaware. Jesus told the dying thief that today he would be with him in paradise (23:43); Paul said to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). So the believer who dies goes at once, consciously, into the presence of the Lord, and waits there with joy for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no purgatory in between. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers are first purified there; but Scripture speaks of the believer going straight to be with Christ, because by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). All live to him.

For worship. Blessed is the God of the living. He called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob over their graves, and he calls himself the God of his people over theirs. The God who spoke from the bush that burned and was not consumed keeps his own through the fire of death, and will raise them on the last day.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes answered, 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For they no longer dared to ask him any question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have spoken well. Only Luke places it here (compare Mark 12:28, 32). These are scribes, many of them Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection and have just watched a rival party demolished on it.

The approval of those who agreed. It is genuine as far as it goes. Not you are the Christ. Not even we will follow you. It is the approval of men who agreed with the conclusion. They came to this chapter to destroy him, and here they are commending him, because on this particular point he was on their side. That is a familiar thing, and it is not the same as faith. A person can be delighted by a preacher who demolishes a position he already disliked, and walk out having received nothing at all. The test of whether a person is listening to Christ is not whether he applauds when Christ attacks somebody else. The scribes are back within two chapters, seeking how to put him to death (22:2).

They no longer dared. The verdict covers all three delegations. The chief priests ended by saying, we do not know; the spies became silent; the Sadducees are not recorded as replying at all. After the third nobody would risk a fourth.

Nobody defeated him in argument. What is left is the arrest, at night, with a bribe, away from the crowd. What happened to him that Friday did not happen because the case against him was strong.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is David's son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them, How can they say that the Christ is David’s son? Now he asks. Three delegations have questioned him and failed. He has one question of his own, the decisive one, and it is about who he is. Note first that he is not denying the premise. That the Messiah would be a descendant of David was not a rabbinic guess but a promise: I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16); there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). A blind beggar had been shouting Son of David at him outside Jericho (18:38). So the question is not whether the Christ is David’s son. It is whether that is the whole of it.

David himself says. The quotation is Psalm 110:1, in Jesus’ day widely taken to be David’s and about the Messiah, and the argument depends on both. Many modern scholars doubt that David wrote it; but the heading names him, Jesus’ hearers did not dispute it, and Jesus builds on it with full confidence. It became the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13).

The Lord said to my Lord. In the Hebrew the first word is the covenant name of God, Yahweh, printed LORD in small capitals; the second is adoni, my lord, a word for a master. God speaks to David’s Lord.

Sit at my right hand. An invitation to share the throne of God, extended to a figure distinct from the speaker: the place where the authority is exercised. Every scribe in the courtyard could recite it. What was missing was not information.

Gabriel had already answered it. The reader of Luke does not have to wait for the riddle to be solved, because the angel solved it in the first chapter. Gabriel told Mary that her son would be given the throne of his father David, and in the same breath that he would be called the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit and so called holy, the Son of God (1:32–35). He is David’s son by human birth, born into David’s house (1:27). He is David’s Lord because he is the eternal Son of God. That is how David could call his own descendant Lord: the child of Mary was the Lord whom David worshipped, come in David’s flesh.

In everyday life. Is your view of Jesus too small? You can believe true things about him, a good teacher, a helper in trouble, and still believe too little. Read Psalm 110 this week and let it change how you pray: not timidly, as to a distant friend, but boldly, as to the reigning King.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.’ David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your footstool. The image is from the ancient world’s pictures of conquest: Joshua had the commanders of Israel put their feet on the necks of five kings (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet; the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). Until does not mean his reign then ends; of his kingdom there will be no end (1:33).

David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son? There is the question, and its whole weight rests on a social fact so obvious that nobody in that courtyard needed it explained. In that world, honour ran upward. A son honoured his father; a descendant honoured his ancestor. A father did not call his son lord, and the further back the ancestor, the greater the honour due. David was the greatest king Israel ever had, and every Jew traced honour toward him. So a psalm in which David calls his own descendant my Lord is upside down. It cannot happen, unless the descendant is something more than a descendant. If David calls the Messiah Lord, the Messiah must be greater than David.

The answer. Jesus does not supply it, but every reader of this Gospel has had it since chapter one. Paul states it in two halves: descended from David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:3–4). Jesus is pointing to himself.

A true expectation that is too small. The scribes had a Messiah who was David’s son and nothing more. Their expectation was true and too small, and a man with an expectation like that will reject the reality when it arrives, because it does not fit.

Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man? Because only such a Saviour could save us: as man he could take our place and die our death; as God his obedience and death have infinite worth and he conquers death. (See Matthew 22:45 for the fuller answer.)

For worship. Jesus is both David’s son and David’s Lord, the root and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16). Every grave of every believer is on the list of things he will put under his feet, and the King who has already risen will see to every one.
verseByVerse.note: A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool — a picture of total victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, 'Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the hearing of all the people. The words are addressed to his disciples in the hearing of all the people: a warning given to one group in front of another, so that both hear it.

Beware of the scribes. The scribes were the Bible teachers, whom ordinary people assumed were the most reliable guides available. He tells the crowd to be careful of them, a warning against their example, as at the Pharisee’s table (11:43).

Long robes. Four marks follow, all about being seen. The long robes marked men of learning and rank, and they walk around in them: not wearing one to a function but promenading.

Love greetings. The respectful titles due to a teacher, paid in the open square. Not receive greetings, which they could not help, but love them.

The best seats. The bench at the front, facing the congregation, and the couches nearest the host, which Jesus had watched guests scrambling for at a Pharisee’s dinner (14:7).

The appetite to be seen. Not one of these is a sin in itself. What is diagnosed, four times over, is an appetite for being looked at while being religious. Any position in which a person is watched being godly carries it, and it does not announce itself. It feels like enjoying one’s work.

The Teacher who took the lowest place. He had said that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (14:11), and within days he would take the lowest place there is, numbered with the transgressors (22:37), and God would raise him to the highest. Every scribe who loved the best seat stood before the only one who deserved it, and who gave it up.

Is it wrong for church leaders to have titles or be honoured? Not in itself. Scripture tells churches to respect and honour those who labour among them, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; 1 Timothy 5:17). The sin is in loving the honour. Leaders should test themselves: would I be content to serve unseen? Do I resent it when I am not thanked? And churches should guard their leaders, not feeding vanity with flattery, but praying for them and holding them to the example of Christ, who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45).

In everyday life. Watch your heart for the love of recognition, especially if you serve in church: the small pleasure when your name is mentioned from the front, and the small sting when it is not. Do one piece of service this week that no one will know about.

For worship. Only once in the Gospel is Jesus dressed in a splendid robe, and it is put on him in mockery (23:11). The only man with a right to the long robe and the first greeting wore one as a joke and went on to the cross without complaint.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who devour widows’ houses. The register changes completely. Long robes and good seats are vanity; this is predation. How did scribes devour widows’ houses? Scripture does not say, and several means were available in that world. Scribes were not supposed to charge for teaching the law, and so depended on the hospitality and gifts of the devout, of whom widows were a notably generous group. A scribe might be appointed to manage a widow’s estate and take a fee from it, or manage it dishonestly. He might accept board and lodging from a woman who could not afford it. He might simply encourage a level of giving that ruined her. What all of these have in common is that none is illegal. They are the abuse of religious standing to extract money from people who trusted the standing.

The most vulnerable. Widows had no earning power, little legal protection and nobody to complain to, and God’s law had singled them out for that reason: you shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child; if you do mistreat them, my wrath will burn (Exodus 22:22–24). These are the men entrusted with teaching that law.

For a pretense. The long prayers are not a separate failing; they are the instrument. The reputation for piety gets a man access to a widow’s confidence and her accounts.

The greater condemnation. The principle has run through this Gospel since chapter twelve: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:47–48). The sentence is heavier because the position was higher, the knowledge greater, and the trust betrayed deeper, and because they used religion to cover their sin. Not many of you should become teachers, James warns, for we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1). There are degrees of punishment as there are degrees of reward, and Scripture reserves its severest language for those who use the things of God to get things from people.

The link. Luke sets the next scene immediately: a poor widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1–4). The chapter that began with the leaders questioning Christ’s authority ends with Christ exposing theirs.

What if this has happened in my church? Then it must be named and dealt with, not hidden. When a leader has used his position to exploit the vulnerable, whether financially, emotionally or sexually, the church’s duty is to protect the victims, tell the truth, involve the civil authorities where the law has been broken, and remove the offender from leadership (1 Timothy 5:19–21). Protecting the institution’s reputation at the victims’ expense is to repeat the scribes’ sin. And if you have been harmed by someone who used God’s name to do it, know that Christ is not on their side. He saw the widows, and he warned the whole temple about the men who devoured them.

Does hypocrisy in the church not prove that Christianity is false? No. It shows that Jesus was right. Nobody has ever condemned religious hypocrisy more severely than he did, here in the temple, in front of the very men who practised it. The gospel never claimed that religious people are good. It claims that all of us, scribes and sinners together, the respectable and the disreputable, need a Saviour, and that this Saviour takes the side of those whom the powerful have used. So the answer to a hypocrite in the pulpit is not to walk away from Christ, but to come closer to the one who saw through the scribes and still went to the cross for sinners.

In everyday life. Is there any place where your reputation for being a Christian gives you an advantage over someone weaker: an elderly relative’s finances, an employee who trusts you? Handle it as before God. And look out for the widows of your church: visit, help, make sure no one is exploiting them.

For worship. God is the defender of widows and the father of the fatherless (Psalm 68:5). And his Son is the true High Priest, who does not devour the houses of the poor but gave his own life for them, and whose prayers for his people are never a pretence (Hebrews 7:25).

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

20.text: <sup>1</sup> One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up <sup>2</sup> and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.” <sup>3</sup> He answered them, “I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, <sup>4</sup> was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?” <sup>5</sup> And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ <sup>6</sup> But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” <sup>7</sup> So they answered that they did not know where it came from. <sup>8</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” <sup>9</sup> And he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. <sup>10</sup> When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>11</sup> And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>12</sup> And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. <sup>13</sup> Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ <sup>14</sup> But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ <sup>15</sup> And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? <sup>16</sup> He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “Surely not!” <sup>17</sup> But he looked directly at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? <sup>18</sup> Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>19</sup> The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people. <sup>20</sup> So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. <sup>21</sup> So they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. <sup>22</sup> Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” <sup>23</sup> But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?” They said, “Caesar's.” <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.” <sup>26</sup> And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent. <sup>27</sup> There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, <sup>28</sup> and they asked him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>29</sup> Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. <sup>30</sup> And the second <sup>31</sup> and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. <sup>32</sup> Afterward the woman also died. <sup>33</sup> In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, <sup>35</sup> but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, <sup>36</sup> for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. <sup>37</sup> But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. <sup>38</sup> Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.” <sup>39</sup> Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” <sup>40</sup> For they no longer dared to ask him any question. <sup>41</sup> But he said to them, “How can they say that the Christ is David's son? <sup>42</sup> For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>43</sup> until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>44</sup> David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?” <sup>45</sup> And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, <sup>46</sup> “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>47</sup> who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

21.title: The Widow's Offering and the Olivet Discourse
21.overview:
Luke 21 is Jesus’ last public teaching, given in the temple. It opens with a contrast to the scribes condemned at the end of chapter 20: a poor widow puts two small copper coins into the treasury, all she had to live on, and Jesus says she has given more than all the rich.

When some admire the temple’s stones, he foretells its destruction and goes on to the Olivet Discourse (compare Matthew 24 and Mark 13). Luke speaks more plainly than the other Gospels about the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and he alone sets the times of the Gentiles between that event and the coming of the Son of Man in glory, which is the final, visible return of Christ.

The chapter closes with the pattern of Jesus’ last week: teaching in the temple by day, the people coming early to hear him, and nights on the Mount of Olives, all moving toward the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses, Jesus watches the rich putting in their gifts, and then a poor widow putting in two of the smallest coins minted. His verdict is that she has given more than all of them, because they gave from what they would not miss and she gave all she had. The context of a corrupt and doomed temple is real, but his words are praise of her faith, not a lament over her.
verseByVerse.theology:
God values giving on a different ledger from ours. The rich men’s gifts are not condemned; they are revalued. Heaven measures the cost to the giver, not the benefit to the fund.

The scene is also a small portrait of the cross, days before it. She gave her whole livelihood; he was about to give his whole life. Complete self-giving is not a heroic exception in the kingdom of God. It is the shape of the King.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church celebrates the total of a giving campaign. The pastor privately knows the costliest gift came from a widow on a fixed income. He has to decide whether the celebration names the total or the sacrifice, and this passage tells him which one heaven has already recorded.

And for anyone whose giving is small: she is remembered in every language on earth two thousand years later, because the Lord noticed, and said so.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 21 is Jesus’ last public teaching before the cross, given in the temple. A poor widow gives more than all the rich (vv. 1–4); the admired temple is doomed, and no date is given (vv. 5–7); his people are warned against false messiahs and panic, and promised words and safety under persecution (vv. 8–19). Luke carefully distinguishes the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 (vv. 20–24) from the visible return of the Son of Man (vv. 25–28), with the times of the Gentiles between them, and ends with a call to watch and pray (vv. 29–38).

The link. Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47), Jesus sees a widow. Luke puts the two scenes side by side on purpose. The men who loved the best seats are condemned; the woman nobody noticed is praised.

The offering box. Mark tells us he was sitting opposite it (Mark 12:41). It was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women, which ordinary Israelites could enter. According to the Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition written down more than a century later, thirteen chests stood there, shaped like trumpets. It is often said that a coin dropped in rang on its way down. If so, the rich are walking past, and it is ringing.

He looked up. Jesus lifts his eyes to watch what people put in. There is Someone at the treasury whose interest is not in the total. He watches how people give. He still does.

The Lord who came to his temple. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom Israel sought would suddenly come to his temple, and that he would come as a refiner of silver, purifying the priests until they brought offerings in righteousness (Malachi 3:1–3). Luke has already told us who the messenger sent before him was (7:27). So the man watching the offering chests is not a visitor with opinions about stewardship. He is the Lord of the house, come to his own temple as the refiner, testing what is brought into it. The rich are weighed and the widow is weighed, and his verdict, in the next breath, will overturn every reckoning the court has made.

Nothing is said against the rich. Their gifts were real, and the temple ran on them. His reckoning is not a rebuke of their giving but a revaluation of it, and that is the more searching thing. It is easy to guard against hypocrisy; you know when you are performing. It is much harder to discover that a gift made in good faith was, on the ledger that finally matters, worth very little, because it cost you nothing.
verseByVerse.note: The offering box was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women.

verseByVerse.quote: and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A poor widow. Poor is penichran: needy, of very little means. And he saw her, the second verb of sight in two verses. In the loudest week of the religious year, with the wealth of Jerusalem filing past, the eye of the Son of God rested on a woman nobody was looking at, holding a sum nobody would have counted.

A widow. In that economy the word described destitution: no wage, little legal standing, nothing beyond gleaning and charity. The law commanded Israel to care for her (Deuteronomy 14:29), and Jesus had just said what the religious establishment did with women like her: it devoured their houses (20:47). She is the wronged party in the very institution she is about to fund.

Two small copper coins. The lepton was the smallest coin in circulation; two of them came to perhaps a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage. In a trumpet-mouthed chest they would have made almost no sound at all. She could have kept one. She gave both.

The widow at Zarephath. Jesus himself had preached on her at Nazareth: of all the widows in Israel in Elijah’s time, the prophet was sent to one in Zarephath (4:25–26). She gave him the last of her flour and oil before feeding herself, and the jar did not run dry (1 Kings 17:12–16). Now one greater than Elijah stands in the temple, and again the eye of heaven passes over the great and rests on a widow. The sermon that nearly had him thrown from a cliff is being lived out in the Court of the Women. His mission, from Nazareth to the treasury, has always moved towards the overlooked.

Does God really notice small things? Yes, and this verse is the proof. Jesus noticed two coins worth almost nothing, in a crowd, in the week of his death. He says the very hairs of your head are numbered (12:7), and a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). So the small, hidden faithfulness of an ordinary life is not wasted: the prayer no one hears, the care of an elderly parent, the coins given from a pension. He sees it. Because he spoke about her, this woman is known wherever the Gospels are read, while the names of that morning’s wealthy donors are gone without trace.

In everyday life. If you have little to give, money, time or strength, give it anyway and do not be ashamed. And look around your church for the people who give quietly out of very little, whom no one thanks. Thank them, help them, and make sure no one is taking advantage of them.
verseByVerse.note: Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than all of them. By heaven’s arithmetic she has given more than all the wealthy donors combined, because God measures not the size of the gift but its cost and the trust behind it.

Out of their abundance. Their overflow, what they would not miss. The money we would never miss is the money we never had to trust God for.

All she had to live on. The widow gives from her lack, the thing she cannot spare: literally her whole life, her whole livelihood. She trusted God for her next meal. And she pictures what Jesus is about to do in a few days: she who gives everything at the treasury points to him who will give everything on Golgotha.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? The arrangement of Luke’s text raises a real question. Only a few verses earlier Jesus condemned the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47); a few verses later he says the temple whose treasury she is filling will be torn down to the last stone (21:6). So some readers conclude that Jesus is not praising her at all but lamenting her, mourning a religious system that has taught a penniless widow to give away her last means of living. It is an honest reading, and the sequence that suggests it is not accidental. This commentary’s view: as in Mark’s account (Mark 12:43–44), the context of corruption is real (20:47; 21:6), but Jesus’ words are clearly praise of her faith and devotion. This poor widow has put in more than all of them is commendation. He is not endorsing the temple, and he is not saying her coins repaired anything; within a generation the whole apparatus would be ash. He is telling us what God saw at that treasury: not the sums, but a heart holding nothing back. The worth of her gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it. It was in the trust of the one who gave it, and God received it even though the building it was dropped into was under sentence. That is a mercy for everyone who has given and served inside a church that was flawed or failing or would not outlast them.

Does Jesus mean that every believer should give away everything? No. He commends her trust and her gift; he does not command everyone to give away all they live on. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has (2 Corinthians 8:12), and a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). And no church may press the poor to give beyond their means; Jesus has just condemned those who devour widows’ houses (20:47). What he does ask of everyone is what she showed: a heart that trusts God more than money, and a gift that costs something.

What does the widow teach me about how much to give? The New Testament gives no fixed percentage, but it gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, in keeping with your income (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Give first, not from what is left over. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe, a tenth, a helpful starting point, and many in comfortable circumstances give more. The widow’s question is not what is the least I must give? but what does it cost me to trust God here? Start where you are, and let your giving grow as your trust grows. Jesus measured her gift not by its size but by what was left in her hand afterwards, which was nothing.

For worship. The rich gave out of their abundance and the widow out of her poverty. Christ alone gave out of both: out of the infinite riches of the Son of God he gave not a portion of his wealth but his very self. Her two coins outweighed the silver of Jerusalem; his one offering outweighs the sins of a multitude no one can number.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Temple, the Signs, and the Cost of Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Someone admires the temple, and Jesus replies that not one stone will be left on another, as in AD 70 it was. He gives no date, only instructions for the meantime: do not be led astray by those who claim to be the Christ or announce that the time is at hand; do not be terrified by wars; and do not read the ordinary catastrophes of history as the signal that the age is over.

Before any of that, the disciples will be brought before kings and governors, as Acts records: their opportunity to bear witness, with a mouth and wisdom promised. The cost is named plainly: betrayal by family, death for some, hatred for his name’s sake. Yet not a hair of their heads will perish.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 16 and verse 18 do not contradict each other. Not a hair of your head is a Hebrew way of speaking of complete preservation (12:7). What enemies can do to a believer is real and may be final in every visible respect, but it cannot reach the person himself, because his Lord rose from the dead.

The disciple is not promised safety; he is promised supply, words when words are needed, and a security no execution can touch. Endurance is remaining under the load today, on grace given daily. And the promises are for suffering for my name’s sake, not for every unpopularity a Christian brings on himself.
verseByVerse.examples: For those whose faith has cost them a family, it was foreseen and foretold, and the promise attached to it in this Gospel is enlargement, not replacement: many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Olivet Discourse. Luke’s version of Jesus’ teaching about the future (Mark 13; Matthew 24) is spoken in the temple (vv. 5, 37), and answers two questions: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will happen at the end?

Noble stones. They were not being foolish. Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Some foundation stones still in place are over forty feet long, and Josephus says that when the morning sun struck the gold-plated front a man had to look away, and that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow.

And offerings. Votive gifts dedicated to God and displayed, among them a golden vine over the entrance, added to cluster by cluster by worshippers. The temple was completed in the early sixties, and within a few years of completion it was gone.

Admiration is not idolatry. The thing admired was genuinely magnificent, genuinely God-ordained and genuinely doomed, and nothing in the stonework told them which of the three was about to matter.

The temple of the LORD. Jeremiah had named the instinct six hundred years earlier: do not trust in these deceptive words, this is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD (Jeremiah 7:4). They were not chanting a lie. They were resting on a building instead of on the One who had asked for it, which is much harder to see in yourself.

The glory of this latter house. When this second temple was first rebuilt, the old men who remembered Solomon’s wept (Ezra 3:12), and God answered through Haggai that the latter glory of this house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). Herod’s gold never made that true. What made it true was a child forty days old carried up its steps and taken into an old man’s arms as God’s salvation (2:22–32), a boy of twelve calling it his Father’s house (2:49), and now a man teaching in its courts day after day. Those admiring the stones are praising the frame while the picture stands beside them. The glory Haggai promised has come, and the stones they praise will soon have nothing left to do.

Is it wrong to love a beautiful church building? No. Beauty is God’s gift, and the tabernacle and temple were made beautiful at his command (Exodus 28:2; 1 Chronicles 22:5). Caring for a building where God’s people gather is good stewardship. The danger is trusting in it, or in any institution: assuming that because the building, the denomination or the tradition is old and impressive, God must be pleased with what happens inside it. The church is not the building. It is the people of God gathered around Christ, and that church will survive any building’s fall.

For worship. Over the temple door hung a golden vine, a fitting emblem, for Israel was the vine God brought out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8). The true Vine (John 15:1) walked beneath it that week, unadorned, and in a few days he would be cut down. Yet from him, and not from the gold, grows the fruit God sought in every age, fruit that no Roman torch can reach.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with gleaming white stone and gifts displayed by donors.

verseByVerse.quote: 'As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
