The days will come. A prophetic formula of judgment. He points at the most permanent things in their world and puts a term on them.

Not one stone upon another. This was the one place on earth where sacrifice could lawfully be offered and where God had put his name. To say the temple would fall was to say that Israel’s whole system of approach to God was ending. Jeremiah was nearly killed for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and a saying about the temple would be brought against Jesus at his trial (Mark 14:58).

The fulfilment. About forty years later, in AD 70, the city fell and the temple burned. The great platform survived, including the Western Wall, but that wall belongs to the platform, not the sanctuary. Of the sanctuary itself, exactly what Jesus said is what is there: nothing.

Was this prophecy written after the event? Some scholars argue that Luke must have written after AD 70 and shaped the saying to fit. It is worth meeting rather than dodging. Many conservative scholars note that Acts, Luke’s second volume, ends with Paul alive in Rome, and says nothing about the fall of Jerusalem, the death of Paul or the death of James, events a Christian historian writing later would have been unlikely to leave out of a history of the early church. And the prediction is not detailed in the way invented prophecy tends to be; it does not mention the fire. The date of Luke is still debated, and honesty says it cannot be fixed beyond dispute. But the saying does not rest on Luke alone: it stands in Mark, and a charge about the temple was brought against Jesus at his trial (Mark 14:58), so many scholars of every outlook accept that Jesus did speak of the temple’s fall. For those who believe he rose, the deeper answer is simpler. Jesus is the Son of God, and the God who declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10) is able to tell his servants what will happen.

The perishable and the imperishable. He will say the counterpart later in the chapter: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (v. 33). The visible is perishable and the spoken word of Christ is not, the exact reverse of how the world grades reality (Isaiah 40:8).

Why did God allow his own temple to be destroyed? Because its work was done. The temple was a shadow; Christ is the substance. He is the true temple, where God dwells with man (John 2:19–21), and his death is the one sacrifice to which all the temple’s sacrifices pointed (Hebrews 9:11–12; 10:11–14). When the veil was torn at his death (23:45), the old way was finished. The fall of the temple in AD 70 was also a judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah (19:41–44). After that, no one could imagine that animal sacrifices were still the way to God. There is one way now, and it is open to every nation: Jesus himself.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, 'Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?' And he said, 'See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they asked him, Teacher, when will these things be? Two questions, and both are about timing: when, and how will we know it is close. In Luke, the question is specifically about the temple’s destruction. It is what any of us would have asked.

And what will be the sign when these things are about to take place? Look at what he does not do. He does not give a date. Not here, and in Luke not anywhere: there is no date in this chapter, and no formula for calculating one. What he gives instead is a series of instructions about how to live in the meantime, and the very first is a warning about people who will answer the question he has just declined to answer.

Not led astray. Jesus’ first concern is not a timetable but protection from deception. The verb gives English planet, the wandering star. To be led astray is to drift off course while still believing you are travelling in a straight line.

In my name. Claiming to be the Messiah. Acts and Josephus both record would-be deliverers in the decades that followed (Acts 5:36–37; 21:38), and every century since has had them.

The name worth stealing. Counterfeiters copy only what is valuable. That false christs would arise for centuries, all borrowing his title, is itself a testimony to the One they imitate. Every impostor must claim what Jesus simply is (22:70), and the test of every voice is whether, like John the Baptist, it is glad to decrease so that he may increase (John 3:30).

The time is at hand. Only Luke adds this. The first claim is about a person; this one is about a clock. Many who would never make the first claim make the second every decade, and Jesus puts them in the same warning.

Do not go after them. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of announced dates, and the wreckage is always made of people: farms sold, savings given away, and then the morning after, when the sun came up as usual.

How can an ordinary Christian tell whether a teacher is leading people astray? Jesus gives the test in the sentence itself, and it is beautifully simple: do not go after them. Watch where the teaching takes the people who follow it. Teaching from God sends a person back to ordinary obedience: his work, his family, his prayers, his neighbour, his local church, and above all to Christ himself. Teaching that leads astray gathers a following around a teacher, doing something exceptional at his direction, on a timetable he supplies. Test every spirit (1 John 4:1). The mark of the false is that it makes you dependent on a man who claims to know something Christ declined to tell you (Acts 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wars and tumults. When you hear: not when you suffer. Jesus is speaking about the effect on the soul of news from elsewhere. He knew, twenty centuries before the phone on the bedside table, that a person can be crushed by events that are not happening to him.

Do not be terrified. Not ordinary fear, but being startled out of your senses, the mind scattering. He is not forbidding grief or concern; the man who reads of a famine and feels nothing has a worse problem than anxiety. He is forbidding the state in which fear has taken over the controls.

For these things must first take place. Must is dei, Luke’s word for the settled purpose of God, the very word Jesus used of his own suffering: the Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22). He puts the same word under the wars. They are inside the plan, not outside it: not caused by God in the way that good is caused by him, but not loose either. What does that mean? God does not do evil or approve of it, and those who start wars are guilty for them (James 4:1–2). Yet nothing happens outside his rule: he governs even the wicked acts of men for his own good purposes (Genesis 50:20). And the cross shows what that word means in God’s mouth. The worst thing men ever did was also a must, and it became the salvation of the world (24:26). The One who says the wars must come is the One who set his face to go to Jerusalem because he must, and the One who holds the plan bore its worst himself for those who live through it.

But the end will not be at once. What crushes a person watching the world convulse is the conclusion drawn from it: that history is unravelling. Jesus flatly denies the inference. Wars are the weather of a long age, and he says so in advance so that nobody has to work it out during the storm.

What should I do when the news frightens me? Not look away, but refuse the false interpretation. When the headline arrives, the question is not is this the end? He has told you it is not. The smaller and more answerable question is: what does love require of me today, in this street, with this news in my head? Pray for the people in it, as specifically as you can. Give if you can. Then do your work and go to bed. And limit what you take in: no one is helped by a mind fed with disaster every hour. God is our refuge and strength, therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way (Psalm 46:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nation against nation. Four categories cover everything that can go wrong on a planet: war, which men cause; earthquake, which nobody causes; famine and plague, often both; and then the sky.

Famines and pestilences. Only Luke includes pestilences. There was a severe famine under Claudius, which Luke records (Acts 11:28), and major earthquakes in the sixties. But these have marked every generation since: the beginning of the birth pains (Mark 13:8), not signs of a date.

Signs from heaven. Only Luke has this. Josephus records portents before the fall of Jerusalem: a star like a sword over the city, armies in the sky, the temple’s eastern gate opening by itself at night.

Not signs of the end. The end will not be at once (v. 9). He is describing the ordinary content of the long age between his ascension and his return, so that his people will not misread it. The plague years of the fourteenth century convinced many that the end had come, as do the wars on the news this month. A man who thinks he is watching the last act does not plant trees. Jesus takes the false interpretation away as a kindness.

The Lord of everything on the list. Read the list against the Gospel Luke has already written. The man who speaks of earthquakes and terrors is the one who rebuked the wind and the raging waves until there was a calm (8:24). The one who speaks of famine fed five thousand in a desolate place with five loaves (9:12–17). The one who speaks of plagues laid his hands on the sick of every kind and healed them (4:40). Every disaster he names is a territory he has already entered as its master. He does not foretell these things as a spectator, and none of them is a coded message about the date. He foretells them as the Lord who will one day end each of them for good.

Why does God allow earthquakes, famines and plagues? Scripture does not give a full answer, but it gives enough to trust him. These things are the fruit of a world under the curse of sin (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 8:20–22), not usually the punishment of particular sufferers for particular sins (13:1–5). They are warnings that this world is not our home and that judgment is coming, calling all people to repentance. And God is not absent from them: his Son entered this groaning world, suffered in it, and will make all things new (Revelation 21:4–5). Meanwhile, they are occasions for the church to show the love of Christ.

In various places. The suffering is distributed, not universal, and that is why the church has always been able to answer it. When the famine is in one place, the harvest is in another, as the believers in Antioch found when they heard of the famine in Judea (Acts 11:29–30). The geography of trouble is the opportunity of the body of Christ.

For worship. The earth shakes, and he is not shaken. The groaning of creation is real, but it is labour, not death throes, and the first of the new creation has already been born: the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18).

verseByVerse.quote: But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But before all this. Luke stresses the order: persecution of the disciples comes first, before the wars and signs. The disciple’s experience of the last age begins not with a sign in the sky but with a hand on his arm.

Synagogues and prisons. Luke alone went on to write the sequel, and every item on this list happens in Acts: Peter and John arrested (Acts 4:3), the apostles beaten (Acts 5:40), Stephen stoned (Acts 7), James killed with the sword (Acts 12:2), believers delivered to synagogues and prisons (Acts 9:2; 16:23).

Kings and governors. Paul stood before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24–26). And the cause is named: not for being difficult, or political, or strange, but because they belong to Jesus.

Before a governor and a king. The Master would go first. Within days Jesus himself would be brought before a governor, Pontius Pilate, and, as Luke alone records, a king, Herod Antipas (23:1–12), and there he made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13). Every disciple who has since stood before a magistrate for his name has stood where the Son of God stood.

Your opportunity. The second word turns the paragraph over. The Greek says it will turn out for you as testimony, and testimony is martyrion, a relative of the word that gives us martyr, though here it still means simply the evidence a witness gives. So God does not merely bring good out of an arrest afterwards. The arrest is the appointment. The courtroom becomes a pulpit. It is hard to see how else a tentmaker from Tarsus, held in chains, could have got a hearing before a Roman governor and a king, and the Lord arranged it.

Paul saw it so. Writing from prison: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard that my imprisonment is for Christ (Philippians 1:12–14).

What if I never face a courtroom? The principle does not require handcuffs. It requires only that following Christ has cost you something in front of other people: the awkward silence when you said where you were on Sunday, the promotion that went elsewhere, the family meal that went quiet when you would not laugh at the joke. Those moments feel like loss, and they are counted as testimony. A watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could have said when it was free. And remember the believers today for whom this is not a metaphor at all: in many countries Christians are arrested, beaten and imprisoned for the name of Jesus exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle it. Decide it now, in advance, and cease to carry it: you will not be anxious.

Not to meditate beforehand how to answer. The verb was used of rehearsing a speech, as a defendant would rehearse his defence. Jesus is not talking about study, which Luke’s own heroes do constantly, but about the anxious drafting of testimony before a hearing: not a ban on preparation but a promise for persecution.

Does this verse forbid preparing sermons or Bible studies? No. Paul settles it by example. This is the man who reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths (Acts 17:2), who quoted Greek poets in Athens, who asks Timothy to bring the books, and above all the parchments (2 Timothy 4:13), and who also, standing before Agrippa, plainly received something he had not written. Preparation and this promise are not rivals. One is the ordinary work; the other is the extraordinary supply at the moment when the ordinary work has been taken away. Prepare diligently when you can. When you cannot, trust him.

A mouth and wisdom. In 12:12 it is the Holy Spirit who will teach them what to say; here it is Jesus himself, for the risen Christ gives his Spirit, and the Spirit speaks Christ’s words. Wisdom is what to say. A mouth is the ability to say it, the part many of us lack: we know the truth and cannot get it past our teeth when it matters.

None able to withstand. Luke shows the promise landing: of Stephen, they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking (Acts 6:10).

Does this mean Christians will always win the argument? Not in the sense that their opponents will be persuaded or that they will be acquitted. Stephen’s hearers could not withstand his wisdom, and they stoned him. The promise is that the truth spoken by Christ’s witnesses will not be refuted, that their testimony will stand, and that God will be glorified in it. The result is in his hands. Your task is to be faithful; his is to give the words and to use them as he wills.

In everyday life. The anxiety this verse addresses is rarely about courtrooms. It is the dread of the question at work or at the kitchen table, or lying awake composing what you should have said. The command is not try harder but settle it. Pray before the conversation, say what you know simply, and leave the rest with him.

parallels.desc: they could not withstand the wisdom of Stephen

verseByVerse.quote: You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even by parents. The list moves outward from the innermost circle. Delivered up means handed over into the power of someone who intends harm: not an argument at a family gathering but a father telling the authorities where his son is (Micah 7:6; 12:52–53).

Delivered up, as he was. The verb is the one Luke keeps for Jesus’ own passion (9:44), and within days Judas, who had shared his table, would deliver him up with a kiss (22:4–6, 48). Jesus is not describing a road he will watch his disciples walk. He is describing the road he is already on.

Some of you. Not all, and he does not say which, though he knows. James would be the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John, as the early church remembered it, would die old.

Hated by all. Hatred that seems universal makes a person suspect the fault is his. But the ground is stated twice in six verses: for my name’s sake. For anyone whose deepest need is to be liked, this sentence is meant to loosen that need’s grip. The Father’s verdict on his Son, you are my beloved (3:22), rests on everyone who is in him, and no crowd can take it back.

Not every unpopularity. A Christian can be disliked for being rude, superior or tactless, and has not been promised anything here. Subtract the name of Christ from your situation, and see whether the hostility goes with it. If it would remain, the remedy is repentance.

What if my family has turned against me for following Christ? Then this verse is for you, and two things in Luke are true for you. First, Jesus said this would happen. The silence at the other end of the phone is not evidence that God has abandoned your family or that you made a mistake. It was foreseen and foretold, by someone whose own brothers did not at first believe in him (John 7:5). Second, he attached a promise to it: there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30). The family is not replaced. It is enlarged, in the church now, and you should let the church be family to you. Keep loving and praying for your relatives, honour them where you can without denying Christ, and leave the door open. Many have come later.

For worship. The Son who was handed over by a friend has become the Friend who hands over no one. He answers the empty chair at the table with a household: his mother and his brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21).

verseByVerse.quote: But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a hair. The sharpest apparent contradiction in the chapter: two verses earlier he said some of you they will put to death (v. 16). The two are measured on different scales, and the second is the true measure. They may lose their lives, but they will not perish.

The idiom. Not a hair of your head is a Hebrew way of speaking of complete preservation (1 Samuel 14:45; Acts 27:34). Jesus has used it once already, in a passage about being dragged before the authorities: even the hairs of your head are all numbered (12:7).

The person is safe. The promise is not that the body is spared but that the person is kept. Stephen was stoned to death, and not a hair of his head perished. Luke wrote both sentences.

Why both sentences can be true. The man who spoke them was about to be put to death, and on the third day he showed these same disciples his hands and his feet (24:39). Death did to Jesus everything it can do, and it could not keep him, and his people are joined to him. Not a hair of your head will perish is, in the end, a promise of resurrection.

By your endurance. Endurance is hypomonē: to remain under the load, like a beam still bearing the weight in the morning (8:15). And the verb is gain, not keep. The life handed over in the losing is handed back larger.

Does my salvation depend on my endurance? Endurance is the evidence and fruit of God’s keeping, not the ground of salvation. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6), and no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). True faith perseveres, and God preserves it. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his people, and they keep going. The call to endure is real, and God uses it as one of the means by which he keeps his people enduring. So the warning and the promise belong together. You must endure; and if you are his, you will, because he will hold you.

What if I do not think I have it in me to last? That is the quieter fear this verse raises in most Christians, and it is not the fear of martyrdom. It is: I do not think I can keep going. Not thirty more years. Not through what is coming. You are not asked to last thirty years at once. Endurance is not a store of strength held in reserve; it is remaining under, today. Nobody is given the grace for a decade in advance. The saints who endured to the end did it the way anyone does: the next morning, and then the one after that, on mercies that are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) and grace that is sufficient for the day (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In everyday life. If you are facing a long trial, an illness, a hard marriage, a grief that will not lift, do not try to carry next year. Ask for today’s grace from the Spirit who raised Jesus and lives in you (Romans 8:11), do today’s faithful thing, and lie down tonight trusting the One who numbers your hairs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Fall of the City and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke gives his Gentile readers the plain meaning of the abomination of desolation: armies around Jerusalem. Jesus tells his people to flee the city, not shelter in it. The fall of the city will be God’s judgment, the days of vengeance Isaiah foretold, and Jesus grieves as he announces it. Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled: a dominion that is real, permitted and bounded.

Then the scene widens from a city to the world: signs in the heavens, nations in perplexity, people fainting with dread, and the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (Daniel 7:13). His people are told to straighten up and raise their heads, because their redemption is drawing near.
verseByVerse.theology:
Serious readers differ on how the fall of Jerusalem (verses 20 to 24) relates to the coming of the Son of Man (verses 25 to 28). This commentary takes the fall of the city as a real judgment in that generation and a foretaste of the last one, and verses 25 to 28 as the final, visible return of Christ. Luke’s verse 24 settles much of the question: he alone writes an interval of unknown length between the trampling of the city and the appearing of the Son of Man, so the objection that Jesus predicted a return that did not come does not hold.

They will see anchors the Christian hope in something public: he will be seen returning.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 25 and 26 describe a suffering common in comfortable countries: not disaster but dread, the strength going out of the body over a thing that has not happened. Jesus does not scold it. He names it, and then tells his own people to lift their heads.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Where Mark speaks of the abomination of desolation, with let the reader understand (Mark 13:14), Luke, writing for Gentile readers, probably gives the plain meaning. It was fulfilled when the Romans surrounded Jerusalem, first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66, then under Titus in AD 70.

Its desolation. The destruction and abandonment of the city, as Daniel had foreseen (Daniel 9:26–27).

Flee to the mountains. Three commands follow, startlingly ordinary: get out of Judea, get out of the city, do not go back in.

Do not enter it. Under any normal siege the countryside empties into the walled city. Jesus tells them to do the opposite, and history shows why: many who fled into the city were trapped, and famine and fighting between factions killed multitudes before the Romans broke through.

The church heard him. The church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophetic word, left before the war reached its height and settled at Pella, east of the Jordan, perhaps when Cestius Gallus withdrew in AD 66. The tradition has been questioned, but it fits what plainly happened: the church was not destroyed when Jerusalem was.

He went in so that they could go out. He tells his disciples to get out of Jerusalem in the week he himself has entered it with his face set (9:51). He enters the doomed city so that his people can leave it. Outside its walls he would bear a wrath far deeper than any siege, and the command to flee comes from the One who, a few nights later, would refuse to flee himself.

Is fleeing not simply running away? A thoughtful reader will feel the question. Should the disciples not have stayed and prayed for the city, and died with it if necessary? Jesus says no, and it is good to have a Lord who will say so. There is a time to stand and a time to go, and the difference is not measured by how brave it feels. Paul was let down the Damascus wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and was not ashamed to tell of it (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). What decides the answer is not courage but calling: flight from danger is cowardice only when it is flight from a post you were given. Nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls. The same applies to Christians facing persecution today: it is not wrong to flee if God opens a way, and it is not wrong to stay if he calls you to.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, as the Romans did in AD 66–70; Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation.”

verseByVerse.quote: for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Days of vengeance. Two things are bolted together here. The first is that this is judgment: covenant language, God’s judgment on Jerusalem for rejecting her Messiah (19:43–44). God had bound himself to Israel with promises for faithfulness and plain warnings of siege and exile for rebellion (Deuteronomy 28:15, 49–52). Vengeance here is not a grudge but the holy God keeping his word, as a just judge keeps the law. And it is quoting Isaiah 61:2, the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, the passage Jesus read at Nazareth, where he stopped in the middle of the sentence, having announced the favour and left the vengeance unread (4:18–19). Seventeen chapters later he finishes the sentence. Yet the year of favour is still being proclaimed to every nation, and the patience that kept the scroll closed at Nazareth has kept the door open for us.

To fulfill all that is written. The prophets had warned of siege and famine on unfaithful Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 28:49–57; Daniel 9:26; Micah 3:12). God does what he has said.

Alas. The second thing is grief. The word is often heard as a threat; here it is the sound a man makes over something unbearable, aimed at the least guilty people in the city: a woman eight months pregnant, a mother with a baby at the breast, on the day the siege begins.

Great distress upon the earth. Upon the earth may mean upon the land of Israel. Josephus describes horrors of famine and slaughter that are hard to read.

Judgment and tears together. The judgment is deserved and it is agonising, and the one who says so had wept over this city a few days before (19:41–42). He does not judge half-heartedly, and he does not judge coldly. I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live (Ezekiel 18:32).

Does God enjoy judging people? No. That is the question underneath this passage, and people really carry it. The answer is standing in the temple court with tears not yet dry, describing a siege a generation off, and grieving in advance for infants not yet born. His judgment is real and it is just, because sin is real and he is holy. But he takes no pleasure in it. And within the week the wrath he is describing will fall in its fullness on him, so that everyone in that city and every sinner in the world who turns to him might not have to bear it. There is no vengeance in Scripture that God has not first been willing to bear himself for those who trust him (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 5:9).

In everyday life. If you have grown casual about sin, let this passage sober you. If you are afraid of God’s wrath, look at who is speaking, and run to him, not away from him.

parallels.desc: the days of punishment have come

verseByVerse.quote: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led captive. Josephus says over a million died in the siege, probably an exaggeration, and that ninety-seven thousand were taken captive, many sold as slaves or made to die in the arenas.

Trampled underfoot. After the second Jewish revolt (AD 132–135), the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city and banned Jews from it. Empire after empire has held it since.

Until the times of the Gentiles. Only Luke has this clause. Every reading agrees on the word until: Gentile dominion over Jerusalem is real, permitted and bounded. And the times of the Gentiles are also the times of Gentile mission, the shape Paul uses: a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:25).

A light for the Gentiles. Over the infant Jesus in this temple Simeon had sung of a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32), and the risen Christ will send his apostles to all nations (24:47). So the times of the Gentiles are not empty time between two catastrophes. They are the age in which the light Simeon held in his arms goes out to every people.

Where Christians differ: the times of the Gentiles. Many Reformed interpreters take the phrase to mean the age of Gentile ingathering and Gentile dominance, running from the fall of Jerusalem to the return of Christ, in which the gospel goes to the nations. Dispensationalists (who see Israel and the church as distinct in God’s plan and expect a future national role for Israel), including teachers many readers have been helped by, understand it as a defined period of Gentile political domination of Jerusalem, and many have seen the founding of the modern state of Israel (1948) and the capture of Jerusalem (1967) as the end of the times of the Gentiles and a sign of the imminent end. Their instinct is a sound one in this respect: they are trying to let the word until mean something, and to take seriously that God has not finished with the people to whom he made the promises. This commentary’s view: Jesus gives no such timetable, and warns against date-setting (vv. 8–9). The times of the Gentiles is the age of Gentile mission and Gentile dominance between the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s return. This fits Luke’s own flow, where Acts carries the gospel out to the nations, and Romans 11:25 measures the term by the ingathering of the Gentiles, not by who governs a city. Christians differ on whether Paul expects a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ or means by all Israel the whole elect people of God (Romans 11:25–27); on either reading, Israel’s salvation is a work of grace through the gospel, not a political event to be calculated.

Is the modern state of Israel the fulfilment of prophecy? Christians hold different views, and they can be held charitably. What this verse will not bear is a calendar. It gives a boundary without a date, deliberately, and every attempt to turn it into arithmetic has expired. The New Testament’s focus is not on territory but on the gospel: the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ, the true offspring (Galatians 3:16, 29), and Jews and Gentiles alike are saved only by faith in him. Christians should pray for the peace of Jerusalem and for all its people, Jewish and Arab, and long for them to know the Messiah. They should not treat the news from the Middle East as a timetable for Christ’s return.

A horizon behind the trampling. The sentence does not deny the trampling. It puts a horizon behind it: the word until is God’s. There is no oppression in this world, including any you are suffering now, that Scripture describes without an end.

parallels.desc: the nations have come into your inheritance
until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in

verseByVerse.quote: 'And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Signs in sun and moon. The discourse now moves from a city to the world and to his return. Every image comes from the prophets, who used it for great acts of God’s judgment: stars withholding their light at the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10), the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:30–31; Acts 2:20).

Literal or picture? This language, in the Bible’s own usage, is the language of God arriving in judgment and of an old order ending, and it is used both of historical catastrophes and of the last day. Whether the sun will literally go dark is not something this passage settles, and a reader should not be told it does. What it plainly announces is that the created order itself will register the coming of its Maker, and that the registering will be terrifying.

The sun’s light failed. On the day Jesus died, darkness lay over the whole land from noon until three, and Luke alone says it: the sun’s light failed (23:44–45). The heavens that will be shaken at his return went dark at his death, because their Maker was bearing the sin of his people. That is why a believer can read this verse without terror. The judgment these signs announce has already fallen once, at noon on Golgotha, on the Son of God in the place of all who trust him.

Distress of nations. Perplexity is aporia: literally no way through, the state of a person who has run out of options. The sea, in Scripture, is a picture of chaos (Psalm 46:3; Revelation 13:1).

Fainting with fear. Strength simply leaving, with foreboding: fear not of what is happening but of what is coming. That is a common suffering in a prosperous country: the scan that has not come back, the redundancy not yet announced. Jesus does not scold this. He knows what dread does to a person.

The powers of the heavens. Once more I will shake the heavens and the earth (Haggai 2:6): the shaking removes what is made, so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:26–27).

Should these verses frighten a Christian? They should sober us, but not terrify us. They describe what the world will feel when its Maker comes in judgment, and they are meant to warn the unbelieving and wake the sleepy. But for those who belong to Christ the same events are the prelude to joy, for Jesus at once tells them that while others faint, they are to lift up their heads. You do not need to fear the day of the Lord if you are hidden in the Lord of the day. If you are not, these verses are his kind warning to come to him now.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man coming. Daniel saw one like a son of man brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and handed a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13–14). He came first in weakness, laid in a manger; he will come again with power and great glory.

In a cloud. Luke alone has the singular, and Luke alone wrote the two scenes that explain it: the voice from the cloud on the mountain (9:34–35), and the cloud that took him out of their sight, with the promise that he would come in the same way (Acts 1:9–11). The cloud is the robe of God’s presence (Exodus 40:34–35). To come in a cloud is to come as only God comes.

They will see. The Christian hope can never be reduced to an inner experience. He was seen when he was born, killed and taken up, and every eye will see him coming back (Revelation 1:7).

There is no secret coming. This passage, like every other New Testament description of the return, speaks of one coming, public, glorious and seen by all (1 Thessalonians 4:16), when the gathering of his people, the resurrection and the judgment come together (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The teaching of a secret removal of the church beforehand is taken up at v. 36.

Where Christians differ: is this the Second Coming, or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some interpreters read this coming as Christ’s vindication, made visible when the temple fell, pointing out that in Daniel 7 the son of man travels to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom rather than down to the earth. This commentary’s view: in Luke the far horizon is in view here. Luke has already set the times of the Gentiles between the fall of the city and these signs (v. 24), and what he describes reaches far beyond AD 70: signs in sun, moon and stars, anguish among the nations of the whole earth, and the redemption of God’s people drawing near (v. 28). The fall of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) was a real judgment and a foretaste. This is the final, visible return of Christ.

Hold the picture. Daniel’s figure, given every people and nation into his hands, is the same figure standing in a temple courtyard, days from being flogged, describing what is coming to men who will run away from him before the week is out. The dominion was always going to be handed to a crucified man.

Straighten up. Two physical commands. Straighten up is the word Luke used of the woman bent double for eighteen years (13:11–13). Raise your heads: lift the chin, which nobody under threat ever does. While the world is fainting, the Christian is told to do the opposite of the natural thing with his own body.

Your redemption. Redemption is apolytrōsis: release, rooted in the freeing of captives by a price paid, here full and final deliverance, including the resurrection of the body (Romans 8:23). The events that terrify everyone else are, for the believer, the sound of the door opening. The world sees the end of everything. The church sees him.

How should I think about Christ’s return day to day? As the believer’s great hope, not a subject of dread or calculation. It means that history is going somewhere; that every injustice will be put right; that the dead in Christ will rise; that our bodies will be redeemed; that we will see him face to face. Paul calls it the blessed hope (Titus 2:13). It should make you watchful in holiness, steady in suffering and generous with this world’s goods, because they are not your final treasure. And it should put the prayer of the early church in your mouth: come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

In everyday life. Practise the posture. When the news is bad, or your body is failing, or the church seems weak, lift your head and say: my redemption is drawing near. Let it change one thing today: the fear you will not feed, the grudge you will let go, the thing you will give away.

For worship. The hands that once straightened a woman bent double will one day straighten a whole bowed creation. He paid the price of our release with his own blood, and he is coming to claim what he bought, body and soul, not to destroy his own but to take them home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–38 — The Fig Tree, the Weight on the Heart, and the Daily Rhythm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the fig tree is deliberately ordinary: trees come into leaf, and everybody knows summer is near. The signs are readable, and what they announce is the kingdom of God. This generation, the people of Jesus’ own day, would see what the disciples had asked about, the fall of the temple, and it came within forty years; the day of his return is not given. Under it all stands verse 33: heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not.

Then, after the cosmos, the kitchen. What threatens readiness is a heart weighed down by indulgence or by the cares of this life, and the remedy is to stay awake and pray.
verseByVerse.theology:
Watchfulness is not scanning the news for prophetic fulfilment but the settled attention of people who live today under eternity.

To stand before the Son of Man is courtroom language. If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Psalm 130:3). The strength to stand is not mustered but asked for, and asked of the very one before whom we shall stand. Jude gives the ground: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
None of this is a call to care less about family or work. It is a diagnosis: what leaves a Christian unready for glory is more often a crowded diary than a scandal.

Verses 37 and 38 give a pattern for anyone overwhelmed by what is coming. Jesus knew he would be crucified within the week, and he spent the days teaching in the morning and sleeping on a hillside. Work in the day, withdraw at night to pray, and do the next ordinary faithful thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at the fig tree. A small phrase is Luke’s alone: and all the trees. The fig tree is sometimes read as a coded symbol for the nation of Israel, and systems of date-calculation have been built on that; the prophets do use figs of Israel (Hosea 9:10). But and all the trees makes it plain that the point is not symbolic botany. Trees come into leaf before summer, and everybody knows it.

In leaf. Signs are readable. You do not consult an expert to know that summer is coming; you look at a branch. The signs are not a cipher for the initiated, but a season a Christian can read from his own doorstep.

What the fig tree does not tell you. It gives no date. It tells you the direction of travel and the nearness of the thing, precisely the amount of information that produces watchfulness rather than arithmetic.

The kingdom of God is near. Not the end is near, not the judgment, but the kingdom. Everything in this discourse has been dark: armies, betrayal, famine, a city under sentence. And all of it announces the reign of God arriving in its fullness. The signs are not the symptoms of a world dying. They are leaves on the branch.

The kingdom is the King. In Luke the kingdom of God is never an abstraction. It came near when he came near. Within days he would tell the Twelve that he assigns them a kingdom, as his Father assigned one to him (22:29), and a dying thief would ask, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (23:42). So the summer the leaves announce is not finally a season of history but the face of the King. When Christians read the branches, they are not reading the weather of the world. They are watching for him, and every leaf says the same thing: the One who came once in humility is on his way back in glory.

If the kingdom is already here, how can it be near? Both are true. The kingdom came in Jesus: the King was among them, healing and forgiving, and he reigns now from heaven (17:21; Acts 2:33–36). But it has not yet come in its fullness, when every enemy is defeated, the dead are raised and the creation renewed. Christians live between the two: the kingdom has come, and the kingdom is coming. The events of history are like leaves on the tree, telling us that the full summer of his reign is on the way.

In everyday life. When you read of the world convulsing, is your emotion dread or expectancy? The difference is whether you believe the thing on the far side of the shaking is a ruin or a King. When bad news comes this week, pray, help where you can, and say quietly, the kingdom is near.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This generation. Taken naturally, this generation means Jesus’ contemporaries, and all means the events leading to and including the fall of Jerusalem, which came within a single lifetime. Sceptics press the point: if all includes the return (v. 27), that generation passed away and he did not come. It is the standard charge that Jesus was a mistaken prophet, honestly felt, and it deserves an answer.

Luke’s answer is eight verses earlier. Where Matthew and Mark keep the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the age closely braided, Luke names the gap: Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (v. 24), an interval of unknown length written into the discourse by Jesus himself. The all that must take place is what the disciples asked about in v. 7: the stones thrown down, the siege, the captivity. Every one of them happened within forty years.

Where Christians differ: what does this generation mean? Some take it to mean the Jewish race, which will last until the end. Others take it to mean the generation alive when the final signs appear. Some critics claim that Jesus was simply mistaken. This commentary’s view: the best reading (compare Mark 13:30) is that Jesus’ contemporaries would see the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, the event the disciples had asked about (v. 7), and they did. Elsewhere in Luke this generation means the people of Jesus’ own day (7:31; 11:29–32). The day of his final coming itself remains unknown, as Mark records Jesus saying (Mark 13:32). Jesus was not mistaken.

The opposite error. Because v. 24 sets a limit on Gentile dominion and v. 32 attaches a generation to fulfilment, people have bolted the two together to calculate a date, and every such attempt has expired quietly. When the apostles asked the risen Christ, he declined: it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). A man who has worked out the date does not need to stay awake. That is why we are not given it.

My words will not pass away. Jesus sets his own sayings against the whole visible universe and says the universe will give way first. Israel’s prophets claimed that permanence only for the word of the LORD: the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus claims it for what he himself says, with no thus says the LORD in front of it. Earlier in Luke he had said that whoever hears his words and does them builds on rock (6:47–48), and after Easter he would point the disciples back to the words he had spoken while he was still with them (24:44). A claim like that is either the gravest presumption or the voice of the LORD himself. The temple stones, lying where he said they would lie, are one witness to which it was; the empty tomb is the greater one.

How can I trust words spoken two thousand years ago? Because they have been tested and have never failed, and because of who spoke them. Within a generation the temple fell as he said. He said he would rise on the third day, and he did. He said the gospel would go to the nations, and you are reading this. And the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures still bears witness to them in the hearts of those who read (John 16:13; 2 Timothy 3:16). The words of Jesus are not old in the sense of outdated. They are older than the world and will outlast it. Build on them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch yourselves. After the cosmos, the kitchen. Jesus names the things that will actually cost his disciples their readiness, and not one of them is on the news. Only Luke has this application.

Weighed down. Made heavy, dull, like eyes too heavy to stay open, as the disciples were heavy with sleep on the mountain (9:32). A heart with too much on it does not become wicked. It becomes slow.

Dissipation and drunkenness. Dissipation is kraipalē, an old medical word for the heaviness in the head the morning after; drunkenness is the night before. Both ask a bottle or a night out for the rest and joy that only God can give, and both leave the heart heavier than before.

Cares of this life. Then the anxieties about ordinary things (8:14): bills, rotas, the boiler, the form that has to go back by Friday. That one is not a sin in the ordinary sense, which makes it the most dangerous item on the list. A man can be sober, faithful to his wife, honest in business, in church every Sunday, and be so occupied with things that will not exist in a hundred years that the return of Jesus Christ is no part of how he thinks about Thursday.

The night the warning was tested. Within days, in the garden, Jesus found the disciples sleeping for sorrow (22:45): not drunk, simply weighed down by grief. And there, under a weight no one else has ever carried, he stayed awake and prayed: not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). He watched when his friends could not; his perfect obedience is counted to all whose watch has failed (Romans 5:19), and he lives to intercede for those whose eyes keep closing (Hebrews 7:25).

Like a trap. A snare works not because the animal is stupid, but because it is head-down in a perfectly reasonable activity when the cord closes. And it will come upon all (Isaiah 24:17): the only question is whether it finds them ready.

Does this mean I should care less about my family and work? No. The remedy Jesus gives at once is not detachment but prayer. Jesus does not tell you to stop paying the bills or caring for your children. He tells you not to let them weigh down your heart. The difference is whether your ordinary duties are done before the face of the coming King, or whether they have crowded him out. Cast your cares on him (1 Peter 5:7), do your work as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23), and let the thought of his coming lighten the load rather than add to it.

In everyday life. If the cares of this week have crowded out every thought of his coming, do not answer that with more guilt. He invites the overburdened to cast their cares on him. Put one minute of looking for his coming into each day this week.

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay awake at all times. The whole discourse funnels into two verbs: stay awake, and pray. No preparations to make, no date to mark. At all times rules out becoming intensely watchful when the news is bad and forgetting when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness. It is nerves.

Strength to escape. Prayer is the means of watchfulness (22:40, 46). The escape is asked for, not announced as automatic, and it is coupled with strength, language for endurance rather than absence: escape from the judgment, and from being swept away by deception and fear.

Where Christians differ: does strength to escape mean a rapture before the tribulation? Many Christians have been taught to hear in this phrase the promise of a removal: that the church will be taken out of the world, secretly, before the worst arrives, the final period of great distress often called the tribulation. Others read the escape as being kept safely through rather than being spared. Those who hold the first view are not careless readers; they are trying to give full weight to the word escape. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that it means being kept faithful through what is coming, so as to stand before the Son of Man at the end, not being removed beforehand. Jesus has just said his followers will be persecuted and some put to death (vv. 12–16), and promised that by their endurance they will gain their lives (v. 19). The escape is paired with standing before the Son of Man, which is plainly the final scene, and the New Testament knows only one, public return of Christ (v. 27). There is no secret rapture. Whatever a reader concludes, the verse gives him something to do, and what it gives him is prayer.

To stand. Legal language: what a man does when the case is called. To stand before him at his coming means to be unashamed and accepted (1 John 2:28). If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Psalm 130:3).

He stood where we could not. Within days the Son of Man would himself stand bound before the council, Pilate and Herod. Pilate found no guilt in him, said so three times, and handed him over anyway (23:4, 14–15, 22–25). The Judge has already stood in the dock in our place, and the sentence we deserved was carried out on him.

Will I be able to stand? That is the fear this verse leaves in many sincere hearts: have I watched enough, prayed enough, endured enough? Read the verse again and see where the strength comes from. It is not mustered; it is asked for. The prayer is not that we might be strong but that we might have strength given, and the one being asked is the one before whom we shall stand. He is not an examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. He is the one supplying the answer to his own examination. No one has ever stood before the Son of Man on his own record. The psalm that asks who could stand answers at once: but with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4). The standing is his doing.

What does staying awake look like in practice? Not sleeplessness or constant anxiety. It means a life awake to God: regular prayer, morning and evening; reading Scripture; gathering with his people; confessing sin quickly rather than letting it settle; living each day as if it could be the day, and planning as if he might not come for a hundred years. It means asking often: if he came today, would he find me doing what he left me to do? Watchfulness is simply faithfulness that remembers he is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day in the temple. Luke ends the greatest prophetic discourse in his Gospel with a timetable. This man has announced the destruction of the temple he stands in, the death of friends beside him and his own return in glory. He knows that within days he will be crucified, and who will betray and deny him. And what he does with the days that remain is: teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again.

Olivet. The Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside. Jesus may have stayed at Bethany (Mark 11:11), or in the open, at the place where he often went to pray (22:39), which is where Judas would find him. He had said it himself: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (9:58). In the last week of his life it was still true. And the mountain he slept on was the one from which he had wept over the city (19:41), the one where he would pray in agony and be arrested, and the one from which he would ascend (Acts 1:12).

Early in the morning. There is no frenzy in him, no last campaign. He teaches, available to whoever comes.

The rhythm of a man who knows the future. Work in the day; withdraw at night to pray; be found in the morning where the people who need you can find you. That is what perfect knowledge of a terrible future looked like when it was lived out by an actual man, and it looked like peace: the peace of someone who knows exactly what is coming and is not afraid, because the Father who holds the whole of it is his Father.

How can I have peace when the future is uncertain? Your future is less known to you than Jesus’ was to him, but it is just as fully known to your Father. Peace does not come from knowing what will happen. It comes from knowing who holds what will happen, and from doing today what he has given you to do. Jesus’ last week shows that faithfulness and peace go together: he did not escape the cross by worrying about it, and he did not lose his peace by facing it. Bring each day to the Father, as he did on the Mount of Olives, and you will find that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards your heart (Philippians 4:7).

In the flow. Jesus’ public ministry in Luke ends here, on the note the temple section began with (19:47–48). Next the leaders and Judas plot (22:1–6), and everything Jesus has said about watching, praying and standing before the Son of Man he is about to live out himself.

In everyday life. The crowds got up before dawn to hear him; you can hear him at your kitchen table. Set aside the first part of the morning, before the phone and the news, to read a passage of the Gospels and pray.
verseByVerse.note: Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside it.

parallels.desc: as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives

21.text: <sup>1</sup> Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, <sup>2</sup> and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. <sup>3</sup> And he said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. <sup>4</sup> For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.” <sup>5</sup> And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said, <sup>6</sup> “As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>7</sup> And they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?” <sup>8</sup> And he said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them. <sup>9</sup> And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.” <sup>10</sup> Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. <sup>11</sup> There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. <sup>12</sup> But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. <sup>13</sup> This will be your opportunity to bear witness. <sup>14</sup> Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, <sup>15</sup> for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. <sup>16</sup> You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. <sup>17</sup> You will be hated by all for my name's sake. <sup>18</sup> But not a hair of your head will perish. <sup>19</sup> By your endurance you will gain your lives. <sup>20</sup> “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. <sup>21</sup> Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it, <sup>22</sup> for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. <sup>23</sup> Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. <sup>24</sup> They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. <sup>25</sup> “And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, <sup>26</sup> people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>27</sup> And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <sup>28</sup> Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” <sup>29</sup> And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. <sup>30</sup> As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. <sup>31</sup> So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. <sup>32</sup> Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. <sup>33</sup> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>34</sup> “But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. <sup>35</sup> For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. <sup>36</sup> But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” <sup>37</sup> And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. <sup>38</sup> And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

22.title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest
22.overview:
Luke 22 tells the last night before the cross. It begins with Judas’s agreement to betray Jesus and the preparation of the Passover, moves through the institution of the Lord’s Supper, the disciples’ dispute about greatness, Jesus’ prayer for Peter and his warning of Peter’s denial, and the agony on the Mount of Olives, and ends with the arrest, Peter’s denials and Jesus before the council.

Luke’s account of the Supper has features of its own: two cups (vv. 17 and 20), a strong look forward to the kingdom, and the dispute about rank placed straight after the bread and the cup, so that the disciples’ argument stands beside Jesus serving them with his body and blood.

The cup Jesus prays about in the garden is not only the pain of crucifixion but the cup of God’s wrath, which he would drink in the place of sinners.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Conspiracy, Preparation, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Passover, the feast of the lamb whose blood turned the destroyer aside in Egypt, draws near, and in that week the chief priests look for a way to kill the Lamb of God. Satan enters Judas, who freely makes his bargain, and Jesus arranges the meal himself, down to a man carrying a water jar.

At the table he says he has earnestly desired this Passover, and he fills its bread and cup with himself: his body given for them, and the new covenant in his blood that Jeremiah had promised. Only then is the betrayer named, his hand on the same table.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper looks three ways. It remembers, as Passover did, bringing a past deliverance into the present (Exodus 12:14). It proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). And it looks forward to the feast of the kingdom, so every communion table is an unfinished meal.

Of the four main views of what happens at the table, set out in the verse notes, this commentary holds the Reformed view: the bread remains bread, and yet by his Spirit the believer truly feeds on Christ by faith. The two words in both sayings, for you, mean on behalf of and in the place of: substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before.

Verses 21 and 22 set God’s determined plan and Judas’s guilt side by side without reconciling them, as Scripture does elsewhere (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23).
verseByVerse.examples:
Some believers fear they could be handed over like Judas. The fear is itself the answer. A conscience that recoils at the thought of betraying Christ is not being handed over; it is being held.

Others stay away from the table because they feel they are not good enough to come. The cup does not commemorate anyone’s fitness. It was poured out for a table that held a traitor, a denier and ten men who would run before morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 22 is the last night before the cross. The leaders plot, Judas sells his Lord, and Jesus, in command of every detail, keeps the Passover with his apostles and turns it into the Lord’s Supper: bread that is his body given for them, a cup that is the new covenant in his blood (vv. 1–23). At the table the disciples argue about rank; he shows them greatness as service, promises them a kingdom, and tells Peter he has prayed for him (vv. 24–38). Then come the prayer on the Mount of Olives and the cup, the betrayal with a kiss, the healing of an enemy’s ear, Peter’s denials and the Lord’s look, and the dawn trial where Jesus declares that the Son of Man will be seated at God’s right hand (vv. 39–71). The one being handed over is the one in charge.

Unleavened Bread and Passover. Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:15–20), and Luke explains for Gentile readers that the two were spoken of as one. Passover was the feast of the lamb. Every family in Israel that could afford one brought a year-old male without blemish to the temple, and on the fourteenth of the month, between the afternoon and the evening, it was killed. Josephus reckoned the lambs slaughtered at a single Passover in the hundreds of thousands. The whole ritual existed to keep one night alive in the nation’s memory: the night in Egypt when the blood went on the doorposts and the destroyer passed over the houses that had it (Exodus 12). That is the week the chief priests choose to kill the Lamb of God, who is our Passover lamb, sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Seeking how to put him to death. The plot has been building for days (19:47; 20:19). They think they are managing a political problem.

For they feared the people. Not God; the people. They needed a quiet arrest, away from the crowds who hung on his words (21:38), at a festival when the city’s population multiplied several times over and Rome was watching. The men entrusted with the worship of Israel are conspiring against the salvation of Israel, and the thing governing their deliberations is a public-order risk assessment. That is the idol of approval at work in religious dress: men who feared the crowd more than they feared God, and so could stand in his house planning to kill his Son. Whatever we fear most, we end up serving (Proverbs 29:25).

Behind them a purpose is running to time. Seven weeks later Peter would set the two truths side by side before a crowd in this same city: Jesus was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and they had killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). The scheming was theirs, freely chosen and fully culpable; and it was the means by which the Lamb was brought to the feast in the very week the lambs died. The priests were thinking about crowds. God was keeping an appointment.

Does God cause people to do evil, then? No. God never puts wickedness into a heart or approves it (James 1:13). The leaders hated Jesus because they wanted to, and they will answer for it. But God is never a spectator who has to improvise around human sin. He governs it, restrains it, sets its limits and turns it to his own good ends, as he did with Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20). That is why the cross can be at once the worst crime ever committed and the best thing that ever happened. Hold both: the evil is real and blameworthy, and it is never out of God’s hand.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; the two names were used together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan entered into Judas. After the temptation in the wilderness the devil departed from Jesus until an opportune time (4:13). Now is that time. He works through a man at his side (John 13:2, 27). Luke supplies none of the theories about disappointed political hopes; he names a spiritual event: the enemy of God entered a man who had walked beside Jesus for some three years.

The stronger man. Jesus had already told the parable of this night. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armour and divides his spoil (11:21–22). The devil has chosen as his weapon the very death by which the stronger man will strip him. Satan enters Judas to destroy Jesus. Jesus lets Judas deliver him up, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).

Of the number of the twelve. Not a hanger-on: one of the Twelve, chosen after a night of prayer (6:12–16), sent out with authority to preach and to heal (9:1–2), who had come back and told Jesus all they had done (9:10). Nearness to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. A person can sit in church every week, know the Bible well and even serve in ministry, and still never have trusted Christ or loved him. Belonging is not being near the things of Jesus; it is being known by him, given a new heart and joined to him by faith (Matthew 7:22–23; John 10:27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Judas was not responsible. Luke’s next sentence answers that: Satan entered him, and then he went away and conferred. He walked to the meeting, opened the negotiation, named his terms and took the money. Every verb belongs to Judas, and Jesus pronounces a woe upon him (v. 22), which would be monstrous if the man were a puppet. Satan does not manufacture desires that were not there. He finds them, feeds them and hands the man the opportunity. Judas had already given way to greed (John 12:6). What entered him found a door already unlocked, and Judas had been turning the key, quietly, for a long time: a coin here, a resentment there, a growing private conviction that he understood things better than his master.

Could Satan enter me like that? Not if you belong to Christ. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt a Christian, accuse him, and sift him hard, as this chapter will show with Peter, but he cannot take possession of one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never one of Christ’s sheep (John 6:64, 70; 17:12). Yet the warning still stands for every Christian: do not give the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:27). Unconfessed sin, nursed resentment and secret greed are exactly the open doors he looks for.

I am afraid I might be a Judas. Some believers are frightened by this verse: they wonder whether the sin they cannot shake is the beginning of a betrayal. The fear itself is the answer, and it should be said plainly. Judas is never once recorded as being afraid of what he was becoming. He was calm; he negotiated; he ate the supper; he came to the garden with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not a conscience being handed over. It is a conscience being held. And the man in this very chapter who did deny his Lord, out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it (v. 32), and was fully restored. Judas went out to a meeting. Peter went out and wept. The difference between them was not the size of the sin (2 Corinthians 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Conferred. Luke writes the sentence as ordinary business: he went, conferred, agreed a figure, consented, and began looking for a window. No struggle is recorded. It reads like the minutes of a meeting, and that is more frightening than a scene of tormented decision. The officers were the captains of the temple police, who would make the arrest (v. 52).

To betray him. The verb is paradidōmi, to hand over. It is the word Jesus had used in his predictions (9:44; 18:32), and the word Paul will use of the Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Judas hands him over for money; the Father hands him over for love; the Son gives himself up (Galatians 2:20). Three handings-over in one act, and only one of them was wicked.

They were glad. The solution has walked in the door by itself, wearing the face of one of his own friends. Their gladness is small and squalid, and it shows what the leadership of Israel had become: relieved, at a problem solved.

Money. Matthew tells us the figure: thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). It is not an arbitrary sum. It is the compensation set in the law of Moses for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and it is the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah’s strange prophecy, the lordly price at which God himself was priced by them (Zechariah 11:12–13). That is the value the guardians of his own house placed on the Son of God: the going rate for a dead slave.

In the absence of a crowd. Both parties want darkness: the priests because their power cannot survive daylight, and Judas because betrayal cannot be done in front of witnesses. (John 3:20).

How could anyone sell Jesus for money? Very easily, and by degrees. John tells us Judas kept the common purse and used to help himself to it (John 12:6). He did not wake one morning and decide to betray the Messiah; he had spent months letting money matter more than the Master, and when the offer came the decision was already mostly made. That is why Paul calls the love of money a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). Most of us will never be offered silver for Christ. But every week we are offered small trades: a dishonest claim, a hidden purchase, a habit of worship quietly traded for overtime we do not need. Each one teaches the heart what it values.

In everyday life. Is any part of what you are doing arranged so that it happens where you will not be seen? Whatever needs the absence of a crowd usually needs it for a reason. Bring that thing into the light today, where the blood of Jesus cleanses it (1 John 1:7), with God first and then, if it is needed, with one trusted person.

For worship. The leaders were glad over a bargain; heaven is glad over a ransom. The one they bought cheaply, in an office by lamplight, had already resolved to buy them at a price no treasury could hold: not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with his own precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). God had settled the price of our redemption before the foundation of the world, and he paid it in full, in the Son they sold.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the captains of the temple police. Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, 'Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Had to be sacrificed. The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, before the meal that evening, by the thousands. Had to be is edei, it must, the word Luke uses all through his Gospel for the fixed purposes of God: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22; 24:26). The law required the lamb on that day, and the purpose of God required the Lamb.

Peter and John. Only Luke names them, the two who will stand together at the centre of Acts (Acts 3; 4; 8). Their partnership begins here, running an errand.

Prepare the Passover. It meant securing the room, buying the lamb, taking it to the temple court to be killed, roasting it whole, buying the bitter herbs and setting out the unleavened bread and the wine: a whole afternoon of ordinary labour, asked of two of his closest friends on the last day of his life. For anyone who feels their tasks are too small to matter: do the errands of your day as service to him, not as time stolen from serving him. Peter and John spent the afternoon before the Lord’s Supper buying groceries.

That we may eat it. Not that you may eat it. He includes himself in the meal, and he is looking forward to it: he will tell them he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with them (v. 15).

Was this a Passover meal? Luke, with Matthew and Mark, says so plainly. John seems at first to put the Passover a day later (John 18:28; 19:14). The more likely explanation is that John’s Passover there means the meals of the festival week, and Preparation means the Friday before the Sabbath of Passover week. Scholars still debate the calendar, and some questions about it remain open; believers hold both accounts true while the details are weighed.
