The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus is the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Should Christians keep the Passover today? Christians are free to learn from a Passover meal, and many find that seeing one explains the Lord’s Supper wonderfully. But we are not bound to keep it. The Passover was a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). The lamb has been slain once for all, and Jesus gave his church a new meal to keep until he comes, which is the Lord’s Supper. To treat the old feast as necessary would be to go back to the shadow when the light has risen.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, 'Where will you have us prepare it?' He said to them, 'Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where will you have us prepare it? A reasonable and slightly anxious question. Jerusalem at Passover was overwhelmed, its population swollen several times over, and rooms went early and to the connected.

A man carrying a jar of water. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar on his shoulder would stand out at once in a crowd of thousands.

Had Jesus arranged this beforehand, or did he know it prophetically? Luke does not say, and both are entirely possible. The parallel is the colt in 19:29–34: two disciples sent, a sign described, a password given, and everything found as told. Jesus may well have made quiet arrangements. What both explanations agree on is the thing Luke is certainly saying: nothing about this night is happening to Jesus. He is arranging it.

Follow him. A secret arrangement, probably so that Judas would not know the place in advance: not to save Jesus’ life, which he had resolved to give, but to keep the supper safe until he had placed it in his friends’ hands.

He is not being taken. He is going. Everything from here to the tomb will look like a man carried along by other people’s decisions. Luke opens the sequence with a man who knows what a stranger will be carrying that afternoon. No one takes my life from me, he had said, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

Does Jesus guide me in the details like this? He does, but usually not in this way. The same Lord governs every detail of your life by his providence, down to the hairs of your head (12:7), and he guides his people through his Word, through wise counsel and through the ordinary sense he gives. He does not promise us coded signs about which street to take, and we should not demand them or treat every coincidence as a message. Pray about the details, read the Scriptures, ask advice, decide with a clear conscience, and then trust that the one who knew about a water jar is not absent from your house move or your job interview.
verseByVerse.note: Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Teacher says to you. The message is a phrase, not an explanation. No name is given. The householder needed only that much: the arrangement was understood, and he counted it an honour to be trusted and asked no further questions. He is never named, and the room he lent has been remembered for two thousand years.

The guest room. The word is katalyma, the same word as the inn at Bethlehem where there was no place for them (2:7). At his birth there was no room; at his death a room is ready. The world that had no space for him in the manger has one large furnished room for him on his last night, and he fills it with a gift the world has fed on ever since.

A large upper room furnished. Furnished means laid out: carpets down, the low couches arranged around the table. It may have been the same upper room where the disciples gathered after the ascension (Acts 1:13), and possibly the house of Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12), though we cannot be sure.

My disciples. On the eve of the night when every one of them will fail him, one betraying, one denying, the rest scattering, he calls them my disciples. He knows exactly what they are going to do. And the room is booked for them, the meal is prepared for them, and they are still his. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1).

What if my home or my gifts seem too ordinary to matter? Then you are in exactly the householder’s position, and he is one of the quiet heroes of the Gospels. Hospitality is not a minor virtue in the New Testament; it is required of elders and commended to all (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). A kitchen table where a struggling believer is fed, a spare room for a missionary, a lift to church: these are rooms lent to Christ. Do not wait until you have something impressive to offer. Offer what you have, and let him decide what it is for.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth borrowed a room, and in it he gave away everything. He took a guest’s place in a borrowed house so that we, who were strangers, might be given a son’s place in his Father’s house, where he has gone to prepare rooms that will never be lent and never be taken back (John 14:2). We lent him an upper room for one night. He gives us a home for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as he had told them. The same construction as with the colt (19:32): the words of Jesus proved reliable in a small domestic matter. Within hours the same two men will hear things that are impossible to receive: that one of them will betray him, that Peter will deny him before dawn, that he himself will be numbered with criminals. If he could be trusted about a man with a water jar, he could be trusted about his death and resurrection.

The last easy verification. Much of what follows has to be believed in the dark. That is the ordinary shape of a Christian life: a stretch where the promises are checkable, and then a season in which nothing is confirmable and all you have is that the same voice was accurate before. That does not make the silence pleasant. It makes it survivable, because the silence of a proven friend is not the silence of a stranger.

And they prepared the Passover. He told them where; they did the work. Foreknowledge in this Gospel never replaces obedience; it directs it. They roasted a lamb, not knowing that they were laying a table for the end of the world’s long night.

Does this mean everything I want will turn out as I hope? No. What comes true is what Jesus has said, not what we have wished. He told these men about a room, and also about betrayal, denial and his own death, and all of it came true. His promises to every believer are many and certain: forgiveness, his presence, the Spirit, the resurrection of the body, a place in his kingdom. He has not promised you the job, the healing or the outcome you are praying for, though you may and should ask. Trust him for what he has said, and leave what he has not said in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the hour came. In one sense it means the appointed time for the Passover meal, which began after sunset. But this is the Gospel in which Jesus has been walking towards something with his face set (9:51), and the chapter in which he will say to the arresting party, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (v. 53). John makes the theme explicit (John 13:1); Luke says it more quietly. The hour came, and he sat down to dinner.

He reclined at table. Not on chairs, as in the paintings, but lying on low couches around a low table, propped on the left elbow, which is why the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus (John 13:23). Reclining had its own meaning. Free men reclined; slaves stood and served. The first Passover was eaten standing, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11), but by Jesus’ time reclining had become the custom, to celebrate freedom. You eat this meal lying down, at ease, because you are no longer slaves.

And the apostles with him. All twelve, including Judas. Luke has told us in v. 3 what one of them has done, and he places him here without comment, reclining with the rest.

Composure that is real. The hour has come, and what he does with it is lie down among his friends in the posture of a free man at a feast of deliverance, with the man who has already sold him somewhere along the same table. This is what composure looks like when it is real: not the absence of dread, for the garden will show you the dread, but the refusal to let dread eat the hours that are still good.

Does it matter whether we sit, stand or kneel at the Lord’s Supper? Scripture does not prescribe a posture, and churches do it differently with clear consciences. Some sit at a table, as the disciples did, to show that we are guests welcomed to a family meal; some come forward; some kneel. What matters is that the posture of the heart is right: humble, because we are sinners, and at rest, because we are free. A believer may come to that table as these men came, as guests whom the Master has invited, not as slaves earning a place.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have earnestly desired. Epithumia epethumēsa, literally with desire I have desired: a Hebrew way of doubling the word to intensify it, the language of aching for something (Genesis 31:30). Only Luke records it.

To eat this Passover with you. And the object of the longing is this: an evening with eleven ordinary men and one traitor, in a borrowed room, eating roast lamb. Of everything available to the Son of God in his last hours, he had set his heart on being at a table with them, men who will before morning argue about rank, fall asleep on him, deny him and run. He does not long for them because he has misjudged them.

Before I suffer. Then, immediately, the shadow. The word is pathein, from the same root as the church’s old name for these events, the Passion. He is dating the meal by his suffering.

Until it is fulfilled. Having named the suffering, he looks straight past it to a far side. The Passover pointed forward, and its meaning would be filled full first in his death, the true Passover sacrifice, and finally in the banquet of the kingdom (13:29; 14:15): the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9; Isaiah 25:6–8). The meal looks back to Egypt, forward to the cross, and beyond the cross to the feast.

Will there really be a feast in the kingdom? Yes, and it is more solid than we imagine, not less. The kingdom’s fulfilment comes when Christ returns, the dead are raised bodily, and God makes all things new. Scripture pictures that renewed creation with a table, food and wine, faces and fellowship (Isaiah 25:6; Matthew 8:11). We need not press every detail, but we must not make it thin and ghostly either. Those who rise will have real bodies, as Jesus did when he ate fish after his resurrection (24:42–43). Whatever the feast is, it is not less than the best meal you have ever eaten with the people you love, and he will be at the head of the table.

Why would Jesus long to be with people like me? Because his love was never based on our quality, and so our failures do not cancel it. He longed for that table knowing every denial to come. The same is true of you. He does not tolerate your company while hoping for better; he has set his heart on you, which is what it means to be chosen in him before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). When you come to the Lord’s Supper feeling unworthy, remember that the first table was laid for men who were about to fail him, and he had ached to share it with them.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, 'Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took a cup. Luke has a cup before the bread and another after it (v. 20), and it looks like a muddle until you know the shape of the meal. By the time the Mishnah (the early written collection of Jewish tradition) was compiled, the Passover was structured around four cups of wine, and something like that order was probably already followed: a cup at the opening, a cup after the telling of the Exodus story, the cup of blessing after the meal, and a cup of praise with the psalms. This first cup belongs to the earlier part of the evening, before the bread; the cup in v. 20 is the one after supper, probably the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16). So Jesus did not invent a new ceremony out of nothing. He took a cup at a meal that already carried centuries of meaning and filled it with himself.

And when he had given thanks. A Jewish host blessed God as King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine. On the night of his betrayal his first recorded word over the cup is thanksgiving.

Divide it among yourselves. He gave it to be shared. The Supper is corporate at its root: a meal of the family, not a private devotion.

Until the kingdom of God comes. He is fasting. Having said how deeply he longed for this meal, he sets the cup down until the kingdom has come: the vow of a man with unfinished business. He will not sit down to the feast until his people can sit down with him, and there is a death between here and there. So the cup he pushes away at this table is the measure of the cup he accepts in the garden. He declines the wine of the feast in order to drink the cup of wrath, so that when the kingdom comes there will be somebody there to drink with.

But did he not drink sour wine on the cross? He was offered it, and John records that he received it just before he died (23:36; John 19:29–30). That was not the festive fruit of the vine at the table of the kingdom. It was the cheap sour wine of soldiers, moistening the lips of a dying man so that he could cry out that it was finished. The vow stands: he has not yet drunk the cup of celebration with his people. He is waiting for the whole family to be gathered home.

Wine or grape juice at communion? Faithful churches differ. Jesus used wine, and many churches use it for that reason. Others use unfermented grape juice to protect those who struggle with alcohol, and point out that Jesus calls it simply the fruit of the vine. Both seek to honour him, and neither should despise the other. What matters is what the cup means: his blood poured out, and the feast to come.

In everyday life. When you next share the cup at church, look around at the people sharing it with you. They are your family at his table, the ones with whom you will drink it new in the kingdom. If there is someone there you are estranged from, go and be reconciled first (Matthew 5:23–24).
verseByVerse.note: The Passover meal included several cups of wine; Luke mentions a cup before the bread and another after supper.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took bread. The four actions are the same as at the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and at Emmaus (24:30): took, blessed, broke, gave. The hand that fed the crowds will be recognised breaking bread on the evening of the resurrection.

This is my body. At this point in the Passover the host probably held up the unleavened bread and spoke of it as the bread of affliction the fathers ate in Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3). Jesus says something else. This bread now speaks of his own body, about to be given in death. He broke it before anyone broke him. He gave it before anyone took him. Nothing about that night was extracted from him.

Given for you. Only Luke and Paul record these words (1 Corinthians 11:24). The preposition is hyper: on behalf of, and in a sacrifice like this one, in the place of. Not merely for your benefit, but in your stead. This is substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before, in the plainest words he ever used about his own death.

Do this in remembrance of me. As Israel remembered the exodus at Passover, the church remembers Christ’s death at his Supper. The word is anamnēsis, and in the Old Testament remembering of this kind is never a private effort of memory but a public act that brings the past event into the present: each generation ate the Passover as though it had itself come out of Egypt. So the Supper is a living proclamation of his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26) and a renewal of the covenant: at the table God sets his promise before his people again, your sins are forgiven for my Son’s sake, and they answer it by taking the bread in faith, as a bride and groom might renew their vows, not to make the marriage but because it is already made.

Where Christians differ: the Supper. Four words have divided the church for five hundred years, and the reader is entitled to know what the argument is about. Roman Catholics hold transubstantiation: at the priest’s word the substance of the bread becomes the actual body of Christ, though everything observable remains bread, and the Mass is offered as a sacrifice. Lutherans reject that but hold that Christ’s body is genuinely present in, with and under the bread. Those who follow Zwingli hold that the bread signifies the body and the Supper is a memorial and a pledge. Calvin and the Reformed churches hold a real spiritual presence: the bread remains bread, and yet Christ is truly given, so that by his Spirit the believer really feeds on him, not with the teeth but by faith. This commentary’s view: Calvin’s view is best. This is my body is a sacramental sign, a visible sign of a promised reality, spoken while his body was at the table, unbroken, in front of them, which settles what kind of sentence it is: he spoke as he always spoke, I am the door, I am the vine. Yet the Supper is more than a memory. The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread a participation in his body (1 Corinthians 10:16): believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit, who joins us to the risen Lord in heaven. Nor is it a sacrifice offered again. Luke’s word is remembrance, not repetition: Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14), and the Supper receives that offering rather than renewing it. The Westminster Confession, which the 1689 London Baptist Confession follows here, puts it carefully: worthy receivers, inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally, receive and feed upon Christ crucified (Westminster 29.7; 1689 30.7).

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? Think of how food works. You do not admire bread; you take it into yourself, and it becomes your strength. At the Supper, as the bread and cup are taken with the mouth, the believer’s heart takes hold of Christ himself, crucified and risen, as the one whose body was given for him. The Holy Spirit makes that real: he lifts our hearts to Christ where he is, and Christ strengthens our faith, assures us of forgiveness and binds us to him and to one another. It is not magic, and it is not merely thinking hard. It is communion with a living Saviour, through means he has appointed.

What if I feel nothing when I take communion? Then you have still received what was given. The Supper does not depend on the strength of your feelings but on the faithfulness of Christ who promised himself in it. Some Sundays the heart is warm; some Sundays it is numb with tiredness or grief. Come anyway, trusting his word: given for you. A child fed by his father is nourished whether or not he notices the taste. And if the numbness persists for months, speak to your pastor; it may be weariness, sorrow or sin that needs care, but it is never a reason to stay away from the means of grace.

How often should we take the Lord’s Supper? Scripture does not fix it. The early church seems to have broken bread often, perhaps each Lord’s Day (Acts 2:42; 20:7), and many churches celebrate weekly; others monthly or quarterly, to guard against it becoming routine. Calvin wished it to be weekly. What Scripture does require is that it be kept, regularly, with self-examination and faith, until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26).

For worship. He asked to be remembered by a meal, not a monument. The Lord of glory, hours from being forsaken, chose bread, the commonest thing on the table, and put into it the most uncommon promise: given for you. Kings are remembered in marble; he is remembered at plain tables in cathedrals, prison cells and village halls. And the One who asked to be remembered never forgets his own. He feeds them with himself by his Spirit, and he will remember them on the day he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After they had eaten. Probably the third Passover cup, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the main meal.

Poured out for you. For Jewish men, blood in connection with a cup was close to unthinkable: the law forbade drinking blood because the life is in the blood and God had given it for atonement on the altar (Leviticus 17:11–14). That is exactly why the words work. He is not inviting them to drink blood; he is telling them what the cup means, and the meaning is atonement. Poured out is altar language, the blood of a sacrifice poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Atonement means that sin is covered and the sinner brought back to God, because a life has been given in his place; the holy God does not shrug at sin, but neither does he leave the sinner to bear it.

The new covenant in my blood. Jeremiah, six centuries earlier, in the ruin of everything, heard God promise a new covenant, not like the one their fathers broke. This one would be different in three ways: the law written on the heart rather than on stone; every member knowing God personally, from the least to the greatest; and the ground of it all forgiveness, for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The law written on the heart means that God’s will is no longer only a rule outside you, pressing in, but a desire within you: you begin to want what he commands, because he has given you a new heart and put his Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:26–27). That promise had stood unfulfilled through the return from exile and the rebuilt temple. Now a man at a supper table lifts a cup and says: here it is, and it is in my blood.

Covenants are sealed with blood. Abraham’s covenant is cut between divided animals (Genesis 15), and Sinai’s is sealed with Moses throwing blood on the people and saying, behold the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). What is new here is not the mechanism but the victim. The covenant at Sinai was sealed with the blood of animals and broken by the people within weeks; the new covenant is sealed with Jesus’ own blood, and so it rests not on our faithfulness but on his (Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:15–22).

Textual note. Some ESV readers will see a note that a few manuscripts omit the end of v. 19 and v. 20. The longer text has overwhelming support, and the same words are found independently in Paul (1 Corinthians 11:23–25) and in Matthew and Mark. No doctrine rests on Luke’s wording alone.

Who may come to the Lord’s Table? Those who belong to Christ: baptised believers who trust him and are willing to turn from sin. Paul tells each to examine himself and then eat (1 Corinthians 11:28). It is not a reward for being good enough; it is for sinners who need Christ. But it is not for unbelievers, nor for those living in unrepentant sin under the church’s discipline. Baptist churches, holding believer’s baptism because in the New Testament baptism follows faith as the disciple’s first public confession, ask that those who come should first have been baptised as believers, and many gladly welcome to the table believers from paedobaptist churches (those that baptise the infants of believers) who love the same Lord, recognising them as brothers and sisters in Christ.

I am struggling with a sin, so should I stay away? Not if you are fighting it. This fear keeps some believers from the table: they are not good enough to come. But the cup does not commemorate your fitness. It commemorates the death that made you fit, and it is offered by the one who poured it out for a table that included a traitor, a denier and ten men who would run. Examine yourself, confess the sin to God, and come as a sinner holding on to Christ. The person who should hold back is the one who has decided to keep a sin and stop fighting it; for him the Supper is a call to repent first, today, and then to come.

Does God really forget my sin? He chooses not to remember it against you. God knows all things, but in the new covenant he binds himself never again to bring your forgiven sins up as a charge, to hold them over you, or to treat you as they deserve (Hebrews 10:17–18). They were remembered once, fully, at the cross, and laid on Christ. When your conscience digs them up again, answer with the cup: this was poured out for me, and God has promised to remember my sin no more.

verseByVerse.quote: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the table. Matthew and Mark have the announcement of the betrayal before the bread and the cup. Luke puts it after, and the effect is stark. In that culture sharing a dish was a pledge of friendship and loyalty. Psalm 41 had already given words to the wound: the trusted friend who ate the psalmist’s bread and lifted his heel against him (Psalm 41:9). In the Son of David that psalm reaches its fullest meaning, and John records Jesus applying it to this very night (John 13:18).

Did Judas receive the bread and cup? Luke’s order makes it look as if he did. But Matthew and Mark put the warning about the betrayer before the Supper, and John has Judas leave after the morsel (John 13:30). Luke often arranges events by subject, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the cup was shared. Either way, he sat at the table with Jesus and betrayed him.

As it has been determined. The word is hōrismenon: marked out, fixed, appointed by God (Acts 2:23; 4:28). The cross is not a catastrophe that overtook the plan; it is the plan. Goes is the language of a man on a journey, walking a road he has chosen.

Woe to that man. The betrayal fulfils a determined purpose and remains entirely the betrayer’s own guilt; Jesus asserts both in one breath and makes no attempt to reconcile them. Woe here is grief as well as doom: the cry of a friend over a man walking to ruin.

If it was determined, how can Judas be blamed? Because he did exactly what he wanted to do. Nobody forced Judas; God did not put a single wicked desire into his heart. He chose freely, for his own reasons, and God in his wisdom used that free choice to accomplish redemption. Scripture never explains fully how both are true, but it insists on both, and so must we. If God were not sovereign, the cross would be an accident; if Judas were not responsible, there would be no sin for the cross to deal with. A man is judged for what he intends, and Judas intended betrayal (Genesis 50:20).

Could Judas have repented? Yes. The offer was real to the very end. Jesus warned him at this table, washed his feet, and in the garden asked him a question that held the door open (v. 48). Judas did not repent because he would not. Nothing in God’s decree stopped a man who wanted to come back; the tragedy is that he did not want to. Scripture calls him the son of destruction (John 17:12), and his end shows a remorse that never turned to God. No one who truly comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37).

A word for the wronged. People who have been badly wronged live between two temptations. One is to conclude that the wrong was outside God’s reach, which makes the world random and God small. The other is to conclude that because God had a purpose in it, the person who did it was not really guilty, a false comfort that leaves the victim unable even to name what happened. This verse refuses both. God’s purpose stood, and the man who did it is answerable. You are permitted to say that what was done to you was wicked, and that God was not absent from it, and you are not required to make those two sentences into one. Where the wrong was abuse or a crime, it must be named, reported and stopped; trusting God’s purpose never means covering it up.

parallels.desc: according to the definite plan of God

verseByVerse.quote: And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of them. Eleven men, some three years in his company, and when a betrayer is announced, not one of them can identify him. Matthew adds that each asked, Is it I? (Matthew 26:22). Serious spiritual defection does not announce itself in advance. It is generally invisible until it is complete, sometimes even to the person concerned.

The eleven looked inward first. If the Lord says one of us is capable of it, I had better start with myself. It was a sound instinct, the opposite of the reflex to run an accusation across everyone we know and stop just short of our own door. So Paul tells the Corinthians to examine themselves before eating (1 Corinthians 11:28), not each other.

The one who knew. Only one man at that table knew the answer, and he did not give it. Jesus had read hearts all through this Gospel (5:22; 6:8), and he knew Judas’s. Yet he did not expose him to the table. The Lord who sees every heart chose to shield the traitor from exposure and to leave the door of repentance open to the last moment.

How do I examine myself without becoming morbid? Examine yourself to find sin and bring it to Christ, not to find a reason to despair. Ask honest, simple questions: Am I trusting Christ, or something I have done? Is there a sin I have stopped fighting? Is there someone I refuse to forgive? Then take what you find straight to the cross and confess it. Do not keep digging once you have looked; the purpose of looking at yourself is to look away to him. The eleven asked, Is it I?, and then they stayed at the table. Self-examination that ends in fleeing from Christ has gone wrong. Self-examination that ends at his feet has done its work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–38 — Greatness, Sifting, and the Turning Season
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The bread has been broken and the betrayal announced, and an argument breaks out about rank. Jesus describes the world they know, where rulers arrange to be thanked as benefactors, and says it shall not be so with them: the leader is to be as one who serves, as he has just served them.

Then he gives them what their ambition was reaching for: he counts their staying with him, and assigns them a kingdom, a place at his table and thrones. He tells Simon that Satan has asked to sift them all, and that he has prayed for him that his faith may not fail, and that when he has turned again he is to strengthen his brothers. Peter protests, and is told the number and the hour of his denial. Jesus warns that the season of welcome is over, in a saying about swords that the next verses show is not a call to fight.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 32 is the perseverance of the saints in one sentence, and it rests on Christ’s prayer, not on the strength of Christians. Peter’s faith held because Christ prayed for him, and he always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

The teaching on greatness in verses 25 to 27 applies the incarnation to authority. The one who serves at the table is the eternal Son, and within a day his serving goes as far as the cross. Authority in the kingdom is real, and it exists for those under it.

Verses 35 to 38 must be read together. Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12, that he will be numbered with the transgressors, and that is why the swords must go. The passage supports neither holy war nor a ban on all force by any authority; it shows that Christ’s kingdom is not advanced by the sword.
verseByVerse.examples:
Anyone who leads anything can ask when they last did something for their people that carried no credit and that nobody would notice. That is the youngest man’s work, and Jesus took it.

Verses 33 and 34 are for anyone who has made God a promise and broken it. His failure surprised Jesus no more than his sincerity did, and being told in advance meant the denial could only ever say: he knew, and he prayed for me anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dispute. The bread has been broken, the cup passed, the betrayal announced, and minutes later an argument breaks out about rank. Only Luke places it here. It was probably about seating, who would lie nearest to Jesus, and the word is philoneikia, literally a love of winning. Not a disagreement they fell into but an appetite they indulged.

Regarded as the greatest. The old argument. They had had it before (9:46), and had been answered then with a child set in front of them. The honest response is recognition: a church can have a deeply moving communion service and a quarrel in the car park afterwards about who was asked to serve at it. Jesus does not shame them. He describes a world they know.

Kings of the Gentiles. They play the lord. The world’s model of greatness is power over others, and it has never needed to be taught.

Called benefactors. Benefactor, euergetēs, was a formal honorific, voted by cities, inscribed on stone and coins, and claimed by rulers who intended everyone to remember what they had done; Ptolemy III of Egypt took it as his official title. Jesus has named the mechanism by which worldly power sustains itself: force that has arranged to be thanked. The tell is not whether a person does good, but whether the doing of good has been arranged so that it is seen, credited and remembered.

He went about doing good. The verb from this word appears only once in the New Testament, of Jesus, who went about doing good, literally benefacting (Acts 10:38). The one true Benefactor never took the title. He took a towel, and then a cross. The kings of the Gentiles had their goodness carved in stone so that it would come back to them. His came back to him as thorns and nails.

Is ambition wrong? Not in itself. Jesus does not tell them to stop wanting greatness; in the next breath he tells them how to have it, and then gives them a kingdom (vv. 26–29). Paul calls it a noble thing to aspire to oversight in the church (1 Timothy 3:1). What is wrong is ambition for yourself: to be seen, ranked and thanked. The test is simple. Would I still want this work if nobody ever knew I did it, and if someone else got the credit? Godly ambition wants Christ to be great and the church to be served, and it is content to be the youngest at the table while that happens.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefactor” was an official title that rulers loved to claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not so with you. Five words, and they carve the church out of the world: the one place where the usual arithmetic of status does not operate. He does not abolish leadership; he redefines it in the same sentence. What is forbidden is not office; it is what office is used for.

As the youngest. In that world the youngest at a gathering did the menial jobs. He fetched, he was interruptible, and everybody’s needs came before his plans.

As one who serves. Leadership in the kingdom is service (Mark 10:43–45). The leader is the one who carries the most weight for others, not the one who is carried.

Who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer and gives the obvious answer himself, which is a way of making sure nobody escapes into cleverness. Everyone in the room knew: the man lying down. By the world’s standards the guest is greater than the waiter, and in every society that has ever existed the served outrank the servers.

I am among you as the one who serves. On the same evening, John tells us, he took a towel and washed their feet (John 13:4–15), including the feet of the man who had already agreed to betray him. This is where the passage stops being about management and becomes about God. The one speaking is the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, holding a basin. And within a day the One who poured the water will pour out his life. Luke does not record here the ransom saying (Mark 10:45); he shows it, the night before the ransom was paid.

Does servant leadership mean leaders have no real authority? No. Elders are to be respected and obeyed (Hebrews 13:17), and parents and others hold real authority from God. Jesus himself is Lord while he serves. The point is the direction in which authority flows: it is given for the good of those under it, never for the comfort of the one holding it. A servant leader still decides, still teaches, still corrects, but he does it as a man carrying others, and he expects to give an account to God for them.

What does this mean in a marriage and a home? The same pattern applies, and it is the key to Christian headship. Scripture calls a husband the head of his wife, and in the same breath tells him to love her as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:23–25). So headship is not a right to be served; it is a call to lead in self-giving love, taking the first step in prayer, in apology and in sacrifice, protecting and providing and putting her good before his own. Christians differ on how far headship reaches, and many egalitarian believers read these verses as mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21); this commentary holds that headship is real, and every faithful reading agrees that it never licenses control. A man who uses headship to control, belittle or frighten his wife has turned it upside down into the Gentile model. Abuse is never tolerated in Christ’s church; a wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church must stand with her.

For worship. Once he told a parable no one else would have dared to tell, of a master who comes home in the night, finds his servants awake, and dresses himself for service, has them recline at table, and comes and waits on them (12:37). At this table the Master was already doing it, and he has never stopped. He serves his people now from the throne, and on the last day the Lord of glory will still be the one who serves: the King of all things waits at his own table.

verseByVerse.quote: 'You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom,
verseByVerse.commentary:
You stayed. Having corrected their ambition, he now satisfies it. He does not tell them to want less; they have been wanting the right thing in the wrong shape. Within hours they will fall asleep on him and scatter, and one will deny him three times. And on the evening before all of it Jesus says: you stayed.

He counts the staying. They did stay: through the hostility, the plots, the crowds falling away when the teaching got hard (John 6:66), the long homeless walk to Jerusalem. The failure coming is real, and it does not cancel what preceded it. He is not scoring the worst night. He sees the whole thing, and he counts the staying.

I assign to you a kingdom. The verb is diatithemai, to appoint or arrange, a word used for making a covenant or a will, and the verb behind the noun covenant (diathēkē). A man about to die is settling his affairs, and what he has to leave is a kingdom (Hebrews 9:16–17). As my Father assigned to me: the Father has given the kingdom to the Son (Daniel 7:14), and the Son gives it to his disciples by the same verb (12:32). They argued about greatness; Jesus gives them a kingdom.

A scramble by heirs. This recasts the whole dispute. They were fighting over a portion of something that was already being left to all of them in full. That is nearly always the shape of status-hunger in the church: a scramble for a slice, conducted by heirs. If we are children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

Does Jesus really count my faithfulness when I keep failing? He does, because he sees what is really there. A Christian’s faithfulness is not erased by his falls, any more than these men’s years with him were erased by one night. That is not because the failures do not matter; Jesus names them honestly. It is because your perseverance is itself his work in you, and he will not despise what he has made (Philippians 1:6). He remembers the cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). If you are still following him after many stumbles, he calls that staying.

parallels.desc: he himself has suffered when tempted
if we endure, we will also reign

verseByVerse.quote: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At my table. The meal is not over; it is adjourned (v. 18). The same table, the same host, the same men, and this time nobody is arguing about seats and nobody leaves in the dark.

Heaven is a table. Heaven is usually left vague and should not be. It is not a choir practice that never ends. It is, in his own image, a table: food, drink, faces, conversation, and the person you most want to be near presiding over it. Everyone who has ever sat at a long meal with people they love and felt the evening going too fast has been given a small, accurate sample of it.

Thrones. The Twelve stand for the renewed people of God. Judging carries the sense it has in the book of Judges, to govern and put right, rather than merely to pass sentence (Matthew 19:28). And all believers will share in some way in his reign: do you not know that the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2)?

What are these thrones? Christians read this in different ways, and the reader should know them. Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years after his return, see here a future earthly reign over a restored Israel. Matthew places it in the new world (Matthew 19:28), the renewed creation. The more likely reading is that the apostles share in Christ’s rule over his people, the true Israel of all who believe, which begins now through their word, the apostolic foundation on which the church is built (Ephesians 2:20), and will be complete in the new creation. Whatever God has still in store for ethnic Israel, which Christians present differently from Romans 11, the promise here is of the apostles’ share in Christ’s reign.

The future is not passive. Christians are going to be trusted with something, as the faithful servant is given authority over ten cities (19:17). And the men handed this promise were not a shortlist of the impressive but provincial men who had spent the last few minutes squabbling about precedence and would spend the next few hours failing.

Will I really rule with Christ? Yes, in the way that fits you and that he appoints. Scripture says those who endure will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12), and that the redeemed will reign on the earth (Revelation 5:10). We do not know the details, and we should not imagine a crowded court of rival kings. But it means that the work you do faithfully now, in small things, is training for responsibility in the new creation, and that heaven will not be idleness. It will be service without sin, weariness or rivalry, under a King we love.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. Having promised thrones (v. 30), Jesus tells the man who usually speaks first that the night ahead will shake him to pieces. The thrones will come not by their own strength but because he prays for them.

Simon, Simon. The doubled name is how Scripture speaks when something enormous is about to be said to one person: Abraham, Abraham; Moses, Moses; Martha, Martha (10:41); Saul, Saul. It is tender and urgent. Not Peter, the rock, but Simon, the name he was born with: he is being addressed as the man he still is, as he is about to fail.

Satan demanded to have you. Demanded a person be handed over, as in Job, where the accuser asks for a man, is granted a limit, and cannot exceed it by a hair (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6). Satan does not have free access to God’s people. He has to ask. And the ESV notes that this you is plural in the Greek: he demanded to have all of you. Satan asked for the whole barn.

Sift you like wheat. Sifting is violent. Satan’s aim was not to shake the chaff out of Peter but to demonstrate that Peter was chaff, to shake them until their faith fell apart.

But I have prayed for you. Here the you is singular: for Peter specifically, who was about to fall most heavily. Satan asked for them all; Jesus names one man. And the one who prayed for Peter on earth now intercedes for his people at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25).

That your faith may not fail. Consider what he did not pray. He did not pray that Peter would be spared the sifting; the sifting comes. He did not pray that Peter would not fall; Peter falls within hours, three times. He prayed for the one thing underneath all of it: that the man would go down and not stay down. Peter fell, but did not fall away. Judas fell away. To fall is to sin badly, even grievously, and then be brought back to Christ in repentance. To fall away is to turn from Christ for good and never return, which shows that the faith was never real (1 John 2:19). The difference is not that Peter was stronger. Jesus prayed for Peter. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints, the truth that everyone God has truly saved will go on believing to the end, because God keeps them: not the strength of our faith but the prayer of our Saviour (John 17:11–15).

And when you have turned again. Repented, returned. The word is when, not if. Jesus knows Peter will fall, and he knows Peter will come back. The restoration is settled before the fall has happened.

Strengthen your brothers. The man about to be the worst failure in the room is appointed to hold up everyone else, because a man who has been carried back knows the way. Restored, he strengthened others (John 21:15–17), and years later he wrote to suffering churches about the devil who prowls like a roaring lion, and about the God of all grace who will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (1 Peter 5:8–10). He had been sifted, and he knew.

Does strengthen your brothers make Peter the head of the church? No. Roman Catholic teaching has seen Peter’s primacy here, and Peter’s leadership among the apostles is plain in Acts. But the commission is personal and pastoral: Peter, restored after his fall, would strengthen the others, as he did in Acts and in his letters. Nothing in it speaks of an office passed to successors, and Paul later rebuked Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11–14).

Why does God allow Satan to sift his people at all? Because God means the sifting for good while Satan means it for harm. Satan wanted to prove Peter was chaff; God used the same night to burn away Peter’s self-confidence and make him a humble shepherd. Trials test faith so that it is found genuine, more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). God sets the limits, and nothing exceeds them (1 Corinthians 10:13). That does not make the sifting painless, but it means it is never pointless, and never outside the reach of Christ’s prayers.

Does Jesus pray for me personally? Yes. His high-priestly prayer reaches beyond the apostles to those who will believe through their word (John 17:20), and he lives to intercede for all who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He does not pray for the church in a vague mass; he knows his sheep by name (John 10:3). When you are being shaken and cannot pray well yourself, the Son is praying for you, and the Father always hears him (John 11:42).

For worship. John the Baptist had said that the winnowing fork is in Christ’s hand, and that he will gather his wheat into his barn (3:17). Satan may shake a disciple, but he does not hold the fork. The One who does had already counted Simon wheat, and prayed over him. The accuser asks; the Son decides; and what the Son has gathered no sifting will scatter.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural — Satan asked for all of them — while in verse 32 it is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter. Sifting shook wheat in a sieve to separate it.

parallels.desc: Satan asks leave to test Job
shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, 'Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.' Jesus said, 'I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ready to go with you. Peter means it entirely. Before the night is out he will strike with a sword in front of an armed crowd (John 18:10) and follow into the high priest’s courtyard when the others have gone. What he lacks is accurate knowledge of himself. He heard a warning and answered with a list of his qualities. That is the quiet idol of self-reliance, the belief that my love for God is the thing that will hold me, and it is often strongest in the most devoted people. One day he would go to prison and, by early tradition, to death in Rome (Acts 12:3–5; John 21:18–19), held up by the Lord who had gone before him. But not yet.

I tell you, Peter. The only time in this Gospel Jesus addresses him as Peter. The rock is about to crumble, and the name he was given is spoken over the moment he will least resemble it.

Three times. The reply is exact: this day, three times, before dawn. Jesus does not say Peter is weak in general; he tells him the number and the deadline.

Why tell him in advance? It cannot be to prevent the denial, because it does not. It cannot be to humiliate him, because Jesus has just promised to restore him. The reason is in the words before: when you have turned again. If Peter had denied Christ without warning, the collapse would have been total. He would have concluded that Jesus had misjudged him, that his discipleship had been a mistake from the start, that there was nothing to go back to. Judas seems to have reached a conclusion of that kind, and it destroyed him. Because he was told in advance, the denial could only ever mean one thing: he knew. He knew, and he prayed for me anyway, and he told me I would come back.

Did the rooster crow once or twice? Mark says the rooster would crow twice (Mark 14:30). Luke gives the general warning, before cock-crow; Mark, whose Gospel early tradition links with Peter’s preaching, gives the precise form. One account is fuller than the other; they do not contradict.

Should I stop making promises to God? No, but make them leaning on him rather than on yourself. Vows and resolutions are not wrong; Scripture is full of people pledging themselves to God. Peter’s mistake was not his devotion but his self-reliance, and his refusal to hear the warning. So make your promises as prayers: Lord, I want to be faithful in this; keep me, for I cannot keep myself. And when you break one, do not conclude that the whole thing was a sham. Confess it, get up and go on. A broken resolution is a reason to trust Christ more, not to stop following him.

In everyday life. Think of a promise you made God and did not keep: the habit you were going to give up, the resolve after a conviction that lasted eleven days. Bring that broken promise to Christ today: he kept perfectly what you have broken, and his obedience, not your record, is counted as yours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9). Then replace it with a humbler prayer: keep me.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?' They said, 'Nothing.' He said to them, 'But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two seasons. The talk at the table looks back to the open doors of chapters 9 and 10 and forward to the hostility of Acts. Everything turns on the sentence that follows: he will be numbered with the transgressors (v. 37). Because the world is about to treat the Master as a criminal, it will treat his servants as his. So the sword saying belongs to the passion story, not to a manual on self-defence.

No moneybag. He makes them answer out loud about the missions when he sent them out unprovisioned (9:3; 10:4), into a countryside that received them.

Did you lack anything? Their answer is one word: nothing. God had provided through people’s hospitality. It is a good question to be made to answer, and worth answering yourself before reading on. Not, has life been easy? but the narrower and more testable one: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word the disciples used, and are surprised by it. And if your honest answer is harder than that, if you have known real want, Scripture does not ask you to pretend: Paul knew hunger and need (Philippians 4:12), and the promise is not that we never lack bread but that he never leaves us (Hebrews 13:5).

But now. The change is not in God’s care but in the world’s welcome. The men at this table will go out to the arrests and courtrooms he described (21:12), and will need to provide for themselves.

The Lord who sent them. It was his name that opened the doors (10:17), and the reason the season is changing is himself. The world that welcomed his messengers is about to reject their Master, and the hostility they will meet is the hostility he meets first, tonight. Disciples share their Lord’s welcome, and they share his rejection (John 15:20).

Sell his cloak. One of the hardest sentences in the Gospels: a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance. A cloak was a man’s coat by day and his blanket by night (Exodus 22:26–27). To sell it for a sword is to say: the danger ahead is now greater than the cold. His own response, when they produce two swords and later when one is used, shows plainly that it is not a licence for the disciples to fight.

Does this verse teach that Christians may carry weapons or use force in self-defence? It is not really about that question, and it should not be made to settle it. Jesus is speaking figuratively of the danger ahead, and when a disciple took him literally he said, enough, and later stopped the sword and healed the wound (vv. 38, 50–51). Christians differ on personal self-defence, and Scripture elsewhere gives the governing authority the sword to punish evil (Romans 13:4). What this passage settles is that the gospel and the kingdom of Christ are never to be advanced or defended by the sword (John 18:36).
verseByVerse.note: The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance, as verses 38 and 51 show.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.' And they said, 'Look, Lord, here are two swords.' And he said to them, 'It is enough.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Scripture must be fulfilled in me. Must, dei: the divine necessity again, the fixed purpose of God written in advance and now arriving.

Numbered with the transgressors. He quotes Isaiah 53:12, the last line of the Servant Song (Isaiah’s poem of the LORD’s suffering Servant), about the servant who poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors, yet bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors. It is the only direct quotation of Isaiah 53 by Jesus in the Gospels, and the lens through which he reads his own arrest (23:32–33). That is also the reason the swords must go. A man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one.

Its fulfillment. Literally has its end. Jesus finds his own name in Isaiah 53, and goes out to the garden to make it true.

Two swords. They take him literally: two short swords or large knives, perhaps used for the Passover lamb. He was telling them the friendly season was over; they heard sword and reached for iron.

It is enough. Not that two swords are enough to fight, which would be absurd against an armed detachment, and Jesus knows it. Rather: enough of this, the weary words of a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong (Deuteronomy 3:26). And when the iron did come out in the garden, he stopped it with a word and mended the only casualty of the night with a touch (vv. 50–51).

Buy a sword, then put it away, so which is it? Down the centuries the church has misread this in both directions. Some have taken v. 36 as a divine licence for the sword and built crusades and holy wars on it. Others have taken v. 51 as an absolute ban on any force whatever, in any hands, for any cause. The passage will carry neither load. The key is the detail easily missed: two swords for twelve men about to be surrounded is not enough for a fight, and Jesus says, it is enough. The single sword-stroke of the whole passion was struck by a disciple, against Christ’s will, and Jesus reversed it. That is Luke’s last word on swords in the kingdom.

What does numbered with the transgressors mean for me? It means he was counted where you belonged so that you could be counted where he belonged. On the cross he was listed among the lawless, and God treated him as the sin-bearer. God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that in him we might become his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21). That exchange is the whole gospel. When your conscience reminds you that you belong in the column of transgressors, answer that Christ has already stood in it, and you have been moved, by grace, to his.

For worship. He was numbered with the transgressors, and he made the most of the company. Hanging between two of them, he heard one ask to be remembered, and answered with paradise (23:42–43). He stooped low enough to be counted among the lawless, and stayed close enough to them to save.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives as was his custom, which is why Judas knew where to find him, and why he had a well-worn path of prayer on the worst night of his life. He tells the disciples to pray for themselves, that they may not enter into temptation.

Kneeling, he asks the Father to remove the cup, the cup of God’s wrath in the prophets, and yields: not my will, but yours, be done. Luke alone records the angel and the sweat like great drops of blood, verses some manuscripts omit. He finds the disciples sleeping for sorrow and wakes them gently to pray.

Then Judas arrives at the head of the arresting party and comes to kiss him, and Jesus meets him with his name and a question. When a disciple cuts off a servant’s ear, Jesus stops the violence and heals the man: this is your hour, he tells the leaders, and the power of darkness.
verseByVerse.theology:
In Gethsemane a true human will, which did not want the cup, freely bent itself to the Father’s will. Where Adam chose his own will in a garden, the last Adam chose his Father’s, and by that obedience the many are made righteous. The silence that met his request to be spared shows that there was no other way for sinners to be saved.

The last healing before the cross was done for an enemy, unasked, by the prisoner. And the hour of darkness was real, with real authority, but it was only an hour, and God had set it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 39 is for anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there: the path that carries a person through such a night is made in the ordinary weeks.

Verse 42 answers a woman facing a diagnosis who wonders whether her honest if you are willing is weak faith: the Son of God prayed it. Verses 45 and 46 are for the believer whose grief has made prayer feel impossible: the Lord wakes his sleeping friends gently.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, 'Pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. At supper Jesus told Peter he had prayed for him (v. 32); now he prays for himself, and tells the disciples to pray (vv. 40, 46). The one who goes to the cross is not a victim swept along but a Son who has prayed his way to it.

As was his custom. The pattern of the week (21:37), and it has two consequences. The first is that Judas knew where to find him (John 18:2). Jesus goes, on the one night when his habits are lethal, to the one place his betrayer would look. He did not hide.

A path already trodden. The second is about prayer. The worst night of his life did not send him somewhere new; when the crisis came he did not have to invent a practice, only keep one. What carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, made in the ordinary weeks when prayer feels unnecessary.

When he came to the place. Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives; the name means oil press. Luke does not name it. He simply calls it the place, as if every reader knew where the Lord prayed.

Pray for yourselves. About to enter the deepest agony any human being has known, he does not ask them to pray for him but for themselves. The words are lifted straight out of the prayer he taught them: lead us not into temptation (11:4). Temptation, peirasmos, is the trial that is coming, testing as well as enticement, which could make them fall. It is a plea born of the self-distrust these men lack. The danger closing in was real and armed, and the only defence he issued was prayer, at the beginning of the scene and again at the end (v. 46).

Does God lead us into temptation? God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does bring his people into testing. The prayer asks to be kept from falling when the test comes; and God promises that he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

How do I build a habit of prayer like this? Start small, regular and fixed, rather than large and occasional. Choose a time and a place, as Jesus had the Mount of Olives: a chair, a walk, the first ten minutes after the children leave. Use the Lord’s Prayer as a frame, the Psalms as words when you have none, and a short list of people to pray for. Expect it to feel dry some days; the habit is not for the good days but for the night when you will need a worn path. Pray with others too, in your church’s prayer meeting, because it is easier to keep a path that others walk with you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, 'Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
About a stone’s throw. Near enough to be seen and heard, far enough to be alone. Luke, who drew on eyewitnesses (1:2), measures the distance.

And knelt down. The customary posture for Jewish prayer was standing. Kneeling was for extremity, a sign of intensity and submission. In Mark he falls on the ground (Mark 14:35).

Father. Whatever else is about to be said, it begins there, and the address never wavers. Even in agony, the intimate name.

Remove this cup. The cup has to be identified correctly, because everything depends on it. In the prophets the cup is a fixed image, and it is not an image of pain in general. It is the cup of the wrath of God: the LORD holds a cup of foaming wine that the wicked of the earth must drain to its dregs (Psalm 75:8); the cup of the wine of wrath for the nations (Jeremiah 25:15); the cup of staggering (Isaiah 51:17). This wrath has nothing of a man losing control about it: it is the steady, holy resistance of perfect goodness to evil. So what makes him shake is not the nails. Jewish martyrs went to terrible deaths with calm defiance; if Jesus were merely facing execution he would be less brave than his own martyrs. What is in front of him is the cup: the undiluted judgment of God against sin, to be drunk in the place of sinners by the only man who never deserved a drop of it.

If you are willing. He does not presume. He asks, and the asking is real: if there is another way, let there be another way. There was not, and the silence that followed that request is the measure of what the cross was for. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of it, there was no other way for you to be saved.

Not my will. The heart of the prayer: total submission. He genuinely did not want the cup, and that is what makes it obedience rather than indifference. Where Adam chose his own will in a garden, Christ says your will in a garden. And this obedience is our salvation: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 10:7–10).

Is it not cruel for a Father to pour out wrath on his Son? Cruelty would mean a Father punishing an unwilling third party, and the Son is nothing of the kind. The Father and the Son are one God, and the Son came of his own will: no one takes my life from me, he said, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). The cross is not God punishing someone else to spare himself trouble. It is God himself, in the person of the Son, bearing the cost of his own justice for those he loves. That is why Paul can say that God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).

Did Jesus have two wills? Yes. He is one person, the eternal Son, with two natures, divine and human, and each nature has its own will. As God he shares the one will of the Father and the Spirit. As man he has a true human will, which recoiled from the cup as any holy human will must, and which he freely and perfectly bent to the Father’s purpose. The church confessed this against those who said Christ had only one will (Constantinople, 681), because a Saviour without a human will could not offer human obedience in our place. Gethsemane is where you see it: a real man choosing, at the cost of everything, to obey.

Is it weak faith to pray if it is your will? No. The Son of God prayed it, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is not a failure of faith; it is the highest thing faith ever does. Pray boldly for healing, for a marriage, for a child: ask, and say what you long for. Then add what Jesus added, not as a hedge but as trust. It is not lack of faith that says, your will be done. It is faith in a Father who knows better than you, and who did not spare his own Son.

For worship. A few hours earlier he had handed his friends a cup and called it the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them. Now, on his knees in the dark, he is shown the other cup, with no mercy mixed in it, and he takes it. He drank the cup of wrath to the dregs so that the cup his people hold is the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13).
verseByVerse.note: A stone’s throw is a short distance. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An angel from heaven. The Father does not remove the cup. He sends someone to help his Son drink it. The angel does not come to rescue Jesus from the cross; the angel comes so that he can get to it. That is often how God answers his people’s prayers too: not by removing the trial but by strengthening them in it (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

He needed strengthening. In his humanity he needed strength. The one who made the angel is being ministered to by it. He was made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17), including the need for help from heaven in the hour of weakness, and so he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44. The evidence really is divided. The two verses are missing from some early and important manuscripts, and present in many others; they were known to early writers like Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the second century. Some copies mark them with a sign showing the scribe knew there was a question. Careful scholars weigh two explanations. Either Luke wrote them and some scribes cut them, or they preserve a true early memory later written in. The first has real force. Some readers in the early centuries were embarrassed by a Jesus who sweated, shook and needed an angel, thinking it made him look too weak, and a scribe who removed these lines would have thought he was defending Christ’s dignity. He would have been removing the proof of his humanity. Many scholars think they are original, and many others do not; most modern Bibles keep them, with a note.

How then should they be read? Read them, and rest nothing on them that rests nowhere else. Nothing in them is unique to them. The agony in the garden is in Matthew and Mark without these verses. Angels attending Jesus after a great trial is already in the record (Matthew 4:11). And a Christ who prays in anguish is not a fragile idea propped up by two disputed lines; it is the settled teaching of the New Testament: in the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7). They are true in any case to what we know of Gethsemane.

Do angels help believers today? Yes, though usually unseen. Angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7). But Scripture never tells us to pray to angels, seek them, or build our comfort on stories of them. The angel in the garden pointed Jesus to the cup, not away from it. Our strength comes from God, by his Spirit and his Word, and whether he uses angels to give it is his business.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44.

verseByVerse.quote: And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being in agony. Agōnia, related to agōn, the contest of the arena: the strain of a mind in fierce conflict. This is not despair. It is a battle of the will, at the limit of what a body can do.

He prayed more earnestly. Under that kind of pressure the human instinct is to stop praying. He went the other way: the worse it got, the harder he prayed.

Like great drops of blood. The detail only the physician records. Luke may mean that the sweat fell in thick, heavy drops, the way blood falls; or he may describe a rare documented condition, hematidrosis, in which extreme distress mixes blood with sweat. Either way the point is not clinical: it went that far.

Falling down to the ground. In a garden, on the ground. Adam was cursed to eat bread by the sweat of his face until he returned to the ground (Genesis 3:17–19). Here the sweat of the last Adam, as Paul calls Christ (1 Corinthians 15:45), falls on the ground of a garden, and the curse of Adam’s sin is borne by the one who came to undo it.

Is anxiety or deep distress a sign of weak faith? Not in itself. There is a strain of Christian teaching that treats visible distress as evidence of weak faith: a believer facing something terrible ought to be calm, and fear is failure. This verse ends that argument. The sinless Son of God, in perfect communion with his Father, doing exactly the Father’s will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it. Anxiety can become sin when it turns to unbelief or grumbling, and we are told to cast our anxieties on God (Philippians 4:6; 1 Peter 5:7). But fear and anguish carried to the Father in prayer are not failure. They are exactly what Jesus did. And if anxiety has become a constant illness, seeking medical help is wisdom, not lack of faith.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish; “like great drops of blood” may be a comparison or describe a rare medical condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, 'Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sleeping for sorrow. Matthew and Mark record that the disciples slept. Only Luke tells us why: from grief. That is a physician’s observation and a kindness. They had spent an evening being told that one of them was a traitor and their leader was going to die, and grief of that weight does not keep you awake. It shuts you down. Luke is gentle with the disciples, mentioning only one return where Mark has three.

Why are you sleeping? There is no long rebuke in those words, and no discussion of their failure at all. Mark records a sharper word to Peter (Mark 14:37), but Luke gives us this: a gentle question.

Rise and pray. The same command as v. 40. He does not say, feel better, or stop grieving. He says, rise and pray, the smallest possible next action. Within hours Peter will fall at a fire.

When grief makes prayer impossible. This names one of the commonest and least-discussed experiences in the Christian life. Bereavement, depression, a marriage coming apart, exhaustion after months of caring for someone, and the believer finds that the very thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do. And then, on top of the sorrow, comes the accusation: a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through something immeasurably worse, and his response is to wake them gently and tell them to pray, not to inform them that they have forfeited anything.

What if I cannot pray at all right now? Then pray the smallest prayer you can, and lean on others and on the Spirit. A groan, a single line, the Lord’s Prayer said slowly, a psalm read aloud: God hears all of it. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, and he intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Ask a friend or your pastor to pray for you and with you. Rest and sleep are not sins; Elijah was fed and allowed to sleep before he was spoken to (1 Kings 19:5–8). And remember that Christ is praying for you while you cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking. He was mid-sentence telling them to pray, and the torches were already coming up the hill.

The plot arrives. Since v. 3 the chapter has been moving towards this: at night, in a garden, guided by an insider, as foretold at the table (v. 21).

Judas was leading them. Luke says it again as though it still cannot be believed. The one who had followed Jesus now leads his enemies.

To kiss him. A kiss was the common greeting of a disciple to his teacher, an act of honour and affection. He could have pointed. He chose the one movement that means, I am yours, and used it as a marker for the temple police. That is what sin does when it is finished: it takes what is good and makes it the instrument. Worship offered to be seen, truth told to wound, a Bible verse used to win an argument, affection used as a lever.

Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Only Luke records these words. Jesus uses his name. This is the last recorded word of Jesus to Judas, and it is not a curse. It is a question, and it is his name, the name Luke listed on the mountain when Jesus chose the Twelve (6:13–16). It exposes the obscenity: betrayal with a sign of love. And still he calls himself the Son of Man, the one who will come in glory (Daniel 7:13). It is best read as what it plainly is: a last door held open, a last appeal to Judas’s conscience. He puts to Judas the thing Judas is doing, in words, at the moment of doing it, and the question hangs there waiting for an answer. This is how the Lord deals with a man walking into ruin: not by ambush, but by naming it to his face while there is still a second in which to stop. And when the question went unanswered, he went on to the cross and died for sinners exactly like the one who kissed him (Romans 5:6).

Why did Jesus choose Judas if he knew? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64, 70), and chose him all the same, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9). That choice did not make Judas a traitor; it gave a man every privilege, some three years of Jesus’ company, his teaching, his miracles and his love, and Judas turned them all down. His story is a warning that nearness to holy things does not save, and a proof that Christ’s love was offered even to the one who sold him.

Was Judas ever truly a believer who lost his salvation? No. Jesus says that of those the Father gave him he lost none except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12), and he had said early on that one of the Twelve was a devil (John 6:70). Judas shared the outward life of a disciple but never belonged to Christ; his faith was never real, and his end showed it (1 John 2:19). The true believer may fall terribly, as Peter did, but Christ’s sheep never perish (John 10:28).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, 'No more of this!' And he touched his ear and healed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
