Lord, shall we strike with the sword? They ask the question and then do not wait for the answer, which is the whole trouble with them in one line. They had two swords (v. 38) and had misunderstood. Before the reply comes, a sword is out and a man is bleeding.

His right ear. John names them both: Peter with the sword, and the servant Malchus (John 18:10). Peter was a fisherman, not a swordsman, and an ear rather than a head suggests a wild stroke the man ducked: in the circumstances, suicidal.

No more of this! Or, let them do this, allowing the arrest. Either way, Jesus stops the violence, the last command he gives before he is bound. He is stopping not an enemy but a friend, not cowardice but reckless courage out of love for him, because the kingdom does not come that way. He would say it under interrogation the next morning: if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). The one thing he would not permit in his own defence was the thing his followers have most often reached for since.

He touched his ear. Only Luke, the doctor, records it. Minutes from being bound, with torches in his face, he stops his arrest to repair the injury done to one of the men who came to take him. Malchus went to work that night to arrest a man and came home whole. The last miracle of healing before the cross was performed on a member of the arresting party, by the prisoner, without being asked. Not merely non-retaliating, but actively mending. We too were his enemies, and he reconciled us to God by his death (Romans 5:10).

Was Peter wrong to defend Jesus? His love was right and his method was wrong. He wanted to protect Jesus from the cross, which is exactly what Jesus had come to embrace, and he reached for the world’s weapon to do it. Christians make the same mistake whenever they try to defend Christ with anger, force, manipulation or political power. The way we stand up for Jesus is by speaking the truth in love, suffering wrong patiently, and doing good to those who oppose us (1 Peter 2:23; 3:15–16).

Does Jesus still heal like this? Christ still heals, often in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence (James 5:14–15). But the instant miracles of his earthly ministry and of the apostles were signs confirming the new revelation of the gospel (Hebrews 2:3–4), and this commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such sign gifts, the miraculous healings, tongues and prophecies that marked the apostles, ceased with the apostolic age, because the New Testament calls them the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Brothers and sisters who believe otherwise, many of whom pray for the sick with great faith and love, are to be loved and listened to. Either way, every healing, through medicine or prayer or both, is his gift, and the greatest healing he gives is the forgiveness of enemies.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. John names the servant Malchus and the swordsman Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, 'Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests. He speaks to the officials, not to the muscle: the leadership itself had come out at night to see it done.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? A robber here, lēstēs, is not a pickpocket but a bandit or an insurgent: a man with a weapon and a hillside. So the question is precise. They treat him as a dangerous criminal: have you come out equipped for an armed rebel? And within hours Luke will show a real insurrectionist, Barabbas, set free while the man they treated as one is condemned in his place (23:18–25).

Day after day in the temple. He was there every day, in the open, in their own building. They chose the olive grove, at night, with a paid informant and a crowd carrying clubs, and the choice tells you who believed his own case would survive daylight.

Your hour. Only Luke records these words. He concedes the hour: it is genuinely theirs, the time God has permitted them to act. He concedes the power: exousia, real authority, the authority of Satan (Acts 26:18). What he withholds is any suggestion that this is more than an hour (4:13). It gets an hour, and it is God who has given it.

What is the power of darkness today? It is the same enemy, still working through human hearts and systems: lies, cruelty, false religion, persecution, and the ordinary pull of the world against God. Christians are not to be naive about it (Ephesians 6:12). But for believers it is a defeated power. God has rescued us from the domain of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). Satan’s hour ended at the empty tomb, and what remains is a beaten enemy’s rage before the end. We resist him with the truth, the gospel, faith and prayer (Ephesians 6:13–18), never with fear.

In everyday life. When darkness seems to be winning, in the news, in your family, in your own heart, remember that it looks permanent from inside. It looked permanent to the eleven men running down that hillside, and by Sunday morning it was over. Say it aloud today about the darkest thing you face: this is an hour, and God has set its length.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–71 — The Denial and the Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter follows at a distance and sits down by the fire among the men who arrested his Lord. He did not decide to deny Christ; he decided to stay warm. A servant girl’s mild charge brings the first denial, and the denials grow worse over an hour. While he is still speaking, the rooster crows, and the Lord turns and looks at Peter. Peter remembers the saying of the Lord, goes out and weeps bitterly.

Inside, the guards blindfold and strike Jesus and demand that he prophesy, while three of his prophecies are being fulfilled that night. At daybreak the council asks whether he is the Christ. He claims that from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They ask whether he is the Son of God, he affirms it, and they need nothing further.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter and Judas both regretted what they had done. Judas’s remorse ended in death; Peter’s tears ended in repentance and restoration. Paul names the difference (2 Corinthians 7:10). The test is not how deep the grief is but which way it faces.

Verse 69 joins Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 in a claim no mere man could make: to sit at God’s right hand, with the work finished (Hebrews 10:11–12). His enemies understood it as a claim to be the Son of God, and he affirmed it. They convicted him under the right law, and were wrong only about who he was.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian leader who has failed under pressure may conclude that he has forfeited his calling. Peter is the answer. The man who denied Jesus three times was preaching Christ in the same city within seven weeks.

Verses 63 to 65 show cruelty with nothing ideological in it. He could have named every man in that room, and he said nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Into the high priest’s house. John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest, and then before Caiaphas (John 18:13, 24). Luke gives us the denial first, then the mocking, then the morning council.

Following at a distance. He was following, which is more than the others managed (Mark 14:50). And he was at a distance: close enough to see, far enough to be nobody, the position of a man who cannot bear to leave and cannot afford to be counted. Many Christians know that distance: not apostasy, and not confession either, but the conversation where you did not lie about your faith and did not mention it.

Led away alone. The Shepherd has been struck and the sheep are scattered (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). He enters the high priest’s house without one friend at his side. Even the little that Peter manages, following far behind, he owes to the Lord who had prayed that night that his faith would not fail (v. 32).

A fire in the courtyard. It was cold (John 18:18), and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm. But inside his Lord is being interrogated, and outside Peter sits shoulder to shoulder with the men who brought him there, faces lit by the same fire.

Among them. This is how the fall actually occurs. Peter did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm. He drifted to the safest available place, sat down with people whose questions he had no intention of answering honestly, and the denial came out of his mouth as the natural consequence of where he was sitting. Nobody plans the third denial. They choose the fire.

Is it wrong to spend time with people who are not Christians? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticised for it (15:1–2), and we are sent into the world, not out of it (John 17:15–18). The danger in Peter’s case was not where he sat but why: he sat there to hide. Be among unbelievers as yourself, a follower of Jesus, friendly, honest and unashamed. The question is not whether you share their fire, but whether you have agreed, without saying so, to keep Christ out of the conversation in order to keep your seat.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, 'This man also was with him.' But he denied it, saying, 'Woman, I do not know him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A servant girl. Luke wants the reader to see how small the pressure was. The accuser is a young female slave, the person with the least standing of anyone present, whose word carried little legal weight.

In the light. He had put himself where the fire was, and the fire showed his face. He was recognised because he was warm. Looking closely is staring intently. That is all: no interrogation, no threat, no soldier.

This man also was with him. Her charge is as mild as an accusation can be: not that he drew a sword, which was true, merely that he was with him. Yet with him is the very essence of discipleship (8:1; Mark 3:14), and that is exactly what he now disowns.

Woman, I do not know him. The first denial, a flat lie, and a few hours earlier he had said he was ready to go to prison and to death (v. 33). He denies not a fact but the person. About three years of the boat, the storm, the loaves, you are the Christ of God (9:20), and the sentence that comes out is that he does not know who the man is.

The one he could not unknow. Peter says he does not know him, and the one fact in that courtyard no lie could touch is that Jesus knew Peter. He had called him from his boat (5:10), named him (6:14), prayed for him by name that very night (v. 32) and foretold this very sentence (v. 34). Peter could disown the relationship with his mouth. He could not dissolve it, because it had never rested on Peter’s hold on Jesus. It rested on Jesus’ hold on Peter, and that held through the denial.

The gap between intention and action. The gap between what Peter sincerely intended and what he did was total, and the force needed to open it was one stare from a slave girl. That is why self-confidence is not a Christian virtue. Peter did not overestimate his love; his love was real. He overestimated what love can do on its own in a cold yard at night. And it is why the previous instruction was, pray that you may not enter into temptation (v. 40). He slept when he was told to pray, then he sat down at the fire, and then a girl looked at him.

I have denied Christ by silence, so what now? Then you are where Peter was, and the way back is the same. Name it to God honestly, without excuses. Remember that Christ was not surprised and has prayed for you. Then, where it is possible, take the next opportunity in the same company to own him plainly. Peter, who denied Jesus before a servant girl, later stood before the very council that condemned him and said, we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:20). Silence can be forgiven, and courage can be given.

In everyday life. Denials of Christ often happen in small moments, before unimportant people: the joke you laugh at, the weekend you describe vaguely. Before work today, ask the Spirit who filled Peter before the council (Acts 4:8) for courage in exactly those moments, and decide now one simple sentence you could say if asked.

verseByVerse.quote: And a little later someone else saw him and said, 'You also are one of them.' But Peter said, 'Man, I am not.' And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, 'Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.' But Peter said, 'Man, I do not know what you are talking about.' And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also are one of them. A little later, the second accusation, from someone else.

Man, I am not. The second denial. Each denial is worse than the last. The first denied the person: I do not know him. The second denies the fellowship: I am not one of them, I have no part in that group. The third will deny the subject altogether: I do not know what you are talking about. Sin does not stay the size it started. The second lie exists to protect the first, and the third to protect the second, and each costs less to tell than the one before.

About an hour. Only Luke notes the time. This is not a moment of panic. Peter had an hour to get up, walk out and repent. He stayed.

A Galilean. The third accuser has evidence: Matthew adds that his accent gave him away (Matthew 26:73). Peter could control what he said. He could not control how it sounded. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

The third denial. Immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. Luke does not even let him finish. God did not send an earthquake to stop Peter. He used a bird doing at dawn what birds do at dawn, and it was enough, because it had been named in advance (v. 34).

The Lord of the rooster. The Lord who knew where a colt was tied (19:30) and who would be carrying a water jar (22:10) knew the hour a bird would crow. Peter’s lies were running to their own schedule, and the rooster was running to Christ’s.

Who accused Peter? The Gospels differ in who accused Peter: a servant girl, another girl, a man, the bystanders. In a crowded courtyard several people likely spoke at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. All four agree on the threefold denial and the rooster. Differences like these are what independent witnesses usually show, and believers hold all four accounts true even where the exact order of voices cannot now be fixed.

Is denying Christ an unforgivable sin? Not for one who comes back. Peter denied him three times, with oaths (Matthew 26:74), and was forgiven and restored. The sin Scripture calls unforgivable is the settled, knowing rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work evil (Mark 3:28–30), and such a person does not want to repent. Hebrews warns of those who fall away and never return (Hebrews 6:4–6). But anyone grieving over a denial and longing to come back is plainly not in that condition. The rooster was not the end of Peter’s story. It was the alarm that woke him.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.' And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord turned. Only Luke records the look. Perhaps Jesus was being led across the courtyard between hearings. And Luke calls him the Lord. Even as a prisoner, he is Lord.

What was in that look? Everything depends on it, and the text tells us by what it produced. It did not produce despair or self-justification. It produced memory, and then tears. So it was not a look of anger or contempt. A man looked at with contempt does not remember a promise; he remembers the contempt. What Peter remembered was words, and surely the ones that came just before the prediction: I have prayed for you, and when you have turned again. So the look said something like: I told you. And I knew. And nothing between us has changed. A look of grief and love, and Peter never forgot it. Jesus does not speak. He is bound, mocked and about to be beaten, and he has no opportunity to cross a courtyard and put a hand on his friend’s shoulder. All he has is a turn of the head. It was enough.

Peter remembered. The word of Jesus came back to him. That is how the Lord still restores his people: by bringing his word back to mind at the moment it is needed.

He wept bitterly. Peter went out into the night, as Judas had gone out from the supper (John 13:30), but their nights ended differently. Judas, seized with remorse, returned the silver and took his own life (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter wept, and lived. Both regretted; only one turned with his regret towards the Lord he had wronged. That is Paul’s distinction between a grief that leads to repentance and salvation and a grief that ends in death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Judas’s story is a warning against despair; it is not a verdict on everyone who has died by their own hand in illness and anguish, whom we leave, with their grieving families, to the mercy of God. What matters is not how hard a man weeps but which way he faces when he does. Jesus had prayed for him (v. 32), and he would be restored (24:34; John 21:15–19).

How do I know if my sorrow over sin is godly sorrow? Look at which way it faces. Worldly sorrow is mainly about me: what I have lost, how I look, what it will cost, and it either hardens into excuses or sinks into despair. Godly sorrow is about God: I have wronged him, and I go to him. It grieves the sin itself, not only its consequences; it confesses; it hopes in Christ’s mercy; and it turns, slowly but really, from the sin. You do not need to measure the size of your tears. If your sorrow drives you towards Christ rather than away from him, it is the godly kind.

Does Jesus look at me like that when I fail? Yes. If you belong to him, his look at your failure is the look Peter received: knowing, grieved, and full of love. He is not surprised by your sin and he has already prayed for you. The look is meant to bring his word back to you and to lead you to tears that end in restoration, not to drive you away. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and his kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4).

For worship. Bound and about to be beaten, the Lord still had eyes for a failing friend. Seven weeks later the man who had wept in the dark preached Christ to thousands (Acts 2:14–41). The look that broke his heart did not end his ministry; it began it. The eyes that turned towards Peter across a courtyard have never once looked at one of their own who has fallen and looked away.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, 'Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?' And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocking him. These are the guards, with hours to fill and a prisoner nobody would ask about (18:32). It is the commonest kind of cruelty: he was available and unable to retaliate, and it passed the time.

Blindfolded. A cruel game, with a rule: blindfold him, hit him, and demand that he name the hand. The mockery aims at the one thing they had heard about him, that he was a prophet. And in the very hours these men demand a prophecy, his prophecies are being fulfilled: the kiss, the denials before the rooster (vv. 34, 61), the numbering with the transgressors. They blindfold the only man in the room who can see anything, and then ask him to prove he can see. Isaiah had heard the Servant say it: I gave my back to those who strike (Isaiah 50:6).

Blaspheming him. The word is blasphēmountes. They will condemn him for blasphemy (v. 71), but they are the blasphemers, insulting the Son of God.

Luke records no answer. He could have named every man in that room. He says nothing: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). What is held back is not merely a retort but legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). The power that made the hands striking his face was under perfect control, restrained by nothing but his own settled will to be struck.

Why did Jesus not defend himself? Because he had come to suffer, not to win the argument. His silence was not weakness but chosen obedience: he was the Lamb led to the slaughter, bearing in his body the punishment our sins deserved. Had he spoken, he could have silenced them; had he struck back, he could have destroyed them; but then there would have been no sacrifice and no salvation. Peter, who watched it, later wrote that he answered insult with no insult and suffering with no threat, but handed himself over to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

How should I respond when I am mocked for my faith? With the same trust, though not always the same silence. Jesus did speak when the truth required it (v. 69), and we too should be ready to give a reason for our hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). But we need not answer every taunt, defend our dignity, or repay insult with insult. Leave your reputation with God. Count it an honour to share a little in his reproach (Acts 5:41), and pray for those who mock you, as he did for those who crucified him (23:34).

For worship. In Isaiah the Servant who gave his back to the smiters also said that he had set his face like a flint, knowing he would not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:6–7). Jesus had set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and here, under a blindfold and a rain of blows, that face is still set. They covered it and struck it, and it did not turn from them.

verseByVerse.quote: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, 'If you are the Christ, tell us.' But he said to them, 'If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. The formal trial asks the question the whole Gospel has been asking: who is this? The angel had told Mary her son would be called the Son of God (1:32, 35); now the council asks it (vv. 67, 70), and he tells them.

When day came. The daylight session was a repair. Later Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, held that capital cases should not be tried at night, so at first light the council met formally to confirm a verdict decided days before (v. 2). The most respectable machinery in Israel is being operated correctly in order to kill the Son of God. Religion is never safer than the heart that uses it: their religion had become the place they hid from God rather than the way they came to him.

The assembly of the elders. The Sanhedrin, Israel’s supreme council, under the high priest.

If you are the Christ, tell us. It sounds like an inquiry and it is not one. The council does not want information. It wants a sentence it can take to Pilate.

If I tell you, you will not believe. Without bitterness and quite unanswerable: a description of a settled state. When Lazarus came out of a tomb their response was to plan another death (John 11:53).

And if I ask you, you will not answer. Earlier that week they had refused to answer his question about John’s baptism (20:7). But he does not stay silent, and what he says next is not a defence. It is a claim so large that the council will need nothing else.

Was the trial of Jesus illegal? By the standards of the later Jewish law code it broke several rules: a night hearing, a hurried verdict, no defence, the judges as accusers. We cannot be sure every rule was in force then, but the Gospels plainly show a trial whose verdict was settled before it began. The deeper point is that the court was right about the law and wrong about the man. God allowed injustice to condemn the just so that the unjust could be justified (1 Peter 3:18). To be justified is to receive the Judge’s own acquittal: not a better feeling but a verdict, accepted in his sight because Christ’s righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 4:5).

What if someone I love keeps asking but never believes? Keep answering with patience, but recognise what Jesus saw: some questions are not requests for truth but defences against it. You cannot argue anyone into the kingdom; only God opens hearts (Acts 16:14). So pray for them more than you debate them, live the gospel in front of them, and give them the plain claims of Christ, as he did here. Then leave them with God. One member of that very council, Joseph of Arimathea, had not consented to its decision and came out for Jesus at the cross (23:50–53), and God changed the heart of a young Pharisee named Saul.
verseByVerse.note: A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at daybreak.

verseByVerse.quote: But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from now on. Then he answers, and gives them far more than they asked. From now on: through his death, resurrection and ascension, from this room, with his hands tied and a death sentence being drafted.

The Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man, brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and given an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus has used it all through Luke’s Gospel; here, before the highest court in Israel, he speaks it with the whole vision in view.

At the right hand of the power of God. Psalm 110:1, the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool, the psalm he had used to silence the scribes that same week (20:41–44). Two Scriptures are folded into one sentence, and together they make a claim no mere Messiah could make: a man to sit down on God’s own throne. The prisoner before them is the judge of all.

Seated, because the work is finished. The right hand is not about geography. It is the position of the one who exercises the king’s authority, and to be seated there is to have the business settled. The priests stood daily, offering sacrifices that could never take away sins; Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at God’s right hand (Hebrews 10:11–12). Luke omits the coming on the clouds that Mark records (Mark 14:62) and emphasises the present enthronement, which begins at the ascension (Acts 2:33–36; 7:55–56).

What is Jesus doing at the right hand now? Reigning and interceding. He rules all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), and he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). His reign is not postponed to a future age; it is happening now, from heaven, as the gospel goes to the nations and the Spirit gathers his people. And he prays for those who are his (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). One day he will come again visibly, in glory, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. Until then the throne is occupied, and nothing in your life is outside his rule.

verseByVerse.quote: So they all said, 'Are you the Son of God, then?' And he said to them, 'You say that I am.' Then they said, 'What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you the Son of God, then? They heard it, and that answers a modern idea: that Jesus never claimed to be divine and the church invented it later. His enemies, sitting in front of him, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion from what he had just said, and put it to him as a question. The then does real work: so it follows that. They have understood v. 69 correctly. A man who takes the seat at God’s right hand is claiming a relation to God that no creature has. The one seated at God’s right hand must be God’s Son. A sceptic may reply that the Gospels were written by the church. True, but that Jesus was condemned by his own leaders and handed to Rome is among the best-attested facts about his end, and it is hard to explain unless he made some such claim.

You say that I am. Not evasion but a recognised way of saying yes (Matthew 26:64), and the council took it as one. There may be more in it. The final words are egō eimi, I am, the words that echo God’s own name given to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and the words Jesus had used before in a way that made men pick up stones (John 8:58).

What further testimony do we need? The trial ends without proof of any crime, because there was never one. In Luke no witness is called; in Matthew and Mark the false witnesses fail to agree. No act is established. They have their charge: blasphemy.

From his own lips. The only evidence the court ever had was his own confession. The charge is blasphemy, a creature claiming the honour of God, and it would be entirely just if the man in the dock were anyone else. They got only one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant. A man who claims this is either guilty of blasphemy or is who he says; the council saw no middle ground, and neither does Luke.

Does Son of God mean only that Jesus was a very godly man? No. Israel’s kings could be called God’s sons, and believers are sons by adoption, but that is not what the council heard or what Jesus meant. He claimed to sit at God’s right hand and to be the Son in a unique sense: the eternal Son, one with the Father (John 10:30), who shares the Father’s nature and glory, became man without ceasing to be God. That is why they called it blasphemy. A merely good man claiming that would not be good.

Who was responsible for Jesus’ death? A small group of leaders handed him over, and Rome executed him; Jew and Gentile together, as the church confessed (Acts 4:27–28). Behind them all stood God’s plan, and the sins of everyone he came to save. It gives no ground for blaming the Jewish people as a whole, and Peter, preaching to Jerusalem, said they had acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17).

Follow him into the house that he enters <sup>11</sup> and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>12</sup> And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.” <sup>13</sup> And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>14</sup> And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <sup>16</sup> For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” <sup>17</sup> And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <sup>18</sup> For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” <sup>19</sup> And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” <sup>20</sup> And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. <sup>21</sup> But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. <sup>22</sup> For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” <sup>23</sup> And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this. <sup>24</sup> A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors. <sup>26</sup> But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. <sup>27</sup> For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves. <sup>28</sup> “You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, <sup>29</sup> and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, <sup>30</sup> that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>31</sup> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, <sup>32</sup> but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” <sup>33</sup> Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” <sup>34</sup> Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.” <sup>35</sup> And he said to them, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” <sup>36</sup> He said to them, “But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. <sup>37</sup> For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.” <sup>38</sup> And they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “It is enough.” <sup>39</sup> And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. <sup>40</sup> And when he came to the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>41</sup> And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” <sup>43</sup> And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. <sup>44</sup> And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. <sup>45</sup> And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, <sup>46</sup> and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>47</sup> While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, <sup>48</sup> but Jesus said to him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” <sup>49</sup> And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” <sup>50</sup> And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. <sup>51</sup> But Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he touched his ear and healed him. <sup>52</sup> Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? <sup>53</sup> When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” <sup>54</sup> Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. <sup>55</sup> And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. <sup>56</sup> Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, “This man also was with him.” <sup>57</sup> But he denied it, saying, “Woman, I do not know him.” <sup>58</sup> And a little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” <sup>59</sup> And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” <sup>60</sup> But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. <sup>61</sup> And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.” <sup>62</sup> And he went out and wept bitterly. <sup>63</sup> Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. <sup>64</sup> They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>65</sup> And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. <sup>66</sup> When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, <sup>67</sup> “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe, <sup>68</sup> and if I ask you, you will not answer. <sup>69</sup> But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” <sup>70</sup> So they all said, “Are you the Son of God, then?” And he said to them, “You say that I am.” <sup>71</sup> Then they said, “What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.”

23.title: The Trial, the Cross, and the Tomb
23.overview:
Luke 23 is the day of the cross. Jesus is tried before Pilate and Herod, condemned, crucified between two criminals, and buried in a new tomb. Through it all Luke keeps one emphasis: Jesus is innocent. Pilate says so three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod finds nothing deserving death (v. 15), a dying criminal confesses it (v. 41), and the centurion says it when he has died (v. 47). The innocent one is dying for the guilty.

Three sayings from the cross are found only in Luke: the prayer for his killers (v. 34), the promise of paradise today to a dying criminal who could bring nothing but a confession and a request (v. 43), and his last words, a prayer of trust from Psalm 31:5 (v. 46).

The chapter ends quietly. The women from Galilee see the tomb and how the body was laid, go home to prepare spices, and rest on the Sabbath, not knowing what the third day will bring.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Trial before Pilate and Herod
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council cannot carry out a death sentence, so the charge has to change. Before Pilate they bring three charges built for a Roman ear: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, and claiming to be a king. The second is a flat lie (20:25). The third is true, and it is the one that will kill him.

Pilate questions him and reaches the right verdict at once: I find no guilt in this man. When the accusers mention Galilee, he sees a way out and sends Jesus to Herod, who has long wanted to see him and hopes for a sign. Jesus answers him not a word. Herod mocks him and sends him back, and Herod and Pilate become friends that day.

Pilate declares him innocent again before the people, and in the same breath offers to flog him and release him. The compromise fails. The crowd asks for Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, guilty of exactly what Jesus was falsely accused of, and the shouting overrules Pilate. He releases the guilty man and hands Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.theology:
The repeated verdicts of innocence are the spine of the chapter. A guilty man dying would pay only for himself. The Barabbas exchange shows substitution in the street before it is accomplished on the hill: a guilty man goes free, unchanged and unreviewed, because another dies in his place. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Verses 23–25 hold two truths together. These men are fully guilty, as Peter told them at Pentecost (Acts 2:23). And behind them stands the purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Pilate handed him over under pressure; the Father gave him up in love.
verseByVerse.examples:
Pilate's sin is not brutality but procedure. He never says he believes Jesus guilty; he simply never acts on the fact that he is not. Responsibility does not transfer: the man who tried hardest not to be involved is named in the creed.

Verse 5 alleges no crime, only disturbance, and it is the oldest complaint made against Christ's people. When the only offence is the truth about Christ spoken kindly, the complaint is a compliment.

Herod had killed the prophet who brought him God's word; now he wanted a trick, and received silence. The believer who fears that God has gone silent on him is answered by the contrast: Herod was not troubled about it. Being troubled is itself a sign that God has not gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, 'We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 23 is the day of the cross. Jesus is declared innocent again and again by Pilate and Herod, yet handed over to be crucified while Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, walks free (vv. 1–25). On the way he warns the weeping women of judgment coming on Jerusalem; on the cross he prays for his killers, is mocked as a king who cannot save himself, and promises a dying thief paradise today (vv. 26–43). Darkness falls at noon, the temple curtain is torn, and Jesus commits his spirit to his Father and dies; a centurion praises God, and a councillor buries him while the women watch (vv. 44–56). Luke’s great theme is the innocence of the one who died: the righteous for the unrighteous, the King enthroned on a cross, opening paradise to the guilty.

The whole company of them. The Sanhedrin, the highest religious body in Israel, marches a bound prisoner across the city to a Gentile, because under Rome it could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). And the charge has to change: a Roman governor would have thrown out blasphemy before lunch.

Three charges. So they make three fresh charges, each designed for a Roman ear: sedition, tax refusal and treason. Misleading our nation means stirring up rebellion, the word a governor most feared to hear at a festival.

Forbidding tribute. A flat lie. They had asked him that exact question in the temple, and he had answered: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s (20:25). He had said pay it; they report that he forbade it. That is how false witness usually works: not fabrication, which is easy to disprove, but a true thing rotated until it points the other way.

Christ, a king. They translate Messiah into king, a rival to Caesar. This third charge is not false. He is the Christ, and a king, but not the kind Pilate feared, and they trust Pilate to hear the word king and stop listening. So the Son of God is brought before the empire on two lies and a truth, and the truth is the one that will kill him.

Is it wrong to defend myself when I am falsely accused? No. Paul defended himself before councils and governors (Acts 24–26), and calmly correcting a lie is often right, especially when others will be harmed by it. Jesus was silent at points in his trial because his hour had come and he had chosen to suffer, not because silence is always the godly answer. The question is your spirit. Speak the truth plainly and without bitterness, refuse to answer lies with lies, and then entrust your name to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). You do not have to win to be vindicated.

For worship. They came for a man they could not execute and found a wording that would do it for them. The one they slandered stood still and let them, because the charge sheet that really mattered was not theirs but ours, and he had come to have it nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). So the King was accused of being a king, and he was one.
verseByVerse.note: The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and a rival king. The tax charge was false.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pilate asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' And he answered him, 'You have said so.' Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, 'I find no guilt in this man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, known for brutality and contempt for the Jews (13:1). He knew what a rebel looked like; he had very likely crucified some.

Are you the King of the Jews? Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him, in an outsider’s political language: are you a pretender to a throne? (See John 18:32–33 for the fuller answer.)

You have said so. The same idiom he used before the council: an affirmation, not a dodge. But it is a guarded yes, true but not in the sense you mean. John fills in what Luke compresses: my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:33–38). It is a yes with the sword taken out of it.

No guilt. And Pilate believes him. Luke means you to count the verdicts: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod (v. 15), a dying criminal (v. 41), a Roman officer (v. 47). Six declarations of innocence, and the execution proceeds. A pagan governor said it of Jesus, and on the last day the holy God will say it of everyone who is in him.

If Jesus was innocent, why did God let him die? Because only an innocent man could die for the guilty. Nothing about the cross is a miscarriage that God later put right. The innocence is not a tragic detail; it is the point. A guilty man dying would settle nothing for anybody, because he would only be paying for himself. Christ, who had no sin of his own, bore the penalty of ours in our place: he died not for his own crimes, but for the sins of others, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). God did not merely permit it; he willed it, out of love (Isaiah 53:10; John 3:16). Scripture calls that exchange justification: the guilty declared righteous by God himself, not because they have become innocent but because Christ’s righteousness is counted as theirs (2 Corinthians 5:21).
verseByVerse.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, saying, 'He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent. Insistent, refusing to accept the verdict; at v. 23 the pressing turns into shouting.

From Galilee even to this place. Judea here means the whole Jewish land (4:44), and from Galilee to Jerusalem is the whole course of his ministry: calling him a rabble-rouser, they unwittingly summarise Luke’s Gospel. But it is a threat assessment: Galilee produced insurgents, and the revolt of Judas the Galilean was still remembered (Acts 5:37). To tell a Roman governor that a Galilean has been stirring people up all the way to the capital is to say the word rebellion without having to prove it. And the mention of Galilee gives Pilate an idea.

One word that is not a lie. Teaching. Stripped down, the accusation is that he has been teaching in public, and people have listened. They cannot produce an act, only an effect. It is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people. It is enough to allege disturbance: the message is divisive, and things were calmer before (Acts 17:6).

How do I know whether the offence is the gospel’s or mine? Sometimes the charge of stirring up trouble is fair, and honesty requires saying so. Christians can be needlessly abrasive, and a good deal of the trouble some believers attract has nothing to do with Christ and everything to do with the manner of the man carrying his name. So ask: Am I being offensive in tone, timing or pride? Have I spoken the truth with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15)? Am I more eager to win than to love? If you can honestly say that the only thing that offended was the truth about Christ, spoken kindly, then the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Galilean. Only Luke records the trial before Herod. He may have learned of it from Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward (8:3), or from Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod (Acts 13:1). The accusers meant Galilee as an aggravating detail. Pilate hears it as an escape route, a way out of a difficult case.

He belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction. Galilee was the territory of Herod Antipas, a client ruler under Rome, in Jerusalem for the Passover. It is not a legal necessity: the offence was alleged in Judea too, and Pilate had every authority to try it. He is not applying a rule. He is looking for a door.

He sent him over to Herod. The door is entirely procedural. He does not release Jesus, which his own verdict required, or condemn him; he transfers the file. That is the characteristic sin of this chapter, and it is not brutality. It is the sin of a man who knows exactly what is right, does not want to pay for it, and finds a mechanism that postpones the decision.

The one who took what was not his. Set Pilate beside the prisoner he is passing on. Pilate holds a responsibility that is truly his, and spends the morning trying to put it down. Jesus stands before him carrying a burden that was never his, the guilt of his people, and he will not put it down for a moment. Pilate looks for a door; Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and will not take one. Pilate wants the decision to belong to someone else; Jesus had already said in the garden, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). The whole trial is a man refusing what is his, before the Man who has taken on himself what is ours.

Responsibility does not transfer. The man who tried hardest not to be involved is the one whose name the church has said in the creed for centuries: suffered under Pontius Pilate. Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (James 4:17).

Can I avoid making a decision about Jesus? No. You can postpone it, refer it, wait for more information or hand it to someone else, but not deciding is a decision. Pilate tried every route around the question and was left holding it. Every person must answer for himself who Jesus is and what he will do with him; a parent’s faith, a spouse’s faith or a church’s faith cannot answer for you. If you have been putting it off, ask the question honestly today, read one of the Gospels through, and ask God to show you the truth.
verseByVerse.note: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was very glad. Herod Antipas is delighted by the prospect of entertainment. This is the man who liked listening to John the Baptist (Mark 6:20) and then had him beheaded to save face at a birthday feast.

Long desired to see him. Since 9:9: John I beheaded, but who is this? He got his wish on the last morning of Jesus’ life.

Some sign. There is the whole man in one clause. He does not want repentance; he killed the man who offered it. He wants a display: curiosity, not faith. Jesus has been reduced, in the mind of a king, to an entertainment that has finally been booked.

He made no answer. Not one word. Herod is perhaps the only questioner in the Gospels to whom Jesus says nothing at all. The silence is not sulking or fear. It is the answer. Herod had silenced the voice of God in John; now God is silent to him, and the mercy of God does not perform on request. Like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7).

Does God ever stop speaking to a man? He does, and Scripture says so more than once (Proverbs 1:24–28; Romans 1:24). But the fear a sensitive believer carries, that this has happened to him, is answered by the very shape of the case. Herod was not anxious about it. He was very glad. A man who is troubled that God may have gone quiet has, in that trouble, the evidence that he has not. If you are worried that you have hardened your heart beyond hope, the worry itself is the Spirit still at work. Come to Christ now; he has never turned away anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Is it wrong to want to see a miracle? Not in itself; God did signs to help people believe (John 20:30–31), and we may ask him to act in power. What is wrong is Herod’s spirit: wanting a show while refusing the message, demanding proof on our terms while ignoring the evidence already given. Jesus called it an evil generation that seeks a sign (11:29). If God has given you his Word, the testimony of the apostles and the empty tomb, you have been given the greatest sign of all, and the right response is not to ask for another but to repent and believe.

For worship. The Word through whom the worlds were made stood before a king and said nothing. He would not perform for the man who had silenced John, yet he walked out of that hall to die for scoffers and killers, and a man brought up with this very Herod would one day be among the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1). His silence to the proud is never his last word to the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Vehemently accusing him. The chief priests have followed him across the city. There is nothing to answer, so the volume has to do what the evidence cannot.

Treated him with contempt. Disappointed, Herod turned to mockery, and it is worse than a verdict. He does not condemn Jesus; he finds him ridiculous. The Greek is exouthenēsas, to count as nothing. It is not hatred, which at least concedes that its object matters, but the judgment of a bored man who decided the whole thing was beneath him. He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3).

Arraying him in splendid clothing. Bright, shining, gorgeous: a royal robe thrown over a prisoner as a joke, because he had been accused of claiming a throne. This is the first of the mockeries (vv. 36–38), and in every case the mockery consists of treating him as what he actually is.

He sent him back to Pilate. Herod found no grounds to condemn him either (v. 15), and Jesus was led back across Jerusalem, it seems still in the mocking robe.

How should I feel when Jesus is mocked today? Grieved, but not surprised and not afraid. Christ has been mocked from the first, and the mockery has always come from people who think they are cleverer than he is. Do not answer with mockery, and do not imagine that his honour depends on you. Pray for the mockers; some of them, like many in Jerusalem, may yet beat their breasts and believe. And let the mockery remind you that every taunt aimed at him is a backhanded confession of who he truly is.

In everyday life. When you notice yourself treating something holy as small, a sermon as a performance to be rated, prayer as a box to tick, the Lord’s Supper as a routine, that is Herod’s contempt in miniature. Confess it, and come back to the one who was counted as nothing first, for you.

parallels.desc: a similar mockery by Pilate’s soldiers

verseByVerse.quote: And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friends that very day. We are not told the cause of the quarrel; perhaps Pilate’s massacre of Galileans (13:1). Luke cares about the cure: Pilate sent the prisoner over as a courtesy, Herod sent him back with a joke attached, and united by their contempt for Jesus, the two men discovered they could work together.

Contempt makes friends. Two people who agree on nothing will warm to each other instantly over a third party they both find absurd; office politics runs on it. A friendship that needs a common enemy is a poor kind of peace.

The fulfilment. A few weeks later the believers in Jerusalem would quote Psalm 2 in prayer, naming both men: the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed (Psalm 2:1–2; Acts 4:25–28). Here is the gathering: a governor and a tetrarch who could not stand each other, reconciled over the body of the Son of God. But the psalm does not end with the plotting. It goes on: as for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill (Psalm 2:6). The gathering of rulers was the very road by which the Anointed went to his throne, and within three days the one they had sent back and forth between them would be raised, declared the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

Does this mean rulers and governments are always against God? No. Scripture tells us that governing authorities are appointed by God for our good, and calls us to pray for them and honour them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). Psalm 2 describes what rulers do when they set themselves against Christ, and it ends by calling them to kiss the Son and be wise. The point here is that even when the powerful unite against him, they plot in vain. The one enthroned in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4), and their plans end up serving his.

For worship. Two rulers found a friendship in despising him, but the true peace made that day was not theirs. By the blood of that same cross God reconciled to himself all things, making peace (Colossians 1:20). Herod and Pilate were joined against the Son; sinners are joined to the Son, and in him to one another, Jew and Gentile, ruler and thief.

parallels.desc: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, 'You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Called together. Pilate convenes a formal assembly and puts his finding on the record with unusual care, and now the crowd is drawn into the decision.

After examining him before you. A formal Roman hearing. Before you: they were present, and no one can afterwards claim the governor rushed it. This is a man building a defensible file, and he is doing it because he already suspects he is going to need one.

Not guilty. The second declaration of innocence (v. 4). And here is the tragedy of Pilate in one motion. He is scrupulous about the record and careless about the man. Everything he does from here is aimed at making sure that when this goes wrong it will not be attributable to him, and none of it at what his own verdict required: to let an innocent man walk out. Nothing prevented him except the calculation of what it would cost him. Underneath the calculation was a god Pilate served more faithfully than justice: his own position. Whatever we cannot bear to lose is what we will, sooner or later, sacrifice someone else to keep.

What is the fear of man, and how do I fight it? The fear of man is letting other people’s approval or anger decide what you do, even when you know what is right. It lays a snare, says Proverbs, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). Pilate’s fear was of the crowd and of Caesar (John 19:12). Ours is usually smaller: the colleague’s raised eyebrow, the family’s disapproval, the online pile-on. The cure is not bravado but a bigger fear: the fear of God, who sees and judges and also loves. Ask, in the moment, whose verdict on me matters most? Then act for an audience of one.

parallels.desc: I find no guilt in him

verseByVerse.quote: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither did Herod. Two rulers, two verdicts of innocence, like the two witnesses the law required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Nothing deserving death has been done by him is the plainest verdict spoken by anyone that day, and the high-water mark of the trial.

Punish and release him. And then, in the same breath, therefore: the conclusion he draws from innocence is a flogging. The verb is paideusas, to discipline, a chillingly domestic word for what was probably a beating lighter than the full scourging, though Roman flogging was no formality. There is no version of justice in which this is defensible, and Pilate knows it. He is bargaining, and what he has put on the table is somebody else’s back.

The chastisement that brought us peace. Pilate’s word comes from the same root as the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Isaiah 53:5: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace. Pilate meant a beating to buy off a crowd, an innocent man punished to keep a guilty city quiet. God meant something infinitely greater by the same innocent suffering: the Servant bearing the punishment due to others, so that those who deserved it might have peace with God. Pilate’s compromise was wicked; the Servant’s substitution was righteous, and it was the only exchange that day that worked.

How decent men do monstrous things. It is almost never a single decision to do evil, but a series of small settlements, each presented as the reasonable middle course. The compromise fails, and for a reason worth naming. Once Pilate conceded that innocence was no protection, there was no principle left in the room to stop at. If the man can be flogged though innocent, the argument against crucifying him though innocent is only a matter of degree, and the crowd could do arithmetic.

What should I do when I am pressured to compromise at work or in my family? First, see the compromise for what it is: not a middle way between two goods but a smaller wrong offered to avoid a cost. Then decide what is right before the pressure peaks, and say it calmly and early, as Pilate should have done. Find out what you actually can and cannot be made to do; often the threat is larger than the reality. Seek counsel from a wise Christian. Be willing to lose something, a promotion, a friendship, a peaceful Christmas, rather than your integrity. And remember that the Lord who stood before Pilate knows what that pressure costs.

In everyday life. Look for one place where you are offering half of something to avoid giving all of it: half the truth to a customer, half an apology to your wife, half obedience to God. None of us has ever given the whole perfectly; the man Pilate flogged did, and his whole obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). So give the whole, not to buy God’s favour but because in Christ you already have it.
verseByVerse.note: To “punish” here means a flogging.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all cried out together, 'Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas'— a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Away with this man. Literally, take this one, the cry later raised against Paul in this city (Acts 21:36). Release to us Barabbas appeals to the Passover amnesty (Mark 15:6).

Textual note. A reader following in a modern Bible will notice the text jumps from verse 16 to verse 18, with verse 17 printed only as a note: Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival. Nothing has been removed from Scripture. Verse numbers are not inspired; they were added in the sixteenth century. Since then far older copies have been found, centuries closer to the apostles, and in the oldest of them this sentence is not there. It appears in later copies and looks very much like a helpful explanation of the Passover custom, written in the margin by a scribe and then copied into the text. So the translators keep the number, print the words in the note, and tell the reader exactly what the evidence is. What is displayed here is not damage to the text but the care with which it has been kept. And nothing in the account depends on it; the custom is attested independently by the other Gospels.

Insurrection and murder. Insurrection is exactly the crime Jesus had been falsely accused of in v. 2. The crowd picks the guilty man, and the Son goes to the cross that had been prepared for the other. Barabbas, of all men, could say literally: Jesus died for me.

Am I really like Barabbas? Yes, and that is the best news you will ever hear. You may never have led a revolt or killed anyone, but Scripture says every one of us has rebelled against God, our rightful King (Isaiah 53:6; Romans 3:23), and that hatred in the heart is murder in his eyes (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). We stood under a just sentence. Christ was condemned in our place, and we were let go. The difference is that Barabbas was released without being changed, while all who trust Christ are not only set free but made new and declared righteous. Seeing yourself in Barabbas is not humiliation for its own sake; it is the door to gratitude.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, 'Crucify, crucify him!' A third time he said to them, 'Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crucify, crucify him! What they shout has stopped being an argument: no charge, no reasoning, two words repeated. A crowd in this state cannot be answered, because it is no longer making a case. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels.

A third time. As Peter had denied him three times, so Pilate declares him innocent three times (vv. 4, 14, 22): three verdicts from the bench, three refusals from the floor.

Why, what evil has he done? It is the right question. It is the only question. And nobody answers it, in Luke or in Matthew and Mark, who record it too. The question hangs in the middle of that loud morning and no one supplies a reply, because there was none. So consider what has actually defeated the governor of Judea. Not evidence, which does not exist. Not law, which is entirely on the other side. Not force, since the soldiers are his to command. Noise. He is beaten by volume, and he knows it, and he gives way anyway.

How do I stand against a crowd? Most people will never face a mob, and almost everyone will face its smaller relatives. A room in which one view is being expressed loudly and confidently exerts a pressure that has nothing to do with whether the view is true, and it works on people who can see perfectly well that it is not true. So decide what you believe before you enter the room. Speak early and simply, before the noise builds. Look for one other person who agrees, and stand with them. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Exodus 23:2). And remember that the question is not, can I see what is right? Pilate saw it three times. It is whether you can still say it when it is expensive, and that courage is the Holy Spirit’s gift to those who ask, not a matter of nerve (Acts 4:29–31).

For worship. Why, what evil has he done? The question still stands, and neither earth nor hell has ever answered it. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). Hearing his own people roar for his death, he called down no fire. He heard them shout crucify, and he went, because the evil that was not his had been laid on him, and he had come to carry it away.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their voices prevailed. Four bleak words. Not the evidence, not the law, not the verdict given three times: the voices. Prevailed means had the mastery, and the mastery belongs to a crowd.

Their demand granted. The word is epekrinen: he pronounced sentence. Luke’s phrasing is almost administrative, and the flatness is the point: a judicial murder processed as a granted application. Pilate chose his position over justice (John 19:12).

Two things held together. These men are entirely guilty (Acts 2:23), and behind the crowd, behind Judas’s price and Pilate’s cowardice, stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; Acts 4:27–28). God’s purpose forced no one: every man in that courtyard did exactly what he wanted to do (see 22:22). And Paul’s verb there is the very verb Luke uses of Pilate in the next breath: paradidōmi, to hand over. Pilate handed him over to a mob. The Father handed him over for us. The same act, and the difference is everything: one was a surrender to pressure, the other was love with nothing forced about it at all.

Was Pilate less guilty than the leaders who handed Jesus over? Less, but still guilty. Jesus told Pilate that he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin (John 19:11): the men who knew the Scriptures, saw the signs and still demanded his death sinned against greater light. But Pilate had the power and the knowledge to stop it and did not. Scripture never lets anyone off because someone else was worse. Each will give an account for what he knew and did (12:47–48), and the creed still names Pilate.

In everyday life. If someone has handed you over, abandoned you to a situation they had the power to stop and would not pay the cost of stopping, take comfort here. That is exactly what happened to him, and he knows it from the inside. Bring it to him today, and tell him plainly what was done.

verseByVerse.quote: He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He released the man. Luke tells us again who Barabbas was, in the same sentence as the release, so that no reader misses who walked out alive.

For whom they asked. They chose a murderer. Peter would say it to them in the temple: you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and killed the Author of life (Acts 3:14–15).

He is not pardoned. A condemned prisoner hears a crowd outside, a door is unlocked, and he walks out into the daylight past a beam being carried the other way. Nobody has said he is innocent, and nothing about him has changed; he goes free because another man is going to die in his place. Substitution is acted out in the street before it is accomplished on the hill. Barabbas walked free because Jesus took his place; sinners walk free because Jesus took their sin, and with it their sentence.

Delivered over to their will. Delivered over is the word of the passion predictions (9:44; 18:32). Not to justice, but to their will, the most complete abandonment a court can perform. And behind it, the Father’s will (Romans 8:32).

Does this passage blame the Jewish people as a whole? No. Luke names the actors: a handful of leaders, a crowd stirred up by them, Pilate and his soldiers. Jesus himself, his apostles and the first thousands of believers were Jews. The charge of collective or inherited guilt, used for centuries to justify hatred of Jews, has no ground here, and Christians must repent of it wherever it appears.

Did Barabbas ever believe? We are not told. Scripture leaves him at the prison door, and any tradition about his later life is guesswork. Perhaps that is deliberate. His story stops at the moment of release so that every reader can step into it. The question is not what Barabbas did with his freedom but what you will do with yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — The Way of the Cross and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the way out of the city a soldier forces Simon of Cyrene, a stranger coming in from the country, to carry the cross behind Jesus, the posture Jesus had described for discipleship (9:23). Women mourn for him, and he tells them to weep for themselves, because of the judgment coming on Jerusalem.

At The Skull he is crucified between two criminals, numbered with the transgressors (22:37). His first word from the cross is a prayer for his killers, while the soldiers gamble for his clothes as Psalm 22:18 had said. Rulers, soldiers and one of the criminals all mock him with the same words: save yourself. Pilate's notice names the only charge ever proved: that he is the King of the Jews.

The other criminal turns. He fears God, accepts his sentence, declares Jesus innocent, and asks only to be remembered. He is promised far more: today you will be with me in paradise.
verseByVerse.theology:
The prayer Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do pleads a real but partial ignorance: they knew they were killing a man, not that they were killing the Author of life. Ignorance is not an acquittal; it is a ground on which to ask. Luke shows the prayer answered in Acts, where Peter tells the same city that they acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17) and thousands are forgiven.

The mockery of v. 35 states the atonement exactly, without understanding it. He could not save himself and save others. The power was not lacking; but to come down would have left everyone he came for still under sentence.

The dying criminal could not be baptised, make restitution or show any fruit. He brought a verdict on himself, a recognition of who Jesus is, and a request, and the answer exceeded it: not some day but today, and not somewhere but with me. There is no purgatory in that promise.
verseByVerse.examples:
Most crosses in a Christian life are not chosen. The diagnosis, the redundancy, the years of caring for a parent were laid on, not volunteered for. Simon did not volunteer either, and he walked closest behind the Son of God.

Verses 27–28 correct a devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, full of sympathy and empty of repentance.

Verses 39–40 answer the assumption that suffering makes people better. Two men suffered the same pain at the same distance from Jesus, and both began by reviling him (Matthew 27:44). One changed, and it was grace that changed him.

And v. 43 is for anyone who thinks it is too late: a confession and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they led him away. A condemned man carried the crossbeam himself, and Jesus set out doing so (John 19:17). The likeliest reason a stranger had to take it over is that, after a night of beatings and the flogging (John 19:1), Jesus could carry it no further.

Help to carry the beam. The one who upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3) apparently could not carry a beam of wood up a hill. That is the measure of how truly he became man. He went to the cross in real flesh, as weak as ours, so that he would be a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and no sufferer who has run out of strength would ever think him far away.

Simon of Cyrene. A soldier picks a stranger out of the crowd, a man arriving with plans for the day, from Cyrene in North Africa, which had a large Jewish community. A Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry a load. Simon was not asked.

Behind Jesus. Only Luke says behind Jesus. That is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (9:23; 14:27). Now a man does it literally, and against his will.

Most crosses are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as though it were a decision, and sometimes it is. But the illness was not chosen. The child’s diagnosis was not chosen. The redundancy, the parent who needs care for a decade, the marriage that became a long endurance: none of it was volunteered for. It was laid on. Simon may have resented every step. And apart from Jesus himself, he is the only man who ever carried the cross of Christ.

Simon’s family. Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), as if his readers knew them, and Paul greets a Rufus in Rome, chosen in the Lord (Romans 16:13). It may be the same family. If so, the man pressed into service that morning did not stay a bystander.

What does it mean for me to carry my cross? It means following Jesus wherever he leads, accepting the cost of belonging to him, and saying no to self when self and Christ conflict (9:23–24). Sometimes the cross is chosen: you give up a sinful relationship, tell the truth at a price, take a stand that costs you. Often it is laid on you: a suffering you did not seek, which you carry not with resentment but behind Jesus, trusting him with it. Your cross is never his cross. He alone carried our sins; we carry only what comes from following him, and he walks ahead.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great multitude of the people. Not all were hostile.

Mourning and lamenting. Only Luke records this formal, audible grief, as at a funeral. There is no hint that Jesus thinks it insincere, and he does not rebuke them for it.

Do not weep for me. Even on the way to the cross he thinks of others. Not because his suffering is not worth weeping over, but because theirs is nearer than they think, and pity is not what he needs from anyone. Some devotion consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, and produces sympathy and no repentance. He did not go to Golgotha to be pitied.

Weep for yourselves. Weep for the judgment coming on Jerusalem (19:41–44; 21:20–24). Their children would see the siege and destruction of AD 70. Grief that fastens on someone else’s situation can be a way of not looking at your own. It is easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face the state of one’s own household.

Is it wrong to be moved by the sufferings of Christ? No. It would be strange to read of the cross and feel nothing, and the church has always sung of his wounds with tears. The question is where the feeling leads. If it ends in a pleasant sadness, it has missed the point.
