If it leads you to see the seriousness of sin, to repent of your own, to trust him and love him, it is exactly what the cross is meant to produce. Do not weep for him as a victim. Weep over the sin that put him there, and then rejoice that he chose to go.

In the flow. These are the last of Jesus’ words over Jerusalem in Luke (13:34–35; 19:41–44). Between the trial and the cross Luke has placed not a word of self-pity but a warning and a grief.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are the barren. In that world childlessness was the standard image of grief and shame (1:25). Jesus says a day is coming when women will be congratulated on it. That is a measurement of horror: the siege of the year 70, when the worst thing that could happen to a woman would look like an escape, because she would not have to watch her children die. He is not saying it with satisfaction; he is grieving. If you have longed for children and not had them, or have lost a child, hear this gently: Jesus is not calling childlessness a blessing, and he is not making light of your grief. He is measuring a horror, and the Lord who said it wept over the very mothers he was speaking of.

Fall on us. A quotation from Hosea 10:8, spoken over the northern kingdom on the eve of its destruction. It is a cry of people who would rather be crushed than face what is coming, and John heard it again at the end of all things, from those hiding from the wrath of the Lamb (Revelation 6:16). Being buried under a mountain is not what they are fleeing. It is the alternative they prefer.

Is Jesus speaking about AD 70 or about the final judgment? Both, in the way prophecy often works. The nearer fulfilment came within forty years, when Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem, as he had foretold (21:20–24). But the words he uses, and Revelation’s use of the same cry, show that the fall of Jerusalem was a foreshadowing of the last day, when all who have refused Christ will face the holy God. The first came exactly as he said, which is a sober warning that the second will too.

For worship. There is a day coming when men will find the presence of God unbearable, and the terror of it is not that he is cruel but that he is holy and they are not. And the one who spoke of that day was walking towards a hill to bear it. The wrath of the Lamb is real; so is the blood of the Lamb, and whoever hides in him will never need to hide from him.

parallels.desc: they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us”

verseByVerse.quote: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry? It has the sound of a proverb, and it probably was one. Green wood is living wood, full of sap; it resists a fire and has to be forced to burn. Dry wood is dead, and goes up at a spark. So the question argues from the lesser to the greater, a form the rabbis used constantly: if this is what happens in the unlikely case, what will happen in the likely one? The application is not stated, which is why readers have taken it two ways, and both are worth having.

Two readings. The first: if Rome and the temple authorities will do this to a man who is entirely innocent, what will they do when the city is full of genuine rebels? Jerusalem burned within a generation. The second goes deeper and does not exclude the first: if judgment falls like this on the green wood, the one man who never deserved a stroke of it, what will it be when it falls on the dry? If judgment begins at the household of God, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel (1 Peter 4:17–18)? What is happening on that hill is the wrath of God against sin, absorbed by a substitute, and even so it produced three hours of darkness and, as Matthew and Mark record, a cry of forsakenness that has never stopped echoing (Mark 15:34). That wrath is not rage; it is the holiness of God meeting sin, as light meets darkness. What happened there has a name, propitiation (Romans 3:25): the wrath falls, but it falls on the sacrifice, and so it is turned away from those for whom he dies.

Is God’s judgment not out of all proportion? This is a question people ask honestly and often: would a loving God really deal with sin so severely? Look at what he was prepared to do to his own Son rather than overlook it. Nobody who has understood Calvary can go on thinking that God takes sin lightly or deals with it cheaply. Sin is no small thing, because it is committed against an infinitely holy God, and the punishment of those who refuse his mercy is conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The cross is not evidence that judgment is mild. It is the fullest evidence available of how serious it is, and, in the same act, the reason a sinner need never face it.
verseByVerse.note: A proverb: if this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will happen to the guilty (dry wood, ready to burn)?

parallels.desc: every green tree and every dry tree

verseByVerse.quote: Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two others, who were criminals. Fulfilling Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus had quoted at the table only hours before: he was numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Here is the numbering, carried out by a Roman work detail.

The place that is called The Skull. Luke gives the meaning of the Aramaic Golgotha; the Latin is Calvary.

There they crucified him. Luke describes it in a single word: his readers knew exactly what crucifixion was. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty, and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. Its purpose was public degradation over hours, and Luke’s restraint is a kind of reverence.

One on his right and one on his left. That is exactly the arrangement James and John had once asked for: grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory (Mark 10:37). When the places either side of him were finally filled, it was by convicted criminals. He is placed among them, in the middle, the place one would give a ringleader.

Why did Jesus have to die by crucifixion? Because crucifixion was a death under curse. The law said that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul explains that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). It was also the most shameful death the world knew, and he despised the shame (Hebrews 12:2), taking the lowest place so that none of his people would be beneath his reach. And it was public: lifted up, as he said, to draw all people to himself (John 12:32).

In the flow. Around the crucifixion Luke sets three sayings found only in his Gospel: a prayer for his killers (v. 34), a promise to a thief (v. 43) and a prayer of trust as he dies (v. 46). Between them come the mockers, three times telling him to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39). The shape carries the meaning: the one who will not save himself spends his dying hours saving others.
verseByVerse.note: Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' And they cast lots to divide his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Father, forgive them. The first of Jesus’ words from the cross in Luke is a prayer for the men holding the hammer. Father: nothing they are doing has changed how he addresses God. Forgive them: the soldiers, the leaders, the crowd. He practises what he taught: love your enemies, pray for those who abuse you (6:27–28). It is the intercession of a high priest, begun before he is dead, for people who have not asked and are not sorry. Stephen would pray the same as he died (Acts 7:60); he had learned it from his Lord.

For they know not what they do. The ignorance is real and it is partial. They knew they were killing a man; they did not know they were killing the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), the Author of life (Acts 3:15, 17). Ignorance does not remove guilt; if it did, no forgiveness would be needed. But it is a ground on which to plead, and Peter pleaded it in the same city (Acts 3:17). And the prayer was answered. At Pentecost thousands in that city, very likely including some who had shouted for his death, repented and were forgiven (Acts 2:36–41), and a centurion at the foot of the cross praised God (v. 47).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer. It is missing from some important early copies and present in many others. But it is very early, widely attested, and fits Luke perfectly; no evangelist is more preoccupied with forgiveness. Some have suggested that a later scribe, looking back on the destruction of Jerusalem, thought the prayer had gone unanswered, or that the Jews should not be forgiven, and let it fall. If so, he stopped reading too soon, because Luke wrote a second volume telling what became of it. Most scholars accept it as an authentic saying of Jesus.

They cast lots. A condemned man’s clothes were the perk of the execution squad, and it is Psalm 22:18 happening word for word: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. The gamblers were the very men he was praying for.

Were they forgiven even if they did not repent? No. Jesus prayed that they would be forgiven, and God answered that prayer by bringing many of them to repentance and faith. Forgiveness is always received through turning to Christ (Acts 2:38; 3:19). Those who went on rejecting him were not forgiven by a blanket pardon. But the prayer shows the heart of Christ towards his enemies, and it means that no one who had a part in his death, and no one today who has despised him, is beyond the reach of his mercy if they come.

Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? You must let go of revenge and bitterness, and wish them good, even before they repent. That is what Jesus did here: he prayed for them, and gave up any desire to repay. Never avenge yourselves (Romans 12:19). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, needs repentance on their side (17:3–4), and forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or crime, forgiveness and reporting it go together; you can forgive from the heart and still let the authorities do their God-given work. Start where he started: bring them to the Father in prayer, and ask him to forgive them.

For worship. If he prayed like that for the men at the foot of his cross, there is no sinner he will refuse who comes to him, and every forgiven believer since has been an answer to those three words.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer “Father, forgive them.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people stood by. No mockery is attributed to the people. They are silent, and they will go home beating their breasts (v. 48). The people watch; the rulers scoff.

The rulers scoffed. The word is exemyktērizon: they turned up their noses, sneered. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Psalm 22:7).

He saved others; let him save himself. He saved others: they concede his miracles in the middle of a taunt. Then the sneer: a saviour who cannot get himself off a cross is no saviour. The soldiers and one of the criminals will repeat it. It is the settled assumption of the whole hill: real power rescues itself.

Exactly wrong, and exactly right. The logic is exactly wrong. He could not save himself and save others. Not because the power was lacking, for he had told Peter that legions were available for the asking (Matthew 26:53), but because the two things could not both be done. To come down would be to leave the work undone and every person he came for still under sentence. So the mockery states the gospel with perfect accuracy and no understanding whatever. Atonement means sinners and God made one again, at one, by sin being dealt with. And this is how it was done: Jesus stayed under the penalty our sins deserved, so that it would never fall on us (Isaiah 53:5).

His Chosen One. They use Peter’s confession (9:20) and the Father’s word at the transfiguration, my Chosen One (9:35), in mockery; chosen is Isaiah’s word for the Servant (Isaiah 42:1). They were quoting the Father’s own delight in his Son back at him as an insult, and their words are true.

Could Jesus really have come down from the cross? Yes, in power. He was the eternal Son, and nothing held him there but his own will and his love for the Father and for us. No one takes my life from me, he said; I lay it down of my own accord, and I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again (John 10:18). That is what makes his staying so glorious. It was not the nails that kept him on the cross. It was the will to save.

verseByVerse.quote: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, 'If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers also mocked him. Jews and Gentiles together. The rulers mocked him theologically; the soldiers are an execution detail passing the time.

Offering him sour wine. The cheap wine soldiers drank, offered as a toast to the king. And this too was written: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (Psalm 69:21).

If you are the King. The phrase was said to him before, in the wilderness: if you are the Son of God (4:3, 9), and the devil departed until an opportune time (4:13). This is that time. Three times on the cross he is told to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39), as he was tempted three times in the wilderness: prove it by using your power on your own behalf. The answer is the same both times: he will not use his power for himself. In the wilderness he answered with Scripture; on the cross he answers with silence.

If God loved me, would this be happening? It is what a Christian hears in a hospital corridor, in a marriage gone cold, in the fourth month of looking for work: if you really were what you claim to be, you would not be in this position; if God loved you, this would not be happening. The shape of that temptation is universal even when the stakes are small. Answer it from the cross. The beloved Son, in whom the Father delighted, was in the worst position any man has ever been in, and it was not because God did not love him but because God was doing the greatest good through it. Suffering is never proof that you are not loved. For the Christian it is always held inside the love that gave the Son (Romans 8:32, 35–39).
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

verseByVerse.quote: There was also an inscription over him, 'This is the King of the Jews.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
An inscription over him. The board carrying the charge, posted as Roman custom required so that everyone who passed knew what he was dying for. It is a legal document.

The King of the Jews. The only charge Rome ever posted against Jesus of Nazareth is that he is who he said he is. Pilate wrote it as a sneer at the men who had forced his hand, and refused to change it: what I have written I have written (John 19:21–22). It was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek (John 19:20), so that every kind of person in the festival city could read it. Without meaning to, Pilate proclaimed to the world who Jesus is: he reigns from the cross.

Why do the Gospels give different wordings? A careful reader comparing them will spot it. Matthew has this is Jesus, the King of the Jews; Mark, the King of the Jews; John, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. This is what happens when four witnesses report a sign written in three languages: each gives the substance, and the substance is identical in every one. It is the ordinary variation of honest testimony, and a set of accounts that agreed word for word would be more suspicious, not less.

In what sense is Jesus a king now? In the fullest sense. He was not only King of the Jews but is King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), raised and seated at God’s right hand, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). He rules now over all things for the sake of his church, gathers his people from every nation through the gospel, and will return visibly to judge and make all things new. His kingdom does not advance by armies or elections, but no throne on earth is outside his rule. To be a Christian is to be his willing subject.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him, saying, 'Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the criminals railed. Two men, the same distance from Jesus, in identical pain, hearing identical words, and they go opposite ways. Railed is eblasphēmei: he blasphemed. Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first (Matthew 27:44), so the difference emerged during those hours, perhaps as the second heard him pray for his enemies.

Set for the fall and rising of many. Old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said that this child was appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel (2:34). Here is that word in its starkest form: one Saviour, a cross on either side, and nothing separating the two criminals except what each made of Jesus. Even while he is dying, every human destiny turns on him.

Suffering does not make people better. People assume that a man facing death will naturally turn to God. These two were nailed up on the same morning for the same kind of crime. Suffering did not soften one of them. Only grace did that.

Save yourself and us! The first man has repeated the rulers’ sneer and added a request entirely about his circumstances: get me down. He wants rescue from the cross, not from sin. That is a real and common form of religion, sincere in hospital wards and financial crises: it wants God to change the situation, and has no view at all about God.

Do you not fear God. The second man’s first recorded words are not about Jesus and not about himself, but about God. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), and here is a dying criminal, hours from the end, with no religious education anyone knows of, arriving at the one thought that no amount of pain had produced in the man on the other side.

Since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? He is not lecturing from above. He includes himself. We are all dying; how can you mock? The whole rebuke rests on this: we are both getting what we deserve, which is a thing almost nobody says about himself.

What does it mean to fear God? It is not cringing terror before a tyrant, but a deep reverence and awe before the holy God who is our Judge, joined, for those who know his mercy, with love and trust. It means taking him seriously: knowing that he sees, that sin matters to him, and that we will stand before him. Those who fear him are drawn to him, not driven away, because with him there is forgiveness, that he may be feared (Psalm 130:4). The thief feared God, and that fear sent him to Christ. That is always where true fear of God leads.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first.

verseByVerse.quote: And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.' And he said, 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we indeed justly. What this man says in two sentences is as exact a statement of the gospel as many Christians could manage. He confesses his guilt without excuse; he says the sentence is right. Repentance is not feeling sorry at being caught; it is agreeing with God about your sin and turning from it to him. This man could not undo a single deed, but he could stop defending himself, and he did. That is true repentance, and it speaks as David did: you are justified in your words and blameless in your judgment (Psalm 51:4).

Nothing wrong. One more witness to Jesus’ innocence, alongside Pilate and Herod, and this from a man who has nothing to gain by saying it: the only declaration in the chapter made by someone who was himself dying.

Jesus, remember me. Astonishing faith. Consider what he is looking at. Not a miracle-worker surrounded by crowds. A man nailed to a beam a few feet away, bleeding, mocked by everyone present, visibly dying, with a Roman notice over his head calling him a king as a joke. And he calls him by his name, Jesus, which means the Lord saves, with no title, and asks to be included in a kingdom that not one visible thing on that hill supports the existence of. At that hour even the disciples seem to have given up hope (24:21).

Faith with everything stripped off it. He has no Bible, no baptism, no church, no time, and no capacity to do a single good work; he cannot even come down and be useful. He has nothing to bring except an honest verdict on himself and a conviction about who the man beside him is. And the request is modest: remember me, do not let me be forgotten when you come into what is yours, as Joseph once asked the cupbearer to remember him (Genesis 40:14).

Is a deathbed conversion real? It can be, and this man is the proof; but there is one such thief, so that none need despair, and only one, so that none should presume. (See Matthew 20:1–2 for the fuller answer.)

Do I need to be baptised to be saved? Baptism is commanded by Christ for every believer (Matthew 28:19), and a Christian who refuses it is disobeying his Lord. But baptism is not what saves; Christ saves, through faith. As far as we know, the thief was never baptised, and on the cross he could not be, yet he was in paradise that day. Baptism is the sign and confession of a salvation already received, which is why this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), holds that it is for those who have believed, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters (those who baptise the infants of believers, as a sign of God’s promise to families) who see it differently. So if you have come to faith, be baptised, gladly and soon; but never think that the water does what only the blood can do.

In everyday life. Measure your own prayers against this one. Many Christians pray apologetically, working out whether they have the standing to ask. This man had none, and asked anyway. Pray the thief’s prayer today, in his words, when you are most aware of your failure: Jesus, remember me.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you. He asked to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied, and each part of the answer gives more than was requested.

Today. Not after an interval of waiting: before the sun goes down on the worst day of his life. Today is Luke’s great word of present salvation: unto you is born this day (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled (4:21); today salvation has come to this house (19:9). There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one: the same day, straight through, from a Roman cross to paradise.

You will be with me. That is the heart of heaven: being with Jesus. Paradise is not described, and it does not need to be (Philippians 1:23). Whatever else heaven contains, its content is a person, and the man who has him has everything in it.

In paradise. A Persian word for a walled garden, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden (Genesis 2:8) and in the New Testament of the place of the blessed dead with God (2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7): Eden restored. The last promise Jesus makes before he dies is that the garden is open again, and he says it to a criminal.

Where Christians differ: purgatory and soul sleep. Roman Catholic teaching holds that most of the saved must pass through purgatory after death, to be purified before they enter heaven. Others teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. And some have tried to move the comma, reading I say to you today, you will be with me, so that today describes when Jesus spoke rather than when the man would arrive. The Greek carries no punctuation, so the question is fair. But truly I say to you is a fixed formula on Jesus’ lips, used scores of times in the Gospels, and not once does it take a trailing today; and it would be a pointless thing to say, since the man could hardly have supposed he was being answered on some other day. This commentary’s view: today goes naturally with you will be with me, as Luke uses the word elsewhere. The thief, a criminal with no time for penance, went straight to paradise with Christ. There is no purgatory: Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient, for by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14), and the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). And there is no soul sleep: believers who die are with the Lord at once, consciously, which is why Paul could call it far better (Philippians 1:21–23), and why the souls under the altar speak (Revelation 6:9–10). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession put it carefully: the souls of men neither die nor sleep, and the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1).

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb, and his soul went to the Father (v. 46), which is why he could promise the thief today. (See John 19:41–42 for the fuller answer.)

Are my loved ones who died in Christ aware and happy now? Yes. They are with the Lord, conscious, at rest from their labours, and blessed (Revelation 14:13). They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware; when Scripture calls death sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), it speaks of the body resting until it is raised and of death’s gentleness for the believer, not of the soul’s unconsciousness. We are not told what they know of us, and we must not try to contact them (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). But we can grieve with hope, because they are with Christ, which is far better.

If they are already in paradise, why do we still need the resurrection? Because God made us body and soul, and he will not leave half of us in the grave. The state of believers between death and resurrection is blessed but not yet complete. Paul longs not to be unclothed but further clothed (2 Corinthians 5:4). At Christ’s return the dead in Christ will be raised with glorious bodies like his (1 Thessalonians 4:16; Philippians 3:21), and the paradise the thief entered that day will become a whole new creation. The thief’s body probably went into a criminal’s grave; it will come out as Christ’s did.

Is it fair that a criminal should be in paradise on the day he died? Not if heaven is a reward for good lives, but it never was. If it were fair in that sense, none of us would be there, because even the best life lived by a sinner falls short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The thief is in paradise on exactly the same ground as the apostle Paul: Christ’s death in his place, received by faith. The objection usually comes from the elder brother in us, the part that has kept the rules and quietly expects to be credited for it (15:28–30). Grace offends the religious as much as it surprises the irreligious, and both need it equally. The real wonder is not that the thief got in, but that anyone does.

In everyday life. Read this verse to anyone who thinks it is too late: a man raised near the church but never committed, dying in a hospice, wanting to know whether there is time. The answer is unqualified. There was no baptism, no probation, no changed life to show. There was a confession, a recognition and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

For worship. The first Adam was driven out of paradise, and cherubim with a flaming sword guarded the way back (Genesis 3:24). The last Adam, dying on a tree, opened it with a word, and walked a thief in. The curse that closed the garden fell on him as he hung on a tree (Galatians 3:13), so that the way in could stand open to the guilty; and for everyone who trusts him, the day of death is simply today, with him.
verseByVerse.note: “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the dwelling of God’s people after death.

parallels.desc: the tree of life in the paradise of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–56 — The Death of Jesus and the Burial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From noon until three darkness covers the land, and Luke says only that the sun's light failed. It is the language of judgment (Amos 8:9). Across the city the temple curtain is torn in two.

Then, with a loud voice, Jesus prays Psalm 31:5 with one word added, Father, and breathes his last. The centurion praises God and says certainly this man was innocent. The crowds go home beating their breasts, and the women from Galilee watch from a distance.

Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented to their decision, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen and lays it in a rock-cut tomb where no one had yet been laid. The Sabbath is beginning. The women see the tomb and how the body was laid, prepare spices, and rest according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.theology:
The darkness speaks of judgment, not merely grief. The blow that fell on Egypt falls here on the Lamb, so that it need not fall on those he dies for.

The torn curtain means the way into God's presence is open. For centuries that room said not yet, and not you. Now we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Luke has no cry of dereliction, but he has not softened the death; he has shown the anguish on the Mount of Olives (22:41–42) and chooses trust for the last word. Both are true.

The burial is not an appendix. Paul lists it among the facts of first importance (1 Corinthians 15:3–5), because it proves Jesus was dead and fixes the place where he would be found alive. Isaiah had written it: and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Mark's centurion speaks of the Son of God; Luke's says innocent, showing a Roman reader that the founder of this movement was pronounced innocent by every competent authority and executed anyway.

Verse 49 is for anyone whose service to Christ goes unrecorded. The women from Galilee had funded the ministry (8:2–3), stayed to the end, saw where he was buried, and were the first to hear that he was alive.

Verse 54 leaves a silent Saturday, and much of the Christian life is lived in such gaps, after the loss and before any sign of hope. The gap is not abandonment: the most decisive work in history had just been finished.

And vv. 55–56 show faithfulness with no feeling left in it: the spices ready, the tomb a walk away, and a whole day of rest because God commanded it. Anyone holding on like that should remember how their Saturday ended.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now about the sixth hour. The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon. So this is not evening coming on early. It is darkness at the brightest part of the day, for three hours.

Darkness over the whole land. The Old Testament had already supplied the meaning. Amos, prophesying judgment: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9). And Egypt had a darkness that could be felt for three days (Exodus 10:21–22), the plague immediately before the Passover lamb. So the sign is not merely grief. It is judgment, and the reason for the darkness is the reason the sky went black over Egypt: God is dealing with sin. Only this time the blow does not fall on a nation. It falls on one man, in the middle of the day, in the dark. The judgment against sin was falling on the Son.

While the sun’s light failed. Not an eclipse, though the suggestion is sometimes made. Passover falls at full moon, and a solar eclipse cannot happen at full moon; besides, no total eclipse lasts more than a few minutes. Luke says only that the sun’s light failed, and leaves the mechanism alone. It was a supernatural darkness.

The curtain torn in two. The second sign happens across the city, where nobody at Golgotha could see it. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s presence, from the rest of the temple. Behind it nobody went: one man, one day a year, with blood, and not without trembling (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). The whole architecture of Israel’s worship was a statement that the way in was closed. Matthew and Mark note the direction of the tear: from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). A tear from the top down is not vandalism; it reads as a verdict, passed from above. Torn: the way into God’s presence is open through the death of Christ. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). And it was a sign that the temple system was ending. Luke places the tearing before Jesus’ death, Mark after it; Luke groups the signs together.

In the flow. Up to this point every voice in the chapter has been human. Now heaven answers without a word, and Luke sets the two signs just before Jesus dies (v. 46), so that the reader hears his last words knowing what the death means: judgment falling, and the way to God thrown open. At his arrest Jesus had said, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53); God has turned that hour into the hour of access.

Can I really come to God directly, without a priest? Yes, through Christ, and only through him. The curtain is torn for everyone who trusts in Jesus. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is our great high priest. You do not need a human priest to confess to, a saint to plead for you, or a holy building to stand in. You may pray to the Father, in Jesus’ name, anywhere, at any hour, about anything. Pastors are given to teach and care for you, and fellow believers to pray with you, but none of them stands between you and God. The way in is open, and it is open because of blood.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' And having said this he breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling out with a loud voice. That was not how crucified men usually died. Death on a cross came slowly, by exhaustion and failing strength, and the end was commonly a fading, not a shout. He chose the moment of his death (John 10:18).

Into your hands. The words are a quotation: Psalm 31:5, into your hand I commit my spirit. Later Jewish tradition used that verse as an evening prayer, said before sleep: Jesus dies with a bedtime prayer. And he added one word to it. The psalm says, into your hand. He says, Father. The relationship is unbroken. Commit is paratithemai, to deposit, to place something valuable into safe keeping. It is not resignation but a deliberate entrusting. Stephen, dying, would say almost the same words, addressed to Jesus (Acts 7:59), because that is what the first Christians did with this sentence: they took it as the pattern for how to die.

Where is the cry of dereliction? A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice something missing, and it should be faced rather than passed over. In those Gospels the cry from the cross is, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Mark 15:34), and Luke does not have it. Has he softened the death? He has not, and the answer is in what he has already given. Luke does not hide the horror of that night: the agony in the garden, and the sweat like drops of blood and the angel sent to strengthen him, which are his alone (though those two verses, 22:43–44, are missing from some early manuscripts). Luke has shown the anguish; he shows it in Gethsemane. What he chooses for the last moment is the other true thing about it, and both are needed. The cry of dereliction tells you what the cross cost. This word tells you how it ended. It is the word of perfect trust, the work finished. After the darkness, after whatever passed in those three hours that no writer describes, the last sentence out of his mouth is the one a child says to a father he is sure of.

He breathed his last. He died. Truly. Not a swoon, not an appearance of death, but the separation of his soul from his body. The Son of God died.

How can I die well? By learning to say this prayer before you need it. Jesus did not invent new words at the end; he used a psalm he had known all his life. So fill your memory now with Scripture and with prayers of trust: Psalm 23, Psalm 31, Romans 8, John 14. Settle your trust in Christ while you are well. Put your affairs in order, forgive those you need to forgive, and tell those you love that you belong to him. And when the time comes, whether slowly or suddenly, you may commit your spirit to the Father with confidence, because Jesus has gone ahead of you and is waiting to receive you (Acts 7:59).
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer.

parallels.desc: into your hand I commit my spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, 'Certainly this man was innocent!' And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion. The first voice after the death belongs to the officer in charge of killing him. A centurion commanded about eighty soldiers, and executions were routine duty for the garrison. He is the last man on that hill who could be moved by sentiment.

He praised God. A Roman soldier praising God at the cross. It is how Luke’s Gospel greets every mighty work of God (2:20; 5:25; 7:16; 18:43), and even here, at a death, someone does it.

Certainly this man was innocent! The Greek is dikaios: righteous, or innocent, depending on the setting. In Mark he says, truly this man was the Son of God (Mark 15:39); a man watching an execution probably said more than one sentence, and each writer has kept the one that serves his account. Luke’s choice is the key to his whole passion narrative. This is the last of the verdicts Luke has been counting, after Pilate’s three, Herod’s and the dying criminal’s, and it comes from the officer commanding the execution squad, a Gentile. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader, who will read in Acts of Christians before magistrates while the charges keep collapsing: their founder was pronounced innocent by every competent authority, and executed anyway. That is not a smaller confession than Mark’s. It is the same verdict from the other side: Mark tells you who he was, and Luke tells you what Rome could not find in him. The righteous one has died for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

Beating their breasts. They came for a spectacle and go home in grief and remorse. That gesture has appeared once before in this Gospel, and it is worth remembering where. A tax collector, standing far off, who would not even lift his eyes to heaven, beat his breast and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner, and Luke says that man went home justified, declared right with God (18:13–14). Here is the beginning of repentance, and it would bear fruit at Pentecost, when the people were cut to the heart (Acts 2:37).

What did the centurion actually understand? Probably not everything. He saw how Jesus died: the prayer for his killers, the promise to the thief, the darkness, the loud cry of trust, and he knew this was no criminal. Whether he believed in Jesus as Lord we are not told. But he praised God, and in that moment he spoke truer words than the council. God often begins with a person there: an honest recognition that Jesus is not who the world says he is. Pray for that beginning in those you love, and do not despise it when you see it.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers but in practice about eighty. Beating the breast was a sign of grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All his acquaintances. His friends, perhaps including some of the disciples. At a distance: Luke used that phrase of Peter in the high priest’s courtyard (22:54), and he uses it again here of everyone who loved him. Luke does not put a single apostle at the foot of the cross by name. These stayed until it was over, at a distance, which is probably where soldiers kept the friends of a condemned man, and where grief itself often stands. My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off (Psalm 38:11).

Alone in the middle of a crowd. Luke’s phrase at a distance echoes the Greek Old Testament wording of the psalms in which a righteous man suffers (Psalm 88:8), and the echo is probably deliberate: the righteous sufferer is dying, and his friends cannot come near. The one who touched lepers, took children in his arms and let a sinful woman wash his feet dies with no one who loves him within reach. He bore the distance as well as the wounds. And because he was left alone, none of his people will ever be: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

The women from Galilee. Luke has told us about them before: Mary called Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager, Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means (8:2–3). They had travelled with him for the length of the ministry, and they had been paying for it. And they are still there, watching the end of everything they had given themselves to.

Watching these things. Watching: eyewitnesses. They see him die, they see where he is buried, and how (v. 55), and they come back with the spices. The unbroken chain of witness that runs from the cross to the empty tomb is held, in this Gospel, by women, whose testimony in that world often carried little weight in a court. God chose them anyway.

What does this say about women in the church? It honours them highly. In the Gospels women were the most faithful followers at the cross, the witnesses of the burial and the first to hear of the resurrection. They supported Christ’s ministry, served him, and were sent to tell the apostles. This commentary holds, with the complementarian reading of the New Testament (men and women equal in worth, given different and complementary callings), that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), and that this is a pattern of order, not of worth. Paul grounds it in creation rather than in the customs of his day (1 Timothy 2:13), which is why we hold to it. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and we honour their love for Scripture while we differ. Women and men are equally made in God’s image and equally heirs of grace (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7), and every church should value, use and thank its faithful women as Luke does.

In everyday life. Faithfulness sometimes means simply staying, watching, not running away. If you are sitting beside someone in a long illness or a grief you cannot fix, your presence is not nothing; it is the ministry of the women at the cross. Stay. And thank someone this week whose quiet service has held your church together.

parallels.desc: my friends stand aloof from my plague

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph of Arimathea. Luke introduces him as a witness whose credentials matter. Arimathea was a town of Judea, perhaps Ramathaim, Samuel’s birthplace.

He was a member of the council. The Sanhedrin, the very body that had condemned Jesus a few hours earlier, so the man about to take the body down belonged to the court that condemned him. Yet Luke calls him a good and righteous man, as he described Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6) and Simeon (2:25) at the start of the Gospel.

Had not consented. Only Luke records this: not the decision only, but the action. Perhaps Joseph was absent from the night hearing, or voted against it. But the passage does not hide the honest question: where was the dissent when it might have mattered? John says Joseph was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). By the time he acts, the man he might have defended is dead. He is neither hero nor coward, but something more recognisable: a believer who was afraid, whose silence had a real cost, and who then did the bravest thing still available at the moment he had left.

Looking for the kingdom. Waiting for it, as Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel and Anna for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Gospel begins and ends with faithful people waiting.

Waiting for a kingdom that had just come. Joseph thought his waiting had ended in failure; in fact it had ended in the very thing he was waiting for. The kingdom of God was not defeated on Friday; it was won, by a King who reigned from a tree and conquered by dying. Joseph went to Pilate believing he was burying the hope of Israel. He was laying in the tomb the King who would walk out of it.

Am I a secret disciple? Many believers are at times: you love Christ, but in some setting, at work, with certain friends or family, nobody would know. Joseph’s story is both a warning and a hope. A warning, because silence when it matters has a cost, and Jesus says that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (9:26). A hope, because Christ did not reject Joseph, and gave him a magnificent act of courage at the end. If you have been hiding, the way forward is not despair but a step into the open: one clear, kind word that shows whose you are.

For worship. A frightened disciple who had kept silent in the council found his courage only when it seemed too late, and the Lord he had failed to defend wasted none of it. His late, trembling love put the tomb, and its emptiness, on the record for ever. A bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3).
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked for the body. Crucified bodies were not usually surrendered, though in Judea the Romans sometimes allowed burial out of respect for Jewish law (Deuteronomy 21:23). To go to the governor and ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to risk being identified, on the record, with the treason. Mark says Joseph took courage and went (Mark 15:43), hours after his own council had procured the execution. Whatever he had been keeping quiet, he is not keeping it quiet now.

A linen shroud. Somebody had to draw the nails and take the weight of the body as it came free, and Joseph, a wealthy councillor (Matthew 27:57), did it or saw it done. The body was wrapped in a burial cloth. John adds that Nicodemus came too, with a great weight of spices (John 19:39).

A tomb cut in stone. Every clause from here does quiet evidential work. A tomb cut in stone: not a shallow grave that could be disturbed, but a chamber hewn out of rock, the kind wealthy families had, with one entrance, sealed with a large stone. And Isaiah had put it in writing seven centuries before, in the same breath as the transgressors: and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9).

A new tomb. A new tomb (John 19:41), so that on Sunday there could be no confusion about whose body was missing. Like the colt on which no one had ever yet sat (19:30), it was set apart for him. And its location was known to a named member of the council, and to the women watching from a few yards away, and therefore checkable by anyone in Jerusalem who cared to walk out and look.

Did Jesus really die, or did he only faint? He really died. Roman executioners were experts in death, and the centurion confirmed it to Pilate (Mark 15:44–45). John saw a soldier pierce his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). His friends handled his body, wrapped it and laid it in a tomb, and his enemies sealed and guarded it (Matthew 27:62–66). A half-dead man, flogged and crucified, could not have rolled away the stone, overpowered guards, and then persuaded his disciples that he was the conqueror of death. The burial is in the creed and in Paul’s summary of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) precisely because it is the proof that he was dead.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone.

verseByVerse.quote: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the day of Preparation. It explains the haste of everything around it. The day of Preparation was Friday, the day on which everything for the Sabbath had to be done, because from sunset nothing could be: food cooked, lamps lit, work finished.

And the Sabbath was beginning. The Sabbath began at sundown. Literally, the Sabbath was dawning, perhaps referring to the lamps being lit, or the first evening star. So they are working against a clock, with no time for the full anointing, and the women note where it is because they can see it is unfinished. Then the sun goes down, and nothing more is done for a day and a half.

The Sabbath rest. On the seventh day God rested from the work of creation (Genesis 2:2). Now the Son rests in the tomb on the seventh day, his work finished (John 19:30). On the first day of the week, the new creation would begin.

The silent Saturday. Luke does not hurry past the silence. Between the last verse of this chapter and the first verse of the next lies a whole day in which nothing is said. God had become man, and was dead, and was in a grave, and it was the Sabbath, and nobody knew anything. There is a great deal of Christian life lived in that gap: the flat interval when the worst has already happened and nothing is moving, prayers seem to land nowhere, and the only thing available is to keep the ordinary rules of an ordinary day, getting up, praying, going to church, while your heart is in pieces. Nothing in this chapter suggests that the gap is a sign of abandonment. The most decisive work in the history of the world had just been finished, and from the outside, on the Saturday, it looked exactly like defeat.

How is Friday to Sunday three days? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1), so three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40) and on the third day mean the same span. All four Gospels say Jesus died on the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42), and theories of a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion have arisen largely to fit a literal count of hours.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday; the Sabbath began at sundown.

verseByVerse.quote: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How his body was laid. The last three verbs of the chapter: they saw, they prepared, they rested. They watched the laying out, and on Sunday they would not go to the wrong tomb.

Spices and ointments. To anoint the body properly after the Sabbath. Mark says they bought spices once the Sabbath was over (Mark 16:1); perhaps they made a start on Friday. They are preparing to anoint a corpse. They did not expect a resurrection. Everything they are doing is the work you do when hope is finished. And they do it beautifully, at speed, with care, for a man who cannot thank them.

The word they had forgotten. The spices are the measure of how completely they had missed what he said. He had told them plainly that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22), and again on the road up to Jerusalem (18:31–33). Their grief was real and their love was real, but their plans had no room for his promise. And the promise did not depend on their remembering it. While they ground spices, the word of the Son of God was quietly on its way to fulfilment, and on the third day it would keep itself.

They rested. Faithful Jews, keeping the law even in grief (Exodus 20:8–10): obedience with nothing left to fuel it. Every instinct they have is to go, and the commandment says rest, so they rest, with the jars ready by the door. Faithfulness can have no feeling in it at all, and it is done because God is God.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? These women lived under the old covenant, and Christ had not yet risen, so their example does not settle the question by itself. Christians hold different views. Many Reformed and Baptist Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath command continues, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day of the week as the Lord’s Day, to be kept holy for worship, rest and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), while the church gladly gathers on the first day, the day of resurrection, without Sabbath rules. This commentary’s view: the second view fits the New Testament best; the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday. Both seek to honour the Lord of the Sabbath, and believers should not judge one another over it (Romans 14:5–6). The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. All agree that the day of rising is a gift, and that weekly rest and worship are wise and good.

In the flow. The chapter that began with the council marching Jesus to Pilate ends with a handful of women resting at home, who will be first at the empty tomb with these very spices (24:1). So the burial is not an epilogue but the first half of the resurrection account. A dead man laid in a known tomb before witnesses is what makes an empty one mean something.

For worship. They rested on the Sabbath with the spices ready, and every one of those jars was wasted, because before they could use them he was up and out, and angels were asking why they sought the living among the dead. Their love brought ointment for a corpse; his love brought them a living Lord. So God lets his people’s faithful grief be overtaken by his joy, and his answer to the tomb is the third day.

23.text: <sup>1</sup> Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. <sup>2</sup> And they began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” <sup>3</sup> And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>4</sup> Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no guilt in this man.” <sup>5</sup> But they were urgent, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.” <sup>6</sup> When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. <sup>7</sup> And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time. <sup>8</sup> When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. <sup>9</sup> So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. <sup>10</sup> The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. <sup>11</sup> And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. <sup>12</sup> And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other. <sup>13</sup> Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, <sup>14</sup> and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. <sup>15</sup> Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. <sup>16</sup> I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>18</sup> But they all cried out together, “Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas”— <sup>19</sup> a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. <sup>20</sup> Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, <sup>21</sup> but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!” <sup>22</sup> A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>23</sup> But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. <sup>24</sup> So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. <sup>25</sup> He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will. <sup>26</sup> And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus. <sup>27</sup> And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. <sup>28</sup> But turning to them Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. <sup>29</sup> For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ <sup>30</sup> Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ <sup>31</sup> For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” <sup>32</sup> Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. <sup>33</sup> And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” And they cast lots to divide his garments. <sup>35</sup> And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” <sup>36</sup> The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine <sup>37</sup> and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” <sup>38</sup> There was also an inscription over him, “This is the King of the Jews.” <sup>39</sup> One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” <sup>40</sup> But the other rebuked him, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? <sup>41</sup> And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” <sup>42</sup> And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” <sup>43</sup> And he said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” <sup>44</sup> It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, <sup>45</sup> while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. <sup>46</sup> Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And having said this he breathed his last. <sup>47</sup> Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” <sup>48</sup> And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. <sup>49</sup> And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things. <sup>50</sup> Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, <sup>51</sup> who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God. <sup>52</sup> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>53</sup> Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid. <sup>54</sup> It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning. <sup>55</sup> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <sup>56</sup> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

24.title: Resurrection, Recognition, and Commission
24.overview:
Luke 24 moves through three scenes: the empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and the appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem. In each the disciples move from confusion towards recognition, and in each they are sent back to what Jesus had said and what the Scriptures had written. The resurrection does not only happen; it explains everything before it and sends the church into everything after it.

On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures to two downcast disciples and is known in the breaking of the bread. That evening he shows the eleven his hands and feet, opens their minds to see that the whole Old Testament is about him, and sends them to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins to all nations, once clothed with power from on high.

The Gospel ends with the ascension and the disciples in the temple, blessing God with great joy. It began in the temple with Zechariah at the altar of incense (1:9), and it ends there, ready to continue in Acts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The women come at dawn carrying spices for a corpse. They were not primed for a miracle. They find the stone rolled away and the body gone, and Luke writes the full title, the Lord Jesus, over the empty place.

Two men in dazzling apparel remind them of what Jesus had said in Galilee (9:22, 44; 18:31–33). The women remember, believe, and tell the eleven, who call it an idle tale. Peter runs to the tomb, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home marvelling, which Luke is careful not to call believing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The resurrection is a bodily event, and Luke records the physical detail, the stone, the body, the cloths, because the claim is not that a spirit survived but that the one who died was raised. If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:14–20).

That women are the first witnesses, named, and dismissed by the apostles, is a strong sign that the account is not invented: a forger would have put the discovery in the hands of a respected man.

And the angels' word remember is the key to the chapter. The failure to understand the resurrection was a failure to believe the word already given.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women's walk to the tomb was obedience with no expectation attached: they were going to finish a burial. Much faithful service has that shape, and it was those carrying the spices who reached the empty tomb first.

Verses 6–8 are practical. Faith rarely fails for lack of material; it fails for lack of memory. In a frightening season, go back to what God has actually said, not to what you feel.

Verse 11 is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool: the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree. And v. 12 describes a real stage on the road. Marvelling is not yet believing, but nobody who ran to the tomb stayed outside it for long.

verseByVerse.quote: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Luke 24 is the first Easter Sunday, told as though it were all one day (Acts 1:3 shows that the ascension came forty days later). Three times in it the disciples are sent back to what Jesus said and what the Scriptures wrote. The crucified one is alive in his body, the whole Bible is about him, and the Gospel that began in the temple with a silent priest ends in the temple with a blessing that never stops.

The setting. The chapter before ended with jars of spices standing ready in a house while the Sabbath was kept (23:56). This one opens with the jars being carried out of the door.

On the first day of the week. Sunday. A whole new week of history began on that morning.

At early dawn. As soon as the law allowed and there was light enough to see the path. This is simply what love does when it has been made to sit still for thirty-six hours.

The spices they had prepared. To anoint a dead body (23:56). Every step of that walk was taken in the belief that they were going to a corpse, which tells heavily against the theory that the resurrection was a story wishful people talked themselves into. These women were not primed for a miracle; their only practical worry, Mark tells us, was who would roll away the stone (Mark 16:3).

The stone rolled away. Luke does not describe the rolling: no earthquake, no angel heaving at it, none of the drama a storyteller would have supplied. He reports the state of things when they arrived: it was open, and somebody else had done it. Matthew tells us an angel of the Lord did it (Matthew 28:2). And the stone was not moved to let him out. The risen Lord who would vanish from a table at Emmaus that evening (v. 31) did not need a doorway. It seems to have been moved to let the witnesses in.

The body of the Lord Jesus. That is the first fact of the Christian faith, and it arrives as an absence: not a vision, not a voice, but an empty shelf in a rock chamber. And note the title Luke chooses at exactly this point, the Lord Jesus, the only time in this Gospel that the full title is used (a few manuscripts lack it, but the earliest have it). He writes it over the empty place where the corpse was supposed to be. The crucified one is the Lord.

Could the body simply have been stolen? Consider who could have taken it. His enemies had every reason to keep it and produce it the moment the apostles began preaching in the same city weeks later, and they never did. His friends were hiding, frightened and disbelieving; men do not go to their deaths, as several of them did, for a story they know they made up. Grave robbers leave the body and steal the valuables; here the linen was left and the body gone (v. 12). And the tomb could not explain the appearances: to the women, to Peter, to two on a road, to the eleven, to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). The simplest explanation of the empty tomb is the one the angels gave.

Why do Christians gather on Sunday? Because this is the day he rose. The first Christians, most of them Jews who had kept the seventh-day Sabbath all their lives, began meeting on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7), and John calls it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). Christians differ on whether that day is the Christian Sabbath, carrying over the fourth commandment, or a day of joyful worship without Sabbath rules. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules, with no one binding another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17), while honouring those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view. All agree that every Sunday is a small Easter, a weekly announcement to the world that the tomb is empty.

In everyday life. Think where you, like the women, are making careful arrangements around something you have already decided is dead: a prayer you have stopped praying, a person you have given up on. God may already have acted.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perplexed. Confused, at a loss, with no way through: a word close to the one Luke used of the nations in perplexity (21:25). The messengers came while they were in that state, not after they had worked something out. Their first thought was not resurrection.

Two men in dazzling apparel. Angels: later the disciples call it a vision of angels (v. 23). Luke calls them men because that is what they looked like. Two: the number of witnesses the law required for testimony to stand (Deuteronomy 19:15), like the two men at the transfiguration (9:30) and at the ascension (Acts 1:10).

Do the Gospels disagree about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Mark a young man, and Luke and John two; the women named and the times differ a little too. Each Gospel is a selective, independent report, and one does not deny two: Matthew and Mark focus on the spokesman. The women seem to have come in more than one group, and Luke himself says some of those who were with us went to the tomb (v. 24). All agree on the empty tomb, the women first, and the message that he had risen. Accounts that agreed word for word would look rehearsed; these look like witnesses.

Frightened. Awe before heavenly messengers. Again and again in this Gospel an angel’s coming has begun with a frightened human being: Zechariah at the altar, Mary in Nazareth, shepherds on a hillside. Here the women go face down on the floor of the tomb.

Why do you seek the living among the dead? It is a gentle rebuke, but more a reorientation. They have come to the right place with the wrong category. Tombs are where the dead are, and everything about their errand was correct except its central assumption. And the phrasing carries a claim no other sentence had yet made. Not, he is alive again, which would put him back where he was. The living: a description, a permanent condition. He has not returned to life like Lazarus, to die again. He has passed into a life that death has no further business with. I am the living one; I died, and behold, I am alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Where might I be looking for Jesus among the dead? The question turns outward, and it has been doing its work on readers ever since. Many people take Jesus seriously as a teacher, an example, a great moral figure of the past, and would be embarrassed to be thought unserious about him, and every one of those categories is a tomb. It is possible to hold him in the highest regard and still be looking for him among the honoured dead, where he cannot be found. Christians can do it too, treating him as a memory, a doctrine or a tradition rather than as a living Lord to speak to today. Seek him where he is: risen, reigning, present by his Spirit, speaking in his Word.

verseByVerse.quote: He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not here, but has risen. Everything turns on these words. Has risen, ēgerthē, is literally has been raised, by God: the resurrection is the Father’s verdict on the Son. The council had condemned Jesus as a blasphemer and Rome had executed him as a rebel; by raising him, God reversed both verdicts in front of the world and declared him to be his Son in power (Acts 2:23–24; Romans 1:4). The tomb was not broken out of; it was opened from the throne. A few manuscripts lack the words he is not here, but has risen, as the ESV notes; the earliest copies have them, and Mark gives the same message (Mark 16:6).

Remember how he told you. Having announced the greatest news ever delivered, the messengers do not explain it. They tell the women to remember. Jesus had said it three times in this Gospel, plainly, with the details: the Son of Man must suffer, be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22); let these words sink into your ears (9:44); and again on the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery and spitting named in advance (18:31–33). The women were among those who heard. So the angels’ remedy for bewilderment is not new information but old information that was not believed when it was given.

The Son of Man must. Must, dei: divine necessity, God’s plan. All of it happened exactly as he said.

Faith fails for lack of memory. What the women are handed in the worst confusion of their lives is not an explanation of the present but a promise made in Galilee months earlier. Faith very rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory, which is why God fills his book with commands to remember, and gives his people bread and wine and says, do this in remembrance of me.

Why does it matter that Jesus was raised bodily, and not just that his spirit lives on? Because everything depends on it. If Christ has not been raised, says Paul, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection is the Father’s public declaration that the sacrifice was accepted and the debt paid: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). Justification here means the Father’s acquittal of a guilty sinner, resting not on anything in him but on Christ’s death in his place, received by faith. It proves he is who he said (Romans 1:4). And it is the firstfruits of our own resurrection; his body raised is the pledge that ours will be (1 Corinthians 15:20). The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, brought to God as the promise that the whole field would follow (Leviticus 23:10). A spirit living on would prove none of this. An empty tomb proves all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They remembered his words. This is the first act of Easter faith recorded by anyone. Nothing has been proved to them; they have not seen him. They have an empty tomb, a message from two figures they could not identify, and a sentence from Galilee suddenly coming back with everything in it they had missed. And it is enough. They believe a promise before any appearance at all.

They told the eleven. No waiting to see whether they would be believed: they remembered, and they went. The eleven had slept in the garden, Peter had denied him, and none of them had come to the tomb. The women had every human reason to nurse a grievance, and none of it appears. The risen Lord let the news of his victory go first to the men who had run away, carried by those who had stayed. The first proclamation of the Christian era was made to a room of disillusioned men who did not want to hear it, and every proclamation since has had roughly the same shape.

Faithful in the background. Luke has tracked this group across three chapters without once putting them in the foreground. They funded the ministry (8:3), watched the crucifixion (23:49), marked the tomb (23:55), and came at dawn. They were the first to be told, and the first to tell.

May every Christian share the good news, women included? Yes, gladly. These women were sent with the message, and in Acts the whole church, men and women, went about speaking the word (Acts 8:4), Priscilla with Aquila explaining the way of God to Apollos (Acts 18:26). Every believer is a witness to Christ, at home, at work, among friends. The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), but that does not silence anyone from telling a neighbour, a child or a colleague that Jesus is risen. Christians who read those passages differently are our brothers and sisters, and on this verse we stand together: the risen Lord sent women first.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary Magdalene and Joanna. Luke names them, and in a document of this kind names are checkable. Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2). Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager (8:3); only Luke names her. Mary the mother of James. Some of them were probably still living when Luke wrote. Named eyewitnesses.

An idle tale. Luke reports the apostles’ reaction without softening it. The word is lēros, and Greek medical writers could use it of the babbling of a delirious patient. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The apostles did not simply doubt the report; they dismissed it as the raving of women unhinged by grief. They were not gullible.

They did not believe them. Two things follow. The first is a strong argument for the truth of the account. A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time, and a pagan critic would later sneer at the whole religion as resting on the word of a hysterical woman. Every instinct of a forger would be to put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke puts it in the hands of women whose report was rejected by the apostles themselves, and he names them. The second is pastoral, for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, and they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree.

Unbelief met by the Lord himself. Luke does not leave the apostles in their scorn. That same evening the Lord would stand among them, show them his hands and feet and eat in front of them (vv. 36–43). He sent no rebuke by the women; he came himself. Their unbelief was met not with a lecture but with his own presence, wounds and all, and that has been his way with doubting disciples ever since.
