Is it wrong to have doubts? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. The apostles began here as sceptics, and Jesus dealt with them patiently and with evidence (vv. 38–43). Many sincere Christians go through seasons of honest questions. The right response is not to hide them or to feed them, but to bring them into the light: read the evidence, talk to a mature believer, pray as the father did, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). What Scripture warns against is not the struggling doubter but the settled refusal to believe what God has made plain. Be merciful to those who doubt (Jude 22), including yourself.

In everyday life. If a friend tells you the resurrection is a fairy tale, do not be rattled: the first people to say so were the apostles. Offer to read Luke 24 and 1 Corinthians 15 with them.
verseByVerse.note: A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time; no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter ran. In Luke’s telling, Peter is the one who runs. This is the man whose last recorded act was to weep bitterly in a courtyard after denying three times that he knew Jesus. He has not been restored yet; that comes later in the day, in a meeting Luke will mention and refuse to describe (v. 34). John tells us that another disciple ran with him (John 20:3–10). And Peter could run because of a prayer: Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail (22:32). Shame’s instinct is always to withdraw, and if the report were true, Peter would have to face the man he had disowned. He ran anyway. Real sorrow for sin moves towards Christ, not away from him; that is the whole difference between Peter and Judas, and it is visible here in a pair of running feet.

The linen cloths by themselves. Stooping to look in through the low entrance, he saw the wrappings lying there without a body in them. This was not the scene of a robbery: nobody unwraps a corpse in the dark and carries it out naked, leaving the valuable linen behind.

Marveling. Not yet believing fully. Luke is precise, and the honesty is a mercy: Peter looked at the strongest physical evidence anyone had yet seen and walked home wondering. Later that day the Lord would appear to him (v. 34).

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit this verse, as the ESV notes, but it is well attested in the earliest and best copies, and John tells the same story at greater length (John 20:3–10).

What if I am still at the marvelling stage? Then you are in a real place on the road, not a disqualified one. Something has begun to move in you; the old explanations no longer fit; and settled faith has not yet arrived. Do what Peter did next: stay near the other disciples, keep listening to the word, and wait for Christ to show himself. Read a Gospel through, slowly. Ask God plainly to make him real to you. Marvelling is not believing, but nobody who ran to the tomb was left outside it for long.

For worship. The denier ran, and grace had already reached him before he knew it: the Intercessor who had prayed for him was alive, and was about to find him. Blessed be the risen Lord, who left the linen lying in the tomb and went looking for Simon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The same Sunday two disciples walk away from Jerusalem. Jesus joins them, but their eyes are kept from recognising him until v. 31, and Cleopas asks whether he is the only visitor who does not know what has happened. He is speaking to the only person who truly knows.

Their account is accurate and not enough: a prophet mighty in deed and word, handed over by their own leaders and crucified. We had hoped, they say, and they offer the third day, which should have sent them running back, as their reason for despair. So he gives them not more evidence but the key: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he shows them what the Scriptures say about himself.

At their table the guest becomes the host, and as he breaks the bread their eyes are opened and he vanishes. They walk the seven miles back that night and find the room already saying that the Lord has appeared to Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it not necessary turns their difficulty upside down. They thought the crucifixion proved he could not be the Christ; he tells them it is why they should have known he was. The suffering was not a detour from God's plan but the way into the glory.

Verse 27 is how the church has read its Bible ever since: the Old Testament is one book with one subject.

And the afternoon's order, Scripture opened and then bread broken, became the pattern of Christian worship. The meal at Emmaus was not the Lord's Supper, but Word and Table belong together.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 16 describes a common condition of the Christian life: he is nearer than you can tell, and the not-seeing is preparation, not abandonment.

Verse 21 is for anyone living inside a we had hoped: their hope was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked, on the very day they gave it up.

And v. 32 answers the Christian for whom the Bible feels dead. The burning came from a person, so the answer is a prayer: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Yet they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way; feeling is a gift, not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day. The same Sunday: the tomb found open, the report dismissed, Peter back from the tomb, and two disciples walking out of the city. Only Luke tells this story in full (the longer ending of Mark mentions it in a sentence, Mark 16:12–13). Two of them: disciples of the wider company, not apostles. One is named Cleopas (v. 18); the other never is. It has been suggested that the unnamed one was his wife, since they share a home, and it is a reasonable guess and no more.

About seven miles from Jerusalem. About sixty stadia, as the ESV notes, around two hours on foot. Where Emmaus was is not certainly known, a small mark of honesty: legends gather round famous places, not villages nobody can now find. They are probably going home, because it is over, to pick life up again.

The Shepherd goes after them. Luke’s whole Gospel has been travelling towards Jerusalem since Jesus set his face to go there (9:51). Everything has been accomplished in that city, and these two are walking away from it. But the risen Lord does not wait for them to come back. The Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost (15:4) goes after two, on foot. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10), and the resurrection has not changed his ways.

Talking with each other. This is what grief does on a long walk: it turns the events round and round, trying to make a shape of them that does not hurt so much, and gets nowhere.

Why did the risen Jesus not appear to everyone? He appeared to chosen witnesses, as Peter later said: God made him to appear, not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose (Acts 10:40–41). The resurrection was not a show to compel belief from the hostile; Jesus had said that those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (16:31). He gave his church reliable eyewitnesses and sent them to tell the world, so that we who have not seen may believe through their word (John 17:20; 20:29).

In everyday life. If you are walking away from something, a church, a hope, a calling, because it seems over, talk it through with another Christian before you settle into the village.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location of Emmaus is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself drew near. Jesus himself: not a messenger, not a vision. And the verb is entirely undramatic: he came alongside and walked with them, as any traveller does who catches up with people going the same way, and let them talk.

Their eyes were kept. A divine passive: God kept them from recognising him until the right moment (v. 31). This is not a failure of observation and not a disguise; it is deliberate, temporary, and lifted later by the same hand. Mary Magdalene also did not recognise him at first (John 20:14).

He withheld himself to give them more of himself. If he had made himself known at the roadside, there would have been joy and no Bible study: the fact without the meaning. Instead he keeps his face hidden long enough to walk them through Moses and the Prophets, so that they would learn to know him first through the Scriptures.

Is Jesus with me when I cannot sense him? Yes. This verse describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is closer than at any point you can identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is not abandonment but preparation. He has promised, I am with you always (Matthew 28:20), by his Spirit who dwells in every believer. These two later said their hearts had been burning the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger. Your feelings are not the measure of his presence; his promise is.

For worship. The Lord of glory, hours out of the grave, matched his pace to two people who had given up on him, and walked with them for two hours while they explained his death to his face. Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it (Genesis 28:16).

parallels.desc: the disciples did not know that it was Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?' And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk? He asks a question he does not need the answer to, as he has throughout this Gospel. Where is your faith? Who was it that touched me? What do you want me to do for you? He is not gathering information. He is opening a door and letting them walk through it in their own words, drawing them out.

Looking sad. The question stops them dead in the road. Two people can talk freely about a grief between themselves, yet when a third person asks about it, the whole weight comes back. Sad is skythrōpoi: the look of someone who has stopped expecting anything.

One of them, named Cleopas. He may be the Clopas of John 19:25, whose wife Mary stood at the cross. If so, perhaps she was the other disciple. An early tradition says Clopas was Joseph’s brother, which would make him Jesus’ uncle by law, but we cannot be sure.

Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days? The irony is complete. He is addressing the only person in the world who truly knows what happened. Everyone else in that city had watched from outside: the crowd saw an execution, the council a problem solved, the soldiers a shift completed. One man knew what had actually taken place on that hill, and he was standing in the road being asked whether he had heard the news. And he does not correct him. He does not say, I was there. He asks another question and lets Cleopas go on. That is the patience of Christ. He listens to a mistaken account of his own death from a grieving man without interrupting to put the record straight, because the man needs to say it more than he needs to be corrected, and everything Cleopas gets wrong will be answered properly a few minutes later.

Is it all right to tell God that I am sad and disappointed? Yes. He asked these two to tell him, and he listened. Around a third of the psalms are laments: honest prayers of grief, confusion and complaint, poured out to God (Psalm 13; 42; 88). Honesty with God is not unbelief; it is faith speaking to the only one who can help. What turns lament into sin is accusing God of wrong or turning away from him. Tell him the whole thing, in your own words, as Cleopas did. Then let him answer you from his Word.
verseByVerse.note: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What things?' And they said to him, 'Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet mighty in deed and word. Two words from him, and he has them telling the story. What follows is a small creed, what these disciples actually believed on Easter afternoon, and everything in it is true, and it is not enough. Jesus of Nazareth: the right man. A prophet: true; Moses had said one would come (Deuteronomy 18:15). Mighty in deed and word, before God and all the people: his ministry was public, and God attested it (Acts 2:22). Not yet the Son of God.

Our chief priests and rulers. The history, accurate to the last detail. They do not blame Rome; they say our leaders did this, and use Luke’s word for Pilate’s act, delivered him up (23:25). So here is a man with the facts entirely straight and no gospel at all: the sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home. They call him a prophet. They do not call him the Christ, and they are about to be told that they had it in the Scriptures all along.

What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing him? A great many people are not hostile to Christianity in the least. Jesus was a remarkable man; his teaching was profound; he was killed unjustly; the world would be better if people lived as he said. All of that is true, and it will not save anybody, because it describes a corpse. Knowing Christ means trusting him as the living Saviour who died for your sins and rose again, and Lord to whom you belong. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). You can tell the difference by asking: do I speak about him, or to him? Do I admire him, or depend on him?

parallels.desc: a man attested to you by God

verseByVerse.quote: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we had hoped. Few tenses are sadder. Not we hope, which is alive; not we never hoped, which is safe. We had hoped is the tense of a thing once real and now over, and everyone who has prayed for something and watched it not happen knows its exact weight. Hope had died.

To redeem Israel. It was not a small or foolish hope. To redeem, lytrousthai, is to ransom, to buy out of slavery, Zechariah’s word when he sang that God had visited and redeemed his people (1:68). They understood redemption mainly as liberation from Rome, and a crucified Messiah seemed a contradiction. They were not wrong to want God to act. They were wrong about the shape and the timing, and that is nearly always where hope goes wrong. It is also where a quiet idol hides. We can want God mainly as the means to something else, a healed marriage, a career, a nation put right, and when he does not deliver it, we decide he has failed us, when in fact he was offering us himself.

The third day. They know it is the third day. He had told them again and again that the Son of Man would rise on the third day (9:22), and here they are reciting the timetable as the reason their hope is finished. That is what unbelief does with evidence. It does not ignore it. It files it on the wrong side of the ledger.

What do I do when my hopes are dashed? First, tell God, as they told the stranger. Then ask whether what you hoped for was God’s promise or your own picture of how he should keep it. These two had the right God and the wrong expectation. God does not always give what we hoped for; he always keeps what he has promised, and often in a far larger way (Ephesians 3:20). Go back to his actual words, as Jesus took these two back to Moses and the Prophets. And remember Romans 8:28: not that every disappointment is good in itself, but that God works all things together for good for those who love him.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some women of our company amazed us. They report the evidence: the empty tomb, the angels, the message. Read what they have and then where they are going, because the gap between the two is the point.

A vision of angels. In their retelling the sight survives and the message, he is alive, is held at arm’s length: it was a vision, they say, and a report filed as a vision requires nothing of anybody.

Just as the women had said. Peter, and, John tells us, another disciple with him (v. 12; John 20:3–10). They have three strands: the empty tomb reported by named witnesses, the announcement of angels, and independent corroboration, all pointing one way. And they are walking to Emmaus.

But him they did not see. That is honest, and it is the sticking point: they have decided in advance that only a sighting will count. The promise from Galilee has not entered the conversation at all. So he does not say, look at me. He spends two hours in the Old Testament, because their problem was never a shortage of evidence. Facts do not interpret themselves.

Is evidence enough to bring someone to faith? Evidence matters, and God has given a great deal of it; the apostles appealed to it constantly (Acts 2:32; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Christianity is not a leap in the dark. But evidence alone does not change the heart. These two had all the facts and were walking the wrong way. What they needed was the Scriptures opened and their eyes opened by Christ himself. So give people the evidence, gladly and honestly, and also give them the Word, and pray, because only God can open eyes (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
O foolish ones. Foolish is anoētoi: not stupid, but failing to put together what they already have, the word Paul uses of the Galatians (Galatians 3:1).

Slow of heart. Not slow of mind: the word you would use of someone who takes a long time to be persuaded of something he already half knows. He does not say slow to believe the women. He says slow to believe all that the prophets have spoken. They believed the glorious parts: a throne, a kingdom, an everlasting dominion. The suffering was on the same pages and had been left unread: the servant despised and rejected, led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53); the man of Psalm 22 with hands and feet pierced; the shepherd struck (Zechariah 13:7). It was all there, and nobody had wanted it.

Was it not necessary. The same divine must as in v. 7, gathering up every passion prediction in the Gospel (9:22; 17:25; 22:37). The cross was not a defeat that ruined God’s plan; it was the plan. They think the crucifixion is the reason he cannot be the Christ. He tells them it is the reason they should have known he was.

That the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Suffering first, then glory (1 Peter 1:11): the pattern of the whole Bible. The Messiah had to suffer to redeem Israel, not by defeating Rome but by dying for sin. And enter into his glory is not a consolation offered after the suffering; it is a destination reached through it. The word is one of movement, of going in by a door, and the door was a cross.

Why was it necessary, and could God not simply forgive? God is love, and he is also just. He cannot pretend that sin does not matter, or treat evil as if it were good, without ceasing to be the holy God. The cross is how he can be both just and the one who justifies the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). The punishment our sins deserved was laid on Christ, our substitute, so that God’s justice was satisfied and his mercy set free. That is why it was necessary: not because God was reluctant to forgive, but because he would not forgive at the cost of his justice, and so he paid the cost himself, in his Son.

Is my suffering a detour from God’s plan? This verse answers the question a suffering Christian most often asks, though it does not remove the pain. If suffering was necessary for the Christ on the way to glory, it is not evidence of a mistake in anyone else’s case either. The same pattern holds for his people: we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). Your hard road is not God having lost the thread. It may be the very door to the glory he has prepared.

parallels.desc: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beginning with Moses. Moses and all the Prophets means the whole Old Testament. Every preacher has wished for a transcript; there is none, because the New Testament carries it on, written by men who had this lesson or learned from those who did. Beginning with Moses, he probably started with passages like these. The offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head and be struck in the doing of it (Genesis 3:15). The promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). A ram caught in a thicket, dying in the place of a son (Genesis 22). A lamb slaughtered and its blood on the doorposts so that death would pass over the house (Exodus 12). A bronze serpent lifted on a pole, so that anyone dying of the bite could look and live (Numbers 21). A scapegoat driven into the wilderness carrying the sins of the people on its head. And all the Prophets: a servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53); a son of man coming with the clouds to receive a kingdom (Daniel 7); a new covenant, with sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31); and the psalms of suffering and vindication (Psalms 22; 16; 110).

The things concerning himself. The word is diermēneusen: he interpreted, a word also used for translating a foreign language. They had heard the Scriptures read every Sabbath of their lives; what they had never had was the key. And the claim is enormous: the Old Testament is not religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book, with one subject, and the subject was walking down a road to Emmaus explaining himself (John 5:39, 46).

How to read the Old Testament. With Christ at the centre: not by forcing Jesus into every verse, but by seeing how every part points to him, prepares for him, or is fulfilled in him.

Where should I start, if the Old Testament feels like a closed book? Start where Jesus started, with the big story, and read it with a few signposts. Genesis 1 to 3, 12 and 22; Exodus 12 and 20; Leviticus 16; Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12; Psalms 2, 22 and 110; Jeremiah 31:31–34. As you read, ask three questions: What does this show me about God? What does it show me about our need? How does it point forward to Christ? Use a reliable study Bible, and read the New Testament passages that quote the Old, especially Hebrews, which draws deeply on Leviticus. Over time the shape of the whole becomes clear.

For worship. The Author of the book had come to read it aloud. Every altar, every lamb and every promise in Israel had been pointing down the centuries at one person, and on the afternoon of the third day that person walked down a road and showed two travellers his own face on every page. The Scriptures were never a puzzle with Christ as one of the pieces; they were his portrait, drawn in advance by the love of the Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, 'Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.' So he went in to stay with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He acted as if he were going farther. Readers sometimes find this uncomfortable, as though it were a pretence. It is not. He is a traveller who has reached the point where his companions turn off, and the courteous thing, the only thing that leaves them free, is to keep walking unless he is asked. He does not force himself on them.

They urged him strongly. Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty, and the roads were not safe after dark. But more: something in those two hours had made them unwilling to let this man walk away. They would tell each other later what it was: their hearts had been burning (v. 32).

Stay with us. They are not asking for more teaching; they think they are doing a kindness to a man with nowhere to sleep. The great moments of the Christian life rarely announce themselves in advance. And the sentence has been the prayer of Christians ever since, for the reason they first said it: the day is far spent. It is in the old hymn: Abide with me, fast falls the eventide.

He went in. He accepts the invitation. He went as far as the door and would not go in until he was wanted, and the moment he was asked he came in and sat down.

If Jesus waits to be invited, does salvation depend on my asking? Our asking is real, and he does respond to it: behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in (Revelation 3:20). But notice who began this whole afternoon. He drew near to them first, unasked, on the road, and it was his words that set their hearts burning so that they wanted him to stay. That is how grace always works. God’s call is effectual, meaning it brings about what it calls for: he opens the heart, and the heart, opened, gladly invites him in (Acts 16:14; John 6:44). So we must ask, and when we do, we find that he gave us the desire to ask. Do not wait to feel sure you are chosen. Ask him in; that you want to is the sign of his work.

In everyday life. Tonight, as the day ends, pray their prayer in your own home: Lord, stay with us. And look for a practical way to open your home this month to someone who would otherwise be alone at evening.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At table with them. It is their house, and at their table the guest becomes the host. That happens wherever he is welcomed. The four actions, taking, blessing, breaking, giving, Luke has recorded twice before: on a hillside with five thousand (9:16), and in an upper room three nights earlier (22:19). These two were probably not in that upper room (22:14), but they may well have seen those hands break bread before, and now the hands were marked.

Their eyes were opened. Another divine passive, the reverse of v. 16 by the same hand. Perhaps they recognised the way he broke bread, or saw the wounds in his hands. Recognition, from first to last in this account, is a gift and not an achievement, and it came at the table after the Scriptures had prepared them.

He vanished. The instant they see him, he is gone. This has struck readers as cruel, and it is the opposite. Once they knew him, they did not need to see him; he would be known through the Scriptures and the breaking of bread. And they do not sit down and grieve his going. They get up and run.

Word and table. The pattern of Emmaus became the pattern of Christian worship: the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken. This is not itself the Lord’s Supper but an ordinary meal in a private house. Yet the church’s instinct is right: the Word preached and the Supper given belong together, as the Reformers insisted.

Why do I not seem to recognise Christ in worship? Sometimes because, like these two, we come with our eyes held by grief or tiredness or distraction. Sometimes because we come expecting only a performance, not a meeting. Recognition is his gift, so ask for it before you go: Lord, open my eyes to see you in your Word and at your table. Come prepared, having read the passage if you can. Listen to the preaching as Christ speaking through his servant. And remember that he was present with these two long before they saw him. A dull Sunday is not an absent Lord.

parallels.desc: he took bread and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: They said to each other, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearts burning. They say it afterwards. It was only when they knew who he was that they understood what had been happening to them for two hours, and that is very often the shape of it: a Christian looks back on a hard year and sees that God was at work in him unnoticed. Jeremiah knew the feeling: a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jeremiah 20:9). In Scripture the heart is the whole inner person, thinking, willing, loving; this is not a mood but something catching light.

On the road, in the Scriptures. While he talked to us on the road: the person. While he opened to us the Scriptures: the book. Neither alone did it. A stranger’s company would not have set a heart burning, and the Scriptures had been read to these men every Sabbath without producing this. It was Christ, in the Scriptures, opening them.

What do I do when the Bible feels dead? This is a question many honest Christians carry privately. The answer this verse gives is not, try harder, and not, find a better method. The burning came from a person, and the request that follows is a prayer rather than a technique: that the one the book is about would open it. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). So pray before you read. Read a whole passage, not a fragment, and look for Christ in it. Read with others sometimes. Keep reading on the dull days; the fire is his to give. And add this, because the reverse error is real: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is not the test. The fire is a gift, not a verdict.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, 'The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!' Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That same hour. The meal is abandoned. It is dark, they have already walked seven miles, and the reason they gave for pressing him to stay, that the day was far spent, applies with equal force to them. They go anyway, back over the same road they had walked out in despair, because there are people in Jerusalem who need to hear this tonight.

Risen indeed. They arrive to a room already alight, and before they can say a word the news is shouted at them. Risen indeed, ontōs: really, truly. It has become the ancient Easter greeting. And Simon: not Peter the rock, but the old name, the one Jesus used when he warned him (22:31). Somewhere in that Sunday the risen Christ met privately with the man who had denied him three times.

The meeting no one described. Luke does not describe it; neither does anyone else. Paul confirms it happened and names Peter first among the witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5). Whatever passed between those two stayed between them. That is worth knowing by anyone whose own worst failure has been dealt with quietly. The church heard that the Lord had appeared to Simon. It never heard what was said.

The breaking of the bread. Luke’s summary of the Emmaus story is the shape of the whole afternoon: the road, and the bread. That phrase would become Luke’s term for the church’s fellowship meal and the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:42, 46; 20:7).

Does God make public everything I have confessed to him? No. Some sins must be confessed to people we have wronged, and some public sins need public repentance, but much of our dealing with Christ is private, as Peter’s was. You do not have to tell everyone everything to be fully forgiven. What God has covered, he has covered (Psalm 32:1). And what he says to you in that private meeting, his forgiveness, his restoration, your new commission, is as real as if it were announced from the housetops.
verseByVerse.note: Simon is Peter.

parallels.desc: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–53 — Jerusalem, the Commission, and the Ascension
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus stands among them, and his first word to the disciples who had failed him is peace. They think they are seeing a ghost, so he shows them his hands and feet and eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

Then he sends them back to the book: everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, and he opens their minds to understand it. Repentance for the forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem, the city that had just killed him. They are witnesses, and they must wait in the city until they are clothed with power from on high.

At Bethany he lifts his hands, as a priest does, and blesses them, and while he is blessing them he is carried up into heaven. They worship him and return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 39–43 rule out a resurrection that is only the survival of a soul, a vision, or a cause living on. It is a body with hands and feet that can be touched and that eats. When Paul calls the resurrection body a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44), he means a body ruled by the Spirit, not a body without flesh. And the wounds remain: the Lamb stands in the midst of the throne as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

Verse 45 shows that understanding Scripture is finally God's gift (1 Corinthians 2:14; Acts 16:14), so the right response to a closed Bible is to ask him who opens it.

The ascension is not the end of the story but the beginning of his reign at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3), as he had told the council (22:69). And the disciples' worship of him, given by Jewish monotheists with no one correcting them, is the first worship of Jesus in this Gospel.
verseByVerse.examples:
Disbelieved for joy is a common form of unbelief among genuine Christians: believers who know the gospel is true and cannot quite accept that they are forgiven. Jesus did not rebuke it or argue with it. He asked for something to eat, and made the moment small enough to be believed.

Verse 48 shows what any Christian is asked for: not answers to every question, but to say truthfully what he knows of Christ. And the commission was given to eleven men who had all failed him days before.

Verse 49 is for anyone in a season of enforced waiting. Stillness can be obedience or disobedience, and both feel like wasting time. These men waited and prayed, on orders, until the power came.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, 'Peace to you!' But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus himself stood among them. He arrives mid-sentence, into a room where he is being discussed, suddenly. John adds that the doors were locked for fear of the authorities (John 20:19). There is no entrance described. One moment the room is full of frightened people arguing about reports; the next he is in it.

Peace to you! The first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church is peace, the ordinary greeting, shalom. But the last time most of these men saw him, he was being arrested in a garden while they ran. If ever there was a moment for a reckoning, this was it, and what he says is, peace to you. Peace with God through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20) was bought on Friday; on Sunday evening the one who bought it stands in the room and says the word. Some manuscripts lack this greeting, as the ESV notes, but the earliest copies have it, and John records the same words (John 20:19).

They thought they saw a spirit. They have just been shouting that the Lord is risen, and when he appears they conclude they are looking at a ghost. That is not a flattering detail, which is why it is worth trusting. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was apparitions, not resurrection. Nobody in that room was expecting a resurrection. They were expecting a haunting, and they were terrified.

What does it mean to have peace with God? It means the war is over. By nature we were God’s enemies, under his just wrath because of our sin (Romans 5:10; Ephesians 2:3). Through Christ’s death that hostility is ended for everyone who trusts him: since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). It is not first a feeling, though it brings calm; it is a status, a settled relationship, which does not rise and fall with your mood. And from it flows the peace of God that guards the heart in anxious times (Philippians 4:6–7).

In everyday life. If you are carrying guilt over a failure you have already confessed, hear the first word of the risen Christ to his failed disciples: peace to you. Receive it today, and carry it to one person you are at odds with.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? He does not scold the doubt. He asks about it, and then he answers it with evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. Gently, he deals with their doubts.

My hands and my feet. Because that is where the nails went. He is not simply proving that a body is present; he is proving whose. The risen Lord is the crucified one. And the resurrection body is glorious, imperishable, and scarred. He did not leave the marks behind in the tomb; he carries them still: the Lamb standing in the midst of the throne, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

Touch me, and see. Physical evidence. Not just a vision, but a body that can be handled. John would write years later of what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we looked upon and have touched with our hands (1 John 1:1).

Flesh and bones. That closes off a whole family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, a vision granted to grieving friends, or a cause living on. It is a body, transformed but real, that can be handled (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

But does Paul not call it a spiritual body? A reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty here, because Paul calls the resurrection body a spiritual body, and that sounds like the opposite of flesh and bones. It is not. Paul is not describing what the body is made of but what it is ruled and animated by, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning that he has no body (1 Corinthians 2:15). A spiritual body in Paul’s sense is a body wholly governed by the Spirit of God: imperishable, glorious, powerful. It is not a ghost. Paul’s whole argument in that chapter is that ours will be like Christ’s, and Luke goes on to show him eating fish.

Where Christians differ: a spiritual or bodily resurrection? Some modern theologians speak of the resurrection as spiritual only: a vision, or the disciples’ renewed faith, or Jesus living on in their memory and mission. This commentary’s view: Luke goes out of his way to insist on bodily resurrection: flesh and bones, wounds, touch, eating. The empty tomb, and Jesus’ own words, rule out a merely spiritual resurrection. As he rose bodily, so will his people: he will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

Could the disciples simply have seen what they wanted to see? Hallucinations, as far as is known, are private experiences of one mind; they are not shared by a roomful of people at once, and they do not ask for fish and eat it. Nor were these men primed for what they saw: they expected a ghost, if anything, and had called the women’s report nonsense that morning (v. 11). And a vision, however vivid, does not empty a tomb in a city full of enemies who wanted the body produced. The appearances came to the unwilling as well as the willing, and they changed frightened men into witnesses who would die rather than deny what they had touched.

What kind of body will I have in the resurrection? A real body, continuous with this one, but transformed. Sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in dishonour, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). No more sickness, ageing, disability or death. Recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, yet changed in ways we cannot fully picture. And the Christian hope is not the escape of the soul from the body. It is the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23), in a renewed earth, and the ground of it is standing in a room in Jerusalem holding out his hands.

In everyday life. If you live with a body that is failing, in pain or limited, read 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 today and say it about your own body: raised in power.

parallels.desc: which we have looked upon and touched

verseByVerse.quote: And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disbelieved for joy. Only a very honest writer would have set that phrase down. The fright has passed. What holds them back now is the paralysis of a person offered something too good to be true: not scepticism, but the fear of letting yourself accept a thing in case it turns out not to be so.

Disbelieving for joy among Christians. There are believers who can recite the doctrine of justification and cannot quite accept that they personally are forgiven, not because they think the gospel untrue, but because they cannot make themselves take it. Jesus does not rebuke it or argue with it. He asks for something to eat.

Have you anything here to eat? It is an ordinary sentence, and a disarming one. The Son of God, three days out of a grave, with the powers of the age to come in his body, asks whether there is anything in the house.

Broiled fish. He did not need it. He ate because they needed to watch him do it. A ghost cannot chew. Peter would later preach that they ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:41). Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

I believe the gospel, but I cannot feel forgiven, so what should I do? Look at what Jesus did here. He did not demand that they feel more; he gave them something solid to look at. Do the same with your own heart. Look away from your feelings to the facts: Christ died for sinners; he rose; he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37); God declares the one who trusts in Jesus righteous (Romans 3:26). Come to the Lord’s Supper, where he gives you bread and wine to take into your hands. Let a trusted Christian remind you of the promises. Feelings often follow facts slowly. Keep looking at him until joy lets itself believe.

parallels.desc: who ate and drank with him

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While I was still with you. He is with them at that moment, eating. So he is marking off a period that has now ended, the years of walking Galilee together, and speaking from the other side of it. And what he does first in the new arrangement is what he did on the road: he sends them back to the book (9:22, 44; 18:31–33).

Everything written about me. Not a few verses, but everything. A man stands in a room in Jerusalem and says that the whole Bible is about him: the garden and the flood, the altar on Moriah and the blood on the doorposts, the throne of David, the laments and the love songs, the exile and the return. He says it of the book God wrote, and it is true.

The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms. That is not a loose gesture at religious literature. It is the threefold division of the Hebrew Bible: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings, here probably named after the first and largest book of the Writings, the Psalms. In other words, the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections, with nothing left out.

Must be fulfilled. The same must that has governed this Gospel from the boy who must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the Son of Man who must suffer. Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). Not that the Old Testament contains some prophecies he happened to satisfy, but that the whole of it is about him, and it had to come out this way.

What am I to do with all the Old Testament? Every new Christian eventually asks it: genealogies, sacrifices, a tabernacle measured in cubits, kings who mostly failed, prophets shouting at a nation that would not listen. Read it as the setting-up of a story whose ending you already know. It is not a different religion stuck on the front of yours. It is the same God, working towards the same person, for two thousand years before he arrived.

Is every Old Testament passage about Christ? The whole Old Testament leads to him: its promises, its patterns and its law find their goal in him. But each passage has its own meaning in its own setting, and that must be read first. Finding Christ is not a matter of hunting for hidden symbols in every detail; it is tracing how each part of the story moves towards him, shows our need of him, or is fulfilled in him.

In everyday life. Read a chapter this week with Christ in mind: Exodus 12, Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22. Ask: what did this mean then, and how does it reach its goal in him?
verseByVerse.note: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he opened their minds. The verb is diēnoixen: he opened, he unlocked, used for the third time in this chapter: their eyes at the table (v. 31), the Scriptures on the road (v. 32), and now their minds in the room. What was hidden from them before (9:45; 18:34) is now revealed.

To understand the Scriptures. These men had the text from childhood. Two of them had just spent an afternoon with the risen Christ expounding it. And they still needed something done to them before they could take it in. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence, education or access, but of a closed mind being opened by God. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him (1 Corinthians 2:14). Luke shows it again in Acts: the Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14).

Two consequences. The first is humbling: if you understand the gospel, someone opened your mind, and you did not do it. The second is freeing: if the opening is his work, then the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask him.

Can an unbeliever understand the Bible? He can understand its words, its history and its arguments, sometimes very well; many scholars who do not believe have explained the text accurately. What he cannot do without the Spirit is receive it as true, see the glory of Christ in it, and believe it savingly. That is why we share the Scriptures with unbelievers and pray for them at the same time. The Word is the means; the Spirit is the one who opens.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written. Everything the risen Christ says about himself in this room is anchored to a text. He might have argued from what had just happened, and it would have been unanswerable: the wounds, the fish, the empty tomb. He argues instead from Scripture, which tells you what he intends the church to stand on when the eyewitnesses are gone.

That the Christ should suffer. That is the half nobody had wanted. Christ means the anointed King, and a suffering King was not what Israel was watching for. It was in the book all the same: in Isaiah’s servant (Isaiah 53), in the psalms of the righteous sufferer (Psalm 22), in the one whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10) and the shepherd struck (13:7).

On the third day. A fair question: where exactly is that written? No verse says in so many words that the Messiah will rise on the third day. The apostles answered two ways. They pointed to particular texts: Peter at Pentecost quotes Psalm 16:10, you will not let your Holy One see corruption, and argues that David’s tomb is still here, so he was speaking of another (Acts 2:25–31); Isaiah’s servant, after being cut off, prolongs his days (Isaiah 53:10–12); Hosea speaks of being raised on the third day (Hosea 6:2), and Jonah supplied the pattern (Matthew 12:40). But the deeper answer is the shape of the whole. A story that runs from a garden lost to a people redeemed by blood, from exile to return, from a valley of dry bones to an army standing up, does not end in a tomb.

In everyday life. Learn to say the gospel in one sentence from Scripture, so that you can give it to someone this week: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, and he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Memorise it today.

parallels.desc: on the third day he will raise us up

verseByVerse.quote: and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentance for the forgiveness of sins. This sentence is still inside thus it is written: the mission of the church is part of what the Scriptures foretold, on the same footing as the suffering and the rising. This is the message, and a great deal gets preached in its place: moral improvement, respectability, a technique for a better life. Repentance, a turning of the whole person from sin to God; and forgiveness of sins, the gift won by Christ’s death, the thing a guilty person actually needs and cannot obtain for himself (1:77; 3:3).

Should be proclaimed. Also written: the mission is part of the Scriptures’ plan. I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6).

In his name. That is the authority and the ground: on his authority, by his power, through faith in him (Acts 2:38). Not in the name of the church, and not on the strength of anyone’s sincerity. Peter would put it flatly: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

To all nations. The scope is the world, and it is the climax of Luke’s great theme. All flesh shall see the salvation of God (3:6). Simeon held a baby and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32). Luke traced his genealogy back not only to Abraham but to Adam (3:38).

Beginning from Jerusalem. The city that had just done it: where the crowd shouted crucify, where the council condemned him, where the cross went up outside the wall. Any ordinary movement would start where it was welcome. The first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it. If that seems unfair, it is the only kind of gospel that could include us: a forgiveness that reached only the respectable would never reach anyone, because no one is. When Peter did preach there, about three thousand were forgiven in a day (Acts 2:41), and Acts follows this exact plan: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

Must people hear of Christ to be saved? Yes. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ, and there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). That is why the risen Lord sends his church to all nations: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14)? The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession hold that elect infants who die in infancy, and others unable to understand the outward call, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 10.3), in ways we are not told. Parents who have lost a little one may rest in the kindness of the Lord who took children in his arms and said the kingdom belongs to such as these (18:16). But for all who can hear, the gospel must be preached, which is why missions are not an optional extra for keen Christians. They are the reason the church is still here.

What does repentance actually look like? Repentance is a turning round: away from sin and towards God, grieving over the sin and hoping in his mercy, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession describe it (Westminster 15.2; 1689 15.3). It starts when you see your sin through God’s eyes, as an offence to him and not merely a harm to you. It lays hold of mercy in Christ, for grief over sin with no hope of pardon only drives a sinner further from God. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself, in the Spirit’s strength, to walk with God in new obedience. In practice that means naming the specific sin to God, putting right what can be put right, removing what feeds it, and starting again the next time you fall, knowing that your standing rests on Christ’s perfect obedience counted as yours, not on the quality of your repentance (Romans 5:19). It is not only the first step of the Christian life but the shape of the whole of it.

In everyday life. Choose one practical thing this month: learn about one unreached people and pray for them by name; give regularly to a missionary; welcome an international student; or speak of Christ to the person in your own Jerusalem, the one nearest you, who seems least likely to listen.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses. A witness is not an advocate and not a theorist. He was present and can say what he saw; he may not embellish or speculate. The word is martyres, and English has narrowed it, because several of the men in that room died for their testimony. The apostles’ testimony is the foundation of the church (Acts 1:22; Ephesians 2:20), and we believe through their word (John 17:20).

Of these things. Christianity is not in the first instance a philosophy or a set of values. It is a report: that a particular man, under a named Roman governor, was executed and buried, and three days later was alive, and here are the people who saw it. Paul staked everything on it: more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:5–6). That is a man saying: go and ask them.

Look at who is commissioned. These are the men who fell asleep in the garden, denied him in a courtyard, dismissed the women’s report as nonsense, and were standing in that room minutes ago convinced they were seeing a ghost. Not one has a record to be proud of. Every one is about to be sent to the ends of the earth on the strength of what he saw. They will not be asked to be impressive. Only truthful.

I did not see the risen Christ, so am I a witness? Not in the apostles’ unique sense: they were eyewitnesses, and their testimony, written in the New Testament, is the foundation that cannot be repeated or added to. But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done for him, and to the truth of the apostles’ report, which he has believed. You do not need to have the answers to every question, or to argue anyone into the kingdom. You are asked simply to say what you know of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed (1 Peter 3:15). The blind man in John 9 could not answer the theologians, but he could say: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise of my Father. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; 2:1–4, 33), promised long before in the prophets: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28–29); I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:26–27). And Jesus himself sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7). Only God can send the Spirit of God. Another claim to divine authority, made almost in passing.

Stay in the city. He has just given them the message, the authority, the scope and the starting point, and then he tells them to wait. They had the greatest news in the world and were forbidden, for the moment, to take it anywhere. Stillness can be disobedience or obedience, and both feel like wasting time. These men were not idle; they devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14). But they went nowhere, on orders, until the power came.

Clothed with power. The verb is the one used for putting on a garment. Power, dynamis, is the power of the Spirit (Acts 1:8). It comes from outside and is put on; it is not a capacity discovered within. Zeal without the Spirit was exactly what Peter had shown in the garden with a sword (22:50).

Stay in the city, or go to Galilee? A reader comparing Gospels will notice a difficulty, which sceptics have pressed for a long time. Here Jesus says, stay in the city; but at the tomb in Matthew and Mark he is going ahead of them to Galilee, and Matthew’s great commission is given on a mountain in Galilee. The objection only bites if all of this happened on one evening, and it did not. Luke’s own second volume says Jesus appeared over forty days (Acts 1:3). Restore that span and the accounts fall into a likely order: appearances in and around Jerusalem on Easter Day and the week after; then Galilee, where Matthew’s mountain and John’s breakfast on the shore belong; then back to Jerusalem for the last days before Pentecost. Luke compresses the forty days. Stay in the city was given and repeated at their end (Acts 1:4), and it governs the last days before Pentecost.

Should Christians today wait for the Spirit as the disciples did? No. Their waiting was for one unrepeatable event, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, which marked the new age. Now every believer receives the Spirit when he believes (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13; Acts 2:38–39). Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach a later baptism in the Spirit, to be sought after conversion, often with speaking in tongues. This commentary holds that the sign gifts, such as tongues and healings, ceased with the apostles, because they served to confirm the apostles’ message while the New Testament was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). It does not believe Scripture teaches a second baptism for all believers, and holds that view charitably towards brothers and sisters who see it otherwise and often shame us by their zeal. We are not waiting for the Spirit to come; we are asking him to fill us (Ephesians 5:18), and depending on his power in everything.

In everyday life. Before your next act of service, the class, the visit, the conversation about Christ, stop and ask for the Spirit’s power, plainly and specifically. And if you are in a season of enforced waiting, of illness or delay or a closed door, use it as they did: pray, stay close to God’s people, and be ready.
verseByVerse.note: The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As far as Bethany. On the slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem: the village of Martha and Mary and Lazarus, where he had wept at a grave and called a dead man out of it (John 11). He goes back there to leave. Acts 1:9–12 gives a fuller account.

He blessed them. That is the posture of the priest. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22), and the blessing given to the priests to speak was this: the LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Numbers 6:24–26). And Luke, who opened this Gospel with a priest named Zechariah going into the sanctuary while the people waited outside for the blessing, and coming out unable to speak a word (1:22), now closes it with a priest whose hands are raised and whose blessing is not silent. Jesus is the great high priest, blessing his people. The hands lifted over them had holes in them.

While he blessed them. He did not finish and then go. He went in the middle of the blessing, as though the blessing never stopped, and he is doing it still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25), his finished sacrifice speaking for them, so that no accusation against them can stand (Romans 8:34). And he was carried up into heaven: not vanished, as at Emmaus, but taken up. This is not an exit from the story but an enthronement, all things put under his feet (Ephesians 1:20–22). The man the world crucified now governs the world, as he had told the council (22:69). And this same Jesus will come again in the same way (Acts 1:11).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit and was carried up into heaven. Some older editions left out several short phrases in this chapter, because a small group of manuscripts lacks them. Then a very early papyrus copy of Luke, published in the twentieth century, was found to contain them, and opinion moved back; that is why the ESV prints them. Mark the direction of that story. The evidence did not erode the text as it accumulated. It confirmed it.

Did the ascension happen on Easter evening? Luke tells us in Acts that it came forty days later (Acts 1:3, 9). Here he gives the story in brief, without marking the passing of time after v. 49.

Why did Jesus have to leave? He said it was for our good: if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you (John 16:7). Ascended, he reigns, intercedes and is present by his Spirit with every believer at once. (See Acts 1:9–10 for the fuller answer.)

Where is Jesus’ body now? In heaven. The risen and ascended Christ is truly human still, with his glorified body, and that body is in heaven, at the Father’s right hand, until he returns (Acts 3:21). That is why Reformed Christians do not believe his body is physically in the bread at the Lord’s Supper. He is present to his people by his Spirit, really and spiritually, lifting our hearts to him where he is. And one day the heavens will open and we will see him, in the same body, with the same marked hands.

For worship. Every earthly priest lowered his hands at last and died; this one was lifted up with his hands still raised. He has gone into heaven as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), a man in our flesh at the Father’s right hand, and the benediction he began on the Mount of Olives will not end until he comes again.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven.”

parallels.desc: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed them

verseByVerse.quote: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They worshiped him. The word is proskynēsantes: they fell down before him. A few manuscripts lack these words, as the ESV notes, but the earliest copies have them. It is the first time in Luke that anyone worships Jesus. These are Jewish men who had said every day of their lives, the LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4); Jesus himself had said, you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (4:8). And they give it, with no one correcting them, to a man they had watched eat fish. That is not a doctrine developed over centuries by a church drifting from its roots. It is monotheists on a hillside outside Jerusalem, on their faces, and Paul’s letters, most likely written earlier still, already speak of every knee bowing to Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11).

How can Christians worship Jesus if only God is to be worshipped? Because Jesus is God. Christians do not worship a man alongside God; they worship the one God who has made himself known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is not a lesser god or a created being. He is the eternal Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1), who took our flesh without ceasing to be divine. So when the disciples fell down before him, they were not breaking the first commandment but keeping it. And the Father wills that all should honour the Son, just as they honour the Father (John 5:23).

With great joy. The strangest phrase, because he had just left. It should have been a bereavement. The good news of great joy announced at his birth (2:10) is now theirs, because they finally understood where he had gone: not another loss but the coronation of the man they loved, alive, reigning, coming back, and about to send his Spirit. Grief looks at an empty sky. They looked at a throne.

Continually in the temple. The Gospel began in that temple, with an old priest at the altar of incense who came out mute and could not give the blessing (1:9–22). It ends in the same building, with ordinary people who cannot stop blessing God. The horn of salvation, the sunrise from on high (1:68–79), the light for revelation to the Gentiles: every promise made at the start has been kept.

The end of Luke, the beginning of Acts. Luke’s first volume ends in worship and joy, waiting for the Spirit. His second tells what the risen Lord continued to do and teach through his Spirit and his church (Acts 1:1), and the story continues in every congregation that gathers on the first day of the week to bless God.

For worship. The Gospel that began with an angel announcing good news of great joy for all the people ends with that joy spilling out of a temple, and it has never been contained since. The one they worshipped on the hillside is alive for evermore, seated on the throne of the universe in our flesh, and he will come again. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever (Revelation 5:13). Amen.

24.text: <sup>1</sup> But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. <sup>5</sup> And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” <sup>8</sup> And they remembered his words, <sup>9</sup> and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. <sup>10</sup> Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, <sup>11</sup> but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. <sup>12</sup> But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened. <sup>13</sup> That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup> and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. <sup>15</sup> While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. <sup>16</sup> But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. <sup>17</sup> And he said to them, “What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, looking sad. <sup>18</sup> Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to them, “What things?” And they said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <sup>20</sup> and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. <sup>21</sup> But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. <sup>22</sup> Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, <sup>23</sup> and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. <sup>24</sup> Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.” <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! <sup>26</sup> Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” <sup>27</sup> And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. <sup>28</sup> So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, <sup>29</sup> but they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. <sup>30</sup> When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight. <sup>32</sup> They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” <sup>33</sup> And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, <sup>34</sup> saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” <sup>35</sup> Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. <sup>36</sup> As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace to you!” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. <sup>38</sup> And he said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” <sup>40</sup> And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Have you anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> They gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate before them. <sup>44</sup> Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” <sup>45</sup> Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, <sup>46</sup> and said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, <sup>47</sup> and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. <sup>48</sup> You are witnesses of these things. <sup>49</sup> And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” <sup>50</sup> And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. <sup>51</sup> While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. <sup>52</sup> And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, <sup>53</sup> and were continually in the temple blessing God.
